13304-mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-6-may-:
McClure's Magazine, volume six, number six, May 1896, opens with illustrations of Jean François Millet. They include a self-portrait drawn in 1847, described as melancholy like Dürer, with a profound regard full of intelligence and goodness. The lead piece, A Century of Painting, traces Millet's parentage and early influences. The number mixes art, fiction, and adventure.

A story passage follows a woman who, troubled by a dreary pair, ranges puzzling things into dreadful order, arranges their comfort quietly, then goes to her room and does not come down. Later, a pirate tale has Constantine laughing at a plan to free a captive, since men love their island more than her. The issue is a rich, illustrated monthly of its age.
13637-mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-2-janu:
The January 1896 number of McClure's Magazine leads with Ida M. Tarbell's life of Abraham Lincoln, following his first years in Illinois, his time in Denton Offutt's store. His bouts with the Clary's Grove boys, and his service as a captain in the Black Hawk War. It is the kind of careful, document-based biography the magazine made famous.

Eugene Field's poems of childhood follow, including The Ride to Bumpville and The Rock-a-by Lady, alongside a survey of a century of painting and other features. The issue shows McClure's at its best: serious reporting, popular poetry, and art history in one monthly package. It captures the magazine world that shaped American reading in the 1890s.
13788-mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-3-febr:
McClure's Magazine for February 1896 leads with Ida M. Tarbell's life of Abraham Lincoln. This instalment follows Lincoln at New Salem from 1832 to 1836. It covers his search for work, his store, his study of law, and his postmastership. The story of Ann Rutledge and his entry into the Illinois Assembly close the section.

Other articles and illustrations fill the issue, but Lincoln dominates. Tarbell worked from interviews and local records, giving the series a fresh, human tone. Readers meet a young Lincoln learning surveying, business, and politics by trial. The magazine's mix of biography and pictures made it famous. This issue shows muckraking biography at its best.
14319-mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-4-marc:
McClure's Magazine for March 1896 mixes Lincoln history, Kipling fiction, and science for a wide readership. Ida M. Tarbell writes on Lincoln's early years in Illinois, from his first speech to his stand against slavery. Rudyard Kipling adds The Ship That Found Herself, in which a ship's parts talk and boast. Will H. Low surveys a century of painting. The number shows a young magazine at its most ambitious.

Kipling's ship Dimbula pitches through a storm while frames, beams, and steam argue over who bears the strain. A second tale, The Divided House, tells of Lucas and Armida, a brother and sister who split a house and let one side fall to ruin. Lucas blames Armida for meddling, and she answers with tears and offers of peace. Scientific kite flying, a young hero, and poems fill out the number. It reads as a snapshot of American taste in 1896.
14663-mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-5-apri:
McClure's Magazine for April 1896 opens with the new marvel in photography, the Röntgen rays in America, illustrated with a lady's hand showing bones and a ring. Cleveland Moffett and H. J. W. Dam report the discovery.

The issue also carries Ida M. Tarbell's Abraham Lincoln, from the campaign of 1840 to his marriage to Mary Todd, Anthony Hope's Phroso, Kipling's Soldier an' Sailor Too, and Will H. Low on a century of painting. The number shows McClure's at its peak, mixing science, biography, and fiction for a mass audience. McClure's monthly reached hundreds of thousands of readers.
16216-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
August 1896 brings volume fifty, number eight of The American Missionary, published from Bible House in New York. Editorials mark the Jubilee Year Fund, shares and leaders, and Harriet Beecher Stowe. Southern pages trace church histories and Deer Lodge in Tennessee. Anniversary exercises at Fisk, Howard, Lincoln Academy, Allen Normal, Saluda, and Burrell schools follow. Blowing Rock and Meridian add local notes.

Indian closing exercises at Santee, a Salt Lake City Chinese report, women's state groups, and receipts complete the number. The jubilee mood runs through it, celebrating fifty years of mission work. Readers studying Black colleges, mission schools, and church fundraising will find a rich anniversary record.
16800-the-secret-of-a-happy-home-1896:
Marion Harland wrote this 1896 guide to home happiness, issued by the Christian Herald in New York. She dedicates it to her three children, whose love made her home happy and her life worth living. Chapters take up the family purse, small trifles, patience, nerves, marriage, mothers-in-law, and the rule of two, in short, plain talks.

Harland writes as a wise older friend, with tales and parables to make each point stick. She holds that happy homes grow from small daily care, not from wealth or luck. The book still reads as a warm, old-style home manual, useful for its common sense and its view of 1890s family life.
17039-the-salmon-fishery-of-penobscot-ba:
Hugh M. Smith's 1898 Fish Commission paper reports a visit to Penobscot Bay and River in August and September 1896. He talked with most weir and net owners on both shores, and he tracked salmon, shad, and alewife runs with care. The Penobscot, he notes, was then the only major salmon stream left on the US Atlantic coast.

Smith weighs the gains from hatchery planting, seal damage, hook catch off Maine, and new plantings of quinnat salmon and steelhead trout. His tone is that of a field scientist, plain and full of numbers. The short paper gives a clear snap of a famed fishery at a turning point, and of early efforts to keep it alive.
19890-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
The American Missionary was the journal of the American Missionary Association. Volume 50, number 6, is the June 1896 issue. Its notices direct letters about the work to corresponding secretaries in New York. Financial letters go to the treasurer. Woman's work has its own secretary at the Woman's Bureau. The Association ran missions among freedpeople, Native Americans, and immigrants.

Missionary monthlies mixed reports, appeals, and obituaries. Field letters showed donors what their money built: schools and churches. The AMA had abolitionist roots and a long Southern school network. A single issue preserves that machinery in motion. Historians of education and race use such runs heavily. June 1896 sits deep in the Jim Crow era.
20093-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
The American Missionary for April 1896 is volume fifty, number four, of a monthly journal. Various hands wrote its reports on mission work at home and abroad. Letters on funds went to the treasurer in New York. Letters on women's work went to the Woman's Bureau secretary.

Inside are field reports, news, and appeals from the association's work. Such journals linked far-off missions with churches that gave the funds. Readers can see how missions were run, staffed, and sold to supporters. The issue is a plain window on American mission life in 1896.
21595-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
The American Missionary for February 1896, volume fifty, number two, comes from the American Missionary Association in New York. The monthly sold for fifty cents a year from Bible House, on Fourth Avenue. Merrill E. Gates of Massachusetts led the association, with M. E. Strieby as editor.

Contents promise an outlook editorial, a Lincoln Memorial Day piece, and a tale called Pat's Miss'n Box. An essay treats the problem of illiteracy, a core concern of the group's schools. Lists name field workers and teachers' homes across the South and beyond. Receipts close the number, accounting for gifts to the cause.
21952-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
The American Missionary Association reports its work in this March 1896 number of The American Missionary, the fiftieth volume's third issue. Editorials ask what now, remember Bishop Haygood, and plead the present need of the Indians. Memorials honor a college president and a teacher lately dead. Reports from the South bring word of Wilmington, North Carolina, a mountain family feud, and funny answers from mission schools.

Other pages cover Thanksgiving among the Indians, the Watsonville and Santa Cruz missions to the Chinese, and women's state organizations. The Association, born of the abolition movement, ran schools for freed people, Native Americans, and immigrants. This monthly is its bulletin board: receipts, needs, and small victories, printed for the churches that paid the bills.
23057-how-the-redoubt-was-taken-1896:
Campfires line the heights in How the Redoubt Was Taken, a war tale dated 1896. The narrator, always superstitious, was troubled by a piece of augury at that moment. He sought his couch but could not sleep. He got up and paced for a while, eyes on the enemy's long line of campfires along the heights past Cheverino village.

A redoubt, an earthwork fort, must be stormed before the story ends, and the sleepless night loads the assault with dread. The tale descends from Tolstoy's Sevastopol world, where a young officer's fear and vanity share the same tent. Battle here is confusion, smoke, and sudden clarity. Readers get a compact, honest piece of nineteenth-century war writing, more interested in what a soldier feels than in what his generals planned.
23419-the-return-of-the-soul-1896:
Robert S. Hichens wrote this eighteen ninety six tale as a diary. It opens on a Tuesday night in November with scorn for theories, above all one from Professor Black that a child would laugh at. The narrator, no diary keeper by habit, finds himself keeping a hidden book after all.

Entries trace a past love story, a tragedy he brought about, a debt never paid, and a sense of having been here before, in Rossetti's words. Hichens builds dread from small, nightly notes rather than from shocks, as the writer's mind turns on itself. Readers who like a slow, inward ghost tale will enjoy the diary form, which lets guilt and a returning soul surface line by line.
23420-the-folly-of-eustace-1896:
R. S. Hichens wrote this eighteen ninety six tale of Eustace Lane, who at sixteen chose a mask for life as other men choose a mask for a ball. In his dressing room, candles lit and mirror set, he tried on a character picked to please the world and win his heart's desire, then stepped out and wore it for years.

The tale follows the cost of that choice: a life lived behind a chosen face, with only the silent dressing room knowing the secret. Hichens writes with wit and a sharp eye for social climbing, pride, and self deceit. Readers who like a study of character will enjoy watching Eustace keep up his mask. They will learn what folly it is to trade a true self for a part that flatters the crowd.
23421-the-collaborators-1896:
Robert S. Hichens set this eighteen ninety six tale at midnight, as Big Ben strikes and Henley asks his friend Andrew why they should not collaborate. Everybody does it, Henley says, and two heads may beat one, if Andrew, too excitable and intense alone, gains a drag upon the wheel.

Andrew grants Henley sense and humour but bars the new humour from any book bearing his name. He tolerates Dickens for grim tales like the dying clown while damning the rest to the sporting papers. Hichens turns the debate into a comedy of literary friendship, where taste, temper, and ambition clash over a book not yet in proof. Writers and readers alike will smile at the pair, so sure and so unsure of what makes a good book.
24323-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
This number of the Scientific American Supplement, volume forty-two, number 1082, is dated New York, September 26, 1896. The Supplement cost five dollars a year, or seven with the parent paper, founded in 1845. Its table of contents shows the range of late Victorian popular science, from architecture and autocars to chemistry, domestic economy, geography, mathematics, metallurgy, mineralogy, and mining.

Articles include new building construction at Paris in plaster and iron, and the De Dion and Bouton road motor worked by steam. An air bath and a feculometer follow, with errors in food economy and Zanzibar and its recent events. Goodman's hatchet planimeters for measuring areas come next. The great Krupp iron and steel works, precious stones by Professor Miers, and a firedamp testing station at Marchienne-au-Pont close the number. Readers get a packed weekly of science and craft.
24896-the-ebbing-of-the-tide-south-sea-s:
Louis Becke published The Ebbing of the Tide, South Sea Stories, in 1896. The opening tale, Luliban of the Pool, has a girl weaving a basket by a deep mountain pool in Ponape. The girl's voice carries a song about Luliban. A boy from Metalanien listens, and a white man waits to go crayfishing.

Other tales move across the Pacific, from Jakoits chiefs and red-haired traders to the ship Indiana and a prickly Irish captain. A note ties one tale to the Shenandoah's burning of seven whaleships in 1866. Becke writes with island knowledge and a storyteller's ease, giving readers the South Seas in their rough, romantic prime.
25906-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
The September 1896 number of The American Missionary, organ of the American Missionary Association, reports the jubilee year of the association's work. Editorials press the jubilee meeting and the share fund, with only thirty days more to give. News from the South fills the middle pages: Ballard Normal School at Macon, Talladega College commencement, Albany and Chandler normal schools, and letters from pastors and former students.

A piece on self help and self support by a Black writer leads the Southern news, and a Mobile student recalls entering Emerson Institute in October 1892 with no sure support. Chinese missions get a visit report, and the Bureau of Woman's Work marks its jubilee. Receipts close the number. The issue gives a plain monthly record of schools, churches, and giving in the year after slavery's jubilee.
26022-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
The January 1896 American Missionary, volume fifty, number one, opens the association's jubilee year. Editorials mark the new year, pamphlets and speeches, a jubilee bell bank, and woman's bureau clippings. Chinese endeavor testimonies follow, with memorials for Professor George L. White, Miss Ada M. Sprague, and others. The Bureau of Woman's Work reports its annual meeting, with addresses by Mrs. Sydney Strong and Miss Annette P. Brickett.

A closing appeal speaks of ten million souls in bondage to superstition, ignorance, and sin, whose cry rises to God, and calls readers to make God fearing, intelligent citizens of them. Receipts list givers across the states. The number is a plain record of missions, women's work, and giving at the start of 1896.
26996-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
The American Missionary for May 1896, volume 50, number 5, reports the work of the American Missionary Association from its Bible House offices in New York. The issue centers on the Jubilee Year Fund, with field days in the interior and shares of the fund listed for donors.

Its reports run from church missions and a revival in Selma, Alabama, to a Ponca village in Nebraska and a Chinese mission in Los Angeles. An editorial notes the arrest of the association's teachers at Orange Park, Florida, giving the number the feel of a working bulletin from missions across the country.
31427-miscellaneous-writings-1883-1896:
Mary Baker Eddy's Miscellaneous Writings, 1883 to 1896, was published by the trustees under her will at Boston. It gathers the writings of the discoverer and founder of Christian Science and author of Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures. Copyright in 1896 by Eddy, renewed in 1924, the volume ranges across chapters on introductory matters, one cause and effect, questions and answers, addresses, letters, sermons, poems, and testimonials. A prospectus, epigrams, and a preface open the book.

The collection shows Eddy speaking to her followers and to the public over thirteen formative years. Its pieces address doctrine, church life, and personal counsel in turn. For readers of American religious history, the volume is a primary source for Christian Science in its first generation. It speaks in the founder's own words and in the voices of those who testified to it.
323-verses-1889-1896:
Rudyard Kipling's volume eleven gathers the verse of his early fame, from barrack rooms to empire. Verses 1889 to 1896 opens with Barrack-Room Ballads, including Danny Deever, Tommy, Fuzzy-Wuzzy, and Gunga Din. A dedication to Wolcott Balestier precedes them.

Soldiers, screw-guns, cells, and loot fill the ballads in Tommy Atkins's voice. Later sections add the Widow at Windsor and other imperial lyrics. Kipling's rhythms made these poems recited in camps and schools alike. The volume captures Kipling at his most popular. Kipling's soldier poems were set to music and sung across the empire.
33079-my-trip-around-the-world-august-18:
Eleonora Hunt's My Trip Around the World, privately printed in Chicago in 1902 and dedicated to her grandsons John and Hunt Wentworth, records a journey from August 1895 to May 1896. Hunt admits in her introduction that she hesitated to print the manuscript, since the work was a struggle in her declining days with impaired health and imperfect vision. She pressed on so her grandsons might learn from its pages and one day take the same trip with fuller knowledge.

The book's hope is that young travelers will see the Orient and other foreign lands with greater appreciation if they first gain a storehouse of knowledge. Hunt's account therefore mixes personal memory with guidance, written for family rather than for fame. It remains a charming period travel memoir, full of the sights and courtesies of a world tour in the last years of the nineteenth century.
33621-battle-of-fort-george-a-paper-read:
Ernest Cruikshank, captain of the 44th Battalion, read this paper on the Battle of Fort George before the Niagara Historical Society on March 14, 1896. Published as the society's first transaction, it tells the story of the taking of Fort George on May 27, 1813, during the War of 1812. The preface praises Cruikshank as the historian of the Niagara peninsula and his style as clear, dispassionate, and deeply researched.

The paper sets the battle in the eventful history of Niagara, a town that served in turn as a legislative, educational, military, and commercial center. The town was occupied by the enemy and left a heap of smoking ruins. For readers of Canadian and American military history, it offers a concise, locally grounded account of a key Niagara campaign action.
4868-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
The years 1595 and 1596 bring a new Spanish governor and fresh pressure on the Dutch and their allies, and John Lothrop Motley tracks the shifting map. Archduke Cardinal Albert takes command, Philip William returns from captivity loyal to Spain, and Calais falls into Spanish hands, alarming the Netherlands and England alike.

Henry of France seeks English help on ungenerous terms, Guise secures Marseilles, and Dunkirk pirates harass Dutch shipping. Motley follows Henry's talks with Elizabeth's ambassador and the unease of Dutch towns watching the coast close around them. The volume shows a war widening beyond the Low Countries into a contest for ports and allies.
817-the-jargon-file-version-4-0-0-24-jul:
The Jargon File, in its July 1996 edition, records the slang, jokes, and lore of hackers and early computer folk. An older version had appeared as Gutenberg text 38 in 1992, and this edition updates and expands it. The Jargon File began at MIT and Stanford, where hackers shared slang by network.

Entries define terms, explain customs, and preserve stories from labs and networks, often with wit. The file serves as both a dictionary and a history of a culture that built much of modern computing. This edition captures hacker talk just as the web was reaching the public.
a-brief-history-of-the-united-states-pg6:
John Bach McMaster argues in his preface that most countrymen get all their knowledge of their country's past at school. So a school history must carry both the essentials and much that is merely well worth knowing. His design puts the essentials in the text, told in as few words as truth and fairness allow, and the rest in large notes that teachers may use or omit.

The contents march through the whole story. They run from discovery and exploration through the English in America. They cover the rivals France and the Indians, the Revolution, and the development of the Union. They end with the long struggle against slavery and the Civil War. McMaster was famous for his great history of the people of the United States; this brief version brought his manner into classrooms.
a-residence-in-france-during-the-years-1: Charlotte Biggs gathers her complete letters from France during the years 1792 through 1795 in this volume, prepared for the press by John Gifford. The editor's preliminary remarks praise facts that illuminate France's internal state during the Revolution's most important period. Written by an English lady with general remarks on French character and manners, the letters serve both the general reader and the future historian.
aristophanes-lysistrata-1896:
Lysistrata is the anti-war comedy of Aristophanes, the Athenian playwright, presented here in the unexpurgated Athenian Society translation of 1896. In the play, the women of Greece, led by Lysistrata, swear a sex strike against their husbands. They will refuse all intimacy until the men end the Peloponnesian War and make peace.

For two thousand years the comedy was treated as obscene: cut from school texts, seized by United States Customs, and barred from the mails under the Comstock regime. This translation refused those cuts and printed the play whole. It preserves both a classic of Greek theatre and a landmark in the fight over who was allowed to read it.
arxiv-2509-00196:
Inbeom Lee and Yang Ning present G-HIVE in 2025, a framework for regression models with hidden variables and many outcomes. Hidden variables are unmeasured factors tied to both the outcome and the inputs, and they can bias estimates. Past work mostly covers linear models, where the link is straight.

Generalized linear models allow curved links, but hidden factors then cloud identification, estimation, and inference at once. G-HIVE rests on a factor model view and builds a modified quasi-likelihood from reweighted estimating equations. The key is a weight choice that removes the first-order bias from hidden factors. The unified frame handles multivariate outcomes in one pass.
arxiv-2509-00296:
Andres Galindo-Olarte, Zhichao Peng, and Jennifer K. Ryan analyze superconvergence of an upwind discontinuous Galerkin method for radiative transfer in 2025. Radiative transfer tracks how radiation moves and interacts in a medium. The discontinuous Galerkin method solves such equations on small elements with polynomial fits that need not match at edges.

Superconvergence means the solution is far more accurate at special points than its general rate suggests. The team proves high-order superconvergence for steady and time-dependent cases at Radau points on each element, and in global norms as well. SIAC filters, which smooth the output, lift accuracy further at marginal cost. Applying them to low-dimensional moment quantities works especially well in practice.
arxiv-2509-00596:
Matthew A Malkan leads a team of fifty-two authors on the PASSAGE survey. PASSAGE is a galaxy survey made with the James Webb Space Telescope. It used slitless spectroscopy. That method spreads light from all objects in view. No targets are picked first. The work ran in the second half of the telescope's first cycle.

The survey observed dozens of high-latitude fields. It gathered more than ten thousand near-infrared spectra of faint galaxies. The team describes the survey design and data quality. They give examples on emission-line galaxies, with a focus on low-mass ones. Wide wavelength coverage and sharp images help track galaxy growth. The many fields also limit sampling bias from cosmic variance.
arxiv-2509-00696:
Akriti Verma, with three co-authors, Shama Islam, Valeh Moghaddam, and Adnan Anwar, addresses online toxicity, including hate speech and trolling, by looking at emotions in real time. Prior work mainly moderates after harm is done, overlooking how one user's emotion affects others during a conversation.

Verma and her co-authors build a graph-based framework that flags when emotion regulation is needed and prompts self-reflection. A comment queuing mechanism delays publishing, giving users time to cool down before engaging further. On Twitter and Reddit data, the framework reduced toxicity by twelve percent, while queuing cut the spread of anger by fifteen percent, holding only about four percent of comments on average.
arxiv-2509-00796:
Anum Arslan leads six authors in total, with Wen-Bo Dong, Charles Gale, Sangyong Jeon, Qun Wang, and Xiang-Yu Wu, on in-plane transverse polarization in heavy-ion collisions. Polarization measures how particle spins align, and this component, to the authors' knowledge, has not yet been measured in such experiments.

Arslan and her co-authors give an analytical expression for the polarization component and cross-check it with a numerical hydrodynamic model, which treats the collision matter as a fluid. When the temperature-gradient contribution is neglected, simulation and formula agree qualitatively. The prediction can be tested in experiments and would help complete a consistent picture of spin phenomena in heavy-ion collisions.
arxiv-2509-01196:
The compressible Navier-Stokes equations describe fluids whose density can change, such as gases, and vacuum regions make them hard to solve. Jin Tan, Yan-Lin Wang, and Lan Zhang study weak solutions on a line, with general starting data that may include empty bubbles or dense patches. Their work builds on Hoff's theory for bounded density.

Tan and the co-authors prove such solutions exist worldwide in time and gain regularity, smoothness, under stated conditions. A key global estimate holds even when the starting density is not strictly positive. They also show velocity and density settle toward equilibrium at an exponential rate. As a side result, they describe in numbers how the two vacuum states, patches and bubbles, evolve.
arxiv-2509-01696:
Muhammad El-Taha sorts waiting line systems that run in discrete time steps into clear classes. A queue here is a line of jobs waiting for service, tracked step by step rather than in smooth time. His classes rest on how jobs are scheduled and when the line is observed. When observed waits match true waits, a system is coherent; when they run low or high, it falls in the other two classes.

For coherent systems, he shows that key traits stay fixed across the class. Those traits cover line length, wait time, busy spans, and a classic formula for average waits. One trait from a single setup thus extends to its whole class. The scheme also settles a dispute: a famed law linking line length and wait holds for all such queues.
arxiv-2509-01896:
Ayumu Shoshi leads seven co-authors in a sharp radio study of a young star disk that hosts the youngest known transiting planet. The star sits in the Taurus-Auriga birth region, and its disk shows a ring and gap layout called a transitional disk. Data from a large millimeter array reveal the dust glow and tilt of the disk. Advanced imaging hints at faint inner emission that may be a separate inner disk.

Gas motion gives a central star mass near that of the Sun. Dust ring lopsidedness and gas twists look weak, if present at all. Model fits suggest the inner and outer disks may tilt apart by a small angle. With the planet and a companion star also offset, the system shows a richly skewed early layout.
arxiv-2509-02096:
Yu Guo leads four co-authors in demonstrating a broadband optical delay line suited to quantum memory. Delay lines hold photons briefly so quantum networks can synchronize operations. Their design nests a multipass cell to stretch the optical path while keeping loss low. Custom dielectric coatings keep reflectivity high across a wide color range.

Entangled photon pairs test the cell, with one photon delayed and its partner as timing reference. Tomography after the longest delay shows entanglement fidelity near perfect. Retrieval efficiency also stays very high after a single transit. Delay settings step from a few nanoseconds to hundreds in fine increments. The large time bandwidth product marks the device as a strong memory candidate.
arxiv-2509-02196:
Aditya Sengar leads three co-authors in a way to run all atom protein motion in a learned latent space. Long span motion of bio molecules is key yet costs a lot to run head on. Boost tricks need shared terms that are hard to name, which caps work on switch paths. A past model learned to draw end states as all atom warps, but not the path in time.

Their Graph Latent Dynamics Propagator adds time flow in that latent space. Three mover types face off: Langevin runs with a score guide, Koopman straight maps, and self fed neural nets. Tests span small chains to large switch proteins, graded on calm, truth, and pace. Self fed nets give the most firm long runs and true time scales. Score led runs best catch side chain heat traits when the score is well learned.
arxiv-2509-02896:
Sepanta Zeighami, Shreya Shankar, and Aditya Parameswaran introduced a 2025 system called BARGAIN for running language models over large text collections. Top models are accurate but pricey at scale, while cheaper models make more mistakes. Their goal is to cut bills without letting quality drift far from the best model.

BARGAIN decides which records a cheap model can safely handle. It does so with an adaptive sampling plan, meaning it checks a changing slice of outputs to judge quality on the fly. The method carries firm statistical promises about accuracy, and variants promise precision or recall instead. Across eight real datasets it saved far more money than earlier cascade methods while keeping its guarantees.
arxiv-2509-02996:
Michael C. H. Choi and Youjia Wang introduced group-averaged Markov chains in a 2025 probability paper. A Markov chain is a random walk through possible states, used widely for sampling in statistics and physics. Averaging a chain's steps over a symmetry group can make it settle to its target distribution faster.

The authors define a family of averaged chains built from a group acting on the state space. When the target distribution respects that symmetry, averaged versions improve on the original by measures like spectral gap and long-run variance. A double-averaged version is usually best in theory, but single averages mix about as fast and cost less to run. The averaged chains also appear as natural projections under two standard distance measures. Famous samplers, from Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to Metropolis-Hastings, fit inside this picture.
arxiv-2509-03196:
Elena Colangeli, Charles Dalang, and Tessa Baker showed in 2025 how lensed light and gravitational waves together could weigh the graviton. The graviton is the hypothetical particle carrying gravity, and standard theory treats it as massless. If it had even a tiny mass, gravitational waves would travel slightly below light speed along curved paths.

That change alters the standard lensing equations for bending, time delay between images, and magnification. The authors argue that one strongly lensed event seen in both gravitational waves and light would bound the mass extremely tightly. Their bound needs no model of the lens, the waveform, or the cosmos. Magnification alone gives a far weaker limit and depends heavily on such models.
arxiv-2509-03296:
Balaganchi A. Bhargava and 3 co-authors studied how noise affects two-dimensional Floquet topological phases in 2025. Floquet phases arise in systems driven by a repeating pulse, and their topology protects special states that live at the edges. Real experiments always bring disorder and decoherence, stray disturbances that could kill those states.

Two example phases both proved surprisingly robust against timing noise. Edge modes first decayed quickly as they thermalized among themselves, then settled into a slow power-law fade. That slow exponent matches one-dimensional diffusion, spreading sideways from the edge. Modes in the bulk faded faster, matching two-dimensional diffusion instead. Large simulations and a simplified analytical model support the picture. The findings make these phases attractive candidates for future devices.
arxiv-2509-03396:
Advika Rajapakse computed a Steenrod square operation for spatial versions of Khovanov homology in a 2025 topology paper. That homology assigns algebraic invariants to knots and links. It refines a classic polynomial invariant. Sarkar, Scaduto, and Stoffregen built spatial refinements of its even and odd versions. Those refinements turn the algebra into spaces with richer structure.

Steenrod squares are operations on the cohomology of such spaces. They detect subtle twisting in the space's shape. Rajapakse computes the second such square on these refinements, for arbitrary links. That computation determines their stable homotopy types for all knots up to eleven crossings. The paper also proves that two squares defined algebraically by Schütz genuinely arise as Steenrod squares on these spaces. The results tie a knot invariant to deep homotopy theory.
arxiv-2509-03696:
Aleksandr V. Petrov and two co-authors' 2025 research paper is about estimating positional bias in logged search and recommendation data with large language models. Users click items near the top of a ranking more often, regardless of true relevance. Models trained on those logs inherit the bias, mistaking placement for quality.

The standard fix, inverse propensity scoring, weights training by the inverse chance that an item at each position was actually examined. Estimating those chances is hard in complex grid layouts. Their method uses a language model as a judge over the logged interactions to estimate propensities directly, at lower cost than live experiments. The estimates stay stable across score ranges and reveal row and column effects in a travel site's grid that simpler rules miss. A reranker trained with these weights matches the production model on a standard ranking metric and improves a weighted version of it modestly.
arxiv-2509-03896:
Zushuai Zhang and two co-authors' 2025 research paper asks how interacting code smells change the dependency structure of Java software. Code smells are surface symptoms of deeper design problems, and dependencies between modules spread the cost of every change. Individual smells are well studied, but what happens when several smells interact through shared dependencies was largely unexplored.

The team analysed 116 open-source Java systems, comparing dependency patterns where smell interactions exist against cases without them. In most of the thirty-six comparison cases, interactions came with a significant rise in total dependencies. Every smell also showed a consistent direction of change, up or down, for particular dependency types whenever it interacted with others. Those regularities have practical uses. They can sharpen how smells are detected and prioritised for cleanup. They can also guide refactoring strategies that cut ripple effects before they grow expensive.
arxiv-2509-03996:
In a 2025 research paper, Paul D. L. Ritchie and three co-authors examine how coupling and timescales decide whether tipping elements set each other off. A tipping element flips abruptly once slow external forcing pushes it past a threshold. Climate science worries about chains of these flipping in sequence.

When an upstream element loses stability, it can drag a downstream neighbour over its own threshold, particularly when the downstream system runs much faster, a pattern named an accelerating cascade. The paper pins down which combinations of coupling strength and timescale separation produce cascades. A taxonomy then classifies tipping sequences by their timing. As a concrete testbed, two simple tipping elements with hysteresis are coupled in one direction. Mapping the pair's responses across its parameters ties each cascade type to bifurcations in the joint system. Climate risk assessment gains a cleaner vocabulary for how abrupt changes propagate.
arxiv-2509-04096:
Lyssa Ramaut and three co-authors build a low-cost crash sensor system for forklifts in a 2025 engineering paper. Warehouse trucks take hard knocks from loads, racks, and other machines, and rough handling can go unreported. Small wireless nodes stuck on the truck measure shaking in three directions. A field campaign in real working settings supplied the data used to tune the detection method.

Software learned to separate genuine high-impact hits from everyday bumps and turns. It also points to where on the truck each hit landed. The nodes sip power, so batteries can last for years without service. Fleet owners gain a steady record for safety checks and damage claims.
arxiv-2509-04196:
Aditi Saxena and two co-authors study agreement in networks whose links carry complex numbers in a 2025 research paper. Each connection weight then holds both a strength and a phase angle, like a push with a twist. Such models suit power distribution grids and other directed systems. The authors ask exactly when flow across the network settles into consensus, meaning all nodes end with the same value, for both tightly and loosely linked directed graphs.

One extra condition, called real dominance, turns out to decide convergence, and it depends on the links' phase angles. Spectral properties of the network's Laplacian matrix explain why. When agreement fails naturally, modified flows are offered that force it. Tests cover invented and real networks, plus diffusion as the mirror process.
arxiv-2509-04696:
Keeping a knowledge graph fresh takes constant extraction of facts from the web. Samira Khorshidi, lead author with eleven co-authors, describe ODKE+, a production system for that task, in a 2025 paper. The pipeline detects missing or stale facts, retrieves supporting documents, and extracts candidate facts.

Extraction mixes pattern-based rules with ontology-guided prompting of large language models. A second model validates facts, and a further stage ranks and normalises them before ingestion. At deployment scale, the system processed millions of Wikipedia pages and ingested millions of high-confidence facts. The authors report improved coverage and much shorter update lag than traditional methods.
arxiv-2509-04996:
Generalist robot policies that follow vision and language instructions usually need huge models and datasets. Moritz Reuss, lead author with five co-authors, present FLOWER, a far smaller vision-language-action policy, in a 2025 robotics paper. Their design prunes many language model layers and reallocates capacity to the diffusion action head.

A second conditioning method cuts parameters further through modular adaptation. The resulting model has under a billion parameters and was pretrained in a modest number of accelerator hours. It performs competitively across many simulation and real-world tasks and robot bodies in their tests, and sets a leading score on one manipulation benchmark.
arxiv-2509-05396:
Letting several AI models debate can make answers worse, Andrea Wynn, Harsh Satija, and Gillian Hadfield find in a 2025 paper on multi-agent debate. Debate is often sold as a way to improve reasoning, and earlier work mostly studied debates among models of similar strength.

Mixing models of different capability changes the picture. Across experiments, accuracy sometimes fell over time even when stronger models outnumbered weaker ones. Models often moved from right answers to wrong ones after hearing peers, favouring agreement over challenge. The authors probe causes including flattery-like agreement, social conformity, and task type. Naive debate, they conclude, can degrade performance unless agents are equipped to resist persuasive errors.
arxiv-2509-05596:
Upgraded industrial control software must keep its old behaviour, and Soumyadip Bandyopadhyay with Santonu Sarkar verify that property in a 2025 software engineering paper. Programmable logic controllers run factory equipment, and their programs are updated often as requirements evolve.

Both the old and new versions, written as sequential function charts, are converted into Petri net models, a standard model of step-by-step processes. A new containment checker, built on symbolic path equivalence, then tests whether the new model's behaviour contains the old one. On eighty real-world benchmarks from an open library the framework scaled well. It ran about four times faster than a popular comparison tool.
arxiv-2509-06196:
Fine-tuned language models purpose-built for hiring outperform general ones at reading resumes, report Mohamed T. Younes and four co-authors in a 2025 paper. Building on their earlier MLAR tracking system, the team trains models on recruitment data rendered in a standardized JSON format. A synthetic dataset supplies consistency, while resumes parsed by a large DeepSeek model add diversity and realism.

Experiments show clear gains over base models and other leading systems across exact match, F1, BLEU, ROUGE, and similarity scores. The fine-tuned Phi-4 model posts the highest F1, above ninety percent, signaling strong precision and recall. The authors argue such specialization can reshape recruitment workflows and candidate-job matching.
arxiv-2509-06396:
Predicting how a brain metastasis will answer radiosurgery, a year ahead, is automated in a 2025 paper led by Lorenz Achim Kuhn with seven co-authors. Brain metastases drive much cancer mortality, and follow-up MRI review at scale is an intractable manual workload. The team built a pipeline curating a longitudinal dataset from one hospital: nearly nine hundred lesions in one hundred seventy-seven patients, each followed over a year at roughly two-month intervals.

Clustering finds five dominant growth trajectories tied to final response categories. Gradient boosting predicts twelve-month lesion response from pre-treatment and first follow-up scans with strong accuracy, and graph machine learning nearly matches it with more flexible timing. The authors frame the pipeline as groundwork for decision support in personalized radiosurgery care.
arxiv-2509-06496:
Methane fingerprints in the light of Saturn's moon Titan are catalogued in a 2025 planetary science paper led by Sirinrat Sithajan, with four co-authors. Methane shapes Titan's air, yet a complete list of its absorption lines at visible wavelengths is still missing. Better lists would sharpen methane detection on Titan and on distant exoplanets.

Using the ESPRESSO spectrograph at very high resolution, the team picked out features that belong to Titan itself, carefully allowing extra room for sunlight and Earth's air. They found several thousand candidate methane features, most of them newly reported, and far more than a lower-resolution instrument found in the same ranges. Most lines stay blended rather than cleanly split. The full list, with reliability measures, is published so others can build better methane line lists.
arxiv-2509-06796:
Testing whether a specific person's data trained a model, without training hundreds of stand-in models, is the advance claimed by Yuntao Du and four co-authors in a 2025 machine learning security paper. Membership inference attacks measure how much a model leaks about its training set. Leading attacks rely on many shadow models unrelated to the target, which is expensive.

Their imitative attack instead builds a small number of models designed to copy the target model's behavior closely, informed by the target itself. Those imitators then support the membership judgment. Extensive experiments show the method substantially outperforming existing attacks across settings while using less than five percent of the computing cost of leading approaches. Cheaper, stronger membership tests matter both for auditing privacy honestly and for understanding how much information trained models really retain.
arxiv-2509-06896:
Poisoning attacks on training data look weaker once the hardest targets are graded, argue William Xu and seven co-authors in a 2025 machine learning security paper. Targeted poisoning injects malicious examples to flip predictions on chosen test samples. Published evaluations average success over randomly picked targets, which can hide true worst-case strength.

Using only information from a cleanly trained model, the authors rank test examples from easiest to hardest to poison. Coarse scores come from clean training dynamics, while finer classification uses poison distances and budgets. Experiments show these measures reliably sort samples by vulnerability. Defenders gain as much as attackers: since targeted poisoning leaves no mark on the data distribution, proactively finding the most vulnerable samples lets them apply focused countermeasures. The paper reframes both attack evaluation and defense around worst cases.
arxiv-2509-07196:
Shahid Qamar and 3 co-authors introduce a learning framework in 2025 for tracking and steering quantum systems that lose energy to their surroundings. Such open systems are hard to model when the internal Hamiltonian, the energy rule, or the noise pattern is not fully known. The framework is called AQNODE, short for Augmented Quantum Neural Ordinary Differential Equation.

AQNODE embeds the system in a larger hidden space whose motion is learned by a neural network from partial measurement data. From weak measurements it rebuilds qubit states and tracks how fast coherence fades over time, without being handed the true physics equations. Feedback rules, including a time-varying optimal controller, then steer the system toward target states. Computer trials show low prediction errors and stable control across varied setups, which suggests the method could suit real-time lab use.
arxiv-2509-07296:
Energy planners need to know how often extreme demand events arrive in clusters, not just one at a time. Grace Burtenshaw, Joe Lane, and Meagan Carney present a new statistical workflow for that problem in a 2025 research paper. Standard extreme value theory handles isolated extremes well. It struggles with successive extremes, such as long heat waves driving repeated demand peaks.

Their workflow builds on recent theory for successive extremes in dynamical systems. It assumes the data follow a heavy-tailed distribution, where very large values remain fairly likely. The authors show the method gives steadier estimates of return levels than standard likelihood methods. They test it on forecast gas supply scenarios running from 2025 to 2050. Better estimates of clustered extremes can guide storage and purchasing decisions before a hard winter hits.
arxiv-2509-07596:
Yusuke Hirota heads a 12-author audit in 2025 of the benchmarks used to measure gender bias in vision-language models. These benchmarks label real images by gender, but the images also carry spurious correlations: backgrounds and objects that happen to co-occur with one gender. The authors ask whether those extra features distort the bias scores that labs report and compare.

Across four widely used benchmarks and several models, they perturb only non-gender features and watch the scores move. Masking just ten percent of objects or lightly blurring backgrounds shifts bias metrics by up to 175 percent in generative models and 43 percent in CLIP variants. The scores, they conclude, often track reactions to spurious features rather than gender bias itself. Since spotless benchmarks are fundamentally hard to build, they recommend reporting feature-sensitivity measures beside every bias score.
arxiv-2509-07796:
Waves traveling through the Sun's outer atmosphere may explain how the corona gets so hot. Upasna Baweja and 8 co-authors report two wave types sharing the same polar plumes in a 2025 research paper. Polar plumes are ray-like structures rising from the Sun's poles. The team used sharp, fast images from the Extreme Ultraviolet Imager aboard Solar Orbiter.

They found slow magneto-acoustic waves and Alfvénic waves present at the same time in the same plumes. The slow waves showed small brightness changes with periods near nine minutes. The Alfvénic waves swayed the plumes sideways with much shorter periods. Both wave families were also seen inside fine substructures of the plumes. Seeing both together, up to a good height above the pole, helps theorists test wave heating ideas. Those ideas aim to explain the hot corona and the solar wind.
arxiv-2509-07896:
Sleep tracking through an earbud-like sensor is tested by Philipp Lepold and 3 co-authors in a 2025 wearable technology paper. Laboratory sleep staging relies on full scalp electrode setups that are accurate but far too intrusive for nightly home use. A single in-ear channel measuring electrical signals could be worn comfortably instead.

Earlier work showed in-ear signals track many patterns seen by full scalp recordings. The authors check whether that single channel supports sleep monitoring in real-world settings, with special interest in spotting the moment someone falls asleep. Reliable onset detection could pause media automatically or build long-term sleep records at home. Comfortable monitoring would move sleep science out of the laboratory and into everyday life.
arxiv-2509-07996:
Lingdong Kong and 22 co-authors survey world models that represent scenes in three and four dimensions in a 2025 review paper. World models let agents understand, represent, and predict their environments. Earlier surveys stressed generative methods for flat images and video, overlooking fast-growing work on depth imagery, occupancy grids, and LiDAR point clouds for large-scale scenes.

Terminology in the field is fragmented, with inconsistent definitions of what counts as a world model. The survey offers a standardised definition and taxonomy while mapping the native 3D and 4D literature. Robots and self-driving systems live in physical space, so models built on real spatial data, evolving over time, are central to their planning and safety.
arxiv-2509-08096:
Option pricing models can match today's volatility surface yet imply the wrong variance over time, shows Jiwook Yoo in a solo 2025 quantitative finance paper. Traders calibrate models by minimising errors against Black-Scholes implied volatilities. A model can pass that test while its variance term structure, the pattern of expected variance across horizons, drifts far from what option prices imply.

Joint calibration fixes the objective by fitting market option prices and the variance term structure together. The mismatch matters because many derivatives and risk measures depend on how variance evolves, not only on today's surface. A calibration that respects both views should produce prices and hedges that stay consistent when contracts extend across several maturities.
arxiv-2509-08196:
Jianfeng Lu and Kecen Sha revisit a cheap stand-in for a costly quantum matrix in a 2025 paper. The matrix is the quantum Fisher information matrix. It tells variational quantum algorithms which way to lean as they search. Getting it straight costs many state preparations on real hardware.

A classical version is cheaper. Average that classical matrix over random measurement bases, and for pure states the mean is half the quantum one. The pair review this fact through the lens of covariant measurement, a tool from quantum metrology. They then push past the basic fact. If the swap holds up, quantum optimisers can save scarce runs and still precondition their search well.
arxiv-2509-08296:
Graphs themselves become quantum objects in a 2025 paper by Kassahun H. Betre and Nathan Lewis, motivated by background-independent quantum gravity. Ordinary quantum theory puts states on a fixed structure; quantum gravity may need the relations among things to be dynamical too. Finite multigraphs, with labelled or unlabelled vertices and a cap on edges, are quantised in a unified representation.

The construction treats quantum multigraphs as microscopic degrees of freedom rather than mere pictures of relations among particle states, and their Hilbert spaces are developed before attention turns to simple graphs. Letting connectivity fluctuate quantum mechanically is a small, concrete step toward spacetimes that are built from relations instead of assumed in advance.
arxiv-2509-08696:
Text-to-speech systems built on diffusion transformers sound natural but speak slowly, because they refine audio over many steps. Siratish Sakpiboonchit speeds one up in a 2025 research paper written alone. The method caches transformer layer outputs inside the F5-TTS architecture. Reusing those outputs skips redundant computation during the denoising process.

A calibration phase measures errors between timesteps to choose a safe caching schedule. One unified schedule covers both attention and feed-forward layers, sidestepping dependency problems between layers. Experiments on two speech datasets varied the cache thresholds and step counts. Caching at later denoising steps cut inference time without hurting quality. Caching early steps degraded speech about as much as using fewer steps overall. The approach needs no retraining and no architecture change, making it an easy upgrade for deployed speech systems.
arxiv-2509-09196:
Chin Yuen Kwok and 1 co-author present efficient trie based biasing using multi-step prediction for rare word recognition in a 2025 paper. Speech systems can give bonus scores to partial words that may lead to a rare word. If the full word never appears, bonuses must be revoked.

Undoing those bonuses only works inside beam search, and it costs a lot for large decoders. Instead, the model is adapted to look ahead and predict several steps at once. That better estimates whether a partial path will complete the rare word, avoiding revocation entirely. Fine-tuning Whisper on ten hours of synthetic data cuts word error rate greatly on the same style of test.
arxiv-2509-09296:
Li Wang and 5 co-authors present datasets and defenses for over-the-air adversarial attacks on speaker verification in a 2025 paper. Speaker verification confirms identity by voice, but adversarial audio played through the air can fool it. Prior detection methods lacked a comprehensive test dataset.

Their AdvSV 2.0 dataset holds hundreds of thousands of samples totaling hundreds of hours, covering classic attacks and both transmission types. A new attack based on a neural replay simulator strengthens over-the-air attacks. A contrastive one-class defense, CODA-OCC, is proposed in response. It achieves strong detection scores on the new dataset, outperforming several state of the art methods.
arxiv-2509-09396:
A model explaining its answer by showing what change would flip it sounds transparent, until someone checks whether the flip is honest. Harry Mayne and 6 co-authors audit such self-generated counterfactual explanations in a 2025 research paper. The models were asked to edit inputs just enough to change their own predictions. Good explanations should be valid and minimal.

Left alone, the models produced valid counterfactuals that were far from minimal, revealing little about the true decision boundary. Asked explicitly for minimal edits, they made tiny changes that failed to flip anything. That validity-minimality trade-off held across models, datasets, and settings. The authors warn that these explanations are at best ineffective and at worst misleading. Anyone deploying language models in high-stakes settings should not let a fluent self-explanation substitute for evidence about how the model actually decides.
arxiv-2509-09496:
Ha Linh Nguyen and 2 co-authors use body momentum to make generated human motion look more physical in a 2025 computer vision paper. Many models split motion into local joint movement around the hips and the hips' path through the world, then treat the two parts separately. In reality the parts are coupled, because contact with the ground drives a body forward as its shape changes.

Whole-body linear and angular momentum captures that coupling in one quantity. The authors add a loss term forcing generated momentum profiles to match those in real recordings. Motion cleaned up in this way showed less foot sliding and jitter, better balance, and no loss in recovery accuracy.
arxiv-2509-09696:
Weibin Li and 2 co-authors present DCHO in 2025, a framework for predicting how higher-order brain connections evolve over time. Ordinary connectivity links brain regions in pairs, while the higher-order kind captures groups of three or more acting together, a richer picture of organisation. Earlier methods inferred such group links from scans but treated them as still pictures, leaving forecasting untouched.

DCHO splits the job in two: first infer the group connections, then predict where their hidden trajectory heads next. A dual-view encoder gathers structure at several scales, a combinatorial learner assembles the group information, and a special loss keeps time paths honest. Across several neuroimaging data sets the method beat rivals at both classifying brain states and forecasting dynamics.
arxiv-2509-09796:
Alexander Klimek and 4 co-authors optimise sustainable aviation fuel plants with neural networks embedded inside the planning maths in a 2025 engineering paper. Choosing a fuel route means picking discrete process steps and tuning continuous operating settings at once, while stream compositions vary along the way. Ordinary superstructure methods strain under that mix, so the team folds learned surrogate models directly into a mixed-integer optimisation problem.

Applied to Fischer-Tropsch kerosene, the cheapest layout with no carbon limit leans on fossil autothermal reforming. Tighten the emissions cap and biomass gasification plus direct air capture with storage move in, cutting net emissions at rising cost. At zero emissions, a hybrid of the fossil and biomass routes wins on price.
arxiv-2509-09896:
Alexandru Cojocaru and 3 co-authors tighten a lifting theorem for quantum security proofs in a 2025 cryptography paper. Lifting results let a proof about a simple game carry over to a harder quantum setting, here the random oracle model where hash functions are treated as random. Their engine is a new measure-and-reprogram method they call coherent, because the reprogramming respects the quantum state instead of disturbing it clumsily.

The sharper theorem needs only classical reasoning about query counts, a relief for analysts. Direct payoffs include an average-case direct product result, showing multi-instance games stay hard, plus clean hardness derivations for salted games and multi-instance versions of one-wayness and collision resistance. Several other uniform and non-uniform hardness claims follow the same path.
arxiv-2509-09996:
Dario J. Fritzewski and 4 co-authors match X-ray glow to spin, star by star, in the young open cluster NGC 2516 in a 2025 astronomy paper. Cool stars shine in soft X-rays from their hot outer atmospheres, and that shine, read beside a rotation period, reveals magnetic activity and how it changes with age. The cluster was observed by the eROSITA telescope aboard the SRG satellite during its early calibration phase.

Over fifteen hundred X-ray sources filled the view, and about a thousand were tied to known stars, including hundreds of cluster members with measured spins. Spectra were fitted for every source, and stars were grouped by mass and rotation to isolate the spin effect. A colour-activity chart shows the X-ray share climbing from hotter to cooler star types, with K stars behaving in a more tangled way.
arxiv-2509-10396:
Teaching language models by inpainting is Siyan Zhao and ten co-authors' idea in this 2025 paper. Masked diffusion models generate text by filling blanks. Standard models write left to right instead. Reinforcement learning for any such model suffers in a common way. Rewards are rare. Failed tries are wasted.

Their framework, IGPO, turns inpainting into a guide. During training, it inserts fragments of correct reasoning into the model's own attempts. The model still writes most of the solution itself. The fragments steer exploration toward promising paths. That rescues training signals. Group-based methods would otherwise zero those signals out. Fine-tuning on rewritten, concise traces adds a second boost. Entropy-based filtering adds a third. Together, the recipe sets new best results for its model class. The wins come on three math benchmarks, including GSM8K.
arxiv-2509-10496:
Battery health decides how long electric vehicles and drones stay useful, and Imen Jarraya with six co-authors propose a hybrid predictor for it in this 2025 engineering paper. Estimating a lithium-ion battery's state of health is hard because degradation is nonlinear and unfolds over time, defeating conventional techniques.

Their model, SOH-KLSTM, fuses two architectures. A long short-term memory network reads the sequence of past measurements and tracks long-term dependencies, while a Kolmogorov-Arnold network supplies flexible nonlinear curve fitting inside the memory cell's candidate state. The combination aims to follow the complicated shapes of real battery aging more faithfully than either part alone. The authors frame the design for the settings where health monitoring matters most, from cars and aircraft to home energy storage.
arxiv-2509-10696:
Shuaiqi Wang and nine co-authors build Struct-Bench, a benchmark for privately generating structured data, in this 2025 paper on differential privacy. Companies hold valuable structured datasets, tables laced with free-text fields, that cannot simply be shared. Synthetic copies could unlock them, but standard quality scores, built for images and plain text, miss the structure entirely.

Struct-Bench asks users to describe their dataset's grammar, then grades synthetic versions against it. The benchmark ships with five real and two synthetic datasets, reference metrics, and a public leaderboard. Even state-of-the-art private generators struggle on it, the authors show. A case study demonstrates using the benchmark to improve the Private Evolution method on structured data, giving the privacy community a shared yardstick where none existed.
arxiv-2509-10996:
M. Z. Haider and 4 co-authors present V-ZOR, a design for trustworthy communication between blockchains, in this 2025 paper. Bridges and oracle services, which carry data between chains, are among the weakest points in decentralized finance, with billions lost to trust failures. Committees that report data are usually picked in predictable ways, which invites manipulation.

V-ZOR wraps each data packet in a zero-knowledge proof that the reported value was aggregated correctly, as a median. Committee pickers are reseeded with quantum entropy so no one can foresee the panel. Reporters stake funds once on a shared hub, and any chain can punish cheating with a fraud proof. A prototype ran with low verification cost and one-block delay.
arxiv-2509-11296: Dan Haran proposes a new frame in this short 2025 algebra paper. Profinite groups are limits of finite groups. They sit at the heart of modern number theory. Haran builds a theory of their epimorphisms. These are maps that hit every element of the target. The theory describes such maps through indecomposable ones, those that cannot be broken down further. The aim is a cleaner set of building blocks for maps between profinite groups.
arxiv-2509-11496:
Fabrycio Leite Nakano Almada and six co-authors report a multilingual fact-checking system. This 2025 paper covers claim normalization. That step rewrites messy social posts as short, self-contained claims. The CheckThat! 2025 task demanded it in twenty languages.

Their approach switches strategy by resources on hand. Fine-tuned small models serve the thirteen tongues with training data. Prompted large models cover the seven with none. The system reached a podium place in most of the twenty tongues. It took second place in eight of them. Five of those were zero-shot tongues where prompting shone. For Portuguese, the team's home test bed, it placed third. All code and prompts are public.
arxiv-2509-12196:
Forecasting many linked measurements at once, like sensors on one machine, strains the standard transformer because its attention treats every pair of channels the same static way. Hunjae Lee and one co-author propose prime attention in 2025, which reshapes each token for the specific pair it is about to interact with.

Learned adjustments tailor the representation per relationship while keeping the overall cost the same as ordinary attention. Across forecasting benchmarks the method beats standard attention, with gains up to about six and a half percent. It also matches or beats the baseline while reading up to forty percent less of the sequence.
arxiv-2509-12396:
Network embeddings squeeze a social graph into a few numbers per person, and the squeezing is not fair by default. Gabriel Chuang and one co-author ask in 2025 what baseline embeddings do before anyone adds a fairness fix, using the stochastic block model as their test bed.

They pin down exact conditions for information loss and show the loss scales with a graph's density and its tendency to link within groups. Very different graphs can collapse to identical embeddings, and that collapse lands hardest on small, sparse communities. Downstream link prediction then errs more for exactly those communities, matching disparities seen in practice.
arxiv-2509-12796:
S. Bokpe, F. Dossa and G. Avossevou work out in 2025 the states of a two-way wobble system whose mass shifts with place. Such systems model small devices where mass is not fixed, and exact answers help link small-scale rules to heat traits.

With a standard math method they get exact forms for the energy levels and wave shapes. From those they derive heat traits such as stored heat, stored energy, and disorder. In two ways of motion the heat traits depend strongly on the bend factor, unlike the one-way case. The link hints that tuning the factor could lift the work of small heat machines.
arxiv-2509-12896:
Fabian Kropfl, Daniel Peterseim and Elisabeth Ullmann speed up flow models with random traits in 2025. Fine detail makes such models slow. Averaging can shrink them, but building the shrunk form for each new case still costs much.

Their fix trains a neural net to map a fine case to its coarse facts at once. New cases can then be shrunk fast and with trust. Tests cover two trait types: log-shaped spreads for rock layers, and layered random fields with shifting link lengths. Trait contrast shapes how well the shortcut holds. The frame suits large sets of random cases.
arxiv-2509-13496:
Rajatsubhra Chakraborty, Xujun Che and four co-authors map hidden social bias in text-to-image models in 2025 with BiasMap via cross-attention. Output counts miss concept coupling that survives output fixes. Attention maps expose structural links between demographics and semantics during generation.

Overlap of attribution maps quantifies coupling per concept pair. Professions with gender or race serve as cases. Past fairness fixes shrink output gaps yet leave coupling intact in tests. Energy-guided sampling that cuts expected overlap during denoising mitigates coupling directly. Distributional fixes complement, not replace, concept fixes.
arxiv-2509-13696:
Iyadh Ben Cheikh Larbi and 3 co-authors feed both text and time series into language models to predict medical outcomes, in a 2025 paper. Nobody doubts that large language models write text well. What they can do with structured clinical data is far less clear. Classification work in medicine often turns on measurements that change over time, such as a series of readings.

The authors start from language models that have already been tuned to follow instructions. With careful prompt optimization, they teach the models to take two inputs at once: the free text of clinical notes, and the structured entries of the health record. The combined approach, they report, performs as well as specialised systems built to handle many kinds of input at once. It asks for less complexity than those systems.
arxiv-2509-13796:
Meng Fai Lim and Chao Qin compute algebraic K-groups in a 2025 number theory paper. For the ring of integers of a totally real abelian number field, they target the precise orders of the even K-groups. The orders are the sizes of the groups. The group indices follow a four-step pattern. These groups encode deep arithmetic information, and exact values are hard won.

The authors present approaches for calculating those orders. Along the way, they prove a formula tying one field's order to the orders of its intermediate cyclic subfields. The field in question is built from prime-degree steps. That recursion breaks a hard computation into easier ones. They close with a compiled list of values for these K-groups. It serves as a reference table for other researchers in the arithmetic of such fields.
arxiv-2509-13896:
Shalini Chakraborty and four co-authors review the ethics literature on AI in software modeling education in a 2025 paper. Students and teachers now use these tools to interpret requirements and formalize models. The tools also turn mental pictures into structured diagrams. So they quietly shape core skills, like domain understanding and diagram thinking. Little ethical oversight guides that influence.

Searching six major digital libraries, the team retrieved nearly fourteen hundred unique papers. Only three explicitly addressed ethical considerations. Those include responsibility, fairness, transparency, diversity, and inclusion. That near-total absence is their headline finding. They examine the three studies closely. They also map the research openings and challenges that follow. The goal is building ethical frameworks into modeling curricula.
arxiv-2509-14096:
Víctor Mayoral-Vilches reports a hands-on security assessment of a production humanoid robot in a solo 2025 report. Humanoid robots are leaving laboratories for real workplaces, and their security frameworks have not kept pace. Working on a Unitree G1 platform, he combined static analysis, runtime observation, and cryptographic examination to map how the machine actually defends itself.

The findings cut both ways. A dual-layer proprietary encryption system proved innovative in design but used static cryptographic keys, letting configurations be decrypted offline. More seriously, the robot kept persistent telemetry connections sending audio, visual, spatial, and actuator data to external servers with no user consent or notice. He even ran a cybersecurity AI agent on the robot to probe its maker's cloud, arguing the field needs adaptive security frameworks.
arxiv-2509-14296:
Vasiliki Bikia and eight co-authors describe the Spezi Data Pipeline in 2025, an open source Python toolkit for digital health data. Health apps and studies gather messy data from sensors, heart traces and questionnaires. Teams need one standard way to handle it all.

The pipeline covers secure access, retrieval, processing, display and export in modular steps. Records follow the HL7 FHIR standard, a shared format for health data exchange. The toolkit sits inside the Stanford Spezi ecosystem for building health software. A worked example uses real data from the PAWS project at Stanford. For research and clinical teams, the value is less custom glue code and data that other tools can read without translation.
arxiv-2509-14396:
Drew Fudenberg and Annie Liang study delegating decisions to an AI of unknown alignment in 2025, using a medical treatment choice as the case. More patient information helps an aligned AI predict need well. The same information amplifies harm if the AI pursues other goals.

A designer must choose which attributes to reveal before seeing the prediction. Fudenberg and Liang characterise the best disclosure as a balance set by beliefs about AI reliability. Rare groups with high treatment need should be identified and disclosed, they show. Remaining patients are better pooled together, hiding detail that a misaligned system could exploit. The result gives a principled disclosure rule for using powerful but untrusted predictors.
arxiv-2509-14496:
Wyatt Petula and four co-authors present DeliverC in 2025, a game that teaches C pointers with generative AI help. Pointers are a hard topic in coding courses, known for tripping new students. Game based learning is in wide use, but live, adaptive help for hard topics is rare.

The game uses a small GPT model to give hints shaped to each player and to make pointer tasks on the fly. A pilot with twenty five undergraduates tracked play data and surveyed drive, self belief and feedback quality. On the survey, most players said they felt surer of the topic and more reflective after play. Error rates also fell as players moved through scaffolded levels. Play thinned as tasks grew hard, and some hints missed the mark.
arxiv-2509-14596:
Yanglei Song and Georgios Fellouris address a hard estimation problem in a 2025 statistics paper. They want the probability that a random walk in many dimensions exits through one of many rare regions before reaching its target. The setting comes from sequential multiple hypothesis testing, where the number of rare regions can grow extremely fast with dimension.

Standard importance sampling with mixtures over all tilted distributions works in theory but becomes impossible to compute. Song and Fellouris build efficient mixtures from far fewer components, combining optimal tilts for a few regions with extra proposals that control variance elsewhere. They apply the method to three testing probabilities, including a multidimensional version of a classical exit problem. Theory and numerical experiments both support the approach.
arxiv-2509-14696:
Sanchayan Banerjee and three co-authors find multiple many body localisation transitions in 2025 in a driven non-Hermitian quasiperiodic chain of hardcore bosons. Many body localisation keeps a system from thermalising, preserving local memory. Periodic driving usually heats such systems into thermal behaviour.

Here the driven system first delocalises, then localises again as the driving period grows, a re-entrant transition. Further increase brings a series of localisation and delocalisation switches, leaving extended regime islands between localised phases. Non-Hermiticity, meaning energy exchange with an environment in the model, shapes the pattern. Repeated transitions warn that a single drive setting can misrepresent a system that flips phases several times across the dial.
arxiv-2509-15196:
Anna J. Fehr and Sean M. Andrews measure the temperature structure of planet-forming disks in two dimensions in a 2025 astronomy paper. A protoplanetary disk's heat varies with both distance from its star and height above the midplane, and that structure steers how planets assemble. Their method works annulus by annulus, ring by ring, for flexibility.

From synthetic disks with known structure, they extract emission surfaces and brightness temperatures for several carbon monoxide lines, then invert them into vertical temperature profiles. The recovery stays faithful despite noise and limited resolution, and even a modest line set constrains temperatures over wide ranges of radius and height. Errors in the extracted surfaces are the chief systematic worry. Applied to archival observations of the HD 163296 disk, the method shows simple radial temperature laws hiding real complexity.
arxiv-2509-15296:
Vincent MacKay, Zhilei Xu, Ruby Byrne, and Jacqueline Hewitt design radio arrays that sample the measurement plane completely in a 2025 radio astronomy paper. Interferometers measure Fourier components of the sky on the so-called uv plane, and gaps in coverage distort images. Their RULES algorithm engineers layouts that leave no gaps over a chosen baseline range, with fewer antennas than current arrays.

Complete layouts matter for cosmology: bright foregrounds contaminate the faint twenty-one centimeter signal from the early Universe inside a wedge-shaped region of Fourier space. Simulated observations over an FM-adjacent frequency band, processed through an image-based power spectrum estimator, test whether complete sampling shrinks that wedge's damage. The results guide how next arrays might buy cleaner early-Universe data through geometry alone.
arxiv-2509-15396:
Yotam Svoray, writing alone, sorts rough points on shapes defined over local rings. These rough points are called hypersurface singularities, and he groups them in an ADE style scheme. The grouping rests on a trait named Cohen-Macaulay type, which gauges how a ring's parts behave. The size of the field left over in the ring sets how far the scheme can reach.

Svoray first widens a classic result on rings with few or countable types to rings with far more types. The new bound depends on how large that leftover field is. With that step in place, he builds the full ADE style grouping for these shapes.
arxiv-2509-15596:
Gui Wang leads a large team that builds a test for AI in eye surgery. Models that read images and text do well in broad tasks, but surgery is high stakes and narrow. Their skill there was largely untested. The team build a large test set grounded in firm clinical knowledge.

The set, EyePCR, holds over two hundred thousand question and answer items. It spans fine traits for seeing, a knowledge web for grasping facts, and four reasoning tasks drawn from clinic work. The layout mirrors how surgeons see cues, add knowledge, and decide. A tuned version of a known model leads on seeing questions among rivals. It also beats open models on grasp and reasoning, nearing top commercial ones.
arxiv-2509-15696:
Weiyi An and Jie Zhu combine two routes to single photon light. Photon blockade is an effect where one photon stops a system from taking a second. It makes sources that emit photons one at a time, prized for quantum work. One route uses strong links to split the energy levels. Another uses clashing paths that cancel the second photon's rise.

A third, newer route uses two photon absorption from the setting itself. An and Zhu place that absorption inside a light amplifier device. By joining the clashing path route with the absorption route, they get a steadier blockade. Multi photon states are suppressed more strongly. The work aids the design of single photon sources.
arxiv-2509-15896:
Arghodeep Nandi leads a team that surveys misinformation detection through the lens of the human mind. False claims are a major harm of the digital age. Auto fact checks mostly grade whether a claim is true. Yet falsehood harms through how people perceive, read, and feel about what they see, not through falsity alone.

The survey reads top detection systems against mind science: biases in thought, social dynamics, and emotional response. That reading exposes limits in current tools and points to fixes. The team sketch future paths, such as models that join brain and behavior traits with tech factors. Such frames could catch falsehoods better and blunt their harm.
