The work is a survey, not a new detector.
arxiv-2509-16996:
Jonathan Morag returns with a solo study of radiation-driven shocks in a 2025 astrophysics paper. When a supernova bursts out, radiation carries the shock through the star's outer layers. Past solutions assumed a fully ionized gas that glows by one process. Morag adds atomic transition lines, which change how the gas blocks and emits light.

Two simplified cases are solved numerically. One shock moves through a uniform medium. The other escapes a falling density profile. A semi-analytic form covers the spectrum when local balance holds. The work rules out some common line tables for breakout work, since bound but ionized species matter.
arxiv-2509-17096:
Ziyou Li, Agnia Sergeyuk, and Maliheh Izadi bring order to prompt management for coders in a 2025 paper. Developers now write prompts as casually as sticky notes, which hurts reuse and reliability. Their tool, Prompt-with-Me, lives inside the coding environment itself. It gives prompts a structured home where they can be stored, found, and maintained.

A user study with a small group of developers showed strong acceptance. Usability scored high and mental load scored low. Users reported better prompts and less repeated effort. The authors distill lessons for the next generation of prompt tools, as prompts become a durable part of software work.
arxiv-2509-17696:
Nestor Arsenov and seven co-authors map the high-redshift cosmic web with quasars as their tracers. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses the Quaia catalogue, which holds hundreds of thousands of quasars across a huge stretch of sky whose selection function is well understood. Quasars shine far, so they can chart structure at epochs galaxies barely reach.

The team reconstructed the matter density field and ran the REVOLVER method, which uses Voronoi tessellation around each quasar to find voids and clusters. Their catalogues list well over ten thousand voids and tens of thousands of clusters. Fifty mock catalogues checked the consistency of the data and the method, and density profiles of the structures were measured at large scales. The work extends cosmic web mapping to earlier times, where it can test the standard cosmological model where it is least probed.
arxiv-2509-17896:
Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, and Denis K Sunko split a three-fermion wave state into fixed and free parts. Their 2025 paper deals with top-spin states of three fermions, the class that holds electrons. The fixed parts, called shapes, exist just to meet the Pauli rule that no two fermions share a state.

The free parts carry the real physics, as bosonic modes built on the shapes. On a top-grade wave state for a lithium atom state, hundreds of basis terms shrink to eleven shape blocks. Just five blocks matter in size. The squeeze shows a clean way to hunt robust few-body linked states.
arxiv-2509-17996:
Claire Voisin studies which field steps are needed for a point to exist on a del Pezzo surface. Her 2025 paper works over a base field with no real-order trait. Cubic surfaces, one such class, are the main focus of the results.

She shows that if a cubic surface has a point over a field step whose size is not a multiple of three, then it has a point at a small step too. That sharpens a past result by Coray, which allowed a larger step. Like gains hold for two lower classes of such surfaces. She also shows a power of a cubic shape is easy to parametrize.
arxiv-2509-18096:
Chaehyun Kim and 7 co-authors open up text-to-image models to find where word sense lands in a picture. Their 2025 frame, Seg4Diff, studies joint attention in a diffusion transformer that holds image and text tokens side by side. Such maps have been little mapped, layer by layer.

One block stands out as a grounding expert: it links text tokens to neat image zones, again and again. Those links yield good masks for what each word names. A light fine-tune with mask-tagged images sharpens that skill. Image quality rose too, which shows the grouping is a real trait of these models.
arxiv-2509-18496:
Young stars inherit the motion of the gas clouds that bore them. Ji-Xuan Zhou, Guang-Xing Li, and Bing-Qiu Chen use that link to map how interstellar gas moves in three dimensions. Their 2025 paper joins gas velocity measures with star motions from the Gaia space mission. The sample covers 102 pairings of young stellar objects with molecular clouds.

All pairings sit within about 3.5 kiloparsecs of the Sun. The team finds the gas traced by these pairs mostly follows the galaxy's rotation. An extra drift of about 8.6 kilometers per second rides on top. Motion within the galactic plane is more energetic than motion up and down. The paper releases a catalogue of 3D velocities in several reference frames. It also lists values for well-known clouds. The catalogue sets a base for studying how gas, stars, and the galaxy interact.
arxiv-2509-18796:
Surgical AI starves for labeled images, and fake images from diffusion models can copy training data too closely. Danush Kumar Venkatesh and Stefanie Speidel present SAADi, a framework that aligns synthetic image making with the end task. Their 2025 paper pairs preferred and non-preferred fake images as judged by downstream models. Light fine-tuning then steers the generator toward the preferred kind.

On three surgical data sets, the aligned images lifted sorting scores by seven to nine percent. Segmentation scores rose by two to ten percent. Gains were largest for underrepresented classes, where data scarcity bites hardest. Repeating the refinement loop added further gains of four to ten percent. The authors frame task-aware alignment as a general fix for sample quality decay. It turns synthetic data from a gamble into a tuned input.
arxiv-2509-19196:
An underwater explosion or volcanic eruption sends a pressure pulse through the ocean, and R. Pethiyagoda and three co-authors model how that pulse evolves. Their ocean is compressible, which matters because water squeezes under pressure, both as the wave passes and in its resting state. Solving the motion equations is eased by a special inner product the authors introduce. It lets them borrow self-adjoint operator theory and work in a space where the acoustic-gravity wave modes are cleanly separated.

Simulations show the pulse first spreading outward in a ring. It then reflects from the surface and the rigid ocean floor, and eventually channels sideways away from the source. Comparing runs with and without the resting compression shows its effect is small but not negligible. The method gives a time-domain picture of both the surface motion and the pressure field below.
arxiv-2509-19296:
Sherwin Bahmani and twelve co-authors teach a video generation model to build true 3D scenes, a system they call Lyra. Learning-based 3D reconstruction normally needs photos of real places from many angles, which are not always available. Video diffusion models, by contrast, have absorbed rich spatial knowledge from watching video, but they output flat frames. The team's self-distillation framework transfers that hidden 3D knowledge into an explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting representation.

A second decoder, trained to emit the 3D representation, is supervised by the ordinary image decoder's output. Training needs only synthetic data the video model generates itself. At run time the system creates 3D scenes from a text prompt or a single image, ready for real-time rendering. It also extends to dynamic scenes from one ordinary video. Experiments report state-of-the-art results for both still and moving scene generation.
arxiv-2509-19396:
Sahil Tyagi and three co-authors present OmniFed, a software kit for federated learning that is built in pieces. In federated learning, models train where the data live. That suits edge devices and big centers where data cannot be pooled and privacy counts. OmniFed keeps four jobs apart: set-up, control of the run, data transfer, and the training logic itself. Users swap in code only where they need to, and the core stays whole.

The kit supports many network shapes and can mix transfer methods inside one run. Well-known training methods are built in. Privacy add-ons include noise-based privacy, encrypted math, and safe merging, plus tools that shrink what gets sent. The authors test several models and methods to gauge speed and quality. Their claim is practical: one stack will ease federated work across unlike settings.
arxiv-2509-19596:
Dark matter may not be perfectly stable; it could decay slowly into invisible particles. Lea Fuß, Mathias Garny, and Alejandro Ibarra build a model where that decay ties directly to neutrino masses. Two near-twin dark particles fill the model, and the heavier one decays into the lighter plus neutrinos over cosmic time. The same mechanism that sets the decay also gives neutrinos their tiny masses.

Settings that match the known dark matter amount also match measured neutrino traits. The decay would leave marks in several places at once. Galaxy surveys could see a telltale fading of structure, a neutrino telescope could catch a diffuse glow, and a gamma-ray line could appear in range of a planned telescope. Few models offer three independent checks. Upcoming surveys will test the idea within years.
arxiv-2509-19996:
Big AI models burn large amounts of energy, yet many tasks could be served by smaller ones. Emilio Cruciani and Roberto Verdecchia propose choosing the model per task with the planet in mind. Their Green AI dynamic selection weighs the task, each model's footprint, and the accuracy the user actually needs. Two methods carry the idea out.

Cascading tries cheap models first and escalates only when needed. Routing sends each request straight to the model judged most suitable. Both aim to cut emissions while holding accuracy loss to a minimum. The paper presents the approach as an intuition with concrete machinery, inviting measurement. Inference, run billions of times, is where AI's footprint concentrates. Picking the lightest adequate model is a lever available today.
arxiv-2509-20496:
Random matrix products drive models from wireless channels to quantum circuits, and James Tian studies their kernel structure in a 2025 arXiv paper. Each product defines a positive definite kernel indexed by time. Shifting time by one step gives a second kernel. Tian asks when the original kernel dominates the shifted one, and what the Radon-Nikodym derivative between them looks like.

Two families of multiplicative walks receive complete answers. One has uneven variances across steps; the other is built from Gaussian Kraus operations. In both, the domination question collapses to a one-step condition on diagonal moments alone. The derivative is then described explicitly by a sequence of fibers over time. The uneven-variance case yields a coordinate formula through a nonnegative matrix. In the Kraus case, the condition becomes a single operator inequality on the generating map.
arxiv-2509-20696:
Humanoid robots often move stiffly when one controller must copy motion, track speed, and keep balance at once. Qingpeng Li and six co-authors split those jobs in RuN, a 2025 paper on natural humanoid locomotion. RuN stands for a residual policy approach built for smooth walking and running.

A pretrained motion generator first supplies a natural, human-like movement pattern across a wide range of speeds. A reinforcement learning policy then adds only a small correction for real physical contact and balance. This split lets the robot shift smoothly from walking to running. The authors test the system in simulation and on a real Unitree humanoid robot, reporting stable and natural movement in both settings.
arxiv-2509-20796:
Internet-of-things devices share data through the cloud, and access rules must be both fine-grained and revocable. Yongjiao Li and five co-authors propose a fast encryption scheme for that setting in a 2025 paper. Their method builds on attribute-based encryption, where access follows user traits.

The scheme adds data integrity checks and supports removing authorized users when access should end. Heavy revocation work is shifted to the cloud, easing the load on small devices. The authors claim adaptive security even under multiple challenge ciphertexts. They aim to balance efficiency, security, and dynamic scaling better than earlier revocable schemes. The design targets outsourced storage where things devices are too weak for heavy cryptography.
arxiv-2509-20896:
Diffusion models make text and images by slowly removing noise, and the steps are usually random. Hideyuki Suzuki, Wataru Kurebayashi, and Hiroshi Yamashita make those steps fixed instead in a 2025 paper. Their method swaps the random reverse chain for a herding algorithm with mildly chaotic dynamics.

Herding drives the state changes in a set, repeatable way. The swap needs no new training and no smooth stand-ins for the discrete states. On text and image tasks, the authors report gains in both speed and sample quality. The method also improves diffusion-based answers to hard combinatorial problems. It is a small change to the sampling stage, offered as a direct replacement that many existing discrete diffusion models could adopt at once.
arxiv-2509-20996:
When sheet metal is bent one way and then the other, it gives back differently than simple models predict. Gyu-Jang Sim and seven co-authors model that reverse-loading behavior in a 2025 materials paper. Ultra-thin sheets buckle under compression tests, so experiments alone cannot map the behavior.

Their crystal plasticity simulations include a back stress model grounded in geometrically necessary dislocations and the boundaries those dislocations form. A single grain-size-dependent parameter captures both the Hall-Petch strengthening effect and the Bauschinger effect, where reversed loading yields early. The model predicts reverse-loading response using only tensile test data. Better springback and formability predictions matter for car bodies and other stamped parts, where trial-and-error tooling is expensive.
arxiv-2509-21096:
Econometricians test whether their instruments are valid using overidentification tests, but weak instruments and uneven error variance can distort those tests badly. Stuart Lane and Frank Windmeijer compare two such tests in a 2025 econometrics paper. One is the classic J-test; the other is the Kleibergen-Paap rank test.

The authors derive the limiting distributions of both tests under heteroskedasticity and weak instruments, as special cases of a robust score test. Simulations show the Kleibergen-Paap test usually behaves better. The J-test suffers severe size distortions, rejecting valid instruments too often. Because test size depends on parameters that weak instruments cannot pin down, they recommend a conservative approach. A classic estimation problem is revisited at the end.
arxiv-2509-21196:
Hao Wu and 7 co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on forecasting turbulence with neural networks. Turbulence is the wild, swirling flow seen in air and water. Long forecasts are hard because small errors grow fast. Past neural methods often lose the true physics over time. The authors aim to fix that failure.

They build a model with two branches that learn two kinds of effects. One branch learns local effects, where flow fades and spreads at small scales. The other learns wide effects that link far parts of the flow. A shaped network layer is shown to act like a true rate of change. Tests support the claim that this split helps long forecasts stay close to real flow.
arxiv-2509-21796:
Soichiro Mori, Tadakatsu Sakai, and Masaki Shigemori ask where the entropy of a black hole comes from, inside string theory. Their 2025 paper, Black Hole Entropy from String Entanglement, shifts the usual question. Instead of entanglement across regions of space, they study entanglement between the spaces of states living on the strings themselves, called worldsheet spaces.

The authors apply this idea to a known duality and its extension to a three-dimensional black hole. They argue that the heat entropy of two- and three-dimensional black holes is matched by string entanglement between folded strings in the dual theory. A replica method on the worldsheet splits the entropy into two parts. One part can be computed exactly and matches the known entropy in a key limit. The other part is left open, with evidence that it holds the rest.
arxiv-2509-22096:
Chen Li, RuGway Wu, and Jörg Schmiedmayer describe a reliable source of entangled atom pairs for matter-wave networks in this 2025 paper. Entanglement between massive particles is wanted for tests of quantum nonlocality, precision measurement, and atom-based quantum processors. Their protocol starts from diatomic molecules made of ultracold atoms and splits them in a controlled way.

The split naturally creates quantum correlations between the two atoms in spin, in position and momentum, and in path. That yields Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen pairs on demand rather than by chance, and richer multi-qubit states through layered encoding. With each atom guided in a matter waveguide, the design scales to hundreds of parallel sources feeding an optical-style network of splitters, shifters, and detectors. Every step builds on established laboratory techniques, so the authors argue it can be built with current technology.
arxiv-2509-22496:
Ruoyu Chen and 8 co-authors explain which image regions drive a multimodal model's words. These models align pictures with text, but how much each token leans on the image stays unclear. Their tool, EAGLE, works as a black box: it needs no access to model internals. It credits a chosen token to compact image regions and splits credit between language priors and visual evidence.

A single objective joins two tests: whether the region suffices, and whether it is needed. A greedy search over thinned image regions optimizes that score. EAGLE also separates what tokens rely on, by modality. Across open models, it beat prior methods on faithfulness and localization while using far less memory.
arxiv-2509-22596:
Qixin Zhang and 7 co-authors coordinate teams of agents online, even when the shared goal lacks the nicest structure. Submodular objectives, where each added agent helps less than the last, admit strong guarantees. Many real goals are only weakly submodular. Their first algorithm reaches an optimal approximation guarantee for the submodular case and also covers two weakly submodular variants, tracked by curvature and ratio parameters.

A second algorithm drops the need to know those parameters in advance, while keeping the same guarantee. Both rest on a new policy-based continuous extension. Unlike the classic multilinear extension, it rounds any set function without loss. Simulations validated both algorithms.
arxiv-2509-22696:
MohammadReza Abbaszadeh Bavil Soflaei and Karim SamadZamini detect cataracts from retinal photos with models small enough for clinics. Cataracts cloud the lens and remain a top cause of vision loss worldwide. Early detection from fundus images can speed treatment. Their pipeline classifies images from a data set with left and right eye photos of five thousand patients.

A Swin transformer scored highest on accuracy and F1. A distilled MobileNet nearly matched it at far lower cost, by learning from the big model. A dual-eye variant that merges both eyes scored close behind. Grad-CAM heat maps showed the networks focus on medically sensible signs, like lens opacity and central blur.
arxiv-2509-22796:
Xingyu Li and 13 co-authors sort Linux kernel security patches by the bug they fix, using language models. Downstream maintainers often delay patches, leaving windows of vulnerability. Critical fixes for out-of-bounds access and use-after-free bugs are hard to spot. Some fixes are deliberately silent, CVE records lag or go missing, and kernel CVE rules have shifted. Prior fine-grained classifiers lack coverage and accuracy.

Their pipeline, DUALLM, pairs a large language model with a fine-tuned small one. It reads commit titles, messages, diffs, and code context together. On recent kernel patches it reached high accuracy and found over a hundred candidate critical fixes. Manual checks confirmed most, and the team built proof-of-concept exploits for two bugs.
arxiv-2509-22996:
Jiří Milička, Anna Marklová, and Václav Cvrček release two corpora of machine-written texts in English and Czech. The aim is a fair test bed for comparing human and model writing. Both corpora copy the shape of known human reference sets. The English one mirrors BE21, a modern Brown Corpus update. The Czech one mirrors the Koditex corpus in the same tradition.

Texts came from models by OpenAI, Anthropic, Alphabet, Meta, and DeepSeek. The range runs from GPT-3 to GPT-4.5. All texts carry token, lemma, and grammar tags under the Universal Dependencies standard. Both corpora are free to download and searchable through the Czech National Corpus.
arxiv-2509-23196:
Few-shot reasoning demos can hurt strong reasoning models instead of helping them. Haonan Wang and 10 co-authors dig into that paradox with high-quality traces. More exemplars steadily lowered accuracy, even when the traces were optimal. Two failure modes explain the drop. Semantic misguidance makes the model copy an exemplar's steps as if the problems matched. Strategy transfer failure blocks reuse of the underlying approach.

Their Insight-to-Solve procedure turns demos into explicit, reusable insights. It then derives a fresh trace for the target problem. An optional self-refinement pass checks coherence. Across benchmarks, the method beat direct answering and test-time scaling rivals.
arxiv-2509-23496:
Random networks laid out in space, with a few heavyweight hubs, raise percolation questions about long crossings. Emmanuel Jacob and 3 co-authors study crossing chances in geometric inhomogeneous random graphs. Vertices come from a Poisson process and carry heavy-tailed weights. Edge chances fall with distance and rise with the pair's weights. The team asks how likely a path is to cross an annulus, the ring between two balls.

Depending on the radii, the degree spread, and how fast long edges fade, crossings turn out to match the chances for one-edge or two-edge jumps. The team also derives escape chances from balls with a strong center. One result gives decay rates for a typical point's component in the subcritical regime.
arxiv-2509-23896:
Brains grown in dishes and brains simulated in silicon are starting to compute together. Dhruvik Patel and 6 co-authors review NeuroAI and its branch of synthetic biological intelligence from a computational angle. They sort the field into hardware, software, and wetware. Synthetic biological systems join the adaptive learning of living neural networks with engineered platforms, serving as test beds for neural computation and biohybrid designs.

Recent advances in organoid intelligence, neuromorphic computing, and neuro-symbolic learning get surveyed. The authors see a new class of systems emerging, ones that compute through the interaction of living tissue and digital algorithms.
arxiv-2509-23996:
Programmers learning with AI help need feedback tuned to what they actually know so far. Yuchen Wang and 2 co-authors propose CoTutor, which upgrades Bayesian Knowledge Tracing with signal processing to model student progress more sharply. Deployed as an AI copilot, it pairs generative AI with adaptive learning technology to deliver feedback and strategy. University trials showed measurable gains in learning outcomes over conventional tools, according to the authors.

Convex optimization and signal processing automate the learning analytics at scale. Pedagogical judgment stays with humans by design. The paper also flags privacy and ethics as open work, framing the system in Richard Hamming's vision of computer-aided learning to learn.
arxiv-2509-24096:
Abduction means proposing a plausible cause for what was observed, a skill that tests of language models rarely target. Kaiyu He and 6 co-authors built GEAR, an automated way to score such hypotheses with no gold answers. It grades a set of hypotheses on three points: each must fit the facts, the set must predict new cases well, and its members must differ from each other.

The team ran nine models on four benchmarks with well over a thousand problems and tens of thousands of candidate hypotheses. Clear gaps between models emerged that gold-answer tests had hidden. A training plan based on GEAR scores, paced by how fast the model learns, improved all three scores and carried over to standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-24196:
Designing a metasurface, a flat sheet that steers light, usually means costly full-wave simulations for each new shape. Huanshu Zhang and 3 co-authors show that a large language model can learn that design task from text descriptions of shapes. Data-driven rivals avoid simulations but need a fresh network and long tuning for each new optical job.

Fed with descriptions of free-form shapes, the model learned to predict spectra and to solve the inverse design task. The team benchmarked open-weight models and traced how accuracy grows with model size at the billion-parameter scale. One-dimensional token models proved practical for two-dimensional shapes. The chat-to-chip workflow aims to make such design far more user-friendly.
arxiv-2509-24296:
Diffusion language models write by refining many tokens at once, and that process opens new jailbreak paths. Zherui Li and 9 co-authors dissect those weaknesses along two axes: moves within one step and moves across steps. They find a harmful bias in the standard greedy remasking choice, and a path effect where early tokens steer the safety of the final output.

Their defense, DiffuGuard, needs no training. One stage adds controlled randomness to remasking to break the greedy bias. A second audits blocks of text using the model's own signals and repairs risky parts. Across four models and six attack styles, attack success fell by about two thirds, with utility and speed kept.
arxiv-2509-24496:
Millions of language models exist, yet how they descend from each other through fine-tuning or distillation is often undocumented. Zhaomin Wu and 5 co-authors define LLM DNA, a compact representation of a model's functional behavior, in analogy to biology. They prove this DNA has inheritance and determinism traits and that it exists at all.

From the theory they derive a training-free pipeline to extract DNA at scale. Across hundreds of models, DNA matched prior findings on small subsets and revealed relationships no one had documented. A phylogenetic tree built from DNA tracks the shift to decoder-only designs and clock-like differences in family speeds.
arxiv-2510-00596:
Stephan Heinemann, Zhi-Chao Liang, and Laurent Gizon published this 2025 solar physics paper tracing a giant swirling mode in the Sun's magnetic skin. Doppler measurements had revealed a slow global oscillation near the poles, an inertial mode with a single wave around the Sun. The authors hunted its fingerprint in long magnetogram records from two instrument networks. Spectral analysis found magnetic wiggles at exactly the mode's known rhythm.

The signal sits between sixty-five and seventy degrees latitude in both hemispheres. Its pattern is mostly symmetric across the equator, as theory would suggest. Peak amplitudes reach only about a fifth of a gauss, a whisper against the Sun's stronger fields. Simple models reproduce the pattern by letting the mode's horizontal flow drag the radial field around. The detection confirms the mode stirs the magnetic field, not just the plasma motion.
arxiv-2510-00696:
Tarhouni, Al-Zubi, and Alouini test machine learning for predicting radio signal path loss in this 2025 arXiv paper on wireless communications. Path loss measures how much a signal weakens between transmitter and receiver, and planners need it to design networks and place antennas. Classic propagation formulas are rigid and often inaccurate in real terrain. The authors focus on the sub-6 gigahertz band around a suburban university campus in Saudi Arabia.

They generated training data with ray-tracing simulation and checked the models against both simulated and measured datasets. Random forest and k-nearest neighbours gave the best accuracy among the algorithms tried. All the learning-based models beat traditional formulas such as COST-231 Hata, Longley-Rice, and the close-in model. The authors present ray-tracing plus machine learning as a flexible, low-cost planning tool.
arxiv-2510-00996:
Xu, Tiulpin, and Blaschko rework classifier-free guidance for autoregressive image models in this 2025 arXiv paper on generative modelling. Autoregressive models build images token by token, and classifier-free guidance normally steers only the first token. That creates two failures: the guidance gap fades as decoding proceeds, and strong guidance distorts the picture's coherence. Their method, SoftCFG, spreads soft, uncertainty-weighted perturbations across every token instead.

Each generated token contributes guidance in proportion to the model's certainty about it, so the signal persists through long sequences. A step normalization rule bounds the cumulative perturbation, which keeps late tokens from drifting. The method needs no training and drops into existing pipelines unchanged. On ImageNet at 256 by 256 resolution it set a state-of-the-art FID score among autoregressive models. Qualitatively, it removed artifacts such as mangled motorcycles and phantom extra hands.
arxiv-2510-01296:
McMillian, Banerjee, and Bueno-Orovio review how deep learning rebuilds three-dimensional anatomy from flat magnetic resonance scans. Clinicians think in volumes, but scanners and time often deliver only slices. Four families of methods, point clouds, meshes, shape-aware models, and volumetric models, compete to bridge the gap.

The survey compares foundations, limits, and performance across heart, brain, and lung imaging. Diseased anatomy, where training data thins out, receives special attention. Public datasets, compute demands, and evaluation metrics are cataloged for practitioners. Multimodal and cross-modality designs mark the frontier the review points toward. Convolutional, adversarial, and diffusion architectures all appear in the surveyed methods. Representation choice drives design, performance, and clinical usefulness together. Shape priors grow more important as the field matures. Pathological cases remain the generalization bottleneck for most approaches. A structured map helps newcomers choose methods wisely the first time.
arxiv-2510-01496:
Fabiano weakens the most famous condition in fixed-point theory by requiring contraction only on average along a path, not at every single step. Banach's principle guarantees a unique resting point for maps that shrink all distances. Many real maps shrink distances eventually while misbehaving locally, escaping the classical theorem.

His path-averaged contractions average iterated distances to judge shrinkage over the long run. Every continuous such map on a complete space still has exactly one fixed point. Picard iteration converges to it as in the classical case. Examples prove the class genuinely differs from the Kannan, Chatterjea, and related families. Long-term contractive behavior is what the averaging condition captures. A comparison table separates the new class from its cousins. Multivalued mappings and common fixed points await future work. Generalizing Banach is a long and honorable tradition. Fixed points anchor equilibrium analysis everywhere.
arxiv-2510-01596:
Tan and co-authors test whether gripping a quantum thermometer harder actually makes it read temperature better. A single qubit probe sits in an environment with memory, where the usual simplifying approximations fail. Exact simulation methods track the probe's signal quality across coupling strengths and temperatures.

Strong coupling disappointed in the moving, non-equilibrium regime, where weak coupling read best. Only at ultra-low steady temperatures did the strong grip help, and modest cold favored weak coupling again. A hybrid optimizer then tuned control settings for each regime. Thermometer design must match grip strength to the temperature range, not maximize it. Memory in the bath means yesterday's interaction still shapes today's reading. Signal-to-noise ratio for temperature is the scoreboard throughout. Particle swarm search, quantum-enhanced, handled the control tuning. Born-Markov shortcuts would have hidden exactly these reversals. Precision is regime-dependent, not monotonic at all.
arxiv-2510-01696:
Hashemi and Nakatsukasa settle a long-open question about a famous matrix shortcut in this 2025 paper. The Sherman-Morrison formula updates the solution of a linear system after a rank-one change to the matrix. Engineers and scientists use it widely because it is simple and fast. Whether it stays numerically stable in floating-point arithmetic had stayed unclear since the 1940s.

The authors show the plain formula can indeed be backward unstable in a common computing scenario. They also answer a question posed by Nick Higham about how the error bound scales. Their fix adds fixed-precision iterative refinement on top of the formula, reusing the factorizations already computed. Under mild assumptions, the refined method provably restores backward stability without losing the formula's speed. In every numerical experiment the team ran, the refined version eventually produced a backward stable answer.
arxiv-2510-01796:
Chen, Lee, Liao, and Shiu question a default shape choice in neural network design in this 2025 paper. A multi-layer perceptron block usually runs narrow at its edges and wide in the middle. Skip connections then operate at the small input and output sizes. The authors flip that pattern into what they call an Hourglass block.

In an Hourglass block, skip connections live at the expanded width instead. The residual computation squeezes through a narrow bottleneck in the middle. A fixed random projection lifts inputs to the wide space and never needs training. The team compared both shapes on generative tasks over popular image datasets. Hourglass designs reached better performance-versus-size trade-offs at every budget they tested. As budgets grew, the best Hourglass models went deeper, with wider skips and narrower bottlenecks. The authors suggest rethinking skip placement in transformers and other residual networks too.
arxiv-2510-02096:
Falk and four co-authors learn representations of neural networks straight from public model hubs in this 2025 paper. Weight space learning treats trained weights as a data type worth embedding. Progress was bottlenecked by model zoos, small curated collections trained at great expense for research. Public hubs like Hugging Face hold vastly more models, but they are messy and undocumented.

The authors design a backbone that tolerates that heterogeneity across architectures and datasets. Trained on downloaded hub models, its representations performed strongly on weight space tasks. They often beat backbones trained on laboratory-built zoos. The diversity of the hub data also carried a bonus: the representations generalized to data modalities never seen in training. The work drops the zoo requirement entirely. Weight space learning can now scale with the public model ecosystem itself. That shift makes the field's data problem look much more tractable.
arxiv-2510-02296:
Liao and co-authors personalize image generators one concept at a time without erasing earlier lessons. Their 2025 machine learning paper presents Concept Neuron Selection, called CNS. People often teach a generator a pet, a face, or a product. Later lessons usually overwrite earlier ones. That failure is known as catastrophic forgetting. CNS finds the small set of neurons tied to each new concept. It fine-tunes only those neurons. It also protects neurons used by concepts learned before.

Tests on real datasets covered single and multiple concepts. CNS reached state-of-the-art quality with tiny parameter changes. The model kept its general text-to-image skill throughout. Older methods stored a separate adapter for every concept. CNS stores only small neuron masks instead. Memory and processing costs drop sharply. Personal galleries can grow without retraining from scratch.
arxiv-2510-02396:
Mirgalooyebayat and Didehvar compute the travel route least likely to infect a commuter. Their 2025 applied mathematics paper models pandemic travel risk. They define a problem called the Least Infection Probability Path. A route is scored by its total transmission risk. Risk grows with crowding, carrier chance, and exposure time. Ventilation, activity level, and personal distance also count. Five transport modes enter the model, from walking to cars. The team applied the model to Tehran transit data. Local routing apps supplied the network details.

One peak hour trip anchored the case study. A mixed walking, subway, and rapid bus route proved safest. It beat car and bus routes by a wide margin. Optimized routing cut infection risk by about fifteen percent. The framework scales to cities with millions of residents. Pandemic planning gains a concrete routing tool.
arxiv-2510-02596:
Bakels, van de Ruit, and Jafarian fit simple linear models to brain activity during a passive wrist task. Their 2025 neuroscience paper uses EEG recordings with a known input. Volunteers sat still while a device wiggled their wrists. The wrist motion followed a rich multisine pattern. That motion served as a measured input to the brain. Subspace identification then learned a linear state space model. One algorithm, PO-MOESP, produced the most accurate model. The model lives in a latent space behind the scalp signals. Linear maps connect that space to neural source regions.

Seven participants supplied verification and validation data. The latent model represented their EEG measurements accurately. Source space findings matched earlier studies of the same task. Linear models stay interpretable where black boxes fail. Brain monitoring tools need models clinicians can read. Richer tasks and better source maps come next.
arxiv-2510-03096:
Azizpour, Navarro, and Segarra teach graph networks to drop useless input features. Each node in a graph may carry many measured traits. Some traits help the task, and others only add noise. Classic importance scores struggle with tangled graph links. Their method tests features while training is still under way. It shuffles one feature's values and watches validation scores. A drop in score marks that feature as load-bearing.

Features that fail the test are cut, one round at a time. The method tracks how each trait's worth shifts as cuts proceed. It works with any graph architecture and any task. Theory ties the test soundly to how such networks use data. Trials confirmed the scores find what truly matters. Flexibility held across harder graph settings as well. Only node classification was shown in full, the authors note. Link prediction and whole-graph tasks are natural next steps.
arxiv-2510-03196:
Caputo and Cavallucci characterize snowflake spaces purely through rectifiability. A snowflake raises all distances in a space to a fractional power. Such spaces matter for embedding problems in fractal geometry. Tyson and Wu characterized snowflake-like spaces years ago. Their result demanded compactness, doubling, and an embedding. This paper strips all three assumptions away. The characterization now holds for every metric space. Ultralimits take the place of weak tangents in the tests.

A space is snowflake-like exactly when its ultralimits behave. Every ultralimit must lack nontrivial metric one-currents. Pure one-unrectifiability of every ultralimit says the same thing. Rectifiable curves, in short, are what snowflakes cannot hide. The proof leans on the authors' general structure theorem. Embedding theory gains a criterion with no side conditions. Analysts can now test wild, noncompact spaces for snowflake nature. The result ties metric geometry to geometric measure theory tightly.
arxiv-2510-03296:
Arrighi, Costes, and Maignan present a 2025 arXiv paper on graph rewriting, where small local rules reshape a network step by step. Physics treats a process as reversible when nearby snapshots in space and time fix each other fully. Graph rules are picked at random spots, so the classic test for reversibility does not fit. The authors build a stricter space and time version of the test for these systems.

The team gives three ways to define space time reversibility for graph rules. One asks for an inverse rule, one lists three broad conditions, and one builds rules that run cleanly both ways. They prove that all three definitions agree, which is the core result. They also give local checks that are enough to guarantee reversibility. An example even shows time dilation, echoing relativity. The work helps designers build network models that can run backward without losing track of the past.
arxiv-2510-03496:
Murugesan and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on stopping robot arms from hitting people before contact is near. Shared workspaces need robots that predict human motion, not just react to it. Their system reads 3D skeletons from a depth camera and forecasts each joint's path with a neural network. A digital twin of the cell tests the forecast and the planned robot motion in simulation first. Capsule shaped safety fields turn forecasts into risk scores that trigger replanning.

In fifty trials, the method avoided every collision proactively in the study. Clearance stayed above two hundred fifty millimeters around the person in those runs. Replanning finished in under two seconds when risk crossed the line. Twin checking also bridges the lag between sensing and updated plans. Factories could run closer human robot teamwork with fewer stops and far less danger to workers on the floor.
arxiv-2510-03696:
Piskala and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper evaluating chatbots by whether users' goals got fulfilled, rather than scoring replies. A conversation can read turn by turn while the user's request fails. Their framework segments conversations into goals, then judges success across turns tied to each goal. The metric is the Goal Success Rate. A taxonomy, Root Cause of Failure, labels why failed goals went wrong. Teacher language models do the judging, guided by goal definitions and standards from experts.

The team applied the system to AIDA, an employee assistant built as a multi agent system. Its goal success rate climbed from sixty three percent to seventy nine percent over six months of fixes. The taxonomy pointed engineers at the earliest defective turn for each failed goal. Rationales from the teacher models keep the verdicts explainable to the teams. The framework is generic enough to port to other bots.
arxiv-2510-03996:
Njungle, Jahns, and Kinsy present this 2025 arXiv paper with a builder's toolkit for neural networks that run on encrypted data. Cloud machine learning services raise hard questions about who can see sensitive inputs. Homomorphic encryption allows computation without decryption, but earlier tools each supported only narrow model types. The authors offer a configurable framework, FHEON, for privacy-preserving convolutional networks.

FHEON provides optimized encrypted versions of the standard building blocks: convolution, pooling, ReLU activation, and fully connected layers. Developers set channels, kernel size, stride, and padding to assemble arbitrary network designs. The team built five known architectures with it, from LeNet-5 up to ResNet-34. Encrypted accuracy stayed within about a point of the plain models for the tested networks. A LeNet-5 model classified handwritten digits in seconds on a home-grade processor. FHEON makes private inference easier for ordinary developers to build.
arxiv-2510-04096:
Mordo and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on training language models to win search ranking competitions. In competitive search, publishers rewrite documents to climb a search engine's rankings for valuable queries. Language models have made such rewriting cheap. The authors ask whether reinforcement learning can produce stronger competitive agents than prompting alone.

Their framework, RLRF, builds preference datasets from the outcomes of ranking competitions themselves, without human-authored examples. An agent learns to modify content for higher rank while anticipating rival agents' strategies. In experiments, the trained agents consistently and beat previously suggested approaches. They stayed effective under ranking functions they were never trained on. They also adapted when opponents played strategically. The authors flag faithfulness to the original document as a key concern for future work. The study shows ranking ecosystems must now reckon with learning agents, not just static optimization tricks.
arxiv-2510-04196:
Ding and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on training multimodal reasoning models that stay capable and safe at the same time. Combining images with text opens jailbreak routes that text-only guardrails miss. Safety fine-tuning applied afterward usually taxes reasoning ability or causes over-refusal of harmless requests. The authors instead mix reinforcement learning signals across modalities, tasks, and objectives inside one pipeline.

Their framework, CoSMo-RL, trains the model CoSMo-R1 with safety and capability rewarded jointly. Mixed objectives are meant to prevent the policy drift that single-objective training produces. Experiments showed improved safety alongside maintained or improved multimodal reasoning and instruction following. The model resisted multimodal jailbreaks better and refused benign inputs less often. A unified training path, the authors argue, beats bolting safety on after capability is built. That ordering question matters for every lab shipping reasoning models.
arxiv-2510-04396:
Bastian Jäckl and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on how screen layout affects visual search. Modern video search tools rank images for a text query, but a person still scans the grid by hand. The team asked which layout of thumbnail images helps people find one known target fastest. They tested seven layouts with 49 volunteers on a known item search task.

Across more than seventeen hundred tasks, layout changed both speed and accuracy in clear ways. Grouping frames by their source video gave the lowest average search time. A four column grid that kept the rank order gave the best accuracy and the fewest missed targets. Sorted grids let users scan dull areas fast, but they pushed good targets to weak spots and raised misses. The authors suggest mixed designs that keep top results in place and sort the rest.
arxiv-2510-04896:
Gabriele Giacometti, Daniele Rizzo, and Dario Zappalà wrote this 2025 physics paper testing whether a shortcut flow equation keeps the universal truths of field theory. Renormalization group flows track how a theory changes with the scale of observation. The proper time flow is a cousin of the functional flow, with limits. Universal numbers, like the coefficients that govern how couplings run, must come out right. The authors check the flow against those numbers.

For a scalar theory, they derive the running of the quartic coupling at one and two loops. The anomalous dimension of the field also matches expectations. For Yang Mills theory they use the background field method. The gauge coupling running comes out through two loops. No term that would break gauge symmetry sneaks into the result. The verdict: the shortcut keeps the universal content of renormalization. That reliability supports its use from statistical models to gravity studies.
arxiv-2510-05096:
Zeyu Zhu, Kevin Qinghong Lin, and Mike Zheng Shou automate a tedious chore of academic life in this 2025 arXiv paper. Turning a research paper into a short presentation video takes hours of slide design, recording, and editing. The video must align slides, subtitles, speech, and a talking presenter. Dense figures and tables make the job harder.

The team first built Paper2Video, a benchmark of 101 papers with author-made videos and slides. Four new metrics judge how faithfully videos convey a paper's content. Their system, PaperTalker, then generates such videos with a team of agents. It refines slide layouts with a tree-search choice method and renders speech and a talking head. Its videos beat existing baselines and cut production time about sixfold.
arxiv-2510-05196:
Daqian Shi and seven co-authors track a population's shifting needs during health emergencies in this 2025 arXiv paper. Officials face huge streams of mixed data with little time to read them. Structured demographics arrive beside free-text feedback from surveys and helplines. Manual expert review is accurate but far too slow.

Their framework fuses the two data kinds into a need-aware graph. A language model reasons over the graph, which is keyed by age, gender, and deprivation levels. The system links feedback to a behavior-science ontology and visualizes subgroup trajectories over time. In their case study, concerns moved from acute infection anxiety toward longer-term mental-health and economic worries. Women reported mental-health support needs more strongly than other groups. The approach suits resource-constrained public health teams.
arxiv-2510-05296:
Zahra Maleki and three co-authors improve camera-based heart monitoring by finding the right skin in this 2025 arXiv paper. Remote photoplethysmography reads pulse signals from subtle skin color changes on video. Picking the wrong pixels ruins the signal, especially when people talk or turn their heads. Existing unsupervised pipelines often grab hair, eyes, or mouth regions by mistake.

Their method, SkinMap, segments skin across the whole body and weights the best regions. It excludes interfering areas while staying robust to movement. The team also releases a new dataset, SYNC-rPPG, with realistic challenging conditions. SkinMap kept heart-rate errors low during talking and head rotation, where rival methods failed. It also detected a diverse range of skin tones accurately. The results support dependable contactless monitoring outside tidy lab settings.
arxiv-2510-05396:
Nilesh Gupta and five co-authors make language-model ranking scale to hundreds of documents in this 2025 arXiv paper. In-context ranking puts the query and all candidates into one prompt. Attention costs then grow quadratically with the list size. The authors look for structure inside the attention of models fine-tuned for this task.

They found attention is dense inside each document block but sparse between blocks. Certain query tokens in middle layers also flag each document's true relevance. BlockRank enforces the block sparsity architecturally, cutting attention to linear cost. A contrastive loss sharpens the query-to-document relevance signal during fine-tuning. On MSMarco, BEIR, and NQ, it matched top listwise rankers while running about 4.7 times faster on 100 documents.
arxiv-2510-05496:
Wadayama presents a numerical method for measuring how much information survives a noisy channel. Mutual information is the key quantity, since it caps how well coded messages can perform. When the channel bends signals through a nonlinear stage, that quantity becomes hard to compute. His 2025 paper builds a bridge from a learnable score function to the answer.

The method learns the score of the channel output by denoising score matching. A classic identity then turns that score into Fisher information along the noise path. Adding that information over noise levels yields the mutual information estimate. Only forward simulation of the channel is needed, never the hard reverse probabilities. Tests check the method against exact solutions and a density-based rival. The estimates stayed accurate across many input patterns and channel shapes. The paper also gives theory and practical guidance for using the bridge.
arxiv-2510-05596:
Zhao and colleagues survey self-evolving agentic AI for wireless networks. Static AI models cannot keep pace with fast-changing radio environments. Self-evolving agents instead update their models, tools, and workflows on their own. Their 2025 paper lays out the concepts, architecture, and open directions.

The authors describe a layered architecture with an autonomous evolution life cycle. Key techniques include tool intelligence, workflow optimization, self-reflection, and evolutionary learning. They also propose a cooperative multi-agent framework with role-specialized language models. A supervisor agent coordinates structured dialogue, feedback, and validation. A case study evolves antenna optimization for low-altitude networks. The framework upgrades fixed antenna tuning into movable antenna optimization autonomously. The system restored degraded beam performance by up to about fifty-two percent. It runs the full cycle from data collection to monitoring without humans. Such autonomy suits next-generation networks that reconfigure constantly.
arxiv-2510-05796:
Baêta classifies valuations defined on convex functions of one variable. A valuation adds over unions and intersections, like volume or surface area for bodies. Classifications in the spirit of Hadwiger's theorem organize whole families at once. Her 2025 paper treats convex Lipschitz functions on the line with compact domain.

The valuations are upper semicontinuous in the natural topology. They are also invariant under translations of the function. A dual epi-translation invariance constrains their behavior under epigraph shifts. Baêta establishes the complete classification under those combined assumptions. Intrinsic volumes on convex bodies are the classical prototype of the theory. Ludwig's school extended Hadwiger-type results to functions in recent decades. Such theorems reduce wild functional spaces to a few building blocks. One variable keeps the classification fully explicit and checkable. Integral geometry supplies many of the motivating applications for valuations.
arxiv-2510-06096:
Bou and four co-authors from Imperial College London and Amazon AGI present a way to audit what a chatbot optimizes in a 2025 paper. Inverse reinforcement learning can infer a model's hidden reward from its behavior. Older methods return one overconfident estimate, and many different rewards can explain the same behavior.

The framework uses Bayesian inverse learning, so it recovers a distribution over objectives instead of a single answer. Auditors can watch it shrink as evidence accumulates, which measures how ambiguity falls. Uncertainty-aware diagnostics flag spurious shortcuts and prompts where the inferred objective should not be trusted. The team showed that a refined, low-uncertainty reward can drive retraining with toxicity cuts matching the original alignment process. Their audit of a detoxified model produced a calibrated, readable objective. The toolkit targets safety teams and regulators verifying model goals.
arxiv-2510-06196:
Faleo and eight co-authors push unfiltered photons toward perfect spectral purity. Photonic quantum technologies need truly indistinguishable photons that interfere cleanly. Down-conversion sources reach high visibility with moderate filtering, but filtering throws photons away.

The team optimized telecom sources by combining two shaping tricks. Gaussian quasi-phase-matching engineers the crystal's nonlinear response, and Gaussian shaping sculpts the pump spectrum. With no spectral filtering at all, they measured the photons by time-of-flight spectrometry. The spectral purity upper bound exceeded ninety-nine point nine percent. Two-photon interference between independent sources reached visibilities near ninety-eight and a half percent. Such numbers rival filtered sources while keeping every photon. For quantum networks on telecom fiber, bright pure unfiltered sources remove an efficiency bottleneck. The recipe simplifies source design, since purity comes from shaping rather than lossy cleanup optics.
arxiv-2510-06596:
Ayush Zenith, Arnold Zumbrun, Neel Raut, and Jing Lin tackle a data problem in computer vision. Their 2025 paper concerns object detection, where models learn to find items in images. Good training sets are scarce and costly to label by hand. Synthetic images from simulations can help, but only if their quality is high.

The team introduces SDQM, a metric that grades synthetic datasets without full model training. It combines sub-scores for coverage, diversity, similarity to real data, and interpretability. In their experiments, SDQM scores tracked the detection accuracy of YOLOv11 closely. Older metrics showed only moderate or weak links to that accuracy. The metric also tells builders how to improve a dataset, not just that it is weak. That guidance can cut the costly cycle of training, testing, and regenerating data. Resource-limited teams stand to gain the most from such a shortcut.
arxiv-2510-06696:
Mojtaba Mojtahedi and Borja Sierra Miranda work in mathematical logic, on the logic of provability. Their 2025 paper introduces a new kind of model for modal logic, called provability models. Modal logic reasons about necessity and possibility, and here the key operator reads as provability in a formal system. Classic Kripke models provide the usual semantics for such logics.

Provability models enrich Kripke models by assigning a logic to each individual world. The first author had used them to prove a completeness result for intuitionistic provability logic. The new paper studies several classical systems, including K, K4, S4, GL, and GLP. A striking result concerns the interpretability logic ILM. It turns out to be complete for exactly the same provability models as GL. The authors also build predicative and decidable versions of the models for GL and ILM. Soundness and completeness for GLP round out the picture.
arxiv-2510-06996:
Roch leads the JETSCAPE collaboration in building better starting conditions for simulations of heavy-ion collisions. Their 2025 paper uses the SMASH transport model to set up each collision event. Hydrodynamic simulations then evolve the hot matter created when nuclei smash together. The starting snapshot shapes everything that follows, especially at finite baryon density.

SMASH supplies event-by-event maps of energy, momentum, and three conserved charge currents. Those currents track net baryon number, electric charge, and strangeness through the collision. A lattice-QCD-based equation of state guides the hydrodynamic phase. The transport start yields stronger local fluctuations in charge and strangeness than rival models. Fast hadrons threatened the numerics by smearing charge conservation. A cutoff fix in their liquefier modules doubled the global charge accuracy at top energy. Realistic starts like these sharpen comparisons with collider data.
arxiv-2510-07096:
Zhu Li and four co-authors give speech synthesizers a sense of sarcasm. Their 2025 paper builds a text-to-speech system that can deliver lines with a sarcastic edge. Sarcasm hides in subtle mixes of wording, context, and tone of voice. Speech research has mostly handled broad emotions like joy or anger, leaving sarcasm nearly untouched.

Their system conditions speech generation on two kinds of guidance. A fine-tuned large language model supplies semantic signals that flag sarcastic intent. A retrieval module fetches real examples of sarcastic delivery to guide the prosody. Both signals feed a VITS speech backbone. Tests beat baseline systems on objective measures of quality. Human listeners also rated the output higher. The sarcastic speech sounded more natural and more expressive to them. Synthesized samples even helped separate sarcasm detectors do their job better. Funnier, more humanlike voices could follow for assistants and entertainment.
arxiv-2510-07196:
Adams and Petruccione review a striking overlap between quantum computing and a bold theory of the brain. Their 2025 article begins with a proposal by Bruce Kane from the 1990s. Kane suggested using the spins of phosphorus atoms set in pure silicon as quantum bits. Those spins keep their quantum state for a very long time, but building a working machine from them remains hard. Matthew Fisher later proposed that similar phosphorus spins inside brain molecules might shape thinking itself.

Both rely on long-lived nuclear spins in quiet surroundings. The computing side still struggles with scale and error correction. The cognition side still lacks proof that such spins stay coherent in the brain and affect neurons. The authors argue the fields can teach each other, since biology might inspire new hardware while computing tools might test the brain theory.
arxiv-2510-07496:
Sayanagi repairs power series rings over the badly behaved base rings that classical algebra avoids. The 2025 paper studies bases of Krull dimension zero that may be non-Noetherian. Over such bases, ordinary power series rings can fail to be flat and can even have infinite dimension, breaking theorems that algebraists rely on. The author considers a modified power series construction designed to preserve good behavior. Over the modified ring, dimension stays finite and flatness survives. Properties familiar from the Noetherian world are then re-examined one by one in this wilder setting.

Versions of Krull's height theorem and of unmixedness generalize successfully to the new construction. A summary table for zero-dimensional semilocal bases shows the modified ring matching the Noetherian column on dimension, faithful flatness, and the Cohen-Macaulay property. The ordinary ring over a non-Noetherian base fails those same tests.
arxiv-2510-07596:
Van Cuyck, Bethermin, Lagache, and Beelen forecast how to dissect the carbon monoxide background of the early universe line by line. Their 2025 paper concerns line intensity mapping, which charts total emission from many faint galaxies at once. Rotational lines of carbon monoxide trace cold molecular gas, the raw material of stars, but they also contaminate maps targeting other lines.

The recovered distribution, combined with bias-weighted line intensities, yields the cosmic molecular gas density out to redshift three. A feasibility study targets one transition with an experiment modeled on the CONCERTO instrument. The method turns a foreground nuisance into a measurement: the same CO glow that pollutes other experiments becomes a census of cold gas across cosmic time.
arxiv-2510-07696:
Chen, Kjos-Hanssen, Koswara, Richter, and Stephan wrote this 2025 theoretical computer science paper on automatic complexity. That measure scores a word by the smallest machine that singles it out among words of its length. The authors study a nondeterministic version of the measure. They gather all words whose complexity stays below a fixed fraction of their length. The question is how hard those word collections are to compute.

For every allowed fraction, the collection turns out to be neither context-free nor readable by certain Boolean circuits. The proof also settles an open question about the one-third case in circuit terms. Along the way, the authors prove a Shannon effect for their complexity measure. Such results draw lines around word patterns. Even words cheap to describe can form languages beyond basic machines. That warning matters for anyone who equates low complexity with easy computation.
arxiv-2510-08296:
D. J. Priour Jr. maps how exposed surfaces behave in piles of randomly placed grains, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Percolation theory studies when clusters first span a whole system. In grain packs, solid clusters connect at one density, while open void networks vanish at a higher density. Priour reads these two thresholds as borders of one surface regime between them.

Between the borders, exposed surfaces either wrap solid clusters like sheaths or line tunnel-like voids. He shows a second-order phase transition flips surfaces from sheaths to tunnels at a middle density. A new geometric method finds these surfaces exactly, with cost growing only linearly in system size. He computed all three thresholds for many grain shapes, including the Platonic solids. For sliced, disordered cubes, the critical porosity at void loss approached five percent.
arxiv-2510-08596:
V. S. Raghu Parupudi argues that perplexity unfairly punishes creative text from language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Reference-free metrics like self-perplexity score text by how predictable the model finds it. Creative writing is surprising by design, so fluency-based scores systematically downgrade it. Parupudi proposes a Confidence Score drawn from the model's output probability distribution instead.

Experiments used gpt-4o-mini on ninety-nine creative prompts. Fluency-based metrics preferred the novel response in zero percent of cases, a total shutout. The Confidence Score preferred novel responses nineteen percent of the time, a statistically significant difference. Its confidence interval for the gap ran from 11.1 percent to 27.3 percent, excluding zero comfortably. The score also separated easy, medium, and hard tasks with non-overlapping intervals. Parupudi presents it as a fairer metric for the creative era.
arxiv-2510-08696:
Yunzhen Feng and co-authors rescue the wasted wrong answers in group-based reinforcement learning for language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. GRPO, the standard recipe, samples groups of responses and rewards the correct ones. Groups with no correct response yield zero advantage and no gradient, wasting substantial compute. The team asks whether these negative groups can teach without extra supervision at all.

Starting from a maximum-likelihood view of reward modeling, they derive an equivalent policy gradient with a modified value function. That value adds a penalty on incorrect responses, weighted by confidence, punishing confident mistakes most. Their method, LENS, gives incorrect generations nonzero, confidence-dependent rewards inside GRPO. With Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-3B on the MATH benchmark, LENS consistently beat the GRPO baseline. Gains were significant on harder problems, where negative groups are most common.
arxiv-2510-09396:
Sajad Khatiri and four co-authors report bringing a research testing tool into industry in a 2025 arXiv paper. The tool, Surrealist, generates test scenarios in simulation and was first built for drones. The team adapted it to the ANYmal quadruped robot, a four-legged machine used for industrial inspection, where safe navigation around obstacles is essential.

A search-based algorithm invents hard obstacle-avoidance cases that manual testing often misses. In a pilot phase, the generated tests exposed one route-planning algorithm with a success rate near forty percent and benchmarked a stronger one near seventy-one percent. The tool then joined the ANYbotics workflow for six months and tested five in-house algorithms. A formal survey of the engineers confirmed its value for finding critical failures, benchmarking fairly, and strengthening the wider testing process.
arxiv-2510-09996:
Qu and co-authors release BurstDeflicker in this 2025 arXiv paper on image restoration. Flicker artifacts mar short-exposure photos taken under alternating current lighting. Rolling shutter cameras expose a sensor row by row, while AC lights pulse in brightness, so the two rhythms clash.

The clash prints dark bands across the image, a non-uniform brightness pattern that ruins otherwise good shots. BurstDeflicker is a benchmark set of data for removing flicker in dynamic scenes, where the subject moves between frames. Motion makes the fix harder, since methods cannot simply average the burst of shots. The dataset lets researchers compare deflickering methods on shared, realistic cases and measure how well each restores even brightness.
arxiv-2510-10696:
Tomáš Grabec and seven co-authors present a new way to visualize how sound waves spread across a material's surface, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Surface ultrasonic waves reveal a material's elastic behavior. That response is captured by a Green's function, which depends on direction and frequency. The team gives the first direct experimental visualization of this function in the frequency domain, including the fine detail caused by elastic anisotropy, where stiffness varies with direction.

Their method builds on transient grating spectroscopy, a laser technique usually used to measure surface acoustic waves. By focusing on very early time signals, they catch ultra-transient oscillations that live far shorter than the usual standing wave patterns. The diffraction from these short lived gratings maps the surface response in exceptional detail, and the maps strikingly reproduce the theoretical Green's functions. They name the technique ultra-transient grating spectroscopy, for contactless study of anisotropic solids.
arxiv-2510-10996:
Ethan Abraham, Junghyun Yoon, Troy Van Voorhis, and Martin Z Bazant revise a cornerstone quantity of electron transfer theory, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Marcus theory predicts reaction rates for electrons hopping between molecules, and its reorganization energy is normally treated as a classical quantity. The team shows the parameter that actually appears in the activation barrier is a quantum mechanical object. It depends on the electronic coupling between the two sides, and it matches the classical Marcus picture only when that coupling vanishes.

This reframing unifies the description of activation barriers across the adiabatic and non adiabatic regimes, which are usually treated separately. The authors put the insight to work by deriving a closed form expression for the curvature of the current overpotential relation in reactions limited by electron transfer at an electrode. The formula now formally covers both inner sphere and outer sphere processes, the two standard reaction classes.
arxiv-2510-11196:
Medical vision-language models explain their answers in fluent chains of thought, but a plausible explanation may not reflect how the model actually decided. Johannes Moll and co-authors test that faithfulness problem in this 2025 arXiv paper on chest X-ray question answering. Their framework perturbs both the text and the image in controlled ways and scores explanations on clinical fidelity, causal attribution, and confidence calibration.

A reader study with radiologists showed the evaluator scores track human judgment within the range of agreement between radiologists themselves. Benchmarking six models, the team found that answer accuracy and explanation quality are decoupled, and that acknowledging an injected cue does not ensure the explanation is grounded in it. Text cues shifted explanations more than visual cues did. Proprietary models scored much higher on attribution than open-source ones, which the authors flag as a deployment risk.
arxiv-2510-11296:
Vision-language models adapted to a new task meet two kinds of unfamiliar data: known classes in new styles, and entirely new classes they must flag as unknown. Lin Zhu and co-authors tackle both problems together in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Their starting observation is that re-aligning the vision and language parts of a model produces a substantial change in an energy score for known-class data.

Their score, called Delta Energy, measures that change and proved more reliable for detecting out-of-distribution inputs than the standard energy score. A training objective that maximizes a lower bound on the score improves generalization to style-shifted data, and the authors prove it yields a domain-consistent curvature property linked to generalization. A unified fine-tuning framework built on these ideas beat recent approaches by 10 to 25 percent in detection quality across benchmarks for both goals.
arxiv-2510-11396:
Waste-to-energy plants must keep burning when the stream of municipal waste swings unpredictably in quantity and composition. Achraf Bouhmady and Othman Cherkaoui Dekkaki state that safety problem in mathematical form in this 2025 arXiv control theory paper. They model safe operation as a robust viability problem: a zero-sum game between the plant's control policy and a hostile disturbance representing the uncertain inflows.

Within a Hamilton-Jacobi framework, the viability kernel, the set of states from which safe operation can be maintained, becomes the zero sublevel set of a value function solving a constrained Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. The authors approximate that kernel on a computer with a Local Lax-Friedrichs scheme. Their experiments show that increasing inflow uncertainty clearly shrinks the viability domain, narrowing the safe operating envelope. The method stays tractable for moderate-dimensional systems and offers a basis for building control policies for plant design.
arxiv-2510-11496:
Phone-grade multimodal AI must fit in a few gigabytes of memory and run on battery power, while cloud models with hundreds of billions of parameters set the quality bar. The AndesVL Team at the OPPO AI Center presents a family of mobile multimodal language models in this 2025 arXiv technical report. The suite spans 0.6 to 4 billion parameters, built on Qwen3 language models with visual encoders.

The report details the architectures, training pipeline, and data, claiming first-tier results among similar-scale models across reasoning, visual question answering, multilingual, and interface benchmarks. For deployment, a 1+N LoRA design and a quantization-aware fine-tuning framework ease task adaptation and compression. Their OKV cache eviction algorithm, with speculative decoding and compression, reached a 6.7 times decoding speedup and up to 30.9 percent memory reduction running the largest model on a MediaTek Dimensity 9500 chip, and models are released.
arxiv-2510-11696:
Wei Huang and a large team from NVIDIA, MIT, and partner universities present QeRL, a cheaper way to train large language models with reinforcement learning. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses a practical bottleneck: such training eats GPU memory and spends long stretches generating trial answers, called rollouts. QeRL shrinks the model with a four-bit number format and trains only small added adapter layers.

The surprise finding is that the noise introduced by shrinking the numbers actually helps, because it makes the model's choices less predictable and encourages broader exploration. A control mechanism adjusts that noise during training. QeRL sped up rollouts by more than half and enabled training of a thirty-two-billion-parameter model on a single high-end GPU for the first time. It also reached higher accuracy than rival low-cost methods on math benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-11896:
Miguel Cárdenas, Alejandro Nettle, and Leandro Núñez revisit the mathematics of the Z pinch, a fusion device where a huge electric current squeezes plasma with its own magnetic field. The snowplow model simplifies the plasma into an infinitely thin cylindrical shell. That shell acts like a piston, sweeping inward and compressing the gas. Their 2025 arXiv paper gives this venerable model a fresh variational treatment.

The authors write down the Lagrangian of the snowplow system, the energy bookkeeping from which motion follows. Applying the Euler-Lagrange machinery then produces the model's equations of motion in a clean form. Next they set a quantitative criterion for judging how well a Z pinch device performs, an operating point measure. Finally, they apply the criterion to one specific Z pinch system as a worked example.
arxiv-2510-11996:
Tanner W. Muturi leads a student team teaching AI to reason about space in cluttered warehouses. Vision-language models falter in such scenes: boxes hide boxes, and questions demand precise distances and relations. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a framework around the Physical AI Spatial Intelligence Warehouse dataset from the 2025 AI City Challenge. The core trick is telling the model where things are, in words.

The team embeds each object's mask dimensions as bounding box coordinates directly inside the prompt. The model thus reasons over explicit geometry instead of guessing from appearance. They fine-tuned the system separately for four question types: distance estimation, counting, multiple-choice grounding, and spatial relation inference. Answer formatting was also aligned with the grader by appending normalized answers during training. The pipeline scored about seventy-three points and placed fourth on the public leaderboard. Structured prompts are a cheap substitute for spatial common sense.
arxiv-2510-12096:
Guozheng Ma and six co-authors rethink sparse training as a scalpel rather than a hammer for deep reinforcement learning. Bigger networks, machine learning's pet trick, often backfire in reinforcement learning, where plasticity loss spoils training. Dynamic sparse training, rewiring links during learning, helps, but prior studies applied it the same way everywhere. This 2025 arXiv paper studies module by module and design by design.

The findings reorder what matters most. Encoders, critics, and actors follow distinct learning habits, and dynamic training helps each its own way. Design improvements, not sparsity tricks, provide the base for scaling up; dynamic strategies then add module-specific gains on top. Comparing the three sparsity regimes fills another gap. The authors distill it all into Module-Specific Training, a practical system that pairs each module with its best regime. It delivers large scaling gains across diverse algorithms without changing them.
arxiv-2510-12196:
Samoldekin and co-authors present two graphics processor based algorithms for process mapping, a 2025 arXiv paper in computer science. Process mapping assigns the tasks in a graph to the processors of a supercomputer so that work stays balanced and communication stays low. The authors aim to bring the recent success of graphics based graph partitioning to this older optimization problem.

The first method uses hierarchical multisection, splitting the task graph along the hierarchy of the machine itself. The second method builds mapping directly into the multilevel partitioning pipeline, speeding up coarsening and refinement steps. In experiments both methods ran more than three hundred times faster than leading processor based tools. The first kept communication costs only about ten percent higher on average, while the second traded some solution quality for even larger speed gains.
arxiv-2510-12396:
The CMS Collaboration searches for dark matter produced alongside bottom quarks and a pair of leptons, in proton proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, in a 2025 arXiv particle physics paper. The target scenario extends the Standard Model with two Higgs doublets plus a pseudoscalar particle that mediates interactions with dark matter. In this model a heavy neutral Higgs boson can decay into a Z boson and the pseudoscalar.

The analysis uses multivariate techniques covering a wide range of masses for the new particles. Observations matched the expectations from known Standard Model processes, so no dark matter signal appeared. The team set upper limits at ninety five percent confidence on the production rate times branching fraction across the heavy Higgs mass range. They also derived constraints on the benchmark model's parameter space and compared them with cosmological expectations, narrowing where such a mediator could still hide.
arxiv-2510-12796:
