Li and co-authors present DriveVLA-W0 in this 2025 arXiv paper, a training scheme for self-driving models that see, read, and act. Such vision-language-action models learn from recorded actions, but those actions are sparse, low-dimensional signals, meaning few numbers per scene, so much of the model's capacity goes undertrained. The authors call this gap a supervision deficit.

Their fix adds world modeling, where the model must also predict future images, which forces it to learn how driving scenes evolve. They built versions for two model families, one using discrete image tokens and one using continuous features, and added a lightweight action expert to keep responses fast. On the NAVSIM benchmark and a much larger in-house dataset, the approach beat earlier baselines, and its advantage grew faster as training data increased.
arxiv-2510-13196:
Desai, Cervantes, and Banerjee simulate a fire plume rising through a plant canopy in this 2025 arXiv paper, a Lawrence Livermore laboratory study. Buoyant plumes from wildland fires interact with vegetation in ways that open grassland models miss, and understanding the turbulence matters for predicting smoke and fire behavior. The authors use large-eddy simulation, which resolves big turbulent motions directly.

With a crosswind blowing, the plume's windward edge gained vorticity while hairpin-shaped vortices tilted along its leeward side, and strong counter-rotating vortex pairs formed as flow spiraled in. A no-canopy comparison showed the canopy's drag made the plume tilt less steeply near the source, delayed its bend-over transition downstream, and damped its far-field wandering. Momentum transfer patterns also differed sharply, with ejections above the canopy and sweeps inside it dominating upstream, and counter-gradient motions dominating on the leeward side.
arxiv-2510-13796:
Wu and co-authors trace where and how symbol grounding emerges inside language models, using causal, mechanistic analysis. Their 2025 arXiv paper revisits Harnad's classic problem: how do words gain meaning from world experience? Recent hints suggested grounding might appear in large models trained without any grounding objective. Where in the network it lives, and what computes it, stayed unknown.

Their controlled framework probes internal computations while models link language to environmental signals. Grounding concentrates in the middle layers of the network, they find. A specific aggregate mechanism does the work: attention heads pool the environmental ground to support word predictions. The pattern repeats in multimodal dialogue and across very different architectures. Both transformers and state-space models show it, while simple recurrent networks do not. The results give practical leads for predicting and steering generation reliability.
arxiv-2510-13896:
Yu and co-authors segment cellular images with a training-free team of AI agents that routes each image to a specialist tool. Their 2025 arXiv paper, GenCellAgent, tackles microscopy segmentation across varying imaging conditions. Specialist models excel narrowly and degrade when microscopes or stains change. Retraining for each lab's setup is slow and annotation-hungry.

A planner-executor-evaluator loop drives the system: choose a tool, run it, then quality-check the result. Long-term memory stores corrections, letting it personalize and self-improve. When conditions drift from a tool's comfort zone, a few reference images adapt it on the fly. Text guidance can segment organelles no existing model covers. Across four benchmarks, routing delivered a mean accuracy gain of 15.7 percent over leading baselines in the reported tests, with organelle scores on new data improving far more, the authors report. Human touch-ups compound the gains through memory.
arxiv-2510-13996:
Lukas Gienapp and co-authors introduce the German Commons, the largest openly licensed collection of German text assembled for training language models, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most training corpora contain text whose licensing is unclear, which blocks truly open models, and the scarcity is worse outside English, where openly licensed material is critically rare.

The team compiled forty-one sources across seven domains, including legal, scientific, cultural, political, news, economic, and web text, all from established providers with verifiable licenses. Cleaning, quality filtering, deduplication, and formatting repairs produced more than one hundred fifty-four billion tokens, each domain licensed at least as openly as CC-BY-SA 4.0, a standard share-alike license. That makes the corpus legally safe for training and redistribution. The authors also release their construction and filtering code, tailored to German text, so the collection can be reproduced and extended.
arxiv-2510-14196:
Anne Kroo and Olav Solgaard introduce a corner-cube reflector that turns optical sensors into remotely readable devices, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Corner cubes return light back to its source. The authors' version encodes a sensor's state into the diffraction pattern of that returned beam, so a reader can measure the sensor without wires or batteries at the sensing point.

Inside the reflector, a reference path and its sensor-modulated partner interfere. They produce an interferometric signal. Phase and amplitude changes can be read from it with a square-law camera over an optical link. Because the readout is optical and the node is passive, the sensor's orientation does not matter, removing an obstacle to deploying coherent interferometric sensing in the field. The authors present the design as a route to scalable, chemically and physically inert sensor nodes for sensing chemical, biological, and physical quantities.
arxiv-2510-14296:
Md Mahadi Hasan Nahid and co-authors rethink schema linking, the step in text-to-SQL systems that matches a question to the tables and columns of a database, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most research improves the SQL generation step and neglects retrieval of schema, even though missing or wrong schema elements cause hallucinations and failed queries.

Their framework retrieves schema in both directions: table-first, choosing tables then their columns, and column-first, choosing columns then their tables, augmented with question decomposition, keyword extraction, and keyphrase extraction. On the BIRD and Spider benchmarks, the method improved schema recall while cutting false positives. SQL generated from the retrieved schema beat full-schema baselines and approached oracle performance without query refinement, closing half the gap between using the full schema and using the perfect one. The authors argue schema linking is a lever for text-to-SQL accuracy.
arxiv-2510-14596:
Markoff and Galaktionovs return, in a 2025 arXiv paper, to the flood of images from camera traps used in wildlife monitoring. Classifiers can only name species they were trained on. Many trap datasets contain animals no classifier knows, so the images sit unlabeled. The authors test whether self-supervised vision models can sort such images with no species training at all, an approach called zero-shot.

They compared clustering methods across three image models, combined with ways of compressing the image features. They also tested a continuous similarity ordering, which lines images up so neighbors look alike. On a five-species test set, one pairing reached 88.6 percent accuracy in the reported runs, and the one-dimensional sorting kept mammals and birds in coherent order across fifteen hundred images. The team deployed similarity ordering in their production platform, where it speeds up browsing and hand labeling for biodiversity work.
arxiv-2510-14896:
Mumcu, Jones, Cherian, and Yilmaz propose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a way to spot abnormal events in video that also explains its flags. Semi-supervised detectors learn from normal footage only, but struggle with anomalies built from object interactions, a person leaving a bag, and their alarms come without reasons. Earlier systems that asked a vision-language model to judge whole frames directly inherited the model's blind spots.

This framework asks a multimodal language model about pairs of objects at different moments, collecting text descriptions of each object's activity and interactions. Descriptions from normal training videos define ordinary behavior. At test time, a new video's descriptions are compared with those references, and mismatches signal anomalies. Because the evidence is text, the system can say what looked wrong. Experiments show strong detection of interaction anomalies, and state-of-the-art results even on datasets without interaction anomalies.
arxiv-2510-14996:
This 2025 arXiv paper by Liao is a reply to critics, not a new study. McMullen and colleagues had commented on his 2025 turbulence simulations, which explicitly include random velocity fluctuations. Such simulations, they said, should show a thermal-fluctuation-dominated range known from the literature. His failure to find one, they argued, contradicts other results. The reply disputes that reading of the evidence.

Liao offers a counter-example: direct numerical simulation results in the literature, which implicitly carry random noise, also show no thermal-fluctuation-dominated range, so published work qualitatively agrees with his simulations on this point. He adds a broader warning. Such noise can hugely influence the statistics of chaotic systems, turbulence included, a danger Lorenz pointed out in 2006. Every approach to turbulent flow, he argues, should carefully check how its own noise affects the statistics it reports, before claiming contradiction with anyone.
arxiv-2510-15296:
Yiming Lin and five colleagues tackle image labeling when each training photo carries only one confirmed tag, even though it may deserve several. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in single positive multi-label learning, where missing tags are the core difficulty. Labels also relate to each other in rich ways, as broader classes contain narrower ones and some tags often appear together.

Their framework places each label as a ball in hyperbolic geometry, a curved space well suited to hierarchies, rather than as a plain point. Balls can nest, overlap, or sit apart, matching inclusion, co-occurrence, and independence between labels. A classifier adjusts its strictness with temperature, and a physics-inspired penalty nudges balls toward sensible layouts. On four benchmark datasets the method matched leading rivals and read more clearly, and its learned label layout tracked real co-occurrence patterns closely.
arxiv-2510-15496:
Jade Leathrum computes the dimensional fingerprint of a family of fractal carpets, in this 2025 arXiv paper written at the University of California, Riverside. The shapes start from a square split into a grid, with some cells deleted at each step and the process repeated on what remains. When enough cells vanish in the right places, the result is a dust type carpet, full of holes yet not itself connected.

Leathrum studies these fractals through fractal zeta functions, a tool from the work of Lapidus and co-authors that encodes a shape's oscillations in a set of complex dimensions. She devises an analytic and combinatorial algorithm that computes those complex dimensions for every dust type Sierpiński carpet modification. Knowing the complex dimensions reveals how the fractal's geometry vibrates across scales. The paper extends earlier work she began under advisors Sean Watson and Erin Pearse.
arxiv-2510-15696:
Carlos Gamboa, Alexandre Street, Davi Valladão, and Bernardo Pagnocelli present a method in a 2025 paper. The method serves energy decisions that repeat every few minutes. Conditions keep changing between decisions. Current robust optimisation models train for one set of data. They need full retraining when new data arrives. That is too slow for online scheduling.

The team built a data-driven uncertainty set that uses context. The solution method reuses earlier work instead of starting over. A new variant of a standard algorithm does this. It keeps cuts from earlier runs valid when context changes. The target is two-stage decisions under uncertainty. Power scheduling is one example. Speed and robustness must coexist there.
arxiv-2510-15996:
Ozan K. Tonguz and Federico Taschin propose watching for distribution shift in learning systems with a classic statistical distance. Models fail when live test data drift away from the training distribution, and in safety-critical uses those errors matter greatly. One defence is to measure the drift in real time and react to it.

The pair use the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, the largest gap between two cumulative distributions, as the drift gauge. They show how that single number tracks the damage to an AI agent's performance. In a traffic test with a reinforcement learning agent at one intersection, even a very small distance value accompanies a travel time rise of about half. They hope the test will help smart transportation agents judge their own degradation live and adapt with better information.
arxiv-2510-16096:
Tina Behnia, Puneesh Deora, and Christos Thrampoulidis probe how the mix of training text shapes what a language model learns. Models train on text that blends plain word patterns, which make speech fluent, with facts linking one word to another. The team built a fake training set where each part can be tuned alone. They can vary how often each fact shows up in new settings.

Richer settings slow a model's grip on facts it was trained on. Gains on facts in new settings hinge on how those settings are built. Sometimes rich variety is the only path to any recall. Some setups break fact recall, others break word patterns, and some break both. By swapping model parts, they trace the new-setting failures to the layers that code words in and out. The testbed lets researchers study effects that large real models blur.
arxiv-2510-16196:
Zheng Huang and nine co-authors work on reading pictures back out of brain scans. A scanner called fMRI tracks blood flow as a person views an image, and AI then tries to rebuild that image. The rebuild runs in two stages: map the scan into a code space, then let an image model draw from that code.

The team finds brain signals resemble the text space of a language model more than any image-based space. So their system, PRISM, turns scans into structured text that names objects, traits, and links between them. One module then draws each object on its own and blends them, cutting object errors. A second module picks the traits and links that best match the brain signal. On real data sets, PRISM beats earlier methods, cutting a key loss score by up to eight percent.
arxiv-2510-16396:
Lead author Yeh Keng Hao, with co-authors Hsu Tzu Wei and Sun Min, studies fast hand tracking. Their 2025 work targets small devices. Their tool, SPLite Hand, finds the pose of a hand in three dimensions. Pose means where each joint sits in space. The work targets headsets and other gear with weak chips and tight power.

SPLite skips empty parts of each image to save work, and a light decoder reads the pose out. Tests on a small Raspberry Pi board ran about three times faster than before. Hand error stayed near nine millimetres on a standard test set. Small, fast pose tools like this one help cheap headsets feel quick and smooth.
arxiv-2510-16996:
Juncheng Dong leads seven co-authors in speeding graphics processor code with agent teams in a 2025 paper. GPU kernels are small programs that run AI workloads. Tuning them is slow, expert work involving memory and scheduling tradeoffs. Single language models often fail at this irregular search.

Their framework, STARK, splits the work among cooperating model agents. The agents follow grounded instructions and manage context dynamically. Profiling feedback guides each round of kernel refinement. The setup mimics how expert engineers iterate on code. On a standard benchmark, it solved tasks where baselines failed. Some kernels ran up to sixteen times faster than before. The results suggest agent teams can automate real performance engineering.
arxiv-2510-17496:
Giacomo Camposampiero, with Michael Hersche and three co-authors, built a hard reasoning test in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their test, called I-RAVEN-X, checks pattern and math reasoning in large AI models. It extends an earlier test with bigger numbers, wider feature ranges, and noisy inputs. The point is to see whether models can generalize, meaning apply a rule in new settings, and stay robust under uncertainty.

Results split the model types apart. Reasoning focused models handled longer rule chains and wider ranges better than standard models. Both types still struggled when inputs were uncertain. They failed to weigh several likely outcomes at once. The test gives builders a clear way to probe these weak spots.
arxiv-2510-17596:
Irene Hiess and Ludwig Kampel settle five long open values in test design in a 2025 arXiv paper. A covering array is a table with a coverage promise. Every small group of columns must show all value mixes at least a set number of times. Testers use such tables to check systems with few runs. The smallest row count that works for given settings is called its covering array number.

Five of these numbers had tight bounds for decades but no exact values. The authors use balanced covering arrays, a stricter kind with even coverage. A computer result rules out balanced tables of a certain size. Their arguments extend that result to plain covering arrays. That settles all five values at once.
arxiv-2510-17796:
Francesco Verdiani and four co-authors use galaxy clustering to measure the cosmos. They study bright red galaxies photographed by the DESI Legacy Survey. Their tools are the power spectrum and the bispectrum of galaxy positions. Both tools sum up how galaxies group on the sky at each scale.

They also cross-check galaxies against lensing maps of the cosmic microwave background. A model with galaxy bias terms describes the clustering they see. The model was tested against a large computer simulation first. Adding the bispectrum made the final values much tighter. The team reports the matter share and how clumpy matter is.
arxiv-2510-17996:
Yifei Luo, with nine co-authors, tests a prediction that star feedback makes small galaxies breathe. Simulations say bursts of star birth blow gas out and pull it back in, shaking the galaxy's gravity well. That shaking should link galaxy size, gas motion, and birth rate in a shared pattern.

The team measures gas motion in about a hundred small star-forming galaxies and sets the data beside matched mock views from the FIRE-2 simulations. A clear trend in the residual gas motion at fixed mass supports the picture. Galaxy readers get rare observational backing for a feedback cycle long seen mainly on screens.
arxiv-2510-18196:
Yoshinari Fujinuma, writing alone, shows that language models used as judges bend their scores to whatever range they are given. Asked to grade summaries on a set scale with no reference, judges cluster their marks according to that scale's shape. The same bias appears across models from one family, which makes switching judges a weak fix.

A contrastive decoding trick counters the pull of the range. Agreement with human grades rose on average across ranges in the tests. Evaluation pipelines that lean on model judges get both a named failure mode and a cheap, practical remedy.
arxiv-2510-18296:
Aayushi Dangol, with Smriti Kotiyal and nine co-authors, interviews teachers about generative AI in a 2025 study. Generative AI tools can draft text, plans, and feedback for classroom use. The study district adopted these tools early, with official policies and industry-led teacher training.

The team held semi-structured interviews, meaning guided conversations with room to wander, with twenty-two teachers. Teachers described why they adopted the tools, why some resisted, and where they drew lines. District policy, professional norms, and care for students all shaped those choices. The findings challenge the simple adopt-and-train story districts often follow.
arxiv-2510-18496:
Anamitra Ghorui and Uday Khedker present a data structure built for program analysis, where information about a whole program flows through its control paths. Pointer analysis is a prime example: tracking which variables may point to which objects creates huge amounts of data, and much of it is duplicated as it propagates. Repeated storage and repeated operations on near-identical data slow the analysis badly.

Their structure, LatticeHashForest, stores such data so duplicates are removed as soon as they appear, and operations can reuse earlier results instead of recomputing them. Unlike older tricks such as hash-consing or decision diagrams, it can also modify parts of large stored structures while keeping the deduplication benefit, and it nests at several levels. The paper describes the structure in detail, gives an abstract model, and supplies a full C++ implementation with tests on example and benchmark programs.
arxiv-2510-18596:
Haojia Lin and his eleven co-authors build the first benchmark for judging reward models that grade computer-using agents. Such agents complete tasks by operating real software, and script-based checkers cannot scale or grade single steps. Reward models could fill that gap, but nobody had tested how well they actually judge an agent's whole run or its individual moves.

The benchmark collects agent runs from ten software categories and seven agent designs, with success rates spanning a wide range, all annotated by experts under strict quality control. Testing seven vision-language models with three prompt styles exposed weak visual reasoning and missing knowledge in current reward models; general models beat specialized ones. The authors also propose an ensemble prompting method, requiring agreement across prompts, as a practical improvement.
arxiv-2510-18796:
Anthony Conway and Daniel Kasprowski define a new obstruction in algebraic topology. The work is motivated by classifying four-dimensional manifolds with boundary. Their object is the relative k-invariant. It belongs to a pair of spaces. One space sits inside the other. The invariant measures whether a certain map can be extended. The map lives on the smaller space and on a two-stage approximation of the larger one.

The authors show the invariant is exactly the obstruction to a section. They prove it is complete in a comparison problem too. Take two pairs of spaces and a map between the smaller members. The invariants decide whether that map extends over the first space's three-dimensional skeleton. Set identifications on the first two homotopy groups must hold. Complete obstructions are prized in this field. Nothing is lost when passing to the invariant.
arxiv-2510-19096:
Long Li and Mourad Sini show that strong contrast in sound transmission through a bubble creates not one resonance but an infinite family of them. The famous Minnaert resonance, the low ringing of a gas bubble in liquid, was known as the smallest member, linked to a single basic vibration mode.

The other resonances sit near shifts of the remaining vibration patterns of the region, pushed slightly off the real axis. Inside the bubble, the field is dominated by mixtures of those patterns, making the extra resonances of Fabry-Pérot type. The fuller picture matters for acoustics, imaging, and bubble-based sensors.
arxiv-2510-19496:
Moshe Kimhi and four co-authors introduce CARES, a small preprocessing module that picks the lowest image resolution a vision-language model actually needs. Big models usually read images at full resolution, and the resulting visual tokens can make up nearly all of the input, wasting compute. Many questions, though, can be answered from a much smaller image.

CARES uses a compact vision-language model to judge when the larger model's answer would stop improving at higher resolutions. It is trained as a classifier over preset resolutions but can output in-between values when running. Across five benchmarks covering documents and natural images, and across several target models, it kept accuracy while cutting compute by up to eighty percent.
arxiv-2510-19696:
Qingjun Jin and three co-authors present a picture-based way to write down gluonic operators, the building blocks of effective field theories for the strong force. Composite terms define the interactions in effective Lagrangians. Their count explodes as the term's dimension grows, which makes a full list extremely hard to build. The problem grows sharper as collider tests grow more precise.

Building on the team's earlier method for making gluonic operators from primitive ones, the new picture scheme gives a systematic way to build the primitives themselves. With it, they derive the primitives behind gluonic terms of lengths two through seven, in general spacetime dimension. The result helps organize operator bases for the Standard Model effective field theory.
arxiv-2510-19796:
Rohith Kuditipudi and five co-authors ask whether the creator of an open-weight language model can prove someone else's black-box model was derived from it. Their approach exploits palimpsestic memorization: models remember training examples seen late in training more strongly. If the creator shuffled the training data randomly, correlations between the suspect model's behavior and that secret ordering become quantifiable statistical evidence.

In the query setting, likelihood scores given to training examples exposed the link across more than forty fine-tuned models with extremely small p-values in nearly all cases. In the observational setting, working from generated text alone, one of their two methods could identify a derivative from just a few hundred tokens. The work gives model creators a practical provenance test.
arxiv-2510-19896:
Filipe Ferreira de Oliveira, Matheus Becali Rocha, and Renato A. Krohling use SHAP scores to choose features for spotting urinary tract diseases, with bladder cancer as the focus. Their pipeline trains three gradient-boosting methods across six binary tasks. Each task separates bladder cancer from other urological or cancerous conditions. Tuning was automatic, and class imbalance was handled with synthetic oversampling.

SHAP-guided feature choice kept or even improved balanced accuracy, precision, and specificity, while using fewer inputs. Since the choice itself can be explained, doctors can see which values drive the predictions. The authors argue the method supports clearer, leaner clinical decision tools for screening and early diagnosis.
arxiv-2510-20296:
Wenqi Jiang presents RAG-Stack, a blueprint for jointly improving the quality and the speed of retrieval-augmented generation systems from the vector database point of view. Such systems fetch documents from a database and feed them into a large language model prompt, which improves reliability. Tuning them is hard because quality and performance depend on many knobs across models, databases, software, and hardware.

The blueprint has three pillars working together. An intermediate representation separates quality concerns from performance concerns in one shared description. A cost model estimates system performance for any such description. A plan exploration algorithm then searches those descriptions for configurations that are both high quality and high performance. Jiang argues this structure should become the standard approach.
arxiv-2510-20396:
Fatma Almaz and Handan Oztekin review Vn-slant helices inside a lightlike cone, a topic in differential geometry. The paper defines these helices in the cone setting and introduces their harmonic curvature functions. It then expresses the differential equations satisfied by those curvature functions using a constant vector field that serves as the axis of the helix.

Necessary and sufficient conditions for a curve to be a Vn-slant helix are given through the asymptotic orthonormal frame adapted to the lightlike cone. As a review, the article gathers definitions, curvature relations, and characterization results in one place. Readers working on slant helices in pseudo-Riemannian settings get a compact reference for the lightlike cone case and its special frame machinery.
arxiv-2510-20696:
Jing Bi and four co-authors study how well machines reason from images. Their models mix visual input with text based reasoning. They often use chain of thought, or step by step prompts. Yet the models still invent visual details that are not there. They also lean too much on text instead of images.

The team tests top models in three stages to find failure modes. Then they propose a new agent based design. It pairs a language model with small visual tools. Those tools check fine details and refine each reasoning step. Their system gained clear ground on the MMMU and MathVista tests. It matched or beat much larger models on those tests. The team plans to release its framework and test suite. That should help others build models that look more carefully.
arxiv-2510-20896:
Zhiwei Shao leads fifty six co-authors in the first direct measurement of galaxy assembly bias, a key systematic for cosmology, using survey data from the DESI instrument. Assembly bias means galaxy content of a dark halo depends on its wider surroundings, not mass alone, which can skew cosmic inferences if ignored.

Their cosmology free method joins a high quality group catalog with weak lensing, reading galaxy counts per group from cross correlations and average halo mass from lensing. On a nearby volume limited sample, occupation clearly varies with large scale density at fixed mass. The direct detection turns a modeled worry into a measured effect that future surveys must handle.
arxiv-2510-21096:
Alain M Dikande, working alone, solves the Kramers escape problem for Brownian particles in bistable substrates whose double well shape can deform. Escape rates govern how particles hop between stable states under thermal noise, a basic process in chemistry and devices.

Three deformations are treated, shifting both minima at fixed barrier height, shifting the barrier at fixed minima. Tuning both together through one deformability parameter, rendered in the record as a single real control. Analytic escape rate expressions are obtained for all three forms. Deformable landscapes model real substrates that flex, so the formulas extend Kramers classic result toward living and engineered matter.
arxiv-2510-21296:
Sukanya Patra and Souhaib Ben Taieb fix a common flaw in anomaly detection: training data that are supposed to be normal often contain hidden anomalies, which drag performance down. Many fixes need access to the training pipeline itself, or advance knowledge of how much contamination is present in the data.

Their framework, EPHAD, works after training, adjusting a model's outputs at test time using fresh evidence gathered then. That evidence can come from a vision-language model such as CLIP, from a classic detector, or from expert knowledge of the field. Tests span eight image data sets, twenty-six table data sets, and one real factory data set. Results hold up across models and contamination levels, showing the patch approach is broadly useful.
arxiv-2510-22296:
Latika Mishra leads a five-author team making titanium dioxide particles in plant juice. The whole-plant extract of Phyllanthus niruri replaces harsher chemistry. That herb is long used in folk medicine. The green route is the synthesis method. The product is deliberately short on oxygen. The flaw changes what the material can do.

Diffraction confirms pure anatase crystals in a tetragonal lattice. Microscopes show clumped spheres averaging about thirty-five nanometers across. Tests verify plant biomolecules on the particle surfaces. They also confirm the oxygen gaps behind two mixed states of titanium. The particles absorb strongly in the ultraviolet. Their band gap narrows to the value the team reports. Magnetic and optical behavior both strengthen over the plain material. The route is offered as a green path to useful nanomaterials.
arxiv-2510-22696: Ivan N Mikhailov, writing alone in a 2025 mathematics note, shows that the Lipschitz distance between two classes of metric spaces is positive. One class lies at finite Gromov-Hausdorff distance from a one point space, and the other from the real line with its natural metric. The positive result means the two classes stay genuinely apart under this stronger stretch based comparison.
arxiv-2510-22996:
Liang Chen, Xu-Feng Zhao, and Shao-Zhe Lu study the Casimir effect at finite temperature for a simple one-dimensional field. Two sharp delta-function potentials act like walls that squeeze vacuum energy between them. The authors compute force and entropy by direct quantization and compare with the standard Lifshitz theory.

At zero temperature both methods give the same force. When warm, the long-distance force settles to a simple form, but Lifshitz theory predicts twice the size found by direct quantization. That factor-of-two gap matters for how physicists model thermal vacuum forces in small devices and tests of theory.
arxiv-2510-23096:
Jiyoung Hong and six co-authors introduce TwinShift, a benchmark for audio deepfake detectors that face new voices and new synthesis tools. Fake audio already fuels fraud and misinformation, and detectors that ace old tests often fail on unseen generators or speakers. Real-world reliability demands testing under strictly unseen conditions.

TwinShift is built from six synthesis systems, each paired with disjoint sets of speakers, so neither side leaks into training. Detectors must handle both shifts at once. The benchmark gives developers an honest measure of robustness before their systems guard calls, media, and identity checks.
arxiv-2510-23396:
Musleh Alharthi, Kaleel Mahmood, Sarosh Patel, and Ausif Mahmood present EMTSF, a mixture of state-of-the-art models for time series forecasting. Transformers moved from language into forecasting with strong results, yet a simple linear model once beat them, sparking debate. Later models such as PatchTST and TimeLLM restored the transformer lead, and follow-up papers challenged each claim in turn.

Against that contested backdrop, the authors combine several top models into one extraordinary mixture. Ensembling diverse forecasters can average out individual weaknesses. Their system targets robust accuracy across the many kinds of series forecasters face in practice.
arxiv-2510-23496:
Cesar Cuenca and Maciej Dołęga study systems of many interacting particles whose spacing follows rules set by a temperature-like parameter. In the high temperature regime, the particles spread out in patterns described by special functions called Jack functions. Earlier work in the series found when a law of large numbers holds there, using generating functions built from those Jack functions.

Here the authors derive a functional equation for the moment generating function of the limiting arrangement, which opens the door to analytic tools. They use it to compute the limiting densities for the pure Jack measures, covering known cases tied to random matrix ensembles. A striking pattern emerges: the limiting measures rest on separate intervals with unit gaps, a crystallization effect. The interval positions match zeros of explicit special functions, which also appear as spectra of certain Jacobi operators.
arxiv-2510-23696:
Elias Bernreuther and four co-authors explore how beam-dump experiments could spot a hidden sector of dark particles. In strongly interacting dark sector models, accelerators can create dark quarks that shower into several dark mesons. If some of those mesons are light and long-lived, they travel a distance before decaying, leaving displaced vertices that detectors can catch.

The authors focus on production through effective operators, with the dark sector's rho-like meson decaying through kinetic mixing. They weigh current limits from NA62 and BaBar against projected reach for SHiP and Belle II. A sizable region of parameter space remains open where SHiP could record several displaced vertices inside a single event. Such multi-decay events would do more than signal discovery: their pattern would reveal the structure of the dark sector itself, turning a detection into a measurement tool.
arxiv-2510-23896:
Kosei Uemura and two co-authors give African languages their own corner of the text embedding benchmark world. Embeddings power retrieval and help stop language models from hallucinating, but the multilingual benchmark still underrepresents African languages, and its few tasks are recycled from translation sets. The authors answer with AfriMTEB, covering fifty-nine languages, fourteen tasks, and thirty-eight datasets, including six new ones.

The new datasets span fourteen to fifty-six languages each and add fresh task types: hate speech detection, intent detection, and emotion classification. Alongside the benchmark, the team presents AfriE5, an embedding model adapted from the mE5 model by cross-lingual contrastive distillation toward African languages. In their evaluation, AfriE5 reached state-of-the-art results on the new benchmark, beating rivals including Gemini embeddings and mE5. The work gives builders a fair test and a strong starting model for African language applications.
arxiv-2510-24196:
Jijun Yang and forty seven co-authors describe a photosensor system built for the RELICS experiment and how it was tested. The surface level detector faces intense cosmic muon backgrounds that can saturate its photomultiplier tubes, blinding them to faint signals. To handle this, the team designed a base with an extended dynamic range.

The system reads out each tube at two points, the anode and the seventh dynode, to widen the range of linear response. Tests of Hamamatsu R8520-406 tubes confirm stable running under positive high voltage and a linear range extended by more than tenfold. A model of saturation and recovery also gauges how muon signals will affect the detector.
arxiv-2510-24296:
Daniel Parrochia examines the meeting of cosmology and philosophy, working alone. Scientific cosmology now has a standard model of an expanding universe, but big questions remain open. Did the expansion begin in a singularity that marks an absolute start, or is our universe one among many, spread across space or time?

Parrochia also revisits the old theological point, held since Thomas Aquinas, that a beginning is not the same as creation. After a brief history of recent scientific cosmology, the article weighs these options and clarifies what science can and cannot settle about the origin of the universe.
arxiv-2510-24696:
Yael Alush, Nicholas C Stone, and Sjoert van Velzen recheck a late glow seen when a star is torn apart by a black hole. At late times the glow often forms a shelf that is treated as flat and still. That flat shelf view comes from models of the disk of torn gas as it spreads.

The team fits the shelf data with a range of shelf shapes and picks the best by a set rule. About a third of cases favor a shelf that shifts with time, a third favor a flat one, and a third show no clear shelf. For clear cases, they fit a disk model lifted by magnet fields.
arxiv-2510-24796:
HaoYang Shang and Xuan Liu coin a term, mutual wanting, for the two way hopes that grow between users and AI chat tools. As chat models shift fast, users form hopes for the new forms, and firms shape what users come to want. Past work has not mapped these two way hopes at large scale.

The pair mined user posts from big AI forums and ran tests across a few chat models. Near half of users used human like words for the tools, and trust words beat betray words by a lot. Users fell into clear want types, and gaps between hope and fact could be gauged. Their frame aims to help firms spot strain at model change time.
arxiv-2510-24996:
Emilio De Santis, Kadmo Laxa, and Eva Locherbach give two new ways to run a perfect fake of a chain that recalls all its past. In such a chain, the next sign's odds rest on the whole run of past signs. Their ways grow from a known trick that pairs the chain with its own past.

One way lets a new sign at times pop up free of the past. The other way works when such free pops can not hap. Both can deal with past links that are thin spread, by use of unknown states in the past set. Rules on how fast past pull fades make sure the runs stop in finite steps, near all the time.
arxiv-2510-25196:
Ji Qiang, Jinyu Wan, Allen Qiang, and Yue Hao use auto slope math to flag chaos in beam paths fast, for use in ring design. To widen the safe zone of a beam ring, teams must know where paths turn wild. Their flag is the size of the tangent map, drawn from tracked paths run in a form that can be sloped by code.

In many cases, one or a few turns of the ring give enough of a read, they show. That cuts the cost of the wild check by a lot next to long runs. As a case, the flag drove the safe zone tune of a known light source ring design. Fast chaos reads can speed each design pass.
arxiv-2510-25296:
Rachel Axelrod, Uri Obolski, and Daniel Nevo study vaccine trials. Their 2025 statistics paper tackles broken blinding in trials. Blinding hides who got vaccine or placebo. When blinding breaks, behavior can change outcomes. People may act differently if they guess their status. Then measured efficacy mixes immune and behavior effects.

Recent work proposed new causal targets for this problem. Those targets need strong assumptions to identify exactly. One assumption rules out unmeasured common causes. Personality traits might violate that assumption in practice. The three authors relax that strong assumption. They derive nonparametric bounds for vaccine effects instead. Bounds give a range rather than one number. They build bounds with linear programming and monotonicity. They test the bounds on synthetic data. One example draws on a COVID-19 trial.
arxiv-2510-25596:
Jiachuan Xu led five co-authors constraining baryonic feedback. Tim Eifler, Elisabeth Krause, and Vivian Miranda helped. Jaime Salcido and Ian McCarthy complete six authors. Their 2025 astronomy paper mixes multiple cosmological probes. Weak lensing and galaxy clustering data are mixed. Cosmic microwave background lensing and cross-correlations join them. Six-by-two-point data come from Dark Energy Survey.

Planck data supply microwave readings. They model baryonic feedback via principal parts. Parts are constructed from the ANTILLES runs suite. A tight correlation links feedback and baryon fraction. A neural network emulator boosts study speed hugely. Speed gains reach about a thousandfold in practice. Simulated studies validate against various systematic effects. Their six-by-two-point result gives a form amplitude value. It indicates weak baryonic feedback in the universe. Tensions appear with Illustris run feedback strength. OWLS AGN feedback also exceeds their constrained value.
arxiv-2510-25696:
Yesmine Abdennadher, Eleonora Cicciarella, and Michele Rossi present a convolutional spiking GRU. Their 2025 paper processes spatio-time data with spiking neurons. Spiking networks enable quick time messaging for sequences. Gated recurrent units are robust recurrent network variants. Classic recurrent networks lose local details in long sequences. Previous spiking GRU methods missed fine local dependencies.

Their cell leverages convolutional operations to preserve local form. Time precision of spiking neurons is integrated. Quick gating mechanisms of GRUs are retained too. The architecture suits time and spatio-time datasets. Benchmarks included speech digits and gesture recognition tasks. Image-based event datasets were also tested thoroughly. Their model outperformed leading GRU variants on average. Quality exceeded ninety percent on sequential tasks. MNIST quality reached over ninety-nine percent there. Efficiency better by sixty-nine percent over SpikGRU. Code is ready publicly.
arxiv-2510-25896:
Prune C. August, Robin Wordsworth, Mikayla Huffman, David Brain, and Lars A. Buchhave ask whether impacts could bring back an atmosphere on a rocky planet after it has frozen out. Planets close to small red dwarf stars are locked with one side in night, so gases can condense as ice on the dark side and the air can collapse. That ice, though, forms a store that an impact could vaporize.

August and the team use a simple energy balance model with random impacts for carbon dioxide atmospheres. Middle sized impactors, five to ten kilometers wide, at plausible rates can rebuild visible, short lived air. For some known rocky worlds, planets may spend half or more of their time with such restored air.
arxiv-2510-26396:
Joel Z Leibo, Alexander Sasha Vezhnevets, William A Cunningham, and Stanley M Bileschi take a practical view of personhood for artificial intelligence. As AI agents start to act on their own, they argue, societies will face many new kinds of personhood at once. The paper asks what to do about that without first settling deep debates about minds.

Leibo and his three co-authors treat personhood as a bundle of rights and duties that a society can grant, split, or tailor to a task. That could let an AI sign contracts or be held to account, without any claim that it is conscious. They also warn of dark patterns, design tricks that use our social habits against us. Their frame aims at tools for governing AI agents in daily life.
arxiv-2510-26696:
Yuliya Bilinskaya, with five co-authors, studies a quantum resource called nonstabilizerness, sometimes nicknamed magic. It marks the states that give quantum computers power beyond easy classical simulation. The team examines it on the information lattice, a way of organising a state's information by scale.

Bilinskaya and the team show that noninteger local information directly signals nonstabilizerness. For states whose short- and large-scale information separate cleanly, noninteger total information at large scales witnesses the long-range form. They propose a folding procedure to split global from edge-to-edge contributions. In a test case, the ordered ground state of a spin model showed long-range magic from global correlations, while the disordered ground state had at most short-range magic.
arxiv-2510-26796:
Dongyue Lu, with ten co-authors, generates four-dimensional content from casual video without camera pose labels. Immersive applications want scenes that move in space and time, built from ordinary footage. Existing video-to-4D methods need hand-annotated camera poses, which are costly and brittle on wild footage.

Lu and the team present See4D, which renders warped views to a bank of fixed virtual cameras instead of predicting a camera path. A view-conditional inpainting model, trained on realistically warped images, fills missing regions across those viewpoints and learns a geometry prior without three-dimensional annotations. An autoregressive pipeline then extends the video along camera splines in overlapping windows. On cross-view generation and sparse reconstruction benchmarks, See4D generalised better than pose- or trajectory-based rivals.
arxiv-2510-26896:
Cristina Gheorghe, writing alone in 2025, studies fixed points in pure math. A fixed point is an input that a map sends back to itself. Her maps are multivalued, meaning one input can lead to a set of outputs.

Some maps fail a Ćirić contraction test, a rule that pulls points closer in a set way. She studies a close, allowed change to such a map that does pass. The question is when the first map still keeps its strict fixed point. She also asks when results stay stable, meaning small changes do not break them. Her results are recast in Takahashi's sense of allowed changes and shown with examples.
arxiv-2510-26996:
Arghavan Rezvani leads five co-authors in presenting MoME, a system for outlining structures in medical scans. The name stands for Mixture of Visual Language Medical Experts. It adapts the mixture of experts idea, where different specialist parts handle different inputs, from large language models to medical vision and language tasks.

MoME selects specialists on the fly and blends multi-scale image features with text embeddings, meaning numeric codes for words. The team tests it on an assembly of ten datasets holding thousands of CT scans. Results show strong, competitive precision across the sets. For readers in medical imaging, the work shows how pairing foundation models with text can yield robust outlining without a single fixed pathway.
arxiv-2510-27296:
Wenfeng Huang, Xiangyun Liao, Wei Cao, Wenjing Jia, and Weixin Si propose FGMamba, a light model that sharpens medical images while cutting scan cost and time. Super-resolution must capture both long-range anatomy and fine frequency detail without heavy computation. Their frequency-aware gated state-space design unifies global dependency modeling and fine-detail enhancement in one compact architecture.

A gated attention state-space module blends efficient sequence modeling with spatial and channel attention, while a pyramid frequency fusion module gathers high-frequency detail across resolutions guided by Fourier transforms. Across five modalities including ultrasound, MRI, and CT, the model tops standard quality scores with under three quarters of a million parameters, beating convolutional and transformer rivals. The results support frequency-aware state-space models for scalable medical enhancement.
arxiv-2510-27396:
Damilola Fasiku and Wentao Tang split a hard tuning problem across many machines in this 2025 paper. The problem is derivative-free optimization: tuning a black-box system whose slopes are unknown. The goal splits into parts held by different machines, tied by shared rules. Exact solves at each step are too costly to demand.

Their scheme builds on ADMM, a method that swaps messages between parts until they agree. A two-level design handles the shared rules: an inner loop updates each part, an outer loop pushes a slack value to zero. Each part is solved loosely by a trust-region solver, one that trusts its local model only near the current point. The slack allowed shrinks in a controlled way. They prove the method settles near a true answer and beats one-machine approaches on hard tests.
arxiv-2511-00096:
Shangyu Lou introduces Urban-MAS, a multi-agent system of language models for human-centered urban prediction in a zero-shot setting. Urban AI tasks such as perception prediction and human dynamics need multimodal, heterogeneous data, and single language models often underperform on domain-specific questions. Three agent types structure the framework, starting with predictive factor guidance agents that prioritize key factors.

Guidance agents steer knowledge extraction so compressed urban knowledge is used effectively by the predicting agents. Urban computing readers get a division of labor among model agents for city tasks. Specialized prompting roles aim to recover the domain expertise a single general prompt misses.
arxiv-2511-00196:
Leonardo Alberro, Noura Limam, and Raouf Boutaba present a quality-of-service-aware data plane model for programmable transport networks serving the 5G user plane. Next-generation services demand per-flow bandwidth assurance, sub-millisecond-style latency goals, and traffic prioritization, while network functions migrate to edge and central clouds, making transport the critical enabler of end-to-end guarantees. Fixed-function infrastructure cannot flex across the diverse profiles standardized for 5G.

Their model supports predictable behavior and fine-grained service differentiation in programmable hardware. Telecommunications readers get a design for meeting strict service guarantees in cloudified networks. Predictability, not average speed, is what industrial and emergency services actually buy.
arxiv-2511-00496:
Pawan Murthy, Anja Lippert, and Andrea Beck compare ways to simulate how lubricant spreads inside high-speed gearboxes. Too much oil wastes energy in churning; too little wears the gear teeth. Spinning parts make direct viewing impractical, so engineers must trust simulations, yet no head-to-head study weighed accuracy against computing cost, and thick grease was barely studied at all.

Four solvers face two benchmark cases, one judged qualitatively and one quantitatively. Two mesh-based Eulerian solvers matched experiments well in chosen cases but cost heavily. A particle-based solver looked right qualitatively yet drifted in numbers. The study then extends to grease, testing how fill volume and gear speed change deposits on the gears. The benchmarks give future solver studies a shared reference frame.
arxiv-2511-00996:
Shuo Guan and colleagues show, end to end, how a space based gravitational wave detector could measure the fingerprint of the electroweak phase transition. That transition was a change in the early universe, when the Higgs field settled into its present state. A first order version of that transition would leave a background hum of gravitational waves.

Simulating the Taiji mission, including instrument noise and astrophysical foregrounds, they reconstruct the hum's spectrum with both Fisher matrix estimates and Bayesian sampling. The spectrum pins down the transition's large scale parameters, which map onto particle physics quantities in an extended Higgs model. Despite degeneracies between parameters, the Higgs self couplings, which govern how the Higgs interacts with itself, can be greatly constrained this way.
arxiv-2511-01296:
Guanjie Cheng and colleagues harden federated learning, where many devices train one shared model without sending raw data to a center. The setup invites attack: gradients can leak private information, and malicious participants can poison the model. Existing defenses tend to be expensive or imprecise.

Their framework, LSHFed, checks gradients by hashing them. A locally sensitive hashing scheme with multiple hyperplanes compresses each high dimensional gradient into a compact binary code, irreversible by design. Malicious gradients can then be detected and filtered from their codes alone, cutting both privacy leakage and transmission cost. Experiments show the model stays accurate even when up to half the participants are colluding adversaries, while gradient verification communication drops by up to a thousand fold.
arxiv-2511-01596:
Hadis Ghodrati Saeini and six colleagues study films one molecule thick. The films build themselves from polyalanine helices, spiral protein fragments that coat a surface in neat patterns. Such films matter for an effect that links molecular handedness to electron spin, with spin-based devices in mind.

The team paired scanning tunneling microscopy with theory. Films of one handedness form hexagonal lattices. Mixed films, with left- and right-handed helices, form rectangular phases with stripes. Computed potentials from tight-binding work explain the split: helices of opposed handedness bind more strongly and pack more tightly. The bright and dark contrast in the microscope images comes from anti-parallel alignment of opposed helices, not from real height changes.
arxiv-2511-01696:
L. Tan Phuc, N. Quang Hung, N. Ngoc Anh, and N. Dinh Dang investigate a puzzling bump in how atomic nuclei emit gamma rays at low energies. This upbend resonance in the radiative strength function matters for neutron capture rates and stellar nucleosynthesis, yet its origin is still debated.

Extending an exact thermal pairing plus phonon damping model, the authors compute strength functions for nuclei from scandium-44 to samarium-153 across odd-odd, odd-mass, and even-even systems, matching the available measurements. The upbend, they find, comes from non-collective particle-particle and hole-hole excitations about three times stronger than the giant dipole resonance. Because it appears only at finite temperature in their framework, the upbend breaks the Brink-Axel hypothesis at very low gamma energies, and a global relation ties its integrated strength to mass number.
arxiv-2511-01796:
Misha Gromov's lecture notes take up a classical question in differential geometry. When can one Riemannian manifold be immersed into another, keeping the immersion's curvatures small? And what stands in the way when it cannot be done?

The lectures develop constructions of immersions with controlled, in the notes' phrase, small curvatures between Riemannian manifolds, working out the flexible methods that produce such maps. Alongside the constructions, they indicate the obstructions. These are the rigid features of curvature that no clever construction can circumvent. They mark the boundary between the flexible and the rigid in this part of geometry. The text is a compact route into Gromov's h-principle circle of ideas, aimed at readers who want both the building techniques and the reasons they sometimes must fail.
arxiv-2511-01996:
Matéo Spriet, Christopher Langrenez, Raymond Brummelhuis, and Stephan De Bièvre ask what makes the Kirkwood-Dirac distributions special among quantum mechanics' many quasiprobability representations. Each Kirkwood-Dirac representation is fixed by two matched sets of commuting observables. It exactly reproduces their Born probabilities for every state. A wider family of such forms shares that property.

The authors first define a natural quantum conditional expectation: the best guess for one observable given another, in a given state, and verify it behaves as one should. They then prove that only the Kirkwood-Dirac representations yield a conditional expectation, given one of the two observable sets, that coincides with this natural one. A state-dependent no-go result falls out along the way, linking anomalous conditional values to the nonexistence of a joint probability distribution for the two observables.
arxiv-2511-02496:
Ronald Katende, a researcher in machine learning theory, argues that the shape of a model's representation deserves to be graded, not just its accuracy. In data-scarce learning, where labels are few, an encoder can pack its latent space wastefully. Katende defines a quality score that adds two geometric penalties, for curvature and for intrinsic dimension, to the usual information bottleneck trade-off between compression and task relevance.

Under smoothness and concentration assumptions, he derives generalisation bounds for the low-label regime in which the intrinsic dimension and covering complexity appear. He characterises the frontier between keeping information and keeping geometry simple. The practical version, V-GIB, adds those penalties to variational bottleneck training. On real benchmarks with label fractions from one to twenty percent, it lifted performance and reduced geometric complexity in several regimes, notably on two image datasets, though no regulariser won everywhere.
arxiv-2511-02596:
Florian Bruse, David Kronenberger, and Martin Lange extend one of descriptive complexity theory's classic bridges between logic and computation. Vardi's theorem from 1982 says that the queries computable in polynomial space, over ordered structures, are exactly those expressible in first-order logic enriched with partial fixpoints. This paper climbs the exponential-space hierarchy: for each level k, the queries computable with k-fold exponential space should correspond to a logic of matching strength.

The authors prove the correspondence, characterising k-EXPSPACE queries as exactly those expressible in higher-order logic of order k plus one, again with partial fixpoints. For levels above the first, the restriction to ordered structures can be dropped, because higher-order logic is expressive enough to manufacture the needed order itself. The result completes a uniform logical picture of a whole hierarchy of enormous complexity classes.
arxiv-2511-02996:
Ailar Mahdizadeh and five colleagues teach a model to link CT scans with the reports doctors write about them. Most vision-language models work on flat images and treat scan slices as separate pictures, losing the body's three-dimensional structure. Their 2025 framework, SCALE-VLP, trains on whole volumes and uses graded matches instead of a strict right-or-wrong pairing between scans and text.

Two additions guide the learning: spatial semantics that preserve anatomy across the volume, and medical knowledge from radiology ontologies. The model then transfers across tasks with no extra tuning. It retrieved the right report far more often than the prior best, lifted abnormality classification by ten points, and wrote reports with strong scores. On an outside data set it still gained, hinting at broad reach.
arxiv-2511-03196:
Feng Wu, Tsai Hor Chan, Fuying Wang, Guosheng Yin, and Lequan Yu align medical data of different kinds, records, images, and notes, using a statistical tool called a copula. Fusing such modalities into one distribution is the core problem of multimodal learning, and simple joining methods flatten how the parts interact. Their 2025 framework models each modality's latent distribution as a Gaussian mixture, then ties the marginals together with a copula that captures complex, higher-order links.

Because the joint model is explicit, it can also generate a plausible representation for a modality that is missing for a given patient. On public MIMIC hospital data sets, the model beat rival fusion methods. The authors release their code, aiming at clinical settings where complete data is the exception.
arxiv-2511-03596:
Kyle F Grosser and co-authors fairly compare four models that predict time to Huntington disease diagnosis. The models, built on repeat length, age, and combined scores, often disagree, and past comparisons risked bias. Testing models on their own training data flatters them, and heavy censoring, with most people still undiagnosed, distorts scores further.

The team explains each model's foundations in plain terms, weighing practical use. External data then test how well each model separates high-risk from low-risk people once censoring is handled properly. Trial designers need honest rankings, since a weak model wastes slots and can mislead hopeful participants. The study offers a cleaner yardstick for a field where timing guides care.
arxiv-2511-03696:
Zihan Li, Dan A Mazilu, and Irina Mazilu design two classroom modules that teach statistical physics through quantum computing with the Qiskit toolkit. Quantum random walks and the Ising model form the pair, each letting students run a system in both classical and quantum form. Side-by-side runs make superposition and interference tangible rather than abstract.

Circuits, sample code, and student activities are laid out for direct adoption in statistical mechanics or modern physics courses. The Ising module ties quantum circuits to collective behavior and phase change, a core physics story. The walk module contrasts ballistic quantum spread with slow classical diffusion. Hands-on contrast, the authors argue, deepens grasp of distributions far better than formulas alone.
arxiv-2511-03896:
Haithem Taha and Kshitij Anand recast incompressible fluid mechanics as a quadratic program through a variational principle. Gauss's principle turns particle dynamics into a least-cost problem. The principle of minimum pressure gradient plays the matching role for fluids. A flow that cuts pressure gradient cost to its least value at each instant must satisfy the Navier-Stokes equations.

That least-cost problem, the pair show, is a convex quadratic program, among the most tractable classes in nonlinear optimization. Using classic mechanics and the Moore-Penrose theory of generalized inverses, they derive an explicit exact solution. Fluid evolution can therefore be computed by solving that program, opening a computing route quite different from standard time stepping.
arxiv-2511-04596:
Fridrik Freyr Gautason and his co-author study holographic Wilson loops in three-dimensional theories. The targets are two families of superconformal Chern-Simons-matter theories with two supercharges. One family has duals in M-theory, the other in massive type IIA string theory.

Geometry gives a universal handle on the semiclassical quantization of probe branes and strings. From that, the pair computes the one-loop partition function for both probes. The result predicts how Wilson loops behave at large N in the dual field theories. For the M-theory family, they conjecture a full perturbative answer written as a ratio of Airy functions.
arxiv-2511-04696:
Jan Strich and three colleagues introduce EncouRAGe, a Python framework for testing retrieval-augmented generation. Such systems pair language models with searched documents, but setups vary wildly between labs. EncouRAGe breaks the pipeline into five modular parts that researchers can swap.

The parts cover type definitions, system building, inference, the vector store, and metrics. Local deployment and repeatable results are design goals throughout. Evaluation spans several benchmarks with twenty-five thousand question pairs and over fifty-one thousand documents. Their results carry a warning: retrieval systems still trail some baselines, so careful local testing remains essential.
arxiv-2511-04896:
Tatsushi Shima, writing alone, restores nuclear recoil to neutrino scattering in collapsing stars. In core-collapse supernovae, the stalled shock needs extra heating to revive. Standard transport treats coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering as energy-neutral, dropping the recoil.

Each scattering actually hands a few kiloelectronvolts to the nucleus, he calculates. Across the hundred-kilometer stalled layer, that trickle sums to a major heat input. The total lands within an order of magnitude of what simulations need for revival. Neutrino spectra and lepton balance stay nearly unchanged. The long failure to revive shocks may trace to this one neglected motion.
arxiv-2511-05796:
Yong Huang and co-authors build SecureLink, a system that verifies drones by fusing fingerprints from two layers of the network stack. Drone radio links are open, so a hostile drone can impersonate a trusted one with stolen certificates. Older checks rely on one data type from one layer, which wobbles when drones move in open settings.

SecureLink aligns radio fingerprints from channel measurements with motion fingerprints from onboard sensors like accelerometers and gyroscopes. An attention-based network fuses the features, trained with a similarity loss, and a one-class classifier decides whether a drone is genuine. The team built the system and tested it on three drone types in varied settings, reporting stronger and steadier authentication.
arxiv-2511-06096:
MinSik Kwon and co-authors run a heat engine whose fuel is quantum coherence itself. Heat engines turn thermal energy into work; this one is fully quantum at every stage. A single spin in diamond draws energy from a coherent bath and stores it in a spin battery, cycle after cycle.

After a few cycles the device produced almost twice the work of its classical counterpart, a clear quantum enhancement, the team reports. They give concrete criteria for when coherence converts into work successfully. The link between motor and battery must itself stay coherent, they stress. The experiment shows a working nanomachine with all parts quantum, a proof that coherence is a usable fuel and not just a curiosity.
arxiv-2511-06396:
Dachuan Lin and colleagues test whether debate between small models can judge language model safety as reliably as one big judge. Safety scoring often relies on costly frontier models acting as judges. The team built HAJailBench, a human-labeled set of more than eleven thousand jailbreak attempts spanning many attack styles and target models.

Their Multi-Agent Judge framework seats a critic, a defender, and a judge agent under one shared safety rubric. On the new benchmark it beat matched small-model baselines and earlier multi-agent judges while costing less than a leading commercial model. Ablations showed a few debate rounds capture most of the benefit.
arxiv-2511-06596:
Z. Bazzi and colleagues publish the largest catalog yet of extragalactic molecular clouds, traced by glowing carbon-rich dust. The James Webb Space Telescope's sharp images of nearby spiral galaxies reveal polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emission that marks molecular gas, even where carbon monoxide stays dark. Sixty-six galaxies from the PHANGS survey supplied the maps.

Cloud finding at two resolutions extracted well over one hundred thousand structures in each version. A linear conversion turned dust brightness into molecular mass estimates, and cross-matching showed about forty-one percent of dust clouds pair with known carbon monoxide clouds. The heaviest clouds gather in spiral arms, surface densities fade outward, and both catalogs are released for star formation research.
arxiv-2511-06796:
Claims that humanoid robots move at human level are common but seldom measured, so MD-Nazmus Sunbeam proposes a system to make the claim testable. Peak torque or speed alone say little about whether a joint delivers the right mix of torque, power, and endurance at real working angles. The system standardizes joint coordinates with a degrees-of-freedom atlas based on biomechanics conventions.

Human-Equivalence Envelopes then define, for tasks like walking, stairs, lifting, and reaching, whether a robot matches human torque and power at the same angle and rate. These feed a Human-Level Actuation Score combining workspace coverage, efficiency, bandwidth, and thermal sustainability. Detailed protocols using dynamometry and power and thermal testing supply every input, and a worked example shows trade-offs that headline specifications hide.
arxiv-2511-06896:
Giacomo Graziani surveys the theory of ruled and rational surfaces, two classic classes in algebraic geometry. Rational surfaces are those birationally equivalent to the projective plane, and ruled surfaces are swept out by classes of lines, loosely like a cylinder or cone. A powerful idea in classifying such objects is the model: choosing, within an isomorphism class, a representative with nice features.

The survey defines and studies suitable models for these surfaces in the smooth complex case. With good models in hand, features of the surfaces themselves become easier to read off and compare. Graziani presents the constructions and the theory around them as a coherent account, giving readers a clear entry into how modern algebraic geometry tames these classic objects through their best representatives.
arxiv-2511-07196:
S V Aksenov, M S Shustin, and I S Burmistrov study how dissipation steers quantum transport through a superconducting device coupled to normal metal reservoirs. Working in a field-theoretic Keldysh system for a quadratic Liouvillian, they extend the Meir-Wingreen current formula and the Onsager response matrix to a superconductor attached to any number of fermionic baths. A Kirchhoff-style rule yields the dissipation-induced loss current and changed quantum kinetic equations.

For wide-band contacts attached to single sites, each contact reduces the degeneracy of the non-equilibrium steady state by one, a result checked numerically on the extended Kitaev model. In low-temperature linear response, degenerate and nondegenerate steady states correspond to quantized and unquantized conductance peaks. Revisiting resonant transport through the Kitaev Majorana mode, dissipation explains the shrinking and asymmetry of its zero-bias peak.
arxiv-2511-07496:
Barath Chandran, Srinivas Anumasa, and Dianbo Liu fight a flaw in diffusion image generators: blended, unrealistic samples. When the learned score field is too smooth, sampling slides between modes and invents hybrids that no data supports. Earlier work named the cause but offered no sampling fix.

Their correction adjusts the score during generation using its Laplacian, a measure of sharpness. A finite-difference trace estimate keeps the extra math affordable in high dimensions. Trials on toy data and images cut hallucinated samples markedly. Because the change acts after training, existing models can adopt it directly. Cleaner samples raise trust in generated media.
arxiv-2511-07596:
Alzate-Trujillo, del Pino, López-Sanjuan, and collaborators rebuild the Milky Way disc history from twelve-filter sky photos. The J-PLUS survey colors separate stellar chemistry well enough to loosen the classic confusion between age and metal content. Combined with Gaia motions, the data cover the disc on galactic scales.

Fitting stellar models to color-magnitude diagrams recovers when stars formed and in which chemical component. Isochrone fitting also yields ages and metallicities for individual stars as history tracers. Separating chemically distinct disc parts clarifies how the disc assembled over time. Wide multi-filter surveys thus become time machines for our own galaxy.
arxiv-2511-07896:
Dengcan Liu, Jiahao Li, and Zheren Fu build reward models on a budget. Reward models steer language model alignment by standing in for human preference, yet they usually demand huge annotation sets and costly fine-tuning. Limited-resource teams are locked out of serious alignment work.

SparseRM mines a sparse autoencoder decomposition of a model internal representations for preference-relevant directions. Those interpretable directions assemble into a lightweight reward model without retraining the giant. Interpretability comes along for free, since each direction can be inspected. Cheaper, clearer reward modeling could democratize alignment and make preference judgments easier to audit.
arxiv-2511-07996:
B Hudson, L Gurvits, E Mooij, A Ricarte, and D Palumbo assess whether very long baseline interferometry can image orbiting pairs of supermassive black holes. Such binaries should form after galaxies merge and are expected sources of gravitational waves. Directly watching their orbital motion would give the first firm electromagnetic proof that close pairs exist.

The Black Hole Explorer space mission is the main case studied. An orbit fitting method using relative positions and Bayesian sampling recovers binary properties from simulated images. Detection needs strong flux and tiny separations, while three yearly observations could pin down orbit size and shape for periods under ten years.
arxiv-2511-08796:
Jiaxing Zhao and three co-authors examine how the birth process of a heavy quark and its antiquark leaves fingerprints on the mesons they later form. Different quantum chromodynamics mechanisms create these pairs with different correlations, and those early links survive into the patterns detectors measure.

Using the EPOS4HQ event generator, the team compares calculated correlations with data on open and hidden heavy-flavor mesons from proton collisions at RHIC and LHC energies. The measured correlations between heavy mesons turn out to mirror the production mechanisms directly. A Wigner density approach for bound-state formation also reproduces the measured spectra of Bc mesons, the rare family binding a bottom antiquark to a charm quark. That agreement lets the authors draw conclusions about where in space the heavy quarks are created.
arxiv-2511-08896:
Sanyukta Adap, Ujjwal Baid, and Spyridon Bakas train neural networks to label the sub-regions inside glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive brain tumor, from stained tissue slides. Reading these slides by hand is the first step of diagnosis, and automated region maps could help researchers understand the tumor's morphology at scale.

A four-step pipeline classifies six histological regions in the BraTS-Path 2024 challenge data. Several EfficientNet variants were tried, and the B1 and B4 sizes performed best, reaching an F1 score of 0.98 under cross-validation on the training set. The same approach scored near 0.55 on held-out validation data and about 0.52 on the hidden test set. That drop is the paper's honest warning: models that shine in training can falter on new hospitals' slides.
arxiv-2511-08996:
Xiran Chen and five co-authors label cell types across two single-cell sequencing technologies that see tissues differently. Whole-cell sequencing misses fragile cells that nuclei-only sequencing catches, and vice versa, so a label learned on one platform should transfer to the other, yet almost no methods attempt the crossing.

ScNucAdapt performs that transfer with partial domain adaptation, a technique suited to label sets that overlap only partly, which matches how cell compositions differ between the platforms. It is tested on both paired datasets, where the same tissue was measured both ways, and unpaired ones. Across those settings it annotates cell types robustly and beats the existing approaches compared. The authors offer it as a practical framework for unifying cell atlases built from mixed sequencing technologies.
arxiv-2511-09196:
Francesca Scarabel, Harry Coldwell, and Tyler Cassidy study an epidemic model where infectivity and waning immunity both depend on time since infection. The model can be read as a renewal equation for new infections or as a PDE for infected density. They focus on infection durations following a gamma law rather than simpler Erlang ones.

The shape of that length spread strongly changes stability of the endemic equilibrium, even with the same reproduction number and mean infectious period. The authors also find bistability, where a stable endemic state coexists with a stable periodic orbit, apparently a first for such models. Common compartmental shortcuts can invent spurious dynamics, they warn, because they quietly fix that shape.
arxiv-2511-09296:
David C. Konijn and ten co-authors report the largest unbiased search yet for radio bursts signaling coronal mass ejections on other stars. A drifting Type II radio burst is the key signature of such an ejection. The team mined 107 star-years of LOFAR survey data for stars within 100 parsecs.

They found two drifting bursts. One was the known two-minute event from the M dwarf StKM 1-1262, the other a new thirteen-minute burst from LP 215-56. Nineteen more bursts lacked the telltale drift. Fitting a luminosity distribution to detections and non-detections gave a slope matching solar Type II bursts closely. That agreement suggests today's scarcity of detections reflects limited sensitivity, not rare eruptions.
arxiv-2511-09396:
Lukas Arana, Julen Etxaniz, Ander Salaberria, and Gorka Azkune build a strong open multimodal language model for Basque, a low-resource language. Commercial multimodal models handle such languages acceptably, but open models lag far behind. The team created their own training and evaluation image-text datasets for Basque.

They trained models on two backbones, Llama-3.1-Instruct and a Basque-adapted variant called Latxa, trying several data mixtures. Surprisingly, only about a fifth of the multimodal training data needed to be Basque for solid Basque benchmark results. A Basque-adapted backbone turned out not to be required either, contrary to expectations. The released resources are meant to help other low-resource language communities do the same.
arxiv-2511-09596:
Mingkuan Zhao and seven co-authors redesign how attention works in large language models so every head earns its keep. In standard attention, all heads scan the same full sequence. Cost grows with the square of context length and in step with head count. Sparse attention methods save compute but usually lose information.

Their SPAttention splits the attention workload into balanced, non-overlapping distance bands, giving each head its own segment.
