Together the heads form one joint computation instead of many duplicated ones, cutting complexity by a factor equal to the head count. The structure also pushes heads to specialize on distinct dependencies. The authors argue principled structural sparsity improves both speed and quality at once.
arxiv-2511-09996:
Alireza F. Pour and Shai Ben-David propose a new learning paradigm for problems where the set of candidate models is so large that sample estimates cannot uniformly match true losses. The standard fixes, structural risk minimization and regularization, lean heavily on prior assumptions chosen by the algorithm designer. Their approach instead leans harder on the empirical data itself and needs fewer a priori decisions.

The authors analyze how well the paradigm generalizes and show its value under several common assumptions: nearby points being similar, domains clustering into label-homogeneous regions, Lipschitz labeling rules, and contrastive learning setups. A practical advantage is that the method can exploit such structure without knowing the true parameters in advance, which is how those assumptions usually fail to help in practice.
arxiv-2511-10296:
Florian Ebmeier, Nicole Ludwig, Jannik Thuemmel, Georg Martius, and Volker H. Franz detect faults in domestic solar thermal systems from the sensor data the systems already collect. Poor installation or maintenance can quietly slash efficiency or damage a system, and per-home human monitoring is too expensive. Their framework flags abnormal states by probabilistic reconstruction: a model rebuilds normal behavior, and poor reconstructions signal trouble.

Evaluated on the public PaSTS dataset of real operating systems with diverse fault types, reconstruction methods detected faults and generalized to systems never seen in training. The approach beat simple and more complex deep learning baselines, and estimating uncertainty that varies with conditions proved essential to performance. The authors also discuss the engineering overhead honestly and argue for simple models.
arxiv-2511-10596:
Ahmed Gamal Eldin argues that brain signals researchers often throw away are not noise but most of the message. His paper starts from a broader claim. Current artificial intelligence excels at pattern recognition but fails at causal reasoning, which in his view requires a physical architecture of coupled oscillators coordinating as a whole.

To test the idea, he analyzed high-density EEG recordings from ten subjects doing a target recognition task, measuring global phase synchronization with the Kuramoto order parameter. Phase and voltage carried largely independent yet coupled information, and synchronization unfolded in a timed cascade across frequency bands. When standard artifact rejection removed eye, muscle, and body signals, the key correlation fell threefold and target discrimination flipped sign. Eldin concludes cognition is whole-body synchronization, not brain work done alone.
arxiv-2511-10696:
Pike D. Liu, Chang Liu, and Yanxuan Yu propose pi-Attention, a sparse attention operator for long-context transformers that works online as tokens arrive. Local attention windows keep costs down but cannot reach dependencies beyond the window, a bottleneck for long-range modeling at moderate depth.

Instead of precomputing a global sparse mask, pi-Attention keeps a streaming working set of local neighbors plus a pi-indexed long-range fetch, fused by an adaptive prior under one shared softmax. The authors analyze causal reachability and minimum depth under this rule and show the per-step cost stays linear in the working set size. Experiments across context lengths from four thousand to thirty-two thousand tokens show consistent gains over local-window and other sparse baselines, approaching dense attention quality.
arxiv-2511-11296:
Shahriar Hasnat Kazi, Niall Adams, and Edward Cohen develop the first online methods for estimating the spectral density of a time series, the curve that shows how its variation splits across frequencies. Streaming inference must work with fixed memory, fixed cost per step, and the ability to adapt as the data source changes. Offline spectral tools assume a stored, stationary record, so they fail those tests.

Their method rests on forgetting factors, which let older data fade as new data arrive. A new online periodogram recovers the offline one's properties when the series is stationary, and a Whittle estimator built on it tunes its own forgetting from the data. Ocean drifter tests show real-time tracking.
arxiv-2511-11396:
Chen Deng, Yong-Feng Huang, and their colleagues model the afterglow of seven short gamma-ray bursts that show a plateau phase, a stretch where fading stalls. Short bursts follow neutron star mergers, and a plateau hints that the central engine keeps feeding energy after the blast. A magnetar, a highly magnetic spinning neutron star, is the leading candidate for that engine, but X-ray-only fits leave its traits tangled together.

Fitting X-ray, optical, and radio data together inside the magnetar injection model untangles those traits. The broader fit yields a weaker magnetic field and a shorter spin period than X-ray-only work, hence a higher injection luminosity. Energy injection reshaped most afterglows.
arxiv-2511-11496:
Hao-Cheng Weng, John Rarity, and their colleagues integrate nitrogen-vacancy centers, diamond defects that sense magnetic fields, with foundry-made silicon-nitride photonic circuits to run eight quantum sensors at once. Single sensors are powerful, but an array can track how fields vary in space and time and follow moving sources. Their platform reads each of the eight localized sensors distinctly and simultaneously, without bulky optics.

With machine learning for multi-point field reconstruction, the array localized a needle tip far smaller than a millimeter with error below the tip's own size and tracked it as it moved. Simulations extend the idea to watching magnetic microrobots built for medical use.
arxiv-2511-11596:
Javier Marín exposes a data problem at the heart of loss given default modeling, the bank task of predicting how much of a defaulted loan will be recovered. About ninety percent of training labels are proxy estimates from pre-distress balance sheets, not real recovery outcomes, so models learn from a contaminated mixture.

On more than twelve hundred corporate bankruptcies from 1980 to 2023, random forests fail badly, scoring worse than predicting the mean. Information-theoretic features based on entropy and mutual information generalize far better, and leverage carries far more signal than firm size. The lesson is blunt: label quality, not model cleverness, limits recovery prediction.
arxiv-2511-11796:
Beatrice Giudici, Michael Gabler, and Hans-Thomas Janka run long-term three-dimensional simulations of thirteen exploding red supergiant stars to watch how chemical elements mix during a supernova. Progenitor masses span roughly twelve to twenty-seven times the Sun's mass, all single, non-rotating stars.

Neutrino heating is treated parametrically to fix explosion energies, nickel yields, and neutron star properties, and each model evolves from core bounce to ten days after explosion. Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities at the shell interfaces, interacting with the reverse shock, drive outward mixing of inner elements. How mixing varies with progenitor structure helps observers read real supernova remnants and spectra.
arxiv-2511-12096:
Xi Chen and Ziyun Jin take on the Calderón problem, an inverse problem that asks what can be learned about a material from voltage and current readings at its boundary. Their setting is a curved space with a special anisotropic structure, in three or more dimensions. The conductivity may depend on both the electric potential and the electric field.

They show that all derivatives of the conductivity, taken at zero field, are uniquely fixed by those boundary measurements. If the conductivity also varies in an analytic way with the field, then the full conductivity can be recovered uniquely. The result extends exact recovery to a quasilinear, direction-dependent case.
arxiv-2511-12196:
Aditi Bhalla, Christian Hellert and Enkelejda Kasneci address driver monitoring systems that must work across camera views and sensor types. Distraction is a leading cause of road deaths, and deep learning can spot risky driver actions. In real cars, though, viewpoint changes and shifts in modality or setting can break a model trained in one setup.

Their two-phase framework first learns features that stay stable across views and still separate actions, using contrastive learning on multi-view data within one modality. It then adapts to a new modality with an information bottleneck loss, needing no labeled data from that modality. The aim is real-time monitoring that deploys across varied vehicles.
arxiv-2511-12396:
Jiacheng Wang and eleven co-authors present DEMIST, a method to synthesize quantitative myelin maps from routine brain scans. A specialized magnetic resonance technique can produce a myelin-sensitive measure tied to multiple sclerosis assessment, but it needs long, dedicated scans. Standard T1-weighted and FLAIR images are far more common.

DEMIST uses a latent diffusion model in two stages. First, autoencoders learn aligned latent forms for the target maps and the body images. Then a conditional diffusion model works in that space. It sits on a frozen foundation backbone. Conditioning is split into semantic, spatial and adaptive parts, with edge-aware losses to keep lesion borders sharp. Evaluation uses a sizable set of scans and subjects.
arxiv-2511-12496:
Jayanand Maurya, Yu Zhang and Hubiao Niu investigate why the main sequence turn-off in the open star cluster NGC 2355 is extended in color, a feature seen in many clusters. Using precise Gaia astrometry and photometry plus spectroscopic data, they test two candidate causes: stellar rotation, which darkens a star's equator, and binary tidal locking.

Turn-off stars show a clear link between rotation speed and color, supporting the rotation account. Spatial analysis adds a twist: fast rotators sit preferentially near the cluster center, contrary to what tidal locking in binaries predicts. The authors argue early interactions between young stars and their disks, rather than binaries, set the spread in rotation.
arxiv-2511-12596:
Oron Anschel and nine co-authors introduce GAPO, a training method that fights mode collapse in large language models, where the model repeats the same few completions even when many valid answers exist. The method extends a popular group-relative policy optimization approach by scoring rewards over the whole group of sampled answers, not each answer alone.

That group view lets training reward properties such as diversity and coverage directly. With a frequency-aware reward that pushes toward uniform sampling over valid completions, GAPO-trained models produce answers that are both valid and more varied. The authors report the approach also generalizes to open-ended prompts and improves diversity without hurting accuracy on standard math, code and knowledge benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-12696:
E. Nikoghosyan and five co-authors present IdentYS, a Python tool for finding young stars in star-forming regions. Young stellar objects glow with extra infrared light from the disks and envelopes around them, which sets them apart from ordinary field stars. Spotting them reliably matters because their numbers and stages reveal how embedded clusters form and evolve. IdentYS automates that search using near- and mid-infrared measurements gathered from surveys.

The tool applies five color-color diagrams, plots that separate young stars from contaminants by their infrared colors. It filters out field stars and distant galaxies that could pollute the sample, then outputs candidate lists with positions, brightness values. An estimated evolutionary stage, Class I or Class II, based on the infrared excess. The authors aim it at statistical studies of young populations, including distant and deeply embedded regions with large datasets.
arxiv-2511-13796:
Nabadwip Sarkar, Debabrata Pramanik, and Lata Mahato settle uniqueness questions for entire functions that share a value with their higher-order difference operators. The core problem asks when sharing one entire function forces two such functions to coincide. Two named conjectures, one by Liu and Laine and one by Zhang and co-authors, framed the open cases.

The authors obtain two results that confirm both conjectures as posed. Several examples accompany the proofs to show the conditions at work and to mark where the conclusions can fail without them. For value distribution theory, the work closes two stated gaps and sharpens the known map of uniqueness for difference operators.
arxiv-2511-13896:
Juan Carlos Oyola Ballesteros and Paulo M. Carvalho-Neto build a new framework for the unsteady Stokes equations, which govern slow viscous fluid flow. Their version uses a Caputo fractional derivative in time, and that nonlocal operator breaks the standard proof tools. Classical Galerkin methods cannot be applied in their usual form.

The pair design new function spaces tailored to the fractional setting and recast weak solutions inside them. With those spaces, a generalized Galerkin scheme goes through rigorously. The work extends the classical theory of these flow equations and lays groundwork for wider classes of fractional partial differential equations in fluid mechanics and nearby fields.
arxiv-2511-14296:
Chinonso Onah, Roman Firt, and Kristel Michielsen build a quantum optimizer that lives inside the feasible set instead of visiting it by luck. Their constraint-enhanced QAOA works in a one-hot product space, where each block of qubits starts in a W state encoding one choice. A depth-optimal encoder prepares those states without ancilla qubits, and a special mixer moves within the one-hot manifold without leaving it.

The authors prove per-block controllability and show the shallow circuit behaves like a unitary design after symmetry averaging, which yields anticoncentration guarantees for finite sampling. Wrapped with a deterministic feasibility checker, the sampler becomes a polynomial-time hybrid solver, and they report advantages on routing-style problems.
arxiv-2511-14596:
Irin Babu Vathachira, Yael Hillman, and Amit Kashi study how binary setup shapes nova eruptions in symbiotic systems. In these systems a white dwarf draws wind from a giant companion star. The team vary donor mass, white dwarf mass, and orbital separation across a wide grid. Accretion follows the classic wind capture picture.

All models show a long term widening of the orbit. Almost all donor mass leaves the system, either in the wind or in nova ejections. That mass loss drives orbital growth more than angular momentum sinks shrink it. Results clarify how initial binary choices control long nova histories. The grid gives a map for interpreting observed symbiotic novae.
arxiv-2511-14896:
Thijs Lenssen, Aleksandr Talitckii, and two co-authors bring a classic robustness test to systems that spread over space. Mu-analysis asks whether a control system stays stable when its model is wrong in structured ways. The authors extend it to partial integral equations, a flexible language for systems such as beams, fluids, and delay systems.

The safety conditions are written in that same framework, using integral quadratic constraints to capture what is not known for sure. Software called PIETOOLS makes the conditions computable in practice. Tests on partial and delay equations show far less caution than unstructured methods. They also give a clear way to trade stability against performance.
arxiv-2511-14996:
Jonas M. Mikhaeil, Donald P. Green, and David Blei propose a new way to measure how each scientific study changes what a field believes at the moment it appears. Standard meta-analysis pools all studies at once, looking backward, which can understate the impact of a study that shook confidence when it landed. Their method, called SMART, scores each study's influence at its entry time.

Crucially, the method lets a new study raise collective uncertainty, for instance by exposing flaws in earlier methods. The authors re-analyze two known data sets, one from psychology and one from labor economics, to show how the sequential view differs. The result is a richer history of how knowledge actually accumulates.
arxiv-2511-15196:
David Yallup benchmarks particle Monte Carlo methods for sampling problems from lattice field theory. Such high dimensional, multimodal sampling tasks have become tests for machine learning assisted samplers. Yallup shows GPU accelerated sequential Monte Carlo and nested sampling form a strong classical baseline. They match or beat top neural samplers on standard scalar field benchmarks.

Both sample quality and wall clock time favor the particle methods in these tests. They also estimate the partition function, which neural samplers typically do not. Only a single data driven covariance is needed for tuning. No problem specific structure is exploited. The results raise the bar for when learned proposals justify their training cost in lattice sampling.
arxiv-2511-15496:
Maria Pilligua and five co-authors introduce a multi illumination data set for evaluating low light image enhancement. Low light photos suffer noise and washed out color. Most learning methods train on one low light level paired with a bright reference. That narrow training hides how methods behave as light varies.

Their data set captures scenes at diverse intensities under controlled conditions with fixed camera settings. Precise illuminance measurements accompany each image. Benchmarks of leading methods reveal large performance swings across intensity levels. Using the multi level structure, the authors propose improvements to enhancement. The resource should push methods toward robustness across real lighting, not just one laboratory level.
arxiv-2511-15896:
Ying Jin and José Zubizarreta propose cross-balancing, a method for causal inference in observational studies. Causal work compares groups that differ by treatment but little else. Groups are often built from background traits alone. Using outcome data to help design that comparison could raise accuracy, yet it risks breaking the statistics. That long-standing problem is what the authors address.

Sample splitting separates error in building balancing features from error in estimating weights. The frame covers features learned as functions and features picked from a large dictionary. Under mild conditions the estimators are consistent, near normal, and efficient. Tests in simulation and an observational case show gains, with less bias and robustness when learned features converge slowly.
arxiv-2511-16496:
Rintaro Masaoka links a condensed matter system to an unusual conformal field theory. The system is a free-fermion model whose bands touch quadratically rather than at the linear Dirac points, a case whose status as a quantum critical point was unclear.

Masaoka shows the model has spatial conformal invariance, and that its ground-state correlations are exactly those of the symplectic fermion theory in one fewer dimension. Explicit maps connect the physical fermion operators to the symplectic fields. In two spatial dimensions that theory is a logarithmic conformal field theory with central charge minus two. The corresponding systems host anyonic excitations despite being gapless, and moving them around loops cycles through degenerate ground states, much as in topologically ordered phases.
arxiv-2511-16596:
Zohar Rimon and four co-authors take a step toward artificial palpation, teaching a robot to examine soft objects by touch the way a clinician's fingers do. Their idea is that an encoder-decoder system can learn a compact representation from a sequence of tactile readings that keeps everything relevant about the object being pressed.

To test it, the team built a simulation environment and a real dataset of soft objects with magnetic resonance images as ground truth. A robot with a tactile sensor collected palpation sequences, and a model learned to predict readings at new positions. The learned representation supported tactile imaging and change detection, going beyond a simple force map. The proof of concept suggests touch data, properly learned from, can reveal an object's hidden interior.
arxiv-2511-16696:
V. Apinyan and M. Sahakyan study a double-layer square-lattice system in which superconductivity and excitonic pairing might coexist. Excitonic pairing binds electrons and holes across the two layers, and the model adds phonon modulations within each layer that can reshape the charge density and the electrons' total energy.

The authors track both pairing channels, and their coexistence, as temperature, intra- and interlayer Coulomb interactions, electron-phonon coupling, doping, and an applied electric field are varied. Superconductivity is shown to arise through the influence of the intralayer phonons on the total charge density. The results bear on the long-standing puzzle of what drives superconductivity in high-temperature cuprates, since layered structures with competing orders are exactly where those materials live.
arxiv-2511-16796:
Liuyuan Jiang, Quan Xiao, Lisha Chen, and Tianyi Chen improve penalty-based methods for bilevel optimization. These nested problems sit behind hyperparameter tuning and meta-learning, where an outer objective depends on the solution of an inner one. Penalty approaches are popular for their first-order simplicity but usually pay with inner loops and tiny step sizes.

A new penalty reformulation decouples the upper and lower variables for problems with coupled constraints, and a sharper smoothness analysis then permits larger steps and lower complexity for alternating penalty gradient descent. Their PBGD-Free algorithm removes the inner loop entirely for uncoupled problems. A novel flatness condition on the upper objective relaxes the usual Lipschitz demand and shrinks the penalty's interference. Experiments on support vector machine tuning and language model fine-tuning validate the gains.
arxiv-2511-17096:
Sanjay Mishra gives a self-contained tour of how simplicial complexes, shapes built by gluing triangles and their higher-dimensional cousins, can be subdivided into finer pieces. The focus is barycentric subdivision, which splits each piece by adding its center point and starring outward. Mishra shows that subdivision leaves the overall shape unchanged, so finer meshes describe the same space.

Formal definitions, worked examples, and detailed diagrams carry the exposition. The paper proves that repeating barycentric subdivision shrinks the mesh below any chosen scale, a fact that underpins simplicial approximation and homology computations. The treatment suits readers meeting the subject for the first time, since nothing is assumed beyond the basics developed along the way.
arxiv-2511-17196:
Yingkai Zhang and three co-authors work on cleaning noise from hyperspectral images, which record light in many narrow bands and serve remote sensing and inspection tasks. Real sensor noise is a messy blend, hard to model exactly. Methods that train on synthetic noise therefore disappoint on real photographs. The team's answer is to decouple the noise: split it into a part that existing models describe well and a remainder that must be learned from real paired data.

A denoising network is first pretrained on generated pairs, giving it prior knowledge of the modeled component. A second network, guided by high-frequency wavelet features, then removes the unmodeled remainder from real images. Joint fine-tuning across stages limits error build-up. On public and self-captured datasets, the framework beat leading methods on complex real-world noise.
arxiv-2511-17296:
Jozef Strecka and Michal Nemcik explore a magnetic material in theory: a chain of octahedra carrying spin one-half Heisenberg couplings in three distinct strengths, placed in a magnetic field. Using variational proofs, an extended localized-magnon approach, and exact diagonalization, they map the chain's magnetic and thermal behavior. In the frustrated regime, two distinct fragmented phases appear, built from singlet patterns on each square plaquette.

Bound magnon states, pairs of excitations locked together, together with localized single magnons, support a general theory that matches the exact numerics across the whole field range. The theory explains magnetization plateaus at one fifth and three fifths of saturation, whose crossing points encode how degenerate the competing phases are. Heat capacity shows double peaks at field-driven transitions. The system also cools well as the field is removed, making it a candidate for magnetic refrigeration.
arxiv-2511-17396:
Tomáš Domes and Pavel Veselý refine ReqSketch, a data structure that summarizes huge data streams well enough to answer quantile questions with relative error guarantees. Such sketches matter when data is spread across machines or sensor networks, because summaries from different sources must merge cleanly. ReqSketch, already adopted in the Apache DataSketches library, is the most space-efficient design with both relative error control and mergeability, but its mergeability proof was notoriously intricate.

The authors introduce adaptive compactors, a refinement that yields a far simpler proof of the error guarantees in the most general merging setting. The refinement keeps the same space bound, update time, and simple algorithm. In specific scenarios, such as merging sketches of comparable size, the new analysis even gives near-optimal space bounds. The paper strengthens a tool practitioners already rely on.
arxiv-2511-17596:
Yassir Benhammou, Suman Kalyan, and Sujay Kumar teach one model to understand broadcast content across text, audio, and video together. Media organizations drown in manual tagging, and most automated systems read only one channel at a time, missing how the channels inform each other. Their Multimodal Autoencoder learns a unified representation by reconstructing all three modalities jointly, trained on the LUMA dataset of aligned multimodal triplets drawn from real media material.

Because the model must rebuild each channel from a shared representation, it discovers semantic structures that survive across modalities, without needing large paired or contrastive datasets. On clustering and alignment measures, the learned embeddings beat linear baselines by a wide margin. The authors present reconstruction-driven learning as a foundation for scalable metadata and cross-modal search in broadcast archives.
arxiv-2511-18196:
Tyler A. Gordon and 11 co-authors rework seven planet transit data sets from the James Webb Space Telescope in one shared way. The COMPASS program studies small planets with the NIRSpec tool, which records how starlight changes as a planet crosses its star. Small signals and steady noise have made some of these results hard to read.

The team models the shape and drift of the light trace to clean the data. They find the fix helps most when each reading uses few groups, and that noise is worst in one mid range of light. Real errors run just a bit above the forecast tool. New limits on what the planet air may hold close the work.
arxiv-2511-18396:
Jinhao Li, Sarah M. Erfani, Lei Feng, James Bailey, and Feng Liu test whether a weak model can train a strong one for image and text sorting. Human review cannot keep pace as models grow past human skill in some lanes. A weak teacher that grades a strong pupil could ease that load, a plan shown to work for text only models.

The team extend the plan to CLIP, a model that sorts images by text match. Their method learns class core points, sharp typical forms of each class, to lift the strong model's sort skill. Gains would show the weak to strong plan ports to mixed media. The work probes a key route to safe growth of strong models.
arxiv-2511-18496:
Tomoyuki Yamakami studies how to train an adiabatic evolutionary quantum system to perform machine learning tasks. The system, a form of quantum annealing driven by input dependent Hamiltonians, is controlled by families of quantum automata. Training it amounts to finding an optimal controlling automaton for a target problem.

Yamakami develops a way to use known quantum methods for counting, amplitude estimation, and close estimation inside that search. A rough speed estimate for the resulting learning methods is provided. The work connects a theory based quantum computing model with useful questions about how efficiently such systems can be taught to solve relational problems.
arxiv-2511-18596:
Onofre Rojas studies a decorated one-dimensional magnet model called a coupled twin-diamond chain, inspired by the magnetic structure of a real copper compound. The model is built from Ising spins, simple up-or-down units, arranged in linked diamond units. By mapping it exactly onto a simpler effective chain, Rojas obtains the full thermal description through a compact transfer-matrix method, a rare exact result for a frustrated system.

The ground state splits into five distinct phases, two of them frustrated with a vast number of equal-energy arrangements. Those regions leave fingerprints as plateaus in the entropy and divide the ordered phases. At low temperature the model shows sharp yet smooth swings in entropy, magnetisation, and response, signs of pseudotransitions, appearing in twin features that the paper charts.
arxiv-2511-19096:
Eni Musta and Joris Mooij examine a subtle question in medical statistics: how can researchers tell if a treatment effect fades over time? The issue shapes booster vaccine advice and long-term cost studies. Simple comparisons of hazard curves in trials can mislead, because the groups still at risk change in uneven ways.

The authors review safer options, including survival curves and newer causal hazard ratios built on principal stratification or controlled direct effects. Those ratios need strong assumptions, though bounds can still be derived. A key warning follows: a causal hazard ratio moving toward one does not by itself prove that protection is fading.
arxiv-2511-19196:
Murat Uzundag and colleagues make the scientific case for observing pulsating white dwarfs with the PLATO space mission. White dwarfs are the dense remains of sun-like stars, and their pulsations reveal what lies inside them. PLATO offers precise brightness measures, long steady monitoring, and wide sky coverage suited to that work.

The team seeks internal structure, chemical layering, slow changes in pulsation modes, and rare new classes of pulsators, across hydrogen-rich and hydrogen-poor types. They build a sample of hundreds of candidates in PLATO's southern field using Gaia data. Simulations with PlatoSim show pulsations as small as a tenth of a milli-magnitude should be detectable.
arxiv-2511-19296:
Fedor Bakharev and Sergey Matveenko study trapped states in a smoothly bent strip. They use a fractional form of the Laplace operator, which spreads its effect beyond nearby points. For the plain operator, bending a guide is known to create bound states below the main spectrum. Those states stay held in the bend. The fractional case is harder because the operator acts at a distance.

Using an extension method, the authors prove such bound states exist here too, with fixed values at the edge. They give rules for how strong the bend must be and how its curve is spread along the strip. A classic bending effect thus carries into the fractional setting.
arxiv-2511-19396:
Jorge Ortigoso-Narro and four co-authors build an embedded system that listens where a moving object is. The device joins camera-based tracking with acoustic beamforming, steering a microphone array's focus in real time. Single-camera depth estimates plus stereo vision locate objects in three dimensions.

The array is a flat concentric circle of small MEMS microphones, compact and power-thrifty, steering across both azimuth and elevation. Tracking output updates the focus continuously, so the captured sound follows the target even among competing sources. Tests show clear gains in signal-to-interference ratio, suiting the design for teleconferencing, smart homes, and assistive hearing tools.
arxiv-2511-19496:
Yang Liu, Xiaolong Zhong, and Ling Jiang present Xmodel-2. 5, a small language model of just over a billion parameters built to serve as the reasoning core of an agent on modest hardware. Large models reason and use tools well but cost too much for edge or budget-sensitive deployment. Their training uses a parameterisation trick that lets settings tuned on a tiny proxy model transfer directly to the full one. Even with its tied embedding design, saving the usual retuning at scale.

A long curriculum of warmup, stable, and decay phases runs on well over a trillion tokens. Switching the optimiser midway through the decay phase lifts the average across thirteen reasoning tasks, the team reports, with all else held fixed. Mixed low-precision training balances accuracy with speed, and checkpoints and recipes are shared.
arxiv-2511-19696:
Aristides Kontogeorgis and Orestis Lygdas compute explicit bases for the de Rham cohomology of cyclic covers of the projective line. Such covers are curves built by wrapping one line around another in a repeating pattern, defined over fields of any characteristic. Cohomology groups measure the curve's shape in algebraic terms.

Both Kummer and Artin-Schreier families are handled. The authors pin down bases for two sheaf cohomology groups through divisor and residue calculations plus a duality pairing, then assemble a basis for the first de Rham group from Čech data. Everything is closed form in the cover's defining equation, ready for work on group actions and p-cyclic covers.
arxiv-2511-20096:
Ahmed, Armaghan, Naweed, and colleagues build an early warning system for forest fires. Their 2025 paper compares top detection models on new data. Catching fires at the smoke-plume stage saves forests. Existing datasets mostly show fires already raging widely. Models trained on them miss faint early signs.

The team generated early-fire images inside a game engine. Red Dead Redemption 2 supplied synthetic smoke and flame scenes. Published real images were merged into the dataset. Four detectors were benchmarked on the combined set. YOLOv7 and its tiny variant faced detection transformers. Transformers entered forest fire prediction here for the first time. YOLOv7 posted the highest accuracy and fastest inference. Its memory footprint suits small embedded devices. YOLOv7-tiny was judged best overall for early warning. Deformable DETR produced fewer false alarms instead. But it missed more fires and ran slower. Watchtower cameras could run the tiny model continuously.
arxiv-2511-20296:
Shi, Jiang, Lian, Yu, and Fu rebuild CT scans from few views with one provable model. Their 2025 paper presents PromptCT for sparse-view reconstruction. Sparse scans cut patient radiation dose substantially. Missing angles leave heavy streak artifacts though. Clinics need one model per view setting today.

Separate models for each setting cost too much storage. Worse, prior networks rarely prove their stability properties. LipNet, their prior network, is Lipschitz by construction. That bound is proved explicitly, not just hoped. A prompt module tells the network the sampling setting. One model then serves many view counts. The unfolding framework embeds LipNet as its prior. Convergence of the iteration is analyzed formally. Simulated and real data both tested the system. Image quality beat benchmark reconstruction methods. Storage costs dropped versus per-setting rivals. Data and code are publicly shared. Hospital deployment gets simpler and safer.
arxiv-2511-20696:
Dan Li, Hye-Bin Shin, and Yeon-Woo Choi tackle in 2025 a headache for brain-computer interfaces: decoding that forgets earlier users. Brainwave signals differ so much between people that a decoder trained on new users overwrites what it learned from old ones. The usual cure stores old recordings and replays them, but privacy rules and memory limits make that unattractive. Their framework, ProNECL, keeps the knowledge while storing no original signals.

Instead of recordings, ProNECL stores one prototype per class: an average feature pattern for each imagined movement. When a new subject's brainwave data arrives, feature alignment pulls its patterns toward the stored prototypes. Knowledge distillation, training the new model to mimic the old one's behaviour, guards earlier learning. On the BCI Competition IV benchmarks, datasets 2a and 2b, the framework balanced remembering old subjects against adapting to new ones better than rival continual-learning methods did.
arxiv-2511-20996:
Jingxi Chen and colleagues teach in 2025 an image model a new trick by recycling one. Editors love layered images, foreground objects separated from background so each can be edited, but splitting a photo into layers is hard and training data is scarce. The team noticed layer decomposition is inpainting and outpainting in disguise: remove the object and fill the background, or extract the object and complete its covered parts.

So they fine-tuned a diffusion-based inpainting model for the job, adding a fusion module mixing text and image context with linear-cost attention to preserve detail. Training used a synthetic dataset built from open-source assets. On background object removal the adapted model gained 1.71 decibels of PSNR, a fidelity score, and cut the FID gap by 9.99 points over baselines. It recovered occluded object parts better than rivals on the MULAN dataset, and a user study backed the gains.
arxiv-2511-21196:
Economists Zhang Xu and Wei Zhao tackle a design problem in 2025: which signals, meaning structured releases of information, can be shared without breaking privacy limits? Their framework ranks signals by the Blackwell order, a standard way to say one signal teaches strictly more than another. The authors describe the full frontier of allowed signals, the best achievable trade-offs between usefulness and privacy.

Xu and Zhao show that this frontier splits into two building blocks. One block is the minimum informative signals, the leanest signals that still reach the privacy frontier for the guarded variables. The other block keeps privacy intact once some information is already out. They characterize the first block completely, then apply the framework to ex-post privacy notions such as differential and inferential privacy, and to limits on average beliefs after release.
arxiv-2511-21296:
Milan Rosko builds in 2025 a toy radar model inside Minkowski spacetime to show a sharp limit on what measurement can ever certify. An observer bounces pulses off a stationary reflector and infers its distance from the round-trip time. Rosko chooses a computable family of distances, each between 1 and 1.5 units, encoding whether a given computer program halts: a hair above 1 gives the halting step, while exactly 1 means it never halts.

Any fixed-precision radar protocol terminates, returning an interval whose error shrinks as precision grows. Yet deciding from finite data whether the reflector sits at exactly distance 1 would solve the halting problem, which is impossible. Rosko proves the consequence: every effective theory sound about such absence claims, statements that no reflector exists beyond a bound, leaves infinitely many true ones undecided. These statements have the logical form called Pi-1 sentences, universal claims no finite evidence can settle.
arxiv-2511-21396:
Rafał Gruszczyński, Paula Menchón, and William Zuluaga give a logical algebra for spatial contact in a 2025 paper bridging geometry and logic. Standard contact algebras describe when two regions touch, using a two-place relation. The extended contact relation, introduced by Ivanova in 2020, uses three places, capturing richer claims like one region connecting two others, and Boolean algebras carrying it are called extended contact algebras.

Gruszczyński and his coauthors recast the ternary relation as entailment, one region's contact forcing a conclusion. They define pseudo-inference algebras, PSI-algebras for short, where a monotone ternary operator replaces the relation outright. The relational members of this class match extended contact algebras exactly, and the strict ones form a discriminator variety. Extending Stone duality, they build descriptive frames and establish three related dualities, giving the structures a unified spatial and logical meaning.
arxiv-2511-21696:
Wei Liu, Muhammad Aamir Ali, and Yanrong An rebuild the calculus of interval-valued functions from new arithmetic, in 2025. Intervals represent quantities known only within bounds, but the classical rules for them have a defective structure where some problems cannot be solved. The space of intervals ends up only semilinear, frustrating rigorous work.

Under the authors' new operations, the interval space turns into a strict linear space, indeed a Hilbert space with distance, norm, and inner product. Derivatives and integrals built on these operations keep every key property of classical calculus while borrowing tricks from multiplicative calculus. The hybrid framework removes the case-by-case switching-point checks that the older gH-derivative demands. The paper proves an existence theorem for such equations and tests the method on examples. Unlike the gH approach, the count of possible solutions does not explode as switching points multiply.
arxiv-2511-21896:
Dabash and colleagues compare two methods for finding symmetries and conserved quantities in f(R) gravity, where Einstein's curvature term becomes a general function. They work with the Reissner-Nordström spacetime, the geometry around a charged, non-rotating black hole, building a canonical Lagrangian for its radial metric functions and the curvature scalar.

The standard Noether approach ties symmetries of the action to conservation laws, and the authors classify its symmetries and write down explicit generators. The Mei approach instead demands that the equations of motion themselves stay unchanged, which suits higher-order theories. For the quadratic model where f(R) equals R squared, the Mei analysis produced eight independent symmetry generators and new conserved currents, some with no Noether counterpart at all in their results. Mei symmetries thus extend the older framework for black hole dynamics.
arxiv-2511-21996:
Zhang and Liu develop error theory for finite element methods simulating incompressible flow, here the steady Oseen equations. The methods use H(div)-conforming elements, which respect the flow's divergence structure. Pressure robustness, velocity errors independent of pressure difficulty, is vital at high Reynolds numbers.

Standard analyses lean on a commuting diagram property of the element pair, which some attractive elements simply lack. The authors prove optimal-order convergence of the velocity error without assuming it, adding vorticity stabilization to handle convection-dominated regimes. They use exact de Rham and finite element complexes to obtain estimates independent of the discrete inf-sup constant, a quantity that usually pollutes such bounds. As a representative example, Stenberg elements demonstrate the framework and bring pressure robustness plus fewer degrees of freedom than classical Raviart-Thomas or BDM elements, thanks to vertex continuity. The method extends to other pairs violating the property.
arxiv-2511-22296:
López-Santiago, Martino, Miguez, and Vázquez-Vilar, statisticians in Spain, help Bayesian inference find a needle-like period. In models of oscillating data, exoplanet radial velocities, pulsating stars, eclipsing binaries, the posterior for the period concentrates in a tiny sliver of parameter space. Samplers with a vague prior waste their effort everywhere else. Their empirical-Bayes recipe first fits a Gaussian process with a periodic kernel to the data, extracting a posterior for the kernel's period hyperparameter by adaptive importance sampling.

That posterior is then passed forward, with no feedback, as an informative prior for the period in the scientist's actual parametric model, while all other parameters keep independent priors. On synthetic and real data the transfer improves inference without biasing it. The method is aimed at the many astronomical time series where the oscillation is the whole scientific target.
arxiv-2511-22396:
Shao and colleagues diagnose a failure mode of vision-language models on satellite and aerial images. The models produce chains of reasoning that are not grounded in the picture, a habit the authors call pseudo reasoning. They blame a Glance Effect: the model takes one coarse look at a large image and then reasons from its own words rather than returning to visual evidence.

Their fix, RS-EoT, forces an alternating loop of reasoning and evidence seeking. A self-play system named SocraticAgent, with reasoner, perceiver, and verifier roles, generates training traces in this style. A two-stage reinforcement learning plan first sharpens fine-grained grounding and then generalises to question answering. The resulting model reached state-of-the-art results on several remote sensing question-answering and grounding benchmarks. Its behaviour showed cycles of checking the image, supporting the claim that the Glance Effect was reduced.
arxiv-2511-22596:
Roskill, Maleubre, Alonso, and Ferreira extend a shortcut for mining non-Gaussian information from the cosmos. Skew-spectra square a map and cross-correlate it with the original, capturing three-point information while reusing power spectrum machinery and avoiding three-point statistics. Until now the trick worked only for scalar fields. The authors generalise it to fields of arbitrary spin, the kind carried by cosmic shear and cosmic microwave background polarisation.

Applying the formalism to weak gravitational lensing, they build statistics from shear field combinations that avoid mass-mapping, a reconstruction step other lensing statistics need. Predictions in the standard model show the statistics' shapes are driven by Wigner 3j symbol behaviour near filter edges. Predictions map how signals respond to parameters such as clustering amplitude and matter density. Which statistics earn a place in survey pipelines, balancing signal-to-noise, robustness, and constraining power, is future work.
arxiv-2511-22696:
Alvarez-Trejos and colleagues bring calibration and fusion to the probabilities inside neural speaker diarization. Diarization answers who spoke when, and end-to-end neural systems output frame-level probabilities per speaker, but the field judges them only by error rate, ignoring whether their confidence scores mean anything. The authors build the first comprehensive framework for calibrating these probabilities and fusing several models' soft outputs, comparing multilabel and powerset representations on the CallHome two-speaker benchmark.

Proper calibration alone cut individual models' error by up to 19 percent relative in the reported experiments, sometimes substituting for missing domain adaptation. Joint calibration in powerset space beat independent per-speaker calibration, 8.26 percent against 9.18 percent error, by modelling speaker dependencies explicitly. Fusing models then calibrating the combination, with dynamic logits fusion, reached 6.543 percent error, beating standard DOVER-Lap fusion by 5.2 percent relative while calibrating only one combined model.
arxiv-2511-22796:
Banerjee, Scammell, and Scheurer work out how to tell where a material's directional preferences originate. In many two-dimensional superconductors, resistance and critical current both vary with direction, signalling broken rotational symmetry. That breaking might originate in the normal metal, through nematic order, or in the superconductor itself, whose remnants, vestigial order, can linger after superconductivity melts. The authors analyse how the two anisotropies correlate in each scenario.

The correlations are fingerprints. When breaking comes only from the normal state with isotropic pairing, the directions of maximum critical current and maximum resistivity sit perpendicular. A nematic superconductor can flip that relation depending on its order parameter's parity, and when the superconductor alone breaks the symmetry, vestigial order gives yet another pattern. The theory also covers finite-momentum pairing with its own vestigial order. Measuring both anisotropies in materials like twisted graphene thus constrains the breaking's microscopic origin.
arxiv-2511-23396:
Jalali and colleagues test a modified theory of gravity as an alternative explanation for the universe's accelerating expansion. In a generalized hybrid metric-Palatini model where spacetime curvature is built both from the metric and from an independent connection. They add a non-minimal coupling between matter and the Palatini part of the geometry. Then show the theory can be rewritten as a bi-scalar-tensor gravity with two scalar fields.

Confronted with cosmic chronometer data, baryon acoustic oscillation measurements from DESI, and the Pantheon+ supernova compilation. The model fits as a good alternative to the standard cosmological-constant picture, though ordinary matter is conserved only at the background level. A statefinder analysis finds its dark-energy behavior crosses from quintessence-like to phantom-like at a redshift near 0.86 in the past, tracks the standard model closely at late times, and turns phantom in the future.
arxiv-2512-00396:
Detecting gait from a wearable sensor could help track Parkinson's disease outside the clinic. Andrea Procopio and co-authors study tiny separable convolutional networks for wearable gait detection in 2025. They work with short windows of triaxial acceleration on resource-constrained devices.

The team compares magnitude thresholding with three one-dimensional convolutional networks, including an ultra-light purely separable model and one with residual connections. They also study optimal sensor placement. Small, efficient models matter because a wearable must run all day on a tiny battery while still catching the gait changes clinicians care about. Short acceleration windows keep the data rate low enough for cheap wearables. Sensor placement decides signal quality before any model runs, so optimizing it matters.
arxiv-2512-00596:
Recommender systems increasingly receive rich multimodal features from language models, but those features are high-dimensional and noisy. Jiahao Tian and Zhenkai Wang present DLRREC in 2025, a framework that denoises latent representations through multimodal knowledge fusion. Treating the features as static inputs decouples them from the recommendation task.

The framework is built on deeply fusing multimodal and collaborative knowledge for representation denoising. Collaborative signals record what users actually chose, grounding the language model's descriptive features. Cleaner representations should sharpen recommendations in media and shopping systems that now lean heavily on model-generated descriptions. Denoising inside the model beats cleaning features once, because the task itself guides the cleaning. For folks who shop or watch on their phones, the gain is picks that feel less random. The noise is wrung out, and the true likes shine through more clearly.
arxiv-2512-00696:
Hasi Hays, Yue Yu, and William Richardson introduce Hierarchical Molecular Language Models in a 2025 paper on cell biology. Artificial intelligence is changing how biologists decode the networks cells use to signal each other. Their idea treats cell signaling as a specialized language with its own parts and rules.

In that picture, signaling molecules act as tokens, the words of the language. Protein interactions supply the syntax, or grammar, that joins them. The effects that follow supply the semantics, or meaning. Framing signals this way lets language model tools work on cell communication. That could help researchers predict how cells respond when signals change.
arxiv-2512-00896:
Jiang Zhou and Changjiang Bu study the spectra of graphs and hypergraphs in a 2025 math paper. A graph's spectrum is a set of numbers from its connection matrix that summarize its structure. The largest of them, the spectral radius, is especially telling.

The authors link the spectral radius to local structures, the small patterns sitting inside a graph. They show that when a certain ratio of spectral values is large, particular local subgraphs or subhypergraphs must appear. They also bound the local vector chromatic number using tensor eigenvalues. Such results let one number reveal what small shapes a network must contain.
arxiv-2512-00996:
Raymond Hinton, Pepa Ramírez Cobo, and Brani Vidakovic present a new view on measuring signal roughness in a 2025 paper. Self-similar signals look alike at many scales, and the Hurst exponent sums up their long-memory roughness. Wavelet methods estimate it by watching how detail energy decays across decomposition levels.

The authors define dual wavelet spectra, an alternative starting point for that estimate. They apply the idea to mammogram classification, where texture differences can separate healthy tissue from signs of disease. A better roughness measure could sharpen such texture-based tools, giving radiologists one more signal in a hard screening task.
arxiv-2512-01396:
Zhiqing Zhong, Jiaming Huang, and Pinjia He build a test for patch backporting. Software grows fast, with new traits and safety fixes. Many users stay on old versions since upgrades can break their code. Backporting moves a fix from a new version to an old one by hand.

That hand work is slow and prone to error. The team made BackportBench to score tools that do it on their own. The test spans more than one language. Good scores would show which tools can keep old code safe with less human toil and less risk of a bad port.
arxiv-2512-01996:
Teaching a humanoid robot to walk inside a simulation is fast now, thanks to massively parallel computing that cut training from days to minutes. Younggyo Seo and co-authors present a 2025 recipe that makes the transfer to a real robot both quick and reliable, despite the jump from virtual to physical.

The transfer is hard because humanoid control is high-dimensional, and randomizing the simulation to cover reality adds further strain. Their recipe builds on off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms, which reuse past experience efficiently. The title's promise is training in about a quarter of an hour. Fast, dependable transfer would let robot skills be developed at software speed.
arxiv-2512-02096:
The James Webb Space Telescope found a puzzling new class of distant objects: compact, red points of light with a distinctive V-shaped spectrum. Shuqi Fu and ten co-authors report in 2025 on two of these little red dots that appear to be turning into quasars.

The dots' broad hydrogen emission lines suggest active galactic nuclei, black holes feeding at their centers, hidden inside. Catching two in transition offers a rare before-and-after view of how these objects evolve. The discovery helps astronomers decide what little red dots are and how they connect to the growth of early black holes and galaxies.
arxiv-2512-02196:
Lead titanate is a crystal with a built-in electric slant: its charges sit slightly off center, and they can be flipped. It is also a semiconductor with useful traits for light-based work. Pietro Pacchioni, Lorenzo Varrassi, and Cesare Franchini compute in 2025 how its bent shape changes its excitons. Excitons are bound pairs of an electron and a hole, and they shape how the crystal takes in light.

A sound first-principles account of the light spectrum was still missing. So was a clear view of what the bent shape does to it. That gap counts, since the crystal is a prospect for splitting water with light and for light-based devices. If bending the lattice steers the excitons, strain becomes a knob for tuning the response.
arxiv-2512-02696:
Omid Reza Heidari, Yang Wang, and Xinxin Zuo adapt object detection for security X-ray scans across different machines. A detector trained on one scanner often fails on another, since devices and settings shift the images. Such domain gaps degrade performance in real screening work.

Their ALDI-ray method adapts the ALDI framework to X-ray object detection. The goal is steady detection of threats despite scanner changes, without full retraining each time. Reliable adaptation matters at airports and borders, where new machines should not mean missed bags or long retraining delays. Scans change when bags move to a new hall, so a tool that adapts on the fly saves real time.
arxiv-2512-02796:
Menhaz Ahammed, Matthew Campbell, and Han-Bom Moon hunt for the simplest curves that fill a surface in algebraic geometry. Their surface is the product of two projective lines, a basic four dimensional stage. A space filling curve there must be smooth and reach every part of the surface.

The authors prove that plenty of minimal degree examples exist, in an explicit sense. The result extends an earlier existence theorem by Homma and Kim. Explicit families matter because geometers can compute with them, testing broader ideas about curves on surfaces over any base field. Plain forms that peers can write down beat vague claims that some curve must exist out there in the dark.
arxiv-2512-02896:
Akankshya Majhi and four co-authors study how ridged walls stir a thick fluid that only flows above a stress threshold. Yield stress fluids, like gels and pastes, resist motion until pushed hard enough. The standard Herschel-Bulkley model treats that threshold as a fixed material constant.

In Couette systems, where fluid is sheared between surfaces, ridges change the flow pattern. The title reports that ridged geometries induce axial flow vortices. Side flows of this kind affect mixing and transport in processing equipment that handles pastes, foods, and slurries every day. Ridges are cheap to make and hard to fake, so flow marks they leave are a fair test of how pastes move in plant gear.
arxiv-2512-02996:
Asim Sharma and Avah Banerjee coax quantum chaos from circuits built by rule, not by lottery. Quantum chaos shows in entanglement spectra that follow Wigner-Dyson statistics and in decaying out of time order correlators. Random circuits reach that behavior, but hardware builders prefer deterministic constructions that repeat across platforms.

The pair studies derandomized Clifford plus T circuits with causal cover architectures. Candidate designs include bitonic sorting networks and permutation based routing circuits. Structured routes to chaos could give benchmarks and random unitary designs that any quantum lab can reproduce exactly. Rule built chaos can be set, set, and set once more with the same end state. Prize tests and shared marks both need that trait to work.
arxiv-2512-03396:
Decisions under deep uncertainty can be framed in two orders. Zachary Van Oosten and Ruodu Wang compare those orders in this 2025 work. A decision maker has a statistic for pure-risk preferences, like expected utility, and faces an ambiguous act.

One framework evaluates the act under each plausible model, then aggregates. The other aggregates first, then evaluates. The order can change the final choice, so the difference matters. Clarifying it helps in finance and insurance, where ambiguity about models is unavoidable. Order effects warn analysts that two sound steps can still yield different decisions.
arxiv-2512-03596:
Health cost studies hinge on whose costs count. Dylan Mordaunt presents a Python tool for that choice in this 2025 work. Studies differ under a health system view versus a wider social view, and guides often urge one of them.

The cost of that choice is rarely measured, though it can flip a funding call. The tool supports fair cost studies across groups and a value-of-view check. It shows how often the two views lead to unlike choices. Clearer counts help leaders fund care that is fair and works well.
arxiv-2512-04096:
Meta's advertising systems must copy messages to thousands of consumers across data centres worldwide, in order and without loss, within seconds. Sushant Kumar Gupta and colleagues describe the system built for that job, Fast ACS, in a 2025 preprint. The design is file-based and leans on two communication styles for its two scales of problem.

Between clusters, the system uses remote procedure calls. Inside a cluster, it uses one-sided remote memory access. Consumers pull messages at their own pace instead of being flooded. Ordering and at-least-once delivery are guaranteed by design. The deployment record is substantial: dozens of production clusters, several thousand consumers per cluster, and terabit-scale internal traffic at peak. Delivery worldwide lands within a few seconds, often under one second at the ninety-ninth percentile.
arxiv-2512-04296:
Fine-tuning a transformer normally means retraining billions of weights; parameter-efficient methods update only a sliver instead. Malyaban Bal and Abhronil Sengupta introduce GRASP in a 2025 machine learning preprint, a fine-tuning scheme built on grouped activation sharing. It also targets a deployment problem: models that must survive noisy, energy-stingy edge hardware.

GRASP partitions token representations in layers into a small number of groups, learning one shared scaling and shifting vector per group. That slashes trainable parameters while keeping task-specific learning. A stochastic variant, StochGRASP, learns Gaussian perturbations to the pretrained weights and trains with a noise-aware loss, modelling hardware variability. On GLUE benchmarks with RoBERTa models and on an E2E generation task with GPT-2, the method matches or beats established approaches. It uses an order of magnitude fewer trainable parameters than LoRA. Under noise, the stochastic variant consistently wins.
arxiv-2512-04796:
Pedro Caro and Alberto Ruiz extend a uniqueness result for the initial-to-final-state inverse problem in quantum mechanics to Hamiltonians with unbounded potentials. The problem asks whether knowing a system's state at one fixed time, for every possible starting state, determines the Hamiltonian that drove it. The authors framed the question to explain why data-driven prediction can work in quantum settings at all. Their earlier work settled the bounded case, where potentials decay fast at infinity. Their 2025 arXiv paper removes that comfort.

The key step proves a family of Strichartz estimates, including the sharp endpoint case of Keel and Tao. A counterexample in the paper shows that Bourgain spaces, a rival tool, cannot capture the needed mixed norms here. That limit result justifies the harder route. Uniqueness for rougher potentials widens the class of quantum systems whose rules can, in principle, be read off from observed behavior.
arxiv-2512-04996:
Qiong Chang, Weimin Wang, Junpei Zhong, and Jun Miyazaki work on making a fast three-dimensional scanning method fit on small hardware. The method, called VANICP, matches up point clouds — the clouds of measured points that describe a surface — by spreading neighbor information outward instead of searching the whole cloud each time. It is quick, but it eats memory, which shuts it out of the modest graphics chips in embedded devices.

The team adds a memory plan that hands out and reuses space for the spreading step only as needed. Built into a new version of the framework, the plan cuts memory use by more than ninety-seven percent while keeping the original speed. The code is released openly, so builders of robots and compact scanners can run accurate point cloud matching on hardware that could not hold the method before.
arxiv-2512-05196:
Davis Welakuh, Vasil Rokaj, Michael Ruggenthaler, and Angel Rubio detail cheaper ways to handle light with many modes when it couples to matter. In cavity quantum electrodynamics, atoms and molecules sit inside structured light fields, and tracking every mode of the field is ruinously expensive. For equilibrium properties, though, the authors show much of that complexity can be cut away without losing the physics.

They lay out a family of approximations: keeping only the electric field's polarization part in one formulation, or replacing the many modes with a few effective ones. The methods are designed to stay accurate from weak to strong coupling and across complicated photonic environments. The team demonstrates them on atomic and molecular models and on a two-dimensional quantum ring, showing the shortcuts are versatile. The work lays groundwork for first-principles simulations of real materials inside optical cavities.
arxiv-2512-05696:
Paula Mellado, Francisco Muñoz, and Javiera Cabezas-Escares study a striped state of charge in a toy system built from two chain-like legs. In a charge density wave, electrons settle into a regular pattern of higher and lower density that need not match the crystal lattice. The team uses a half filled, four band ladder model. A slight shift between the legs creates a moiré pattern that flattens energy bands near the Fermi level.

Once short range repulsion between electrons is switched on, the pattern that forms is excitonic, driven by bound pairs of electrons and holes. The wave's shaking splits into two collective modes: a gapped amplitude mode, and a gapless sliding mode carried by long lived neutral phasons. The results warn that even tiny mismatches between layers can reshape charge order in layered materials. They also suggest the puzzling charge wave in hafnium tritelluride is excitonic.
arxiv-2512-05896:
János Engländer turns a classic puzzle about lonely passengers into a moving process. The original problem, due to Tóth, seats passengers at random in empty buses and counts the lonely ones. More buses tend not to reduce the lonely count. Engländer's step is to treat the number of buses as time itself. At each moment the state is Tóth's seating with that many buses, and all passenger counts couple into one object: the detachment process.

Detachment is the event where every passenger sits alone. The paper studies when detachment happens and how clumping behaves. Four critical time scales govern the story, tied to the passenger count, its square, and logarithmic corrections. Modeling passengers with a Poisson distribution simplifies the analysis, aided by a comparison theorem with a new proof. The process is a clean lens on random occupancy.
arxiv-2512-05996:
Yi Liu, Jingyu Song, Vedanth Kallakuri, and Katherine Skinner teach one model to find, outline, and count fish underwater, using only sparse hints for training. Underwater imagery is murky, and dense labeling is expensive. FishDetector-R1 is a unified multimodal framework working under weak supervision. On the standard DeepFish benchmark it beats baselines clearly: detection accuracy up twenty percent, segmentation quality up ten, counting errors down by roughly a third.

Two ingredients drive the gains. A detect-to-count prompt forces the model's detections and its count to agree spatially, so the fish it lists are the fish it numbers. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards tunes it further. The improvements transfer to other underwater datasets. Surveys could run on a model trained from points and prompts. Automated counting would change how widely ocean health gets measured.
arxiv-2512-06196:
Charlie Masters, Marta Grzeskiewicz, and Stefano Albrecht present ARCANE, a way to steer long running AI agents while keeping their goals open to view. When an agent works for hours, its owners need to see what it is being scored on. They also need to change that scoring without training the system again.

ARCANE turns user wishes into short written rubrics: weighted lists of checks that anyone can read. A team of model based agents drafts and refines these rubrics from the task at hand. The rubrics are learned with a tuned training method that balances clear wording, faith to the user's wishes, and low cost. In tests on hard tasks that need many steps and tools, the rubrics gave compact scores and let users swap goals, such as favoring right answers over short ones, at run time.
arxiv-2512-06296:
Sooho Moon and Yunyong Ko argue that the usual scores for fact guessing systems grade them with a blind spot. These systems fill gaps in webs of facts, such as who directed a film or where a person was born. Standard scores can be too lax or too strict about near misses, and they favor facts about famous things over rare ones.

Their framework, PROBE, adds two lenses to grading. One step rescales each guess by how strict the grader wants to be. The next adds the scores up in a way that gives rare items their fair weight. On real fact webs, the authors show that old scores can puff up or shrink a model's true skill, while PROBE gives a steadier picture. Better grading matters because labs pick which models to build on based on these very scores.
arxiv-2512-06396:
Shovan Roy presents AgenticCyber, a team of AI agents built to watch for cyber threats across many kinds of data at once. Enterprise networks and smart device fleets face attacks that no single tool sees whole, because logs, camera feeds, and sound each sit in their own silo. AgenticCyber assigns specialist agents to cloud logs, surveillance video, and room audio, and has them reason together through large multimodal models.

The system was tested on public data sets for each stream: cloud activity logs, crime video frames, and city sound clips. Roy reports it caught threats with high scores, answered in well under a second, and cut the average time to respond by a large share compared with standard intrusion systems. Its modular design aims to scale across company networks and device fleets, shifting defense from fixed tools that wait for alarms toward agents that act early.
arxiv-2512-06596:
The XRISM Collaboration reports the first direct measure of gas motion in the hot heart of the Virgo galaxy cluster, around the giant galaxy M87. Clusters hold gas in a vast hot atmosphere, and the central black hole stirs it through feedback. The Resolve instrument on the XRISM satellite reads gas speeds from the shifts of X ray lines, and Virgo is the closest case where this can be done in detail.

Near the center the gas churns with a wide spread of speeds, falling off steeply within a short span. Bulk motion stays close to M87 itself. If the central spread were pure turbulence, it would run near the speed of sound, with much of the pressure from motion, not heat. Models mixing shocks, sound waves, and turbulence fit. Among clusters XRISM has seen, M87's core is the most disturbed.
arxiv-2512-07296:
Qidi Peng and William Wu take on the practical problem of simulating self-similar processes, random curves whose statistics look the same at every zoom. Such processes model everything from river flows to financial volatility, yet simulation recipes tend to be one-off crafts, each built for a single process with its own constraints and flaws. A general, efficient simulator has been missing.

The authors first review the leading recipes for specific processes and improve several of them. Then they propose a method meant for the whole class: a modified inverse Lamperti transformation converts self-similarity into stationarity. A tamer property that standard machinery can handle, and converting back yields the desired process. The method is demonstrated on the two workhorses of the field, fractional Brownian motion and its sub-fractional cousin.
arxiv-2512-07696:
C. Ganot and twenty-nine co-authors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on Type Ia supernovae. These explosions serve as standard candles for measuring cosmic distances. Their brightness must be standardized with care.

The team builds a large, uniform sample from the Zwicky Transient Facility. Thousands of spectra from its second data release feed the work. Flux calibration is tightened using photometry that is accurate to the percent level. On a subset of explosions near peak light, they replay a special method. The Twins Embedding method once achieved remarkably low scatter in brightness. Its three steps are applied here. The phase correction proves precise. A color standardization step, called Read Between The Lines, also performs well. It beats the standard SALT approach while using one fewer parameter. The full method stalls, limited by the survey's modest spectral quality.
arxiv-2512-07796:
Sridhar Mahadevan wrote this 2025 paper on building large causal models from language models. Traditional causal inference builds small models from experiments and numeric data. Mahadevan wants causal maps that span whole fields of knowledge instead.

His system, DEMOCRITUS, mines a strong language model for causal claims. It proposes topics, poses causal questions, and extracts plausible statements. Those fragments arrive scattered, ambiguous, and sometimes in conflict. The hard problem is weaving them into one coherent structure. Claims become relational triples inside a large causal model. New categorical machine learning methods were invented for that weaving. The paper focuses on the system side of the construction. A six-module pipeline carries text in and organized models out. Cost profiling shows where scaling the system currently bottlenecks. Trials span archaeology, biology, climate, economics, medicine, and technology. Limits of the current system are discussed frankly at the end.
arxiv-2512-07896:
Alexander Chipps, Daniel Forgette, and Kerri Cahoy wrote this 2025 space engineering paper. Small satellites now travel beyond Earth orbit on interplanetary missions. Their designers need thermal predictions, yet pro tools are costly and demand deep training.

Their answer is SATMO, an open-source thermal model for CubeSats. The MATLAB program uses six nodes to represent the satellite's heat balance. It targets low-altitude circular orbits around Earth and other solar system bodies. Mission planners in the early, sketchy stages are its audience. A Mars-orbiting CubeSat serves as the worked example in the paper. Outputs show what temperatures each configuration of the craft will face. Validation runs against the industry standard, Thermal Desktop, come out close. Temperatures agree within a narrow margin across Earth, Venus, and Mars cases. Quick trade studies become possible without a specialist's toolbox. Interplanetary small-satellite planning gains an accessible first pass at thermal design.
arxiv-2512-08096:
Georgios Chionas, Olga Gorelkina, Piotr Krysta, and Rida Laraki, researchers in economics and computer science, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is privacy in blockchain transactions, where users may want to sell the right to execute a transaction without exposing their economic preferences. They model users whose welfare falls as more of their private information leaks.

First, they study an order flow auction in which a user auctions execution rights to specialist agents called searchers. They characterize the optimal auction, a sealed bid design, and show how the level of privacy affects revenue and user welfare. Next, they analyze a Dutch auction variant where price and privacy both fall over rounds. Finally, they build a two sided privacy marketplace with many users and searchers. Their posted price mechanism keeps both sides honest, balances the budget, and still guarantees a constant share of the best possible social welfare.
arxiv-2512-08396:
Barbara Baldoni, Mickael Delcey, Yoann Cheny, and colleagues, engineers and physicists in France, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They use physics informed neural networks to measure how granular materials flow. Sand, grain, and powders have rheological parameters that normally demand complex, costly experiments to pin down, yet those numbers decide how silos empty and how piles collapse.

Their test case is simple: a column of granular material collapsing under gravity. The network learns the flow fields from synthetic data while recovering the rheological parameters at the same time. As a bonus, it reconstructs the pressure field inside the material, something experiments can barely reach. The proof of concept worked on synthetic data. The authors present the method as data driven rheometry for granular matter, ready to be tried on real experiments. Such tools could make designing with powders and grains far less trial and error.
arxiv-2512-08696:
Nathan Dalaklis and Yan Mary He study multifractal analysis for equilibrium states of holomorphic maps on complex projective space. The map has degree at least two, and the work focuses on a uniformly expanding set where the dynamics are non conformal. Equilibrium states come from Holder continuous potentials, a standard class in dynamics.

Instead of Hausdorff dimension, the authors use a newer volume dimension theory to define local dimension spectra. They show each spectrum forms a Legendre transform pair with the temperature function, matching the pattern known in the conformal case. As a use of the main results, they also prove a conditional variational principle for those spectra. The work extends multifractal formalism to a broader non conformal setting, giving tools to describe how local scaling varies across the expanding set.
arxiv-2512-08896:
Gang Liu and coauthors report the results of the Open Polymer Challenge, a community competition for predicting polymer traits with machine learning. Progress toward sustainable polymers has been slowed by a lack of large, high quality, open data sets. The challenge releases a new benchmark with ten thousand polymers and five traits, including thermal conductivity, density, and glass transition temperature.

Participants had to work under realistic limits: small data, uneven labels, and mixed study sources. Winning methods used feature augmentation, transfer learning, self supervised pretraining, and targeted ensembles. The report draws lessons on data preparation, distribution shifts, and consistency across study groups. Those lessons can guide future large polymer data efforts. The models, study, and released data, including a data generation pipeline covering many more properties, form a new base for molecular machine learning in polymer science.
arxiv-2512-09496:
Anissa Alloula and colleagues challenge a standard assumption in machine learning fairness: that training data should always be balanced across demographic groups. Unequal representation can hurt a model's performance on underrepresented groups, yet recent results show imbalanced data sometimes helps a subgroup. Sometimes a subgroup's performance is unaffected even if it is missing from training entirely.

The authors propose the latent separation hypothesis. A fine-tuned model's dependence on subgroup representation, they argue, is set by how far apart the subgroups sit in the pretrained model's internal representation space. They formalize the hypothesis, back it with theory, and validate it across four vision and language datasets. Regularization experiments add early evidence that the effect is causal. Their practical message is that measuring latent subgroup separation can guide real decisions about data collection and balancing when fine-tuning foundation models, instead of balancing by default.
arxiv-2512-09596:
