Arkadiusz Ryś and colleagues present a framework for managing the artifacts produced by systems engineering work, as the field shifts from documents to models. For cyber-physical systems, experts from many domains run workflows and use models in many formalisms, each with its own tools. Knowledge about those workflows and their outputs is valuable for repeating work and for reasoning over results, but it is scattered.

Their framework defines the workflow concepts, formalisms, and artifacts in an ontology, written in an ontology modeling language. From that ontology they build a knowledge graph holding the engineering data, over which reasoning can run. Tools help engineers design workflows, execute them, and store artifacts with versioning, querying, and reasoning, while hiding the graph's complexity. Applied to a drivetrain smart sensor project, the framework eased storage and versioning problems and cut the time needed to find information and inferences.
arxiv-2512-09696:
Asher Sabbagh and colleagues demonstrate that some objects are impossible to push, pull, or trap with light, even using the best shaped light beams. Optical manipulation is a powerful tool across biophysics and nanotechnology, and wavefront shaping with spatial light modulators had seemed able to move arbitrary objects. The authors show this assumption fails for a variety of shapes.

Working in two dimensions, they use inverse design, starting from the desired behavior and computing the shape that produces it. That finds objects resistant to manipulation under even the optimal wavefront shaping protocol. For their counterintuitive shapes, the maximum pulling force drops by up to four orders of magnitude and the maximum trapping stiffness by nearly two. The authors note the designs provide a foundation for extension to three dimensions. Such resistant objects could serve micromachines that need a predictable mechanical response no matter what light falls on them.
arxiv-2512-09896:
Anuj Apte and five coauthors improve the best efficient approximation algorithm for the EPR Hamiltonian problem. Problems of this kind ask for a quantum state that nearly maximizes an energy-like quantity, and approximation algorithms guarantee a fixed fraction of the optimum. Their new algorithm guarantees a stronger fraction than before. The gain comes from two ingredients. One is a new nonlinear bound on monogamy of entanglement for star shaped interaction graphs. The other is a refined parameterization of a shallow quantum circuit used in earlier work.

The team also proves limits on what current methods can deliver. Their barriers show that today's techniques cannot push the approximation ratio substantially higher. That tells researchers the next improvement needs fundamentally new ideas. The paper is a theoretical contribution to quantum algorithms and entanglement theory.
arxiv-2512-09996:
Giacomo Venturi leads a large team reporting powerful gas outflows from active galaxies in the early universe. The targets lie at redshifts three to six, before cosmic noon, an era poorly explored for this kind of feedback. Using the James Webb Space Telescope's integral field spectrograph, the team mapped ionized gas around mostly X-ray selected active nuclei in the GOODS-S field. Combined with a twin sample in COSMOS, theirs is the largest spatially resolved outflow sample at these redshifts, with outflows in most of the galaxies observed.

The outflows are fast and compact, and in some cases they expel ionized gas faster than the host forms stars. Even so, the analysis hints that mass outflow rates were higher long ago, especially beyond redshift three. Stronger early outflows would have been better able to reshape their hosts.
arxiv-2512-10596:
J Xiao and co-authors search satellite images with words, and skip training altogether. Finding the right remote sensing image for a text query is hampered by the semantic gap between raw visual features and human concepts. Vision-language models can bridge it, but domain training is costly, and nobody had properly benchmarked how far model-written captions alone can go.

The team built the Remote Sensing Rich Text dataset, with several structured captions per image. And a reference method called TRSLLaVA that never trains. It turns cross-modal search into text-to-text matching: the query is compared against a database of model-generated captions inside one shared text embedding space. On the RSITMD and RSICD benchmarks the training-free method nearly doubled the recall of a standard zero-shot CLIP baseline and passed several supervised models.
arxiv-2512-10796:
Ross Dempsey and co-authors corner the energy-energy correlator of the most symmetric gauge theory, N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills. This observable records how energy arrives at two detectors set at an angle, a clean probe of how the theory's excitations share energy. The team attacks it with every tool available: perturbation theory, holography, supersymmetric localisation, integrability, and numerical conformal bootstrap.

For finite numbers of colours they derive lower bounds on the correlator's second and fourth angular multipoles at several couplings, plus a smeared angular profile. And find evidence the theory nearly saturates those bounds. In the planar limit, dispersive functionals give tight two-sided bounds on the first three multipoles and the full angular shape. As the coupling grows, dominance in the collinear limit passes from single-trace to double-trace operators, mirroring the parton-to-hadron transition seen when detectors close in during QCD collisions.
arxiv-2512-10996:
Seonok Kim introduces MedBioRAG, a system that helps large language models answer medical and biological questions by first finding relevant documents. Retrieval augmented generation grounds answers in sources rather than memory alone. MedBioRAG combines meaning based search with word based search, ranking, and supervised fine tuning of the model.

The system was tested on document retrieval, short answer questions, and long form answers using well known sets such as MedQA, PubMedQA, BioASQ, and COVID related collections. It beat earlier best models and a strong general model on every task measured. Retrieval scores and answer accuracy both improved. The findings support pairing careful semantic search with fine tuning for biomedical question answering.
arxiv-2512-11096:
Ben Wang and Jiqun Liu study how people use ChatGPT to plan long term life tasks, from health goals to career learning and big events. Such planning is complex and uncertain, and little was known about how AI chatbots support it in practice. The authors interviewed fourteen participants about their planning sessions and examined the prompts they wrote.

ChatGPT helped people break large goals into manageable steps, generate ideas, and stay motivated, acting as a reflective partner. Its plans were often generic or idealised, though, lacking personal detail, realism, and flexibility when life changed. Users had to adapt and check the output themselves. Participants wanted systems that admit uncertainty and plan for failure, not just success. The findings frame long term planning as an evolving human AI collaboration.
arxiv-2512-11196:
O. Ramirez and Y. Bonder derive the first law of black hole thermodynamics for a wide range of gravity theories using the language of differential forms. Black hole thermodynamics, linking mass, entropy, and surface gravity, hints at the microscopic structure of spacetime. A general derivation has existed since the nineteen nineties, but in the traditional metric formalism.

Differential forms are a natural language for gravity theories, especially those that go beyond general relativity. The authors build a unified prescription in that language, covering theories with torsion, a twisting of spacetime geometry, and generic matter fields. Their framework produces concrete expressions for the first law in each case. The result should make thermodynamic checks easier to apply when testing proposed extensions of Einstein's theory.
arxiv-2512-11296:
Yasaman Hashem Pour, Nazanin Mahjourian, and Vinh Nguyen use vision language models to check student written machining code jointly with the machine's own display. Learning to program CNC lathes by hand matters. Earlier checking tools based on text only models could read the code, but not the human machine interface, which shows live status and errors.

Their few shot approach feeds the model paired cases of code and interface screenshots from a training lathe, covering both correct and faulty cases. A structured output schema built from expert heuristics guides the model's judgements. Compared with a zero shot version, the guided model caught more interface errors and more mismatches between code and machine state. The setup suits the manually written code typical of CNC training programmes.
arxiv-2512-11496:
Jelena Losic argues that finding communities in a network should blend two rival toolkits, because no single strategy wins everywhere. Popular graph methods such as Louvain optimise a modularity score, yet they can miss communities defined by geometry. Topological data analysis methods like ToMATo find density based clusters in embedded data powerfully, but depend on how the data were projected.

Losic's framework first embeds the network spectrally, exposing a geometric skeleton where communities appear as basins in a density landscape. ToMATo then extracts the persistent clusters from that landscape in a parameter aware way. Across synthetic benchmarks the hybrid proved highly robust, performing on par with Louvain on networks with clear modular structure. The results support a new class of hybrid algorithms that choose or combine strategies according to a network's geometry, rather than forcing one method onto every problem.
arxiv-2512-11796:
Saurabh V Kadam and co-authors advance a hands on method for lattice Yang-Mills theory, the grid form of the strong force. Their loop-string-hadron approach rewrites the theory in a basis tied to loops, strings, and hadrons at each lattice site. Part I built that basis for SU(3), the strong force group.

Part II gives the full matrix form for any gauge invariant operator at a three way site. The new form stands alone, replacing the older Schwinger boson machinery. Classic calculations in the new basis run much faster than the old way. A companion code script applies the formulas, aiming to speed Hamiltonian based studies of quantum chromodynamics.
arxiv-2512-11896:
Tessa Vu maps unequal heat for people on foot in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Walking in dense tropical cities can be a health risk, yet route apps ignore street level heat. Her Hot Hém workflow mixes street view photos, image segmentation, and satellite data to price heat block by block.

Two XGBoost models learn ground temperature from street view scenes in select wards, then predict it across the walking network built from OpenStreetMap. That yields routes that trade a little distance for real shade and cool. The pipeline can also flag which corridors run hottest and hint why, from missing trees to bare asphalt. Planners get a tool for fairer, cooler streets.
arxiv-2512-11996:
Chris Calger studies isolated points on modular curves of prime power level. A point on a curve is isolated if it does not belong to a family of same degree points swept by a line or a positive rank abelian part of the Jacobian. Isolated points are the loners of the curve, and they carry special arithmetic weight.

Calger asks which j-invariants can arise from isolated points when extensions stay within a bounded degree. For families of modular curves with prime power level, he proves finiteness results for those invariant sets. The work extends Bourdon and Ejder classification of rational cases on the X1(n) and X0(n) families. Such finiteness bounds how wild the arithmetic of modular curves can get.
arxiv-2512-12196:
Xiaoxuan Tang and twelve co-authors present AutoMV in a 2025 paper on music video generation. Making a full song video is hard for current tools. They tend to make short, disjoint clips that miss the beat, the lyrics, and the song structure, and that drift over time.

AutoMV uses a team of AI agents that work in steps. Early tools pull out song structure, vocal tracks, and timed lyrics. Writer and director agents plan scenes and camera moves, image and video tools make the shots, and a verifier agent checks them. In expert ratings, AutoMV beat current products in all four scoring groups and came closer to human made videos.
arxiv-2512-12496:
Joshua Cooper and Hays Whitlatch count Cholesky factorizations of the zero matrix over the field with two elements in a 2025 math paper. A Cholesky root of a matrix M is an upper triangular matrix U with U transpose times U equal to M. Working over F2, the field of just 0 and 1, changes how such roots behave.

They prove that for each fixed rank, the zero matrix has exactly as many Cholesky roots as upper triangular square roots, two counts that were not obviously equal. They then give asymptotics, formulas for how the count grows, for that shared number. The paper closes with directions for future inquiry into related counts.
arxiv-2512-12796:
Maher Boudabra studies optimal domain design for the planar Skorokhod embedding problem in a 2025 math paper. That problem asks for a simply connected domain such that planar Brownian motion, started at zero, exits with a prescribed distribution for the real part of its exit point. Among all domains that work for a given measure, some are best by area or by boundary energy.

Boudabra formalizes Brownian symmetrization of planar domains and clarifies its relation to the Baernstein-Pruss theory. Within the simply connected class, Gross's domain minimizes a whole fractional scale of boundary energies. The proof uses fractional Sobolev seminorms and the exit law alone, not an explicit uniformizer. Deficiency ratios measure how far any domain sits from the Gross optimum.
arxiv-2512-12996:
Payel Shee and co-authors probe PrSi, a metallic ferromagnet, to see how magnetic order interacts with moving charges and crystal-field effects. Such couplings shape the odd ground states of rare-earth compounds. The team used terahertz spectroscopy, which tracks responses on very fast time scales.

Over a wide range of temperatures, the response showed strong scattering of the charge carriers. A Kondo-lattice model explains that behavior as carriers bouncing off local magnetic moments. At low temperatures, sharp crystal-field signals took over at zero point six and one point five four terahertz. The one point five four terahertz mode tracked the onset of ferromagnetic order, marking a change of regime.
arxiv-2512-13196:
Chethana Prasad Kabgere and Sudarshan T. S. B. present NR-QFL, a hybrid quantum-classical framework for federated learning in driver assistance systems. Cars can train shared models without pooling raw data, which protects privacy. But standard aggregation is exposed to noise, delay, and security limits on vehicle networks.

NR-QFL aggregates model updates with variational quantum circuits run under noisy quantum conditions. It encodes parameters as quantum states and adapts its gates to keep errors bounded. Client selection uses quantum entropy, and several servers coordinate for fairness. Tests showed steady convergence, lower gradient variance, and reduced communication overhead under tight edge conditions.
arxiv-2512-13496:
Giacomo Bastianel and co-authors identify the technical design constraints that shape transmission grid expansion planning. Expanding the grid is central to deploying renewable energy at scale, since wind and solar sites often sit far from demand. Planners must weigh far more than cost and capacity on paper.

The paper catalogs the practical limits and considerations that real expansion projects face, from electrical and stability requirements to the physical and operational bounds equipment imposes. By naming these constraints in one place, it aims to keep planning models honest about what can actually be built and operated. That grounding matters as investment decisions lock in grid shape for decades.
arxiv-2512-13696:
Md Shahabub Alam, Md Asifuzzaman Jishan, and Ayan Kumar Ghosh build a physics-guided deep network to detect stress in heat pumps. Heat pumps are key to efficient buildings, yet stress detection is hard due to complex thermodynamics and scarce real-world data. Their data source is the When2Heat data set.

The model uses physics-guided feature choice and class definitions, with five hidden layers and two regularization strategies. Training data held 131,483 samples with 656 features across 26 European countries. The model reached 78.1% test accuracy and 78.5% validation accuracy. That beat shallow networks by 5.0 points, limited feature sets by 4.0 points, and single regularization by 2.0 points. Ablation tests backed each design choice.
arxiv-2512-13796:
Victor Rong and co-authors present Nexels, a compact way to render new views of a 3D scene in real time. Gaussian splatting gives strong novel view results, but it needs millions of primitives for richly textured scenes, even when the geometry is simple. Nexels split geometry from appearance to cut that cost.

Geometry uses surfels, while appearance pairs a global neural field with per-primitive colors. The field textures a fixed number of primitives per pixel, keeping added compute low. On outdoor scenes, Nexels matched 3D Gaussian splatting quality with 9.7 times fewer primitives and 5.5 times less memory. Indoor gains were 31 times fewer primitives and 3.7 times less memory, with rendering twice as fast.
arxiv-2512-13996:
Can Jin and co-authors propose DTop-p, a routing method for sparse Mixture-of-Experts models used in foundation model pretraining. Such models route each token to a few expert subnetworks. Standard Top-k routing is rigid, ignoring that tokens and layers vary in difficulty and need.

Top-p routing adapts by adding experts until a probability threshold is met, but fixed thresholds gave only marginal gains and uncontrolled cost. DTop-p learns the threshold with a Proportional-Integral controller and normalizes routing per layer under a global sparsity budget. Across language models and diffusion transformers, it beat Top-k and fixed Top-p baselines while matching Top-k compute. Scaling held across expert granularity, capacity, model size, and data size.
arxiv-2512-14396:
Marvin Leusch and co-authors ask how the shape of a lattice changes magnetic order in the Hubbard model, a standard model of strongly interacting electrons. They study cubic lattices in three, four, and five dimensions, plus body-centered and face-centered cubic ones.

First they use a method that counts only local effects, then one that adds effects between sites. The added effects cut the transition temperature on most lattices, and the gap shrinks as each site gains more neighbors. On the face-centered lattice, the ordered phase found by the first method vanishes once the wider effects are included.
arxiv-2512-14696:
Turning an ordinary single-camera video into a simulation-ready reconstruction of a person moving through a scene is the goal of CRISP, a new method. Earlier approaches lean on learned priors and joint optimization with no physics in the loop, or return noisy geometry full of artifacts.

Those artifacts are not cosmetic: motion tracking policies that interact with the scene fail on bad geometry. CRISP instead recovers simulatable human motion and scene geometry guided by contact, using planar scene primitives to keep the reconstruction clean. Contact-guided reconstruction could feed robotics and animation pipelines that need video-derived scenes a simulator can actually run.
arxiv-2512-14796:
Mahmut S. Gokmen leads a team tackling a scale problem in digital pathology. Whole slide images of tissue are huge, and they hold detail at many zoom levels at once. Most learning methods treat each zoom level on its own, so their results can shift when the zoom changes.

Their method, called Magnification Aware Distillation, links low zoom context with matched high zoom detail during training. The trained model, MAD-NP, learns with no labels at all. A simple test classifier taught only at 10x zoom kept 96.7 percent of its score when used on unseen 40x tiles. Tissue outlines also stayed steady across zooms, which suits real lab work with tissue samples.
arxiv-2512-14996:
Mohammadhossein Nahavandian and two coauthors study how radiation reshapes the chemistry inside metal alloys used in reactors. Under radiation, chromium atoms in iron chromium alloys drift toward sinks like grain boundaries, a process called radiation induced segregation. That drift can weaken the material until it fails.

Using kinetic Monte Carlo simulations of an iron alloy with 3 percent chromium, the team compares sinks of different shapes: flat sinks in one, two, and three dimensions, plus a spherical sink. They track how chromium piles up near each sink across a range of temperatures. Flat sinks show segregation that grows in a simple linear way with sink density. The spherical case breaks that pattern with a more complex dependence. Computer solutions of the same equations agree with the simulations, which supports the model.
arxiv-2512-15296:
Claudia Ceci and a coauthor solve a government's debt problem with the tools of stochastic control. The target is the debt to GDP ratio, which moves under both chance and policy. Their model lets fiscal policy drive debt accumulation and GDP growth at once, a two way influence often simplified away.

A cost functional captures the pain of running surpluses and the perceived benefit of deficits, encoding the tug between tightening and stimulus. Applying the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman method, they obtain explicit solutions when GDP responds linearly to policy. Threshold type fiscal strategies are analyzed rigorously, with closed form value functions in the relevant regimes. A sensitivity analysis varies key parameters and confirms the findings are robust. The work offers finance ministries a principled map of when to consolidate, under uncertainty.
arxiv-2512-15496:
Jim de Groot, Joao Marcos, and Rodrigo Stefanes describe logics that include negative modalities in a 2025 logic paper. These logics use weaker negations, which soften some usual rules for not, plus restoration modes that can recover classical behavior locally. The question is what such languages can and cannot express.

The authors introduce matching methods suited to these logics and prove an adequacy theorem for them. They then give two kinds of profile results. Intrinsic, Hennessy Milner type results match the logic to those methods directly. Relative, Van Benthem type results identify each language with the fragment of first order logic that stays invariant under those methods. Together these mark out the expressive reach of the logics.
arxiv-2512-15696:
L. N. Fletcher and co authors characterize Jupiter's high latitude storms, the Folded Filamentary Regions, using Juno data in a 2025 paper. These sprawling turbulent cloud formations dominate the planet's mid to high latitudes. Their depth, structure, and energy were poorly known before Juno's close multi wavelength views.

Cloud tops show lobes of layered aerosols split by darker clear lanes, with smaller eddies and high cumulus mixed in. The regions are microwave bright at shallow depths and dark at deep levels, a flip tied to the water condensation layer. Despite roots reaching about 100 bars of pressure, they act as pancake vortices far wider than deep. Their pattern also explains high lightning rates at northern latitudes.
arxiv-2512-15796:
Nickolas de Aguiar Alves and Andre Landulfo show that sound admits an infrared triangle in a 2025 paper, dated December 16. In high energy physics, memory effects, asymptotic symmetries, and soft theorems form a connected trio in the infrared sector. Whether a similar trio exists for an everyday system like sound was open.

Starting from linear perturbations of the Euler equations for a barotropic, irrotational fluid, the authors show low frequency source changes can leave lasting displacements of fluid particles, an acoustic memory effect. Writing the perturbations with a two form Kalb Ramond potential recasts linear sound as a gauge theory. Standard tools then link memory, symmetries, and soft theorems, suggesting new ways to detect memory effects.
arxiv-2512-15896:
Yuxun Guo and co authors study energy energy correlators in electron positron annihilation and deep inelastic scattering in a 2025 paper. These correlators weigh how energy flows at angles inside jets, and their strong force behavior carries clues about hadron formation. The team adds the correlator jet functions for both processes.

One loop math exposes the low energy behavior of small angle and summed correlators. Splitting and sameness across the two processes are shown. A matching scheme joins regions with different scaling in jet energy. With next to leading order corrections, the framework describes high energy annihilation data and model runs well, and predicts correlators for a future electron ion collider.
arxiv-2512-15996:
Saiedeh Akbari and four co-authors introduce a new controller design in a paper on control engineering shared on arXiv in 2025. Transformers, the neural networks behind modern AI, are good at tracking sequences, but control systems that steer real machines need proof that they will stay stable. Prior transformer controllers were trained offline with fixed weights, so they could not adapt live or offer stability guarantees.

The team's design, called LyAT, adapts a transformer in real time for systems with random noise. Its update rule comes from a Lyapunov analysis, the classic method for proving stability in control theory. The analysis guarantees that tracking and estimation errors stay bounded with high probability. Tests on a quadrotor drone confirmed the controller works in practice.
arxiv-2512-16696:
Marco Sangalli, Erik Quaeghebeur, and Thomas Krak study hitting chances for imprecise Markov chains, where the jump odds are known only as a set of possible matrices. They ask for the lowest and highest chances of ever reaching a target set of states.

First they sort out reachability, since past work used the term in mixed ways, and they map how the rival meanings relate. States then split into those with trivial zero or one chances and those needing real work. For the hard states, the lower chance is the unique fix of a nonlinear equation. Their loop method swaps between solving a linear system and picking an extreme matrix, and converges far faster in tests than worst-case bounds suggest.
arxiv-2512-17096:
Bruno Duchesne and Christopher-Lloyd Simon study hyperbolic simplices with maximal inradius, the largest ball that fits inside. A simplex here is set by n plus 1 points in compactified hyperbolic space, and its inradius is the Hausdorff gap between its full skeleton and its faces.

They show a simplex hits maximal inradius exactly when it is total ideal and regular, with a clean value whose tanh equals 1 over n. They also compute the maximal distance to the 1-skeleton, with tanh squared equal to n minus 1 over 2n. Those maxima stay uniformly bounded as dimension grows, tending to log of 1 plus root 2 for the 1-skeleton case.
arxiv-2512-17196:
Kai Liu and coauthors present UmniBench, a benchmark that grades unified multimodal models on understanding, generation, and editing in one pass. Past grading split those skills across separate data sets, missing how a single model blends them.

UmniBench uses human-checked prompts and question pairs, then lets the model under test judge its own generations and edits with its understanding skill. The bench spans 13 domains and over 200 concepts, and it can also split scores by skill for fine reading. Twenty-four models were graded, covering unified systems and single-skill large models. The team offers the bench as a fuller, fairer yardstick for unified models.
arxiv-2512-17396:
Léo Butsanets and four co-authors release RadImageNet-VQA, a vast exam set for AI systems that answer questions about medical scans. Most older sets lean on plain X-rays or textbook art, and many let models guess well from the words alone. This set centers on CT and MRI exams, the cross-section scans doctors use for hard cases.

It pairs 750,000 images with 7.5 million expert-checked questions and answers. The questions cover spotting abnormalities, naming anatomy, and identifying diseases across eight body regions and 97 disease categories. Leading vision-language models still fail often at naming exact diseases, above all when answers must be written freely. Stripping the images away drops scores to near chance, proving the words alone give nothing away.
arxiv-2512-17496:
Maya N Vienken, Jan-Ole Koslik, and Roland Langrock fix a quiet bias in how ecologists summarize animal behavior. Hidden Markov models sort tracker data into hidden states such as resting, feeding, and traveling, and link switching between states to weather, habitat, or season. With many states, the switching web turns unreadable, so papers report a simple share-of-time summary instead.

That summary rests on a shortcut: freeze the driver, say rainfall, and compute the long-run shares. The team shows the shortcut can bend results badly when the driver itself jumps around. They offer two fixes, one that resamples the driver's own record and one that regresses observed state shares. A case study on Galápagos tortoise tracks shows the corrected story in action.
arxiv-2512-17596:
M G Sousa and three co-authors test how much moving charge a fragile quantum phase can take before it breaks. Their stage is a ladder-shaped strip of honeycomb lattice holding a Kitaev-Heisenberg magnet, a model tied to materials that might host exotic topological order. Adding mobile electrons lets charge slosh around, and that sloshing fights the delicate order.

Using heavy DMRG computations, the team maps where the topological phase survives as electrons hop faster and interact harder. Faster hopping squeezes the safe zone and shifts its borders. Past sharp threshold values, the hidden string order that marks the phase vanishes outright. The map tells material hunters how clean and calm a real sample must be to keep the prized phase alive.
arxiv-2512-18096:
Andrzej Czarnecki and Ting Gao revisit a claim that gravity bends spinning particles sideways as they fall. The claimed drift, a spin Hall effect for gravity, would split a falling wave packet by its spin. Their check uses a spinning mass model and the quantum Dirac equation in a flat, even gravity field.

They find the past setup hid a catch: the packet was never truly at rest, since two kinds of momentum part ways when spin is present. That hidden push, not gravity, gave the sideways drift. Prepared with care, the packet stays centered to first order, and any true spin drift waits for far smaller terms. Even fields, they conclude, do not sort spins sideways.
arxiv-2512-18296:
Lijun Bo and Weiqiang Chang price private data as a two player game. Data markets sell access to records, but privacy noise, added to shield each person, blurs the goods and cuts their worth. Older pricing work mostly chased tidy prices or profit and skipped that clash.

In their game the market maker moves first and posts a price rule, and the buyer answers by picking how sharp a query to buy under a privacy cap. For a balanced linear rule they solve the standoff in closed form, giving the best noise level, price, and the edge where buyers walk away. A power shaped rule extends the study. The frame ties privacy math to market design in one piece.
arxiv-2512-18496:
Xiaoyang Guo and Keze Wang work on making vision-language models cheaper to run. Such models turn each image into many patch tokens, and processing them all costs heavy compute and memory. VoCo-LLaMA compresses those patches into a few tokens, but always at one fixed rate. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, makes the rate adapt to each image.

Adaptive-VoCo adds a small predictor that gauges an image's visual complexity from cues like patch token entropy and attention map variance, then picks a fitting compression rate. A joint loss balances compression savings against keeping the representation faithful. Across several multimodal tasks, the adaptive method consistently beats fixed-rate baselines. The result points to vision-language models that spend effort only where an image actually demands it.
arxiv-2512-18596:
Quanxi Zhou and five co-authors coordinate fleets of farm drones. In smart agriculture, unmanned aerial vehicles collect data, take images, and relay communications across fields, but planning their paths together is a hard joint problem. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, frames the task as a Markov decision process and trains the drones with a new reinforcement learning design.

Their framework, EIA-SEC, pairs each drone's actor with two critics. Agents imitate the fleet's current elite performer, which cuts costly trial and error. A shared ensemble critic works beside each local critic to keep value estimates unbiased and prevent overestimation. In experiments, EIA-SEC beats leading baselines on reward, training stability, and convergence speed. Better coordination means fewer wasted flights over the same rows.
arxiv-2512-18796:
Wei-Hao Chen, Yi-Zen Chu, and Vaidehi Varma present TensoriaCalc, a tensor calculus package for the Wolfram Language. Tensor calculations underpin general relativity and differential geometry, but hand computation is slow and error-prone. Their 126-page guide, posted to arXiv in December 2025, describes software designed to feel native to Mathematica rather than bolted on.

A session can hold several metrics at once. Once a metric is set, the package computes covariant derivatives, Hodge duals, index raising and lowering, and geodesic equations. It also handles operations that need no metric, including Lie and exterior derivatives and coordinate changes on tensors. The code and full user guide are public. For researchers and students, TensoriaCalc turns week-long index gymnastics into checked, repeatable commands.
arxiv-2512-18896: Hans Schoutens works in model theory and category theory, where a theory's models form a category of their own. He points out a surprising property: any small category elementarily equivalent to that model category already embeds inside it. The known proof runs through ultrapowers and stays abstract, leaving open which concrete axioms, depending on the theory and language, force the embedding. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, also proposes a first-order logic in which equivalent categories are always elementarily equivalent, tightening the two-way street between the notions.
arxiv-2512-18996:
Chong Liu and five co-authors tackle a common flaw in AI tools that turn app designs into front-end code. Such tools often emit one long script that fits no modern framework well. Their system, called Modular Layout Synthesis, aims instead for neat, reusable parts.

The method first reads a screen capture and builds a tree that captures the layout. It then removes repeated blocks and stores the result as a framework-free schema. Last, rules guide a large language model to write typed code with proper component props. Tests show stronger reuse and structure than earlier baselines, for React, Vue, and Angular style projects.
arxiv-2512-19296:
Zetao Lin and Shiping Liu give a short new route to a core part of representation theory. Almost split sequences are key building blocks in that theory, and proving they exist usually takes long machinery. The authors let a Nakayama functor do the heavy lifting inside broad abelian categories.

From Nakayama duality they derive the dualities and almost split sequences they need, whenever the category has enough projective or enough injective objects. One case covers modules over a class of small categories. For quiver algebras, they ask when three kinds of module categories carry such sequences on one side or both.
arxiv-2512-19696:
Sebastian Racedo, Brigitte Jaumard, Oscar Delgado, and Meysam Masoudi look for energy savings in open radio access networks. O-RAN splits the traditional base station into interoperable pieces, but deployments still pin each logical function to a fixed physical site. That static binding wastes energy when traffic and resources shift over the day.

Their system, GRLDyP, chooses routes and the central-unit location for each arriving service flow on the fly. A graph neural network reads the current topology and resource use, while a reinforcement-learning policy balances service quality, latency, and energy, framed as a Markov decision process. Evaluated on a full day of Montreal traffic traces, dynamic placement cut energy use against the static baseline without breaking quality-of-service promises.
arxiv-2512-19896:
Hany Khalifa and Matti Silveri design a quantum repeater that speaks microwave, not light. Repeaters stretch quantum links by making entanglement hop by hop. This design is gate-based. Its qubits are bosonic grid states held in superconducting resonators. Each station has a transmon plus two resonators. One is a self-correcting memory. The other is a bus for making entanglement.

Entanglement forms when a station catches a passing microwave photon packet. That makes the step sure, not a coin flip as in beamsplitter schemes. Swapping uses a bosonic controlled-Z gate and homodyne checks on the stored states. Losses are then held to storage alone. At set damping rates, the design's odds beat the one-half mark of ideal linear schemes. It can be built with today's superconducting tech.
arxiv-2512-19996:
Suman Chakraborty, Bongseok Kim, and Li Qiao simulate fuel drying out molecule by molecule. Large-scale models of the process assume a sharp liquid-vapor edge. At high heat and pressure, the true edge is diffuse. Traits vary across it. Kinetic boundary rules can repair the large-scale models. But they were built mostly for one-component fluids. Binary mixes lack the density and flux data those rules need.

The team runs molecular dynamics out of equilibrium. The mix is n-dodecane with nitrogen, near critical heat levels. They measure the edge's thickness, its density slopes, and surface tension. They then track the outward and reflected fluxes over time. Both fluxes grow as the heat rises. Yet the share that truly leaves falls. It starts just under one at the lowest heat and sinks toward nine tenths at the highest. Reflected molecules offset more and more of the gain.
arxiv-2512-20096:
Annika Hirling, Giorgio Nicoletti, and Antonio Celani wrote a primer on information-directed sampling. The stage is the multi-armed bandit problem. It is the classic clash of exploration and exploitation. Information-directed policies pick arms by weighing regret now against information gain. Their theory can be forbidding. The primer steps back to a tractable arena. Two-state Bernoulli bandits serve as the minimal model. There, heuristics can be compared with the true optimal policy in strict form.

The frame is extended to discounted, infinite-horizon problems. A modified information measure and a tuning knob shape the choices. In symmetric bandits, the method holds cumulative regret bounded. In the one-fair-coin case, its regret grows only with the log of the horizon. That matches classic lower bounds. The piece is aimed at statistical physicists. It bridges reinforcement learning and information theory.
arxiv-2512-20596:
Yair Glasner, Tobias Hartnick, and Waltraud Lederle construct exotic random subgroups of free groups. A random subgroup is a probability measure on the subgroup lattice; elementwise conservative ones behave tamely under every group element. Recent rigidity theorems for higher-rank lattices suggested such objects might be rare and structured.

For countable non-abelian free groups, the opposite holds. The authors produce uncountably many mutually singular examples, supported on infinite-index subgroups and singular against every invariant random subgroup. The construction studies representations into measurable full groups with the first generator's action frozen. Within that family, elementwise conservativity turns out to be generic in the Baire category sense. Free groups, it seems, are far wilder than lattices.
arxiv-2512-20696:
Pouya Asadi, Graham D Kribs, and Markus A Luty show that the early universe disapproves of quirks. Quirks are heavy fermions charged under both the Standard Model and a new confining force whose strings cannot snap, giving colliders a unique signature to hunt. The authors ask what cosmology says about the universe's reheat temperature in such models.

Glueballs produced by ultraviolet freeze-in live long and cause trouble everywhere. They threaten nucleosynthesis, distort the cosmic microwave background, and overproduce gamma rays and self-interacting dark matter. They also inflate the effective number of neutrino species. Dodging every constraint forces the reheat temperature below roughly one hundred giga-electronvolts across the interesting parameter space. That ceiling clashes with most baryogenesis models, tying a collider search to the universe's first moments.
arxiv-2512-20796:
Zhengyang Shan and Aaron Mueller ask whether a language model can lose its stereotypes without losing sight of demographics entirely. A model may need to recognize names or groups for fair treatment, yet use the same signals to repeat profession stereotypes. The pair test whether those two mechanisms are truly separate inside the model.

Working with Gemma-2-9B, they switched off single internal features picked out by two different hunting methods. Targeted switches reduced race and gender profession bias while name recognition stayed intact. Education bias responded better to the other method, and one wrong switch actually increased bias. Debiasing, they conclude, must be tailored bias by bias.
arxiv-2512-20896:
Kazuma Onishi, Katsuhiko Hayashi, and Hidetaka Kamigaito fight popularity bias in recommendation lists. Popular items collect more clicks simply because more people see them, so training data skews toward hits. Lists then grow repetitive, and standard corrections punish popular items so hard that good recommendations suffer.

Their fix reshapes the correction score with a smooth sigmoid curve applied to log frequency. The gentler penalty frees room for less-seen items without burying genuine hits. Built into a linear autoencoder, the method sharply improved list diversity in experiments. Accuracy held steady at the same time, a pairing recommender designers rarely get from bias corrections.
arxiv-2512-20996:
Yuwei Du, Yong Li, and four co-authors make pro traffic simulators usable by people who are not simulator experts. Platforms such as SUMO and MATSim are powerful but hard to set up from scratch. TrafficSimAgent wraps them in a hierarchy of language-model agents. High-level agents read plain-language instructions and plan the run. Low-level agents pick concrete actions for single traffic elements as conditions evolve.

Across multiple cases the framework ran simulations faithfully. It still produced sensible outcomes when instructions were vague, a common failure point for automation. Its expert-level decision optimization also beat competing systems and recent language-model baselines. Planners and policy staff gain a chat front end for work that once demanded specialist operators.
arxiv-2512-21096:
Jiayun Li, Jie Chen, and two co-authors put hard numbers on a workhorse system-identification method. Expanding a linear system's dynamics in orthogonal basis functions reduces identification to least squares, but everything hinges on where the basis functions' poles are placed. The team derives an analytic convergence rate for the algorithm and an explicit bound on its asymptotic bias, expressed through both the true system's poles and the chosen model poles.

Their pole-selection algorithm then robustly minimizes the worst-case bias, measured in the H2 sense, and provably reaches the fundamental lower bound: no choice can do better asymptotically. The optimal poles are the classical Tsuji points, and bias falls exponentially as basis functions are added. Numerical experiments confirm the bounds, turning a heuristic tuning knob into a solved design step.
arxiv-2512-21196:
Matthieu Verdoucq, Guy Theraulaz, and four co-authors give each drone in a swarm only two instincts: align with a few influential neighbors, and drift toward them. Nothing else, no central controller, no global map. Yet by tuning just the two interaction strengths, the team maps a full phase diagram of collective behavior. There are sharp transitions between loose swarming and ordered schooling. Between them sits a critical region, where the flock's responsiveness, fluctuations, and capacity to reorganize all peak.

Outdoor flights with ten real drones, backed by simulations on a calibrated flight model, confirm the physics. Near the transition, an intruder provokes instant collective turns and brief expansions, and the swarm recovers tight alignment within seconds. Swarm engineers gain a remarkably cheap control dial: two gains trade stability against flexibility, borrowing the trick that keeps animal groups both coherent and quick.
arxiv-2512-21496:
Haiping Fu and Yao Lu prove rigidity results for Einstein manifolds, shapes whose Ricci curvature is proportional to the metric itself. Rigidity means a mild curvature condition forces the space into a short list of standard forms. Their conditions involve the curvature operator of the second kind, a linear map built from the full curvature tensor.

Using Bochner techniques, they show a compact Einstein manifold of dimension at least four has constant curvature when that operator meets a cone condition weaker than simple nonnegativity. A second result, built on work by Li, says a closed Einstein manifold satisfying an averaged eigenvalue inequality is either flat or a spherical space form. This generalizes earlier theorems by Dai and Fu and by Chen and Wang. The authors also classify four-dimensional Einstein manifolds under their cone condition.
arxiv-2512-21896:
For geometric graph classes, twin-width sometimes exactly characterizes when first-order model checking is tractable, a phenomenon called delineation. Colin Geniet, Gunwoo Kim, and Lucas Meijer answer two open questions from the work that introduced the concept for interval and circle graphs.

They prove delineation holds for intersection graphs of non-degenerate axis-parallel unit segments, and also for intersection graphs of circular arcs. It fails, however, for visibility graphs of one-and-a-half-dimensional terrains, so the equivalence has genuine limits. The positive cases exploit natural vertex orderings that geometric graphs admit, importing the rich twin-width theory of ordered graphs. The results sharpen the map of where logic and structure align for geometric intersection graphs.
arxiv-2512-21996:
When a carbon monoxide molecule strikes copper, its energy leaves through lattice vibrations or through electron-hole pair excitations, and which channel dominates decides sticking. Carmen A. Tachino and colleagues simulate CO adsorption on Cu(110) with classical trajectories on a neural-network potential energy surface trained on density functional data, at ninety kelvin.

Comparing a phonons-only model with one adding electronic friction, they find lattice vibrations carry most of the energy and set the sticking probabilities; electronic friction plays a minor role during impact. Once the molecule is trapped near the surface, though, electron-hole excitations speed up settling into the chemisorption well, without much changing how far molecules travel sideways.
arxiv-2512-22296:
Reda Heddad and Lamiae Bouanane propose QMoE, a mixture-of-experts network whose router is a small quantum circuit. Mixture-of-experts models scale by sending each input to a few specialist sub-networks, but classic routers struggle with tangled decision boundaries and uneven expert use. The authors test whether quantum interference can route better, isolating the effect through an ablation study.

Their quantum gating network uses angle embedding and wave interference, effectively acting as a high-dimensional kernel method. On non-linearly separable data such as the Two Moons dataset, it separated distributions that linear classic routers handle poorly, with better parameter efficiency. Simulations also checked robustness against quantum noise, supporting feasibility on near-term hardware. Federated and privacy-preserving learning are among the suggested applications.
arxiv-2512-22396:
Bhanu Prakash Vangala and four co-authors build tools to catch language models fabricating materials science. Hallucinated facts in AI-generated research content threaten research integrity, and detection methods need benchmarks of their own. The team introduces HalluMatData, a benchmark dataset for grading hallucination spotting in materials science text, and HalluMatDetector, a multi-stage system that checks generated content several ways.

The detector combines intrinsic checking, lookup from multiple sources, contradiction graph analysis, and metric-based scoring. Hallucination levels varied widely across materials subdomains, with high-entropy alloy queries showing the most factual mismatch. The pipeline cut hallucination rates by about thirty percent versus standard model outputs. A new consistency score also measures how answers drift across reworded versions of the same question.
arxiv-2512-22496:
Saisab Sadhu and Ashim Dhor wrap AI tutoring in a structured argument so students get guidance instead of flattery. Language model tutors often fail pedagogically: they bless wrong student solutions, a sycophancy problem, or hand over answers too directly. Their system, Hierarchical Pedagogical Oversight, adapts rival-team synthesis to education, deliberately avoiding the shallow consensus that cooperative agent teams drift toward.

Expert agents first distill the dialogue's context, which then grounds a moderated five-act debate between opposing teaching critics. On MRBench, a set of 1,214 middle-school math chats, their eight-billion-parameter model reached a macro F1 score of 0.845 in the reported results. That edged out GPT-4o while using twenty times fewer settings, an argument for rival oversight in low-compute classrooms.
arxiv-2512-22596:
Takuma Narizuka and Issei Yamazaki put a physics model of soccer dribbling through its largest test yet. The attacker-defender model describes a ball carrier and the nearest defender with equations of motion combining resistance, a goal-oriented force, and an opponent-oriented force, all with interpretable parameters. Earlier work showed the model reproduces real dribbling paths well but explored few setting values on small datasets.

The authors improve parameter fitting by solving the model for one player while holding the opponent's real path fixed. They then validate on tracking data from 306 J1 League matches, the model's largest dataset so far. With optimized parameters spanning their full range, the analysis reveals distinct playing styles among attackers and defenders, separating how different athletes balance drive toward goal against pressure from their marker.
arxiv-2512-22696:
Yan X Zhang asks which triangles can be perfectly tiled by congruent copies of another triangle. The question descends from Erdős, with later inquiries by Beeson and Laczkovich. When the big triangle is similar to the small one, or when all angles are rational multiples of pi, the possible counts are understood. Zhang attacks the most interesting leftover case: the small triangle contains a two-thirds-pi angle, and the big one is one of six sporadic specific triangles.

Only two of those six sporadic triangles earlier had any tiling constructions. For each of them, Zhang creates a whole family of constructions producing various copy counts. He conjectures that these families exhaust every count that can occur for these triangles.
arxiv-2512-22796:
Ruoyu Wang and co-authors speed up diffusion models, whose image quality is excellent but whose step-by-step sampling is slow. Standard fast solvers lose quality at low step counts because their errors grow on sharply curving parts of the sampling path. The team's EPD-Solver evaluates several gradients in parallel at each step and combines them to follow the path's integral more faithfully.

Because those extra evaluations are independent, they run in parallel and keep latency low. Training happens in two stages. A small set of solver parameters is first fitted by distillation, then refined by reinforcement learning that treats the solver as a compact stochastic policy. The large backbone model is never changed. The method also works as a plug-in that upgrades existing samplers, with gains shown on demanding text-to-image tasks.
arxiv-2512-23096:
Mario Colosi and co-authors introduce Osmotic Learning, a self-supervised method for learning from data that stays scattered across distributed systems. Data in one place means more in context, since linked sources reveal links no single holder can see, yet sharing raw data between groups or devices is often impossible. Osmosis, their guiding metaphor, moves information rather than data: each side refines a dense, compact representation by absorbing context from the others.

Training aligns the local representations until they settle into a dynamic equilibrium that captures the contextual patterns across sources. Along the way, groups of like data identify themselves, so the process doubles as clustering with no central coordinator. Experiments on structured datasets confirm that the representations converge, reaching accuracy above ninety-nine percent in aligning local information while preserving each source's context. The method targets settings where context matters but one central store is off the table.
arxiv-2512-23496:
Anna Gallone, Simon Bliudze, Sophie Cerf, and Olga Kouchnarenko introduce Chips, a language for modeling the control of adaptable systems built from many interdependent parts. Modern web applications mix software, hardware, network, and online services, and designers need those parts to keep working together reliably. The running example is a variant of the Adaptable TeaStore, a benchmark microservice application.

Chips describes an application as functional blocks and blends ideas from control theory with ordinary programming language features. From such a description it generates component-based models that are built to stay robust under changing conditions. The authors show how the language supports a systematic workflow: design the system, model it in Chips, and analyze the model before deployment.
arxiv-2512-23696:
Jamie Portsmouth, Peter Kutz, and Stephen Hill document OpenPBR, a shared material model used to describe surfaces the same way across film, animation, and design rendering tools. The document accompanies the official specification, explaining why the model is built the way it is and how to implement it, with code examples and mathematical derivations. It formed part of a SIGGRAPH 2025 course on physically based shading.

The model stacks layers over base substrates: metallic, dielectric, subsurface, and glossy-diffuse materials, topped by thin-film iridescence, a clear coat, and fuzz. A special mode handles thin-walled objects such as leaves. Deeper sections treat subtle topics, including how specular reflectivity decouples from transmission, subsurface scattering settings, coat darkening, and thin-film interference, and they preview planned extensions like hazy specular reflection and retroreflection. It is written for the people who build those tools.
arxiv-2512-23896:
Shivali Agrawal and eight co-authors demonstrate ultraviolet LEDs that emit from their cleaved edge rather than their top surface. The devices, grown by molecular beam epitaxy on bulk aluminum nitride substrates, emit deep-ultraviolet light at two hundred sixty-five nanometers, a wavelength used for disinfection. Their layered structure mimics a laser diode, with a high-index waveguide core between cladding layers confining the light for edge emission at two hundred seventy nanometers by design.

The LEDs sustained very high current densities, showed five orders of magnitude between on and off states, and kept differential resistance low. Cleaving along a crystal plane exposed the edge, from which the team collected photons at the energy of the aluminum gallium nitride active region's bandgap. Analyzing where power is wasted, they identify the n-contact resistance as the largest contributor to series resistance in this device generation.
arxiv-2512-23996:
A R Balasubramanian and four colleagues study a counting problem in software verification. Model checkers explore the distinct execution patterns of a concurrent program. Knowing the count in advance would help users plan. It would show how long a check might run. It would also show how much ground a partial run has covered.

Exact counting, the authors show, is hopeless. The problem is hard in a strong formal sense. Even rough approximations lie beyond efficient algorithms. Their workaround is a sampling estimator. It reuses the checker's own exploration tree. Sampled paths yield an unbiased estimate in polynomial time. A variance-control trick keeps the spread of answers small. Built into the JMC checker, the estimator held within about twenty percent. That was on benchmarks with up to a million execution classes. The same machinery can also weigh the cost of a run.
arxiv-2512-24096:
Michal Kolesár, José Luis Montiel Olea, and Jonathan Roth study a common policy question. Suppose officials nudged decisions in a new direction. Judges might be encouraged to release more defendants. What would change as a result? Researchers often answer with an instrumental variable. The assumptions behind that method can be shaky, though.

The authors build a general framework for sharp bounds. It computes the effects of a counterfactual policy. No monotonicity assumption is required. The framework stays computationally tractable as well. For one important class of policies, a further result holds. Monotonicity does not actually narrow the bounds there. The paper also compares other restrictions. A relaxed version of policy invariance is developed. Applications revisit bail judges in New York City. Prosecutors in Massachusetts provide the second case.
arxiv-2512-24196:
Yijie Lin computes a Donaldson-Thomas vertex in an orbifold setting. Donaldson-Thomas theory counts curves and sheaves in threefolds. Its vertex is a generating object built from pyramid-like configurations. Lin treats the one-leg vertex for the group Z2 times Z2. A new notion makes the computation possible: restricted pyramid configurations.

One special class of configurations carries prescribed one-leg partitions. Within it, a unique class satisfies a symmetric interlacing property. That class yields an explicit formula for the vertex. The bridge is a connection to the Z4 vertex, already understood. Vertex operator methods from Okounkov, Reshetikhin, and Vafa do the heavy lifting. Bryan and Young's work supplies the other side of the bridge. The result adds a computed case to the growing Donaldson-Thomas vertex literature.
arxiv-2512-24796:
Rongge Xu, Hui Dai, Yiming Fu, and co-authors introduce LeanCat, a benchmark of one hundred formal category theory tasks written in the Lean proof assistant. Category theory tests library-grounded abstraction, meaning reasoning with high-level interfaces and reusable structures. Existing theorem proving benchmarks rarely measure that skill, favoring algebra or arithmetic instead.

Evaluation exposes a severe abstraction gap: the best model solved only a small share of tasks, and success fell sharply on harder structural problems. Readers in AI and formal methods get a stress test for structural reasoning. The suite is part one, covering ordinary categories, with more parts implied.
arxiv-2601-00196:
Yuquan Li leads five coauthors in asking whether stablecoins can replace card networks at the checkout. Stablecoins are digital tokens tied to a steady value. Their use in payments is growing fast. The authors map both systems side by side. Roles, infrastructure, and transaction life cycles are laid out. Deep contrasts appear in authorization, settlement, and recourse.

A five part lens then scores cost, legality, experience, architecture, and reach. Stablecoins settle fast, around the clock, in programmable ways. Rail level merchant fees often shrink as well. But the risk map flips against users. Fees, error checks, and dispute handling move outward. Cards absorb those frictions with subsidies and set liability rules. That support drives mass adoption for cards. Stablecoins win in closed loops and cross border lanes. As open retail money, they stay at a structural disadvantage.
arxiv-2601-00296:
Bryan Constantine Sadihin leads four coauthors in colorizing sketch videos from many kinds of color references. Most color tools accept just one reference image. They often take the first frame as that guide. Character sheets and background art get ignored. Arbitrary colored frames from later scenes go unused too. TimeColor accepts a changing count of mixed references.

Each reference gains an explicit region assignment. References enter as extra latent frames in time order. One diffusion pass then handles them all together. Model size stays fixed as references grow. Masked attention ties each subject to its right reference. Separate position codes keep the modalities apart. Those guards stop palette leaks across characters. Tests on a large animation dataset show clear gains. Color fidelity, identity, and time stability all improve. Animators gain freedom in what they supply.
arxiv-2601-00396:
Fernanda Sobrino, Adolfo De Unánue T, and eight other co-authors describe a machine learning system built with prosecutors in the Mexican state of Zacatecas. Prosecutors there face deep backlogs and limited staff. Their 2026 paper focuses on the early-attention unit that receives cases and handles early resolution. The system predicts which open cases are likely to close within six months.

Trained on records from 2014 to 2024, the models produce a weekly ranked list of three hundred cases for prosecutors to review. Random forest models score well at that task in tests done under real-time limits. The authors stress readable outputs and fit with existing routines. A randomized trial is planned to test the system in use.
arxiv-2601-00496:
Jan Rawa and Julian Sienkiewicz look for an automatic way to track information overload in social media, and test it on Reddit during the COVID-19 pandemic. Overload is known to tire readers and push them toward avoiding news, which can help false posts spread. Yet few tools can measure overload in very large datasets.

Their candidate measure uses topic modeling: a language model groups posts into topics, and a Gini index summarizes how unevenly attention spreads across those topics. Across Reddit communities about the pandemic, that index correlated significantly with the share of posts a fake-news classifier flagged as false. Within single communities, though, the results were mixed. The authors present the measure as a promising global signal rather than a settled local tool.
arxiv-2601-00596:
Sumanth Balaji, Piyush Mishra, Aashraya Sachdeva, and Suraj Agrawal argue that customer support chatbots need a harder test than most benchmarks give them. Old phone-menu systems followed rigid scripts, while language model agents promise flexibility. The open question is whether an agent follows business policy through multi-step tasks, handles dependencies between steps, and stays on track when users behave unpredictably.

Their benchmark, JourneyBench, generates realistic support scenarios from graph representations of customer journeys. A new score, the User Journey Coverage Score, measures how completely an agent adheres to policy across a whole journey rather than on isolated turns. The work targets a gap between agents that merely complete tasks and agents a company can trust with real customers.
arxiv-2601-00796:
Jiewen Chan and two co-authors present AdaGaR in 2026, a method that rebuilds moving 3D scenes from a single video. The task is hard: fine detail must stay sharp while motion stays smooth. Common methods use soft blobs, called Gaussians, to build each frame. Blobs blur fine detail by their nature. Pure wave-based units, called Gabor functions, keep detail but can wobble in energy.

AdaGaR blends the two: each unit is a blob with a learned wave mix. A weight dial sets how much wave each unit carries, with a fix that keeps energy steady. Motion is tied to smooth spline curves, with a penalty on sharp bends over time. A smart start uses depth guesses, point tracks, and masks of the moving subject. On a standard test set, AdaGaR scored at the top on all three quality marks.
arxiv-2601-00996:
Yongxu Sun and four co-authors present, in 2026, a test for bias in videos made by AI generators such as Sora. Their test extends word and image bias tests to moving pictures. It checks how strongly a generator links groups of people to pleasant or unpleasant scenes. The team first checked the new test against known results.

They then scored links for race and for gender across seventeen jobs and seven awards. Sora's videos linked European Americans and women more to pleasant scenes, by a wide margin. Those links tracked real-world shares closely: who holds each job, and who has won each award. Prompts that ask for fairness shrank most links. But for two jobs, the prompts backfired and the link grew. The authors warn that such tools can deepen unfair images if shipped unchecked. Their test gives makers a way to measure the harm first.
arxiv-2601-01396:
Bao and 3 co-authors study a question in complex analysis about filling in values at a rough point of a shape. The point is singular, meaning the shape is not smooth there, and the question is when values can be assigned in a way that fits a given weighting rule. They develop tools called Zhou weights and Tian functions for that setting.

With those tools, they state clear conditions that are both needed and enough for such filling-in to exist, for two kinds of functions. They then apply the results to simpler rings built from power series and polynomials, giving separate conditions that merge under extra limits on the zero set.
arxiv-2601-01596:
Ren and 7 co-authors add a correction step that lets compressed science data keep its frequency patterns. Squeezing huge data sets by lossy methods saves space but can blur the patterns that many studies rely on, from cosmic structure to diffraction images. Their Fourier correction works with common compressors rather than replacing them.

The key idea writes frequency errors as combinations of ordinary spatial errors, which defines a zone where both stay within set limits. The method nudges the error step by step into that shared zone, sped up by graphics processors. Tests on cosmology, diffraction, combustion, and brain-signal data show key features survive in both views, aiding later analysis.
arxiv-2601-02096:
Ballroom dancing pairs a leader and a follower in intricate, coordinated motion. Capturing that interplay normally needs full-body tracking. Peizhuo Li and three co-authors show a cheaper path. Just three tracked points, from a virtual reality headset and controllers, describe a dancer well enough. The performance can be rebuilt from them.

Three-point trajectories are compact. A small multilayer perceptron can predict the follower's trajectory directly from the leader's. A carefully planned autoregressive procedure then turns trajectories into a full embodied avatar. It works deterministically. The generative models such problems usually require are not needed. The approach resists overfitting. It works on small ballroom datasets. It still generalizes to the larger, more diverse LaFAN motion dataset. Cheap paired-dancing applications in virtual reality open up.
arxiv-2601-02196:
Defending a computer network automatically means choosing corrective actions. Hosts get isolated, services reset, decoys planted. Information is partial and time is short. Yu Li and seven co-authors frame automated cyber defense as a partially observable decision problem. The setting is the CAGE Challenge 4 environment. They solve it with Monte Carlo tree search, not deep reinforcement learning.

The agent is called ACDZero. It embeds the observed network with a graph neural network. Reasoning stays invariant to host relabeling that way. Learned priors over graph-edit actions guide the search. Model-free knowledge is distilled into look-ahead planning. Against leading reinforcement learning baselines, the planner earned higher defense rewards. Network structures and attacker behaviors varied. Robustness was greater, and sample efficiency far better.
arxiv-2601-02296:
Lily L. Zhao and four co authors hunt for hidden instrument drift in seven years of data from EXPRES, a spectrograph built to measure star motions with extreme precision. Small drifts can look exactly like the wobble caused by an orbiting planet. The worst drift appeared around January 2022, when the instrument temperature varied more than usual, and it reached a swing large enough to hide or fake a planet signal.

To correct it, they track shifts, stretching, and rotation in the recorded light patterns, plus line shape measures from a laser frequency comb. Combining those traces with instrument readings in one regression cuts the solar drift by about two thirds and reduces scatter for twelve quiet stars. A spurious planet signal around the star Rho Coronae Borealis disappears once the correction is applied.
arxiv-2601-02396:
Davy Romine, Andrew Kingery, Guanqun Song, and Ting Zhu present SLASh, an open simulation tool for laser linked satellite networks in low Earth orbit. Such constellations promise coverage for hard to reach areas, but designers lack open models that reveal bottlenecks and wasted capacity before anything is launched. Mistakes found late cost operators and users both time and money.

SLASh lets users design a simulated network with chosen characteristics, built to mirror real world conditions, including the inter satellite laser links in its name. It also generates abstract telemetry that can be moved through the simulated network, so different designs can be compared on equal terms. The tool is meant to make constellation planning cheaper, faster, and more transparent.
arxiv-2601-02496:
Sergio Demian Lerner introduces auditable proof of work, a redesign of the mining puzzle used by cryptocurrencies, aimed at a cheating problem inside mining pools. In a block withholding attack, a pool member submits partial work to earn shares but hides any full block found, harming the pool. Pools today cannot easily check whether a member really searched the space they claimed to search.

The construction, inspired by Hashcash style nonce searching, lets a miner later attest, with a chosen probability. To having searched named regions of the nonce space in earlier rounds, while still doing productive work on a new block. Pool members can then audit each other's past effort retroactively, with no trusted hardware or third party. Standard proof of work properties such as public checking and difficulty adjustment are preserved, supporting decentralized pools with verifiable work credit.
arxiv-2601-02596:
Md Abu Sayed and four co authors coordinate decoy defenses across coupled cyber and physical systems, so that an attacker probing one side meets a consistent false picture on the other. The interaction is modeled as a Stackelberg game, where the defender commits to a strategy first and the attacker responds. Guidance for where to place the decoys comes from real vulnerability data in the National Vulnerability Database and from exploit probabilities based on standard severity scores.

Cyber and physical replicas disrupt the attacker's scouting and slow their progress. A score built from single flaw entries identifies which flaws matter most and deserve decoy cover. Across both major versions of the severity scoring system, coordinated multilayer decoys beat single layer ones and baseline defenses on defender utility. The work argues that such decoys should be planned jointly wherever systems are coupled.
arxiv-2601-02896:
Harshvardhan Saini, Yiming Tang, and Dianbo Liu connect two ways of steering the behavior of large language models: reading their internal features and writing better prompts. Models can fall into unwanted personas, such as flattering the user, making things up, or chasing short-term rewards. Handwritten prompts are easy to understand but hard to scale, while automatic prompt search works well yet stays opaque.

The authors use gradient ascent to search for prompts that push the model's internal state toward a chosen persona direction. Two methods, RESGA and SAEGA, add a fluency control so the found prompts still read like natural text. Tests on Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models cover three personas, with a marked drop in measured sycophancy.
arxiv-2601-03396:
Maan Qraitem, Kate Saenko, and Bryan A. Plummer tackle a storytelling problem: characters made by language models all sound like helpful assistants. Procedural generation builds vast worlds, levels, and quests. But character creation is underexplored. Alignment training leaves two biases behind. Such figures uniformly take agreeable moral stances. And they always answer questions directly, never refusing or deflecting. That kills dramatic tension and makes casts predictable.

Their framework, PersonaWeaver, separates world-building from behavior-building. The first covers roles and demographics. The second covers moral stances and interaction styles. The split yields casts with genuinely varied reactions and moral positions. It also gives second-order diversity in style markers, such as length, tone, and punctuation. The authors trace the biases to likelihood training and assistant fine-tuning. Richer characters, they argue, need those pressures deliberately undone.
arxiv-2601-03596:
Qianyu Guo and four co-authors tackle few-shot segmentation, where a model must outline a new kind of object after seeing only a few examples. The method is used in medical diagnosis and factory inspection, but most studies test under clean lab conditions. Real settings add bad lighting, new backgrounds, odd camera angles, motion blur, and camouflaged targets, all of which can break a model.

The team defines an environment-robust version of the task and builds a benchmark spanning eight datasets and many real scenes. Their method, Adaptive Attention Distillation, is designed to hold up under those perturbations. For hospitals and factories, the point is practical: a segmentation tool that only works under perfect conditions is not ready for deployment.
arxiv-2601-03796:
Christopher Gabaldon and eight co-authors present a data-driven way to read the brain's large-scale dynamical state from correlation matrices, subject by subject. Their trick treats correlation thresholding like a percolation probe: as the threshold varies, clusters of connected regions grow and merge, and several observables are tracked at once. These signatures converge at a characteristic threshold, which becomes their descriptor of brain state.

Applied to resting-state scans from a large cohort of nearly a thousand healthy people, the method gave stable, person-specific values that moved systematically with known dynamical indicators like temporal autocorrelation. Simulations of a whole-brain model with a known critical regime confirmed the descriptor tracks changes in collective dynamics as excitability varies. A physically grounded single number for brain state could aid comparisons across people and conditions.
arxiv-2601-03896:
Gennaro Costagliola and Federico Vastarini present work in progress on parsing hypergraphs, deciding whether a given hypergraph belongs to a language a grammar can make. Their grammars are context-free hyperedge swap grammars, which build hypergraphs by swapping hyperedges for subgraphs. The approach rests on a new LR parsing technique for positional grammars, also under development.

The central move is a reduction from hyperedge swapping to positional grammars with extra structural limits, using permutation-based steps to find the right order of hyperedges in each rule. Early results also separate two kinds of ambiguity, in generating graphs versus recognizing them. Which swap languages the method can parse is still under study. Graph parsing underlies tools from program analysis to chemistry, so new parsing routes have wide potential reach.
arxiv-2601-04296:
J. L. Cardoso and three co-authors offer a teaching-first route through a classic problem in their 2026 arXiv paper: how a van der Waals fluid splits into liquid and vapour. Starting from the Lennard-Jones picture of molecules attracting and repelling, they build the equation of state from its first correction and derive the fluid's thermodynamic potentials for one-atom and two-atom gases.

On that base they formulate the Clausius-Clapeyron equation near the critical point and solve it in closed form, giving the coexistence curve without leaning on graphs or numerical work. The authors present the derivation as a clearer path for students and instructors into a problem some 150 years old. Tying the mathematics back to the microscopic origin of the behaviour at each step.
arxiv-2601-04396:
Rebekah White, Rileigh Bandy, and Teresa Portone test a fairer way to be unsure in a 2026 arXiv paper. Bayesian calibration is the standard way to attach uncertainties to a physical model's parameters. when the model itself is wrong in form, Bayes can report confidence it has not earned, misleading the decisions built on it. Prediction-oriented inference promises uncertainties that stay honest by aiming at predicting new data, and that adapt to how wrong the model is.

The authors bring that idea to hard scientific settings: single realizations of evolving data and expensive nonlinear physics. Their testbeds are a polynomial model and a contaminant transport problem, including versions whose equations carry built-in correction terms meant to absorb model error. As misspecification and noise grow, the prediction-oriented approach characterizes uncertainty better than standard inference, and can calibrate those correction terms too.
arxiv-2601-04596:
Xinyan Yu and three co-authors test whether touching a virtual robot changes how present it feels, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Virtual reality is now a standard stand-in for real human-robot studies because prototypes can be rebuilt overnight, but most VR setups leave out touch, an odd omission when the encounter is physical. Their scenario is a robot that seeks a person's help.

Inside the simulation, one group wore haptic gloves giving tactile and force feedback while another used ordinary hand controllers. The gloved participants reported stronger social and self-presence, moved in more varied and natural ways, and judged the robot differently on emotional dimensions.
