Brian M Cho and two co-authors provide anytime-valid tests for the conditional mean function, the function mapping covariates to expected outcomes, covering global nulls and contrasts between functions.

Under mild conditions, their tests control type-I error at all times beyond a minimum sample size, achieve power one, and attain optimal sample complexity relative to Gaussian location testing. Inverting the tests yields function-valued confidence sequences. Synthetic and real-data experiments confirm power while preserving error rates under continuous monitoring. Experimenters in adaptive trials, treatment assignment, and fairness auditing gain inference they can trust mid-stream.
arxiv-2602-08196:
Quantum graphs, networks of wires joined at vertices, model electrons moving through structured materials, and disorder can trap their waves in place. Oleg Safronov studies Schrödinger operators on quantum graphs whose edge counts between points follow orbits of a shift of finite type, a symbolic dynamical rule.

For these systems, he proves Anderson localization: wave functions concentrate in bounded regions instead of spreading across the graph. The result links spectral theory with symbolic dynamics, showing that a combinatorial coding rule for the graph's edges suffices to produce localization. Mathematical physicists gain a rigorous localization theorem for a class of graphs where geometry is governed by a finite-type shift.
arxiv-2602-08296:
Multi-tenant GPU clusters suffer congestion when training jobs share oversubscribed networks, degrading throughput for over a third of jobs. Anton A. Zabreyko and two co-authors present MonkeyTree, the first system to attack congestion through job-migration-based defragmentation rather than routing or flow scheduling.

Because a job's rings send just one flow across racks for each rack the job touches, congestion-free placements exist abundantly and are reachable with few migrations. MonkeyTree formulates defragmentation as an integer linear program minimizing worker movements, and once low fragmentation is reached, new arrivals disturb only a few racks, making it self-reinforcing. Cloud operators gain a placement-level fix for a problem routing alone cannot solve when traffic exceeds capacity.
arxiv-2602-08396:
Drone swarms can act as flying cell towers in cities, disaster zones, and remote areas, but tracking ground users and keeping the drones in sync is hard. Akanksha Sneh and two co-authors propose doing both jobs with the same millimeter-wave radio standard used for communication. Their arXiv paper builds the sensing into the link itself, avoiding extra hardware.

The system, based on IEEE 802.11ad, senses targets in five dimensions at once: range, speed, azimuth, elevation, and polarization. Simulations with realistic urban models confirm that the swarm can track ground targets in all five. Readers get a lean design for drone networks that see and talk through one radio, cutting cost, weight, and power.
arxiv-2602-08896:
Finding the right peer reviewer is slow work, and Yehua Huang and four co-authors attack it with data and language models. Their OmniReview data set merges several academic platforms through a disambiguation pipeline, yielding 202,756 verified review records. On top of it sits a three-level evaluation ladder, from broad recall down to pinpointing the exact expert.

Their method, Pro-MMoE, uses language-model-written scholar profiles to preserve fine expertise detail, paired with a mixture-of-experts design that balances competing goals. It reaches the best score on six of seven metrics, beating embedding-only approaches that compress expertise away. The package offers editors a more realistic, interpretable reviewer recommender.
arxiv-2602-08996:
Video language models give weak sports coaching, and collecting feedback data for every sport is expensive. Arushi Rai and one co-author use rock climbing as a test case for a cheaper route. They supplement existing feedback from a different sport with freely available web material from the target domain, such as competition videos and coaching manuals. That extra data teaches the model climbing-specific judgment without new annotation.

Standard text metrics also fail coaching quality, so the paper proposes two better ones: specificity and actionability. Together, the data recipe and the new metrics enable more useful, practical feedback generation under limited annotations, with lessons that should carry to other sports.
arxiv-2602-09096:
Type Ia supernovae serve as cosmic yardsticks, yet their fainter Iax cousins break the pattern and puzzle astronomers. A large team led by Erez A. Zimmerman presents SN 2024vjm, possibly the faintest supernova ever observed. A deep pre-explosion image from the recently launched Euclid mission shows its progenitor system is dimmer than the helium-giant candidate for SN 2012Z. It is also dimmer than the companion or remnant proposed for SN 2008ha.

The faintness points to a subdwarf helium star donating mass to a white dwarf, and argues strongly against a massive-star origin for this explosion. Weak mass transfer that fails to fully disrupt the white dwarf fits the picture, though such models still struggle with the very faintest Iax events. The result tightens the hunt for what makes these odd explosions.
arxiv-2602-09296:
Frederic Gmeiner and three co-authors bring PointAloud, a set of AI-backed, pointer-first exchanges for think-aloud computing, the practice of catching users' spoken thoughts during software tasks. Current ways strain: users forget what is caught, are not urged to speak, and miss or are cut off by feedback, while speaking must feel worthwhile through handy AI help.

PointAloud offers on-the-spot urging to speak out, low-clutter feedback, and rich-in-context write-ups of work steps beside early AI help. A study with 12 users probes its worth for write-ups and human-AI joint making. The paper ends with design notes for pointer-first, AI-backed think-aloud flows, aiming to make spoken musing a natural part of computing work.
arxiv-2602-09396:
Streaming reinforcement learning sees each transition once and discards it, a frugal regime for on-device agents that starves them of samples. Value losses alone struggle to build good representations from such fleeting data. Nilaksh and four co-authors extend self-predictive representations into the streaming pipeline in their 2026 paper, aiming to squeeze more learning from every frame. Naive transfer fails, since highly correlated streaming samples destabilize training.

The fix combines orthogonal gradient updates against the momentum target with handling for gradient conflicts from streaming optimizers. Across three game suites, the method systematically beats existing streaming baselines. Analyses of the learned latent space confirm markedly richer representations, closing much of the gap left by the missing replay buffer. The approach stays light enough to train on just a few processor cores.
arxiv-2602-09696:
Solving large-scale linear systems is a base of science and factory compute. Classic repeat solvers strain as unknowns grow, while fully quantum linear solvers demand fault-proof kit far beyond near-term reach. Shigetora Miyashita and Yoshi-aki Shimada propose a quantum-boosted paired gradient method in their 2026 paper. A fault-proof quantum method only builds a wave-shaped initial guess for a classic paired gradient solver.

Total runtime and resource needs are estimated for a joined quantum-HPC platform on the three-dim Poisson rule. A central feature is the tunable split of the state number between quantum and classic solvers, letting flexible split of compute effort. Under open design guesses, regimes emerge where the hybrid beats purely classic ways. It needs far fewer quantum kit than end-to-end quantum linear solvers, pointing to quantum devices as boosters within high-performance work.
arxiv-2602-10196:
Guarded measures in ABJM theory reduce, via SUSY pinning, to finite-size matrix sums, but instanton shifts remain hard to compute step by step. A 2026 paper led by Bercel Boldis, with two co-authors, develops a bootstrap setup for supersymmetric Wilson loops and free-energy instanton shifts, building on earlier methods. Exact working links and fit conditions in the Fermi-gas version of the ABJM matrix model drive the math.

The setup yields exact proofs of several free-energy links before known only as guesses, from refined shape string theory or high-care numbers. Applied to half- and sixth-BPS Wilson loops, it fixes their deep shifts, showing broad gaps and finding new shape traits of instanton effects. The results expose the tangled deep structure and duality network of ABJM theory.
arxiv-2602-10496:
Yongzhong Xu studies the shape of transformer training in a 2026 paper. Overparameterized models live in large parameter spaces, yet their learning paths may be far simpler than their size suggests. Controlled modular arithmetic tasks make that shape visible.

The headline finding is sized collapse. Despite a parameter space of size in the hundreds, training paths quickly settle onto execution sheets of only three or four sizes. The collapse holds across random seeds and moderate difficulties, though each run orients its surface differently. The paper links this structure to sharp focus concentration and to slope alignment effects, arguing that small shape explains several familiar training phenomena.
arxiv-2602-10596:
Z. Zhou and seven co-authors design an optical readout for cryogenic detectors in a 2026 paper. Low-temperature tests like liquid xenon dark matter detectors must carry signals out of cryostats, traditionally through coaxial cables and vacuum feedthroughs. That route suffers attenuation and crosstalk.

The new analog optical system converts raw electrical signals into light. The light intensity tracks the electrical size linearly. Fiber carries it out of the cold setting, and it converts back electrically while keeping the waveform. The approach offers low attenuation over long distances and reduced crosstalk across feedthroughs. Wave size multiplexing adds channel room, giving cryogenic tests a cleaner path from sensor to data acquisition.
arxiv-2602-10696:
Miao Lu and four co-authors make assortment tuning robust to shifting tastes in a 2026 paper. Retailers choose product subsets to maximize revenue under customer choice conduct, and data-driven methods learn those choices from history. But preferences shift and choice models misspecify, so learned assortments transfer poorly and revenue falls.

The new system accounts for possible distributional shifts in customer choice rather than trusting a nominal model. It models preference drift from a baseline choice model and optimizes against plausible shifts, trading some nominal results for resilience. The approach speaks to any retailer whose yesterday's customers differ from tomorrow's. Toughness, the paper argues, is worth more than an assortment tuned to a world that no longer exists.
arxiv-2602-10796:
Jie Jiang and ten co-authors match expressivity with parallelism in sequence modeling in a 2026 paper. Transformers are expressive but costly; linear sequence models are fast but bounded by shallow, single-step updates. Iterative methods like test-time training add power yet break hardware parallelism through token-level and step-level serial dependencies.

Their model, PRISM, approximates the gate-residual-direction iteration pattern of test-time training in a parallelizable form. A write-forget decoupling plan isolates nonlinearity within the injection rule, while a two-stage proxy system sidesteps stated solvers' serial dependency. A short convolution anchors the initial residual, letting the model iterate in parallel. The design aims at sequence models that are both strong and hardware-friendly.
arxiv-2602-11696:
Global symmetry alone can force a quantum system to stay gapless, with no energy gap above its ground state, and anomaly matching has been the main tool for proving such enforcement. Takamasa Ando and one co-author introduce a second mechanism based on symmetry spans. In a span, one symmetry embeds into two larger symmetries at once, so any gapped phase with the full symmetry must restrict compatibly from both sides.

When no compatible gapped phase exists, gaplessness follows. The mechanism works even with only discrete and non-anomalous continuous symmetries, both of which admit concrete lattice realizations. The authors build explicit spans that enforce gaplessness in one space and one time dimension, realize them in conformal field theories, and write down lattice Hamiltonians carrying the needed symmetry embeddings.
arxiv-2602-11796:
In 1987 Frankl proved an influential stability result for the Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem, which bounds the size of an intersecting family by its distance from the nearest star family or trivial intersecting family. It extends the Hilton-Milner theorem in a far-reaching way. Eduard Inozemtsev and one co-author now prove the analogue for permutations, provided the number of items is large.

That analogue gives a similar extension of a Hilton-Milner type result for permutations proved by Ellis. Stability results of this kind matter because they say more than a maximum size: they describe what near-extremal families must look like, tying them close to the obvious extremal examples. The permutation version carries that structural insight into a setting where symmetry and ordering complicate the picture.
arxiv-2602-11896:
Metamerism in color vision means two lights with unlike spectra can look the same. Vincent Lostanlen and one co-author propose a musical version of the effect: two music fragments with unlike sound waves can sound the same. This report describes a method to generate musical matches from any audio clip, based on joint time-frequency scattering in Kymatio, open-source Python software for GPU computing and automatic differentiation.

The report gives a math description of JTFS plus excerpts from the Kymatio source code. It reviews prior work on the method, with links to related algorithms such as spectrotemporal receptive fields, modulation spectra, and Gabor filters. For audio research, metamers offer a controlled way to probe what listeners actually hear versus what waveforms contain.
arxiv-2602-12196:
Text reasoning in AI has raced ahead, but spatial reasoning in early maths still lags, and that gap matters in classrooms. Mohamed Huti led this work with nine co-authors, presenting the Visual Reasoning Benchmark, built from 701 real primary-school exam questions from Zambia and India. Tasks include analogy, pattern completion, and spatial matching, shown as raw images with little text.

Models handle static skills such as counting and scaling fairly well, yet hit a spatial ceiling on folding, reflection, and rotation. That uneven edge, which the authors call a jagged frontier, risks wrong marking, false hints, and reinforced pupil errors. The benchmark thus maps where classroom-ready visual tools stop being safe to trust.
arxiv-2602-12296:
Traffic lights that adapt to real flows can cut waits, fuel use, and queues, but they need a good picture of the road. Maojiang Deng led this work with three co-authors, joining deep Q-network and proximal policy optimisation methods to tune signal timing. Roads are split by a formula mixing logarithmic and linear parts, giving variable cell lengths rather than fixed blocks.

Each state carries three channels: vehicle count, average speed, and space occupancy. Signal phases form the action set, each run for a fixed green time, and rewards blend waiting time, speed, and fuel use, each scaled and weighted by priority. Simulations in SUMO with TensorFlow and Python show the variable-cell, multi-channel method beating fixed-cell rivals, including when transferred across ranges.
arxiv-2602-12396:
Spin-orbit coupling splits spin-degenerate bands in crystals without inversion symmetry, even when time-reversal symmetry holds. Fan Yang led this work with two co-authors, using point group representations to classify four types of spin-orbit terms in periodic solids: Rashba, Dresselhaus, Weyl, and Ising. Each type is allowed by different crystal symmetries, beyond the two famous cases alone.

The team builds reciprocal-space energy formulas for each type of opposite-spin splitting, plus minimal tight-binding models capturing all types for subgroups of two high-symmetry groups. They also list all nodal features in the band structures, separating lines forced by crystal symmetry from those forced by time-reversal alone, and name materials hosting each inversion-breaking effect. The classification complements recent work on magnetic systems without spin-orbit coupling, and it grounds studies of superconductivity and collective effects in such materials.
arxiv-2602-12696:
Medical and satellite images often come with different sets of channels, which makes it hard to reuse a trained vision model on a new setup. Most past work retrains the whole model for each new channel mix, leaving the simpler route of probing a frozen model largely untested. Umar Marikkar and three co-authors show that borrowing probe tricks from other fields works poorly here, sometimes worse than training from scratch.

Their answer is channel-aware probing, which treats each channel on its own before combining them. One part encodes channels separately, and another pools within each channel first and only then merges across channels. Across three multi-channel benchmarks, the method beat standard probing, matched training from scratch, and nearly closed the gap to full fine-tuning of the same pre-trained models.
arxiv-2602-12796:
Rebuilding a 3D surface from photos with Gaussian splatting is fast and looks sharp, but the scattered points often lose fine surface detail. Xiao Ren and five co-authors propose GSM-GS, a framework that tightens the geometry from two sides at once. For single views, it splits the scene by texture, using image gradients to separate rich and flat regions, then applies depth-guided filtering that protects detailed areas.

For multiple views, a geometry-guided method links point clouds across frames and builds normal constraints that keep views consistent. Tests on public datasets show the method keeps rendering quality high while improving geometric accuracy. The payoff is surface reconstruction that holds onto small-scale structure instead of smoothing it away, a common weakness of plain splatting approaches.
arxiv-2602-12896:
Open problems drive a field forward, and this document gathers them for billiards and quantitative symplectic geometry. Sixteen contributors, led in the listing by Bernhard Albach, offer problems to an open problem list compiled after a workshop at the University of Heidelberg in July 2025. The contributions span the shared territory of billiard dynamics and symplectic geometry.

As a collection rather than a single argument, its value lies in curation: researchers can see which questions the community judges important and where progress might unlock new results. Workshop discussions shaped the list, giving it the character of a field consensus rather than one author's agenda. For newcomers, it is a map of open frontiers; for specialists, a checklist of challenges worth attacking.
arxiv-2602-13096:
Bartnik's quasi-local mass assigns a mass-like quantity to a two-sphere's worth of boundary data: a metric, two scalar functions, and a one-form. Stephen McCormick and Markus Wolff construct Einstein initial data with boundary matching Bartnik data of a special form, with constant scalar functions and vanishing one-form. Outside a compact set, the data agree with spherically symmetric Schwarzschild initial data of controlled mass.

As an application, they bound the Bartnik mass for such data beyond the time-symmetric setting, a step past earlier results that assumed time symmetry. They also build initial data on a cylinder linking this class of boundary data to time-symmetric data, so that non-time-symmetric estimates can be drawn from prior time-symmetric ones. The constructions give quasi-local mass theory firmer footing outside its symmetric comfort zone.
arxiv-2602-13496:
Ecological decisions lag because biodiversity data takes so long to travel from sensor to analyst. Edge computing moves processing to the sensor itself, with on-device AI cutting reliance on data transfer and constant connectivity, shifting monitoring from passive logging toward autonomous, responsive sensing. In practice, though, adoption is fragmented, with trade-offs and challenges rarely reported in a clear way.

This review analyzes 82 studies from 2017 to 2025 across acoustic, vision, tracking, and multi-modal systems, pooling hardware, model tuning, and wireless links. Papers grew from 3 in 2017 to 19 in 2025, across four system types from TinyML microcontrollers to cloud pipelines, each trading power, compute, and communication differently. Aude Vuilliomenet leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14196:
Han-Xiang Hu and five co-authors build a 2026 arXiv model of cosmic-ray acceleration at shocks. Their nonlinear extension of diffusive shock acceleration adds cosmic-ray backreaction on the shock precursor, plus an upstream-escape mechanism that yields an exponential high-energy cutoff. The cosmic-ray pressure gradient slows upstream flow, stretching the precursor.

In that stretched precursor, higher-rigidity particles sample a larger velocity gradient and gain harder spectra. A momentum-dependent loss term ends acceleration and steepens the spectrum near the cutoff. The compression ratio is set dynamically by matching injection from thermal leakage with nonlinear shock modification, with wave heating as stabilizing feedback. Applied to young supernova-remnant settings, the model aims to reproduce DAMPE observations.
arxiv-2602-14296:
Yifan Wu and 14 co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv way to train web agents with no costly real sites. Getting paths from real sites is pricey and hard to check, since state shifts stay hidden and outside checkers prove mixed. AutoWebWorld instead builds web sites as finite state machines, turned into live sites by coding agents.

Because states, acts, and shift rules are plain, checking turns programmatic: each act is checked against set rules, and task win means reaching a goal state in the machine graph. A fully auto search-and-check line made over 11,663 checked paths from 29 varied web sites at low cost, giving scalable, checkable training data for self-run web agents.
arxiv-2602-14496:
Haojie Hu and five co-authors trace a 2026 arXiv likely fate for JWST's overmassive black holes. The scope found hundreds of huge black holes at redshifts 4 to 7. A notable share sit in galaxies whose black-hole-to-galaxy mass ratios top local values by 1 to 2 orders of size.

Their birth demands heavy seeds or fast seed growth, testing co-growth models. Applying model black-hole and galaxy plans to dark-matter halo merger pasts from N-body runs, in the Shin-Uchuu view, the paper tracks later change. Early change of overmassive black holes is ruled by stunted feeding, slowly shrinking mass ratios toward normal. Less heavy black holes, by contrast, feed super-Eddington early, slowly raising their ratios, hinting at a return toward local scaling links over time.
arxiv-2602-14596:
Ban Q. Tran and four co-authors probe a 2026 arXiv quantum-assisted physics-informed neural network for parabolic partial differential equations. Physics-aware nets code ruling laws into training goals, and quantum widenings aim to lift picture power while staying fit for near-term quantum hardware. One- and two-size heat formulas serve as classic benchmarks.

Two quantum-aided designs differ in code design. In the first, a classic feed-forward neural net makes trainable trait maps for quantum data coding, called FNN-TE-QPINN. In the second, the code stage is built fully by a tuned quantum circuit, called QNN-TE-QPINN, yielding a fully quantum trait map. Findings stress the key role of code design and back hybrid quantum-classic approaches for heat-type formula modeling.
arxiv-2602-14796:
Don Rolih and Rok Zitko study the proximity effect in a single-layer Hubbard model coupled to BCS superconductors inside a phase-biased Josephson junction. Two distinct gapped solutions appear: a Mott-like insulating phase and a proximitised superconducting phase, split by a first-order transition with hysteresis.

In the insulating phase a large correlation charge gap strongly suppresses the critical current. The superconducting phase behaves as a zero-junction whose proximitised gap closes at a phase of pi, yielding a correlated metal. Phase bias and junction transparency thus switch the device between conducting and insulating regimes. Strong correlations meet superconductivity in a tunable junction.
arxiv-2602-14896:
Pedram Bakhtiarifard and others ask why deep nets squeeze so well, by trim, by bits, and by pupil nets, with scant loss in score. Their guess, told in code-size terms, is that trained weights hold more form and less code-size than chance start weights, and squeeze tools reap that saved code-size.

A raw weight count, they argue, claims more than a trained net truly holds. Their Mosaic-of-Motifs plan tests if form, not size, tells why nets squeeze. Deep nets thus gain a code-size tale for a squeeze all users know.
arxiv-2602-15196:
DeVries and colleagues explain the quantized angular momentum of rotating Q-balls. Non-topological solitons such as Q-balls may contribute to cosmological dark matter. Grasping their formation and evolution in the early universe requires grasping spinning lumps with nonzero spin. Rather than taking as given the form of scalar field layouts that produce spinning Q-balls, the team derives it, yielding the well-known discrete spin.

That work brings added insight into spinning soliton traits, including a method for finding their typical angular velocity. By studying spinning lumps in two spatial dimensions, the team tests these traits in detail. Formula guesses for the lumps and their defining values are built, shown to agree with numerical results, and shown to exhibit the general traits of spinning lumps.
arxiv-2602-15296:
Sen and colleagues use GPS carrier phase data to search for exotic low-mass fields emitted by the binary neutron-star merger GW170817. GPS is a planet-scale network of atom clocks enabling tests of fundamental physics beyond navigation. Ultra-relativistic fields would leave a spread, anti-chirp mark in clock rate series, delayed after the LIGO-Virgo detection.

The team builds median fake rate data from eighteen Rb clocks tied to a hydrogen maser, searching pulse length, coming delay, and frequency. No real signal is seen after noise and tests. They derive 95 percent lower bounds on the link scale of square links driving shifts in fine-structure value. These limits beat prior bounds for ELF levels near ten to the minus eighteen electronvolts to ten to the minus fourteen eV. This shows old world satellite-clock networks allow backward searches for new physics using years of clock data.
arxiv-2602-15396:
Shin and colleagues offer paired Schrödinger Bridge pairing, a making setup that finds best paths in spaces in two steps. Spread nets often give very bent paths and rough score goals due to a blank, fresh flow that sets free data-noise links.

First, they treat the Schrödinger Bridge forward flow as a link build task and learn it through a data-to-energy sampling view that moves data to a start. Then, they learn the reverse making flow with a plain pairing penalty guided by the best link. By working in a fresh mode, ASBM gives greatly direct and lean sampling paths. Versus prior works, ASBM grows to high-sized data with clearly better calm and speed. Wide tests on image making show ASBM lifts truth with less sampling steps. The team shows the power of the best path via shrinking to a one-step maker.
arxiv-2602-15796:
Murthy works alone on upper bounds for the triple product property, or TPP, in subgroups of finite nilpotent groups of class two. The TPP holds for three non-empty subsets S, T, and U of a group G when an equation in their elements equals one exactly when primed elements equal unprimed partners. For G, the TPP ratio is the maximum product of subset sizes divided by group size, over satisfying subgroup triples.

The paper proves four bounds. First, the ratio is below the square root of the centre index for class-two groups. Second, the ratio is at most p for p-groups with a cyclic commutator subgroup of order p. Third, the ratio equals one for p-groups with a large centre, with index between p squared and p cubed. Fourth, the ratio equals one for p-groups with character degrees of one or p.
arxiv-2602-16196:
Coordinating large crowds of interacting agents is hard because the joint state-action space grows exponentially with agent count. Emile Anand and coauthors introduce GMFS, a graphon mean-field subsampling design for scalable cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning with mixed interactions. Mean-field methods ease the burden by aggregating interactions, but they assume uniform interactions. Graphon designs capture mixed interactions yet grow costly as agent numbers rise.

GMFS subsamples agents by interaction strength, approximating the graphon-weighted mean field. It learns a policy with sample complexity polynomial in the subsample size and a gap to optimal that shrinks with the square root of that size. Numerical simulations in robotic coordination verify the theory, with GMFS achieving near-optimal results. The design thus offers a scalable route to cooperative learning where agents differ and crowds are large.
arxiv-2602-16396:
Pavel Spurný and Jiří Borovička report an observation of a Geminid fireball, recorded by the Czech Fireball Network in December 2012. The fireball stands out for its record penetration to thirty-two and a half kilometres, and for the likelihood that a small fraction of its mass survived and landed on the ground. No deeply penetrating Geminid with data this precise and reliable had been observed before.

The authors compare this event with many other Geminids. For Geminids over ten grams, the terminal altitude limit stays near thirty-eight kilometres. This Geminid is the exception, penetrating six kilometres deeper. In flight it slowed from thirty-six kilometres per second to under seven. At a quarter of a kilogram, it is the fastest meteorite candidate ever observed. It survived dynamic pressure of two megapascals, ranking among asteroidal bodies behind meteorite falls. The authors also show a similar earlier claim was flawed.
arxiv-2602-16496:
James Reeves leads eighteen coauthors on the soft X-ray view of the ultra-fast outflow in the nearby quasar PG 1211+143. In December 2024 the quasar was watched at once by XRISM Resolve and XMM-Newton, letting iron and soft X-ray outflows be studied together at high resolution. This paper reports the XMM-Newton grating spectrum, finding three lower-ionization counterparts of the iron velocity zones.

The soft X-ray absorbers are somewhat less ionized than their iron counterparts, with opacity mainly from iron L-shell lines and highly ionized oxygen. Comparing the two sets of absorbers shows the outflow fits a density profile falling with radius, while the lower-ionization zones likely come from denser gas clumps. Pure electron scattering seems too weak to drive the wind alone, adding evidence that quasar disk winds are clumpy.
arxiv-2602-16596:
Thomas Michel, Debabrota Basu, and Emilie Kaufmann design Sequential Membership Inference attacks for models that change over time. Modern AI models go through many updates, and privacy audits usually inspect only the final model. The new attacks exploit the whole model sequence, inserting a target canary at a controlled time. For empirical mean computation, the authors develop an optimal attack, SeMI*, and derive its power.

Access to the sequence proves more powerful than scrutiny of the final model alone. The attack's power depends on statistics just before and after insertion, an isolation property the authors exploit for practical white-box and black-box attacks against models trained with differentially private SGD. Tests show higher power than snapshot baselines and tighter privacy audits, giving auditors a sharper tool.
arxiv-2602-16696:
Huan Souza and Pankaj Mehta ask if simple, parameter-free routes can match single-cell foundation models. Single-cell RNA data show strong, stable statistical structure. Large transformer models such as TranscriptFormer embed genes in a latent space and have set state-of-the-art scores on cell-type classification, disease-state prediction, and cross-species learning. Those models cost a lot of compute.

Using plain, interpretable pipelines built on careful normalization and linear methods, the authors match or near-match those scores across common benchmarks. They even beat foundation models on out-of-distribution tasks with new cell types and organisms absent from training. The finding calls for stricter benchmarking and suggests cell identity may be captured by simple linear codes of gene expression.
arxiv-2602-16896:
Jesús López and Eduardo Orozco-Ospino study electron speedup by microwave-driven plasma wakefields in rectangular waveguides. Plasma-based speedup draws interest as a route to compact particle accelerators, thanks to large electric fields plasmas support. Recent work has shown wakefields excited by high-power microwave pulses in plasma-filled waveguides. Yet conditions for efficient electron speedup there remain poorly mapped.

Three-dimensional particle-in-cell runs trace injection and energy gain under reduced and fully self-consistent models. Speedup hinges strongly on injection phase and initial velocity. Best results come when electrons are pre-accelerated near the group velocity of the driving pulse. For the parameters tried, gains on the order of hundreds of kilo-electronvolts arise over meter-scale lengths, with a near-monoenergetic spread under suitable injection conditions.
arxiv-2602-17196:
Yahong Wang led a nine-author team cutting the cost of running multimodal language models. Such models process hundreds of visual tokens per image, so inference grows expensive, and token pruning helps, but choosing when and where to prune has stayed guesswork tied to fixed layers. The paper brings a matrix-entropy view to the problem and spots an Entropy Collapse Layer, where visual information drops sharply and consistently.

That layer gives a principled place to prune. EntropyPrune scores each visual token's information value and drops redundant ones without attention maps, while a spectral trick with dual Gram matrices speeds the entropy math greatly. Tests across varied benchmarks beat strong pruning rivals on accuracy and efficiency, preserving nearly all performance on a popular seven-billion-parameter model while cutting compute by over two thirds. The method also scales to high-resolution and video models.
arxiv-2602-17396:
Laurenz Kremeyer led a six-author team assessing direct electron detectors for ultrafast electron diffraction work. Such tests use photo-induced changes in electron scattering intensity across 2D detectors to report on dynamic phenomena in molecules and materials. Hybrid pixel counting units promise improved sensitivity and signal-to-noise with near-zero readout noise and dark counts plus new acquisition modes like shot-to-shot normalization from high frame rates.

But these units suffer count losses at high fluxes even in continuous-wave beams, and how that translates to ultrashort pulse exposures was unknown yet critical. The paper shows count losses worsen significantly in pulsed tests, with units saturating above a couple of electrons per pixel per pulse, severely constraining bunch charge for single crystal samples. Scaling plans to optimize signal-to-noise and a complete measurement uncertainty model are developed and tested on a large dataset.
arxiv-2602-17596:
Saveliy Baturin studies the loss landscape of shallow ReLU networks. He asks if two low-loss parameter settings can be joined by a path that never climbs far above their loss level. The net has one hidden layer, constrained first-layer weights, and a penalty on the output layer. The data term is convex and globally Lipschitz.

A finite-width construction links any two points of a common sublevel set. It swaps an older quadratic estimate for a direct Lipschitz bound, then moves active units monotonically to exploit positive homogeneity. Sphere covering and cluster merging yield explicit thickening rates, with exact connectivity in one dimension. Approximation rates transfer to barrier decay rates, and Huber and cross-entropy tests back the theory with small certified gaps.
arxiv-2602-17696:
Zongmin Li and team test whether large language model safety can be secured by constraining parameter regions. The field often assumes safety regions exist: parameter subsets whose change directly steers safety conduct. The authors run a systematic evaluation of four safety region identification methods, spanning single weights to full transformer layers, across four model families of varied sizes.

Using ten safety identification data sets, they find that identified safety regions overlap only modestly, as measured by IoU. Overlap drops further when regions are refined with utility data sets of non-harmful queries. Current techniques thus fail to pin down a stable, dataset-agnostic safety region. The result cautions against safety fixes that rest on carving out a fixed parameter zone.
arxiv-2602-17796:
Annu Bura and team investigate the origin of coronal picoflare jets, tiny jet-like eruptions that may feed coronal heating and solar wind acceleration. Using ultra-high-resolution extreme ultraviolet imaging from the Extreme Ultraviolet Imager aboard Solar Orbiter, they study tiny coronal jets seen off-limb in the Sun's polar regions. Most show a bright spire plus a dark eruptive jet component.

Eleven jets were analyzed in detail. Their spatial and temporal scales match previously reported jetlets, while their kinetic energies run two to three orders of magnitude lower, placing them in the picoflare regime. Dark structures generally move slower than bright ones. Comparison with coordinated spectrograph and imaging data, plus radiative-MHD simulations with the Bifrost code, shows a one-to-one match between dark counterparts and cool chromospheric surges beside the bright spire.
arxiv-2602-17996:
Xing Yang and team model strontium titanate with an extended mean-field theory for the two-dimensional Hubbard model in degenerate dilute electron gases. Their theory gives the dome shape of the transition temperature against chemical potential seen in experiments. It shows tunable s-wave and d-wave symmetries shifting with doping. At low temperatures the mean-field picture holds, but pairing breaks down as temperatures rise.

Charge-density-wave order rivals superconductivity, raising the effective electron mass as chemical potential falls and growing stronger with interaction strength and temperature. Spin-density-wave order proves rare and fragile, while an added magnetic term gives subtle band splitting. The authors read these results as a sign that electron interactions drive its transport anomalies, with ways to tell electron-only effects apart from electron-phonon effects. The work offers guidance for raising transition temperatures in dilute systems.
arxiv-2602-18296:
Muhammad Tayyab Khan and three co-authors link 2D engineering drawings to 3D CAD models for factory automation. Their 2026 paper notes that process planning, inspection, and digital-thread work all need one specification tying CAD geometry to dimensioning and tolerancing callouts, datums, and surface demands. Yet 2D drawings still carry most manufacturing intent in auto, aerospace, shipbuilding, and heavy machinery.

The deterministic-first framework enriches drawing callouts, then scores them against candidate features on type fit, tolerance-aware size agreement, and context consistency, with engineering heuristics. Only stubborn ambiguities go to constrained language-model reasoning and a single human review. On twenty real CAD-drawing pairs the system reached mean precision near eighty-four percent, recall near ninety percent, and an F1 score near eighty-six percent. Every pipeline piece earns its keep in ablation tests.
arxiv-2602-18396:
Ehsan Lari and two co-authors built PRISM-FCP, a federated conformal prediction framework that survives hostile clients. Their 2026 paper notes existing robust methods mostly police calibration, leaving training-stage poisoning to separate tools. PRISM-FCP instead treats the coupling between training and calibration together.

During training, clients share only a fraction of parameters per round, which shrinks each hostile client's perturbation energy in the aggregate by that same fraction, a win when it outweighs slower optimization. During calibration, the server filters suspect clients with characterization vectors before estimating the conformal quantile. Tests on synthetic benchmarks and two UCI datasets, under Gaussian, ALIE, and sign-flipping training attacks, show near-nominal coverage with favorable communication-performance trade-offs.
arxiv-2602-18596:
L. S. Sonith and one co-author follow YY Herculis's 2021 outburst. Their 2026 paper reports a hot-type classical symbiotic outburst followed up with the Himalayan Chandra telescope. It coincides with secondary minima. About twelve similar brightenings were reported between 1890 and 2020, with only the 1993 outburst studied spectroscopically.

Monitoring from 2021 to 2023 covers about one and a half cycles, tracing spectral evolution over one period. Temperature and luminosity estimates from emission lines show orbital phase dependence, with phase zero point five, the secondary minimum, most reliable. The hot component measures one hundred forty-one thousand kelvin and one thousand twenty solar luminosities during outburst. It falls to one hundred thirty thousand kelvin and eight hundred thirty solar luminosities after one cycle at phase zero point five. Temperature estimates suggest YY Her shows hot-type (2021) and cool-type (1993) behavior, like AG Dra, and calcium-two absorption variations confirm the ellipsoidal effect in minima.
arxiv-2602-18896:
Vector quantisation powers many generative models, yet its codebooks often collapse. Most code vectors go unused in training. Hao Lu, with five co-authors, offers a new explanation in 2026. The cause is the nonstationary nature of encoder updates. As the encoder drifts, unselected codes receive no updates and slowly die.

Two methods address the problem. Non-Stationary Vector Quantisation propagates encoder drift to non-selected codes through a kernel rule. Transformer-based Vector Quantisation adapts the whole codebook with a lightweight mapping, while preserving convergence to the k-means solution. Tests on CelebA-HQ show near-complete codebook use and better reconstruction than baseline variants. The work gives a principled, scalable basis for future quantisation-based models.
arxiv-2602-18996:
Matching an object across camera views is hard when one view is egocentric and the other exocentric. Shannan Yan, with nine co-authors, proposes a framework in 2026 based on conditional binary segmentation. A query mask for the object is turned into a latent code, which guides localisation of the same object in a target video.

Cycle-consistency training adds a strong self-supervisory signal. The mask predicted for the target view is sent back to the source view, rebuilding the original query mask. That bidirectional constraint needs no ground-truth annotations. It also enables test-time training at inference. Experiments on Ego-Exo4D and HANDAL-X benchmarks show the optimisation objective and test-time strategy achieve state-of-the-art performance. Code is publicly available.
arxiv-2602-19296:
When a student asks a human tutor for help mid-lesson, judging whether that help worked is tricky, since students seek help exactly when they are stuck. Kirk Vanacore and five co-authors offer a framework for measuring the session-level effects of on-demand tutoring inside adaptive learning systems. It pairs sample construction with deep knowledge tracing, a method that estimates what a student has mastered, and then uses doubly robust estimation with causal forests.

Applied to more than 5,000 middle-school tutoring sessions, the method finds a clear gain. Asking for help raises next-problem correctness by about four percentage points, with a smaller gain on the next skill. Effects varied across sessions, with bigger gains where starting mastery was lower, and slightly smaller gains for low-income students. Talk time did not reliably mark the best sessions. Readers get a template for judging tutoring, including AI tutors.
arxiv-2602-19396:
Jailbreak prompts that read fluently and coherently slip past simple detection rules. Amirhossein Farzam and four co-authors study a hard case. An attacker hides a harmful goal by reframing the request to win compliance, keeping intent intact while changing how it looks. Defenses keyed to structural clues or goal-specific signatures fail against such flexible attacks, so the paper works at the level of model activations.

The team builds a self-taught framework that disentangles semantic factor pairs in a frozen language model's activations, instantiated for goal and framing. They create GoalFrameBench, a corpus with controlled goal and framing variations, to train their ReDAct module. Their FrameShield detector, working on framing representations, lifts detection across model families with minimal extra computation.
arxiv-2602-19496:
Tracking gene readouts over pseudotime helps map gene control networks, but single-cell data are noisy and high-dimensional. Mohammad Aamir Sohail and three co-authors introduce a quantum Hamiltonian-based model of gene readouts. In it, gene interactions are encoded in a parameterized Hamiltonian, and quantum measurement outcomes stand in for activity profiles. A scalable variational quantum algorithm, VQ-Net, learns the parameters and infers networks.

Finite-sample recovery promises show correct parameter values with polynomial scaling in the number of genes. On synthetic data, VQ-Net beats classical state-of-the-art methods by over 25 percent on edge recovery and over 50 percent on parameter-sign recovery. Applied to glioblastoma single-cell RNA data, the method finds biologically meaningful structure, linking quantum models to cancer biology.
arxiv-2602-19696:
Some climate and ecological systems can tip abruptly once a threshold is crossed, yet a brief crossing does not always spell disaster. A 2026 arXiv paper by Sacha Sinet and four co-authors studies overshoot in systems made of linked parts, where one slow part drives another, and asks when such an overshoot stays safe.

Earlier work had found an inverse-square rule for safe overshoot in single systems driven from outside. Here the authors extend that rule to coupled systems, writing it in terms of how far apart the parts' timescales sit and how strongly they interact. They test the rule on two simple models: ocean circulation linked to the Amazon rainforest, and ocean circulation linked to the Greenland Ice Sheet.
arxiv-2602-19796:
Rashba spin-orbit coupling in a finite semiconductor nanowire gives a canonical low-energy model, but finite wires behave differently from textbook boxes. A 2026 arXiv paper by Nico Leumer and three co-authors studies such finite wires, alone and when paired with a conventional superconductor.

Even in the normal wire, spin-orbit coupling mixes more than two momentum states into each eigenstate, and the allowed wavevectors follow a transcendental equation rather than a box rule. With superconducting pairing, electron and hole channels complicate the mix further. The authors derive an approximate quantization rule near the phase boundary. They also give a condition for exact zero-energy states. Such states can occur in both topological and trivial phases, and they feed transport through reflection and transmission, depending on how localized they are at the edge.
arxiv-2602-20096:
Many low-mass stars are unresolved equal-mass binaries that look brighter than single stars with the same properties. A 2026 arXiv paper by Zachary Way and three co-authors separates such binaries from single K and M dwarfs using Gaia DR3 XP spectra, and catalogs over twenty-one thousand found by overluminosity.

The training set holds nearby stars with pristine astrometry and photometry, excluding stars flagged as unequal-mass systems. Random forest regression models predicted magnitude and colour from spectral coefficients, dropping stars brighter than predicted after each round until the model converged on single stars alone. Applied across nearby Gaia DR3 stars, the model flags about thirteen percent of the sample as overluminous, taken to be unresolved binaries. Combined with multiplicity surveys across projected separations, these yield a nearby catalog, setting lower bounds on the multiplicity fraction for stars between a tenth and seven tenths of a solar mass.
arxiv-2602-20196:
AI agents increasingly need direct, structured access to app data and actions. Production setups still struggle to state and check the governance properties that matter. Least privilege comes first, then controlled writes, steady failures, abuse blocks, and clear audit trails. A 2026 arXiv paper by Genliang Zhu and four co-authors introduces OpenPort Protocol, a specification for opening app tools through a secure server-side gateway.

OpenPort works with any model and runtime and binds to existing tool systems. Discovery depends on access. Response formats stay stable, with coded reasons machines can act on. The access model joins integration keys, scoped rights, and rule-based policy constraints. Writes follow a risk-gated flow. Drafts and human review are the defaults. Time-bounded auto-running is allowed under clear policy, and high-risk steps face extra controls. Readers gain a specification for governing agent tool access rather than merely enabling it.
arxiv-2602-20396:
Jörg Martin and Stefan Haufe argue that multivariate feature importance needs causal context. Explainable AI aims to reveal which features matter, letting people check models or even spark discoveries. Yet the standard Shapley-value approach, used in a purely data-driven way, can mislead. Even with two features, collider bias and suppression can create spurious links when one feature is judged only in the observational context of the other.

Causal knowledge of the data-generating process is needed to spot and correct such misleading attributions. The authors propose cc-Shapley, an interventional version of standard Shapley values that uses the causal structure to judge each feature in the causal context of the rest. Theory shows it removes spurious links from collider bias. Tests on synthetic and real-world datasets show links vanishing or reversing when moving from observational to cc-Shapley values, against univariate importance.
arxiv-2602-20496:
Stepwise stereo matching is exact but heavy: its looping nets block use on edge devices. Jintu Zheng and three co-authors study stepwise fixes and find depth updates are sparse in space and repeat over time. Their system, Pip-Stereo, cuts all three. Step-by-step round pruning cuts repeat steps, shrinking looped work to one-pass use. Shared one-camera depth priors need no own one-camera encoder. FlashGRU, a loop unit built for the chip, uses set gaps and input-output-aware design.

FlashGRU runs over seven times faster than convolutional GRUs, with about seventy-seven percent lower peak memory and about eighty-one percent fewer memory requests. Pip-Stereo runs frames in seventy-five thousandths of a second on a Jetson Orin NX and nineteen thousandths on an RTX 4090. It matches stepwise models and far beats current real-time rivals in scores and new-scene use.
arxiv-2602-20996:
Voltage graphs label directed edges with group elements, and a classical construction builds a larger derived graph from them. Bjorn Schafer and Mariusz Tobolski generalize that Gross-Tucker construction to quantum graphs in this 2026 arXiv paper, for finite abelian groups. Remarkably, starting from a classical voltage graph can still produce a true quantum graph, one that is quantum isomorphic to a classical graph.

The main result is a quantum version of the Gross-Tucker theorem, characterizing exactly which graphs arise as derived graphs of voltage graphs. Readers get a bridge between classical combinatorics and quantum graph theory, with a precise classification of what the construction can and cannot produce.
arxiv-2602-21096:
Radio systems that send facts and power at once need aerials that serve both kinds of users. Muhammad Zeeshan Mumtaz, Mohammadali Mohammadi, Hien Quoc Ngo, and Michail Matthaiou propose spread-out smooth opening arrays for that job in this 2026 arXiv paper. Each meta-sheet carries smooth currents sending out EM waves through channels told by the dyadic Green function.

The authors cut total power use subject to spectral-yield and energy-gathering quality needs, under equal power shares. A two-layer tuning method handles power shares with fines for need misses. Tuned current patterns cut power use by sixty-five percent against equal shares and sixty-one percent against a single-site array, at equal opening size and transmit power.
arxiv-2602-21596:
Trung X. Pham and three co-authors uncover a hidden meaning bottleneck in guided codes of diffusion transformers. Diffusion transformers lead class-guided and multi-mode generation, yet their learned guided codes stay poorly understood. This first orderly study finds notable overlap.

Class-guided codes show extreme angular closeness, past 99 percent on ImageNet-1K, while continuous-guidance tasks like pose-guided image making and video-to-audio making pass 99 percent too. Meaning data packs into a small subset of slots, with head slots carrying the main signal and tail slots adding barely anything. Cutting low-size slots, removing up to two-thirds of code space, leaves making quality and trueness largely unharmed and sometimes improves them. The findings reveal a meaning bottleneck and suggest chances for leaner guiding tricks.
arxiv-2602-21796:
Nonlinear magnetization precession and spin waves anchor modern magnonics. P. I. Gerevenkov and four co-authors study nonlinear magnetization motion in a thin layered iron film driven by brief laser pulses, in regimes of uniform precession and traveling spin wave packets. Precession roughness, higher harmonics, and dynamic rectification are shown in experiments.

Solving the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation shows these effects stem from asymmetry in the energy curve and need no real threshold. That asymmetry arises readily when an outside field near the anisotropy field is applied close to the hard axis. The work links energy profile shape to nonlinear effects, paving the way for magnonic tools with controlled harmonics and nonlinear spin wave mixing.
arxiv-2602-21896:
Jan Neuser and three co-authors present prodiabatic elimination, a new way to drop fast variables from light-matter systems. It builds on the older adiabatic method, but adds higher-order fixes and noise terms through a careful expansion of operators. The result works far better than the standard method, yet stays simple and cheap to use.

The team tries it on two cases: a driven, lossy Jaynes-Cummings model, and a three-level setup in a two-mode cavity that runs stimulated Raman adiabatic passage. Both cases show the new method is tough and wide-ranging, a handy tool for open quantum systems.
arxiv-2602-21996:
After a gas leak at a chemical plant, responders want fast forecasts of where the plume will drift. Full physics simulations of wind and spread are too slow for urgent what-if questions. Lisa Kühn and three co-authors compare shortcut methods, called model order reduction, that shrink such simulations while keeping them accurate. Their test case is a two-dimensional benchmark for airborne contaminant transport in complex settings.

The study weighs two families of methods, intrusive and non-intrusive variants built on proper orthogonal decomposition, against measures like accuracy, cost, and ease of use. It lays out a workflow for uncertainty-aware prediction, starting from model choice and ending with honest error bars. Emergency teams gain a clearer guide to which shortcut to trust when minutes matter and many scenarios must be run.
arxiv-2602-22196:
AI runs on the labor of data workers, who are often treated as spare parts rather than teammates with real skill. Yujia Gao and five co-authors study how to enact fairer principles in practice, through multilingual, iterative, hands-on tagging workshops with journalists and activists. Their case material centers on news stories of gender-related violence.

The workshops, rooted in feminist thought, foster dialogue, build community, and challenge who counts as a knower in tagging. The authors show that honoring context and pluralism in practice may require bounding context and working toward tactical convergences. The paper bridges a gap between proposed principles and lived practice, offering two practical lessons for hands-on data work.
arxiv-2602-22496:
Telling a controlled-NOT gate apart from single-qubit gates in quantum circuits was recently linked to the resource of state texture. Alexander Greenwood and three co-authors revisit that protocol. They show a more general fidelity-based version succeeds for nearly all laboratory bases. They then broaden the view to resource theories, one per choice of reference pure state. That family sets core resource requirements without the shortcut of the original "grand sum".

Extending from single resourceless states to convex sets via a convex-roof construction, they recover single-qubit measures of known theories like imaginarity and coherence. Finally they introduce fixed-point resource theories. These cover fixed-point instances of state texture, genuine coherence, purity, and athermality. For these theories, the team shows weak monotonicity of a fidelity-based lower bound under free operations. Strong-monotonicity violations appear for the convex-roof logarithmic measure.
arxiv-2602-22596:
Yuci Han and four co-authors improve novel view synthesis from very few photos. Given sparse, unconstrained snapshots of a real scene, the goal is to render fresh viewpoints that stay consistent and free of artifacts. Existing diffusion-based fixes fine-tune only the UNet part of a pretrained model, leaving other parts frozen, so details still drift.

BetterScene instead works inside the Stable Video Diffusion pipeline, adding temporal equivariance regularization and a vision-foundation-model-aligned representation to the variational autoencoder. A feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting model renders features for the enhancer, producing continuous, artifact-free views. On the demanding DL3DV-10K dataset, BetterScene beat leading methods for diverse real-world scenes.
arxiv-2602-22696:
Shinnosuke Nozue and six co-authors widen the playbook for persuasive dialogue agents. Current agents lean on a narrow set of preset tactics that miss real-world complexity. The team borrows proven strategies from social psychology, behavioural economics, and communication theory into one cross-disciplinary design framework.

Tests ran on two datasets: Persuasion for Good, a focused in-domain case, and DailyPersuasion, a broad mix of scenarios. The framework posted strong results on both, lifting persuasion success and generalizing well. It shone brightest with people who started out least willing to be persuaded, tackling a central weakness of persuasive agents head-on.
arxiv-2602-22896:
Zebin Yang and five co-authors cut the cost of robot vision-language-action models. These models fuse language reasoning with 3D visual understanding for manipulation tasks, but their compute load blocks real-time use. The key observation is that actions differ in importance: critical steps need precision, lesser ones tolerate variance.

DySL-VLA sorts layers into informative layers, always run, and incremental layers, skippable on demand. A prior-post skipping guide decides when skipping starts, and a skip-aware two-stage distillation trains a standard model into the lean form. On the Calvin dataset, it beat Deer-VLA on success length by about two percent, cut trainable parameters nearly eighty-six fold, and ran nearly four times faster than RoboFlamingo at equal accuracy.
arxiv-2602-22996:
Filipe S. Ribeiro and three co-authors bound chiral cosmic media parameters with fast radio bursts. Treating the interstellar medium as a cold, ionized chiral plasma within Maxwell-Carroll-Field-Jackiw electrodynamics, they derive the time delay between two travelling signals. The delay is expressed in modified dispersion measures with chiral contributions, and the Faraday rotation angle in modified rotation measures.

Combining dispersion measures and redshift data from a set of bursts constrains the chiral parameter magnitude between ten to the minus twenty-six and ten to the minus twenty-four gigaelectronvolts. Faraday rotation formulae and rotation-measure data tighten the upper bounds on the MCFJ parameters to ten to the minus forty-three gigaelectronvolts, among the most stringent limits of their kind.
arxiv-2602-23196:
Amir Abboud and two co-authors prove that three versions of a hypothesis about triangle detection are in fact the same hypothesis. A recent paper by the authors proposed a dichotomy rule for when triangle detection gets easier in graphs that avoid a fixed pattern H as a subgraph. The natural extensions to induced H-free graphs and colored H-free graphs look much harder at first glance.

The main contribution is a reduction from the induced case to the non-induced case, using a modified pattern H-prime that preserves the two features the dichotomy cares about: three-colorability and triangle count. A similar reduction covers the colored case, and a key ingredient is a self-reduction to unique triangle detection, via a new color-coding-style argument, that preserves induced H-freeness. The equivalences unify the three settings under one rule.
arxiv-2602-23296:
Quang-Huy Nguyen and two co-authors tackle uncertainty quantification in federated learning, where models train across many agents without pooling raw data. Without reliable uncertainty estimates, federated systems risk deploying overconfident models at under-resourced agents, causing silent local failures behind satisfactory global scores. Existing federated methods handle data heterogeneity or model heterogeneity alone, missing their joint effect on coverage across agents.

Their method, FedWQ-CP, balances empirical coverage with efficiency at both global and agent levels under dual heterogeneity. Calibration takes a single agent-server round: each agent computes conformity scores, derives a local quantile threshold, and sends only that threshold plus its calibration sample size. The server averages the thresholds by weight into a global threshold. On seven public data sets for classification and regression, the method maintains agent-wise and global coverage while giving the smallest prediction sets or intervals.
arxiv-2602-23696:
Yongzhong Xu studies total setting paths of model training under AdamW, finding a main low-dim drift line, the backbone, holding 60 to 80 percent of long-horizon shift from the start. That line stays highly stable over rolling training windows yet turns slowly across phases, above all after goal re-tuning.

Per-batch gradients show near-noise-floor match with the backbone, whereas tuner-built updates match strongly with it. The structure thus comes from built-up tuner motion rather than instant shape. Swapping AdamW for SGD-family tuners kills this structure, and cutting beta-2 smoothly weakens backbone grip and reheat bounce-back. Reheat tests show transverse probe modes can be briefly re-excited without much shifting built-up backbone drift. The results shift focus from instant gradient traits to built-up update motion in model training.
arxiv-2602-24096:
Yuxuan Zhang and nine co-authors present DiffusionHarmonizer, an online generative enhancer that bridges neural reconstruction and photorealistic simulation for autonomous robots. The 2026 paper notes that neural methods can rebuild scenes from real data at scale, but renderings often show artifacts in novel views.

DiffusionHarmonizer transforms imperfect renderings into temporally consistent, more realistic outputs with a single-step temporally conditioned enhancer. That enhancer is converted from a pretrained multi-step image diffusion model. It runs fast enough for online simulators on one graphics card. Training relies on a custom curation pipeline that builds synthetic-real pairs. The system markedly raises simulation fidelity in research and production settings.
arxiv-2603-00296: Li and colleagues propose SWAP, a training method that trims needlessly long chains of thought in large reasoning models step by step. Earlier outcome-only rewards with whole-trajectory length penalties cannot tell essential steps from redundant ones, so compression stays blunt. SWAP scores each step by how much its log-probability moves toward the right answer, then shifts penalty mass onto low-value steps while sparing key reasoning. Tests show reasoning length down about two-thirds on average while accuracy rises 5.7 percent over the base model.
arxiv-2603-00496: Hiraki and three colleagues offer a fast axiomatic rival to SHAP for explaining which input features drive a prediction. Framing attribution as a cooperative game, they combine two polynomial time closed form rules into ESENSC_rev2, preserving the null player property. Tests on tabular prediction show it tracks exact SHAP closely while scaling far better as feature counts grow. Theory proves the rule is uniquely fixed by efficiency, null player, restricted marginality, inessential game, and cost cutting axioms.
arxiv-2603-00996: Kim and four colleagues propose sustainable care as a design lens for children's encounters with social issues like climate change, conflict, and inequality online. Much of what children see is tuned for attention through fear and urgency, pushing caring young people toward anxiety or withdrawal instead of action. Their full-day workshop gathers researchers and practitioners to map this landscape and set a research agenda for child-computer interaction.
arxiv-2603-01296: Boumali studies the one-dimensional Generalized Klein-Gordon Oscillator within Doubly Special Relativity, swapping the usual linear non-minimal coupling for a general interaction function. The resulting split, SUSY-like Schrödinger form has a real spatial spectrum ensured by Hermiticity or, for complex cases, by eta-pseudo-Hermiticity or PT balance. It uses a sound metric inner product. DSR then enters through the energy rebuild map, and the paper gives closed-form Magueijo-Smolin and Amelino-Camelia branches.
arxiv-2603-01496:
Hiroyuki Kasahara and Weina Zhou ask what being in the womb during the Great Chinese Famine did to later schooling. Their 2026 study faces a hard bias: boys exposed before birth died at higher rates, so survivors are not a fair sample. That bias can hide or distort the true long-term harm.

To cut the bias, they compare exposed children with their own same-sex siblings who were not exposed. Famine strength is scored from county and year records of excess deaths. On average, exposure raised illiteracy by a similar amount for boys and girls. It also cut years of schooling by a similar amount for both sexes. The matched pattern helps separate famine harm from survival bias in fetal-origins research.
arxiv-2603-01596:
Switching a Python project from one code library to a twin library takes care and a lot of hand edits. Matthias Kebede, May Mahmoud, Mohayeminul Islam, and Sarah Nadi bring that switch into the editor in this 2026 work. Their earlier command-line tool used a language model to do the full switch on its own.

The new plug-in, MigMate, runs inside the VS Code editor that many coders use daily. It shows each planned change and lets the coder confirm edits before they apply. That review step keeps a human in charge of a change that can break a project. In an early user study, the plug-in cut the time for a switch task each time it was used. Users also rated it highly on a standard ease-of-use scale.
arxiv-2603-01696:
Haonan Jia, Shichao Dong, Xin Dong, and colleagues stop image captions from dropping key visual facts. Their 2026 work starts from a flaw: large vision-language models often omit or distort what an image shows. Loss is hard to measure, since text and image live in different forms.

Their insight is that a good caption should let a search find the same image again. Their frame, CIM, scores captions by how well retrieved images match the source in two ways. Reinforcement learning then trains the model to cut that measured loss, with no extra hand labels needed. Results beat even supervised fine-tuning on caption quality in their tests. On one hard benchmark, relation reasoning improves by a fifth for a mid-size open model.
arxiv-2603-02096:
Yiweng Xie, Bo He, Junke Wang, and colleagues compress streaming video memory so models can watch live feeds cheaply. Their 2026 framework, FluxMem, needs no training and adapts its compression to each scene. Streaming understanding piles up visual tokens fast, which inflates latency and memory for multimodal models.

A temporal module first removes redundant tokens across adjacent frames of the stream. A spatial module then merges repetitive regions within each frame into compact representations. Self-adaptive rules set the compression rate from scene statistics, not from manual tuning. Online benchmarks reach new top results under real-time settings in their tests. Latency and peak memory drop sharply on one benchmark, while offline performance stays strong with far fewer visual tokens.
arxiv-2603-02296:
Rajeev Singh and Alexander Soloviev study spinning fluids on a curved expanding backdrop in this 2026 paper. Relativistic fluids from heavy-ion collisions can carry spin as they expand. A recently found backdrop expands sideways with finite reach inside ordinary spacetime. It differs from the classic Gubser flow, which spreads without bound and has rounder symmetry.

Within perfect-fluid spin theory, the authors derive exact equations for every spin part. Faster early expansion and a causal edge keep spin effects more tightly localized here. One spin part, around the flow axis, wobbles as it fades, unlike the Gubser case. That contrast marks this backdrop as a distinct test bed. It suits spin studies in expanding fluids of finite size.
arxiv-2603-02396:
Dennis Gross verifies an AI policy for blood platelet stocks in this 2026 paper. Platelets expire within five days, so blood banks walk a tight line. Too much stock wastes a scarce resource, while too little risks lives. Reinforcement learning can learn good ordering policies, but its neural choices are opaque.

His tool, COOL-MC, pairs learning with formal checking and explanation methods. It builds a Markov chain from only the states a trained policy can reach. Checks confirm a low stockout risk and a low overflow risk over a long horizon. Explanations show the policy watches inventory age most, not weekday or pending orders. Swapping mid-large orders for smaller ones barely changed safety. The study is a first formal audit of such a policy.
arxiv-2603-02596:
Wenzhe Tong, Yicheng Jiang, Chi Zhang, and colleagues estimate ground contact for tensegrity robots in this 2026 paper. Tensegrity robots are light and resilient, built from rods and cables under tension. Their soft, spread-out ground contacts make state estimation hard. Dedicated contact sensors are one fix, but add weight and wiring.

Their graph network reads only built-in sensing: motion units and cable-length histories. The robot's threefold symmetry is baked into how the network passes messages. That symmetry boosts sample efficiency and generalization across poses. Predicted contacts feed a leading Kalman filter for pose estimation. Simulations show higher accuracy and better scores than baselines while using a fifth of the training data. Pose estimates stayed low-drift and physically consistent.
arxiv-2603-02696:
Shenghua Feng, Jie An, Naijun Zhan, and Fanjiang Xu ask when the averages of a random system can be computed exactly. Their 2026 paper studies stochastic differential equations, which describe motion driven by both steady drift and random noise. Moments, meaning averages of powers of the state, underpin formal checks of such systems but rarely have closed forms.

The authors define moment-solvable equations and give a symbolic procedure that tries to build a small linear system governing any chosen moment. They then name a broad class, marked by a block-triangular shape, where this always works for polynomial moments. That class strictly extends linear equations and covers many nonlinear models. Experiments confirm the procedure performs well in practice.
arxiv-2603-03196:
Paolo Angella, Vito Paolo Pastore, and Matteo Santacesaria extend a sensing method to signals that live in endless dimensions. Deep learning models now serve as priors to rebuild signals from few readings, beating older sparsity tricks. But the math behind them assumed finite lists of numbers, while real signals are often curves.

Their frame works in Hilbert spaces, where curves are points in an endless space. They extend two key tools, local coherence and a recovery guarantee, to that setting. The headline result: the needed reading count tracks the prior's true size, not the display grid. Tests on a flow equation confirm the math. With very few readings, a lower-grade model even steadied the rebuild.
arxiv-2603-03296:
Ke Yang and eight colleagues give language model agents a memory that plugs into any task. Long-term memory helps agents in complex settings, but existing designs are either built for one task or generic yet weak, drowning the model in raw retrieved history. Their 2026 module, PlugMem, draws on cognitive science: what matters for decisions is abstract knowledge, not raw experience.

PlugMem compresses episodes into a compact knowledge graph holding two kinds of knowledge: facts about the world and prescriptions for action. Retrieval then reasons over that knowledge instead of verbose traces. Tested unchanged on three different benchmarks, covering long conversations, multi-hop retrieval, and web tasks, PlugMem beat other generic memory designs and even task-specific ones. It also packed the most information per unit of memory under a shared analysis.
arxiv-2603-03596:
Marcel Torne and seventeen colleagues give robot policies a memory with two timescales. A robot cooking dinner must remember which recipe stages are done, a long-horizon fact, and also where the object in its grip went when its own arm hides it, a short-horizon one. Feeding raw past observations to the policy handles neither well. Their 2026 approach, Multi-Scale Embodied Memory, splits memory by kind.

Short-horizon memory is video, compressed by a video encoder into recent visual context. Long-horizon memory is text, holding abstracted semantic facts about progress. Mixed together, the two let vision-language-action policies complete tasks lasting up to fifteen minutes, like cleaning a kitchen or making a grilled cheese sandwich. Policies also adapted their manipulation strategies in context, using memory to change approach mid-task.
arxiv-2603-03696:
Weitao Zhang, Han He, and Jun Zhang chart how a star's outer atmosphere brightens as the star spins faster, and where that brightening stops. The data come from China's LAMOST survey, whose calcium emission lines measure chromospheric activity for solar-like stars. This 2026 paper, the third in its series, cross-matches the activity catalog with rotation periods from the Kepler and TESS space telescopes, assembling more than eleven thousand stars.

Activity climbs with rotation rate until it saturates, then flattens no matter how fast the spin. The saturation point shifts systematically with surface temperature, arriving at longer periods for cooler stars. Saturation shows most clearly in stars with thick convective zones and fades for hotter stars. Recalibrated basal flux indices, which strip out the quiet floor of emission, sharpen the rotation connection throughout.
arxiv-2603-03896:
Tiantong Cheng and Hongbo Cheng ask whether a quantum-corrected anti-de Sitter black hole carrying global monopoles can split into two. The black hole may host regular or phantom monopoles. The authors test the possibility of fragmentation against the second law of thermodynamics: a split is allowed only if the total entropy does not decrease. They derive the entropies of the original black hole and of its would-be fragments, with the difference depending on quantum-gravity oscillations, the monopole factors, and the anti-de Sitter environment.

Both kinds of monopole keep the black hole intact, because the entropy difference is negative. Strong quantum fluctuation can reverse the sign when one fragment is tiny and the other huge, and a large enough AdS radius can also make fragmentation favorable near equal masses. The work clarifies how quantum corrections and environment decide black hole stability.
arxiv-2603-03996: Yin and Liu model accretion flows in Sagittarius A*, the compact radio source at the Galactic center. Nearby pulsar observations reveal unusually large Faraday rotation, indicating strong fields and low-beta plasma at large scales. Gas capture begins below tens of thousands of Schwarzschild radii, where gas pressure dominates. Assuming magnetic-field accretion falls with distance by a power law, a small disk below tens of Schwarzschild radii should carry a supersonic wind above it. Flow between tens and tens of thousands of radii is then convection-dominated.
arxiv-2603-04296: Ritter-Gutierrez and colleagues turn whispered speech into normal voiced speech, preserving words and speaker identity. Whisper and voiced recordings misalign in time, and paired examples are scarce, which makes the task hard. FlowW2N trains only on synthetic time aligned pairs, using speech recognition embeddings stable across synthetic and real whispers. A layer selection rule balances content detail against cross domain stability, and the method leads on CHAINS and wTIMIT intelligibility. It cuts word error rate by 26 to 46 percent over earlier work with only 10 inference steps.
arxiv-2603-04396: John Campbell introduces abelian-normal numbers, a twist on Champernowne's classic normal numbers. Normality preserving selection rules motivated counting subwords as equivalent up to permutation, normalizing counts by equivalence class size. That definition links combinatorics on words with probabilistic number theory. Every normal number is abelian-normal, raising the question whether an abelian-normal number can fail to be normal. Campbell constructs such a constant explicitly, answering yes with a concrete example.
arxiv-2603-04596: Schlossberger and colleagues find the fundamental linewidth limit for Rydberg EIT in thermal vapour.
