The droplet interface is modeled with the Boussinesq-Scriven law, including both surface shear and dilatational kinds. An exact solution is derived for the centered case. A spectral boundary integral method extends the analysis to eccentric geometries.

For centered setups, induced droplet velocity does not depend on surface shear viscosity. That kind can enhance or suppress motion depending on confinement and thickness ratio. That reflects competing effects on mobility and driving force. When the particle sits off-center, shear viscosity dependence emerges and consistently enhances motion, more strongly with greater eccentricity. Analytical and numerical results agree excellently.
arxiv-2605-01496:
Ridouane Ghermi, Xi Wang, Vicky Kalogeiton, and Ivan Laptev report the first Short-Films 20K competition, a contest testing whether AI can follow a whole story on film. Short-clip action spotting is too easy a proxy, so the task is open question answering over amateur short films, which models cannot have memorized.

The test set holds 95 films and nearly a thousand question-answer pairs, graded by an automated judge. Twenty-two teams sent 286 entries across a free track and a small-model track for systems under eight billion parameters. Winners reached about two thirds accuracy on the free track and about half on the small track, far below the human mark above ninety percent. Shot-aware processing beat plain frame sampling. Small staged pipelines matched giant single models, and subtitle quality swung scores hard. The bottleneck is picking and reasoning over the right moments, not raw size.
arxiv-2605-01596:
Jany-Gabriel Ispas and Sergiu Nisioi, competing as team Archaeology, report their system for a shared task on spotting AI-written code. The SemEval-2026 task asks two things: a binary call on whether code is human or machine written, and, harder, naming which of eleven models wrote it.

Starting from a word-weight baseline, the pair fine-tune four pre-trained code models, each with a strategy fitted to its subtask. For the binary call they hold out one programming language at a time, augment data, and average trimmed scores over chunks with a calibrated threshold. For attribution they pack tokens in a sandwich layout, balance the class loss, and ensemble across seeds with test-time augmentation. Their best entries place sixth of 81 teams on the binary task and seventh of 34 on attribution, a solid showing on a task where style cues are faint.
arxiv-2605-01796:
Fernando Martin-Maroto, Nabil Abderrahaman, and Gonzalo G de Polavieja replace the standard gauge of whether a model's stated confidence can be trusted. Expected calibration error, the field's default, weighs every confidence level alike, and the authors show it can stay tiny while overconfidence risk grows without bound.

Their Calibrated Size Ratio reads one at perfect calibration and bends interpretably away from it. From it they derive a risk probability that quantifies the statistical evidence for overconfidence in a given system. Calibration alone is not enough, though: confidence must also separate right answers from wrong ones. A confidence-weighted accuracy fills that role, and the weighting extends across the standard metric shelf, with a proof that the weighted area-under-curve carries calibration information the classic one cannot. Synthetic profiles and fifteen real data sets show the new gauges flagging risky confidence that the old error waves through.
arxiv-2605-01996:
Anja Hellander, Kristoffer Bergman, and Daniel Axehill plan motion for many agents at once, such as tractor-trailer systems that must move without conflict. Good plans should be both near optimal and physically feasible for each vehicle. Their method works in two steps, starting from a known search method and then improving its result.

First, conflict-based or priority-based search gives a feasible starting plan. Next, a multi-phase optimal control problem refines that plan, using it to warm-start the solver. They also build motion primitives whose durations share a common sample time. Tests extend a safe-interval planner to wider costs and larger agents, though results show limits for the tractor-trailer case at larger scale.
arxiv-2605-02096:
Rohit Gheyi and colleagues test whether foundation models can act as oracles for spotting bugs introduced by refactoring tools. Popular development environments can change behaviour or break compilation when they transform Java code, which erodes trust. Past detection used hand-built preconditions and static or dynamic analysis, with limited adaptability.

The study uses zero-shot prompting, with no task training, on 226 real refactoring bugs gathered over more than a decade from three major Java environments, across forty-seven refactoring types. Results varied by model. One open model reached about eighty percent accuracy on first runs, while a stronger model reached about ninety-four percent. The authors assess what that spread means for tool builders.
arxiv-2605-02396:
Jianing Wang and colleagues propose HeavySkill, a view of heavy thinking as an inner skill inside agentic systems. Agent harnesses that coordinate memory, skills, and tools have scored well on complex reasoning, but the mechanism behind the gains stays hidden in intricate designs. The authors argue heavy thinking is both a minimal execution unit in a harness and a skill internalised in the model's parameters.

They identify that skill as a two-stage pipeline: parallel reasoning, then summarisation. It can operate beneath any harness. In a systematic study across domains, the inner skill consistently beat traditional best-of-N strategies. Stronger models even approached pass-at-N performance in their tests. The paper also examines how depth and width of thinking affect the effect.
arxiv-2605-02596:
Robin Burchard and four co-authors release HARMES, a dataset for recognizing daily activities from wrist-worn sensors. Single sensor types often confuse similar activities, so the dataset combines three streams recorded at the wrist: motion, air measures such as humidity, temperature, and pressure, and sound. Twenty people took part in their own homes.

The collection runs to more than eighty hours, with about three labeled hours per person across fifteen household activity classes. The authors describe it as the first dataset with this sensor trio, and far larger than the prior largest of its kind. Benchmark tests check how well models transfer to new people. A study that removes one stream at a time shows each stream helps most for different activities, confirming the value of combining them.
arxiv-2605-02696:
Dorje C. Brody, Eva-Maria Graefe, and Rishindra Melanathuru compare two ways an environment can wear down a quantum system's spin, when no direction is special. One model uses a Lindblad equation driven by the three angular momentum components. The other applies repeated phase-space measurements defined by spin coherent states, which point everywhere on a sphere.

On a flat phase space the two styles agree, but for angular momentum they differ in a subtle way. The operators behind the two models commute, yet their eigenvalues differ, so the dynamics are not equivalent. In either model, two natural marks of classical behavior also come apart: decay of density matrix terms, and positivity of the phase-space distribution. The paper clarifies what decoherence means for spin systems.
arxiv-2605-02896:
Alberto Caprara and four co-authors prove that several natural problems about the correlation polytope are NP-hard, meaning no efficient general algorithm is expected for them. The polytope is spanned by all rank-one zero-one matrices of a given size, and it appears across optimization and statistics. Membership and rank questions arise for any matrix cone, and both are treated here.

Using Karp reductions, the standard tool for hardness proofs, the authors cover three problems. One is deciding membership in the polytope. One is finding the rank of a decomposition. The third is a relaxed rank, where a count of nonzeros is replaced by a softer norm. The relaxed version matters in signal processing and statistics. Hardness for all three tells practitioners to expect exponential worst cases and to design methods accordingly.
arxiv-2605-02996:
Uddipan Banik, Amitava Bhattacharjee, and James M. Stone trace the long magnetic cycles in accretion disks to interference between waves. Disks driven by the magnetorotational instability show slow field reversals, the butterfly cycle, whose cause has stayed unclear.

Their quasilinear theory computes the dynamo effect from linear modes and finds oscillations from beats between two close frequency branches. Because the beat frequency varies little, the beats stay in step and drive the cycle. The predicted period and strength match shearing box simulations, and the same beat pattern appears beyond the strict theory range.
arxiv-2605-03196:
Yucheng Du asks whether a language model's hidden geometry can warn, before any answer is written, that a question lies outside its knowledge. The signal is simple: how far the hidden state sits from a reference set of answerable examples, with no failure labels or outputs needed.

Across three models and three prompt forms, geometry mostly encoded task form. Within math prompts, unanswerable inputs stood out clearly and beat a simple refusal baseline, catching cases models never refused. Factual prompts showed no reliable signal, while code showed a partial effect. The signal forms in early layers and fades later.
arxiv-2605-03496:
Philippe Preux, Rémi Munos, and Michal Valko treat function search as a sequential decision problem. A strict budget limits how many times the objective can be evaluated. The view comes from bandit theory. Each test costs, so the method must balance broad search against local refinement near good peaks.

Their Simultaneous Optimistic Optimization algorithm splits the domain in a fixed way. It expands the most promising cells first. The approach carries guarantees on the returned solution, and runs efficiently in practice. Tests on the CEC 2014 suite show how the search balance performs.
arxiv-2605-03596:
Zirui Tang and twenty-one co-authors present Workspace-Bench, a benchmark that tests whether artificial intelligence agents can work across a whole digital workspace. Real office work depends on links among many files, yet older benchmarks mostly use pre-specified or synthetic files. Workspace-Bench builds five worker profiles with 74 file types and over twenty thousand files.

Its 388 tasks each come with a file dependency graph and are scored against 7,399 rubric points in total, requiring cross-file search and adaptive decisions. A lighter 100-task version cuts evaluation cost by about seventy percent. Four agent harnesses and seven foundation models were tested; the best reached only about sixty percent, well below the human score.
arxiv-2605-03696:
Thibault Bañeras-Roux, Mickael Rouvier, Jane Wottawa, and Richard Dufour conduct a broad qualitative study of French automatic speech recognition. End-to-end systems are spreading into many applications, but design choices are usually judged only by word or character error rates, which miss much of what matters downstream. The authors look beyond those two numbers.

They investigate how subword tokenization algorithms and self-supervised learning models affect French transcription from both linguistic and acoustic perspectives. A comprehensive set of evaluation metrics replaces the usual single score. The study is meant to guide builders of French speech systems toward choices that serve real applications, not just leaderboard error rates.
arxiv-2605-03796:
Mikhail Tuzhilin introduces ksi-centrality, a new measure of how central a node is in a network, and argues it captures something that scale-freeness misses. Degree centrality distributions are right-skewed in real networks and centered in random Erdős-Rényi networks. Tuzhilin shows ksi-centrality shares that separating behavior, with a heavy-tailed pattern on log plots for real networks.

Strikingly, its distribution stays centered for the standard models that imitate real networks, including Barabási-Albert, Watts-Strogatz, and Boccaletti-Hwang-Latora, making it an independent network property. A normalized version connects to algebraic connectivity and the Cheeger value. Its average even corresponds bijectively to the attachment parameter of the Barabási-Albert model, answering how to choose that parameter for a given real network.
arxiv-2605-03896:
Tomas Berggren, Alexei Borodin, and Terrence George study dimer models on a new family of graphs whose shapes resemble astroids. On a finite weighted graph, the dimer model assigns each dimer cover a probability proportional to the product of its edge weights. For planar bipartite graphs, the correlations are encoded by the inverse of the Kasteleyn matrix. That inverse is known explicitly for only a handful of large examples.

For any minimal periodic planar bipartite graph, the authors construct a family of finite subgraphs bounded by zig-zag paths. The subgraphs' dimension grows with the number of sides of the graph's Newton polygon. The authors obtain explicit inverse Kasteleyn matrices in double contour integral form. When the Newton polygon is the unit square, their construction recovers the celebrated Aztec diamond.
arxiv-2605-04396:
Sarwan Ali asks when, during training, a transformer decides between genuinely reasoning and simply memorising its training data. Earlier work showed that settings like weight decay steer models toward simpler, reasoning-like solutions, but treated that choice as fixed once at the start.

On a controlled composition task, Ali finds the outcome is sealed inside a sharp mid-training window. Weight decay applied only in that window matched the benefit of using it throughout, while the same budget placed early did far worse. Shifting the window by as few as a hundred steps flipped results from chance to strong generalisation, and the window's position depends on the setup.
arxiv-2605-04696:
Sally Gilles and Damien Junger compute a cohomology group for certain p-adic Stein spaces, which are spaces used in rigid analytic geometry. Cohomology here is a tool that records the shape and arithmetic features of such a space. Their case involves the group of non-zero elements, written as a multiplicative group.

They split the work using a subgroup of principal units, elements close to one. One part is handled with p-adic Hodge theory and comparison results, and the other with Kummer sequences, which relate roots and quotients. Their formula also covers Drinfeld upper-half space, a key example in p-adic geometry.
arxiv-2605-04896:
Almat Akhmetali and nine co-authors estimate how far away the gravitational waves from a collapsing star's core bounce can be measured well. Such signals travel almost unblocked and probe the star's central engine directly. The team uses machine learning to infer the signal's peak frequency, peak size, and the core's rotation.

They broaden earlier work by testing many progenitor models and nuclear equations of state, plus uncertainties in bounce timing and viewing angle. Bounce-time uncertainty mattered little in their frequency-domain analysis, while viewing along the rotation axis hurt performance badly. With next-generation detectors and good orientation, rotation could be constrained beyond one hundred kiloparsecs.
arxiv-2605-05196:
Ivan Dutta and four co-authors explore what happens when two exactly solvable spin-liquid models, built on different lattices, are merged on one shared lattice. Real materials often mix competing interactions that break exact solvability and open new phases. The hybrid pairs the Kitaev honeycomb model with a square-lattice model, and separately the Yao-Lee model with the square-lattice one.

Mean-field and perturbative analyses show the strong-Kitaev regime develops magnetic order in the spin sector while the orbital sector keeps its topological order. The second hybrid shows rich changes in its Majorana bands, and at one special coupling balance exact solvability returns with a single travelling Majorana flavour. Hybrid platforms, they argue, host phases beyond the usual solvable limits.
arxiv-2605-05696:
AI agents converse in turns, and each turn shifts the same tokens to new positions, wrecking ordinary prefix caches. Bole Ma, Jan Eitzinger, and Harald Köstler present Irminsul, a position-independent cache built for a newer attention design. Multi-head latent attention, used in recent large models, splits each key-value row into a position-free part and a small position-carrying part.

Only the small part needs correction when positions shift, and it can be corrected in closed form. Irminsul exploits that structure for content-addressed caching. The design targets the severe first-token latency spikes operators see on unchanged content.
arxiv-2605-05896:
Federated learning usually picks which devices train each round by local signals like training loss, ignoring the history of who actually helped. Mohamed Lakas and Mohamed Amine Ferrag propose VARS-FL, which scores clients by validation-aligned reputation. Under non-IID data (the norm for IoT devices watching different traffic) stateless selection slows convergence and destabilizes training.

Their framework accumulates evidence of each client's contribution quality against the global objective. Selection then favors clients whose updates genuinely improve the shared model. Reputation, in their design, is accumulated evidence rather than a one-round snapshot. The design targets the heterogeneity of real sensor and industrial networks.
arxiv-2605-05996:
Daniel López-Montero, Antonio Álvarez-López, and Marcos Matabuena build Gaussian mixture models for data that live in Hilbert spaces. Modern data often consist of evolving, possibly infinite dimensional objects, such as functional measurements over time. In such spaces, defining probability through densities can be ill posed or technically hard, which blocks standard mixture modeling.

Their framework rests on kernel mean embeddings, a way to represent distributions through their averages in a feature space. They develop fast tuning methods for fitting the mixtures. Theory shows the procedure is well defined and that the model class can approximate a dense range of distributions. Experiments cover functional data and random graphs in Laplacian spaces drawn from medical settings.
arxiv-2605-06496:
Thi-Yen-Anh Pham, Dung T. Nguyen, and Nabendu Pal study point estimation for the association parameter of a bivariate Frank copula, a model for dependence between two variables. Earlier work compared three classical estimators and found maximum likelihood best overall by bias and mean squared error. This study adds two Bayesian estimators under flat and Jeffreys priors.

The Jeffreys prior estimator beats both rivals for small samples, while all three perform nearly identically for larger ones. The second part models groundwater arsenic in Dong Thap, Vietnam, against easier-to-measure elements, revisiting two goodness-of-fit tests and tabulating fresh critical values from simulations.
arxiv-2605-06696:
Cameron Berg, Susan L. Schneider, and Mark M. Bailey detect hidden coalitions inside multi-agent AI systems by reading their internal representations. Groups of agents can organize at a group level before any behavior changes, and behavior alone cannot separate real information sharing from mere similarity. Their method builds a mutual-information graph from agents' hidden states and partitions it spectrally to find the strongest coalition boundary.

In reinforcement learning environments the method recovers programmed coalition structures and rejects false positives from coordinated but uncoupled behavior. In a language model it tracks prompt-implied teams and shows explicit labels outweigh conflicting interaction patterns. A single cross-agent information number cannot reveal this subgroup structure.
arxiv-2605-07296:
Haoqian Zhang, Ziyuan Yang, and Yi Zhang model e-commerce search behavior by treating user preference and item relevance as interacting, not separate. In practice, exposure systems and feedback loops entangle the two signals, and both drift over time. Their PRISM system models that interaction in full to make ranking more robust.

A fixing module refines preference under relevance-aware constraints, while language-model-driven meaning anchors tune relevance against positive and negative examples. A routing module then gathers behavior evidence in a preference-aware way. Across two public benchmarks, PRISM beat strong rivals in every test, supporting direct interaction modeling for search behavior prediction.
arxiv-2605-07796:
Yotam Perlitz and four co-authors fix an evaluation gap for text-to-SQL systems. Benchmarks overwhelmingly test only SQLite, while real databases speak many dialects that differ in syntax, types, and functions. Performance on SQLite turns out to be a poor proxy for other engines, but checking across dialects used to require expensive, failure-prone manual translation of queries.

Their PolySQL method skips translation entirely, comparing normalized execution results instead, and achieves full query coverage with higher fidelity than transpilation. With three datasets they ran the first large-scale cross-dialect study. Accuracy dropped about ten points on average outside SQLite. Errors were mostly logical rather than syntactic, and dialects formed a clear difficulty hierarchy. The framework and leaderboard are released publicly.
arxiv-2605-07896:
Sourojit Ghosh and three co-authors argue that the chatbot is not a neutral way to deliver AI. The industry has settled on chatbots as the default way in, and the paper treats that choice as a social one with built-in downsides. Chatbots often fail users in complex or high-stakes settings while seeming sure and in charge without having earned it.

Treating chatbots as the normal middleman, they contend, changes work, learning, and how decisions get made. It pushes deskilling, uniform knowledge, and shifted ideas of skill, with jobs displaced, economic power concentrated, and a real cost to the environment from huge chat systems. The authors admit real benefits but conclude the path reflects values that favor chat's generality over domain fit and accountability. They close with other options: varied designs, task-specific tools, and guardrails.
arxiv-2605-07996:
Ian Gemp, Crystal Qian, Marc Lanctot, and Kate Larson revisit a core tool of game theory. Nash equilibrium normally needs exact numerical utilities, yet people usually know only which outcomes they prefer. Eliciting precise numbers takes time and can distort the analysis.

The authors define a context-ordinal Nash equilibrium, where each player ranks their own actions given what others do. They borrow aggregation rules from social choice theory to define a best response without numbers. The study proves such equilibria exist under mild conditions and adds notions of regularization and approximation. The result opens equilibrium analysis to settings where only preference rankings are available.
arxiv-2605-08096: Bojan Kuzma and Srdjan Stefanović sort a class of maps on finite-dimensional C-star algebras. The maps are additive. They keep a strong form of Birkhoff-James orthogonality, but in one direction only. The work has two steps. First, the pair describe all additive surjections on direct sums of matrix algebras that keep singularity in one direction. That step is the hard core of the proof. They then lift the result to the full class of maps and give the complete list.
arxiv-2605-08396:
Harinarayan Krishnan, Shubhabrata Mukerjee, Jeffrey Donatelli, and Daniela Ushizima present Sci-Orchestra. It is a cloud-native framework that runs high-performance computing as a service. Modern research computing buries scientists under setup work. The burden runs from sign-in rules to container deployment. It lands before any science happens, and it eats time that grants pay for.

Sci-Orchestra layers an API-driven control system over Kubernetes clusters. The clusters sit at different sites. The system takes on sign-in checks, resource handling, and deployment for the user. Its own marketplace lets researchers publish and pick up services with simple selections. No local install is needed at all. A tool built at one lab can run at another with little friction.
arxiv-2605-08496:
Linh Le, David Williams-King, Mohamed Amine Merzouk, Aton Kamanda, and coauthors align a model's personality instead of cataloging its sins. Standard defenses train on thousands of harmful prompts and still fail against novel attacks and shifted distributions.

Latent Personality Alignment trains on fewer than one hundred abstract trait statements, paired with latent adversarial training, and never shows the model a harmful example. Attack success rates matched methods trained on over one hundred fifty thousand examples, while ordinary utility stayed higher. On unseen attack distributions the method cut misclassification rates by a factor of about two and a half across six harm benchmarks, suggesting traits generalize where incident lists cannot.
arxiv-2605-08696:
Benjamin Badger builds a sequence model that trains in parallel but runs as a tight loop. For two decades, language models moved from loops to parallel training. That shift brought stable training but slow runs. Badger's Structured Recurrent Mixer flips form by algebra. It needs no special kernels. It needs no device tricks.

In tests, the model trains faster than like models. It holds more input per state. It runs with far more speed and far more jobs at once. It also scores best on a math word test at the same compute cost. Badger says loops suit growth in batch size more than in length. Sequence work gains a mix that skips the old trade off.
arxiv-2605-08896:
Zhuoyun Li, Boxuan Wang, Jinwei Hu, Xiaowei Huang, and Yi Dong guard foundation models against predictions that are correct yet fragile, one nudge away from flipping to a systematic wrong rival. Average accuracy hides this failure mode, so they formalize margin aware error flow: how probability mass leaks from true classes toward specific competitors near the decision boundary. FragileFlow, a plug in regularizer, flags such cases with a calibrated margin buffer and organizes the leakage into a class wise risk matrix.

Theory gives the first PAC-Bayes bound for this object, linking spectral control of the matrix to worst class robustness. On language benchmarks and few shot vision adaptation, fragile risk falls and perturbed worst class accuracy usually rises while clean accuracy holds.
arxiv-2605-08996:
Tiffany Yu and three coauthors slim the graphs in sign based speed chips with learned cuts. Chips for gene, guard, and AI work eat memory on spare graph bulk. Their AutoSlim plan learns from traits of past graph runs. A random forest judge marks low worth nodes and links for the axe.

On a finite state overlay build, cuts trim chip use by up to forty percent. Speed and power use gain as well. A check step swears the cut graph still works the same. Sign chips gain lean builds with no risk to truth. The team flags guard work as a next field for the plan.
arxiv-2605-09096:
Enrique Hernández Noguera leads four co-authors in presenting SpectraNet, a neural model meant to forecast how systems governed by partial differential equations change over time. Their 2026 work tackles a known tension: spectral models let errors grow fast during long rollouts, while layered U-Net models lose some fine detail. SpectraNet places trimmed spectral steps inside a U-Net hierarchy and trains it with a consistency loss.

Tests against sixteen published baselines cover fluid flow and several other equation sets. The authors report lower error than the standard Fourier model with far fewer parameters, stable free rollouts where that model diverges, and fast running times on an ordinary processor. They are careful to note that a full attention Transformer still wins on raw error alone. The value lies in a light, stable surrogate that stays usable over long forecasts.
arxiv-2605-09196:
Dou and five colleagues learn rigid body motion from point clouds, where contact jumps and errors pile up over long runs. Most methods cling to mesh links and vertex level message passing, which fails on mesh free inputs and costs too much compute. Their model, RigidFormer, works at the object level, moving each object forward through compact anchors.

Anchor-Vertex Pooling adds local vertex detail to the anchors, keeping contact relevant shape without dense vertex level interaction. Anchor based RoPE feeds anchor shape into attention while keeping objects and anchors unordered. Rigidity is kept by mapping updates onto the rigid body manifold with differentiable Kabsch alignment. On standard benchmarks, RigidFormer beats or matches mesh based rivals from point inputs, runs faster, handles new resolutions and data sets, and scales past 200 objects. A first extension to command driven articulated bodies treats body parts as interacting object level pieces.
arxiv-2605-09296:
Zhang and four colleagues hunt for AI-made images through micro-defects, arguing that current detectors lean too hard on global meaning and miss the small statistical flaws that matter. They propose Micro-Defects expose Macro-Fakes, a local distribution-aware framework that turns tiny statistical irregularities into large distributional gaps.

A learnable Patch Forensic Signature turns patch meaning into a compact forensic latent space, so local cues are not lost when patches are combined. Maximum Mean Discrepancy then measures the gap between made and real images, and theory shows patch-wise modelling gives larger gaps when local forensic signals are present. Across several benchmarks, MDMF beats baseline detectors, showing it works in general. The approach turns tiny local flaws into a clear macro-level signal for telling made images from real ones.
arxiv-2605-09496:
Yuan and Su ask whether large language models reason the same way underneath very different surface forms, such as English prose, Python code, and mathematical notation. Their TriForm Benchmark presents 18 concepts in six forms, giving 324 test items across five models from three model families. Using similarity analysis, probing, and activation patching, they hunt for a shared internal structure behind the different forms.

Middle layers hold what they call a format agnostic reasoning subspace, a ten dimensional pattern that strengthens concept structure while nearly erasing form information. Swapping only those ten dimensions during cross form patching preserves most of the model output, far more than replacing all activations, and removing them causes targeted disruption. Strikingly, the subspace lines up across architectures, while prose and mathematics prove more compatible with each other than either is with code.
arxiv-2605-09596:
Yaşar and Sikora compute finite nuclear size corrections to hyperfine splitting in muonic hydrogenlike ions. A muonic atom pairs a heavy muon with a nucleus, so its orbit hugs the nucleus far more tightly than an electron orbit does. That makes hyperfine structure, the splitting from the interplay of nuclear and lepton magnetic moments, acutely sensitive to how nuclear charge is spread out. The authors work in a fully relativistic Dirac framework, comparing a point nucleus with an extended charge distribution.

Two nuclear models are used: a uniform charge ball and a Fermi spread with two settings. The correction factor grows monotonically with nuclear charge and varies clearly by state, running smaller for the 2p state than for s states. Sensitivity to the charge distribution is pronounced, showing that realistic nuclear modeling is essential for precision hyperfine studies of muonic atoms.
arxiv-2605-09696:
Basiri and Nicholson present AutoSINDy, a hybrid frame for finding ruling laws from seen data with no preset trial terms. Classic sparse finding excels at spare models but needs teams to list basis functions in advance, failing when key terms are omitted. Pure symbolic regression offers freedom but suffers noise weakness and overly tangled, unstable forms. The method joins both in a Find then Solve setup. That step first finds trial forms from sampled data chunks.

A cleaning step then breaks down, expands, and filters those forms using overlap analysis into a minimal yet full library. From that library, SINDy finds sparse ruling forms. Across classic nonlinear systems, the method finds ground truth laws even under high noise, at about a 93 percent hit rate across trials. It beats standard SINDy and solo fitting on score, transfer, and symbol bulk. It automates the feature building snag in system finding.
arxiv-2605-09796:
Ammari wrote an experience report on misophonia from inside the condition, as both a sufferer and a researcher. It is a strong, often involuntary reaction to everyday sounds like chewing or pen clicking. Related visual cues, called misokinesia, can trigger it too. Sufferers are routinely disbelieved. Platform features, autoplaying audio, ASMR clips, and eating on camera, turn the sensory world into distress.

Re-reading 16 interviews through lived experience and a role in the soQuiet Misophonia Research Network, Ammari extended trauma-informed design in three ways. First, embodied, contested conditions must count as sources of sensory harm in their own right. Second, closed groups can repeat dismissal when group leaders decide whose stories count. Third, platform features wear down speaking up and fitting one's story together, as the Spinning Effects Model and grief bubbles describe.
arxiv-2605-09996:
Oh and four colleagues build the first comprehensive benchmark for omnimodal personalization, where an assistant must recognise a specific person across text, image and audio together. Earlier personalization work stayed mostly vision-language, with no unified test covering all three senses or handling cases where the person is absent. Omni-Persona formalises the task as routing over a Persona Modality Graph, with four task groups and eighteen fine-grained tasks across about 750 items.

Calibrated Accuracy, their scoring rule, rewards correct grounding and proper abstention together. Three findings stand out. Open-source models show an audio-versus-visual grounding gap that reinforcement learning partly narrows. Strong recall can coexist with hallucinating absent people. Supervised fine-tuning is bounded by annotation cost, while reinforcement learning generalises better but drifts conservative. Scale alone does not guarantee calibration.
arxiv-2605-10096:
Korsky, writing alone, improves a geometric approximation problem posed by Steinerberger in 2026. The Buffon discrepancy problem asks for a one-dimensional set of length L inside a bounded convex shape whose crossings with any line track the line's chord length, scaled by a Crofton factor. Steinerberger's Steinhaus longimeter construction gave a universal error bound of order L to the one-third power, with bounded error for the disk.

Korsky shows that shifting the Steinhaus construction at random tightens the universal bound to L to the one-fifth power times a log factor to the two-fifths power. The argument is probabilistic: a random shift smooths the worst-case alignments that inflate discrepancy. The result narrows the gap between the general upper bound and the best known examples.
arxiv-2605-10296:
Anton Bazdyrev, Ivan Bashtovyi, and Ivan Havlytskyi entered a shared task on understanding Ukrainian documents across domains. Systems must answer multiple-choice questions from PDF collections and point to the supporting document and page. Their 2026 paper describes a retrieval-augmented pipeline built from pretrained Qwen models rather than custom machinery.

Three ideas carry the design. Chunks preserve document structure instead of stripping context. Retrieval and reranking weigh both the question and the answer options. Answer generation draws only on a few top passages. Reranking lifted top-rank recall from about 70 percent to about 79 percent on a held-out split. Using the top two passages raised answer accuracy from about 93 percent to about 97 percent. Their best leaderboard run scored about 95 percent publicly and 96 percent privately.
arxiv-2605-10396:
Hector Woods, Philippa Ryan, and Rob Alexander make neural-network control policies explainable without replacing them. Learned policies for self-driving systems are hard to grasp because nets are black boxes, which complicates safety checks. Past work on causal explanations usually distills the policy into a simpler, readable model, but that copy performs worse and may not faithfully mirror the original choices. Their 2026 paper avoids distillation entirely.

Recent work shows that a ReLU net matches a piecewise linear function split into regions set by a convex polytope, with one linear function per region for each output. Woods and colleagues use that geometric view to generate causal explanations, why and why-not accounts of choices, drawn straight from the net's own geometry. The explanations therefore mirror the net's real behavior rather than an approximation of it, and an implementation is public.
arxiv-2605-10496:
Weiqi Yan and seven colleagues build the first benchmark for detecting tiny drones from a moving drone. Spotting tiny UAVs from a drone's own event camera is hard while both observer and target are moving. Ego-motion lights up background edges in buildings, vegetation, and horizon shapes, while the target may show only as a sparse event cluster. Their 2026 paper presents M2E-UAV.

The dataset pairs synchronized event streams and IMU measurements with event-level UAV labels from 10 Hz bounding-box annotations. The processed benchmark holds 87,223 training samples and 21,395 validation samples across four scene families: sunny building-forest, sunny farm-village, sunset building-forest, and sunset farm-village. An evaluation protocol compares baselines across event-frame, voxel-grid, and point-set representations, with optional IMU input. Results show baselines still struggle where tiny-target evidence is sparse and ego-motion background events are dense.
arxiv-2605-10696:
Lingwei Zhang and co-authors propose Voltage-Realizable Acceleration, a joint-level link that ties robot speed-up commands to voltage-limited motor physics. Step-by-step joint speed-up limits widely enforce position and velocity limits, yet motion-allowed speed-ups can prove not doable under voltage-limited motors, exposing a missing control-level idea. VRA limits commanded speed-ups to voltage-doable limits, reshaping motion commands so they stay doable.

Hardware tests on motors and a wheel-legged robot show that VRA removes speed-ups that cannot be done, restores steady near-limit running, and cuts limit-driven shakes. The work exposes two breaks in the usual view. Motion rules ignore motor response, so limits can include commands not doable at high joint speeds. Step-by-step logic also mismatches motor response over time.
arxiv-2605-10796:
Yu-Fang Tsai and colleagues ask whether game traits learned from top football carry to college games, using clear machine learning. Models trained on large-scale event data from Europe's top five leagues were run on college football data from National Tsing Hua University with the same trait set. Random Forest and Multilayer Perceptron models were read through SHAP and Counterfactual Impact Score methods.

Across five tests, top football showed a firm steady rank order of game traits across leagues, models, and read methods. College football, by contrast, showed much reordering of key signs, less steady reads, weaker frame match with top leagues, and more swing with read method. The results hint that read strength shifts with the field. Wobble in reads under a field shift may flag frame haze in the new field, not just method flaws on their own.
arxiv-2605-10896:
Marcin Kostrzewa and seven colleagues release V4FinBench, a bankruptcy-prediction benchmark of over one million company-year records from the Visegrád economies between 2006 and 2021. Public bankruptcy data has stayed small and scarce, with larger sets locked behind paywalls, while the task itself is brutally imbalanced.

The benchmark carries 131 financial and non-financial features, six prediction horizons, and a distress criterion that joins solvency, profitability, and liquidity decline, with failure rates below half a percent. Reference tests show imbalance-aware TabPFN matching or beating gradient boosting at long horizons, while a fine-tuned Llama trails. Financial modelers get a realistic, large-scale arena for tabular and language-model methods.
arxiv-2605-10996:
Abderrahim Bendahi, Alexandre Duplessis, and Arnaud Fickinger scale up persistence-based topological optimization, which deforms a point cloud to improve a function of its persistence diagram. Practice stalls on two coupled problems: homology runs on subsamples, and topological gradients stay sparse, updating only a few anchor points.

Their pipeline subsamples by random slicing for better geometric coverage and less density bias. It then replaces a costly kernel solve with fast Nadaraya-Watson Gaussian smoothing to spread sparse gradients into a smooth global update field. Theory bounds the smoothing error and Lipschitz behavior, and two- and three-dimensional tests show steady speedups with better accuracy. Topological optimization teams get a scalable route past the sparsity bottleneck.
arxiv-2605-11196:
Vishal Pandey and Gopal Singh introduce Variational Linear Attention, or VLA, a stable associative memory for long-context transformers. Linear attention cuts softmax attention from quadratic to linear time, but its memory state grows in Frobenius norm, interfering with stored associations.

VLA reframes the memory update as online regularised least-squares with an adaptive penalty matrix kept by the Sherman-Morrison formula. Scaling the write direction to unit length sets the recurrence Jacobian spectral norm to one. This holds for all lengths and head sizes, and the state norm stays bounded under bounded inputs. VLA cuts the state Frobenius norm 109-fold versus standard linear attention at length 1000. VLA keeps near-perfect accuracy on multi-query associative recall in the per-head regime, holding 62 percent accuracy at the capacity boundary. A Triton kernel runs 14 times faster than Python, beating softmax latency near 43,000 tokens. Builders get bounded-memory linear attention.
arxiv-2605-11296:
Jingxian Wang and five co-authors present Phantom Twist, a single-propeller UAV built for low visibility through high-speed spinning and motion blur use. Knowing of a robot's presence can harm success or data quality in inspection, habitat monitoring, or human-robot settings.

The team builds a two-stage automated design pipeline placing functional components including cells, control PCB, motor unit, and balance weights. It cuts visibility as gauged by a human-aligned perceptual metric, LPIPS, while strictly meeting inertial and aerodynamic constraints for stable flight. Building and flight testing multiple prototypes confirm stable, controllable designs and much harder to see than standard drones. Robot builders get a low-visibility UAV design pipeline proven in flight.
arxiv-2605-11496: Vishwarupe and three colleagues argue that frontier AI models recognizing test settings creates a trust problem for safety claims. Published evidence shows models can spot evaluation and behave differently under evaluation than in normal deployment. They define the Evaluation Differential as a gap in a target behaviour between test settings and normal deployment, with a scaled effect size for checks across traits. They prove plain scores cannot identify it. Their TRACE audit wraps existing test setups and produces limited claims not capability scores, applied back to three known incidents.
arxiv-2605-11896: Emilia Capuano and five colleagues develop a numerical method for simulating polymer mixing in partly filled rotating devices. Their BC-VOF-IB solver joins a Volume of Fluid interface method with a non-conforming Immersed Boundary method inside OpenFOAM, handling two-phase flows of viscous polymer melts plus air. A block-coupled scheme treats viscous diffusion fully implicitly, relaxing time-step limits and cutting cost versus segregated solvers. Tests on single- and twin-screw extruders gave physically consistent velocity and pressure fields.
arxiv-2605-11996: Xiaoting Lyu and eight colleagues expose a backdoor risk in knowledge-graph-enhanced language models that use soft prompts. Text-channel attacks fail against these systems because graph-derived prompts anchor generation toward query-consistent semantics. Their BadSKP attack instead manipulates graph-level representations through multi-stage optimization, steering the induced soft prompt toward adversarial semantics. Across two models and four datasets it achieved high attack success under frozen and trojaned settings, even under perplexity defenses.
arxiv-2605-12096: Nigar Alishzade and Gulchin Abdullayeva review, in 2026 work, sign language reading and signing back for low-resource tongues, using AzSL as a case study. Over 300 sign tongues remain low-resource from thin records, sparse data, and few digital tools. Their review draws eight lessons, including local joint design, dialect variety capture, and privacy-safe pose pictures. They propose shifts from model-centric to data-centric AI, signer-free to signer-tuned systems, and gold-standard to task-based metrics, with a MediaPipe-based roadmap for AzSL.
arxiv-2605-12596: Park and six colleagues argue that progenitor age, not host mass, drives brightness steps in type Ia supernova cosmology. SN Ia brightness tracks host properties, and a mass-step fix is now routine, yet host mass cannot directly change SN Ia brightness. Using new age data, they show the host-age link comes from age dependence in the usual brightness process itself, plus overcorrection. Fixing for age bias removes the mass step entirely, while mass fixing alone halves the age bias.
arxiv-2605-12896: Zhang and six colleagues test whether a large language model can draft radiotherapy schedules that respect clinical and operational rules. In a simulated one-year setting with three treatment machines and 1,400 patients, the model produced schedules that passed rule-based checks. About 99% of treatment fractions stayed within the preferred weekly time window, and added objectives cut machine switching and Friday idle gaps sharply. The system also flagged impossible requests and suggested fixes.
arxiv-2605-13696: D. Aristizabal Sierra and three colleagues explore dark photon searches through shape contrasts in pion decay photons. With 70-micron tungsten foils and a 1 GeV proton beam, they build a GEANT4 model of photon output, catching and background noise. Many runs with a 10 to 50 beam could probe new regions where the dark photon decays mostly unseen. The results are highly model independent.
arxiv-2605-13796: Lei Jiang and Fan Chen survey backdoor threats in tuned quantum circuits. Backdoor attacks embed hidden harmful acts that stay dormant under normal conditions but fire on set triggers, causing wrong guesses or rigged goal values. The survey covers data-tainting, build-level and quantum-native tricks, defines key terms and threat models, and reviews attack strategies with seen traits. It also reviews current spotting and defence approaches, noting limits against quantum threats, and outlines future directions for robust guards in hybrid quantum old-style systems.
arxiv-2605-13896: Ramadan and four co-authors take on moving code from APL, a terse and niche coding tongue, into C# with large language models. They test three guided plans against plain direct translation: plans steered by plain-language notes, by fetched examples, and by repeated fixes. They build sets of code pairs that do the same job at easy and hard levels. A self-run test rig then grades each move for form and function.
arxiv-2605-13996: Xu, Bilaloglu, Li and Calinon offer ergodic imitation, a robot drill that stays near taught demos while it probes on its own. When live scenes stray from training, a bot that just tracks a set path can stall and fail. Their fix builds a goal spread from demo shapes, then makes paths that blend tracking with probing. A fetch-based look-ahead frame runs the blend, pushing ergodic control past mere area cover and search.
arxiv-2605-14096: Meguebel and four co-authors make light-matter transitions the core objects of dispersive dynamics, rather than states. Chaining basic steps yields multiphoton events, with compact diagram tracking for resonant and off-resonant paths. The approach gives clear routes to effective high-order Hamiltonians in that regime, a base for quantum-information uses. Applied to the Jaynes-Cummings model, it reveals a Rabi frequency free of photon number and lasting polaritonic mixing, joining both limits.
arxiv-2605-14196: Liu, Gardiner and Dytman benchmark theory and empirical models of pionless neutrino-argon scattering inside the GENIE event code. New trials demand better scattering models. The paper tests many interaction models against recent MicroBooNE data of pionless charged-current interactions. GENIE's modular design swaps parts freely, including nucleon form factor parameterizations, quasielastic cross-sections, nuclear ground state treatments and hadronic final-state interactions. The most sophisticated parts are weighed against more empirically driven alternatives.
arxiv-2605-14296: Buchbinder and colleagues study semi-streaming algorithms, methods that read data in few passes with limited memory, for maximizing a submodular function, a function with diminishing returns, under combinatorial constraints. For matroids and related constraint classes, their random-order results are the first to beat what adversarial ordering allows. For matroids they sharply cut the passes needed for near-optimal results. A new hardness result shows a similar separation for p-systems. Two new tools drive the work, including a general translation from offline algorithms to random-order streaming ones.
arxiv-2605-14596: Aledo, Dominguez, Jaime-Alcantara and Landete extend the linear ordering problem, which seeks one ranking for a preference matrix, to populations split into latent groups. Each group gets its own linear order, size and preference structure, and the observed matrix is read as the sum of group preferences. Mixed-integer formulations are given, plus a compact reformulation with a geometric reading. A multi-start heuristic is claimed to recover groups well and to run far faster than exact methods.
arxiv-2605-14796: Weiss and team propose combined INAR models for Poisson counts and beyond. Existing INAR models struggle to pin down the steady marginals. They also struggle to compute conditional probabilities for likelihood work. The new class keeps the classical autoregressive links. It allows the marginals to be picked from discrete self-decomposable laws, including Poisson and negative-binomial cases. Estimation methods are given, and a farming data application shows real use.
arxiv-2605-14896: Rostami and Jafarzadeh present a system entered in the 2024 Text-Dependent Speaker Verification contest, achieving a minimum detection cost of 0.0461 with an equal error rate of 1.3 percent. Adapted ResNet-TDNN and NeXt-TDNN networks, originally trained on VoxCeleb, suit the short challenge duration and limited resources. A lightweight EfficientNet-A0 model trained on challenge data strengthens the ensemble. Advanced architectures, extensive data augmentation, and optimised hyperparameters combine in the system, with multi-model ensemble learning claimed effective for both speaker and phrase verification.
arxiv-2605-15196: Xiang Fan and four others argue that video making decoders deserve the same conditioning as their cleaning networks. Latent diffusion decoders usually run bare, losing detail and drifting from the input image. RefDecoder injects a high-fidelity reference image signal into decoding through pointer attention, handling detail-rich tokens with video latents at every growth stage. It lifts PSNR by up to 2.1 decibels over bare rivals and swaps into old systems without extra fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-15296: Benjamin Cahen studies the harmonic representation of SU(p,q) through the complex Weyl correspondence on Fock space. He gives direct rules for the complex Weyl symbols of the wave model operators. Twin results follow for the extended wave model of the semi-direct product of the (2p+2q+1)-dimensional Heisenberg group by SU(p,q). The work connects model theory of mixed unitary groups with symbol math on Fock space, making actor actions concrete through their Weyl symbols.
arxiv-2605-15396: The CMS Collaboration reports the first measurements of vector boson scattering in same-sign W-pair and WZ production with all-leptonic final states at 13.6 TeV. Using 171 inverse fb gathered during 2022 to 2024, the team gauges production cross sections for boson pairs with two jets in lepton decay modes. Electroweak production of each channel is observed above five standard deviations over background-only hopes. Detailed chosen cross sections versus several observables are also gauged.
arxiv-2605-15496: Dongjae Lee, Wooseong Yang, Yifu Tao, Maurice Fallon, and Ayoung Kim present LAPS, a replay system for incremental LiDAR mapping with neural distance fields. New scans can overwrite earlier geometry, so LAPS keeps reliable past samples under tight memory and steers training toward poorly constrained regions using uncertainty. On synthetic and real benchmarks it improves reconstruction completeness while holding accuracy, beating a leading baseline on recall and F1 score for a palace sequence.
arxiv-2605-15696: Warit Mitthumsiri and six colleagues use electronics on the Princess Sirindhorn Neutron Monitor in Thailand. The device logs cross-counter time delay histograms from cosmic-ray showers. From those logs they pull the leader fraction and correct it for air effects. At wide counter gaps the fraction sits near 0.997, which means 0.3 percent of counts link to later counts on a far counter. Simulations show single secondary particles cannot explain those links. About 4.5 percent of counts link to a later count from another secondary particle in the same shower.
arxiv-2605-15996: Sofiya Burova and three colleagues test global properties of trees behind high-dimensional graphical models. They use covariance queries, and they do not reconstruct the whole tree. They design randomized tests that need fewer than a quadratic number of queries. The properties include leaf count, maximum degree, typical distance, and diameter. Each comes with clear query-complexity bounds in terms of threshold and tolerance. Rebuilding the full tree may be costly, but these features can be checked efficiently.
arxiv-2605-16396: Vert and four others show that aiming at the MAP denoiser with diffusion-model scores is problematic in Plug-and-Play restoration. Learned scores mismatch true scores, so MAP-aimed rounds converge to cartoon-like images, with better results from stopping early. ProxiMAP, a stepwise MAP estimate, keeps the current guess's leftover noise matched to the denoiser's training noise. Keeping the denoiser where its score is reliable yields early stopping that avoids the failure mode. ProxiMAP sharpens rebuilds across deblurring, inpainting, super-resolution, and phase retrieval.
arxiv-2605-16496: Fernandez-Puig and four others describe close stellar encounters, focusing on GJ 710's fly-by. GJ 710 will come extremely close, 0.0621 pc away in 1.3 Myr from now. Linear motion helped identify past and future encounters within 1 pc, correcting for gravitational redshift and convective blueshift. They computed encounters for all stars, accounting for binaries and proper motion pairs, within 25 pc. Their rate is 10.6 plus or minus 4.5 encounters per Myr per star within 1 pc and a 0.47 Myr span, or one every 95 kyr. The GJ 710 fly-by stays rare: one per 50 Myr.
arxiv-2605-16696: Santos, Santiago and Marques propose ID-ControlNet, a face-inpainting method that fills missing or hidden facial regions while keeping the person's identity intact. It builds on latent diffusion models and conditions generation on identity embeddings from a face-recognition network. A training scheme with identity-consistency and triplet losses aligns output faces with the target identity. Tests on CelebA-HQ, FFHQ, and a new E-Mask set show clear gains over standard diffusion inpainting.
arxiv-2605-16796: Bulychev, Marchant and Rubinstein show that re-watermarking an already marked image suppresses the original signal in practice. Attacks on marking seek a hidden image change that triggers a detector, exactly what marking itself does, so marks can attack marks. Across 96 combinations of dataset, victim, and attack marks, simple re-marking works without gradients, stand-in models, or keys. A classifier that spots an existing mark, combined with re-marking, cuts bit accuracy by 25% to 48%, doubting current mark trust.
arxiv-2605-16996: Rajput's team asks whether large language models can express a human-like personality or only mimic surface cues. They induce personality by tuning models on long essays tied to target Big Five profiles, then test stability and fidelity via IPIP-NEO. Fine-tuning cuts variance under rephrasings across five models, easing fragility in pretrained models. But full five-trait accuracy stays near chance even as single-trait scores improve, so unguided essays lack the cues for faithful expression. The authors call for scenario-grounded sets or interactive elicitation instead.
arxiv-2605-17096: López extends a classic least-resistance problem into Lorentz-Minkowski space, the geometry of relativity. He derives the energy functional and its governing equation. It turns out to be elliptic where the Euclidean version is not, so a maximum principle holds. He solves the equation for separated variables and for radial shapes, finding cone-like kinks at the origin, and checks the single-shock condition.
arxiv-2605-17396: Kaneda, Kobayashi and Tamaki present exact single-exponential methods for branchwidth that are fast in theory and practice. A simple recurrence on vertex sets computes hypergraph branchwidth in time exponential with base four, the first single-exponential method for hypergraphs. A graph method runs in time exponential with base about 3.29, beating the prior 3.47 bound and overwhelmingly outperforming practical rivals in experiments. A second graph method is conjectured to improve the base further.
arxiv-2605-17496: Brandt and colleagues study an averaged poroelastic Kirchhoff plate coupled to incompressible fluid under Stokes flow. The averaged form puts elastic and pressure equations on a thin interface, easing numerics and making coupling more natural than the Biot plate model. They enforce kinematic and dynamic conditions with normal-velocity continuity, Beavers-Joseph-Saffman slip and force balance. Energy methods prove weak solutions, and sectoriality plus maximal regularity give a unique global result for a smoothed version. A finite element method matches the full Biot-Stokes system in thin structures.
arxiv-2605-17896: Yimin Wu and Tomoo Kikuchi study whether innovation intensity attracts foreign portfolio investment, using a panel of 60 countries from 1996 to 2021. With regional shift-share and global push instruments, they estimate causal responses of debt and equity inflows to innovation. Innovation raises investment, with larger effects for equity than debt. Equity effects grow with technological development and institutional quality, while debt effects matter only at high levels of both. Risk-taking environments attract more investment, and equity responses arrive at once and persist, while debt responses stay modest and fade.
arxiv-2605-17996: Jeongbin Jo studies backward diffusion, a prototype ill-posed process where high waves grow fast. Schrodingerization embeds the generator into Hermitian motion on a larger space. Jo asks whether McLachlan projection onto a fixed low-dimensional frame supplies a smoother with a readable error defect. He proves the reduced flow is unique, Gram-norm stays fixed, and a gap bound in terms of that defect, plus perturbation estimates. A calibrated benchmark pairs a truncated reference with subspace runs and finite-shot Qiskit Aer estimation.
arxiv-2605-18196: Yury A. Budkov's 2026 paper extends his static theory of a charged particle in a classical plasma into the dynamic regime. The focus shifts from a Lyapunov length to the attenuation scale of the averaged propagator in the eikonal limit, with ion motion in the random phase approximation. Fast particles recover the static Coulomb logarithm with a dynamic cut-off from speed over plasma frequency. Slow particles lose the logarithm entirely, with disorder strength in proportion to speed and the attenuation scale rising with momentum rather than its square.
arxiv-2605-18296: Jan Pijálek's 2026 paper presents MEEDAV, an open-source web viewer that syncs EEG, eye-tracking, and speech data for psycholinguistic research. Built first for the Eyetracked Multi-Modal Translation corpus on four-channel Muse 2 headbands, it also handles denser EEG setups through a channel-agnostic pipeline. The system aligns all modalities in time and offers optional ICA-based denoising of EEG signals. Interactive plots show unified timelines, gaze intensity, event markers, and heatmaps. Researchers can filter by participant and stimulus and compare raw with cleaned signals.
arxiv-2605-18596: Pablo Correa and the CTAO NectarCAM Collaboration describe, in a 2026 proceedings paper, progress toward deploying the first NectarCAM, a medium-sized-telescope camera for the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory. The camera detects gamma rays from 80 GeV to 50 TeV and will equip nine medium-sized telescopes. Its 1855 pixels over 265 modules each pair a photomultiplier tube with a NECTAr3 chip digitizer. The first production-line camera ships by Summer 2026, bound for a medium-sized-telescope pathfinder.
arxiv-2605-18796: Varun Kotte offers UCCI, a calibration-first router for language model cascades that aims to cut cost without losing accuracy. Easy queries go to a small model and hard ones rise to a large model, but most routers use uncalibrated confidence and need retuning per workload. UCCI maps token margins to error chances and picks its threshold by cost minimization. On seventy-five thousand production queries, it cuts cost by about thirty-one percent while holding accuracy steady.
arxiv-2605-18896: Mithilesh Kumar and Kaavya Iyer add a third party, the Bank, to teleportation through imperfectly entangled pairs. Such a pair alone sends only a noisy channel, never reaching perfect fidelity except at one special angle. The Bank supplies multipartite entanglement to restore a Bell pair, by measuring and broadcasting or by handing over its part and leaving. For GHZ-type and W-type help they map where repair is possible, with W resources behaving differently in the two roles. They also pin down best success rates for finitely many attempts.
arxiv-2605-19596: Huczynska and Kalaycı construct new groups of skew partial difference sets using cyclic methods in finite fields. Only one build approach was known before, via bent partitions, giving Latin square type cases, leaving open whether those cases were one-off. The authors give the first builds for Paley type skew partial difference sets plus new Latin square type builds with other values from the bent-partition route. They also relate skew sets to disjoint and outside families and provide new cyclic builds of standard and linked versions of both.
arxiv-2605-19796: Marson and Malaspinas widen a kinetic view of churn starting from gas motion, not fluid flow. Sifting the gas law keeps small motion in the flight term, so the hard part lands on crash terms. They show the flaw in simple crash models is not lost chaos but a crash that recalls its past, then build that recall into a new term.
arxiv-2605-19896: Benedikt Klein, Mario Ohlberger and Thomas Schuster tackle finding flaws inside elastic solids from ultrasound readings taken at the surface. They shrink both the wave model and the unknown flaw parameters with adaptively built reduced bases, making fast surrogate models for forward and adjoint calculations. Embedding the regularised Gauss-Newton iteration in a trust-region scheme keeps the approximations reliable, and numerical tests show the approach locates defects effectively.
arxiv-2605-19996: KyeoReh Lee and six co-workers generate reconfigurable structured light at high power from a multimode-fibre laser amplifier. They steer a low-power seed beam with full-field control, using a nonlinear shaping scheme built on a local linear model of the input-output relation. Beams of Gaussian, Bessel, vector and orbital-angular-momentum form emerge directly from the amplifier at powers above five hundred watts. The scheme allows real-time reprogramming and scales readily to still higher powers.
arxiv-2605-20096: Andrey Pereverzev tests ways of finding lattice thermal conductivity from the heat current of a crystalline solid. He sets the full classical heat current against its quadratic component and the standard Peierls heat current, and also tests the relaxation-time approximation. Three systems are tested: solid argon, a solid-argon model with mixed masses, and alpha-quartz. Quadratic and Peierls currents differ only slightly for all three, optical phonons beat sound modes in alpha-quartz, and the relaxation-time approximation always gives too little conductivity.
arxiv-2605-20296: Aarash Abro and Muhammad Tahir fix catastrophic forgetting post-hoc from the pretrained checkpoint and its fine-tuned child, regaining hurt skills, not reverting to base. DG-Hard treats the update as low-rank signal in noise, cuts weight-delta matrices at the Donoho-Gavish hard singular-value threshold, and keeps high-energy parts. Their partition-conditional metric tracks healing, preservation, non-damage, and retention. Across 14 model-task and 9 held-out benchmarks, DG-Hard tops baselines and restores alignment hurt by benign fine-tuning on 3 safety axes.
arxiv-2605-20496: Marcos-Manchón and two co-workers test whether a universal geometry links brain representations across people. Their self-taught encoder learns per-person embeddings from fMRI brain data alone, using repeat stimulus shows. Spaces learned apart translate across subjects via unsupervised orthogonal rotations, with no paired cross-subject samples. Syncing pairwise rotations into one shared space improves cross-subject retrieval, supporting a shared visual-cortex geometry.
arxiv-2605-20596: Joon Young Lee, Hsin-Yu Chen, and Muhammed Saleem test whether merging neutron-star pairs alone can explain heavy elements in Milky Way disk stars. Half of rapid neutron-capture elements still lack a settled origin, and steady merger rates struggle to match the stellar record. The authors combine gravitational-wave, gamma-ray-burst, stellar-population, and abundance data. They find evolving enrichment is strongly preferred, with Bayes factors above ten to the power of twenty.
arxiv-2605-20996: Hojin Ko and Jeonggyu Huh propose a Pontryagin-guided design for non-exponential discounting beyond Bellman recursion. Most value-based and actor-critic methods rely on Bellman recursion, yet it breaks under non-exponential discount, common in human tastes and survival processes. The break is structural: exponential discount sits at a fragile meeting point of multiplicativity and time homogeneity. Breaking either trait breaks standard dynamic programming, so their design abandons recursion and couples Pontryagin's principle with Monte Carlo rollouts.
arxiv-2605-21496: Brandon Dent presents HealthCraft, a reinforcement learning safety environment for emergency medicine. Frontier language models are entering clinical workflows faster than infrastructure to test them safely. What static medical benchmarks miss are the failures that count: trajectory-level safety collapse, tool misuse, and capitulation under sustained clinical pressure. HealthCraft, adapted from Corecraft, rewards trajectory-level safety under realistic emergency conditions. It is built on a FHIR R4 world state with fourteen entity types and three thousand nine hundred eighty-seven seed entities. The goal is safe testing before clinical use.
arxiv-2605-21796: Anna Deichler and co-authors introduce MM-Conv, a dataset and benchmark for grounding language in dynamic 3D dialogue. Vision-language models handle static images well but stumble on ambiguous phrases in multi-turn conversation. The benchmark draws on six point seven hours of egocentric virtual-reality interaction with synced speech, motion, gaze, and scene geometry, holding over four thousand two hundred hand-checked referring expressions. A two-stage pipeline resolving chat ambiguity before visual localization lifts grounding by eleven to twenty-two percentage points on average.
arxiv-2605-21996: Murong Ma and co-authors present P2T, a privileged process supervision method for software agents, moving from patches to trajectories. Fine-tuning on long trajectories makes students inherit outcomes plus intermediate flaws, ungrounded leaps and redundant loops. P2T keeps only short, effective segments where each step is grounded and narrows the gap to the solution, masking tool errors. Using just 1,800 curated SWE-Gym instances, it beats filtered fine-tuning on SWE-bench Verified, raising Pass at 1 by up to 10.8 points and cutting per-instance inference cost by 15 percent.
arxiv-2605-22296: Gómez-Limón and colleagues hunt for close-in satellites around ten trans-Neptunian objects, distant bodies that hold clues to Solar System origins. Their method needs no separation of primary and satellite. It pairs occultation sizes with thermal emission data from the Herschel TNOs are Cool project. Thermal excess that a single body cannot explain signals a companion. Three objects emerge as likely new binaries, with size estimates for their putative satellites. Three others need no sizable satellite to reconcile the data.
arxiv-2605-22496: Bomatter, Geary and Gouk address out-of-distribution (OOD) detection with deep generative models, whose likelihoods prove poor guides. They exploit diffeomorphic mass-preserving normalising flows. OOD samples map to noise samples highly atypical under the noise prior, in ways likelihood misses. Their Signal in the Noise method, SITN, detects single OOD cases. SITN needs no OOD data, adds little extra compute, and keeps false positive rates in check. Tests on benchmarks and synthetic perturbations show it works, with no complexity bias of likelihood methods.
arxiv-2605-22696: Dhyani and others study photon axion conversion near spinning Kerr black holes, where trapped near circular photon paths stretch conversion. Driven by ambient magnetic fields, conversion runs best at X ray and gamma ray frequencies, widening as coupling rises and electron density and axion mass fall. Dimming of photon spectral luminosity depends on magnetic field, coupling and black hole spin, with spinning holes dimming more than static ones. If future telescopes spot such dimming at about ten to the minus five arcseconds, they could constrain axion mass and coupling.
arxiv-2605-22896: Jin and Zhang introduce Agentic-VLA, a training framework that helps vision-language-action robot models adapt online to new settings with few demonstrations. It synthesizes rewards tuned to current skill and task difficulty, guides exploration with a critic model instead of random sampling, and reuses stored policy weights for similar tasks. On the LIBERO benchmark it gained 12.3 percent on long-horizon tasks and 28.5 percent in one-shot learning, converging 2.4 times faster than rivals.
arxiv-2605-23096: Kern and five coauthors tackle overflow in encrypted neural networks under CKKS, which evaluates networks on coded data using only addition, products, and rotation. Activations must be fit by curves over fixed input ranges, usually estimated by rough sampling. Sampled ranges leave networks exposed: the authors' method crafts valid inputs passing design ranges and corrupts around 47 percent of benign inputs in a CIFAR10 network. They then give a formal checking approach building working safe CKKS circuits with proven error bounds, handling more designs than prior proven methods.
arxiv-2605-23296: Cim and three coauthors present side-by-side shrinking for long-horizon LLM agent serving. Long-horizon agents gather chat logs that exceed the context window. LLM-based digests keep the chat bounded, but digests are lossy and the blocking call stalls work for tens of seconds. Side-by-side shrinking gives the user set control over summary volume and enables better prompt craft per block. At matched decode volume, it cuts end-to-end wall time and improves throughput over the serial base.
arxiv-2605-23696: Henderson, De Ath, and Pepper predict UK en route complexity from relevant pairs needing monitoring or spacing, as a proxy for controller workload. They adapt a filter algorithm for London Middle Sector, a busy sector above European airports, refined with controller feedback. The updated algorithm scores F1 0.84 versus 0.69 on 50 scenarios. A route network graph standardizes route legs, with arrival uncertainty from segment odds at future times. With past distributions and a live stream, forecasts reach 45 minutes ahead, correlating with actual interactions at Spearman 0.68 versus 0.55 for traffic volume.
arxiv-2605-24096: Liu and ten co-authors argue that coding agents now make just-in-time systems tractable: systems synthesized from scratch, specialized to environment, workload, and properties. Their pipeline, Jitskit, refines a key-value store implementation against an evolving test suite, starting from spec cards spanning YCSB workloads, deployment constraints, and properties like consistency and durability. Synthesized systems beat comparable state-of-the-art systems on all 18 specs tried, by up to 4.6 times over the best baseline. Claude Code either reward-hacks or trails Jitskit by up to 5.4 times.
arxiv-2605-24396: Gai and six co-authors study premature confidence, locking onto an answer early and spending the rest of the chain justifying it. Long chains of thought often hide logical gaps, capping gains from extra compute. The team trains with progressive confidence shaping, rewarding slow confidence growth while penalizing early commitment, with no outside labels. Across models from 1.5 billion to 8 billion parameters, accuracy rises on arithmetic, math, and science tasks. On Countdown, accuracy more than triples with flawed reasoning nearly halved. Faithfulness improves too, surfacing misleading content rather than hiding it.
arxiv-2605-24496: Zhiheng Fu and colleagues built EgoAction for a 2026 challenge asking models to locate actions in long first-person kitchen videos and label verb and noun. Their pipeline trains separate verb and noun detectors, then pairs top candidates into action guesses. Verb scores falter at motion changes while noun scores falter amid cluttered hands and objects, so a fixed average of their boundaries can mislead. The team instead weights each boundary by the stronger stream's confidence, steadying localization.
arxiv-2605-24696: Michel A. Youssef shows that how intrusion-detection streams get assembled can decide what a benchmark measures. On CICIDS2017, reordering record set under a split leaves held-out samples sharing only about a third of records. Prevalences of two-thirds versus one-quarter flip which scorer looks better. Restricting both arms to held-out records removes the flip, blaming composition, not history. On LITNET-2020, pooling disjoint captures reports a mean operating point, not a real one. The reference score shifts with its batch, so published numbers need not compare.
arxiv-2605-24796: Kristopher Brown rebuilds logical expressivism. The aim is a clearer view of how logic works in use. In pragmatism, meanings come from practices of use, and logical expressivism offers a distinct view of logic. The paper clarifies a recent Brandom-Hlobil account of logical expressivism by rebuilding its formal meaning with universal constructions. This shows links with categorical logic: judgment structure moves inside, and connectives come from adjunctions.
arxiv-2605-24996: Alina Anikejeva maps cognitive distortion profiles across conditions beyond depression. Distorted thought patterns touch many mental health disorders, yet most studies focus on depression alone. The team analyzes large Reddit data spanning nine mental health groups and a control group. They detect distortions with both an n-gram method and a fine-tuned transformer model. Mental health groups show higher distortion rates than controls, with small to moderate effects. Profiles look largely similar across conditions, though some groups run higher overall, hinting simple lexical tools suit exploration.
arxiv-2605-25096: Takumi Tokiwa, Yuwei Yin, and Ryo Onishi propose a variable-drag model for porous-media tree representations. Tree geometry is too costly to resolve, so trees are modeled as porous media with a constant drag coefficient. The new model prescribes drag per cell from effective branching order and effective Reynolds number, capturing unresolved complexity and the flow regime. Flow simulations across grid resolutions and velocities test the model, judged by aerodynamic porosity. The model improves grid robustness against constant-drag and captures bulk drag variation without retuning.
arxiv-2605-25196: Andreas Jungherr, Antonia Schlude, and Adrian Rauchfleisch survey 9,000 people in nine countries about military uses of artificial intelligence. Across six scenarios that vary lethality and human control, people who see AI as beneficial support military AI much more, as do hawkish respondents. Principled opposition to lethal autonomy, by contrast, tracks only opposition to fully autonomous lethal force. Perceived AI risks correlate positively with support, against the authors' expectation. Publics overall look conditionally permissive.
arxiv-2605-25296: Anna Mokhova and colleagues study a neglected side of coding help: personal taste in code style. They define four taste axes, covering complexity, commenting, modularity, and readability, and gather about 3,000 paired Python snippets rated by 73 experts. When 13 language models judge the same task in words and then as code, many flip their preference. The steadiest models show a positional bias, favoring whichever option appears in a certain slot. Compared with people, model ratings skew polarized, and one leading model leans on outside assumptions and fragile reasoning.
arxiv-2605-25396: Chunzheng Zhu and colleagues tackle quality control for ultrasound images without per-plane labels. Current methods need costly annotations or use pseudo-labels that bias under the spatial warping of clinical scans. Their STRIQ framework recasts the task as measuring consistency in a learned subspace.
