A registration aligner matches query images to stable anchors distilled from unlabeled data, while an orthogonal subspace module separates plane-specific knowledge to prevent interference. Tests on two datasets show top correlation with clinical quality scores, enabling live guidance and later audit.
arxiv-2605-25796: Huo and colleagues present SAMark, a watermarking system robust to rewrites. Sentence-level marking breaks under paraphrase. SAMark removes order dependency with a green region in semantic space that does not depend on step order. Multi-channel hyperbolic scoring boosts signals while cutting noise from aligned cases, and range-aware filters add soft controls against meaning repeats. Under paraphrase attacks it reaches over 90 percent true hits at 1 percent false alarms. It beats the rival by over 30 percent on average.
arxiv-2605-25996: Casagrande, Manacorda and Fodor explain why defects in beating active matter move with no flow and no self-push. The stuff is made of units that swell and shrink in rhythm. Motion comes from a ratchet effect: links between local beats and mutual shoves break left-right balance and time balance. Lopsided spinning defects then drift under noise. That cause sets a switch between spiral waves that link slow defects and fibre-like waves that link fast ones, much like faulty heart rhythms.
arxiv-2605-26096: Faisal, Natarajan and Poremba round almost commuting Hamiltonians into ones that commute, keeping locality. Such Hamiltonians sit between classical constraint problems and quantum many-body physics, tractable yet richly quantum. Real ones rarely commute exactly, so near-commutation matters. The authors give a locality-preserving rounding method mapping any two-local qubit Hamiltonian with small term commutators to a nearby commuting one. The rounded system stays within order m times epsilon to the one-third of the original. Consequences include faster simulation for almost commuting systems.
arxiv-2605-26196: In 2026, McKenna McCall and three colleagues tested written explanations of trusted execution environments, sealed-off spaces that guard code and data, on people without technical training. They built draft explanations from existing ones and tried them in test tasks with 966 online workers. Plain explanations that named concrete threats a sealed space blocks improved grasp most. Yet even the best explanations barely moved desire to use the guarded tools, hinting that words alone will not settle privacy worries.
arxiv-2605-26296: Marco Refuto studies symmetries at future null infinity for Schwarzschild space-time, where asymptotic conformal generators close an extended BMS algebra thanks to superdilations. He looks at the related nontrivial charge, which rules out the idea that superdilations are pure gauge. Their effect on a pair of sky watchers reads as an angle-tied redshift, tied to the local flux of the charge. The paper thus marks them as genuine effects with a redshift sign.
arxiv-2605-26496: Fengfa Li and four colleagues unify pruning and upcycling for device-ready expert models with Dense2MoE. Training experts from scratch costs too much, while upcycling bloats parameters and pruning hurts accuracy. Guided by Roofline theory, Dense2MoE prunes bandwidth-heavy attention modules from redundant layers via Layer Fusion UpCycling, repurposing their feed-forward networks as experts. Selective token routing caps active parameters while keeping core abilities. With modest continual pretraining, public dense models become device-ready expert models beating dense, compressed, and upcycled baselines on latency versus accuracy.
arxiv-2605-26596: Haoran Zhang and Zhaohua Sun show why squeezing prompts token by token breaks agents that act through tools. Across seventeen test cells, generic squeezers kept rewards near zero, since they cut the very tokens that carry actions: names, brackets, and verbs. Their AGORA tool instead compresses whole steps, guards format and recent content, and scores relevance with a small trained model. It keeps at least three quarters of full-prompt performance in eight of nine cells.
arxiv-2605-26696: Ahmed, Al-Badawi, and Sakallı test two time-machine shapes in a modified gravity theory: the Ori compact-vacuum-core metric and a four-dimensional Misner-space variant. That theory couples curvature, matter, a scalar field, and its kinetic term. Both shapes solve the modified field equations with anisotropic matter, and their chronology-violating zones survive. The added scalar field thus gives no chronology protection, matching the earlier Li time-machine result.
arxiv-2605-26896: Smykalla and Mariano relate three versions of forcing, the technique Cohen introduced for independence proofs: model theory, Boolean-valued models, and topos theory. Folklore holds the three equivalent in mathematical content, but the literature lacks explicit links. They present new results toward establishing those links, moving the equivalence claim from folklore toward proof.
arxiv-2605-26996: Quang and Phung Nguyen Ngoc Anh prove a characteristic-function bound for two meromorphic functions that weakly share three small functions with bi-weights. When the bi-weight product exceeds the sum plus two, the characteristic of the first function is bounded by roughly twice that of the second. A small error term vanishes as the weight parameter grows. The result gives a clean estimate for weakly shared small functions.
arxiv-2605-27296: Jiashuo Wang and colleagues probe how well language models grasp cultural style in translated movie titles and ad slogans. Their C4STYLI benchmark contrasts Hong Kong and mainland Chinese stylized text, testing both recognition and generation. Models diverge from human judges, and in Hong Kong their recognition leans on surface wording rather than deeper stylistic structure.
arxiv-2605-27496: Theodoros Perdikis, Nader Alharbi, and Michail Tsagris cluster data on spheres and higher-dimensional spheres with elliptically symmetric distributions. They fit the angular Gaussian and the projected Cauchy models with an iterative fitting routine. Tests compare the two on cluster count and cost, and the mixtures group earthquake data and data on higher spheres.
arxiv-2605-27696: Piotr Wyrwinski, Kacper Dobek, and Krzysztof Krawiec propose STROP, a discrete tokenizer that learns variable-length visual programs. A length head trained with a four-phase curriculum calls the active prefix in one forward pass, without post-hoc search or preset compression rates. At about 250 bits per crop, the adaptive model beats fixed-length baselines on segmentation by about 2 to 3 points.
arxiv-2605-27996: Lamparth and colleagues warn that fixing one bias in reward models can simply push optimization onto a correlated proxy. They formalize this reward bias substitution and prove audit scores alone cannot distinguish genuine fixes from substitution or overcorrection. In live RLHF tests, a length penalty curbed verbosity yet drove the policy toward overconfidence while factual accuracy fell.
arxiv-2605-28096: Topuz and colleagues simulate how clots first form after tiny vessel injuries under fast, shearing blood flow. Their particle model resolves red cells, platelets, and stretch-sensitive von Willebrand factor in a microchannel. Clots grow through platelet-factor aggregates to a size set by flow forces alone, then shed pieces as drag grows, capping further growth.
arxiv-2605-28496: Ryo Nikkuni adds a new minimal example to the theory of intrinsically linked simplicial complexes. He had earlier built several minimal n-complexes that must contain a non-splittable two-component link, an (n-1)-sphere plus an n-sphere, in every embedding into 2n-dimensional space. This paper presents one more complex with the same forced-link property. The short work thus extends a small family of minimal complexes whose embeddings cannot avoid linking.
arxiv-2605-28696: Stephen Dolan, Jake McKean, and Laura Munteanu characterize final-state interactions in energy estimation for DUNE and Hyper-K. Tests need guesses held at the MeV level, but hadrons from neutrino-nucleus scatters reinteract with matter. Using event codes, they review motion-based and heat-based gauges, spanning old in-nucleus showers and an Einstein mean-field treatment. Model changes create doubts at or above the needed care scale, with Hyper-K hit by pion soaking and DUNE by hadron energy splits between visible and unseen sources.
arxiv-2605-28896: Prasanth K K studies how LoRA adapters change language model internals, using sparse feature nets. He builds a delta setup picking out the adapter-specific share to the inner stream. He then trains adapter-specific sparse nets across Gemma-2-9B layers at LoRA ranks 4, 8, 16, and 32, matching learned spaces against base dictionaries. Across layers and ranks, the LoRA-base feature match is rather weak. Adapter-specific nets rebuild delta signals better than base ones. Feature density rises with rank and depth while shape drift stays fairly stable.
arxiv-2605-29396: Zhihao Liu studies safety robustness from the optimizer view. Safety training aims to reduce harmful conduct while keeping general utility, but safety effects can be fragile. Lightweight tweaks such as weight noise, activation noise, or quantization can easily weaken safety conduct. Their hybrid method first performs standard first-order safety training and then applies zeroth-order passes. Only a few such passes toughen safety while keeping utility. Layer-wise weak-spot gauges let updates focus on key layers with modest cost.
arxiv-2605-29496: Xueqing Wu and three colleagues diagnose why post-training lifts reasoning more than perception in vision-language models, a gap that bottlenecks reasoning. Using two tasks that separate seeing from reasoning, they trace the supervised fine-tuning gap to token imbalance. Perception fills a smaller share of training text, while the reinforcement gap comes from rewards tracking reasoning more than perception. Reweighting that loss and adding a perception-aware reward raise end-to-end scores. The reweighting gain reaches 18.2 points, and the fixes transfer to benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-29696: Alexander S. Blum, Dean Rickles, and Karim Thébault argue rigour in physics is endogenous, governed by internal norms, often implicit, local, and changing. Physicists sought rigour to remove barriers to calculation and clear concepts, not for its own sake or a higher truth standard. They support this thesis with a case study of the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, 1962 to 1967, drawing on archival material and the published record. Their hypothesis is that rigorisation via the inner product, not the equation's statement, was the crucial step in Wheeler's and DeWitt's work.
arxiv-2605-29796: Yunbo Tang and six colleagues teach search agents when to stop searching. Agentic search systems often miss their knowledge limits, searching when internal knowledge suffices and pressing on past enough evidence. The waste shows up as slow answers and heavy compute, the flaw called over-search. Their frame, SAAS, models the search boundary from rollouts with search on and off, then turns it into penalties that curb needless searches. A staged curriculum that puts reasoning first guards against reward hacking, and tests show over-search falls with accuracy intact.
arxiv-2605-29896: Tiantian Liu and eight colleagues present NdOF, a honeycomb rare-earth chalcohalide, as a platform for multipolar states. Tuning doublets with a field offers a route to multipolar states, yet observation in materials remains rare. Raman spectroscopy identifies four excitations, and a Zeeman-crystal-field analysis reproduces splitting into branches. Magnetization and susceptibility across a wide field range fit a crystal-field model for the angular momentum manifold, confirming the scheme. The ground-state doublet evolves from dipolar to dipolar-multipolar character with field, with pressure as another knob.
arxiv-2605-29996: Angelo Faccia, Ermanno Citraro, and Francesco P. Andriulli model head tissues as a lumped RC circuit. Full numerical simulation costs too much for rapid prototyping or live use, so their circuit mimics a three-layer head to fifty kilohertz. It carries frequency-dependent conductivity and permittivity in the electro-quasi-static regime, using few impedance elements for key signal paths. Tests with a dipolar brain source match semi-analytical scalp voltage peaks across skull thicknesses and eccentricities. Tissue dispersion and capacitive branches were weighed, both adding to fidelity.
arxiv-2605-30596: Svendsen and colleagues tackle a barrier to modular AI: separately trained models settle into incompatible internal coordinate systems. Relative representations bridge models by mapping coordinates to similarities against shared anchor points. But random anchors and cosine similarity miss the stretched geometry of modern architectures. Learning anchors as robust semantic prototypes and using a geometry-aware similarity that keeps magnitude information and ignores affine shifts, they enable near-lossless transfer and stable zero-shot communication between unlike models. The approach works even for small language models of different sizes.
arxiv-2605-30996: Pecile and colleagues test whether inequality in online interaction is stable across time and platforms. A small subset of users captures most action while most stay small, a pattern often fit by power laws. From user-post networks, they count active posts and passive likes and comments, using divergence-based models, inverse coefficient of variation, and a log-transformed Gini index. They find interaction inequality stays stable over time within each platform, across varied systems. This reflects structural constraints on visibility and participation.
arxiv-2605-31096: Zhang and colleagues bring grounded thought inside language models with reinforcement learning. Grounded chain-of-thought helps fine detail, but forcing object boxes often hurts results versus plain text thought. They guess that place skills move inside text thought, since forced grounding hurts answer guesses. Their iVGR method moves place skills into text thought via dual-stream training. It lines up text and grounded streams through a shared reward, letting place skills work without grounding. Tests show iVGR beats rivals on fine-grained benchmarks, while open to tool use.
arxiv-2605-31196: Jun Wang, Xiaohao Xu and Xiaonan Huang benchmark whether vision-language models can judge robot collision risk from what they see. Their TouchSafeBench holds 2,940 simulated indoor episodes with multi-view depth, trajectory maps and simulator contact labels, testing current-state classification and imminent-collision warnings. The best mean Macro-F1 score remains under 50 percent, and depth cues do not automatically become body-collision evidence. Visual fluency, they conclude, does not imply physical accountability.
arxiv-2605-31396: Commandeur, De Schutter and Yorke-Smith review how electric fleets manage power demand and charging plans. The switch to electric fleets promises cleaner air, less noise, climate benefits and more energy flexibility. Battery vehicles bring planning challenges absent from diesel fleets: varied charging speeds, jumpy prices and scarce chargers. Handling this tangle needs solutions balancing cost savings and toughness, with links between transport and power grids. The review draws on grey literature: industry reports, company papers and technical blogs. It names trends and gaps to guide future research.
arxiv-2605-31596: Kheirandish and team propose KLIP, a metric for detecting localized distribution shift in inverse problems via KL-divergence with diffusion priors. Existing methods often need knowledge of the shifted distribution, fail on subtle shifts, and work on full images. KLIP measures the gap between diffusion prior and posterior, needing no calibration data. It can flag whole images as out-of-distribution as well as localize shifted patches within an image. Tests show it detects subtle shifts, such as healthy liver scans versus those with tumors.
arxiv-2606-00096:
Kim, Tan, and Kim discover that visual AI agents work best when they explore diversely, not when they use their tools most, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Visual chain-of-thought agents call tools like cropping and search to gather evidence. Studying harder tasks, including 3D spatial reasoning and medical question answering, the authors identify tool-use collapse: during training, models stop calling tools while their accuracy still rises. Forcing tool use back up yields only marginal gains despite higher usage.

The explanation is diversity. Both training and tool pushes narrowed the range of tried solution paths, trapping models in local optima. Adding an entropy regularization term, which rewards exploration, produced the best performance even as tool use fell. The authors frame tools as training scaffolding: supports that build reasoning skill, then become unneeded. Their project page presents this as a reason to favor exploration breadth over tool frequency.

arxiv-2606-04096:
Daniel Belkin and colleagues show in 2026 how to learn the noise pattern of a quantum device far more precisely. The best method is maximum likelihood estimation, which fits the model that best matches the data. But it is usually too costly for systems with many qubits.

Their method, MET, reuses a fast existing approach as a guide. Then it corrects that approach's bias with a model-free random estimate. This keeps the cost close to the cheap method while gaining most of the costly method's accuracy. Tests used real process tomography data from a four-qubit system. Noise estimates improved a lot, with almost no extra cost. The authors sketch how to scale the idea up.
arxiv-2606-04396:
Khandelwal and Gupta present a reinforcement learning method for diffusion language models, which generate text by unmasking tokens in parallel, in a 2026 arXiv paper. That process leaves a trace showing which tokens became confident and which stayed unstable. Earlier methods grade the whole response at once, or branch it into costly tree searches. Their method, CAPR, summarizes the trace into a path state and trains a value head scoring each block of tokens.

CAPR redistributes the final reward across blocks by the tokens revealed in each one, giving fine-grained signals without tree expansion. Rollout cost falls to about three quarters of flat rollouts and three fifths of tree rollouts. Across Sudoku, Countdown, GSM8K, and Math500 tests, on two LLaDA model families, CAPR set best results so far for this class. On Sudoku it matched the strongest tree baseline at under a third of the per-step compute.
arxiv-2606-04496:
The Belle and Belle II Collaborations measure how matter and antimatter versions of a particle decay differ, using two large datasets from Japanese colliders, in a 2026 arXiv particle physics paper. They study B mesons decaying into a K-short particle, a neutral pion, and a photon, and extract two time-dependent CP violation parameters, called S and C, which quantify the asymmetry. The data cover about 772 million and 521 million Upsilon(4S) decays collected by Belle and Belle II, respectively.

In the region dominated by the K-star resonance, the combined measurement gives S near 0.09 and C near minus 0.09, each with an uncertainty larger than the value itself. In the higher-mass region, S comes out near minus 0.32 and C near minus 0.07, again with wide uncertainties. All values agree with Standard Model predictions, and the combined result is more precise than previous measurements.
arxiv-2606-04596:
Positional bias in summaries of several videos is the subject of a 2026 arXiv study by Huangchen Xu and coauthors. A multimodal model, meaning one that reads video and text together, may judge the same video differently by slot. The slot is simply the place where that video sits among the others fed to the model.

The team built a test set from activity and news videos covering cooking, home life, leisure, and news. They ran nine open and commercial models on pairs and groups of four videos in rotated orders. Scores often fell for videos placed in the middle, even when a simple early versus late score looked small. Giving models more images or longer answers did not reliably remove that middle drop across all settings. Simple prompt changes helped only in part, so the authors urge building models that ignore input order.
arxiv-2606-04696:
Hartman and Kalma prove a result they call the no-core principle in this 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. A stationary action is a group action kept steady, on average, by a chosen random walk on the group. A core is a set meeting almost every orbit, or path of one point, in only finitely many points.

They show that any such core with positive size must sit, apart from rare exceptions, on finite orbits. They then apply that finding to random subgroups chosen by a stationary rule rather than a fixed one. An end is a way the graph linked to a subgroup stretches off toward infinity. For such subgroups, that graph can have zero, one, two, or endlessly many ends, but no other count. Their contrast case builds special subgroups of a free group whose graphs have exactly any chosen larger count.
arxiv-2606-05296:
Dae Yon Hwang and colleagues introduce Agentic Monte Carlo in this 2026 arXiv paper, a way to optimize black-box language model agents without ever training them. The strongest agents often run behind APIs, so their parameters cannot be tuned by reinforcement learning, and their behavior can only be steered at test time. The method exploits an equivalence between reinforcement learning and Bayesian inference.

Instead of training, Agentic Monte Carlo samples from the optimal policy, treated as a posterior distribution over trajectories whose prior is the black-box agent itself. Sequential Monte Carlo does the sampling, guided by a learned value function that steers the agent toward rewarding trajectories while the underlying model stays unchanged. Validated on three environments from the AgentGym benchmark, the method improved over prompting baselines. It even outperformed Group Relative Policy Optimization, a reinforcement learning method, as its test-time compute budget was scaled up.
arxiv-2606-05396:
Cristina Carleo and colleagues run a feasibility study on separating refusal from capability in language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper, motivated by defensive labeling needs. Safety-aligned code models refuse prompts to inject a specified weakness into safe code. Using Python and the SQL injection weakness class as a case study, the team tested the Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct family at three sizes on samples from two datasets.

Refusal proved size- and context-dependent. The largest model refused every prompt, the mid-size one refused most on one dataset but almost none on the other, and the smallest was never blocked. Abliteration, a low-rank weight edit that projects out the refusal direction, cut refusal to zero or near zero at all sizes while keeping validity above 93 percent. Post-edit injection success stayed capacity-bound, high for the larger models and lower for the smallest, separating willingness from capability.
arxiv-2606-05596:
Hou and co-authors blend privacy with multi-goal selection in a 2026 arXiv paper. Many tasks pick a small set that scores well on several goals at once. Each goal shows diminishing returns, the mark of a submodular function. The data behind the goals can be sensitive, though. Nobody had yet combined this selection task with differential privacy, the standard guard against leaking private facts.

The team offers two algorithms with proven quality guarantees. One extends the classic greedy method, which grabs the best next item each round. The other trims scores first, then applies the same greedy logic. Both weave in privacy noise sized to the formal guarantee. Tests on two standard tasks, maximum coverage and facility location, check the trade-offs. The methods stayed effective and fast while holding the privacy promise. The paper opens a task family that privacy research had skipped.
arxiv-2606-05796:
Arquint verifies a small arithmetic routine at the heart of RSA key generation in a 2026 arXiv paper. The extended greatest common divisor routine in Go's standard library was ported from BoringSSL. The port was assumed faithful. Careful checking found two deviations, and each breaks the routine's invariants. One changes how coefficients update during the loop. The other quietly widens the allowed input range.

Arquint fixed the update bug in the Go code, and the fix also ran about twenty-four percent faster on average. For the wider domain, an existing BoringSSL proof was ported and extended. Correctness and termination of the fixed code are proven in Gobra, a verifier for Go. Hard arithmetic lemmas were proven in Lean and imported. The effort also used AI agents to refine proof attempts against error messages. Well-reviewed standard library code, the paper warns, can still hide subtle breaks.
arxiv-2606-06096:
Paavo Parmas and colleagues let policy gradients optimize the return statistic the user cares about in a 2026 arXiv paper. Standard methods chase expected return, a mean. Deployments often care about tails: worst-case risk, trimmed averages, medians, or the best of several tries. OrderGrad estimates gradients for order-statistic objectives directly. Sorted sample rewards are combined through rank weights, forming L-statistics.

Changing only the weights recovers value-at-risk, conditional value-at-risk, trimmed means, medians, and best-of-K criteria. For any sample size and weight vector, the estimator is unbiased for its objective. Implementation is a reward transformation dropped into standard policy-gradient or reparameterized updates. Variance behavior is analyzed alongside. Tasks where mean optimization mismatches deployment, including language-model math post-training, test the method. One estimator family covers risk-averse, robust, and exploratory learning. Means were a default, the authors imply, not a destiny.
arxiv-2606-06296:
Christian Hägg and Boris Shapiro study when a certain transform of a domain stays algebraic in this 2026 arXiv paper on complex analysis. An algebraic oval is a closed loop cut out by a polynomial equation. The exterior Cauchy transform integrates over the region inside the oval, weighted by distance to an outside point. The question is when that transform can itself be written with polynomial relations, rather than needing transcendental functions.

The authors recast the problem on a fixed Riemann surface, where only the poles of an integrand move as the outside point varies. Their main theorem gives a residue criterion. If the lifted boundary separates the surface and bounds a suitable chain away from the fixed poles, the transform is algebraic, with an explicit residue formula. Every smooth oval on a rational curve passes the test. The paper ends with open questions about nonseparating ovals on cubic curves.
arxiv-2606-06496:
Johannes Conrad lays theoretical groundwork for a strange kind of turbulence in this 2026 arXiv paper. Polymer laden fluids can turn turbulent with no inertia at all, purely from elastic stresses. Modeling this elastic turbulence defies the tools that work for ordinary flow. There, symmetries tightly constrain any approximation. Conrad sets up the problem in the Martin Siggia Rose path integral framework, the field theory language for random dynamics.

His main tool is an algorithm that derives Ward identities from the equations of motion. These are exact constraints that follow from symmetries. Applied to a simplified extended Burgers model, the method yields an enlarged identity set. That set strongly restricts which closure schemes are allowed. The sobering conclusion: the stress sector has far fewer protecting symmetries than the velocity sector. That is exactly why renormalization methods struggle more here than in classical turbulence.
arxiv-2606-06596:
String theory computes how strings scatter by adding up contributions from surfaces of every shape. Barman works through a delicate corner of that machinery in this 2026 arXiv paper on minimal superstring theory, a stripped down version of the theory that is easier to solve. He studies instanton effects, rare tunneling events that add small corrections beyond the usual step by step expansion.

Barman computes three quantities for the cosmological constant operator in the two type 0 variants of the theory: two disk amplitudes and one annulus amplitude. Some of the integrals blow up where surfaces pinch off. He regulates them with string field theory. He also fixes exactly where the picture changing operators must sit. Those operators are special insertions the superstring needs. After every contribution is tallied, the results match the scaling pattern predicted by the DDK-KPZ framework precisely, a strong check on the method.
arxiv-2606-06696:
Models that read medical images and answer questions about them often score well on familiar tests, then stumble in new clinics. Ryan D'Cunha and a large team introduce a tougher yardstick in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their benchmark, called MMBU, spans thirty five kinds of biomedical imaging, from chest X-rays to microscope views of cells, with detailed labels attached.

The benchmark tests naming what an image shows, naming it with a marked location, and drawing boxes around objects, in both open and closed answer formats. The team ran fifteen open models and two leading commercial systems through it. Medical tuning helped some models, but overall accuracy stayed low, detection was poor, and results wobbled across data sets. High scores on older, narrower tests, the authors warn, can hide weak basic perception that this broader benchmark exposes.
arxiv-2606-06796:
Tiny electrostatic actuators sit inside countless sensors and switches. Ichida, Kakuno, and Yamane analyze how those devices fail in this 2026 arXiv paper. The device is a parallel plate actuator, a MEMS structure where voltage pulls a plate toward its twin. Pull too hard and the plate snaps down. Engineers call that collapse pull-in, and the final contact touchdown.

The authors study a second order equation for the plate's motion. The spring behind the plate can be soft, linear, or hard. Their tools are geometric: compactification, center manifolds, and blow-up methods. These tools tame behavior that runs off to infinity. Pull-in turns out to mark where solutions degenerate. Touchdown is a blow up reached in finite time. Building on the well understood linear spring, they map the whole structure for soft and hard springs too.
arxiv-2606-07196:
Locating brain activity from scalp sensors is a guessing game with far more possible sources than sensors. Morik and co-authors teach a classical solver to improve itself in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sparse Bayesian methods estimate both the sources and the noise level, but their update rules are fixed formulas. The dynamics cannot adapt to the data at hand.

The team unfolds the classical solver into a neural network whose layers mirror its iterations. Crucially, the network starts out exactly reproducing the original algorithm. Training then adds structured correction terms, from simple learned biases to attention based refinements. The Bayesian skeleton stays intact and interpretable throughout. On synthetic EEG benchmarks with uneven sensor noise, corrected versions reconstructed sources better. Input adaptive corrections performed best. The work offers a template: learn inside a trusted algorithm, not instead of it.
arxiv-2606-07796:
Anwar Shah and co-authors build an autonomous cyber defence for connected vehicles in this 2026 arXiv paper. In the Internet of Vehicles, cars, roadside units, and cloud services talk constantly, and attackers adapt as defenders respond. Static detectors trained offline miss that moving, partly hidden contest. The team models defence as reinforcement learning under partial observability, acting without knowing the attacker's intent.

Their system, Q-BIRD, encodes the defender's uncertainty as a quantum-inspired belief state, built from probability amplitudes rather than ordinary probabilities. That belief feeds a policy network choosing cost-aware responses such as alerting, throttling traffic, or isolating a vehicle. In simulation against an adaptive attacker that probes and evades, Q-BIRD cut cumulative mean damage by about sixty percent and damage variance by about ninety percent. Attack success fell by half, and survival probability rose by about forty-six percent, relative to a standard policy baseline.
arxiv-2606-07896:
Dineth Jayakody and Dushan Wadduwage find why optical neural networks fail at visible wavelengths, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffractive neural networks compute with light itself, passing it through patterned layers performing a learned transformation. Working versions exist at terahertz frequencies, but visible ones lag, a failure long blamed on fabrication difficulty.

The authors identify a different culprit: the thin-layer approximation used in training, which pretends each diffractive layer is infinitely thin. At visible wavelengths the low-index materials available force relief structures thick enough that light diffracts inside the layer itself, breaking the approximation. Their fix is a differentiable beam-propagation layer that models each element as a finite-thickness volume, so training matches fabrication. Under full-wave simulation validation, classification accuracy rose from fifty percent to ninety percent with no re-optimisation. The layer bridges efficient optical design and devices that behave as designed.
arxiv-2606-08096:
Ruoyu Su and co-authors at the University of Oulu tackle a data-cleaning problem that quietly corrupts software engineering research, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Studies of open-source projects measure how developers are coupled through the code they touch, but commit records carry only names and emails, and one developer often appears under several aliases. Without de-duplication, the same person counts as several, distorting the measurements.

The team builds a scalable identification pipeline plus guidance for choosing within it. They start from an Indel string-similarity baseline, then use language-model-assisted matching with manual validation to assemble a large dataset of duplicate identities. On it they train and compare classical machine learning models of varying complexity, scoring precision alongside training and inference time and energy use. The deliverable is a benchmark of which approach best trades accuracy against cost at scale.
arxiv-2606-08296:
Thorstad revisits a central argument about the risks of advanced artificial intelligence in this 2026 arXiv paper. The shutdown problem is the worry that a faulty agent might resist being turned off. A catastrophic version asks how to guarantee shutdown before an agent causes existential harm. Many arguments have been offered to suggest this problem is genuinely hard. That claimed hardness supports broader claims about existential risk and motivates a search for technical fixes.

Thorstad argues for two conclusions. First, existing arguments do not show that solving the catastrophic shutdown problem is hard. The step from agent incentives to a machine that cannot be stopped is weaker than advertised. Second, concern about the problem has pushed researchers toward fixes that impose a high safety tax. Such fixes degrade model performance a lot in exchange for added control. The paper urges a reassessment of how much weight the shutdown problem should carry.
arxiv-2606-08396:
Rubiano works out explicit rules for reordering products in a family of noncommutative algebras, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Normal ordering rewrites any product in a standard form, with variables in a fixed order. The algebras here are the twenty-six double Ore extensions of a specified type in the Zhang-Zhang classification. Rubiano fixes an ordering of the four generators and derives the theory.

The paper gives closed two-letter formulas for the relations and recursive coefficient systems for mixed words and multinomial expressions. Most internal coefficients are quantum or skew-commutative in flavor. The Jordan families produce Lah-Whitney arrays, triangular number tables of Stirling type. A SageMath implementation accompanies the paper, letting readers verify the reductions directly. The result is a complete toolkit for this algebra family, ready for use in symbolic work by hand or by machine.
arxiv-2606-08496:
Jingyi He and colleagues improve the tools that explain what a language model's internal features mean, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sparse autoencoders split a model's dense internal states into sparse features. Each feature hopefully matches one interpretable concept. Explaining those features in words remains a central challenge. Current methods work open-loop: they generate an explanation once and never use feedback to refine it.

Their framework, SAEExplainer, closes the loop by using activation scores as an objective reward signal. A candidate explanation is tested against how the feature actually activates. The explainer model is trained, through preference optimization guided by those scores, to correct itself over two rounds. This cuts explanation hallucinations and reinforces causal triggering patterns.
arxiv-2606-08796:
Wang and colleagues speed up mechanics simulations by marrying finite element solvers to neural operators, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Finite element methods, the standard for stress and deformation problems, grow expensive where behavior turns complex or shapes get irregular. A neural operator is a trained network that predicts a simulation's solution directly. The team's earlier hybrid split each problem into regions, but overlaps wasted interface calculations, and the learned part needed tidy grids.

Their framework removes the overlap. A Schwarz alternating method passes traction, the force across a boundary, from the neural region to the finite element one, cutting the iteration count. A Point-DeepONet lets the neural region work on scattered point clouds, so irregular and non-convex shapes become possible. Strain and stress come from the displacement output by the governing equations, not separate training. Tests on three benchmarks showed bounded error growth over the time horizons tried.
arxiv-2606-09396:
Ke Wang and his colleagues propose PriFT, a way to make supervised fine-tuning of language models generalise better, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Supervised fine-tuning trains a model on fixed demonstrations token by token. Tokens that clash with what the pretrained model already expects can distort its knowledge and cause overfitting. Earlier fixes weighted tokens using the model being trained, which lets the weighting drift as training proceeds.

PriFT instead measures prior support, how well each target token is already supported by the frozen pretrained model, and uses that stable signal to weight training. Two versions use either the token's pretrained probability or its cumulative probability mass. Across mathematics, code generation, and medical question answering, swapping in the pretrained signal improved every reweighting rule tested. On a mathematics benchmark, the mass-based version beat the strongest earlier baseline by about nine points on one pass-rate measure.
arxiv-2606-09696:
Vadim Kaloshin, Illya Koval, and Yi Pan prove that a common flaw in orderly motion breeds wavy invariant surfaces in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is Hamiltonian mechanics, the math of systems that keep their energy. In tidy cases, motion sticks to torus-shaped surfaces that look like flat graphs. KAM theory says most survive small nudges.

The flaw is isoenergetic degeneracy, a point where the tidy test fails at fixed energy. The team shows that for typical such systems, a small generic nudge creates meandering tori. These surfaces are still smooth and invariant, but they fold back and are no longer graphs. Some nudges yield meanders of every order, nested without end. Past sightings of such folds came from numeric runs on single cases, like Rossby waves and the Kepler problem. This is the first broad proof that the folds are the rule, not the fluke.
arxiv-2606-09896:
Tianxing Bu and his co-authors unify two ad markets that share one screen in this 2026 arXiv paper. Guaranteed delivery deals promise set ad volumes at set prices. Real-time bidding sells the rest by snap auctions. Split tools or crude rank rules fail to weigh snap cash against long-run pledges, most of all when one page view holds many slots.

Their HMAF frame runs a plan-calibrate-execute loop. An offline planner parcels out the pledged stock under hard caps. A live tuner then gauges how strongly the two streams should clash. Rank calls across slots are made listwise, in real time. The system ships at Meituan, a giant food delivery platform. There it lifted the pledged delivery rate by three point seven two percent. Total ad revenue rose by one point five nine percent.
arxiv-2606-10096:
James Peng and his team tackle estimating the average of many probability distributions when each one is barely observed, in a 2026 arXiv paper on statistics. The natural center is the Wasserstein barycenter, whose quantile function averages the individual quantile functions point by point. Plugging in the sample distributions directly gives a severely biased estimate under such sparse sampling, which motivates a new approach.

Instead of estimating each unit's distribution or the full population law, they characterize the distribution of latent unit-level quantiles at a fixed level. That distribution can be written through marginal curves of the observations, opening a route to less biased estimates. The problem arises in settings like vaccine studies, where each participant contributes few measurements. The paper develops the theory for pointwise estimates of the barycenter's quantile function, a building block for honest summaries of distributional data collected under real-world sampling limits.
arxiv-2606-10296:
Keramati and his team ask whether a debating AI's internal confidence betrays the quality of its reasoning, in a 2026 arXiv paper on language model testing. Their setup pairs two agents: a Constructor that builds cases and an Auditor that critiques them. A language-model judge scores each agent's reasoning on rule following, justification quality, and evidence grounding, plus a critical-failure flag.

Experiments in the rubric-scoring domain reveal a steady four-phase confidence path across debates. A large role gap appears: confidence aligns with judged reasoning quality roughly twice as strongly for the Constructor as for the Auditor. Confidence-based spotting of critical reasoning failures is far more often right for the Constructor than the Auditor, with reported scores well above chance for one role and near it for the other.
arxiv-2606-10396:
Liu and his team convert a family of equations written in bilinear form into ordinary nonlinear form, in a 2026 arXiv paper on integrable systems. Hirota bilinear equations encode famous wave laws through a special derivative rule, and Jarmo Hietarinta listed bilinear equations of sine-Gordon and nonlinear Schrödinger type while searching for integrable ones.

They provide a recipe converting both the sine-Gordon type and nonlinear Schrödinger type bilinear equations into nonlinear forms. Nonlinearization for cases involving Hilbert transforms, which appear in Benjamin-Ono type models for internal water waves, is also treated. Bell polynomials, a counting tool for tracking derivatives of nested functions, are used throughout the conversion, and worked examples show each case. The full dictionary between bilinear and nonlinear versions helps researchers move results between the two fields of such systems.
arxiv-2606-10696:
Nermeen Abou Baker and Handmann test a segmentation model on rubbish in this 2026 arXiv paper. Meta's Segment Anything Model, SAM, segments almost any object in an image without task training, thanks to training on 11 million images and over a billion masks. Waste sorting is a sterner test: waste scenes bring occlusions, deformable and transparent objects, and items that blend into backgrounds. The authors evaluate SAM's generalisation on 3 waste segmentation datasets, then fine-tune it.

Fine-tuning changes the picture. The tuned SAM-ViT-H model beats the state of the art on the Zerowaste and TACO datasets, with intersection-over-union gains of 30 points. On TrashCan 1.0 it comes close, trailing the best by 1.44 points. The authors conclude SAM should not be wasted as a zero-shot curiosity: fine-tuned, it generalises to a messy task that badly needs cheap, expert-level annotation.
arxiv-2606-10796:
Lyu and colleagues diagnose depression from clinical interviews without training in this 2026 arXiv paper. Supervised detectors need labelled interviews, which privacy makes scarce and expensive. Dep-LLM runs entirely on frozen language models, mirroring how psychiatrists reason. A first module decomposes each one into five clinically aligned themes and extracts evidence-grounded rationales. A second scores each one's reliability from token-level entropy, amplifying trustworthy signals and suppressing uncertain ones. A third fuses the confidence-weighted factors into a diagnosis.

On the DAIC-WOZ and E-DAIC benchmarks, it improves on the zero-shot baseline for all 21 foundation models, across 9 metrics including accuracy and macro F1. It also outperforms trained models and the closed-source commercial models, despite using no training labels and no fine-tuning. Every step yields a readable rationale and a score, so the diagnosis arrives with its logic attached.
arxiv-2606-11196:
Tian and four co-authors present PoQ-Judge in a 2026 arXiv paper, for decentralized LLM inference. Providers in such networks serve model answers and earn rewards under Proof of Quality, paying for good outputs. Scoring quality normally needs a reference answer that live serving lacks. PoQ-Judge trains judges grading question-output pairs with no reference at all.

Three judges span a quality-cost frontier. A TextCNN judge has ten million parameters and answers in under a millisecond. A MiniLM cross-encoder has twenty-two million, and a DeBERTa judge one hundred eighty-four million. All train on UltraFeedback, then fine-tune on GPT-labeled data. On three hundred held-out cases, the DeBERTa judge correlated with the ground-truth proxy at 0.747 Pearson, beating every reference-based evaluator the team had before. A cascade protocol saved 72.7 percent of cost. Scores split sharply by task: 0.830 on question answering, only 0.199 on summarization.
arxiv-2606-11396:
Kumar, Iba, Zarrin, and Berenson present PLUME in a 2026 arXiv paper, a world model for dexterous robot hands. Multi-finger manipulation is sensitive to physical parameters like object shape, pose, and friction. Simulation gives large-scale data with known values, but at deployment the true ones are unknown. Domain randomization may fail for precise tasks like screwdriver turning, where strategy must adapt to them.

PLUME learns to evolve a belief over parameter values and the dynamics conditioned on them. Its latent space represents different physical parameters, and rewards, to inform planning. The model aligns to true dynamics through online parameter inference, without retraining or fine-tuning. On simulated screwdriver turning, valve turning, bucket lifting, and disk flicking, plus a hardware screwdriver task, PLUME transferred its simulation-trained policy zero-shot. It beat state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning and behavior cloning baselines.
arxiv-2606-11496:
Takou, Benito, Vezvaee, Lidar, and Brown learn error models straight from experiment data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Decoders for quantum error correction rely on detector error models, which encode each error's probability and which detectors and logical observables it flips. The authors show estimating these probabilities from experimental syndromes is feasible, avoids separate device benchmarking, and yields decoder priors that reduce decoded logical error rates.

They evaluate on open-source surface-code memory data from Google's Willow chip and run analogous experiments on IBM's ibm_miami processor. Despite the devices' different error scales, estimated models improve logical error probabilities over baseline device-informed models in both cases, typically by five to ten percent, with larger IBM gains. The gains come without additional calibration circuits, decoder fine-tuning, or supervised fitting to logical outcomes. The method exploits spatial and temporal unevenness in the syndrome history, capturing signatures of the real noise.
arxiv-2606-11596:
Shirantha Welikala, Zihao Song, Hai Lin and Panos J Antsaklis design controllers for networks of linked systems in this 2026 arXiv paper. Examples include power microgrids and robot teams. Their guiding idea is dissipativity, a property saying each part stores or sheds energy in a controlled way, so the whole network stays well behaved from disturbances to performance outputs.

The design is hierarchical. Local controllers come first, so each subsystem carries its own dissipativity guarantee. Global controllers and the network wiring are then designed together, exploiting those guarantees while keeping interconnection costs low. Everything reduces to a sequence of linear matrix inequality problems, a tractable class of optimisation, avoiding slow non-convex searches. Because real dynamics are often unknown, a data-driven version works from recorded trajectories alone, using a matrix S-lemma for bounded unknown disturbances. A DC microgrid example shows robust voltage regulation and current sharing.
arxiv-2606-12096:
Smith and co-authors give an exact test for when a set of quantum controls can do anything, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Any quantum computation is a sequence of changes generated by Hamiltonians, rules steering a system's energy and motion. The controls here are Pauli strings, products of basic single-qubit operations across all qubits, the two-level units of quantum hardware. A set is universal if it can generate every operation.

For Pauli strings alone, they prove a condition both necessary and sufficient for universality, and easy to check. Adding one general Hamiltonian, they give a sufficient condition from its expansion in the Pauli basis, necessary in some cases too. Two payoffs follow. First, a full criterion for any Hamiltonian paired with complete single-qubit control on every qubit. Second, proof that an XYZ Heisenberg Hamiltonian becomes universal with local control of just two neighboring qubits.
arxiv-2606-12396:
Jin Yao and co-authors give self-driving language models a dedicated sense of three-dimensional space, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language-action models describe scenes and reason in words, yet their driving can float free of the dense 3D world. Feeding in frozen 3D features does not guarantee the policy uses them. Sparse box and map losses give only thin spatial signals. VLGA adds geometry as a fourth modality beside vision, language, and action, with its own expert network.

The geometry expert is trained to reconstruct the full 3D scene, supervised per pixel against LiDAR point maps. On open-loop nuScenes tests, VLGA posts the lowest trajectory error among rival methods and a three-second collision rate of just 0.18 percent on the reported protocol. On closed-loop Bench2Drive it scores 79.08, topping the strongest prior system. Gains concentrate exactly where driving is hardest: tight, spatially demanding scenes.
arxiv-2606-12596:
Linden extends a time-series fix to panel data and shows, by simulation, that it beats the alternative, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Panel data track many units over time, and their errors often show autocorrelation, echoes lasting several periods. Panel estimators with corrected standard errors handle only first-order echoes. Linden extends the Prais-Winsten transformation to autoregressive order in the Beck-Katz framework, shipped as the Stata package xtpraisk.

The Monte Carlo study spans autoregressive orders one to three, three autocorrelation patterns, panel sizes and series lengths, two thousand replications per condition. It achieves higher power than the Driscoll-Kraay rival in every condition. Its standard errors stay honest, with ratios near one, so the power is real efficiency, not cheating. The rival underestimates standard errors and inflates false positives at short series lengths, worsening as the order rises, though the flaws fade as series lengthen.
arxiv-2606-12696:
Cardenas-Castillo shows a short laser pulse makes the quantum geometry of graphene ripple like a wave, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Graphene is a layer of carbon atoms in a honeycomb lattice. Its electrons are described by Bloch states, and the quantum metric measures how those states change across momentum. In static graphene this geometry is fixed, but the author solves the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for a pulsed drive and watches it move.

Near the Dirac points, where graphene's bands meet, the quantum metric develops a wave-like pattern mirroring the Floquet bands the pulse creates. The momentum and time parts of the metric evolve differently, and the pattern persists after the pulse passes. The pulse also generates a Berry curvature wave, entirely absent in static graphene. Part of the metric wave is a Fisher information wave carried by changing electron densities, measurable in pump-probe experiments.
arxiv-2606-12996:
Bean's doctoral thesis studies critical sets in Latin squares, the smallest partial fillings that determine a Latin square uniquely, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A critical set is a subset of a completed Latin square that extends back to that square in exactly 1 way, with no proper subset having that property. The concept, introduced by John Nelder in 1977, asks for formulas for the largest and smallest critical sets at each order.

The thesis gives bounds on the maximum number of intercalates, the smallest Latin subsquares, in Latin squares of even and odd orders. It also gives a lower bound on the largest critical set size for order 4m. A construction builds on the discovery of a critical set of size 17 in a Latin square of order 8. It verifies that critical sets of size n squared over 4, plus 1, exist for every even order n at least 6.
arxiv-2606-13496:
Lei and colleagues present BudCache in this 2026 arXiv paper, a method for speeding up diffusion models under a fixed budget. Caching reuses calculations across denoising steps, exploiting the redundancy between steps. Methods decide each step's caching by error thresholds, which leaves the runtime unpredictable and hard to control in deployment. BudCache inverts the formulation: the budget is fixed in advance, and the method searches for the caching policy that best preserves output quality within it. The space of step choices is huge.

To search it, the authors combine simulated annealing, an optimisation method, with deterministic hill climbing. The search finds policies within minutes and adds no overhead at inference time. When budgets are tight, a cache-aware schedule alignment step adapts the time discretisation to the policy, reducing the truncation errors caching introduces. The approach suits serving, where operators need guaranteed latency.
arxiv-2606-13596:
Dipendra Gupta and colleagues experimentally study how skew changes turbulent mixing layers in this 2026 arXiv paper. A mixing layer forms where two parallel streams of different speeds meet, a canonical problem in turbulence research. Real shear flows, however, are often three-dimensional: the incoming streams are skewed rather than parallel. The team develops and validates a method for generating skewed mixing layers in the lab. Turning vanes near the splitter plate's trailing edge deflect the mean flow sideways, and cross-wire anemometry measures the evolution.

Relative to the planar setup, the skewed layer shows steady reductions in mean flow and turbulence levels, with deviations reaching roughly forty percent. Despite those differences in size, the basic character of the mixing layer survives: it still grows and organises in familiar ways. The results matter for flows from combustors to ventilation, where assuming planar behaviour can overstate mixing by a wide margin.
arxiv-2606-13796:
Khelifa, Turner, and Venkataramanan ask where diffusion models end up when trained again and again on their own output. Diffusion models generate images by reversing a gradual noising process. Recursive training causes model collapse, a drift away from the true data pattern. Their 2026 arXiv paper proves what final pattern the recursion reaches, and how fast, even when learning is perfect.

The culprit is early stopping of the reverse process, a step needed for numerical stability. Each round shaves off fine detail, and the proofs show high-frequency content fades first, in a clear spectral pattern. Fresh real data mixed into each round slows the drift but cannot remove it. Tests on the CIFAR-10 image set track eight generations. With only ten percent fresh data, about half the high-frequency energy was gone by generation ten. With ninety percent fresh data, the loss stayed below fifteen percent.
arxiv-2606-13896:
Romero, Lv, and Karimzadeh test how well satellite-image foundation models transfer to new jobs. These geospatial models learn from unlabeled remote sensing data, then adapt to tasks like crop mapping or flood detection. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies six models from three training families: joint-embedding, reconstruction, and multimodal. Transfer was measured on classification, regression, and segmentation benchmarks under varied label budgets.

No ranking held everywhere: the best model changed with task and setup, though TerraMind usually sat near the top. Layer probing found task information often more accessible in middle transformer blocks than in the final layer. In segmentation studies on PASTIS and Sen1Floods11 data, decoder design and fine-tuning choices mattered as much as the model itself. Fine-tuning, they found, rewrites models unevenly. The strongest shifts localized to the first linear layer of the multilayer perceptron in each transformer block.
arxiv-2606-13996:
Ding, Hou, and Yin settle how long small waves survive around an obstacle before nonlinearity destroys them. The equation is a two-dimensional quadratic quasilinear wave equation in an exterior domain, outside a convex obstacle, with small initial data of size epsilon. In three dimensions the analogous lifespan is exponentially long. In two, the expected sharp lifespan, a constant over epsilon squared, was open. Their 2026 arXiv paper proves it, for Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions alike.

The lower bound uses a Friedlander radiation field adapted to the problem, a careful trial solution, and new space-time decay estimates. For radially symmetric solutions of a class of such equations, they derive the matching upper bound and determine the sharp constant explicitly, from the radiation field's profile along outgoing rays. Closing both sides pins the lifespan's exact order and, in the symmetric case, its precise prefactor.
arxiv-2606-14796:
Ehsani and co-authors review how AI coding assistants create technical debt in a 2026 arXiv paper. Technical debt is the future rework cost of quick, sloppy choices. Their multivocal review covers one hundred four sources. It mixes formal publications with grey literature like blogs and industry reports. It maps how language-model-assisted development generates debt and what countermeasures exist.

They find these tools amplify traditional code, design, and documentation debt. They also add new kinds. Fast-integration debt arises when rapidly generated code prizes speed over quality. It cascades into governance debt and rising maintenance costs. Prompt, ethical, data, and provenance debt are further emerging categories. Suggested strategies include human-in-the-loop frameworks and prompt engineering. Tools like SonarQube detect debt indicators. No standardized benchmarks or model-specific metrics exist yet.
arxiv-2606-14896:
Smith and co-authors compare spiral galaxies by arm count in Euclid telescope data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Using the Euclid Quick Data Release 1 catalog with arm counts from the Zoobot classifier, they contrast two-armed and three-armed spirals. Two-armed galaxies show larger light concentrations but lower stellar masses and star formation rates on average than three-armed ones.

At fixed stellar mass, two-armed galaxies remain more concentrated, extending trends known nearby out to redshifts between zero point four and one. Their lower star formation is explained by their lower masses, since rates match at fixed mass. A bend appears in the concentration-mass relation for two-armed galaxies above a characteristic mass, and their concentrations decline with redshift. About sixty to seventy percent of Euclid spirals are two-armed and fifteen to twenty percent three-armed, while one-armed spirals are rare and light.
arxiv-2606-14996:
Hemming and coauthors simulate how magnetic monopoles form and vanish in a grand unified model in a 2026 study. Grand unified theories predict monopoles in huge numbers, yet none have ever been observed. One proposed fix is monopole sweeping, where biased domain walls drag monopoles into annihilation. The authors test that idea directly in an SU(3) gauge theory with an adjoint scalar.

Simulations track symmetry breaking, monopole and wall formation, and the survivors as model parameters vary. The final monopole density depends critically on epsilon, a parameter controlling how abundant the biased walls are and how fast they decay. For small but nonzero epsilon, very few monopoles or walls survive in the runs. That regime could solve the monopole over-abundance problem without inflation doing all the work. The scenario also predicts a stochastic background of gravitational waves from the decaying walls. Magnetically charged black holes appear as another possible remnant.
arxiv-2606-15196:
Franklin and coauthors study highness notions for Scott rank in a 2026 mathematical logic paper. Scott rank measures how complex the description of a mathematical structure must be. Highness describes an oracle that is powerful for some task, here computing isomorphisms. The authors define highness for Scott rank and for its computably defined variant. They ask which degrees count as high at each rank level.

The paper characterizes both notions through the ability to compute definable sets. A degree is high for a rank when it can compute sets at levels of the definability hierarchy. The characterization pins highness to thresholds rather than vague strength. The authors analyze the index sets of structures having a Scott rank. Those index sets record how hard it is to recognize structures of each rank. A discussion treats highness for noncomputable Scott ranks. The work sharpens the boundary between structural and computational complexity.
arxiv-2606-15396:
Yu and coauthors build CHILLGuard in a 2026 paper, a safety guardrail tuned for Chinese language model content. Guardrails screen model outputs for harmful material, but existing ones follow Western norms and miss Chinese regulations, cultural context, and implicit phrasing. The team defines a fine-grained taxonomy of five broad and thirty-one narrow risk categories matched to Chinese rules. They then construct training data at scale, expanding sources with retrieval, rewriting prompts to create implicit harmful samples, and calibrating labels by multi-model voting.

The resulting sets hold four hundred five thousand training samples and a test set of fifty-two thousand. Training pairs a generator with a classifier under a preference optimization method adapted to the model itself. CHILLGuard beats the comparable guardrail by a wide margin on its benchmark F1 score. Fine-grained, locally grounded moderation like this is what deployment in a specific regulatory culture requires.
arxiv-2606-15596:
Konstantinides and Passalidis analyse a risk model in 2026 where insurance claims and investment returns interact over an infinite horizon. Claim vectors arrive by one counting process, and one stream of logarithmic returns discounts them, weakly dependent throughout. The counting process is an inhomogeneous renewal process, and the returns have independent but non-stationary increments, outside the classical setting.

Under a moment condition, they derive an asymptotic formula for the chance that discounted claims ever enter a rare set, for heavy-tailed claims. The formula embodies a multivariate single-big-jump principle: extreme outcomes come from one claim, not many moderate ones. Restricting claims to multivariate regular variation yields explicit formulas under weaker moment conditions. Since the classical Kesten-Goldie theorems fail here, the proof discretizes the process to get asymptotics uniform in the number of terms. Insurers can price the tail risk of claims and markets from the formulas.
arxiv-2606-15896:
Kordos and colleagues present LoComposition in 2026, a learning formulation for quadruped locomotion that separates concerns which standard reward engineering entangles. Rewards carry the task, constraints the operational limits, energy minimisation the gait preference, and perception the terrain adaptation. Explicit gait priors, targets for air time, contact counts, and foot clearance, are removed, in favour of whatever gait emerges.

Against a conventional complex-reward baseline, the formulation traverses terrain comparably while cutting cost of transport by fifty-six percent and operational-limit violations by ninety-six percent. Ablations show each component earning its place: removing one exposes a distinct failure mode, from inefficient bounding gaits to terrain-blind energy use. The learned policies transfer zero-shot to a Unitree Go2 robot using LiDAR-based elevation mapping. The broader claim is a design principle: organise locomotion learning around what a robot must reconcile, not the gait pattern it should copy.
arxiv-2606-15996:
Benkrane, Luciano, and Sheykhi examine the Sharma-Mittal entropy's implications for black holes and emergent gravity in 2026. The Sharma-Mittal entropy is a two-parameter generalisation containing both the Rényi and Tsallis entropies as cases. They check its gravity realisation against the Bekenstein bound, the universal entropy limit, and find it consistent, joining the Rényi and Bekenstein-Hawking entropies in the right limits.

Landauer's principle, the cost of erasing information, fed into black hole thermodynamics gives a modified mass-loss law for one-bit erasure, behaving differently for small and large masses. Inside Verlinde's entropic gravity framework, the entropy deforms the force law: the acceleration departs from Newton's at large distances. At one parameter ratio, the deformed law reproduces a MOND-like regime, tying the entropy parameters to MOND's acceleration scale. The framework links black hole heat, information bounds, and the infrared changes usually invoked for dark matter.
arxiv-2606-16096:
Fang and colleagues show single-shot mid-infrared spectral imaging in 2026, using the optics itself to sort colors. Mid-infrared light reveals chemical identity through molecular vibration fingerprints. Snapshot capture in this band has lagged, because sensitive detectors are scarce and encoding is weak. The team instead lets phase matching do the encoding during frequency upconversion.

Different colors leave at distinct angles inside a 4f imaging layout, so one exposure encodes the spectrum without added dispersive parts. Speckle light adds a second encoding layer, and the data are packed and rebuilt by computer. Upconversion to visible light enables room-temperature imaging with ordinary detectors. The system nears 1 photon per pixel per pulse across the range from 2.5 to 4.0 micrometers in the reported tests. Making encoding part of the imaging process itself could ease chemical camera design.
arxiv-2606-16196:
Chhetri and colleagues propose an interpretable test in 2026 for spotting medical images outside a model's training distribution. Neural networks excel at medical imaging but overgeneralize under distribution shift, a safety risk in clinics. Most detectors rely on opaque internal signals whose meaning is unclear. The authors instead probe whether a prediction rests on the right clinical concepts.

Sparse autoencoders first learn class-specific concept vectors from in-distribution data, splitting dense features into sparse, meaningful parts. At test time, the method perturbs deeper-layer features with the predicted class's concept vectors and watches output stability. In-distribution samples should barely move, since their features align with class concepts. Out-of-distribution samples prove far more sensitive in validation across endoscopy, histopathology, and eye imaging. Clinicians confirm the learned concepts match meaningful visual patterns, and such samples lack strong class-dominant concept activations.
arxiv-2606-16296:
Lai and Ota examine in 2026 how gravitational waves respond, at one-loop level, to a time-dependent resonant scalar field. The setting is flat Minkowski space, and the tool is the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, which tracks real-time evolution rather than scattering amplitudes. The authors build an adiabatic regularization scheme adapted to unequal-time correlation functions.

The leading divergence matches the familiar structure already known from simpler backgrounds. The moving background, however, induces extra local divergences tied to the wave's own derivatives and amplitude. These are absorbed by local counterterms: a Weyl-squared term, a time-dependent Ricci scalar term, and a time-dependent cosmological constant. Comparing with the tadpole stress tensor reveals a mismatch beyond leading order in this toy model. The authors argue the mismatch comes from holding the background fixed off shell, and should vanish once the background obeys its own equations.
arxiv-2606-16396:
Man and co-authors speed up image restoration in 2026 by swapping the denoiser inside plug-and-play methods for a spherical encoder. Restoration recovers a clean image from degraded measurements by balancing data fit against a prior over natural images. Plug-and-play schemes usually borrow that prior from a denoiser or a slow diffusion model. SP3 instead projects the working image onto the natural image manifold, using the tightly structured latent space of a spherical encoder.

Alternating that projection with a closed-form data-consistency step, under half-quadratic splitting, converges stably with no gradient computation at inference. Across restoration tasks, perceptual quality matches state-of-the-art zero-shot diffusion and flow methods while running 33 to 630 times faster, per the report. The trade-off is explicit: prioritizing perceptual realism weakens classical distortion scores, and the method cannot deliver minimum mean square error solutions.
arxiv-2606-16696:
Padmanabhan, Miyazawa and Horii introduce VENOM in a 2026 humanoid robotics paper. Teaching one robot body to copy human motion is hard, and teaching many different bodies with one model is harder. Most cross-body trackers split the problem, controlling the upper and lower body separately, which limits expressive whole-body motion.

VENOM is a GPT-based tracker, using the transformer sequence model best known from text, trained on motion data from several humanoids at once. It tracks the entire body jointly, with no split into upper and lower controllers. The team also built a shared dataset of states, actions and rewards for multi-humanoid tracking. In simulation, VENOM beats a plain supervised network trained on the same pooled data. It also nearly matches specialist reinforcement learning experts at tracking, despite receiving no reward feedback during its own training, while keeping the robot stable.
arxiv-2606-16796:
Luo and colleagues measure cosmic-ray ionization in two nearby star-forming clouds in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Cosmic rays ionize molecular gas, driving its chemistry and evolution, yet where the low-energy rays come from is unsettled. Recent work found high ionization rates near massive star-forming regions and young stars.

The team uses hydrogen narrow self-absorption, a dip in radio spectra that traces cold gas, toward IC 348 and NGC 1333. In both clouds the ionization rate falls as gas column density rises. The striking result is the gap between them: IC 348 shows rates about ten times higher than NGC 1333. Modeling the low-energy cosmic-ray spectrum, guided by gamma-ray data, reproduces both profiles. The contrast points to local acceleration sources beyond newborn stars, such as stellar-wind shocks, possibly the same sources behind a gamma-ray excess. Cloud structure shifts the values but cannot erase the disparity.
arxiv-2606-16996:
Tien and Shen speed up open-vocabulary image segmentation in a 2026 computer vision paper. A user can ask for any class by name. But running a big segmentation model at full resolution for every class in a vocabulary wastes enormous effort. Each image holds only a few classes.

Their framework, ActiveSAM, builds on the frozen Segment Anything Model 3 and needs no training. First it tidies and expands the class prompts. A cheap low-resolution preview then estimates which classes are actually present in the image, using presence scores only and skipping the heavy segmentation head. Just the surviving classes are decoded at full resolution, grouped through bucketed prompt multiplexing. A final calibration step suppresses low-confidence background pixels. Across eight benchmarks, ActiveSAM beats the strongest prior training-free system on accuracy while running several times faster on large-vocabulary sets. It also proves most robust when images are corrupted.
arxiv-2606-17096:
Yu, Wang and Liang derive how wall treatments shift high-speed boundary-layer instability in a 2026 fluids paper. Thin coatings and porous walls change transition to turbulence by admitting or absorbing pressure at the surface. Until now each treatment needed its own analysis.

The authors build one admittance formulation for trapped compressible Rayleigh modes. For a rigid-wall mode, they prove a sensitivity law: the complex wave speed shifts linearly with wall admittance, through an explicit coefficient from the rigid-wall eigenfunction. Its imaginary part gives a phase criterion telling whether a treatment stabilizes or destabilizes. Matched asymptotics show that viscous and thermal wall layers, blind-pore coatings and shallow roughness all collapse to the same boundary condition, admittances adding. Computations at Mach 4.5 confirm the coefficient and display the effects: porous walls damp, viscous walls damp, and reactive roughness can flip sign. One formula now prices very different wall physics.
arxiv-2606-17696:
Zhan presents a 2026 arXiv paper introducing FllumaOne, a data set of computer-aided design models stored as executable code rather than finished shapes alone. An editable CAD model carries its construction history: the sketches, features, and parameters that let an engineer change it later. FllumaOne generates each model from a Python program in a dedicated CAD system. It then aligns the program with a feature tree, the final geometry, surface points, plain-language notes, and standard renderings for each sample.

Programs survive only after the geometry kernel, solid checks, and export checks all pass, so the code truly rebuilds what it claims. The main release holds a hundred thousand samples across four bands of design complexity. A small code model fine-tuned on the data produced programs that almost always ran and exported cleanly. The set targets reconstruction, program synthesis, and editable reverse engineering.
arxiv-2606-17796:
Anju and Romeo write a 2026 algebra paper on finite rank operators acting on a Hilbert space, using the cross-connection method from semigroup theory. That method, started by Hall and Grillet, rebuilds a semigroup from linked families of its ideals. Here the authors apply it to the normal category of finite-dimensional subspaces of a space and its dual.

They describe the cross-connection semigroup in detail and show it forms a normed algebra matching the algebra of finite rank bounded operators. Compact operators and their spectra are then characterized through normal cones in the subspace category. A closing theorem shows that closing this algebra yields the full Banach algebra of compact operators, tying an abstract construction to a central object in functional analysis.
arxiv-2606-18496:
Reynolds introduces Neural Phase Correlation, a learning-based method for finding the correspondence between two images, in a 2026 computer vision paper. Correspondence is about the transformation linking two observations rather than their content, yet most learned methods encode each image alone and let similarity scores or decoders infer the mapping.

Classical phase correlation is the exception, measuring the link directly in the frequency domain, but its fixed Fourier basis confines it to simple global shifts. Reynolds extends it by learning the basis on which the transformation decomposes, keeping the relational structure while allowing dense, non-rigid deformations and even unitary dynamics. On a cardiac MRI benchmark the method matched or beat baselines in both registration directions, and on echocardiography data it matched leading results without scoring machinery. Applied to pairs of evolved quantum wavefunctions, the same framework recovered the unknown oscillator's energy levels from data alone.
arxiv-2606-18796:
Xu proves enough conditions for a class of spaces central to domain theory to be well-filtered, in a 2026 general topology paper. Well-filteredness is a compactness-like trait of non-Hausdorff T0 spaces. It underlies much of domain theory. People have sought workable criteria that ensure it.

Xu gives property Q: two conditions on the poset of a space's nonempty compact saturated sets, ordered by reverse inclusion. Infima of such sets must exist. And a directed-supremum separation condition must hold. The main theorem shows every d-space with property Q is well-filtered. The Smyth power space construction, which builds a space whose points are the compact saturated sets, always has property Q. So it preserves well-filteredness. As a use, for a complete lattice carrying an order-compatible d-topology, a distributivity condition on the lattice makes the space well-filtered.
arxiv-2606-18896:
Iubini and colleagues present a 2026 physics paper on heat and particle flow in photonic diamond lattices threaded by a synthetic magnetic flux. The lattice can enter Aharonov-Bohm caging, where interference flattens every energy band and traps light in place. Adding Kerr nonlinearity, which makes the material response depend on light intensity, changes how the trapped light then moves and carries energy.

The authors map the equilibrium phase diagram and then attach hotter and colder reservoirs to the two ends. At weak nonlinearity, tuning the flux to the caging point switches the lattice from a conductor to an insulator.
