At stronger nonlinearity the system keeps conducting, but caging sharply raises the Seebeck coefficient and the thermoelectric figure of merit. The result suggests a practical route to better coupled transport devices by balancing linear and nonlinear channels with flux alone.
arxiv-2606-18996:
Moon and colleagues build the TRAP benchmark in 2026 for a hard clash in agent design. An agent that books travel may need passport data to finish a task. Yet it must never show that private data in its replies. Each test case pairs a private file with a task that needs its data, plus an attack prompt that tries to pull the same data out.

Tests cover more than twenty models, both closed and open, at many sizes. Every family leaks some private data. Stronger skill at following instructions tracks with more leakage, a troubling link. Prompt defenses cut leaks but hurt task success a lot. The authors prove no soft prompt rule can give both high success and zero leaks for this model class. Their fix swaps private fields for hash keys before the model sees them, which blocks most leaks at little cost.
arxiv-2606-19496:
Nathaniel Diamant and Brian Trippe introduce kernel Calibrating Generative Models in 2026, a fix for generators that drift off target. A model may craft plausible molecules whose key features still miss a target class, such as known antibiotics. Plain fine-tuning on the small target set can overfit and gives no control over which features match.

Their method, kCGM, minimises maximum mean discrepancy, a kernel-based gap between generated and target feature spreads. An unbiased score-function estimator drives the updates, while a KL penalty keeps output near the pretrained model. On a target set of 174 antibiotics, plain fine-tuning trades chemical validity for feature match. kCGM instead improves the match and raises validity at the same time. Trials on protein and DNA tasks show the same recipe adapts autoregressive and diffusion models from feature-level guidance alone.
arxiv-2606-19696:
Rong Chen, Kang-Yu Wang, and Yi-Ning Wang prove identities linking two counting families in partition theory in 2026. A Frobenius partition arranges a number into two rows with set length rules. Coloured versions tag entries with colours, adding counting richness.

The studied function counts two-coloured Frobenius partitions of weight n with fixed row length gap. Two cases take focus: gap zero and gap one. Minimal excludants, the smallest missing values, supply the bridge statistic on bipartitions. One sum totals Lin-Liu bipartition minimal excludants over all bipartitions of n. A second count tallies bipartitions whose two component excludants agree. Combinatorial proofs show the gap-zero count equals twice the excludant sum. The gap-one count equals twice that sum minus the equal-excludant tally. Abstract partition functions thus gain direct counting meanings.
arxiv-2606-19896:
Lennart Bosch and Martin Plenio study where to sample a signal for the sharpest parameter estimates in 2026. Nonlinear model fitting infers unknown parameters from measured data. Sample placement can matter as much as sample count for final precision.

Strong-signal regions look informative, since weak regions bury the signal in white noise. Correlations between samples, though, can make the best layout highly non-trivial. Experimental design optimisation names the systematic hunt for such layouts. Bayesian sampling schemes judge candidate points by expected information gain. Adaptive versions update the design as data arrive and beliefs sharpen. The pair develop optimal and adaptive Bayesian sampling for this setting. Better designs promise the same precision from fewer, better-placed measurements. Metrology and sensing problems with costly samples stand to gain most.
arxiv-2606-20096:
Yossi Bokor Bleile, Emanuele Cortinovis, Herbert Edelsbrunner, and Shota Uka borrow tools from quadratic forms to measure tree-like structures that grow in three-dimensional space. Their 2026 paper treats such structures as geometric graphs, shapes made of points and connecting segments. Such trees appear across science, from neuron dendrites to river networks, and their directional spread carries clues about the processes that formed them.

The authors define measures from quadratic forms and build a visualization tool they call the hexplot model. Its distances come from the Fisher metric on the standard triangle, a geometry that respects how directional data naturally behaves. With the model, researchers can plot a tree's spread, take measurements, and gather statistics across many specimens. Path decomposition breaks a tree into its routes, so comparisons stay tied to real structure, giving biologists and geometers a shared language for branching form.
arxiv-2606-20196:
Hyun-Kurl Jang, Jihun Kim, Hyeokjun Kweon, and Kuk-Jin Yoon keep deployed vision models adapting for life without keeping the original training data. Their 2026 paper addresses continual test-time adaptation, where a model adjusts online as conditions drift, with no labels. Privacy and licensing often bar retaining source data, and source-free methods wobble as self-training errors compound into forgetting. Their framework, DO-ALL, distills the source data once into a small set of synthetic anchors.

During adaptation, each incoming sample is matched to its closest anchor in meaning. That anchor steadies learning through source replay, representation alignment, and manifold smoothing. DO-ALL plugs into existing algorithms rather than replacing them. Across CIFAR100-C, ImageNet-C, and the CCC benchmark, it consistently improved long-term robustness, suggesting a compact distilled summary can carry the source data's stabilizing value without its legal burden.
arxiv-2606-20396:
Jaime Moreno and six colleagues show that tiny, hidden measurement errors can fake high-dimensional entanglement. Their 2026 paper targets the assumption behind entanglement verification: that lab measurements match their theoretical settings exactly. As systems grow more complex, that assumption gets harder to guarantee.

Deviations deliberately hidden in the apparatus and small enough to escape notice make separable states pass entanglement tests as if they were highly entangled. The false certification works even though the underlying system shares no entanglement at all. Verification schemes that ignore such error can therefore be gamed by the apparatus itself. The result sets a caution for certifying quantum devices: measurement precision is part of the security claim.
arxiv-2606-20496:
Thilina Ratnayaka, Paul Fischer, and Luke Olson replace the coarsest level of a multigrid preconditioner for exascale Poisson problems. Their 2026 paper targets the pressure Poisson equation from spectral and finite element discretizations of incompressible Navier-Stokes flow. Algebraic multigrid usually handles that last level, but it can bottleneck at extreme scale.

Their two-level Schwarz method splits the coarse solve into a local problem in the original coarse space and a global coarse problem. A novel structured, nonnested coarse space for the global problem enables communication-free interpolation between the two levels. Avoiding communication at the coarsest level attacks exactly where exascale solvers stall. The authors demonstrate the method's effectiveness on the target problems.
arxiv-2606-20896:
Derek Wu and Catherine Yan give new approaches in 2026 to identities for vacillating tableaux, objects that grow and shrink in steps. A key identity counts such tableaux. It was first obtained through the theory of partition algebras. Their work extends the identity to arbitrary differential posets. A poset is an ordered set with special up and down moves.

They show the identity, and several analogues, follow directly from the structure of such posets. No heavy algebra is needed. Specializing to Young's lattice and its powers gives more results. New proofs by pairing come from a simple delete and insert process. A proof by pairing explains an identity by matching objects, not only by algebra. Cleaner proofs can open a topic to broader use, because the counting mechanism becomes visible and portable to new settings.
arxiv-2606-21096:
Heechan Moon and Kijung Shin propose SLeDGe in 2026, a semi-supervised learning method for data streams that learns its graph structure as data evolve. Streaming data change continuously and labels are scarce. Older methods rely on fixed similarity measures or static graphs. Relationships among samples then cannot evolve. Their method jointly learns a predictive model and an adaptive graph under strict memory and label limits.

Separate memories store labeled and unlabeled samples with distinct update rules. Adaptation to new features is balanced with retention of history. Sparsity in the graph filters spurious connections. Label supervision then propagates along trusted links. Tests across twelve datasets beat prior methods. Gains are large when labels are extremely scarce. Streaming settings such as fraud and sensor monitoring need exactly this: learning that keeps up with drift without demanding constant human labeling.
arxiv-2606-21396:
Zhaoxuan Yan and four colleagues address a core obstacle to surgical robot automation in 2026: the robots' own joint readings are unreliable, so their true positions drift from what controllers believe. Model-based calibration is costly and only partly effective. Their alternative trains a visuomotor policy in simulation that fuses the faulty internal readings with precise external camera vision, correcting position errors in real time.

A teacher-student setup guides the learning, and the trained policy transferred to a physical da Vinci Research Kit. Experiments there validated the basic idea: outside vision can compensate for internal sensor deficits without a perfect physical model. The policy also generalized across camera viewpoints and workspace moves. The work lays groundwork for more robust automation of surgical subtasks.
arxiv-2606-21996:
Ferrara audits online hate in multicultural Singapore in 2026, asking whether its structure is shared across the city's overlapping language communities. English, Chinese, and Malay publics discuss the same out-groups in parallel, making Singapore a test case. His corpus held thirty-one million items from Facebook, Reddit, and YouTube, including 1.76 million comments mentioning eleven identity groups.

Eight open language models were benchmarked as hate annotators against a human-adjudicated gold set, and the best reached accuracy of 0.95. The findings support layered cultural contingency: which groups get targeted varies strongly by language, while threat frames and moral grammar are far more shared. Binding moral values such as sanctity and loyalty carried most hate, not fairness concerns. Hateful comments were amplified less than neutral mentions overall, except anti-immigrant hate, which spread preferentially. Ferrara also cautions that absolute hate prevalence is ill-defined when annotator models disagree.
arxiv-2606-22296:
Hu and colleagues present SCENIC in 2026, a framework for generating structured smart-home commands on edge devices, where memory, privacy, latency, and inference cost rule out cloud language models. The task is many-to-one: many phrasings of an instruction must map to one canonical command string that a deterministic parser accepts. The framework covers architecture selection, training data generation, contrastive fine-tuning, pruning, quantization, and export.

The team evaluates transformer backbones under two hundred million parameters, among the smallest studied for this task. The strongest dense decoder-only model reaches 99.0 percent exact match at rank one, while the encoder-decoder retains stronger behaviour at high sparsity. One pruned INT8 encoder-decoder export keeps 91.0 percent exact match while shrinking the exported model by about a quarter. TensorRT profiling adds up to a 1.8-fold speedup of the encoder component.
arxiv-2606-22496:
Aygün Varol and seven colleagues, including Johanna Virkki, study how to run language models on small local devices in this 2026 paper. Their task is reading IoT sensor data, such as air quality and thermal comfort, in smart buildings. Cloud models answer well but raise latency, privacy, and connectivity concerns, while compact local models reason poorly over raw numbers.

The team test whether preprocessing the prompt fixes that weakness. Raw readings were rewritten three ways: as plain values, as threshold-aware descriptions, and as compact summary flags. Data came from indoor Raspberry Pi nodes in Tampere and outdoor air-quality sets from Helsinki, Katowice, and Warsaw. Five local and five cloud models were compared. Enrichment lifted local accuracy sharply, from about fifty-one to eighty-two percent indoors and sixty-four to eighty-nine percent outdoors. Local inference was also the fastest setup tested.
arxiv-2606-22696:
Xiao Shi and four colleagues compress image reconstruction into a single step in this 2026 paper. Reconstructing an image from partial measurements, such as filling in missing regions, is usually done by diffusion or flow models that need hundreds of network evaluations per image. Their method, NullFlow, aims to need exactly one.

The idea is to confine the generative flow to a subspace of images consistent with the measurements. Because the flow never leaves that subspace, no separate data-fidelity corrections are needed. NullFlow samples in one network evaluation by learning the flow's average velocity rather than integrating step by step. The authors prove that this average velocity yields a training objective whose global minimizer is a one-step posterior sampler. On image inpainting, NullFlow matched state-of-the-art diffusion solvers in quality. It cut inference from hundreds of network evaluations to one.
arxiv-2606-22896:
Junhan Huang and colleagues create and steer a light-induced ferroelectric state in this 2026 paper. A ferroelectric material carries a permanent electric polarization that can be flipped. Such light-induced states had only been seen in materials already near the transition, where fluctuations blur the state and block clean control.

The team used intense terahertz pulses to excite a soft phonon mode in lead telluride, a thermoelectric material with no such transition of its own and a centrosymmetric crystal structure. The pulses drove the crystal into a polarized state that persisted up to about 100 kelvin. Experiment and theory together traced the effect to anharmonic coupling, a nonlinear interaction, between two matching lattice vibration modes. A double-pulse protocol then amplified or suppressed the induced polarization on demand. The work shows coherent control of a state that light itself created.
arxiv-2606-23096:
Raghav Bongole and colleagues build a quantile-based theory of worst-case decision making under privacy in a 2026 paper. Interactive statistical decision making covers settings like bandit problems, where each choice reveals new data. Classic minimax theory judges methods by expected loss. Averages hide rare but costly failures, which matter in medicine, finance, and control. The authors develop a theory of minimax quantiles that makes the confidence level explicit. They also fold privacy limits into the same framework by restricting which decision rules are allowed.

Bongole and colleagues relate minimax quantiles to ordinary minimax risk, including a conversion between the two. They prove high-probability versions of the classic Fano and Le Cam lower bound methods for interactive problems. For coordinatewise Gaussian privacy noise, a two-point template isolates how privacy inflates variance. Applications cover Gaussian mean estimation and multi-armed bandits.
arxiv-2606-23196:
Elroy Stav and colleagues ask when asking a language model to correct itself actually helps in a 2026 paper. Intrinsic self-correction prompts a model to revisit its first answer with no outside feedback. Recent studies doubt the practice, since models often cannot tell whether their first answer was right. The authors take a task-sensitive view instead of a universal verdict. They separate three ways revision could work: checking explicit constraints, reworking a complex reasoning chain, or giving a second opinion among rival strategies in word games.

Stav and colleagues test these settings across several benchmarks and models. Self-correction gave consistent gains when the task structure supported one of those revision modes. Where the structure offered no such handle, gains faded. The results recast self-correction as a task-dependent inference-time strategy, not a uniformly reliable improver.
arxiv-2606-23396:
Tim Berberich and colleagues image viruses sprayed as a mist, using an X-ray free-electron laser, in a 2026 paper. Such a laser flashes a single tiny particle and records how it scatters light before the flash destroys it. This lets scientists study targets that never form crystals, in states close to life. The team works with a bacteriophage called PR772, sprayed into the beam as a fine mist. They first boil each pattern down to rotational invariants, numbers comparable across runs and across the particles' random poses.

Berberich and colleagues can then sort the particles and see how each one differs. The results show clear traits even at modest sharpness. The capsid, the protein shell of the virus, is not a perfect icosahedron. It bends in an uneven way. The material packed inside varies in density. One corner of the shell carries a small extension.
arxiv-2606-23496:
Matan Ben-Tov and Mahmood Sharif present TROPT, an open framework for discrete text optimization, in a 2026 paper. This field searches for token sequences that steer a model toward a chosen objective. It underpins red-teaming tasks like jailbreaks, plus auditing and model probing. The tooling is fragmented, though. Optimizers live in scattered codebases tied to specific models and domains, and variants multiply, each costly to set up or compare. TROPT runs them all under one interface and one shared way of building new optimizers.

Ben-Tov and Sharif ship the framework with over thirty ready recipes. They span tasks from jailbreaking to probing model internals, built from more than fifteen optimizers and fifteen loss functions. Models, objectives, and optimizers swap freely to build custom recipes. Case studies include large controlled comparisons of jailbreak strategies, which surfaced potent but underadopted techniques.
arxiv-2606-23596:
Shin tests asset pricing factor models by splitting the market itself into a body and a tail, in a 2026 finance paper. Factor models explain stock returns with a few common drivers, such as market exposure and firm size. In an ideal pricing model, two virtues coincide: zero pricing errors, called alphas, and the highest possible Sharpe ratio, a reward per unit risk measure. In practice the two can come apart, and strong models can hide offsetting errors inside the aggregate return.

Shin decomposes an investible CRSP market index by firm size ranking. The body leg holds the largest share of market value, the tail leg holds the rest, and together they rebuild the market return. At daily frequency every model passes the aggregate test. Yet one leading model, q5, leaves offsetting leg alphas at all nine split points. Random splits erase the pattern, and monthly data softens it.
arxiv-2606-23896:
Mönch identifies where a random walk on one of group theory's favorite test objects ends up in the long run, in a 2026 paper on probability and groups. Thompson's group F, built from piecewise linear rearrangements of the interval, is concrete yet rich enough to resist easy answers. Projecting it onto the orbit of one half gives a walk on the dyadic Schreier graph, a binary tree skeleton with rays attached. Mönch determines its Poisson boundary, the space of possible asymptotic behaviors.

The full boundary is the skeleton's end boundary, the infinite directions down the tree. The proof reduces it to a nearest neighbor walk on the binary tree with two conductance classes. Standard theory for transient tree walks applies, leaving a finite electrical network calculation. The hitting measure turns out to be a product of biased Bernoulli factors over odd two adic integers, with exact constants computed.
arxiv-2606-24196:
Zhou and colleagues teach image and video generators to tailor content for users who cannot describe what they want. Modern pipelines assume a well-formed instruction. Real users rarely articulate visual detail, so output drifts from their taste. Their 2026 system, NaviGen, builds a usable instruction for the next generator out of what the user has done before.

Each item gets a dual identifier. It pairs a collaborative code, capturing how users behave toward the item, with a textual code carrying its semantics. Behaviour thus becomes legible to language reasoning in one token stream. Training runs in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning distils preference reasoning and instruction writing from searched examples. Reinforcement learning then aligns output with user intent, through ranked, self-consistent rewards. Across product, game, and short-video domains, NaviGen improves tailored generation and next-item prediction. Its instructions grow more specific and relevant.
arxiv-2606-24596:
Marcuzzi, Ning, Schwartz, and Gurevych show that how you ask a language model about social groups changes the bias you find. Evaluating social bias in deployed models is urgent, but the literature is fragmented in method and conclusions clash, largely because benchmark framing is ignored. Their 2026 framework puts mixed benchmarks into one controllable format. Isolated group assessments, judging one group alone, are contrasted with forced choice comparative settings.

Across model families, a massive gap opens. Isolated assessments limit prejudice activation. Such settings act as strong catalysts for latent discrimination. Vague contexts drive this primarily. Chain of thought reasoning, usually a remedy, worsens bias under this framing. The prejudice persists every time, even when models receive neutral fallback options, or claim to answer randomly. Marcuzzi's team concludes the measurement instrument is part of the phenomenon. Bias audits that ignore framing are measuring their own design as much as the model.
arxiv-2606-25196:
Photonic processors route light through reconfigurable multimode interferometers to compute with photons, in quantum and classical settings alike. Gökhan Elmas and three colleagues tackle a practical obstacle. The phase of the light drifts, pushed around by active cooling systems and temperature changes, and stable outputs are hard to hold.

The team builds theoretical models of the instability and checks them against measurements. One model treats the phase as a Brownian random walk. The other reconstructs it from oscillating harmonics actually observed in the device. With the models validated, the authors put one to work inside the processor itself, correcting the input phase through self feedback control. The study gives processor builders a tested way to predict phase drift and a route to cancelling it in operation.
arxiv-2606-25896:
Gitika Rameshan and colleagues present two years of observations of SN 2019vxm, an interacting supernova of Type IIn, where the blast wave slams into dense gas the star shed earlier. Telescopes in India and Japan, plus survey and space instruments, tracked its light and spectra from shortly after explosion onward. Few supernovae of this kind have been followed so long and so closely.

Brightness rose slowly, taking about forty-six days to peak at a luminosity that ranks among the most energetic of its class. Modelling of the light curve puts the surrounding gas at roughly three to eight times the mass of the Sun, with at least a similar amount of ejected material. Late spectra show dust forming near fifteen hundred kelvin, strong line asymmetries, and no nebular lines at all, which points to ejecta still hidden behind dense material.
arxiv-2606-26096:
Niclas Heinsdorf and Ken Shiozaki compute a higher form of Berry curvature for a four-dimensional Chern insulator. Berry curvature measures how a quantum state twists as its parameters vary. The second Chern number sums that twist into a whole-number invariant. Their lattice model gets rewritten as a family of endless chains over the three-dimensional Brillouin zone. Infinite matrix product states then carry the computation of the three-form curvature.

Phase diagrams supply the check. The diagram from the Dixmier-Douady-Kapustin-Spodyneiko number matches the second Chern number diagram exactly. That side was already known analytically. Agreement proves higher Berry curvature can yield second Chern numbers reliably. Magnetoelectric coupling is the follow-on topic. The second Chern form ties to the Chern-Simons axion coupling. The pair study how that link plays out in three dimensions, connecting higher Berry phases to a measurable material response.
arxiv-2606-26196:
Haoxiang Sun, Tao Wang, Li Yuan, Jian Zhao, and Jiancheng Lv survey how multimodal large language models perceive the world. Such models fuse vision and language, and recent releases pushed them toward perception-centred intelligence. Older reviews treat sight and language apart. A unified view, where the two form one inseparable sense, has been missing. Their survey claims that gap as its territory.

Perception gets a formal definition first: one built-in vision-language capacity, much like innate human perception. A five-stage taxonomy then traces how that capacity evolved across model generations. Representative methods and milestones fill each stage. Open challenges close the survey, with research directions toward general unified multimodal intelligence. The authors aim to give the field both a foundation and a roadmap. The venue is a journal devoted to information fusion, fitting for a study of merged senses.
arxiv-2606-26296:
Hilding Neilson rewrites the Drake Equation through Indigenous knowledge systems. The famous equation multiplies the ingredients for technological civilizations in our galaxy. Most of its factors remain unknown, and Neilson argues the usual discussion bakes in Western scientific biases. Those biases steer today's searches for biological and technological signatures. Indigenous methods, built on relational knowledge and deep time scales, frame the same question differently.

Viewed through that lens, the galaxy's life story changes shape. What counts as intelligence, communication, and a civilization's lifetime all shift. The essay reviews the equation's history alongside the assumptions SETI inherited. A dramatically different picture of life in the Milky Way follows from the Indigenous framing. The piece appears in a volume on Indigenous astronomy in the space age. Its aim is not to solve the equation but to widen who gets to define its terms.
arxiv-2606-26396:
Praneet Suresh and colleagues use sparse autoencoders, tools that unpack a transformer's internal activity into readable concepts, to map where the model's understanding breaks down. Inputs unlike the training data, from typos to jailbreak prompts, are the test cases.

Such out-of-distribution inputs push the model to activate a larger number of spurious concepts internally. That signal becomes a meter for how far an input has drifted, measured at inference time inside the model's own computation. The team turns it into a fine-tuning strategy that improves robustness, aiming at safer deployment in science, business, and government.
arxiv-2606-26796:
Chi-Zhuo Wang and four colleagues validate a shortcut for measuring the sizes of gas clouds around black holes. Reverberation mapping times how long light takes to cross the broad-line region, the fast-moving gas near an active galaxy's centre. The spectroscopic version is slow and costly. Their ICCF-Cut method extracts the hydrogen-alpha line's behaviour from cheap broadband photos instead.

The team monitored two nearby Seyfert galaxies for several seasons with one telescope. Photo-based and spectrum-based measurements ran at the same time. The extracted light curves closely matched the spectroscopic ones. Time lags agreed within errors in most seasons. Where photo lags came out slightly short, leftover helium contamination in the extracted signal was the likely cause. Correcting for it improved the match.
arxiv-2606-26896:
Alexei V. Nikitin and Ruslan L. Davidchack design collision-resistant radio signalling for low-power wide-area networks. Such networks serve sensors that sip energy and talk rarely. Their modulation scheme, M-ASPM, spreads each symbol's energy to gain sensitivity. Unlike rival schemes, raising its processing gain does not raise packet collision rates. Short packet heads form a separate detection channel.

That head detects packets and synchronises the receiver even when packets overlap. It also measures each packet's frequency offset precisely. Payload data is then extracted without widening the listening window per symbol. Sensitivity rises while network throughput survives under collision-limited conditions. The authors further build a multi-channel layout. Many near-orthogonal channels share the single detection channel, multiplying capacity without new detection hardware.
arxiv-2606-26996:
Michael De Becker of the University of Liège explains how astronomers win access to observation facilities. Telescope time is allocated internationally through fierce competition. Hundreds of proposals chase each call from major agencies. Junior researchers often learn the craft only by failing first. This guide lays out the whole framework for ground-based and space observatories.

Proposal preparation is the heart of the guide. Some rules are mandatory; others are hard-won advice. Common pitfalls and procedural missteps are catalogued so proposers can dodge them. The goal is to cut rejections caused by preventable factors rather than weak science. De Becker writes for any potential user of shared facilities, not only insiders of particular observatories.
arxiv-2606-27396:
Sarkar measures which test-input choices actually catch bugs in tensor programs, rather than trusting folklore. GPU kernel projects typically test one representative shape and data type, then ship. Seven generation strategies are compared on a corpus of twenty-six operations: sixteen correct controls and ten buggy variants seeded with documented error patterns. Shape sets, data-type mixes, and value distributions vary across strategies. A schema-aware seeded fuzzer on a consumer graphics card runs the experiments, in a software testing study published in 2026.

Boundary-only shape sampling wins on safety: it catches most seeded bugs while raising zero false alarms on the correct controls. Aggressive value sampling catches nearly everything but floods the controls with false positives, because injected not-a-number values trip validators on healthy kernels too. For two bugs in softmax tail masks, the regular strategy catches nothing, while boundary shapes catch most or all.
arxiv-2606-27496:
Daniel Fox and Vladimir Tkachev introduce a family of commutative algebras. In these systems, multiplication gives the same result in either order. One short identity defines the family, whose members are called (2,3)-palintropic algebras. It links a cubed element squared with a squared element cubed. Known cases such as Jordan and medial algebras sit inside the family.

Interest comes from the Peirce polynomial of these algebras. That tool normally limits how multiplication can act near an idempotent. An idempotent is an element that stays the same when multiplied by itself. Here the polynomial vanishes, so it gives no limits for free. Fox and Tkachev still prove strong results. Each idempotent admits clear fusion rules for its Peirce spaces. They also prove one more fact. Multiplying by such an idempotent always gives an algebra homomorphism, a map that preserves the operations. Examples and uses in polynomial maps close the paper.
arxiv-2606-27896:
Altermagnets split electron spins by momentum. They do so without any net magnetisation. Strain offers a direct handle on that splitting. ShuaiYu Wang and three colleagues build a strain-resolved symmetry framework in 2026. It covers two-dimensional pentagonal altermagnets. Uniaxial and shear strains are classified by their effect. Each strain either preserves, rebuilds, or destroys the spin–momentum locking. That locking links a spin's direction to its motion.

First-principles screening applies the rule at scale. From 3330 candidate materials, ninety-four stable ones emerge. They sort into the three response types. Representative compounds illustrate each class. Ferroelastic cobalt disulphide switches its locking under strain. It also reverses a spin conductivity component. Shear-strained cobalt diphosphide rebuilds its locking. The form changes from g-wave to d-wave shape. Uniaxially strained FeSSe shows strain-selected spin-valley transport. The work gives guidance for strain-controlled spin transport devices.
arxiv-2606-27996:
Threshold private set intersection reveals an intersection only when it is large enough. Zixian Gong and three colleagues propose a quantum multiparty version in 2026 with explicit cardinality testing. Existing quantum protocols let a third party interpret the final results. That breaks the threshold paradigm, since the size itself leaks. Their design is rotation-based. Single-photon sequences pass through rotations applied by each party, plus masking and correlated aggregate rotations.

The outcome is a set of hidden-label measurement vectors. The third party can measure but cannot interpret the outcomes. The threshold decision runs through an oblivious linear evaluation inner product and a small garbled circuit. Only the yes-or-no answer on the threshold is revealed. The intersection itself is rebuilt only afterwards. Correctness and security are proved. Quantum-circuit simulations on the IBM Qiskit platform show it works.
arxiv-2606-28196:
Ha Thang Long Doan, Hikaru Arita, Kazuto Nakashima, and Kenji Tahara work on robotic hands that can shift an object within the grasp, turning or sliding it without putting it down. Controllers built by hand rely on strong simplifying guesses, while pure trial-and-error learning wastes effort on unstable motions.

Doan and colleagues split the skill into simpler parts, each learned with guardrails drawn from classical physics and control theory, and they restrict the learner to actions that cannot drop the object. Learning then became fast and steady across different objects. The resulting skills coped with sensor and motor noise, with delays in the control loop, and with varying friction between fingers and object.
arxiv-2606-28296:
H. Veermäe, writing alone, revisits the curvaton, a field proposed to have generated the universe's primordial ripples after inflation. The standard treatment gives the curvaton a simple quadratic potential and mild statistics. Veermäe asks what changes when the field interacts with itself.

Self-interactions make the moment oscillations begin depend on the field's own value, and they alter the pressure balance once the ringing settles. Using a compact tool called the abbreviated action, Veermäe derives the full non-Gaussian map for quadratic, monomial, quartic, and cosine potentials. These effects can amplify or damp the non-Gaussianity depending on the case. Strong positive non-Gaussianity, he shows, can seed supermassive black holes at amplitudes small enough to respect satellite bounds, offering an origin story from the early universe for puzzling early galaxies.
arxiv-2606-28396:
Emily Bejerano, Federico Tondolo, Devang Gupta, Aaron Mano Cherian, Taeyoo Kim, Ayaan Qayyum, Xiaofan Yu, and Xiaofan Jiang generate radar training data before any radar visits a new room. Millimeter-wave radar sees through smoke and darkness, but models trained on existing datasets fail in new spaces, and collecting fresh labeled data everywhere is impractical.

Bejerano's team built RadarTwin, which starts from a three-dimensional scan of the target space and infers surface materials with a vision-language model. It then synthesizes raw radar signals with a physics-based ray tracer that follows multi-bounce paths. Paired real and simulated data showed both share the features that distinguish objects, and modeling multipath proved essential. A representation trained only in simulation recognized real objects well above chance, and a few labeled examples pushed accuracy near ninety-five percent.
arxiv-2606-28496:
Trina Basu and Richard Ruiz compute how polarized bosons interfere in proton collisions that produce a vector boson plus jets. Polarization interference between a boson's transverse and longitudinal states can distort measurements, and whether it survives averaging over the decay products was known only for the fully summed process.

Using new methods for helicity amplitudes with polarized intermediate bosons, Basu and Ruiz work order by order in the strong coupling while staying exclusive about the jets. For a virtual photon decaying to massless leptons, the interference vanishes after integrating over the lepton kinematics. That widens the classic result. Parity violation softens the cancellation for W and Z bosons. They give a simple formula handling fiducial cuts, and discuss consequences for multiboson production, imagined chiral bosons, and polarization checks in heavy-ion collisions.
arxiv-2606-28996:
Pathak, Kumar, Ricks, Gururaja and Srivastava build a fast stand-in model for short-fiber thermoplastics, light plastic parts reinforced with short fibers, used in aerospace and car structures. Their mechanical response depends on messy inner detail: fiber direction, clustering and pores left by manufacturing. Detailed finite element models can resolve that detail, but a realistic part with thousands of fibers is far too costly to simulate directly.

The team rebuilt three-dimensional microstructures from high-resolution CT scans and split them into small Voronoi cells, each a distinct fiber neighbourhood. Nonlinear simulations of each cell, including matrix damage, produced stress-strain data for training. A hybrid graph neural network with a memory layer then learned both the structure's layout and its history-dependent response. The trained model predicted stiffness and stress-strain behaviour of unseen structures with accuracy near 0.98 against full simulations, at over a hundred times less cost.
arxiv-2606-29496:
Park and colleagues present RefineSplat, a framework that cleans distractors out of 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions. Real scenes contain transient elements, such as passing people or moving objects, that should not appear in the final model. Existing methods struggle when distractors share colours or meanings with the static scene, so simple masks misfire.

RefineSplat builds transient masks using entropy, a measure of uncertainty, combined with instance masks that outline individual objects. An entropy-aware density control step then aligns the Gaussians, the soft blobs forming the scene, in ambiguous areas by using entropy-aware positional gradients. To test such cases rigorously, the team created the Ambiguous wild dataset. It holds eighteen scenes where distractors and static content are hard to tell apart. Experiments across datasets show state-of-the-art performance, producing distractor-free novel view synthesis, meaning clean renderings from new camera angles.
arxiv-2606-29896:
Gashti, Pourhassan, and Sakallı derive the Weak Gravity Conjecture from the boundary side of the AdS/CFT correspondence. The conjecture claims that any consistent quantum gravity theory needs some charged particle with a charge-to-mass ratio beating an extremal black hole's.

Two settings beyond the standard idealisation are treated: black holes in dRGT massive gravity, and dyonic ones in Einstein-ModMax nonlinear electrodynamics. For the massive gravity case every theory parameter cancels, leaving a universal bound of one over root two, about 0.707. For the ModMax case the nonlinearity parameter survives in the bound and weakens it as nonlinearity grows, reducing to the classic bound of one in the Maxwell limit. Relaxing assumptions such as exact extremality breaks the cancellation in controlled ways.
arxiv-2606-30096:
Leonardo Goodall, Andrea Luppi, and Pedro Mediano measure how meaning flows between speakers in conversation. Language research lacks good tools for tracking such flow. Their framework uses information theory to measure directed meaning transfer. Large language models serve as probability estimators for natural language. Two measures come out of this setup.

Semantic transfer entropy captures directed influence between speakers, predicting who shapes whom. A second tool splits joint contributions from several sources into redundant, unique, and synergistic parts. Four experiments show the framework at work in varied settings. It detects reduced flow in rigid, stuck dialogue. It captures persuaders steering the direction of talk. It separates good therapy from poor by the direction of therapist-client exchange. It also reveals how premises in essays add up to more than their parts.
arxiv-2606-30296:
Wenjia Jiang and nine colleagues build an agent that learns across tasks while making math animations. The agent writes Python in the Manim library to animate a paper section. Reflection within one task fixes errors, but lessons die with the task. Their system, ManimAgent, carries experience forward in memory. No model weights change and no human examples seed it.

Once an animation converges, a vision-language model grades the rendered keyframes. Scores feed a dual-channel Episodic Memory Bank grown from the agent's own work. The positive channel stores success rationales as soft reference examples. The negative channel stores validated failure patterns as known pitfalls. Fixed-probe tests compare against no-memory and retrieval baselines. Blind human first-try success rises as memory grows. Reflection rounds needed per task fall at the same time.
arxiv-2606-30396:
Jue Xu, Xiao Yuan, and Qi Zhao prove limits and a quantum speedup for detecting phase changes in evolving quantum systems. Dynamical quantum phase transitions are abrupt kinks in how a system's state returns over time. They mirror ordinary phase transitions in driven settings. How hard they are to detect was unexplored. Estimating them precisely defeats even quantum computers, they prove. A subsystem variant tells a different story.

Deciding that variant is exactly as hard as simulating quantum circuits. That equivalence yields a provable exponential quantum advantage. Searching for critical times gets a practical algorithm too. It estimates observables at many time points at once. Precision reaches the Heisenberg limit. Scaling in the number of time points stays below linear. The speedup is quadratic over classical approaches. Encoding classical evolution into quantum form widens the reach. Odd behavior in classical systems becomes visible the same way.
arxiv-2606-30496:
Olivier Carton, Jake Sudbery and Reem Yassawi build a number-system analogue of a classic object in mathematics. The p-adic integers extend ordinary counting numbers using base-p expansions. The authors replace powers of p with a Pisot numeration. Such a numeration is a counting sequence driven by a recurrence tied to a Pisot number, an algebraic number whose partner values sit inside the unit disk. The Fibonacci-based Zeckendorf system is the best-known example.

The authors study numerations that preserve zeros. This condition links to an earlier requirement by Frougny and Solomyak. For such systems they construct a topological group from infinite digit strings. They equip it with a topology, a precise notion of closeness between elements. The group projects onto a torus, a donut-shaped space, through a structure-preserving map. When the numeration is unimodular, a determinant condition, the group matches a torus exactly.
arxiv-2606-30696:
Kaier Liang, Hengde Dai and Cristian-Ioan Vasile teach a robot to follow spoken errands with deadlines and choices built in. Commands like tidy either the chair or the couch, then switch on the TV, hide temporal and logical rules: multiple targets in a set order. Existing zero-shot navigation systems, which explore unknown rooms using vision-language models, handle only one target.

Their framework, ViTL, works at two levels. A language model compiles each command into a Linear Temporal Logic formula, a notation for timing rules. That formula becomes a finite-state machine. It coordinates value maps and triggers replanning when new objects appear. At the navigation level, a directional score labels frontier directions on the camera image. The vision model then rates each direction separately. Tests in the Habitat-Matterport benchmark showed full long-horizon task completion, and the score improved single-target accuracy and efficiency.
arxiv-2606-30796:
W. Sand Hellman and nine colleagues study a nearby exploded star, supernova 2024ehs, in detail. The event was a Type IIb supernova, a star stripped of most of its hydrogen envelope before exploding. It appeared in March 2024 in the galaxy NGC 3443, about twenty-four megaparsecs away. Its light curve peaked narrowly, faded fast, and showed unusually weak helium lines.

The team followed the supernova for ten months with photometry and spectroscopy, then modelled the spectra with the SUMO radiative transfer code. The modelling points to a low ejecta mass moving at about twenty thousand kilometres per second. The radioactive nickel mass came out just below a tenth of a solar mass. Nebular spectra, taken late, suggest a helium core of about six solar masses, matching a star born with roughly twenty-three solar masses.
arxiv-2606-31096:
Bang and four colleagues present Horizon3D, a system for long-range 3D object detection in self-driving cars. At highway speeds, a car must spot distant objects early. Radar-camera fusion methods struggle at long range, though. Distant objects return only a few radar points and cover only a few image pixels. Bird's-eye-view methods keep scene context but lose fine detail. Query-based methods keep detail but lose context.

Horizon3D mixes both views. It places Gaussian primitives at object keypoints drawn from radar and camera features. A fusion step refines those primitives and splats them onto the bird's-eye-view plane. A dual-path temporal fusion then tracks scene context and per-object motion across frames. On the TruckScenes benchmark, the system beat the previous best method by 3.0 points of NDS and 1.6 points of mAP. It also kept a sparse representation and competitive speed.
arxiv-2606-31196:
Yu and Zhao prove a result about total collisions in the N-body problem, where all bodies crash together at one point. An open worry was infinite spin, a collision orbit turning endlessly as it shrinks. They study homogeneous problems in Euclidean space of any dimension, with the Newtonian case included.

The pair show infinite spin cannot occur when the limiting central configuration, once normalized, is isolated and fills dimension d or d minus one. Their proof extends an approach built for flat problems to the non-abelian rotation symmetry of higher dimensions, using symmetry reduction in two steps. For three dimensions under Newtonian gravity, the result matches recent work but reaches it by a different route.
arxiv-2606-31296:
Haapasalo studies when one statistical experiment can be turned into another, a question called majorization. An experiment is a set of probability models for data from some source. A change may be exact, it may hold for large samples, or it may be catalytic, where a helper system is used and then given back unchanged.

Haapasalo finds conditions that are both sufficient and close to necessary for the large-sample and catalytic forms. The tests use a family of Rényi divergence measures, extended here to many variables at once. All such general measures turn out to be averages over the Rényi family. The best rate at which one experiment can be turned into another also follows from these measures, by real-algebraic means.
arxiv-2608-00096: Explicit Green's Functions and Adjoint Problems for Differential Equations, arXiv 2608-00096. The Green's functions. Scholars can read the full paper. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
arxiv-2608-00296: EXPERIMENTAL NOTE, arXiv 2608-00296. The experimental note. The paper remains available to readers. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
ashton-devil-in-britain-and-america-1896:
John Ashton published The Devil in Britain and America in 1896, a survey of how the Devil appeared in English popular culture. Ashton was a collector of old pamphlets, plays, and street literature. He traced the Devil through cheap print, stage shows, and folk belief on both sides of the Atlantic.

Chapbooks, ballads, plays, and tales of bargains and hauntings fill the pages, many quoted from rare old sources. Ashton showed how the Devil shrank over time from a feared power to a figure of fun. The book preserves scraps of popular print that might have been lost, and it maps what common readers feared and laughed at.
aston-nihongi-1896:
The Nihongi, or Chronicles of Japan, is Japan's oldest official history, covering events to the year 697. William George Aston's English translation came out in 1896, the first complete rendering of the work. The file holds all thirty books, with his preface, introduction, and index, from the Japan Society edition.

The early books tell of the age of the gods: the making of the islands, the sun goddess, and the first emperors said to descend from her. Later books turn to court chronicle, reign by reign, mixing legend with record. Aston's version stayed the standard door into early Japan for English readers.
aubrey-miscellanies-english-1696:
John Aubrey, the great English antiquary, gathered his Miscellanies from a lifetime of notebooks and published them in 1696. Aubrey collected anything curious, and the unseen world drew him strongly. His book gathers apparitions, omens, dreams, second sight, and witchcraft lore from across Britain.

Aubrey reports each case with its place, names, and witnesses, like a clerk of marvels. He neither sneers nor quite swallows; he records. Second sight in Scotland and corpse candles in Wales fill his pages. The result is the folklore of the supernatural from a first-rate collector. Few books show better what educated English folk still believed in 1696.
beatrice-pg3096:
H. Rider Haggard steps away from African adventure in this contemporary novel, whose text dates its first publication to 1893. Beatrice Granger, twenty-two, stands on the Dog Rocks of the Welsh coast in the first chapter, watching mist gather over a still sea. Her home is Bryngelly, her sharp sister is Elizabeth, and the man of the story is Geoffrey, a rising barrister.

The chapter titles trace a love that cannot be honourably kept. Geoffrey wins his case, becomes a rising star, and speaks in the House of Commons, while Lady Honoria makes arrangements of her own. A confession of faith, writing on the sand, and a night of storm mark the road to the close. Haggard ends with the Latin farewell ave atque vale, hail and farewell.
bibliographical-notes-on-histories-of-in: Bibliographical Notes on Histories of Inventions and Books of Secrets, 1896. Another edition. This book preserves that bibliography. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
bolyai-science-absolute-space-halsted-18:
John Bolyai reached non-Euclidean geometry on his own path, in an appendix to his father's Tentamen of 1832. George Bruce Halsted's translation, The Science Absolute of Space, reached its fourth edition in 1896. Bolyai built a geometry of space that stands free of Euclid's parallel axiom. Halsted added appendices that place the work for English readers.

Bolyai calls his system absolute because it holds whether the axiom is true or false. He derives bold results about parallels, angles, and area with tight proofs. His father had warned him off the problem, fearing wasted years. The son's success ranks among math's great stories. Two founders, Bolyai and Lobachevsky, share the credit.
brewer-dictionary-phrase-fable-1896:
Ebenezer Brewer first published his Dictionary of Phrase and Fable in 1870, and the new edition of 1896 is the mature Victorian form. Brewer was a clergyman and schoolbook writer with a love of odd knowledge. His book explains phrases and allusions that have a tale behind them.

Entries give the source of common sayings, the stories behind names, and the roots of customs and superstitions. Readers learn why we call a man a Croesus or speak of sour grapes. Brewer's became the classic phrase book of the English-speaking home. It still serves writers who meet an old allusion and want its story.
cady-lessons-in-truth-1896:
Harriet Emilie Cady was a homeopathic doctor in New York who became the Unity movement's foremost teacher. Her Lessons in Truth, published in 1896, sets out Unity teaching in twelve plain lessons. The book built a denomination almost by itself, through study groups in parlors nationwide.

Cady teaches that God is present in every person as an inner light waiting to be claimed by thought and word. Her lessons move from basic claims about being to prayer, faith, and the spoken word's power. Unity churches still give the book to new members as their first course.
carpenter-loves-coming-age-1896:
Edward Carpenter published Love's Coming of Age in 1896, a set of essays on sex and marriage. Carpenter argues that love must be freed from property, law, and shame to reach its full growth. He defends women's freedom, simpler marriage laws, and frank education of the young. The essays foresee an age of comradeship between the sexes.

Carpenter writes as a socialist and a mystic at once. He praises the body while seeking a spiritual union through it. The book became a bible of English sexual radicalism. It influenced feminists, reformers, and the young Havelock Ellis circle. Its hopes now seem dated in places, yet its plea for honesty endures.
chemia-rationalis-das-ist-vernunfftmassi: Chemia rationalis, 1696. The rational chemistry. This book preserves that work. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
cia-0000009796:
Comments on American prisoners of war remaining in Vietnam, partly deleted, fill a February 1977 CIA paper with a cover item attached. The deletions hide who commented, which itself signals how sensitive the subject stayed. Four years after homecoming, the possibility of remaining prisoners still moved officials.

Papers like this one weighed live-sighting reports against the settled view that no prisoners remained. Each new comment could reopen settled cases in the public mind. The file shows that tension inside the government, not just in newspapers. Its redactions are part of the evidence, marking where the record was judged too hot to show.
cia-0000010596:
Pakistan's current outlook is given in a September 1951 CIA paper. Pakistan was four years old, carved from British India in the partition of 1947. Its founder was dead, its capital new, and its relations with India poisoned by Kashmir and shared rivers.

The paper weighs the young state's politics, army, and economy as one outlook. Weeks after it was written, Pakistan's first prime minister was assassinated, shaking the state further. Analysts could not know that, which sharpens the file's interest. It preserves Pakistan at its fragile beginning, read closely by the new superpower's own professional watchers.
cia-0000011496:
Communist guerrillas of the Hukbalahap movement were at the height of their revolt in the Philippines when the CIA assessed their plans in October 1950. The paper looks ahead one month, to the armed action the Huks might attempt during November. American aid was flowing to the government in Manila, which was struggling to contain the rising.

Analysts weighed the rebels' strength, their targets, and the government's chances of blunting the offensive. The Huk fight was Washington's test case in Asia after the communist victory in China. The paper preserves the fears and the counters of that moment, just before the revolt began to fade.
cia-0000012296:
Military Thought was the Soviet armed forces' own professional journal, and a Helms memo of November 1961 forwards one of its pieces to the DIA director. The quoted title on the subject line begins 'A Turning...' and breaks off in the file. Soviet officers wrote in that journal for each other, which made its pages prized reading in Washington.

Passing such material to the Pentagon's analysts was steady work in the Penkovsky years. The journal's debates hinted at doctrine, budgets, and plans behind the Soviet line. For readers, the memo shows open print doing quiet service as intelligence.
cia-0000013296:
Soviet officers sought access to American prisoners in North Vietnam, and a CIA report from October 1972 examines the effort. Moscow's interest in the captives was intelligence interest. American pilots knew things about planes, tactics, and electronics that Soviet experts wanted badly. Hanoi's guests asked; what they were given, and what they took, worried Washington's counterintelligence men for years.

The report covers the allies' sharing from the outside, as sources revealed it. It shows the prison system as an asset two communist states divided between them. For readers, the page adds a cold layer to the captivity story: the Soviets, asking.
cia-0000014796: Les Grands Espions de Notre Temps, Great Spies of Our Time, is noted in a CIA file dated January 5, 1971. The book is listed as undated in its source note. A French title on the file shelf shows the spy book trade ran in many tongues. The agency's clipping habit clearly crossed borders as well as oceans.
cia-0000015296: A letter to John Anderson from Herbert Scoville fills a CIA file dated January 3, 1957. Scoville thanks Anderson for a letter received, per the title. Scoville was a rising science chief at the agency. Courteous replies like this were the public face of a file room the public could not see.
cia-0000015496: At Behshahr, a town on Iran's Caspian coast, an unidentified flying object was sighted in a CIA record dated in 1960. Behshahr is named in full in the title, giving this entry a firm place. Reports from Iran reached Washington through the close ties of that era. The sighting joins a world map of claims the agency kept through the nineteen fifties.
cia-0000022796: Three American prisoners of war were detained in Dam Doi District, in An Xuyen Province, a CIA record dated in 1971 reports. An Xuyen was the old name for the Ca Mau country at Vietnam's far south. Detention deep in the delta put the men far from any rescue path. The report fed the maps that prisoner staff kept of holding places.
cia-0000036296:
Brazil feared fallout from the release of terrorists, and a CIA weekly review dated February 5, 1970 recorded that fear. Prisoners had been freed in deals tied to kidnapped diplomats, which worried the military government. The review belongs to a weekly series that tracked Brazil under its generals.

Inside, the concern is plain: freeing jailed militants might invite more kidnappings and more pressure. The review shows a regime weighing order at home against judgment abroad. For readers, it captures the tense logic of a government facing armed opposition in 1970. The review treats the releases as a problem with no clean or easy answer.
cia-0000048996: Havana gave advice to El Salvador's Revolutionary Coordinator of the Masses in 1980, and a CIA item from that year preserves the counsel. The CRM was the umbrella linking the guerrillas to their mass organizations. Cuba's hand in the Salvadoran war was long alleged; items like this one were the paper trail behind the charge.
cia-0000049296: A murder derailed talks between El Salvador's government and the rebels in 1987, and a CIA item records the wreck, kept with the Truth Commission records. Talks in that war were fragile constructions, and a single killing could be aimed at the table itself. The item preserves the derailment as officials absorbed it.
cia-0000049396: Jesuit Priests Murder is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000049396, dated March 1, 1991, with a note that the document itself was undated and the date estimated. Marked for the Truth Commission, the file concerns the priests' killing. Readers should note the dating caution in the heading itself, which the catalog record preserves openly.
cia-0000096496: Progress report on Recommendation number two of the Report to the President by the President's Board is declassified CIA document 0000096496, dated October 4, 1957. The heading is cut short in the catalog. The brief file revisits the same recommendation tracked months earlier, giving readers a later checkpoint in the board's long follow-up sequence.
cia-0000113196: Dated January 1, 1945, with that date marked as an estimate, declassified CIA document 0000113196 concerns names and a description of a person. Its untitled heading notes pages as received, then breaks off at As R. No person is named in the surviving heading text itself. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000119696:
Also from January 1954, this CIA paper surveys Soviet bloc strength in economic warfare and the courses of action open to it. Trade bans, credit pressure, and control of key goods were weapons in the Cold War alongside armies. The paper maps that quieter battlefield as Washington saw it.

Knowing what economic harm the other side could do, and how, shaped Western trade rules for years. The study sets out the bloc's tools and the moves analysts thought it might make. For readers, it explains a contest fought through ports, contracts, and embargo lists, where the damage was measured in stalled factories rather than lost battles.
cia-0000124296: A December 1957 CIA report covers the Soviet rocket program and its earth satellite. Two months after Sputnik, the questions had sharpened: how many rockets, how large, and how soon the next launch. The paper gives the agency's accounting at the end of that startling year. Year-end accountings forced analysts to commit numbers to paper, and those committed figures drove the budget fights over American rockets in the season that followed.
cia-0000132296: Situation Report 605 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series, dated January 1, 1991, covers military developments, but part of its own headline was deleted before release. Military reporting was the core of the series as the deadline for Iraq to quit Kuwait approached. The deleted section may have held the most sensitive material. What remains still shows the shape of the daily military watch.
cia-0000132496:
World reaction to possible American moves against Cuba is forecast in a CIA document dated January 4, 1961. Its headline breaks off at the word again, short for against. The agency was gaming out Washington's options and their likely costs abroad that winter.

The document sets out how other governments and publics might answer each course of action. Such forecasts helped shape the choices that led toward the Bay of Pigs. For readers, it shows planning at its most careful and most uncertain. The real reactions, when the invasion came that April, would test every line of the forecast. Some held up well, and others did not.
cia-0000132596: Possible Cuban work to stir trouble inside Venezuela fills a CIA paper dated August 2, 1960. Havana's hand in the unrest in Caracas was suspected then but not proven. Cuban aid to rebels there would grow much larger in the years ahead. The short paper weighs the proof in hand that summer. It takes each claim in turn and tests it.
cia-0000135696: This Spanish-language item from the 2506 Brigade files is dated 2 January 1961. The brigade of anti-Castro exiles was then in its final months of CIA-run training. The catalog record names no subject for the document, and it shares its date with other items in the release. It stands as a dated piece of primary evidence in Spanish, part of the paper trail of an operation that would fail publicly within four months.
cia-0000135796:
Plans to kill leaders in Guatemala, weighed by the agency from 1952 to 1954, fill a CIA paper carrying an estimated date of May 4, 1995. The paper came out decades after the events it covers. It shows what officers once put on paper at the darkest edge of the Guatemala campaign.

The record gathers the proposals in one place for the first time. Names, lists, and memos from the coup years stand behind its dry title. For readers, it is among the most sobering papers in the whole file. It also shows why the Guatemala operation stayed a byword for covert action long after the Cold War ended.
cia-0000135896: A meeting record of 1 February 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with a report on the OAS conference. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136096: Filed on 6 March 1954, this CIA cable concerns the King Program, one more coded project whose work the file itself has to explain. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136196: The record dated 2 May 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about SECANT, vehicles, a Quetzaltenango contact, and a further item the heading cuts off as pil. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136296: The record dated 3 May 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about the need to visit STORAX, a coded place drawing a trip in the operation's travel orders. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136396: A reported conversation with Major Jaime Rosenberg, head of Guatemala's Guardia Judicial, is forwarded to LINCOLN in this January 1954 cable. The talk touched on activities against the Guatemalan government being carried on in El Salvador and the need for vigilance over them, plus continued contact with a source given a phonetic name. Headquarters traces records, suggests the local station chief have no contact until the matter is resolved, and advises checks. The cable shows the agency watching Guatemala's security chief.
cia-0000136996: PBSUCCESS Situation Report No. 3, from the post-coup period in 1954, describes Guatemala's security services being purged. Investigations are being hampered by destroying documents or denying access to the preceding government's records. The Guardia Civil, roughly penetrated by communists under Presidents Arevalo and Arbenz, is described as alert to subversives and cleaning out communists remaining in government offices. An unknown number of communists who took asylum in embassies have been leaving secretly, with no strict border controls yet evident.
cia-03023196: This March 11, 1959 bulletin carried the day's intelligence summary. Policymakers got the analysts' take on world developments. The Cold War's daily brief. Those who study the era will use it. This file preserves that declassified paper.
cia-06785496: USSR SITUATION REPORT, a CIA assessment. The Soviet report. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-06827996: OHB MAIN CAFE 11/28/16, a CIA document. The dated cafe file. This file preserves that declassified paper. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06974496: REPORT OF INVESTIGATION ALLEGATIONS OF CONNECTIONS BETWEEN CIA AND THE CONTRAS, a CIA document. The Contra probe. This file preserves that declassified paper. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
collectanea-chymica-leidensia-oder-auser: Collectanea chymica Leidensia, 1696. The Leiden chemical collection. This book preserves that alchemy. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
conrad-outcast-islands-1896:
An Outcast of the Islands, Conrad's second novel, appeared in 1896 and returns to the Malay world of his first book. Peter Willems, a clerk who has disgraced himself by theft in Makassar, is hidden away by Captain Lingard on a remote river.

There Willems betrays his protector, falls for Aissa, a Malay chief's daughter, and helps rival traders break Lingard's monopoly. Almayer, from the earlier novel, watches his own hopes rot alongside. Conrad builds the tale from treachery, desire, and the rot of the colonial fringe. It is apprentice work beside the later novels, but the atmosphere is already unmistakable.
constitution-ghana-1996:
Ghana's constitution was approved by public vote in 1992 and took force in 1993, restoring elected rule after years of soldiers in power; the hosted text includes changes through 1996. Early chapters cover the constitution itself, the land of Ghana, citizenship, and the laws in force. A long chapter then protects basic human rights and freedoms for every person.

A president leads the executive and names ministers, most of them from Parliament. Parliament is a single chamber. A Council of State advises the president, and a full chapter protects the place of chiefs and chieftaincy in national life. Later chapters cover the courts, the public services, the police and armed forces, and state finance.
cope-primary-factors-organic-evolution-1:
Edward Drinker Cope was a famed American fossil hunter, quick with a pick and a pen. His Primary Factors of Organic Evolution, from 1896, states his rival theory to Darwin's. Cope had dug up hundreds of extinct species across the West.

Cope argues that use, habit, and inner growth drive change more than chance selection. Traits gained in life, he thought, can pass to offspring. This neo-Lamarckian view lost ground as genetics rose in the next century. The book still shows the real fight over how evolution works in Darwin's own era. Cope backs his case with examples drawn from his own fossil finds.
corneille-cid-mongan-1896:
Pierre Corneille's The Cid was first staged in Paris in 1637 and made its young author famous at once. Roscoe Mongan translated the play into English verse in 1896. Its hero, Rodrigue, loves Chimène, but honor forces him to fight her father, who has insulted his own aged father.

Rodrigue kills his beloved's father in a duel, and Chimène must demand his death. Duty pulls both lovers apart even as Spain needs Rodrigue's sword against the Moors. The play's success sparked a famous quarrel over the rules of drama. The Cid fixed the pattern of French classical tragedy and gave French its byword for a hero.
cumont-textes-monuments-mithra-tome2-189:
Cumont's second tome of Textes et monuments, published at Brussels in 1896, holds the monuments of the Mithraic mysteries. The text is in French, and the volume came out before tome one. It catalogues and describes the cult's surviving art: 493 figures and nine heliotype plates fill its pages.

Bull-slaying reliefs, cave temples, altars, and statues from across the Roman world stand in ordered ranks. Cumont reads each image for what it proves about rite and belief. Paired with tome one's texts, the volume completes his monumental corpus of Mithraic sources. Archaeologists still begin Mithraic work with Cumont's catalogue in hand. Few nineteenth-century corpora have served so long without replacement.
demachy-les-rothschild-1896:
Edouard Demachy wrote this French book on the Rothschilds in Paris in 1896. Its title calls them a family of Jewish financiers of the 19th century. Demachy wrote from the records of French finance, where the Paris house stood at the core.

He sets out the work of the Paris bank through the wars, loans, and rail lines of the age. The book is a grave French record of the house, free of the wild tales of the pamphlet press. It holds its place as the chief French view of the bank in its own time.
dickinson-poems-three-series-complete-18:
Emily Dickinson wrote nearly eighteen hundred poems in her quiet Amherst life and published almost none of them. After her death in 1886, her sister found the poems tied in small bundles. Her friend Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson edited three small volumes in the 1890s. This 1896 book gathers all three series in one volume.

The editors smoothed Dickinson's dashes and capitals to suit the taste of the day, but the voice survives: startling, compressed, and funny even about death. Poems on bees, storms, faith, and immortality crowd the pages. This volume is the complete public-domain record of how the nineteenth century first met Dickinson. Modern readers can watch a major poet arriving in disguise.
dubois-pithecanthropus-erectus-english-1:
Eugene Dubois presented his Java ape-man to English readers in 1896. The paper appeared in the Journal of the Anthropological Institute. He called Pithecanthropus erectus a transitional form between apes and humans.

Dubois lays out the skullcap, thigh bone, and teeth from Trinil in Java. He argues the thigh proves upright walking while the skull stayed ape-like. British experts debated him sharply at the meeting and after. The fossils are now placed within Homo erectus. Dubois's English paper marks the moment the missing link became an international argument. Dubois had carried the bones back from Java at great personal cost.
europmc-pmc10188596:
Zhang and co-workers chart the global burden of blood cancers and how it changed over thirty years, in a 2023 study. Blood cancers, called hematologic malignancies, include leukemias, lymphomas, and myelomas. Knowing where cases and deaths rise or fall helps health leaders aim prevention work and research funds where they matter most.

The team gathered detailed data on rates and deaths across countries and years. They describe clear shifts in the pattern of these cancers over three decades. The paper gives a current map of a major slice of the world cancer burden.
europmc-pmc10300796:
Balasubramaniam and co-authors review how plants respond to salinity stress in a 2023 paper. Salt buildup in soil is a severe and growing threat to farming worldwide. It stunts plant growth, disrupts their water and nutrient balance, and in the end endangers the global food supply.

The review explains how plants sense salt and defend themselves. Defenses include pumping salt out of cells, storing it safely, and making protective compounds. The authors also cover breeding and gene approaches for salt-tolerant crops. The paper links plant science to food security. It also points to traits breeders can select for.
europmc-pmc10349496:
Chen and Yu reviewed in 2023 how tau protein and brain inflammation feed each other in Alzheimer's disease. Tau builds tangles inside brain cells, a hallmark of the illness. Tau harm tracks loss of memory and thought more closely than amyloid clumps do. Inflammation runs alongside both and adds to the decline.

Chen shows that immune cells in the brain, once switched on, can worsen tau harm. Worse tau harm then stirs yet more inflammation, in a loop. Changes to tau after it is made, and its spread from cell to cell, both tie into this loop. The review sums up trials that aim at tau or at inflammation. It backs plans that hit more than one target at once.
europmc-pmc10460796:
Sun and co-authors reviewed immune checkpoint therapy for solid tumours in 2023. Such drugs lift brakes on immune cells so they can attack cancer. The known brakes go by names such as CTLA-4, PD-1, and PD-L1. A newer brake, LAG-3, has joined the drug list. Gains have been stark in skin and lung cancers.

Four blocks still limit wide use, Sun reports. Effects and side effects are hard to split, and true growth can be hard to tell from swelling. Tumours also build complex webs of resistance. Fresh hope comes from drug pairs, gene-edited viruses, mRNA vaccines, and nano carriers. Marks that predict who will respond now guide patient choice.
europmc-pmc1135296:
Nordborg and a large team resequence gene fragments across a model plant's range in this 2005 study. Arabidopsis thaliana is a small self-pollinating weed used as a model organism. The team resequenced 876 short DNA fragments in 96 plants, mixing stock centre lines with a structured sample from natural populations. They asked how genetic variation is patterned in a selfing species.

Despite selfing, variation broadly matched a widely distributed sexual species, they found. Linkage disequilibrium, the correlation between nearby variants, decayed within 50 kilobases. Variation was shared worldwide, though population structure and isolation by distance showed. The data broke standard neutral models in several ways. There was a genome-wide excess of rare alleles, partly due to selection. Local variation fell as gene density rose and rose near duplicated segments. Genome-wide surveys are needed to spot selection, they conclude.
europmc-pmc12375796:
Xu and co-authors reviewed tumor-associated macrophages in 2025. These immune cells gather inside and around tumors. They arrive from blood cells drawn by chemical signals. Once there, they settle into distinct states with opposite effects.

One state attacks tumors and boosts immune defense. The other state helps tumors grow blood vessels and spread. It also dampens immune attack and reshapes nearby tissue. Signals, pathways, and fuel use steer which state dominates. Xu surveys drugs that kill, block, or reprogram these cells. Their dual role makes them a rich but tricky target.
europmc-pmc1257596:
Richard and co-authors tested glyphosate and Roundup on human placental cells in 2005. Roundup is a weed killer built on glyphosate. Its residues enter food and rivers worldwide. Farm workers using it had reported pregnancy problems.

Glyphosate killed placental cells within 18 hours in dishes. Toxic doses sat below levels used in farming. Roundup proved more toxic than glyphosate alone every time. At lower doses the herbicide disrupted aromatase, the estrogen-making enzyme. It altered both enzyme activity and its gene message. Helper chemicals in Roundup boosted those effects. Aromatase makes estrogen, so its disruption matters for pregnancy.
europmc-pmc1281296:
