Norwich is the capital town of Norfolk, England. Joseph Jacobs wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Only London, Oxford, and Cambridge name Jews earlier. The death of William of Norwich darkened it in 1144. That was Europe's first blood accusation case.

Jurnet was the town's great Jew of that age. A fine of 6,000 marks fell on him in 1186. The riots of 1190 slew those found at home. Others of the community survived in the castle. Isaac of Norwich financed on a national scale. A king's fine of 10,000 marks struck him in 1218. His account book for three years still survives. Four Jews were hanged in 1238 after a charge. Arson twice hit Jewish houses the year before. Records fix the Jewry's streets with rare precision.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ostrog-11796:
Ostrog is a Russian city in the province of Volhynia. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote its long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish group most likely rose there in the late thirteen hundreds. Lutsk, a near town, had a strong Jewish group by then. The first print word of Ostrog Jews dates to 1532.

That word deals with a tax on horned beasts from Wallachia. One Ostrog Jew bought 1,500 oxen in that trade. In 1536 Ostrog Jews stood charged before the king. They were said to have dodged the due tax on herds. They said they paid the due tax in Poland in full. In 1550 Solomon Luria became rabbi of Ostrog. His fame drew pupils from far and wide to the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pappos-b-judah-:
Pappos ben Judah was a sage of tales in old Israel. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the first half of the second century. He was a fellow captive of Akiba, the great sage. That was in the hard days under Emperor Hadrian.

In those days it was barred to study the Torah in public. Akiba put his life at risk to teach his pupils still. The mild Pappos warned him to stop that brave work. Spies were all round them, Pappos told him in fear. Akiba told him the tale of the fox and the fish. The Torah was life itself to the Jewish folk, he said. The two men met once more by chance in a jail. Pappos praised Akiba, who was jailed for the Torah's sake.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philip-iv-12096:
Philip the Fourth was king of Spain in the 1600s. He was born at Valladolid in 1605 and died in 1665. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Men called him the poet king for his love of art.

Philip left state affairs to his favorite, Olivares. Spain lacked men and money after the expulsions. Olivares invited Spanish-speaking Jews back to Madrid. He promised them a synagogue and free worship. The grand inquisitor fought the plan as a danger. Intolerance won, and Philip pledged expulsion instead. Olivares fell from power in 1643.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pizmon-12196:
A pizmon is a hymn built around a refrain. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It usually crowns the selihot, the penitential prayers. Cantor and congregation sing it in turns. Its stanzas are measured and set in meter.

The word most likely comes from Greek psalmos. Sephardim use the term more widely, though. Any major hymn in stanzas can bear it. Such hymns carry their own old melodies. Ashkenazim keep famous pizmonim for the Days of Awe. Their refrains let the whole room answer together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-porto-riche-geo:
George de Porto-Riche was a French poet and playwright born at Bordeaux in 1849. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His parents were Italian. He first worked in a bank as a young man. The bank let him go for his love of verse.

Porto-Riche then read law, but soon gave it up. Verse was his true work, he found. His first book of poems came out in 1872. More books of verse followed across the years. One sad little book tells of his lone childhood. His first play was staged at the Odéon in 1873. Plays then joined poems in his life's work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raunheim-saly-s:
Saly Raunheim was an American mining engineer born on June 7, 1838. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Frankfort on the Main. He died in New York City on September 9, 1904.

The article traces his study at Heidelberg and Freiburg. In 1863 he bought a zinc mine for a French banker. It sold two years later for two million francs. It had cost only thirty thousand francs. In 1879 he moved to the United States. With the Lewisohn brothers he formed a Montana mining company. He later developed copper mines in New Mexico. The entry joins mining skill with a sharp eye for value.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-restraints-on-a:
Restraints on alienation limit a person's power to sell land. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Many legal systems know such limits. Jewish law's strongest form was the year of jubilee.

The article draws its rules from Leviticus chapter 25. Sold farmland returned to its owner at jubilee. The key line says the land is God's, not man's. Walled city houses could be redeemed for one year only. After that year the sale became final. Village houses stayed redeemable forever under the law. Levite city houses could never be sold away. The entry shows land held as a trust, not a possession.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rodosto-turkish:
Rodosto is a Turkish port on the Sea of Marmora. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It lies seventy eight miles west of Constantinople. Turks call it Tekfur-Dag.

The article says a Jewish community existed there by the twelfth century. Benjamin of Tudela found four hundred Jews in 1173. Noted rabbis Moses, Abijah, and Jacob lived among them. The community stayed undisturbed for centuries, they say. It never gained great importance, though. A seventeenth century wonder worker wrote on divination there. Cemetery stones mark its chief rabbis across centuries. In 1905 about twenty eight hundred Jews lived in Rodosto. They had a synagogue, a school, and heavy communal debt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rossi-giovanni-:
Giovanni Bernardo de Rossi was an Italian Christian Hebraist born in Castelnuovo on October 25, 1742. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In 1769 he became professor of Oriental languages at Parma for life.

De Rossi gathered manuscripts and old prints to collect variant Bible readings. Like Kennicott before him, he wanted the Old Testament text compared copy by copy. That work forced him to map the early history of Hebrew printing. His Annales of Hebrew typography, from 1795 and 1799, founded that field. He also compiled a dictionary of Hebrew authors and their works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sa-id-ben-hasan:
Sa'id ben Hasan of Alexandria was a Jewish convert to Islam of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His book argues from Scripture for the mission of Mohammed.

The work, Masalik al-Nazar, tries to prove that mission genuine from the Bible. Like other controversialists, Sa'id accuses the Jews of corrupting the text. He charges that they swapped other names for Mohammed's and Ishmael's there. His preface tells how he converted in May 1298, after a dream. A voice bade him recite the opening sura, and he recovered from illness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-sanwel-b:
Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel, called Sanwel, ben Enoch. He was a Polish rabbi who flourished in the seventeenth century. Samuel was born at Lublin. He served as a dayyan, a judge on a rabbinical court. He held that post first at Jassy and later at Mayence.

Samuel wrote Dibre Shemu'el, a book of sermons on the Pentateuch. Only part of it survives today. The surviving part covers Genesis, Exodus, and Leviticus. It was printed at Amsterdam in 1678. A second edition appeared at Venice in 1702. The entry rests on the old Hebrew bibliographies of Benjacob, Fürst, and Steinschneider.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarajevo-turkis:
Isidore Singer and Samuel Wessel wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Sarajevo. The city is the capital of Bosnia. About 1850 Omar Pasha let its Jews settle anywhere in the city. Until 1878, when Austria-Hungary took Bosnia, all local Jews were Sephardim. They were called Spanioles. After 1878 an Ashkenazic congregation formed from newcomers.

The Ashkenazim built a handsome synagogue in the Moorish style. It was dedicated on September 30, 1902. Many of them worked as lawyers and physicians. The Sephardim were somewhat more numerous and generally Orthodox. In 1895 Sarajevo held 4,060 Jews in a population of 41,543. The two congregations now dealt warmly with each other. Their members even intermarried. Ties between Jews and non-Jews were also unusually cordial.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schomberg-isaac:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Isaac Schomberg. He was an English physician. Schomberg was born at Cologne on August 14, 1714. He died in London on May 4, 1780. He was a son of Meyer Löw Schomberg. He studied medicine at Leyden and took his degree there. He then practiced in London.

Schomberg's career turned on a feud with the Royal College of Physicians. In 1746 the censors summoned him to be examined. He sent an excuse they called indecent. The college barred him from practice. After baptism, Cambridge gave him a doctorate by royal mandate in 1749. He passed the college's tests, yet admission was still refused. With Moses Mendez he mocked the fight in a satire, The Battiad. The college relented in 1765, admitting him as a licentiate. He won a fellowship in 1771.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seixas-13396:
Cyrus Adler, L. Hühner, and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on the Seixas family. The family founder came from Portugal to the United States in 1730. Abraham Seixas, born in New York in 1750, served in the American army. He carried dispatches for General Harry Lee. Benjamin Mendez Seixas helped found the New York Stock Exchange.

The family's star is Gershom Mendez Seixas. Born in New York in 1745, he led Shearith Israel congregation for about fifty years. At the Revolution he backed the Patriot cause at once. When the British fleet appeared in 1776, his flock shut the synagogue and left town. Seixas carried the Torah scrolls to Stratford, Connecticut. In 1780 he helped found Mickvé Israel in Philadelphia. He died in New York in 1816.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shamhazai-or-sh:
Shamhazai, whose name means seizer of the heaven, is a fallen angel in Jewish legend. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. An old Aramaic version links him to the giants of Genesis. He and his fellow angel Azael fell from heaven before the Flood.

A midrash tells how the pair challenged God over mankind. God warned that earthly passion would master them too. They begged leave to live among men and honor His name. Once on earth, desire for human women overcame them at once. The entry retells a tale used to explain evil, angels, and the Flood generation in one sweep.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shklov-13596:
Shklov is a Russian town on the Dnieper, in the government of Moghilef. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Jews settled there early, likely in the sixteenth century. Its spot on the Russia-Poland border brought repeated war.

Cossacks destroyed Shklov in 1655, the entry records. Swedes sacked it in 1708 under General Löwenhaupt. Napoleon's army invaded and pillaged it in 1812. Jews formed most of the town and suffered most each time. By 1905 about 12,000 Jews lived there, near eighty-eight percent. They ran two synagogues, many prayer houses, a hospital, and schools. Their trade in wheat and goods ran wide across the region.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-jose-b:
Simeon ben Jose ben Lekonya was a tanna of the fourth generation of rabbinic teachers. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was a contemporary of Judah ha-Nasi, the Mishnah's editor. He educated the son of his brother-in-law Eleazar.

Only a few legal sentences by Simeon have survived. He explained the thirty-nine kinds of Sabbath work cleverly. The word melakah, work, occurs thirty-nine times in Torah, he said. That count is inexact, the entry admits frankly. Simeon seems to have skipped some passages on purpose. His homilies compare Israel to rock and stones enduring. Nations are potsherds that break either way they fall. If the pot falls on the stone, woe to the pot. The entry keeps a neat parable of survival.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-skuteczky-damia:
Damianus Skuteczky was a Hungarian painter of genre and portrait works. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Kis-Györ on February 9, 1850. He studied at the Kunstakademie under Geiger. A state scholarship then let him travel to Italy, where he settled at Venice.

His scenes of Venetian life first made his name. His Evil Tongues, shown at the Vienna Exposition, drew wide notice. In 1885 he returned to Hungary for good. He lived by turns at Budapest and at Neusohl. His best-known works include Daily Bread and Schadenfreude. He also studied the history and technique of Renaissance art.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tell-el-amarna-:
Tell el-Amarna is the ruin of an Egyptian royal city. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and George A. Barton wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its name comes from local Bedouin tribes. The ruins sit on the Nile's east bank in middle Egypt. Rock-cut tombs ring the dead city's site.

Amenophis the Fourth built the city early in his reign. He broke with all gods except Aten, the sun disk. Thebes resisted his reform with old religious interests. So he founded a fresh capital free of them. A palace and Aten temple rose at the site. Nobles' houses gathered around the new court. After his death the old religion reasserted itself. The court moved back to Thebes soon after. The entry tells of a capital built for one god.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tiktiner-judah-:
Judah Löb ben Simhah Tiktiner was a Russian rabbi of the eighteenth century. Schulim Ochser wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He served as head of the rabbinical court at Zagora. Later he lived at Wilna.

His book Shalme Simhah appeared at Wilna in 1806. It ran to two volumes of legal novellae. The notes treat the halakot of Asher ben Jehiel. An opening section lays out basic principles of the Talmud. Casuistic writings by Tiktiner follow those principles. The work stops short of completion, though. It reaches only as far as the treatise Ta'anit. Steinschneider and Benjacob cataloged the book for later scholars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trenel-isaac-14:
Isaac Trenel was a French rabbi who directed Paris's central rabbinical school. Isidore Singer and Israel Lévi wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Metz in 1822, he died at Paris in 1890. He studied Talmud under his uncle at Marmoutier. Further study followed at Merzig in Prussia.

After Metz's rabbinical school, he served briefly at Besançon. He resigned and moved to Paris as a charity secretary. He then assisted the chief rabbi of Paris. In 1856 he became director of the Ecole Centrale Rabbinique. The school moved to Paris in 1859. He kept the directorship until his death. With N. Sander he compiled a Hebrew-French dictionary. He also wrote a study of Hillel the Elder.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vidal-naquet-sa:
Samuel Emanuel Vidal Naquet was a French financier. He was born at Paris on August 22, 1859. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied law in Paris and joined the bar in 1882. In 1885 he entered his father's bank.

On his father's death, Vidal Naquet became the bank's chief. Since 1888 he and his brother Charles have edited a market paper. The paper is called Cote de la Bourse et de la Banque. He wrote many of its lead articles himself. Readers knew him as a top French expert on financial law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiener-jacques-:
Jacques Wiener was a Belgian engraver of medals. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hoorstgen, in the Rhine Province, in 1815. He died at Brussels on November 3, 1899. At thirteen he went to Aix la Chapelle for training. His uncle Baruch, an artist, taught him there.

Wiener studied further in Paris from 1835. In 1839 he settled in Brussels as a medal engraver. His fame rested on fidelity to minute detail. He designed the first Belgian postage stamps. In 1849 he arranged their making in England. Overwork cost him his eyesight in 1872. Belgium's king sent condolences at his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolflein-of-loc:
Wolflein of Lochamen was a medieval song maker in Bavaria. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He is known for one book of songs from about 1450. That book is called the Lochheimer Liederbuch. It holds folk songs of Germany in set order.

One song in the book bears lines in Hebrew letters. The lines speak of love to a woman named Barbara. A phrase in a second song was used by Jews alone. Those clues point to a Jewish hand in the book. Yet one song holds a Christian grace at meals. A female name like Barbara was rare among Jews then. So the entry leaves his faith an open case. It rests on small clues in the songs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-b-eleaza:
Yizhak ben Eleazar of Caesarea was a teacher of law in the 300s. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He taught in the old synagogue of that port town. His pupils and friends loved him with rare warmth. One man set him as high there as God in Zion.

His rulings treat a wide range of daily law. One treats trade deals told to a pupil of his. One treats fraud in the sale of goods to men. One treats the writ that frees a wife from her man. One treats the tithe on dates and on date honey. One treats signs found on a corpse in the field. He passed on the words of two older sages as well. He was famed for his skill at the cook's art too.
kadambari-ridding-1896:
C. M. Ridding Englished Banabhatta's Kadambari in 1896, the first complete English rendering of the great Sanskrit prose romance. Bana began the tale in the seventh century and his son finished it after his death. Lovers are born, die, and are reborn across lives, with a parrot narrating much of the tangled story.

The prose piles clause on clause in famous, breathless splendor, a style Indian critics rank supreme. Reincarnation lets the plot fold love and loss into a vast, looping design. Ridding's translation gave the West its fullest taste of a book India calls the crown of prose fiction.
king-babylonian-magic-sorcery-1896:
Leonard W. King published Babylonian Magic and Sorcery in 1896, the first English book on its subject. King edited a series of cuneiform prayers against witchcraft. The leading group is called the Prayers of the Lifting of the Hand.

Babylonians who believed themselves cursed used these rites for relief. The prayers ask gods to break spells, drive off demons, and restore health. King prints transliterations and translations from tablets in the British Museum. Victorian readers could hear ancient Mesopotamia's fears in its own words. The book pioneered the English study of Babylonian ritual texts. Assyriology students still cite its editions.
le-plongeon-queen-moo-egyptian-sphinx-18:
Explorer Augustus Le Plongeon argued that Maya rulers carried their culture to Egypt. His 1896 book Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx tells that bold story. Le Plongeon dug in Yucatan and photographed its ruins for years.

He reads Maya texts as the tale of Queen Moo and her kin. Their line, he claims, crossed the sea and raised the Sphinx. His photos of ruins remain useful to scholars today. His grand links won few believers, then or now. The book is dated but fun, a diffusionist dream in full sail.
leadbeater-devachanic-plane-1896:
C. W. Leadbeater mapped the home of souls past death in The Devachanic Plane, his guide of 1896. Leadbeater was a chief voice of the new creed in its next crop. Devachan is the bright plane where the soul rests and grows ere its next birth on earth. He claims to have seen it by hid sight.

Each rank of soul gets its own zone and bliss in his map. The guide mates his prior map of the plane of dreams. Fans took both as fact for years. The book is a core text of the creed's scheme. Leadbeater claimed his sight was trained by adepts of the East. Doubts dogged those claims, yet his maps of hid planes still shape occult art.
leibniz-new-essays-langley-1896:
Alfred G Langley published his translation of Leibniz's New Essays Concerning Human Understanding in 1896. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz wrote the work in 1704 as a reply to John Locke's Essay, but it appeared only in 1765, after both men were dead. Langley gave English readers the full text.

In dialogue form, Leibniz answered Locke point by point, defending innate ideas against the blank slate. He argued that the mind holds truths as veins in marble hold a statue's shape. The essays range over perception, language, and the nature of substance. They form Leibniz's fullest statement of his rationalism, and a model of how two great philosophers can disagree with courtesy and depth.
levi-magical-ritual-of-the-sanctum-regnu:
A. E. Waite turned Eliphas Levi's hand writ rites into print in The Magical Ritual of the Sanctum Regnum, out in 1896. Levi left the rites in draft at his death. Waite, a young sage of the occult in London, shaped and glossed them for use in English.

The rites show Levi as a hands-on mage, not just a sage of books. Calls, signs, and tools fill the pages. The book links Levi to the Golden Dawn, the group then at work in London. It is a bridge twixt two ages of rite. Waite was young when he did this work, yet his name soon led the field. The care here shows why groups sought his hand.
levi-transcendental-magic-1896:
Eliphas Lévi's Transcendental Magic appeared in English in 1896, in Arthur Edward Waite's translation of Lévi's Dogme et Rituel. Lévi, a French writer and former seminarian, had set out a full system of magic in the 1850s. Waite's version carried that system to English readers.

Lévi taught that one hidden force, pictured as astral light, lay behind magic, myth, and sacred symbols. Ritual, will, and imagination were the tools for working with it. He drew on Kabbalah, tarot, and church teaching to build a single scheme. The book sparked the occult revival of the late nineteenth century and shaped nearly every magic order that followed.
lewis-the-monk-1796:
Matthew Gregory Lewis wrote The Monk while still in his teens. The book came out in 1796 and shocked the town at once. Its hero, Ambrosio, is a famed priest in Madrid. Pride and lust drag him down a path of crime and black rites.

A nun who bleeds and roams, a robber band, and the Inquisition fill the tale. A young nun's fall and a mother's curse add to the grim store. The book pushed the Gothic line to its wild edge for its age. Age has not dulled its power to shock and to hold a reader.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
Motley's tenth volume spans the dark winter of 1618 and 1619. Political and religious parties trade growing rancour across the Netherlands. Spanish intrigues exploit the divisions, and King James proves inconsistent. Barneveld, the Republic's guide for a generation, lies hidden from sight.

Amid the crisis, Brewster and Robinson's congregation worships at Leyden. Motley recounts their decision to leave Holland for America. Robinson's farewell sermon and prayer mark their parting. The Pilgrim story thus enters this Dutch history near its tragic close. The winter setting underscores the Republic's internal gloom, Motley writes. His sympathy rests plainly with the fallen Advocate throughout.
marsh-pithecanthropus-erectus-java-1896:
O. C. Marsh, Yale's famous fossil hunter, weighed in on the Java ape-man in 1896. Eugene Dubois had reported skull and thigh bones from Trinil in Java. Marsh's short notice appeared in the American Journal of Science.

Marsh reviews Dubois's evidence and gives a cautious American welcome. He treats the bones as a real form between apes and humans. The piece carried weight because Marsh had named many dinosaurs himself. For English-speaking science, his verdict helped make Pithecanthropus a serious subject rather than a traveling curiosity. His notice ran only a few pages, yet it traveled widely.
maspero-struggle-of-nations-1896:
Gaston Maspero turns to war and realms in The Struggle of the Nations, in English from 1896. It is the mid tome of his three tome past of the old East. Egypt, Syria, and Assyria clash in an age of great kings. Chariots, sieges, and state craft fill the tale as realms rise, strike, and fade in turn.

Maspero had run digs and site guards in Egypt at first hand. That grit grounds his grand sweep. McClure's English prose keeps his grace. Fans of the old East still start with this set. This tome is its war book.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-2-january-18:
McClure's Magazine for January 1896 is volume six, number two. Ida M. Tarbell's life of Lincoln again leads the issue. This part shows his first trials in Illinois as a young man.

Lincoln clerks in Denton Offutt's store and meets the Clary's Grove boys. He studies grammar, runs for the assembly, and serves in the Black Hawk War. Poems by Eugene Field and a tale by Herbert D. Ward add lighter fare. Murat Halstead tells how Blaine lost the race for president in his day. A piece on the sun's light adds science to the month's mix. Elizabeth Stuart Phelps starts Chapters from a Life in this issue too.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-3-february-1:
February 1896 brings volume six, number three of McClure's Magazine. Tarbell's Lincoln leads again, now in New Salem from 1832 to 1836. He seeks work, buys a store, and starts to study law.

Lincoln serves as postmaster, surveys with a grapevine chain, and meets debt. The tale of Ann Rutledge stands in this part of the life. Ian Maclaren and Anthony Hope give fiction, and Will H. Low writes on painting. Murat Halstead treats the sad close of Garfield's term as president. A tale of the fastest railroad run adds speed and risk. Robert Louis Stevenson's Touchstone gives the issue a famed short tale.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-4-march-1896:
McClure's Magazine for March 1896 is volume six, number four. Tarbell's Lincoln enters the bar and moves to Springfield in this part. His first speech and first protest against slavery stand in the heads.

Rudyard Kipling gives the tale The Ship That Found Herself. Eugene Field and John Hay add verse and a tale of a young hero. Cleveland Moffett writes on the science of kite flying for weather work. Robert Barr adds a dramatic tale, and Will H. Low goes on with painting. Notes at the end treat a search for justice and the real Lincoln. Kites that draw down electric force show the age's bold science.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-5-april-1896:
April 1896 brings volume six, number five of McClure's Magazine. Two pieces lead on a new marvel in photography. They treat the Rontgen rays and their first use in America.

Pictures show bones through flesh, a ring on a lady's hand, and a frog. Tarbell's Lincoln reaches the campaign of 1840 and his wedding to Miss Todd. Anthony Hope starts Phroso, and Kipling gives a soldier and sailor poem. Mrs. E. V. Wilson's Rachel and more of a life close the issue. Notes praise the funds raised for short tales that year. New Lincoln pictures and a Grant life are flagged for readers too.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-6-may-1896:
McClure's Magazine for May 1896 is volume six, number six. Will H. Low's Century of Painting leads this issue. His subject is Jean Francois Millet, the French painter of farm folk.

Low tells of Millet's roots, his early sway, and his life at Barbizon. He shares his own short knowledge of the man and his studio talk. A self drawn portrait and Millet's joke coat of arms face the piece. Low weighs the place time and shared views have given the painter. Millet's own words on his pictures are quoted in the piece. Low lets the painter's talk stand beside his own judgment.
mctaggart-hegelian-dialectic-1896:
Studies in the Hegelian Dialectic, published in 1896, is J. M. E. McTaggart's first book, a critical exposition of Hegel's method. McTaggart, the Cambridge don who became idealism's most rigorous English voice, here tests the dialectic joint by joint.

He follows Hegel's categories as each passes into its opposite and is preserved in a higher unity, asking at each step whether the move is earned. His verdict is mixed: the method survives, much of its application does not. The book is lucid where its subject is not. It began McTaggart's lifelong project of rebuilding metaphysics with an auditor's conscience.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-being-s:
Volume five of the St. Cloud letters opens book two at letter one. The writer dates it from Paris in September 1805. He has come back to court and watched the Sovereign's levees.

Napoleon was warm and mild before he left to be crowned in Italy. He came back from Milan peevish, abrupt, and rude at his first audience. A naval hope helps explain the swing, the writer argues. Nelson's acts crushed the fleet plan that had raised his mood. A female friend of Madame Bonaparte knew part of the cause. Fleets and kingships weigh more than temper in his account.
mooney-ghost-dance-1896:
James Mooney worked for the Smithsonian and lived among Native peoples, recording their beliefs with care. His 1896 report studies the Ghost Dance faith that spread across the West after 1889. It closes with the Sioux outbreak of 1890 and the killing at Wounded Knee.

Mooney traces the faith to the Paiute prophet Wovoka, who preached peace, dance, and the return of the dead. He prints songs, letters, and firsthand accounts from many tribes. He also shows how fear and rumor among settlers turned a peaceful faith into a crisis. Because he listened before he judged, his report remains a founding work of American ethnography.
openalex-w1989230896:
Jeruza Neyeloff, Sandra Fuchs, and Leila Moreira wrote this guide. Their paper is dated 2012 in the catalog record. Meta-analysis combines results across many primary studies. Reviews of observational studies are often the only option. Standard statistics packages can be hard to use for it.

The guide shows each step inside a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. It focuses on descriptive data tasks for beginners. Forest plots, the summary graphs of meta-analysis, are covered. Step-by-step detail lowers the entry barrier for clinicians. No costly specialist software is required for the method. The paper serves researchers with modest tools and budgets.
openalex-w2063294396:
Gianfranco Grompone, Patricia Martorell, Silvia Llopis and colleagues tested a probiotic strain in tiny worms. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. Resisting oxidative stress helps healthy ageing. Live food bacteria might offer such protection. Evidence for that idea was scarce.

The team fed many bacterial strains to nematode worms. They then exposed the worms to oxidative stress. One Lactobacillus strain protected the worms clearly. Survival rose, and lifespan rose by about a fifth. Gene tests linked the effect to a known longevity pathway. The strain also calmed inflammation in human gut cells. The results mark it as a probiotic candidate. Human benefits still need direct testing.
openalex-w2105334596:
Serguei Chatrchyan and colleagues in the CMS Collaboration measured the new Higgs-like boson in a four-lepton channel. Their paper appeared in Physical Review D in 2014. In this channel the boson decays through Z particles. Four electrons or muons form a very clean signal. Data came from two LHC runs.

The boson appeared as a narrow bump in the data. Its measured mass sat near the accepted Higgs value. Its total width was very small, as expected. Production strength matched the standard model prediction closely. Spin and parity tests favoured the standard Higgs pattern. Rival spin options were ruled out strongly. The channel gave the sharpest early Higgs portrait.
openalex-w2142566496:
Leandro Rezende, Maurício Lopes, Juan Pablo Rey-López, and colleagues published this overview in PLoS ONE in 2014. They gathered what systematic reviews say about sedentary behavior, meaning long waking time spent sitting. Their aim was to sum up the health evidence and grade how well the reviews themselves were done.

From over a thousand review titles, twenty-seven reviews were included. In children and teens, the best reviews gave strong evidence linking more sitting time with obesity. Evidence was moderate for blood pressure, cholesterol, self-esteem, social behavior, fitness, and school results. In adults, strong evidence linked sedentary behavior with death from all causes combined.
openalex-w2153136696:
Lewis Kuller, Russell Tracy, Waldo Belloso, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Medicine in 2008. Within the SMART trial of HIV treatment strategies, patients assigned to intermittent therapy died more often than those on continuous therapy. The team asked whether inflammation and clotting markers in blood help explain that gap.

Stored samples from trial members were tested for six markers tied to inflammation and blood clotting. A case-control study compared patients who died with matched survivors. Higher marker levels near study entry and before death were linked to higher odds of dying. A second study tracked how the two treatment strategies changed these markers over the first month after assignment.
openalex-w2166063496:
Allison Aiken, Dara Salcedo, M. Cubison, and colleagues published this study in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics in 2009. During the MILAGRO campaign, they analyzed fine particles over Mexico City with a high-resolution mass spectrometer. The work, part one of two, covers what the particles are made of and where their organic share comes from.

Organic material made up about half of the fine particle mass, matching a 2003 study. A factoring method split the organics into three main types: fresh traffic-like emissions, aged oxygen-rich material, and biomass burning smoke. The aged type alone supplied almost half the organic mass. A small nitrogen-rich local type also appeared, and a filter-based method gave broadly matching source shares.

Jackson Sá-Silva, Cristóvão de Almeida, and Joel Guindani published this essay in the Revista Brasileira de História e Ciências Sociais in 2009. Writing in Portuguese, they offer theoretical and methodological notes on documentary research. Their aim is to spark debate about how students, teachers, and researchers use documents in everyday research work.

The essay first defines documentary research and sets it beside bibliographic research, noting where they match and differ. It then examines what counts as a document. Next come criteria for a first pass over written documents: checking their origin, context, and trustworthiness. The essay closes by laying out the steps of documentary analysis in order, giving beginners a clear path into the method.

Julie A. Y. Cichero, Peter Lam, and Catriona Margaret Steele led the team behind this paper in Dysphagia, published online in 2016. It presents the IDDSI framework for naming texture-modified foods and thickened fluids. Such foods help people with dysphagia, or swallowing difficulty, eat and drink more safely. Dysphagia affects about eight percent of the world's population.

A volunteer committee from many professions built the framework through systematic review and wide consultation. Their survey drew over two thousand responses from thirty-three countries. It found dozens of different names for a handful of food texture and liquid thickness levels. Respondents strongly backed international standardization. IDDSI therefore sets one global set of terms and definitions. It is meant for patients of all ages, in all care settings and cultures.

Luiz E. O. C. Aragão, Liana O. Anderson, and Marisa Gesteira Fonseca lead a team tracking Amazon fire emissions in Nature Communications in 2018. Brazil cut Amazon deforestation sharply after 2004, through a national action plan. Deforestation rates fell about two-thirds by 2015 compared with the earlier average. Carbon emissions from clearing fell with them.

Drought years tell a different story, the authors show. In the 2010 drought, fire emissions ran far above the following wet year, reaching over half of global land-use emissions that year. Fires in human-modified regions increasingly burn independently of fresh clearing. The paper's title states the result: drought-related fires counteract the decline in deforestation emissions. Protecting the Amazon's carbon gains therefore means fighting fire, not only chainsaws. Climate-driven drought makes that task harder each decade.

Alok Sharma, Edwin Vans, Daichi Shigemizu, and colleagues published this methods paper in Scientific Reports in 2019. It presents DeepInsight, a way to turn data that are not images into images. The converted images can then be fed to convolutional neural networks, the models that excel at picture analysis.

The method matters because small, telling differences in genomic and other data are hard to spot directly. Image-based networks pull out features on their own, with no extra extraction step. They can also catch complex patterns and hidden correlations in data. By reshaping raw values into pictures, DeepInsight lets deep networks work on data far beyond photos. The authors offer it as a general tool for data science.
openalex-w3169375696:
Concepción Marcos, David Díaz, Katharina Fietz, and colleagues systematically review what marine protected areas give to nature and society. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Marine Science in 2021. Protected areas restrict fishing and other uses in parts of the sea. Many exist mostly on paper, with weak rules and little enforcement.

The authors gather evidence on ecosystem services, the practical gains ecosystems provide to people, from these protected zones. They also weigh wider social goods and benefits, such as food, income, and recreation. Sorting strong claims from weak ones matters, because protection is expanding fast. The review helps managers judge what well-run protected areas can truly deliver.

Rita Alaggio, Catalina Amador, Ioannis Anagnostopoulos, and colleagues introduce the fifth edition of the WHO classification of lymphoid tumours, in Leukemia in 2022. It is the world reference for naming cancers of the lymph system, such as lymphomas. Its terms feed into global disease codes used for health records everywhere. A new edition therefore shifts daily practice in labs and clinics.

The article lays out the thinking behind the fifth edition and its main changes. It explains how new evidence on genes and disease behaviour reshaped several groups. Earlier editions grew from a 1990s expert scheme and were revised as knowledge deepened. An overview of the companion myeloid tumour classification was planned separately.
openalex-w4293212596:
The Astropy Collaboration, led by Adrian Price-Whelan, Pey Lian Lim, N. Earl, and colleagues, reports on the Astropy Project and its latest core release. Their paper appeared in The Astrophysical Journal in 2022. Astropy is a community-built set of Python tools that gives astronomers shared, basic software functions. The core package, now at version 5.0, underpins many specialised astronomy packages.

The article summarises what the core package does and what the wider project has changed. It describes links with observatories and space missions that rely on the tools. It also covers Learn Astropy, the project's teaching arm. The authors close with the challenges of sustaining volunteer-driven software that a whole field now depends on.

Dan Eisenberg, Scott Shikora, Edo Aarts, and colleagues present the 2022 indications for metabolic and bariatric surgery. The statement comes from the American and international bariatric surgery societies, ASMBS and IFSO. It appeared in Obesity Surgery, with the journal issue dated 2023. Such statements define which patients weight-loss surgery is recommended for. Obesity is now recognised as a chronic disease, tied to lasting low-grade inflammation and immune problems.

Worldwide surgical experience has grown greatly since the last indications were written. Long-term studies have proven the surgery an effective and durable treatment for severe obesity. The new statement updates patient selection to match that evidence. It aims to end outdated limits that kept proven treatment from people who could benefit.
openalex-w7204250996:
Emílio de Magalhães Garavini led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on antiphospholipid syndrome as an underdiagnosed cause of repeated blood clots. In this autoimmune condition, antibodies push the blood toward clotting, and patients can suffer thrombosis again and again. Searching two sources, the team found over twenty-five hundred papers and selected twenty-five that met their criteria.

The syndrome was clearly linked to recurrent clotting events, with the highest risk in patients whose blood carried the lupus anticoagulant or tested positive for all three antiphospholipid antibodies. Diagnosis and lab interpretation remain tricky, the authors note, and stopping after a first event depends on anticoagulation tailored to each patient. They urge clinicians to consider the syndrome whenever thrombosis recurs with suggestive features.
openalex-w7204469096:
Ana Carolina Jansen Pereira Cirino Prado and Denison Melo de Aguiar released a Portuguese-language legal paper in Brazil in 2026 on regulating private health insurance in the state of Amazonas. Brazil's supplementary health rules impose the same obligations nationwide, but they are executed in territories with very different care capacity. The study reviews studies, records, and official data, mainly from the national regulator, using Amazonas as its territorial case.

Medical care ties concentrate heavily in Manaus, they find, while health regions across the vast state show real care deserts, with long distances, hard logistics, uneven services, and weak internet links. Adding high-complexity tools to the national coverage list widens the gap between promised coverage and what is locally on offer. The authors propose uniform national rights delivered through regulation that fits each territory.
openalex-w7208774396:
Daiane de Lourdes Alves Velho leads a team of six authors on digital curriculum and school inclusion in contemporary culture. Their qualitative study reads three works published in 2026 on educational media, teaching practice, and curriculum problems in special education within ordinary classrooms. The analysis sorts the material into four themes: technology as curriculum, teacher guidance and training, accessibility and assessment, and the institutional conditions behind digital schooling.

Digital resources earn their place, the authors find, when they serve clear learning goals, speak in varied formats, and come with real conditions of use. Poor connections, too few devices, broken training, and access barriers can deepen inequality instead. For inclusion, quick one-off adaptations are not enough: diversity belongs inside curriculum planning itself, with teachers mediating the tools rather than merely handing them over.

Marcus Nascimento Coelho leads a team with a made-up classroom scene, and a hard question inside it. A young child in a preschool PE class asks the teacher: if he can, why can't I? The he is a classmate with autism who plays by adapted rules. The team reads the scene with Jean Piaget's work on how young minds grow. They also use the national curriculum and Brazil's inclusion laws.

The scene is a teaching tool, not a real case. It lets the authors probe how small children grasp difference, rules, and fair play. To call one child special, they warn, is not enough. That label can shrink what inclusion means. PE, planned with care, can do more. It can help all the children see that fair does not always mean the same.
openalex-w7213365596:
Sara Broll Zanini and Mauricio Pereira da Silva Filho study basal cell carcinoma care in midwest Santa Catarina, Brazil. Their 2026 paper uses records from a university hospital's surgical oncology service. Basal cell carcinoma is described as the most common skin cancer worldwide.

The team reviewed electronic records for patients treated between January 2025 and March 2026. They recorded age, sex, clinical features, lab findings, and treatment paths. Patients were mostly older adults, with a mean age near seventy, and women were slightly more numerous. The study maps how patients move through care locally, which can help the hospital plan services and follow-up.
openalex-w7215033896:
Ana Patrícia Rodrigues Pimentel, Laysa Victória Guerra Araújo, and Marli Terezinha Vieira wrote a 2026 legal study of the fundamental right to a healthy work environment in Brazil. Their bibliographic and documentary review maps the national inspection tools and public responsibilities meant to protect workers. A healthy workplace, in their framing, covers physical and psychosocial integrity, not merely the absence of accidents.

Brazil's regulatory framework is robust on paper, they find, yet a wide gap separates the formal right from its material realization. State operational weaknesses and the practice of monetizing risk, paying extra instead of removing danger, widen that gap. The authors call for a shift from a compensatory legal model, which pays after harm, to a preventive paradigm. That shift demands deep changes in institutional and business postures so dignity is protected in daily working life.

Mateus Oliveira Carvalho led a 2026 ecological study comparing hospital care for acute heart attack in three northeastern Brazilian states: Alagoas, Pernambuco, and Sergipe. Using the national hospital information system for 2021 to 2025, the team counted nearly twenty-two thousand admissions and compared hospital deaths, average length of stay, and average admission values across the states.

Alagoas stood out on every indicator: its hospital mortality was clearly higher than in the other two states, and it also showed the longest average stay and the highest average admission value. Pernambuco and Sergipe did not differ clearly from each other. Because the data are aggregated, the authors caution, the study cannot say which clinical or organizational factors explain Alagoas's worse results; patient-level and care-organization studies must follow.

Luis Henrique Francisco Martins and Claudio Alexandre de Souza ran a maker-space workshop with parents at a public school in Foz do Iguaçu, Paraná. Their 2026 action research studied what it did for creativity and family ties. The project joined educational robotics, design thinking, and a Family Day event for fifth-grade families.

Ten parents answered questionnaires and took part under observation. Afterwards they rated the experience highly and, most telling, strongly agreed they could teach their children what they had learned. The authors argue that well-guided maker activities can widen access to creative practice in public education and pull families closer to the school at the same time.

Arthur Felipe Rodrigues Silva led a six-author integrative review, published in 2026, on women's health during the climacteric, the transition from reproductive to non-reproductive life. The review gathers what the literature says about these women's needs, their vulnerabilities, and the care that serves them best.

Twenty articles were sorted into three themes: symptoms and quality of life, sexuality and social conditions, and health education and service organization. Hot flushes, mood and urinary symptoms, lifestyle, schooling, and family relations all shaped quality of life, while education helped women cope. Weak professional training in primary care stood out as a gap. The authors ask for care that is complete, fair, and humane.
papus-tarot-of-the-bohemians-1896:
Papus built the French school of tarot, and A. P. Morton put that school in English in The Tarot of the Bohemians, out in 1896. The French text had come first, in 1889. Morton keeps its keys, charts, and grand claims: the cards hold the lore of old Egypt and the Jews in sign form.

Card past card gets its gloss, rank, and star links. Rules for spreads close the book. English fans at last could learn the French scheme at first hand. The work still stands as that school's main text in English.
plaw-104-100-1996: Public Law 104-100 was enacted on February 1, 1996. It names the United States Post Office building at 24 Corliss Street in Providence, Rhode Island, as the Harry Kizirian Post Office Building. Section 2 covers later mentions. Any law, map, rule, paper, or other record that names that building shall be read as naming the Harry Kizirian Post Office Building. The text is two short sections, and its bill was H.R. 1606.
plaw-104-101-1996: Public Law 104-101, approved February 1, 1996, names a single federal building. It designates the Federal building at 1550 Dewey Avenue in Baker City, Oregon, as the David J. Wheeler Federal Building, and directs that every reference to that building in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, and other records be read under the new name. Nothing else in federal law is changed by the act, whose full text runs to two sections plus a legislative history noting House Report 104-412.
plaw-104-102-1996:
Arizona land and a settled dispute are the subjects of Public Law 104-102, the Saddleback Mountain-Arizona Settlement Act of 1995, approved February 6, 1996. It provides for the transfer of certain lands to the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community and the city of Scottsdale.

Congress finds that both the Community and Scottsdale claimed a 701-acre tract called the Saddleback Property. It lies inside the city, against the north boundary of the reservation. The land holds Saddleback Mountain and scenic, historic terrain along Shea Boulevard. The Resolution Trust Corporation had taken it in 1989 from a failed savings and loan. After it was noticed for sale, the two sides sued. Then they negotiated a settlement agreement instead of fighting the case out.
plaw-104-103-1996:
Public Law 104-103 exists for one month: March 1996. Approved February 8, 1996, it guarantees the timely payment of Social Security benefits that month. At the time, Congress and the Treasury were locked in a fight over raising the public debt limit.

Its findings say Congress intended to pass a debt limit increase before March 1, 1996. In the meantime, beneficiaries should be assured their checks would arrive on time. The law therefore lets the Secretary of the Treasury issue United States obligations before March 1. The amount equals the March benefits payable under title II of the Social Security Act. Those obligations do not count against the debt limit. The exemption ends with the first debt limit increase or on March 15, 1996, whichever comes first.
plaw-104-104-1996:
Promoting competition and cutting regulation in American telecommunications is the stated aim of Public Law 104-104, the Telecommunications Act of 1996, signed February 8, 1996. Congress says the act seeks lower prices, higher quality services, and rapid deployment of new telecommunications technologies.

The law works mainly by amending the Communications Act of 1934. Its first title, on telecommunications services, builds a part on development of competitive markets, with new sections on interconnection and on procedures for negotiation, arbitration, and approval of agreements between carriers. In plain terms, it sets rules meant to let rival companies connect to and compete over the networks that the older law had treated as a regulated monopoly system.
plaw-104-105-1996:
Public Law 104-105, the Farm Credit System Reform Act of 1996, amends the Farm Credit Act of 1971. Its aim is to ease the rules on the farm credit system. It was approved February 10, 1996, as H.R. 2029 in the 104th Congress.

Its first title rebuilds the farm mortgage market run through the Federal Agricultural Mortgage Corporation. Sections set definitions, the company's duties and powers, and how mortgage marketing facilities qualify. They also cover the backing of qualified loans. Required reserves and subordinated participation interests are ended, pools must be spread out, and small farms get their own section. Further sections set how much capital the company must hold. They cover how the rules are enforced, how capital can be rebuilt, and even how the company could be shut down. A second title then turns to easing the rules.
plaw-104-106-1996:
For fiscal year 1996, Public Law 104-106 is the National Defense Authorization Act, approved February 10, 1996. It funds military activities of the Department of Defense and military construction. It also funds defense activities of the Department of Energy. And it sets personnel strengths for the Armed Forces for that year.

The act is organized into five divisions. Division A holds the Department of Defense funding lines, beginning with procurement. Division B covers military construction, and Division C covers Department of Energy national security programs. Divisions D and E reach beyond the military. They reform federal acquisition laws and the running of computer systems across the Federal Government.
plaw-104-107-1996:
Public Law 104-107, approved February 12, 1996, is the Foreign Operations, Export Financing, and Related Programs Appropriations Act for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1996. It is a spending law. It appropriates money out of the Treasury for American activity abroad.

Title I covers export and investment help, starting with the Export-Import Bank of the United States. The bank may spend within its funds on hand and its borrowing limits. But no money may support exports of nuclear equipment, fuel, or technology to a non-nuclear-weapon state. The bar covers a state that has detonated a nuclear device after enactment. A separate subsidy pays 786 million dollars toward the cost of direct loans, loan guarantees, insurance, and tied-aid grants. That money is available until September 30, 1997.
plaw-104-108-1996: Public Law 104-108, approved February 12, 1996, names the federal building at 1221 Nevin Avenue in Richmond, California, as the Frank Hagel Federal Building. A second section covers later mentions. Any law, map, rule, paper, or other record that names that building counts as naming the Frank Hagel Federal Building. The act began as H.R. 2111, with a Senate companion, S. 1076. Its legislative history is printed after the two sections.
plaw-104-109-1996: Public Law 104-109, approved February 12, 1996, makes technical corrections in laws relating to Native Americans. It does not set new policy; it fixes wording. One section amends the act restoring federal services to the Pokagon Band of Potawatomi Indians, changing Bands to Band, rolls to roll, and similar plural forms throughout its membership provisions. Another corrects the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians and the Little River Band of Ottawa Indians Act, amending a heading and membership list provisions in the same word-level fashion.
plaw-104-110-1996:
Public Law 104-110, approved February 13, 1996, extends the power of the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to run certain programs. It also requires reports from the Secretary. The law amends title 38 of the United States Code, the veterans' title, mostly by moving deadline dates forward.

Title I lists the extensions one by one. Priority health care for veterans exposed to toxic substances runs to the end of 1996. Drug and alcohol abuse and dependence programs run to the end of 1997. A pilot program for care options outside nursing homes runs to the same date. Other items adjust negotiated interest rates and mortgages for energy efficient improvements. They widen loan asset sale powers and cover agreements for housing help for homeless veterans.
plaw-104-111-1996:
Ruth and Billy Graham receive a congressional gold medal under Public Law 104-111, approved February 13, 1996. Congress states its findings first: the Grahams have made outstanding and lasting contributions to morality, racial equality, family, philanthropy, and religion.

The findings note that Billy Graham, America's most respected evangelical leader for half a century, reached one hundred million people in person at his crusades and billions worldwide on television. They also credit the couple's newspaper column, fourteen books, and the Ruth and Billy Graham Children's Health Center in Asheville, North Carolina. The act then authorizes the Speaker and the President pro tempore to present the medal, and directs the Secretary of the Treasury to strike it.
plaw-104-112-1996: Public Law 104-112, approved March 5, 1996, designates the United States courthouse at 197 South Main Street in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, as the Max Rosenn United States Courthouse. Its only other section provides that references in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, and records to that courthouse shall be read as references to the new name. The bill, H.R. 1718, is recorded in its printed legislative history as passing the House in December 1995 and the Senate the following February.
plaw-104-113-1996:
Federal labs and private business meet in Public Law 104-113, the National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995, approved March 7, 1996. It amends the Stevenson-Wydler Technology Innovation Act of 1980. The changes deal chiefly with inventions made under joint research and development agreements.

Congress finds that bringing technology to the marketplace is central to the nation's economic, environmental, and social well-being. Federal labs can speed new products through joint agreements, it says, but selling them depends on business. The act therefore makes it easier for companies to obtain exclusive licenses to inventions from joint research with federal scientists. In return, the government receives fair payment.
plaw-104-114-1996:
Public Law 104-114, the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity Act of 1996, known as LIBERTAD, was approved March 12, 1996. Its stated aims are to seek international sanctions against the Castro government in Cuba and to plan support for a transition government leading to a democratically elected government there.

Title I works on strengthening sanctions. Its sections cover enforcement of the economic embargo of Cuba, a ban on indirect financing, and United States opposition to Cuban membership in international financial institutions. Other sections address aid to Cuba from the former Soviet states, television broadcasting to Cuba, and reports on other countries' commerce with and assistance to Cuba. Support for democratic and human rights groups and international observers is also authorized.
plaw-104-115-1996:
Guaranteeing that Social Security and other federal funds stay fully invested during the 1996 debt limit standoff is the job of Public Law 104-115, approved March 12, 1996. Federal trust funds normally hold United States obligations. The debt ceiling threatened that routine investment.

The law lets the Secretary of the Treasury issue obligations to each federal fund before March 30, 1996. The total may reach the amounts deposited in the fund during a short window. It may also cover the face amount of the fund's obligations maturing then. Those special obligations do not count against the public debt limit. The exemption ends on the first debt limit increase enacted afterward, or on March 30, 1996, whichever comes first. A federal fund is any federal trust fund or government account to which the Treasury issues such obligations.
plaw-104-116-1996: Public Law 104-116, approved March 15, 1996, is a joint resolution making further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1996. In substance it moves dates. In Public Law 104-99 it strikes March 15, 1996 in five sections and inserts March 22, 1996. It makes the same one-week change in Public Law 104-92. It also adds bill numbers, H.R. 1977 and 2127, to mentions of two regular appropriations acts named in the earlier law. Nothing else is funded or changed.
plaw-104-117-1996:
Members of the Armed Forces serving with the peacekeeping efforts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, and Macedonia get combat-zone tax treatment under Public Law 104-117. The law was approved March 20, 1996. It says their service shall be treated, for tax purposes, as if it were performed in a combat zone.

A qualified hazardous duty area is one of those three countries. In it, service members are entitled to special pay for duty subject to hostile fire or imminent danger. For personnel there, the act lists the Internal Revenue Code rules that follow combat-zone rules. They cover exclusion of combat pay and the income taxes of members who die. They also cover estate tax treatment, telephone service taxes, and joint returns where a spouse is in missing status. Postponement of deadlines for tax acts is on the list too.
plaw-104-118-1996: Public Law 104-118, approved March 22, 1996, is another joint resolution making further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1996. It extends the stopgap funding dates by one week. In five sections of Public Law 104-99, March 22, 1996 becomes March 29, 1996. In one section of Public Law 104-92, the same date becomes April 3, 1996. The whole operative text is those date swaps. The resolution passed both houses on March 21, the day before approval.
plaw-104-119-1996:
Hazardous waste land disposal rules gain flexibility under Public Law 104-119, the Land Disposal Program Flexibility Act of 1996, approved March 26, 1996. It amends the Solid Waste Disposal Act to make certain adjustments in the land disposal program and provide needed flexibility.

The central change adds a new paragraph to section 3004(g). Waste identified as hazardous based solely on one or more characteristics is freed from the land disposal restrictions and related treatment requirements if two conditions hold. It must be treated in a system that discharges under a Clean Water Act permit, meets pretreatment requirements, or uses a zero discharge system with equivalent treatment. And it must no longer exhibit a hazardous characteristic before it is managed in any land-based unit.
plaw-104-120-1996:
Public Law 104-120, the Housing Opportunity Program Extension Act of 1996, approved March 28, 1996, extends certain housing programs for fiscal year 1996. The programs are administered by the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development and the Secretary of Agriculture.

Its multifamily housing section deals with section 8 assistance. At an owner's request, the Secretary may renew for one year, at current rent levels, a section 8 contract for a covered project. The project must expire or end during fiscal year 1996. A low-income housing preservation provision tells the Secretary to use set amounts. The terms come from a House-passed bill. Its March, July, and August 1996 dates are each pushed forward by about six weeks.
plaw-104-121-1996:
Public Law 104-121 carries a program in its name: the Contract with America Advancement Act of 1996, approved March 29, 1996. Its preamble says it provides for enactment of three named measures. It also provides for a permanent increase in the public debt limit.

Title I is the Senior Citizens' Right to Work Act of 1996. It raises the Social Security earnings limit for people who have reached retirement age. It sets a monthly exempt amount that steps up year by year. The amount starts at just over one thousand dollars a month for taxable years ending after 1995 and before 1997. It rises in later years. The other promised pieces, named in the act's opening line, are the Line Item Veto Act and the Small Business Growth and Fairness Act of 1996.
plaw-104-122-1996: Public Law 104-122, approved March 29, 1996, heads itself Further Continuing Appropriations, Fiscal Year 1996. Its first section again extends the stopgap laws. It moves dates in Public Laws 104-99 and 104-92 to April 24, 1996, and makes two small wording changes in other statutes. Its second section does more. It appropriates an additional 198 million dollars for Assistance for Eastern Europe and the Baltic States. The money serves Bosnia and Herzegovina, including demining help and an economic revitalization program in Bosnia.
plaw-104-123-1996:
Alaska mining land changes hands under Public Law 104-123, the Greens Creek Land Exchange Act of 1995, approved April 1, 1996. It provides for the exchange of lands within Admiralty Island National Monument. It also ratifies an agreement behind that exchange.

Congress finds that the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act created the monument. It also gave special provisions for developing the Greens Creek Claims. Those provisions supplement the general mining laws under which the claims were staked. The Kennecott Greens Creek Mining Company holds title to the claims. The surrounding area has further unexplored mineral potential. Talks between the Forest Service and the company produced an agreement. It allows exploration and development on terms consistent with protecting the monument's values. The findings say that agreement requires Congress's approval to take full effect.
plaw-104-124-1996: Public Law 104-124, approved April 1, 1996, is a one-sentence law. It amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to repeal the saccharin notice requirement, by striking paragraph (p) of section 403 of that act, the misbranding section, codified at 21 U.S.C. 343. That is the entire operative text. The bill was H.R. 1787, with a Commerce Committee report, and the printed legislative history shows House passage in December 1995 and Senate passage in March 1996.
plaw-104-125-1996: Public Law 104-125, approved April 1, 1996, is a joint resolution granting Congress's consent to added powers for the Bi-State Development Agency. That is the Missouri-Illinois compact body. The recitals explain that the states had conferred the added powers by a 1993 Missouri act and a 1994 Illinois act. The original compact terms required Congress's approval before such powers could be exercised. The consented powers take effect January 1, 1995. Congress reserves its rights to alter or repeal the consent. It may also require information from the agency.
plaw-104-126-1996:
Vermont and New Hampshire towns may build water systems together under Public Law 104-126, approved April 1, 1996, which grants Congress's consent to the Vermont-New Hampshire Interstate Public Water Supply Compact. The full text of the compact is printed inside the resolution.

Article I states the policy plainly. Municipalities in the two states may need joint public water supply facilities to avoid duplication of cost and effort and to gain economies of scale. The compact defines those facilities broadly: publicly owned water sources, storage, treatment, transmission and distribution facilities, and ancillary facilities, whether or not they qualify for federal or state construction grants. Municipalities means cities, towns, village districts, and other local units that can build and run such systems and raise revenue by bonding and taxation.
plaw-104-127-1996:
Public Law 104-127, the Federal Agriculture Improvement and Reform Act of 1996, approved April 4, 1996, modifies the operation of certain agricultural programs. It is the 1996 farm bill, and its table of contents shows how widely it reaches across farm policy.

Title I is the Agricultural Market Transition Act. Its second subtitle creates production flexibility contracts, with sections on authorization, contract elements, amounts available for payments, payment limits, violations, transfers of interest in contract land, and planting flexibility. The next subtitle covers nonrecourse marketing assistance loans and loan deficiency payments, beginning with loan availability and loan rates. The structure signals a shift toward fixed contract payments and flexible planting, carried out contract by contract with enrolled farms.
plaw-104-128-1996: Public Law 104-128, approved April 9, 1996, is the Federal Tea Tasters Repeal Act of 1996. Its purpose, stated in the bill's own heading line, is to eliminate the Board of Tea Experts by repealing the Tea Importation Act of 1897. The operative section repeals that act, codified at 21 U.S.C. 41 and following, and a third section makes the repeal effective on the date of enactment. The whole law is three short sections, followed by a legislative history for H.R. 2969.
plaw-104-129-1996: Public Law 104-129, approved April 9, 1996, is a joint resolution waiving certain enrollment requirements for two bills of the 104th Congress. Enrollment is the printing of a passed bill, traditionally on parchment, before it goes to the President. The resolution waives sections 106 and 107 of title 1, United States Code, for the enrollment of H.R. 3019 and H.R. 3136, and provides that either enrollment shall be in whatever form the Committee on House Oversight certifies to be a true enrollment. It changes no program or policy.
plaw-104-130-1996:
Public Law 104-130, the Line Item Veto Act, approved April 9, 1996, gives the President line item veto authority over appropriations, new direct spending, and limited tax benefits. It adds a new Part C, Line Item Veto, to title X of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974.

Under the new section 1021, after a bill or joint resolution has been signed into law, the President may cancel certain items in whole. He may cancel any dollar amount of discretionary budget authority. He may cancel any item of new direct spending, or any limited tax benefit. Three findings are required first: the cancellation will reduce the federal deficit, will not impair essential government functions, and will not harm the national interest. Congress must then be notified by a special message within five calendar days, excluding Sundays.
plaw-104-131-1996: Public Law 104-131, approved April 24, 1996, is a joint resolution making further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1996. Its whole effect is a one-day extension. It amends Public Law 104-99 by changing April 24, 1996 to April 25, 1996 in five sections. It makes the same change in one section of Public Law 104-92. The resolution was considered and passed by the House and Senate on April 24. That was the same day it was approved. The timing shows how close to the deadline the stopgap funding had run.
plaw-104-132-1996:
Public Law 104-132, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996, approved April 24, 1996, states its purposes in its first line. The purposes are to deter terrorism, provide justice for victims, and provide for an effective death penalty. Its table of contents shows a long act built in titles.

Title I is habeas corpus reform. Its sections set filing deadlines and govern appeals. They amend the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure. They also amend the statutes known as section 2254 and section 2255. Those statutes govern challenges to state and federal convictions. Limits on second or successive applications and special death penalty litigation procedures follow. Title II is headed Justice for Victims. Its first subtitle makes victim restitution mandatory, with sections on orders of restitution and conditions of probation.
plaw-104-133-1996: Public Law 104-133, approved April 25, 1996, does a single small thing to the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act. Its title states it exactly: the act extends for two months the authority for promulgating regulations under that act. The operative text amends one clause of section 107(a)(2)(B), striking the words 18 months and inserting 20 months in their place. Nothing else in the statute is altered. The bill was H.R. 3034.
plaw-104-134-1996:
The sample for Public Law 104-134 shows a bigger law than its catalog title suggests. Approved April 26, 1996 as H.R. 3019, the text names itself the Omnibus Consolidated Rescissions and Appropriations Act of 1996. It makes appropriations for fiscal year 1996 as a further downpayment toward a balanced budget.

Section 101 enacts the Departments of Commerce, Justice, and State, the Judiciary, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1996. It does so as if that act had been passed as the regular appropriations act. Its Title I funds the Department of Justice. It starts with general administration salaries and expenses at 74 million dollars. That sum includes money for the Facilities Program 2000. It also includes money for oversight of Immigration and Naturalization Service activities. The printed text notes it follows the hand enrollment signed by the President, without corrections.
plaw-104-135-1996: Public Law 104-135, approved April 30, 1996, names the Federal Justice Building in Miami, Florida, as the James Lawrence King Federal Justice Building. The building stands at 99 Northeast Fourth Street, according to the naming section. A second section covers later mentions. Any law, map, rule, paper, or other record that names that building counts as naming the new name. The bill was H.R. 255, reported by the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
plaw-104-136-1996: Public Law 104-136, approved April 30, 1996, names the federal building and United States courthouse at 125 Market Street in Youngstown, Ohio. Their name is the Thomas D. Lambros Federal Building and United States Courthouse. A second section covers later mentions. Any law, map, rule, paper, or other record that names them counts as naming the new name. The act began as H.R. 869 and was reported in House Report 104-365.
plaw-104-137-1996: Public Law 104-137, approved April 30, 1996, names the United States Post Office-Courthouse at South 6th and Rogers Avenue in Fort Smith, Arkansas. Its name is the Judge Isaac C. Parker Federal Building. A second section covers later mentions. Any law, map, rule, paper, or other record that names that building counts as naming the new name. The bill was H.R. 1804, with House Report 104-367.
plaw-104-138-1996: Public Law 104-138, approved April 30, 1996, names the United States Customs Administrative Building at the Ysleta/Zaragosa Port of Entry, 797 South Zaragosa Road in El Paso, Texas, as the Timothy C. McCaghren Customs Administrative Building. Its only other provision is the standard references clause, treating every mention of the building in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, and other records as a reference to the new name. The measure was H.R. 2415, reported in House Report 104-415.
plaw-104-139-1996: Public Law 104-139, approved April 30, 1996, redesignates a federal building in Menlo Park, California. The building at 345 Middlefield Road, until then known as the Earth Sciences and Library Building, becomes the Vincent E. McKelvey Federal Building, and all references to it in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, and other records are to be read under the new name. The act, H.R. 2556, passed the House in December 1995 and the Senate in April 1996.
plaw-104-140-1996: Public Law 104-140, approved May 2, 1996, is a joint resolution making corrections to Public Law 104-134, the omnibus appropriations act enacted the week before. It inserts a title heading. It repeals two Forest Service paragraphs and a section of the veterans and housing appropriations act, plus one section. It replaces an Interior section with a direction that the Secretary convey to the Daughters of the American Colonists, without payment, the 1933 plaque marking the site of Fort San Carlos. The plaque stands at the Great Southern Hotel in Saint Louis.
plaw-104-141-1996:
Historically Black Graduate Professional Schools keep their place in a federal grant program under Public Law 104-141, approved May 6, 1996. It amends section 326 of the Higher Education Act of 1965. Under that section, those schools may receive grants when the Secretary of Education finds they make a substantial contribution to graduate opportunity for African Americans.

The findings give the stakes in numbers stated in the law. The health professions schools in the program train half the nation's African American physicians. They also train half its African American dentists and half its African American pharmacists. And they train three quarters of its African American veterinarians. A majority of their graduates practice in poor urban and rural areas. The operative change is one deletion: section 2 strikes the second sentence of section 326(b), eliminating a grant renewal limitation.
plaw-104-142-1996:
Public Law 104-142, the Mercury-Containing and Rechargeable Battery Management Act, approved May 13, 1996, sets out to phase out the use of mercury in batteries. It also provides for low-cost collection and recycling, or proper disposal, of used nickel cadmium batteries, small sealed lead-acid batteries, and certain other batteries.

Congress finds it in the public interest to teach the public about collecting, recycling, and disposing of such batteries. One national set of labeling rules, the findings say, will greatly help such programs. The labels cover regulated batteries, rechargeable goods, and the boxes they come in. The act also urges people who use rechargeable batteries to take part in drop-off for recycling. Definitions follow, starting with the EPA Administrator and the button cell.
plaw-104-143-1996:
California's Trinity River gets three more years of restoration money under Public Law 104-143, the Trinity River Basin Fish and Wildlife Management Reauthorization Act of 1995. The law was approved May 15, 1996. It amends the Trinity River Basin Fish and Wildlife Management Act of 1984. It extends the availability of money for restoring fish and wildlife in the river.

A clarification of findings changes how success is measured. Restoration is judged not only by returning adult anadromous fish spawners. It is also judged by whether tribal, commercial, and sport fisheries can take part fully. Better in-river and ocean harvest chances are the test. The findings also say the Secretary needs more authority to run a management program. Its long-term goal is restoring the basin's fish and wildlife populations. Those populations in turn support ocean salmon and steelhead harvests.
plaw-104-144-1996:
Alabama and Georgia's shared river valley is the subject of Public Law 104-144, approved May 16, 1996. It grants Congress's consent to an amendment of the Historic Chattahoochee Compact between the two states. Consent matters because interstate compacts need it before they take effect.

The amended articles state the compact's purpose. It is to promote the cooperative development of the Chattahoochee valley's full potential. The goals are historic preservation and tourism.
