The articles also establish a joint interstate authority to help. That body is the Historic Chattahoochee Commission, with 28 members. They must be residents and qualified voters of the party states and counties served. Seats are allocated by county in the text. Two members each come from Barbour, Russell, and Henry counties in Alabama, among the first named.
plaw-104-145-1996:
Public Law 104-145, Megan's Law, approved May 17, 1996, amends the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994. Its subject is stated in its first line: to require the release of relevant information to protect the public from sexually violent offenders.

The act rewrites the release of information subsection of the state registration program statute. Information collected under a state registration program may be disclosed for any purpose permitted under state law. More than that, the designated state law enforcement agency must release relevant information that is necessary to protect the public. Any local agency it authorizes must do the same. The information is about a specific person required to register. One limit is absolute: the identity of a victim of an offense requiring registration shall not be released.
plaw-104-146-1996:
Programs for people with AIDS are revised and extended by Public Law 104-146, the Ryan White CARE Act Amendments of 1996, approved May 20, 1996. It amends the Public Health Service Act parts that came from the Ryan White Comprehensive AIDS Resources Emergency Act of 1990.

The general amendments begin with the grant program for metropolitan areas. Case numbers reported to the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention decide who qualifies. A metropolitan area qualifies where more than 2,000 cases of acquired immune deficiency syndrome have been reported. The count covers the most recent five calendar years with available data. New subsections add rules about population. The amendments continue through the act's grant machinery in the same detailed, section-by-section style.
plaw-104-147-1996:
Water research funding runs through fiscal year 2000 under Public Law 104-147, approved May 24, 1996. It amends the Water Resources Research Act of 1984 and extends its authorizations of appropriations. The act works by editing that statute's findings, purpose, and grant provisions.

In the findings, environmental quality gains a companion concern, the productivity of natural resources and agricultural systems. Two new findings say long-term planning and policy development are essential. The goal is to ensure an abundant supply of high quality water. The findings also say states must have the research and problem-solving capacity to manage their water resources well. The purpose section adds a matching aim: encourage long-term planning and research to meet future water management, quality, and supply challenges. A grants section then takes up matching funds.
plaw-104-148-1996: Public Law 104-148, approved May 24, 1996, authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to acquire the Shadmoor Parcel. It is about 98 acres along the Atlantic Ocean in East Hampton, Suffolk County, New York. The land joins the Amagansett National Wildlife Refuge, with acquired lands managed as part of it. A second section orders corrections within thirty days to the Coastal Barrier Resources System map for the Fire Island Unit. The changes move a boundary to the Sunken Forest Preserve. They remove Point O'Woods Association land from the areas shown as otherwise protected.
plaw-104-149-1996:
School lunchrooms gain room to maneuver under Public Law 104-149, the Healthy Meals for Children Act, approved May 29, 1996. It amends the National School Lunch Act to give schools greater flexibility in meeting the Dietary Guidelines for Americans under the school lunch and school breakfast programs.

The single operative section replaces one subparagraph of section 9(f)(2). A school food service authority may use any reasonable approach, within guidelines the Secretary sets in a timely manner, to meet the nutrition requirements. The listed options include using the school nutrition meal pattern in effect for the 1994-1995 school year. And one limit binds the government rather than the school: the Secretary may not require a school to conduct or use a nutrient analysis to meet the requirements.
plaw-104-150-1996:
Public Law 104-150, the Coastal Zone Protection Act of 1996, approved June 3, 1996, renews the Coastal Zone Management Act of 1972. That act is the main federal framework for helping states plan and protect their coasts. This law adjusts its aid programs.

One section reauthorizes help for developing state coastal programs. It replaces the years 1991 through 1993 with 1997 through 1999. It also doubles a stated figure from two to four. The same section then schedules the program's end: the development assistance subsection is struck effective October 1, 1999. A heading about submittal of state programs for approval is left behind. Further sections, beginning with help for coastal zone enhancement, continue the reauthorization.
plaw-104-151-1996: Public Law 104-151, approved July 1, 1996, designates the United States courthouse in Washington, District of Columbia, as the E. Barrett Prettyman United States Courthouse. The courthouse stands at 3rd Street and Constitution Avenue, Northwest, as the designation section states. A second section provides that any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that courthouse shall be deemed a reference to the E. Barrett Prettyman United States Courthouse. The bill was H.R. 3029, with a Senate companion, S. 1510.
plaw-104-152-1996:
Public Law 104-152, the Anti-Car Theft Improvements Act of 1996, approved July 2, 1996, amends the anti-car theft provisions of title 49. Its aim, stated up front, is to increase the utility of motor vehicle title information to state and federal law enforcement officials.

Three kinds of change follow. Dates move: a system date in section 30502 shifts from January 31, 1996 to December 31, 1997, and a section 30503 date moves to October 1, 1998. The system itself is renamed, from National Automobile Title Information System to National Motor Vehicle Title Information System, everywhere it appears in chapter 305. And authority is delegated by swapping names in the text, striking Secretary of Transportation and inserting Attorney General across five sections, with the reverse swap made in section 30502.
plaw-104-153-1996:
Fake goods are the target of Public Law 104-153, the Anticounterfeiting Consumer Protection Act of 1996, approved July 2, 1996. The act aims to control and prevent commercial counterfeiting. Its findings explain why Congress treated fake trademarked and copyrighted goods as more than a nuisance.

The findings connect fake goods with organized crime. They say fakes deprive real trademark and copyright owners of large revenues and goodwill. They call the trade a multibillion-dollar drain on the United States economy. It eliminates American jobs and threatens consumer health and safety. Section 3 then makes counterfeiting a racketeering offense. It adds four crimes to the racketeering statute: trafficking in counterfeit labels, criminal copyright infringement, taping live music without permission, and trafficking in goods or services bearing counterfeit marks. A later section applies the act to computer programs, their manuals, and packaging.
plaw-104-154-1996: Public Law 104-154, approved July 2, 1996, names a bridge that did not yet exist. It names the bridge set to be completed in the year 2000. That bridge replaces the bridge on Missouri highway 74, spanning from East Cape Girardeau, Illinois, to Cape Girardeau, Missouri. Its name is the Bill Emerson Memorial Bridge. The usual references section follows. Mentions of the bridge in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, and other records count as mentions of the new name. The bill, S. 1903, passed both houses on June 25, 1996.
plaw-104-155-1996:
Public Law 104-155, the Church Arson Prevention Act of 1996, approved July 3, 1996, amends title 18 to clarify federal jurisdiction over offenses relating to damage to religious property. Its findings open the act, and they describe a problem Congress judged serious enough for federal intervention.

Congress finds that arson, destruction, and vandalism of places of worship, and violent interference with religious exercise there, pose a serious national problem. The incidence of church arson had recently increased, the findings say, especially against places of worship serving predominantly African-American congregations. Local jurisdictions had tried to respond, but the problem was widespread and interstate in scope. The findings close by citing Congress's authority under the Commerce Clause, and under the Thirteenth Amendment for race-motivated interference with holding or using religious property.
plaw-104-156-1996:
Public Law 104-156, the Single Audit Act Amendments of 1996, approved July 5, 1996, streamlines and improves chapter 75 of title 31, the chapter commonly called the Single Audit Act. That chapter governs audits of federal awards handled by state and local governments, tribes, and nonprofits.

The stated purposes run in five parts. The amendments promote sound financial management, including effective internal controls, for federal awards run by non-federal entities. They establish uniform requirements for audits of those awards, promote efficient and effective use of audit resources, and reduce burdens on state and local governments, Indian tribes, and nonprofit organizations. Finally, federal agencies should rely on and use the audit work done under the chapter to the maximum extent practicable. The act then rewrites chapter 75 in full, starting with definitions and audit requirements.
plaw-104-157-1996: Public Law 104-157, approved July 9, 1996, names the United States Post Office building at 102 South McLean in Lincoln, Illinois. Its name is the Edward Madigan Post Office Building. A second section covers later mentions. Any law, map, rule, paper, or other record that names that building counts as naming the new name. The bill, H.R. 1880, passed the House in December 1995 and the Senate in June 1996.
plaw-104-158-1996:
Scattered federal parcels in Gilpin County, Colorado are traded away under Public Law 104-158, approved July 9, 1996. It is an act to provide for the exchange of certain lands there. The findings describe land the Bureau of Land Management administers. That land is part of the Royal Gorge Resource Area in the Canon City District.

About 133 separate tracts are involved, ranging from about 38 acres down to much less than an acre. The Bureau's planning process identified them as suitable for disposal. Yet their nearness to existing communities gives them fair market value. The act's purpose is to use that value in exchange. It disposes of federal lands with limited public utility. It acquires lands with important values for permanent public management. Those values include public access, recreation, fish and wildlife habitat, riparian lands, wetlands, and scenic beauty. The exchange itself, involving Lake Gulch, Inc., is directed in section 2.
plaw-104-159-1996: Public Law 104-159, approved July 9, 1996, names the United States Post Office building to be located at 7436 South Exchange Avenue in Chicago, Illinois. It shall be known as the Charles A. Hayes Post Office Building. Its references section covers later mentions. Any law, map, rule, paper, or other record that names that building counts as naming the new name. The bill was H.R. 2704, passing the House in December 1995 and the Senate in June 1996.
plaw-104-160-1996: Public Law 104-160, approved July 9, 1996, designates the Federal building and United States courthouse at 235 North Washington Avenue in Scranton, Pennsylvania, as the William J. Nealon Federal Building and United States Courthouse. A second section provides that references in laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records of the United States to that building and courthouse shall be deemed references to the new name. The act was H.R. 3364, with House Report 104-611 from the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
plaw-104-161-1996:
A government film gets a path to American audiences under Public Law 104-161, approved July 18, 1996. It provides for distribution within the United States of the United States Information Agency film entitled Fragile Ring of Life. It sets aside two statutory limits that normally keep such agency material from domestic release.

The steps are spelled out in one section. The Director of the Information Agency shall make a master copy available to the Archivist of the United States. Once a person seeking domestic release shows that the necessary United States rights and licenses have been secured and paid for, more steps follow. The Archivist shall reimburse the Director's expenses. He shall deposit the film in the National Archives. And he shall make copies available for purchase and public viewing within the United States.
plaw-104-162-1996:
Bulgaria's products win normal American trade treatment under Public Law 104-162, approved July 18, 1996, which authorizes extending nondiscriminatory, or most-favored-nation, treatment to them. It works by ending the application of title IV of the Trade Act of 1974 to Bulgaria.

The findings build the case. Bulgaria had received most-favored-nation treatment since 1991. It had complied with the freedom of emigration requirements of title IV since 1993. It had reversed many years of Communist dictatorship. It had set up a republic under a constitution, with a government chosen by vote. And it had begun market reforms, including the sale of state firms to private owners. Bulgaria was also joining the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and the World Trade Organization. Congress notes that the United States Trade Representative intended to negotiate to preserve Bulgaria's two-way trade commitments in line with those bodies.
plaw-104-163-1996:
Public Law 104-163, the National Children's Island Act of 1995, approved July 19, 1996, requires transferring title to certain real property in Anacostia Park to the District of Columbia. The transfer is meant to ease building National Children's Island. The island is described as a cultural, educational, and family-oriented park.

Definitions fix the ground precisely. The Islands are Heritage Island and the part of Kingman Island south of Benning Road. They sit within the District and the Anacostia River. They are part of United States Reservation 343, as shown on a filed plat and a 1994 land title survey. National Children's Island itself means the recreation park together with a children's playground. Both are developed and run under the District's Children's Island Development Plan Act of 1993. The playground covers the lands south of East Capitol Street.
plaw-104-164-1996:
Public Law 104-164, approved July 21, 1996, amends the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 and the Arms Export Control Act to improve certain defense and security assistance provisions. It also authorizes the transfer of naval vessels to certain foreign countries, as its opening line states.

Title I, Defense and Security Assistance, is organized in chapters visible in the table of contents. Chapter 1 covers military and related assistance. It covers terms of loans and added requirements under the Foreign Military Financing program. It also covers drawdown special authorities and transfers of excess defense articles. Some articles are for certain European countries. Later chapters take up international military education and training, with assistance for Indonesia named. They also take up antiterrorism assistance and training. A further chapter covers international narcotics control assistance, with its own notification and waiver provisions.
plaw-104-165-1996:
Ten acres of Forest Service land in Missouri may be sold under Public Law 104-165, approved July 24, 1996. It authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to convey lands to the city of Rolla. The property is the Rolla Ranger District Administrative Site in Phelps County. It was conveyed to the United States by C.D. and Oma A. Hazlewood in a deed recorded May 6, 1936.

Consideration is the fair market value, set by an appraisal acceptable to the Secretary under the Uniform Appraisal Standards for Federal Land Acquisition. Rolla must pay in full within six months of the conveyance. Or, at the city's option, it may pay in twenty equal annual installments. The payments start the following January 1. The money goes into the Treasury's Sisk Act fund. The city must also agree in writing to hold the United States harmless from claims. Those claims include hazardous materials claims relating to the property.
plaw-104-166-1996:
Traumatic brain injury becomes a named federal prevention program under Public Law 104-166, approved July 29, 1996. It amends the Public Health Service Act to provide for expanded studies and new programs on such injury. It adds a new section 393A to part J of title III.

The Secretary, acting through the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, may run projects to reduce the rate of traumatic brain injury. He may act directly, or through grants and contracts to public or nonprofit private groups. Technical help for planning and running the projects is included. Named activities include research into effective prevention strategies. They also include public information and education programs. Those cover prevention and the injury's public health consequences. The act defines traumatic brain injury as an acquired injury to the brain. It excludes dysfunction from congenital or degenerative disorders and from birth trauma.
plaw-104-167-1996: Public Law 104-167 is the Mollie Beattie Wilderness Area Act, approved July 29, 1996. It renames an Alaskan wilderness. Section 702(3) of Public Law 96-487 is amended: Arctic National Wildlife Refuge Wilderness becomes Mollie Beattie Wilderness. The law also lets the Secretary of the Interior place a monument honoring Beattie. It marks her work for fish, wildlife, and waterfowl conservation and management. The monument stands at a fitting spot he picks within that wilderness. The act itself is just two sentences long; its bill was S. 1899.
plaw-104-168-1996:
Taxpayers gain a second round of legal protections under Public Law 104-168, the Taxpayer Bill of Rights 2, approved July 30, 1996. It amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Its table of contents lays out the protections title by title.

Title I creates a position of Taxpayer Advocate within the Internal Revenue Service. It expands the power to issue Taxpayer Assistance Orders. Title II modifies installment agreement rules. It requires notice of the reasons for terminating an agreement. It also provides agency review of a termination. Title III turns to abatement of interest and penalties. It expands authority to abate interest. It provides review of an IRS failure to abate interest. And it extends the interest-free period for paying tax after notice and demand.
plaw-104-169-1996:
Gambling's growth prompts a federal study under Public Law 104-169, the National Gambling Impact Study Commission Act, approved August 3, 1996. The act's stated purpose is to create the National Gambling Impact and Policy Commission, and its findings explain why Congress wanted fresh facts.

The most recent federal study of gambling, Congress finds, was completed in 1976. Since then legalization had increased substantially over twenty years, and state, local, and tribal governments had made gambling a source of jobs and revenue. New forms, including electronic gambling and gambling over the Internet, could affect interstate and international matters under federal jurisdiction. Questions about social and economic impacts lacked recent, comprehensive information, so the act establishes the National Gambling Impact Study Commission to conduct a comprehensive study of those impacts in the United States.
plaw-104-170-1996:
Pesticide and food safety law is amended together by Public Law 104-170, the Food Quality Protection Act of 1996, approved August 3, 1996. As its opening line states, it amends both the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act and the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

Title I is headed Suspension-Applicators and works on the pesticide statute's suspension rules. Section 6(c)(1) is rewritten. With one exception, no suspension order may issue unless the Administrator has issued a notice of intention. The notice says he intends to cancel the registration or change the classification of the pesticide. He may issue the notice at the same time as the order. Emergency orders get their own timing. The Administrator may issue one before the notice. But he must then proceed to issue the notice within ninety days of the emergency order. The amended text enforces that deadline.
plaw-104-171-1996:
Romania follows the same trade path as its neighbors in Public Law 104-171, approved August 3, 1996, authorizing the extension of nondiscriminatory, most-favored-nation treatment to Romanian products. Seven findings in the act explain Congress's reasoning before the operative sections.

Romania emerged from brutal Communist dictatorship in 1989. It approved a new constitution and elected a parliament by 1991. It held local, parliamentary, and presidential elections under the new order. Its economic reforms included a two-tier banking system and a modern tax system. They also included freed prices, a tariff-based trade regime, and rapid privatization of industry and nearly all agriculture. Romania had received most-favored-nation treatment since 1993. It had complied with the Trade Act's freedom of emigration requirements. It also belonged to the World Trade Organization. Unconditional treatment would let the United States use its full WTO rights.
plaw-104-172-1996:
Sanctions aimed at oil money and weapons are imposed by Public Law 104-172, the Iran and Libya Sanctions Act of 1996, approved August 5, 1996. As its first line states, it sanctions persons making certain investments in Iran or Libya. The investments must directly and significantly help those countries develop petroleum resources. It also sanctions persons exporting items that enhance Libya's weapons or aviation capabilities or its petroleum development.

The findings give the reasons. Iran's efforts to acquire weapons of mass destruction and delivery means, and its support of international terrorism, are said to endanger United States national security and foreign policy interests. Denying Iran the money to sustain its nuclear, chemical, biological, and missile programs takes more than existing initiatives, the findings say. Libya, the findings add, had failed to comply with three United Nations Security Council resolutions. It had supported terrorism, and sought weapons of mass destruction.
plaw-104-173-1996: Public Law 104-173, approved August 6, 1996, gives more time to build two West Virginia power projects. They are FERC Projects No. 6901 and 6902. On the license holder's request, the Commission shall push the start date so that it ends on October 3, 1999. The step follows section 13 of the Federal Power Act, with its good faith, due diligence, and public interest tests. If a license had expired before enactment, the Commission shall reinstate it as of its expiration date. The same deadline applies.
plaw-104-174-1996:
Sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds may load, but not run, certain machines under Public Law 104-174, approved August 6, 1996. It amends the child labor provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 for minors under eighteen who load materials into balers and compactors meeting American National Standards Institute safety standards.

The new paragraph in section 13(c) is carefully bounded. Young employees may load materials into scrap paper balers and paper box compactors, but not operate them or unload materials from them. A machine counts as safe only if it meets the named ANSI standards, Z245.5-1990 for balers and Z245.2-1992 for compactors, or a later standard certified as at least as protective. It must also have an on-off switch with a key-lock or similar system kept in the custody of employees eighteen or older, and the switch must stay off during loading.
plaw-104-175-1996: Public Law 104-175, approved August 6, 1996, makes one change for federal appeals judges. It amends the last sentence of section 46(c) of title 28, United States Code. A circuit judge who took part in an in banc hearing of a case may keep taking part in deciding it after taking senior status. The act adds that ground alongside the existing eligibility wording. The bill was S. 531, reported by the House Judiciary Committee. It passed the Senate in September 1995 and the House in July 1996.
plaw-104-176-1996:
Two states share one lake's management under Public Law 104-176, approved August 6, 1996. It is a joint resolution granting Congress's consent to the Jennings Randolph Lake Project Compact between West Virginia and Maryland. The compact covers natural resource management at the lake project. It also covers enforcement of laws on natural resources and boating there. The project lies in Garrett County, Maryland and Mineral County, West Virginia.

The compact's recitals note that both states approved it. The Army Corps of Engineers, the project's federal builder, concurred. Congress had authorized the Jennings Randolph Lake Project for the North Branch of the Potomac River under Public Law 87-874. Its purposes were flood control, water supply, water quality, and recreation. The recitals also cite the Flood Control Act of 1944. Under it, the Chief of Engineers may build and run public park and recreation facilities in reservoir areas for boating, swimming, and bathing.
plaw-104-177-1996:
Federal employees acting for their own associations are the subject of Public Law 104-177, the Federal Employee Representation Improvement Act of 1996, approved August 6, 1996. It amends title 18 to allow members of employee associations to represent their views before the United States Government. It widens an exemption in section 205.

The rewritten subsection says nothing in the conflict rules prevents an officer or employee from acting without compensation. He must act consistently with faithful performance of duty. He acts as agent or attorney for a person facing disciplinary, loyalty, or other personnel proceedings. It also covers representing a cooperative, voluntary, professional, recreational, or similar nonprofit organization. Most members must be current federal or District employees, or their spouses and dependent children. Exclusions follow: the exemption does not reach claims, proceedings where the group is a party, or matters involving federal grants or contracts for the group.
plaw-104-178-1996: Public Law 104-178, approved August 6, 1996, repeals an old restriction in the federal criminal code. It strikes section 437 of title 18, United States Code. That provision dealt with federal employees contracting or trading with Indians. The act makes the matching change to the table of sections for chapter 23 of that title. The repeal takes effect on enactment. It applies to any contract obtained, and any purchase or sale occurring, on or after that date. The bill was H.R. 3215, reported by the Judiciary Committee.
plaw-104-179-1996:
The ethics office of the federal government is reauthorized by Public Law 104-179, the Office of Government Ethics Authorization Act of 1996, approved August 6, 1996. It amends the Ethics in Government Act of 1978 to extend the authorization of appropriations for the Office of Government Ethics for three years.

Section 2 adds a gift acceptance authority to that act. The Director may accept and use, on behalf of the United States, gifts, donations, bequests, or devises. They may be of money, use of facilities, personal property, or services to aid the office's work. No gift may carry conditions inconsistent with law. And none may require spending appropriated funds that are not available. The Director must also set written rules for judging whether accepting a contribution would reflect unfavorably on the office's fairness and objectivity. The rules also judge whether it would compromise the integrity, or the appearance of integrity, of its programs.
plaw-104-180-1996:
Public Law 104-180, approved August 6, 1996, is the Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1997. It appropriates sums out of the Treasury for those programs, beginning with Title I, Agricultural Programs.

The first account funds the Office of the Secretary of Agriculture at 2,836,000 dollars. It includes capped amounts for outside employment. It also includes amounts for official reception and representation expenses shared with the Foreign Agricultural Service. Two riders limit the money's use. No funds from the act may pay department personnel to carry out one cited paragraph of the 1996 farm act, Public Law 104-127. And none may be used to enforce another cited subsection of it. Executive operations, starting with the Chief Economist, follow in the same line-item pattern.
plaw-104-181-1996:
Two cities with one name, split by a state line, agree to help each other's police under Public Law 104-181, approved August 6, 1996. It is a joint resolution granting Congress's consent to the Mutual Aid Agreement between the city of Bristol, Virginia, and the city of Bristol, Tennessee. It prints the agreement in full.

The recitals cite Virginia and Tennessee statutes authorizing mutual law enforcement assistance. They say the cities want a set plan for rendering aid. The plan covers times when an emergency demands law enforcement beyond either city's existing capabilities. Each city will respond to calls from the other only on request. The request must come from the senior law enforcement officer on duty for the requesting city, or that officer's designee. The response follows the plan the agreement lays out.
plaw-104-182-1996:
Public Law 104-182, the Safe Drinking Water Act Amendments of 1996, approved August 6, 1996. It reauthorizes and amends title XIV of the Public Health Service Act. That part is commonly known as the Safe Drinking Water Act. Findings come early, in section 3, before the amendments begin.

Title I's contents show the act's reach. Sections cover definitions and general authority, then risk assessment, management, and communication, and standard-setting. Treatment technologies for small systems, a limited alternative to filtration, and ground water disinfection follow. Named contaminants get their own section on arsenic, sulfate, and radon, alongside recycling of filter backwash. The list shown in the sample is rounded out by state primacy, enforcement and judicial review, and public notification. Variances and small systems variances, exemptions, lead plumbing and pipes, and capacity development complete it.
plaw-104-183-1996: Public Law 104-183, the Developmental Disabilities Assistance and Bill of Rights Act Amendments of 1996, approved August 6, 1996, extends that act by reauthorizing four of its funding authorities in identical terms. Sections on allotments for states, protection and advocacy of individual rights, university affiliated programs, and projects of national significance are each amended the same way. Each strikes the fiscal years 1995 and 1996 and inserts the fiscal years 1995 through 1999. The whole law is those four short reauthorization sections, as S. 1757.
plaw-104-184-1996:
Washington's water system gains a financing tool under Public Law 104-184, the District of Columbia Water and Sewer Authority Act of 1996, approved August 6, 1996. It amends the District of Columbia Self-Government and Governmental Reorganization Act. The change lets the District's Council authorize revenue bonds for water and sewer facilities.

Section 2 permits issuing revenue bonds for wastewater treatment activities. It adds water and sewer facilities to an existing bond power sentence. A new definition paragraph explains the term broadly. The plants include works for getting, treating, storing, and sending out water. They also include works for collecting, storing, treating, and transporting wastewater and storm drainage. Disposal of liquids and solids resulting from treatment is covered too. A second amendment lets revenues be used to make payments on the bonds. It inserts the water and sewer wording into the payment provisions.
plaw-104-185-1996:
Royalties from federal oil and gas leases are the concern of Public Law 104-185, the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Simplification and Fairness Act of 1996, approved August 13, 1996. Its stated aim is to improve the management of royalties from Federal and Outer Continental Shelf oil and gas leases.

Section 2 begins by amending the definitions in the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1982. A lessee is any person issued a federal oil and gas lease or assigned operating rights in one. New defined terms follow. An adjustment is an amendment to a filed report, with any added payment or credit. It rectifies an underpayment or overpayment. An administrative proceeding is an Interior Department process where a demand, decision, or order is subject to appeal. And an assessment is a fee or charge other than royalty principal, interest, or penalties.
plaw-104-186-1996:
Public Law 104-186, the House of Representatives Administrative Reform Technical Corrections Act, approved August 20, 1996, provides for a representational allowance for Members of the House. It also makes technical and matching changes to various laws. The changes follow from reforms in the House of Representatives.

Title I handles allowances and accounts. Its sections cover the allowance itself. They cover adjustment of House allowances by the Committee on House Oversight and limits on that committee's authority. They also cover clerk hire employees of Members, payments from House accounts, and reports of payments. One section provides that the annotated United States Code for Members is paid from the allowance. Another covers Capitol Police citation release. Title II then gathers technical and matching amendments and repeals tied to the reforms. It starts with sections on the election of Representatives.
plaw-104-187-1996: Public Law 104-187, approved August 20, 1996, redesignates the United States Post Office building at 245 Centereach Mall on Middle Country Road in Centereach, New York, as the Rose Y. Caracappa United States Post Office Building. References in any law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that building are to be read as references to the new name. The bill, H.R. 3139, passed the House on July 30, 1996 and the Senate on August 2.
plaw-104-188-1996:
Public Law 104-188, the Small Business Job Protection Act of 1996, approved August 20, 1996, packs several purposes into its opening line. It provides tax relief for small businesses, protects jobs, creates opportunities, and increases workers' take home pay. It also amends the Portal-to-Portal Act on wages for employees using employer owned vehicles. And it amends the Fair Labor Standards Act to increase the minimum wage rate. At the same time it gives employers flexibility on minimum wage and overtime compliance.

Title I covers small business and other tax provisions. A subtitle on expensing and related items follows an underpayments section. It increases expense treatment for small businesses. It covers employee tips, storage of product samples, certain charitable risk pools, and dues paid to farm organizations. Employment tax status of certain fishermen, tax-exempt bond rules for first-time farmers, and newspaper distributors treated as direct sellers also appear.
plaw-104-189-1996: Public Law 104-189, approved August 20, 1996, renames the Dunning Post Office in Chicago, Illinois. It becomes the Roger P. McAuliffe Post Office, at 6441 West Irving Park Road. A references section covers later mentions. Mentions of that post office in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, and other records count as mentions of the new name. The act, H.R. 3834, passed the House on July 30, 1996 and the Senate on August 2.
plaw-104-190-1996:
Buyouts for a downsizing aid agency are authorized by Public Law 104-190, approved August 20, 1996. It lets the Agency for International Development offer voluntary separation payments to employees who choose to leave. The act is a single long section of definitions and conditions.

An eligible employee is defined as someone employed by the agency under an appointment without time limitation. He must have been employed continuously for at least twelve months. The exclusions matter as much. An employee who could get an immediate annuity on leaving is out. Reemployed annuitants are out too. So are employees who could get disability retirement. And so are employees already facing forced separation for misconduct or poor performance who have been given specific notice. Those boundaries shape the offer as a tool for planned departures, not a general payout.
plaw-104-191-1996:
Public Law 104-191, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, approved August 21, 1996, states a cluster of aims in its first line. It makes coverage easier to carry and keep in the group and individual markets. It combats waste, fraud, and abuse in health insurance and health care delivery. It promotes medical savings accounts. It improves access to long-term care. And it simplifies how health insurance is run.

Title I is Health Care Access, Portability, and Renewability, and its first subtitle sets group market rules through the Employee Retirement Income Security Act. The new part 7 sections increase portability by limiting preexisting condition exclusions. They bar treating participants and those covered unfairly based on health status. They also guarantee renewability in multiemployer plans and multiple employer welfare arrangements. Preemption, state flexibility, and special rules for group health plans follow.
plaw-104-192-1996:
War crimes become a federal crime under United States law in Public Law 104-192, the War Crimes Act of 1996, approved August 21, 1996. It amends title 18 to carry out United States obligations under the Geneva Conventions, adding a new chapter 118, War Crimes, with a single section 2401.

The offense is defined plainly. Whoever, inside or outside the United States, commits a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions shall be fined or imprisoned for life or any term of years. If death results to the victim, he shall also be subject to the death penalty. The reach is limited by a circumstance: the person committing the breach, or the victim, must be a member of the United States Armed Forces or a United States national. Grave breach takes its meaning from the Geneva conventions of August 12, 1949 and their protocols.
plaw-104-193-1996:
Public Law 104-193, the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996, approved August 22, 1996, is the welfare reform law enacted as part of the fiscal year 1997 budget process. Its table of contents shows a large act organized in titles, beginning with cash assistance.

Title I is Block Grants for Temporary Assistance for Needy Families. Its sections open with findings, create the block grants to states in the Social Security Act, and address services provided by charitable, religious, or private groups. Data and study sections follow. They cover grandparents as primary caregivers, data processing reports, and alternative outcomes measures. Conforming amendments reach the Social Security Act, the Food Stamp Act of 1977, and other laws. Later sections require a prototype counterfeit-resistant Social Security card. They also deny assistance and benefits for certain drug-related convictions.
plaw-104-194-1996:
The District of Columbia's budget for fiscal year 1997 is funded by Public Law 104-194, the District of Columbia Appropriations Act, 1997, approved September 9, 1996. It appropriates sums for the government of the District and other activities chargeable against District revenues for the year ending September 30, 1997.

The federal payments lead the text. A federal payment to the District of 660 million dollars is made under the District's self-government act. A federal contribution of about 52 million dollars goes to the Police Officers and Fire Fighters', Teachers', and Judges' Retirement Funds. A further 5.7 million dollars is paid in lieu of reimbursement for expenses of Presidential inauguration activities, to be apportioned by the District's Chief Financial Officer among the act's headings. A federal contribution for repair of the drinking water system follows.
plaw-104-195-1996:
School districts sitting on federally taken land are protected by Public Law 104-195, approved September 16, 1996, which amends the Impact Aid program. It provides a hold-harmless for amounts of payments relating to the federal acquisition of real property. It adds new subsections to section 8002 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965.

One subsection covers former districts. Where a district was formed after 1938 by consolidating two or more former districts, a special election is allowed. For any fiscal year after 1994, the agency may elect to have its eligibility and payment amount set only for the former districts it designates. It must have been eligible under the old 1950 act for fiscal year 1994 or earlier. The hold-harmless subsection then sets floors. For fiscal year 1995, an eligible agency shall receive not less than 85 percent of what it received for fiscal year 1994 under that older law.
plaw-104-196-1996:
Public Law 104-196, the Military Construction Appropriations Act, 1997, approved September 16, 1996. It appropriates money for military construction, family housing, and base realignment and closure for the Department of Defense. The money covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 1997.

The Army account comes first, at 565 million dollars. It covers acquisition, construction, installation, and equipment of public works, military installations, facilities, and real property. The money is available until September 30, 2001. Of that amount, no more than about 50 million dollars may go to study, planning, design, and architect and engineer services. More is allowed only if the Secretary of Defense finds more necessary and tells the spending committees. The same paragraph rescinds about 2 million dollars from an earlier Army construction appropriation in Public Law 103-110. Navy construction, with its own rescissions, follows.
plaw-104-197-1996:
Congress funds itself in Public Law 104-197, the Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 1997, approved September 16, 1996, making appropriations for the legislative branch for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1997. Title I is headed Congressional Operations, and it begins with the Senate.

Expense allowances are listed person by person. Ten thousand dollars goes to each of the Vice President, the President Pro Tempore, and the Majority and Minority Leaders. Five thousand goes to each Whip. Three thousand goes to each Conference Committee chairman. The total is 56 thousand dollars. Representation allowances give each Senate leader fifteen thousand dollars. Salaries of officers and employees are funded at about 74 million dollars. They are paid without regard to the limitations that follow in the text, starting with the office of the Vice President.
plaw-104-198-1996:
Pueblo of Isleta land claims get a courtroom under Public Law 104-198, approved September 18, 1996. It confers jurisdiction on the United States Court of Federal Claims. The court is to hear, determine, and render judgment on the tribe's land claims against the United States. The usual time limits in title 28 and the 1946 Indian claims law do not bar the case.

The claims concern lands in New Mexico or any adjoining state, held by aboriginal title or otherwise. The United States acquired them without adequate compensation. As adequate compensation, the court may award interest at five percent per year from the date of acquisition. Jurisdiction covers only claims accruing on or before August 13, 1946. The claims must be filed within three years of enactment. A second section says awards to other tribes on the same lands shall not count as a defense, estoppel, or set-off against the Pueblo's claim.
plaw-104-199-1996:
Public Law 104-199, the Defense of Marriage Act, approved September 21, 1996, states its purpose in its opening line: to define and protect the institution of marriage. It does so in two operative sections, one on state powers and one on definitions in federal law.

Section 2 adds a new section 1738C to chapter 115 of title 28. It provides that no state, territory, or possession of the United States, or Indian tribe, shall be required to give effect to a same-sex marriage from another state. More exactly, it covers any public act, record, or judicial proceeding respecting a relationship between persons of the same sex that is treated as a marriage there. It also covers a right or claim arising from such a relationship. Section 3 then adds a definition of marriage and spouse to chapter 1 of title 1, governing how Acts of Congress are read.
plaw-104-200-1996: Public Law 104-200, approved September 22, 1996, makes technical corrections in the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1982, and the corrections are single words. It changes provision to provisions in one definition. It inserts the word so in one sentence and the word not in another. It changes rate to date, owned to owed in two sentences, dues to due, and it to its. That list of seven word-level fixes is the entire act. The act began as H.R. 4018 and passed both houses in September 1996.
plaw-104-201-1996:
Public Law 104-201 is the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1997, approved September 23, 1996. Like its fiscal 1996 counterpart earlier in this set of laws, it authorizes appropriations for military activities of the Department of Defense. It also covers military construction and defense activities of the Department of Energy. It prescribes personnel strengths for the Armed Forces for that year.

This year's act is organized into three divisions rather than five. Division A holds the Department of Defense authorizations. Division B holds the military construction authorizations. Division C holds the Department of Energy national security authorizations and other authorizations. Division A opens with Title I, Procurement, whose first subtitle authorizes appropriations service by service: Army, then Navy and Marine Corps, then Air Force.
plaw-104-202-1996: Public Law 104-202, approved September 24, 1996, names the Department of Veterans Affairs medical center in Jackson, Mississippi, as the G.V. (Sonny) Montgomery Department of Veterans Affairs Medical Center. Any reference to that medical center in a law, regulation, map, document, record, or other paper of the United States is to be considered a reference to the new name. Unusually for a naming law, it sets its own start: the designation takes effect at noon on January 3, 1997. The bill was S. 1669.
plaw-104-203-1996:
Cambodia's products receive normal trade treatment under Public Law 104-203, approved September 25, 1996, which extends nondiscriminatory, most-favored-nation treatment to them. Section 2 makes the change in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule. It strikes the name Kampuchea from general note 3(b). The change is effective for goods entered on or after a Federal Register notice.

The findings are candid about the country receiving the benefit. Congress finds that repression by the Cambodian government had recently increased. Corruption was contributing to substantial environmental degradation. Still, Cambodia had made some progress toward democratic rule after twenty years of undemocratic regimes and civil war. It was rebuilding its market economy. Unconditional treatment would help that economy develop on free market principles. It would promote United States exports in Southeast Asia. And it would encourage further progress on human rights and democratic rule.
plaw-104-204-1996:
Public Law 104-204, approved September 26, 1996, is the Departments of Veterans Affairs and Housing and Urban Development, and Independent Agencies Appropriations Act for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1997. It funds two large departments plus sundry independent agencies, boards, commissions, and offices.

Title I covers the Department of Veterans Affairs. Its first account, under the Veterans Benefits Administration, pays compensation and pensions. About 18.7 billion dollars covers compensation benefits, pension benefits, burial benefits, and related payments. The money is authorized across many chapters of title 38, to remain available until expended. A proviso caps at about 26 million dollars the amount of that money to be paid back to general operating expenses. The line-item pattern continues through the act for housing programs and the independent agencies.
plaw-104-205-1996:
Public Law 104-205, approved September 30, 1996, is the Department of Transportation and Related Agencies Appropriations Act for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1997. Title I funds the Department of Transportation, beginning with the Office of the Secretary.

That office receives about 53 million dollars for necessary expenses. Part of the money shall be used to investigate anticompetitive practices in air transportation. It shall also enforce a cited title 49 section, and report progress to Congress by the end of the fiscal year. Up to 40 thousand dollars may be allocated for official reception and representation. A proviso credits up to one million dollars in user fees for the electronic tariff filing system. Another bars using funds to maintain custody of airline tariffs. Those tariffs are already available to the public at no cost. The Office of Civil Rights follows at about 5.6 million dollars.
plaw-104-206-1996:
Public Law 104-206, the Energy and Water Development Appropriations Act, 1997, approved September 30, 1996, makes appropriations for energy and water development for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1997. Title I, unusually, covers the Department of Defense in its civil role, through the Army Corps of Engineers.

Corps money is to be spent under the direction of the Secretary of the Army and the supervision of the Chief of Engineers. It is for rivers and harbors, flood control, beach erosion, and related purposes. The first account, general investigations, provides about 154 million dollars, available until expended. The money pays for collecting basic information. It also pays for restudying authorized projects, and preparing surveys, plans, and specifications. Named projects with set amounts follow immediately: Norco Bluffs, California at 180 thousand dollars, the San Joaquin River Basin's Caliente Creek at 150 thousand, and Tampa Harbor's Alafia Channel at 100 thousand.
plaw-104-207-1996: Public Law 104-207, approved September 30, 1996, waives certain enrollment requirements for any bill or joint resolution of the 104th Congress making general or continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1997. It waives sections 106 and 107 of title 1, United States Code. Those sections govern printing the enrollment of such an appropriation measure on parchment or otherwise. The waiver covers measures presented to the President after its enactment. In place of the waived form, the enrollment shall be whatever the Committee on House Oversight certifies to be a true enrollment.
plaw-104-208-1996:
Readers should note a catalog mismatch here: the entry title names the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, but the text in this sample is something else entirely. Headed as Public Law 104-208 and approved September 30, 1996, the document identifies itself as the Omnibus Consolidated Appropriations Act, 1997, enacted as H.R. 3610, making omnibus consolidated appropriations for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1997.

Division A begins the spending. Section 101 enacts the Departments of Commerce, Justice, and State, the Judiciary, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1997, as if it had passed as the regular act. Its Justice Department title opens with general administration salaries and expenses of about 76 million dollars. That sum includes the Facilities Program 2000. It also includes a cap on positions and spending for the Department Leadership Program. Whatever the catalog title says, the pages a reader gets are an omnibus spending law.
plaw-104-209-1996: Public Law 104-209, approved October 1, 1996, authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to acquire certain interests in Waihee Marsh for inclusion in the Oahu National Wildlife Refuge Complex. The marsh lies on the northeast coast of the island of Oahu, Hawaii, and consists of approximately 36 acres, as determined by the Secretary, along both sides of Kamehameha Highway. Any lands and interests acquired under the act shall be managed by the Secretary as part of that refuge complex. The bill was H.R. 1772, with House Report 104-528.
plaw-104-210-1996:
Donated food gets legal protection under Public Law 104-210, approved October 1, 1996, which encourages donation of food and grocery products to nonprofit organizations for distribution to needy individuals. It gives the Model Good Samaritan Food Donation Act the full force of law, renaming it for Bill Emerson.

Section 1 converts the model act to permanent law and transfers it to the Child Nutrition Act of 1966. It strikes model from headings and inserts Bill Emerson Good Samaritan. Gross negligence means voluntary, conscious conduct. The person must have known the conduct was likely to harm another's health or well-being. The liability rule then protects donors. A person or gleaner who donates apparently wholesome food in good faith to a nonprofit is not subject to civil or criminal liability. The protection covers claims arising from the food's nature, age, packaging, or condition. Parallel protection covers the nonprofit.
plaw-104-211-1996:
About eight thousand acres join the Goshute Indian Reservation under Public Law 104-211, approved October 1, 1996. The law amends Public Law 103-93, the Utah Schools and Lands Improvement Act of 1993. Its aim is to provide additional lands in Utah for the reservation. It inserts a new section 11 into that act.

The added lands, public lands and lands belonging to the State of Utah, comprise about 8,000 acres of surface and subsurface estate. They are declared part of the Goshute Indian Reservation once two things happen. The state lands must be conveyed, and the United States must accept title. The Secretary of the Interior may acquire the state-owned lands through exchange, subject to valid existing rights. The 1993 act's other provisions on transferred lands apply here too, with one cost shifted. The Goshute Indian Tribe pays for appraising the lands, before the transfer is made.
plaw-104-212-1996:
Two wildlife refuges, in Nebraska and Rhode Island, are reshaped by Public Law 104-212, approved October 1, 1996. Its titles separate the jobs: Title I revises the boundary of the North Platte National Wildlife Refuge, and Title II expands the Pettaquamscutt Cove National Wildlife Refuge.

For North Platte, the act terminates the Fish and Wildlife Service's secondary jurisdiction over about 2,470 acres. Those acres are shown on an August 1995 relinquishment map. The act also revokes Executive Order 2446 of August 21, 1916 for that land. For Pettaquamscutt Cove, the Secretary may acquire Foddering Farm Acres. The farm is about 100 acres adjacent to Long Cove in Rhode Island. It is bordered by Foddering Farm Road and Point Judith Road, as shown on a May 1996 map. The refuge boundaries are revised to include the acquired area.
plaw-104-213-1996:
Alabama takes over a federal fish hatchery under Public Law 104-213, the Carbon Hill National Fish Hatchery Conveyance Act, approved October 1, 1996. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey the Carbon Hill National Fish Hatchery to the State of Alabama. The state Game and Fish Division will use it as part of the state fish culture program.

The conveyance must happen within 180 days of enactment, without reimbursement. The property is the hatchery on County Road 63 at Carbon Hill in Walker County, about 67 acres. It comes with all improvements and related personal property. That includes buildings, structures, equipment, easements, leases, and water rights. A reversion clause guards the purpose. If the state uses the property for anything detrimental to fishery resources management and fisheries-related activities, title reverts to the United States. The state must return it in substantially the same or better condition.
plaw-104-214-1996:
Penalties for attacking witnesses and juries are tied to the underlying case by Public Law 104-214, approved October 1, 1996. It amends title 18 with respect to witness retaliation, witness tampering, and jury tampering, in three parallel changes to sections 1513, 1512, and 1503.

Each amendment sets the same kind of ceiling. If retaliation occurred because of attendance at or testimony in a criminal case, the maximum prison term is set by a comparison. It is the higher of the term otherwise provided by law or the maximum term that could have been imposed for any offense charged in that case. Tampering under section 1512 gets the same rule when the offense occurs in connection with a criminal trial. For section 1503, the higher maximum applies where the offense occurs in connection with a criminal trial and involves the threat of physical force or physical force itself.
plaw-104-215-1996: Public Law 104-215 is the Crawford National Fish Hatchery Conveyance Act, approved October 1, 1996. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey the hatchery to the city of Crawford, Nebraska, for use as a city park. The transfer is free and must occur within 180 days. The property is 5.95 acres, with its buildings, equipment, easements, leases, and water rights. If the city uses it for any unauthorized purpose, all title reverts to the United States. The city must return it in substantially the same or better condition.
plaw-104-216-1996: Public Law 104-216, the Federal Trade Commission Reauthorization Act of 1996, approved October 1, 1996, authorizes appropriations for the Federal Trade Commission by amending section 25 of the Federal Trade Commission Act. The amendment adds two caps to that section: not to exceed 107 million dollars for fiscal year 1997, and not to exceed 111 million dollars for fiscal year 1998. That is the whole operative change. The bill was H.R. 3553, with a Senate companion, S. 1840, and reports from both houses' commerce committees.
plaw-104-217-1996: Public Law 104-217, the Carjacking Correction Act of 1996, approved October 1, 1996, amends title 18 to clarify Congress's intent in the federal carjacking prohibition. Its one operative change inserts words into section 2119(2). The change extends a cross-reference. It now includes any conduct that, if it occurred in the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the United States, would violate section 2241 or 2242 of title 18. Those are the aggravated sexual abuse provisions. The bill was H.R. 3676, with House Report 104-787.
plaw-104-218-1996:
Mother Teresa becomes an honorary citizen of the United States under Public Law 104-218, a joint resolution approved October 1, 1996. It confers the honor on Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu, also known as Mother Teresa. Its recitals stress how rare the honor is. The United States had conferred honorary citizenship only three times in more than two hundred years.

The recitals praise her tireless work with orphaned and abandoned children, the poor, the sick, and the dying. She founded the Missionaries of Charity in 1950 and took in people rejected as unacceptable, regardless of race, color, creed, or condition. Her honors included the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize and the 1985 Presidential Medal of Freedom. Within the United States, her order had established soup kitchens, shelters for women and for unwed mothers, and homes for the dying. It had also set up prison ministry, nursing homes, and programs for children.
plaw-104-219-1996: Public Law 104-219, approved October 1, 1996, clarifies the rules governing removal of cases to federal court by changing a few words in section 1447(c) of title 28. The first sentence of that subsection now speaks of any defect other than lack of subject matter jurisdiction, where it previously said any defect in removal procedure. That single phrase substitution is the entire act. The bill was S. 533, with House Report 104-799, passing the Senate in June 1995 and the House in September 1996.
plaw-104-220-1996: Public Law 104-220, approved October 1, 1996, repeals a redundant venue provision, as its title says. Section 1 repeals subsection (a) of section 1392 of title 28, United States Code, the venue statute. It also makes a technical amendment to subsection (b). The amendment strikes its opening words (b) Any and inserts Any. The surviving text thus reads as a single provision. Nothing else is changed by the act. It began as S. 677, with House Report 104-800 from the Judiciary Committee.
plaw-104-221-1996: Public Law 104-221, approved October 1, 1996, designates the United States Courthouse under construction at 1030 Southwest 3rd Avenue in Portland, Oregon, as the Mark O. Hatfield United States Courthouse, with the usual clause treating references to the courthouse in federal records as references to the new name. Two sections ride along: Franklin Delano Roosevelt memorial commissioners who leave Congress may, with approval, serve one more year, and the act takes effect January 3, 1997. The bill was S. 1636.
plaw-104-222-1996: Public Law 104-222, approved October 1, 1996, authorizes construction of the Smithsonian Institution National Air and Space Museum Dulles Center at Washington Dulles International Airport. Section 1 gives the Smithsonian's Board of Regents the authority to construct the center. Section 2 sets the funding condition in one sentence: no appropriated funds may be used to pay any expense of the construction authorized by the act. The bill was S. 1995, passing the Senate in July 1996 and the House that September.
plaw-104-223-1996:
A trust fund for tribal infrastructure is created by Public Law 104-223, the Crow Creek Sioux Tribe Infrastructure Development Trust Fund Act of 1996, approved October 1, 1996. It provides certain benefits of the Pick-Sloan Missouri River basin program to the Crow Creek Sioux Tribe, and its findings tell the history behind the benefit.

Congress approved the Pick-Sloan program in the Flood Control Act of 1944 to develop the country, irrigate land above Sioux City, Iowa, and protect areas from Missouri River floods. The Fort Randall and Big Bend projects, major parts of that program, generate substantial hydropower and store substantial water. But they overlie the reservation's western boundary and inundated the tribe's fertile bottom lands, its most productive farmland and its homeland. The findings note that Public Law 85-916 authorized acquiring 9,418 acres of Crow Creek land for the Fort Randall project.
plaw-104-224-1996: Public Law 104-224, approved October 2, 1996, repeals an unnecessary medical device reporting requirement, in its title's own words. Its single section amends section 1862 of the Social Security Act, codified at 42 U.S.C. 1395y, by striking subsection (h). No replacement text is added and nothing else in the statute is touched. The bill was H.R. 2366, reported by the Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, passing the House in November 1995 and the Senate in September 1996.
plaw-104-225-1996: Public Law 104-225, approved October 2, 1996, names two Asheville, North Carolina buildings together as the Veach-Baley Federal Complex. One is the Federal building at the corner of Patton Avenue and Otis Street. The other is the United States courthouse on Otis Street. Its references section covers later mentions. Any law, map, rule, paper, or other record that names those buildings counts as naming the Veach-Baley Federal Complex. The bill was H.R. 2504, with House Report 104-416.
plaw-104-226-1996: Public Law 104-226, approved October 2, 1996, repeals the Medicare and Medicaid Coverage Data Bank. Section 1 repeals section 1144 of the Social Security Act, the data bank provision added by the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1993. It then makes conforming amendments undoing that act's related changes. One sits in the Medicare provisions of section 1862(b)(5). One sits in the Medicaid state plan requirements of section 1902(a)(25). And one sits in the data matching definitions of title 5, where a clause is struck. The bill was H.R. 2685.
plaw-104-227-1996:
Public Law 104-227 is the Antarctic Science, Tourism, and Conservation Act of 1996, approved October 2, 1996. It implements the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty. Title I amends the Antarctic Conservation Act of 1978, starting with its findings and purpose.

The new findings record that for well over a quarter of a century, science has been the main activity of the federal government and United States nationals there. More recently, American tourist interest in the region has increased. The National Science Foundation is the lead civilian agency there. It has long been responsible for ensuring that United States science and tourism, and their supporting logistics, are run with an eye to preserving the region's unique values. The amendments also swap the older Agreed Measures on Antarctic fauna and flora for the Protocol. The Protocol becomes the foundation for conserving the region's resources.
plaw-104-228-1996: Public Law 104-228, approved October 2, 1996, names the Federal building at 1655 Woodson Road in Overland, Missouri, as the Sammy L. Davis Federal Building. A references section covers later mentions. Any law, map, rule, paper, or other record that names that building counts as naming the new name. Its bill was House bill 3186, with House Report 104-609. It passed the House in June 1996 and the Senate that September.
plaw-104-229-1996: Public Law 104-229, approved October 2, 1996, names a courthouse before it is built. It designates the Federal building and United States courthouse to be constructed at a site on 18th Street between Dodge and Douglas Streets in Omaha, Nebraska, as the Roman L. Hruska Federal Building and United States Courthouse. References to that building and courthouse in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, and other records are to be read under the new name. The bill was H.R. 3400, with House Report 104-610.
plaw-104-230-1996: Public Law 104-230, approved October 2, 1996, designates the United States courthouse under construction at 611 North Florida Avenue in Tampa, Florida, as the Sam M. Gibbons United States Courthouse. All references to that courthouse in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, and other records are to be deemed references to the new name. A third section delays the act's own start: it becomes effective on January 3, 1997. The bill was H.R. 3710, with a Senate companion, S. 1977.
plaw-104-231-1996:
Government records move online under Public Law 104-231, the Electronic Freedom of Information Act Amendments of 1996, approved October 2, 1996. It amends section 552 of title 5, the Freedom of Information Act, to provide for public access to information in an electronic format.

The findings rehearse what the older act does. It requires agencies to make certain information available for public inspection and copying. It lets any person obtain agency records, subject to exemptions, for any public or private purpose. Since 1966, Congress finds, the act has disclosed waste, fraud, abuse, and wrongdoing. It has identified unsafe consumer products, harmful drugs, and serious health hazards. Now agencies increasingly use computers to conduct business and store publicly valuable records, the findings say. Agencies should use the new technology to enhance public access to those records and information.
plaw-104-232-1996:
A shrinking commission is kept alive by Public Law 104-232, the Parole Commission Phaseout Act of 1996, approved October 2, 1996. Its stated purpose is to extend the Parole Commission to oversee cases of prisoners sentenced under prior law, while reducing the commission's size.

Extension works by substitution: in the Sentencing Reform Act provision on the commission, ten years becomes fifteen years. The commission may also act with any quorum of commissioners it prescribes by regulation. The reductions then arrive on fixed dates. Effective December 31, 1999, the commission may have no more than two commissioners, with the least senior leaving first. Effective December 31, 2001, it consists only of its Chairman, who may then delegate specified powers to hearing examiners, with the Attorney General acting in the Chairman's absence.
plaw-104-233-1996: Public Law 104-233, approved October 2, 1996, reauthorizes the Indian Environmental General Assistance Program Act of 1992 in a single sentence. It amends section 502(h) of that act by striking the figure 15,000,000 dollars and inserting the words such sums as may be necessary, converting a fixed authorization ceiling into an open-ended one. That is the entire law apart from its heading. The bill was S. 1834, with Senate Report 104-338 from the Committee on Indian Affairs, passing the Senate in August 1996 and the House in September.
plaw-104-234-1996:
Goods from the West Bank and Gaza Strip gain a route to duty-free entry under Public Law 104-234, approved October 2, 1996. It is headed West Bank and Gaza Strip Free Trade Benefits. It amends the United States-Israel Free Trade Area Implementation Act of 1985. The change gives the President proclamation authority for articles of the West Bank, the Gaza Strip, or a qualifying industrial zone.

A new section 9 authorizes the President to proclaim the elimination or modification of any existing duty. The duty must apply to a qualifying article. The article must be wholly the growth, product, or manufacture of the West Bank, Gaza Strip, or a qualifying zone. Or it must be a new or different article of commerce made there. It must be imported directly from there or from Israel. A content test applies: materials and processing costs from those places must reach 35 percent of appraised value on entry.
plaw-104-235-1996:
Public Law 104-235, the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act Amendments of 1996, approved October 3, 1996, modifies and reauthorizes the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act. Its table of contents shows Title I amending that act section by section, after opening findings.

Subtitle A, the general program, covers the Office on Child Abuse and Neglect and the Advisory Board on Child Abuse and Neglect. It also repeals the Inter-Agency Task Force on Child Abuse and Neglect. It provides for a national clearinghouse for information on child abuse. It also covers research, evaluation and assistance activities, grants for demonstration programs, and state grants for prevention and treatment programs. Definitions, authorization of appropriations, a rule of construction, and technical amendments close the subtitle. Subtitle B then establishes a program of community-based family resource and support grants.
plaw-104-236-1996:
Sex offenders are tracked nationally under Public Law 104-236, the Pam Lychner Sexual Offender Tracking and Identification Act of 1996, approved October 3, 1996. It is an act to provide for the nationwide tracking of convicted sexual predators. Section 2 adds a new FBI database section to the 1994 violent crime act's registration subtitle.

The new section 170102 defines its terms by borrowing them from the existing registration statute. It also defines a minimally sufficient state sexual offender registration program. Such a program must require registration of offenders convicted of the listed offenses. It must transmit all information gathered to the FBI as the section directs. It must meet the statute's checking rules. And it must require each covered person to register for not less than ten years from the stated starting date. The database gives those state registrations a single federal destination.
plaw-104-237-1996:
Public Law 104-237, the Comprehensive Methamphetamine Control Act of 1996, approved October 3, 1996, aims, in its opening line, to prevent the illegal making and use of methamphetamine. Findings come in section 2. The act is then built in titles aimed at points in the drug's supply chain.

Title I addresses bringing the drug and its precursor chemicals into the country. It supports control efforts abroad and penalizes making listed chemicals with intent to import them into the United States. Title II works on making the drug at home. It covers seizure and forfeiture of regulated chemicals, and a study on preventing sales of production agents. It raises penalties for making and possessing equipment. It adds iodine and hydrochloric gas to list II. It sets civil penalties for firms supplying precursor chemicals. It also covers court orders, cleanup payback for secret lab sites, and record retention. Title III increases penalties for trafficking and manufacture.
plaw-104-238-1996:
Families of fallen officers receive college help under Public Law 104-238, the Federal Law Enforcement Dependents Assistance Act of 1996, approved October 3, 1996. It provides college help to dependents of federal law enforcement officials killed or disabled in the performance of their duties. It adds a subpart to the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968.

The existing part is relabeled Subpart 1, Death Benefits. The new Subpart 2 covers college help to dependents of civilian federal law enforcement officers killed or disabled in the line of duty. Its purposes are threefold. First, to enhance the appeal of service in civilian federal law enforcement. Second, to extend higher education to deserving persons who, because an eligible officer died or was totally disabled, might not otherwise afford it. Third, to let family members reach the educational status they would have attained had a parent or spouse not been killed or disabled.
plaw-104-239-1996:
A standby fleet for national defense is established by Public Law 104-239, the Maritime Security Act of 1996, approved October 8, 1996. It amends the Merchant Marine Act, 1936 to revitalize the United States-flag merchant marine. It restructures title VI of that act into vessel operating assistance programs. A new subtitle covers the Maritime Security Fleet Program.

The Secretary of Transportation shall establish a fleet of active, militarily useful, privately owned vessels. The fleet will meet national defense and other security requirements. It will also maintain a United States presence in international commercial shipping. The fleet, known as the Maritime Security Fleet, consists of privately owned United States-flag vessels covered by operating agreements under the new subtitle. The older operating-differential subsidy program remains as subtitle A. So the act pairs an existing subsidy structure with a defense-ready fleet held in commercial service.
plaw-104-240-1996: Public Law 104-240, approved October 8, 1996, makes a two-word change with a practical effect stated in its title. A county-run health insuring organization may qualify for an exemption from certain Medicaid requirements. It may do so even though it enrolls Medicaid beneficiaries residing in another county. The text amends a cited subsection of the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1985. It inserts the words or counties after the word county. The amendment applies to quarters beginning on or after October 1, 1996. The bill was H.R. 3056.
plaw-104-241-1996: Public Law 104-241, approved October 9, 1996, gives more time to build three Arkansas power projects. They are FERC Projects 4204, 4660, and 4659. On the license holder's request, and after reasonable notice, the Commission may extend the start-of-work period. The extension may run up to three straight two-year periods. It must follow section 13 of the Federal Power Act, with its good faith, due diligence, and public interest tests. The extension takes effect when the Commission's own earlier extension for the project expires. Its bill was House bill 657.
plaw-104-242-1996: Public Law 104-242, approved October 9, 1996, extends building time for two FERC power projects, No. 4244 and 10648. Despite section 13 of the Federal Power Act, the Commission may grant more time. On the license holder's request, and after reasonable notice, it may extend each project's start deadline by up to three straight two-year periods. The step follows that section's good faith, due diligence, and public interest standards. The act takes effect for each project when the Commission's prior extension expires. It began as House bill 680, with a Senate companion, S. 1012.
plaw-104-243-1996: One Ohio power project is the subject of Public Law 104-243, approved October 9, 1996. It is FERC Project 9423. The law lets the Commission extend the deadline for starting work by up to three straight two-year periods. The license holder must ask, with reasonable notice given. The extension overrides the time limits in section 13 of the Federal Power Act. It stays subject to that section's good faith, due diligence, and public interest tests. It applies once the Commission's earlier extension has expired. Its bill was House bill 1011.
plaw-104-244-1996: Public Law 104-244, approved October 9, 1996, allows more time under the FERC license for Project No. 3701. On the license holder's request, the Commission may extend the start-of-work period by up to three straight two-year periods. The step follows section 13 of the Federal Power Act and its good faith, due diligence, and public interest standards. If the license expired before enactment, the Commission is directed to reinstate it effective June 1, 1995. Its bill was House bill 1014, reported by the House Commerce Committee.
plaw-104-245-1996: Public Law 104-245, approved October 9, 1996, reinstates the permit for an Oregon power project, FERC Project 7829. It also extends its deadline under the Federal Power Act. Despite the permit's expiration, the Commission shall, at the license holder's request, reinstate the permit effective May 23, 1993. It shall extend the start-of-work period so that it ends on May 25, 1999. The short act does nothing else. It began as House bill 1290, with Senate companion S. 538.
plaw-104-246-1996: A West Virginia power project gains time under Public Law 104-246, approved October 9, 1996. It is FERC Project 7307. On the license holder's request, the Commission shall extend the start-of-work period so it ends on September 26, 1999. The step follows section 13 of the Federal Power Act, with its good faith, due diligence, and public interest tests. If the project's license had expired before enactment, the Commission shall reinstate it as of its expiration date. The same deadline then applies. Its bill was House bill 1335.
