plaw-104-247-1996: Public Law 104-247, approved October 9, 1996, allows more time under the FERC license for the Mt. Hope Waterpower Project, Project 9401. On the license holder's request, and after reasonable notice, the Commission may extend the start-of-work deadline until August 3, 1999. The extension overrides the limits in section 13 of the Federal Power Act. It stays subject to that section's good faith, due diligence, and public interest tests. The act is a single section. Its bill was House bill 1366, with Senate companion S. 611.
plaw-104-248-1996: Public Law 104-248, approved October 9, 1996, amends title XIX of the Social Security Act, the Medicaid title, with technical fixes about physicians' services. One fix corrects a cross-reference to the unique identifier system. It changes subsection (v) to subsection (x) in section 1902(a). It is effective as if included in the 1990 amendments. Another fix corrects billing rules for services to children and pregnant women. It adds certification in family practice, pediatrics, or obstetrics by the board recognized by the American Osteopathic Association.
plaw-104-249-1996: Public Law 104-249, approved October 9, 1996, extends the deadline under the Federal Power Act for a Kentucky power project, FERC Project 10228. At the license holder's request, and after reasonable notice, the Commission shall extend the start-of-work period. The extension adds not more than three straight two-year periods to its earlier extension. It follows section 13's good faith, due diligence, and public interest tests. The law takes effect when that earlier extension expires. Its bill was House bill 2501, with House Report 104-507.
plaw-104-250-1996:
Animal drugs get a reworked approval process under Public Law 104-250, the Animal Drug Availability Act of 1996, approved October 9, 1996. It amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to improve the process of approving and using animal drugs, and its amendments are written as changes to that act's sections.

Section 2 rewrites the definition of substantial evidence of effectiveness in section 512(d). Substantial evidence now means evidence from one or more adequate and well controlled investigations. The examples include a study in a target species, a study in laboratory animals, a required field investigation, a bioequivalence study, or an in vitro study. The evidence must come from experts qualified by scientific training and experience. It must let such experts fairly and reasonably conclude the drug will have the effect its labeling claims. Conforming amendments follow.
plaw-104-251-1996:
Railroad workers' unemployment benefits start sooner under Public Law 104-251, the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Amendments Act of 1996, approved October 9, 1996. Its stated purpose is to reduce the waiting period for benefits payable under the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act.

Section 2 replaces the waiting period paragraph of section 2(a)(1). Generally, benefits are payable to a qualified employee for each day of unemployment in excess of four during any registration period within a period of continuing unemployment. For the employee's first registration period in an initial period of continuing unemployment in a benefit year, the threshold is seven days instead. Strikes carry a longer wait. Where the Board finds unemployment due to a work stoppage from a strike at the employee's last workplace, no benefits are payable for the first fourteen days of that unemployment.
plaw-104-252-1996: Public Law 104-252, approved October 9, 1996, extends the deadline for starting work on an Illinois power project, FERC Project 3246. At the license holder's request, the Commission shall extend the start deadline until October 15, 1997. The step follows section 13 of the Federal Power Act, with its good faith, due diligence, and public interest tests. The extension takes effect when the Commission's previous extension expires. The Commission may also reinstate the project's license as of its expiration or termination. Its bill was House bill 2630.
plaw-104-253-1996:
Two Louisiana wildlife refuges gain ground and money under Public Law 104-253, approved October 9, 1996. It increases the amount authorized to be appropriated to the Department of the Interior for the Tensas River National Wildlife Refuge. Section 1 rewrites the authorization in the refuge's 1980 establishing act. It reads: beginning October 1, 1995, not to exceed 20 million dollars to the Department of the Interior.

Section 2 expands a different refuge, the Bayou Sauvage Urban National Wildlife Refuge. The Secretary may acquire about 4,228 additional acres. Roughly 3,928 acres lie north of Interstate 10 between Little Woods and Pointe-aux-Herbes. About 300 acres lie south of Interstate 10 between the Maxent Canal and Michoud Boulevard. Those southern acres contain the Big Oak Island archaeological site. All are shown on an August 1996 expansion map on file with the Fish and Wildlife Service.
plaw-104-254-1996: Public Law 104-254, approved October 9, 1996, extends the Federal Power Act deadline for two Pennsylvania power projects. They are FERC Projects 4474 and 7041. On each license holder's request, and after reasonable notice, the Commission shall extend the start-of-work date for each project until September 26, 1999. The step follows section 13's good faith, due diligence, and public interest tests and the Commission's procedures. The extension takes effect for a project when the Commission's earlier extension for it expires. Its bill was House bill 2695.
plaw-104-255-1996: Public Law 104-255, approved October 9, 1996, names the building at 8302 FM 327 in Elmendorf, Texas. The building houses United States Postal Service operations. Its name is the Amos F. Longoria Post Office Building. Mentions of it in federal records are to be read under that name. A second section amends the postal statutes' definition of an institution of higher education. It adds a nonprofit organization that coordinates a network of college-level courses. The courses are sponsored mainly by nonprofit schools for older adults. The bill was H.R. 2700, amended in the Senate.
plaw-104-256-1996: Public Law 104-256, approved October 9, 1996, extends the Federal Power Act deadline for two North Carolina hydroelectric projects. For Project No. 10812, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission shall, on request and after notice, extend the construction start period by not more than three consecutive two-year periods; for Project No. 6879, the Commission may grant the same length of extension. Both follow section 13's good faith, due diligence, and public interest standards and take effect as the projects' earlier periods expire. The bill was H.R. 2773.
plaw-104-257-1996: Public Law 104-257, approved October 9, 1996, reinstates the license for an Ohio power project, FERC Project 3218. It also extends the project's construction deadline. Despite the license's expiration, the Commission shall, at the license holder's request, reinstate the license effective September 25, 1993. It shall extend the start-of-work period so that it ends on September 24, 1999. No other provision appears in the act. It began as House bill 2816, with House Report 104-511 from the Commerce Committee.
plaw-104-258-1996: Public Law 104-258, approved October 9, 1996, extends the deadline for starting work on a Kentucky power project, FERC Project 6641. At the license holder's request, the Commission shall extend the start deadline until June 15, 1998. The extension follows section 13 of the Federal Power Act, with its good faith, due diligence, and public interest tests. It takes effect when its earlier extension expires. The Commission may also reinstate the project's license as of its expiration or termination. Its bill was House bill 2869.
plaw-104-259-1996:
Uranium mill tailings cleanup is extended, with a long tail, by Public Law 104-259, approved October 9, 1996, which extends the authorization of the Uranium Mill Tailings Radiation Control Act of 1978. Section 2 rewrites that act's section 112(a), the part on when the program ends and what it may spend.

The Secretary's power to carry out cleanup ends on September 30, 1998, with two exceptions. Groundwater restoration power continues without limitation. And the Secretary may keep operating the site in Mesa County, Colorado, known as the Cheney disposal cell. He may receive leftover radioactive material from processing sites there. He may also receive byproduct material from near the Monticello, Utah milling site. Operations run until the cell fills to its design limit or September 30, 2023, whichever comes first. Section 3 then adjusts cleanup at active processing sites under the Energy Policy Act of 1992, raising one stated figure from 5.50 to 6.25 dollars.
plaw-104-260-1996: Public Law 104-260, approved October 9, 1996, amends the Clean Air Act. It exempts traffic signal synchronization projects from certain Environmental Protection Agency requirements. A new paragraph in section 176(c)(4) covers conformity rules. Compliance with the Administrator's rules for transportation plans, programs, and projects funded or approved under title 23 or the Federal Transit Act is not needed for such projects. The waiver holds before they are funded, approved, or used. Later regional emissions analyses must still consider such projects' effects on emissions. They feed later conformity decisions.
plaw-104-261-1996: Public Law 104-261, approved October 9, 1996, accepts the request of the Prairie Island Indian Community to revoke its charter of incorporation issued under the Indian Reorganization Act. The charter, issued July 23, 1937 under section 17 of that act, is surrendered and revoked in the act's first section. Two riders amend tribal water rights settlement acts by moving deadlines. The Jicarilla Apache Tribe act's December 31, 1996 becomes December 31, 1998. The San Carlos Apache Tribe act's same date becomes June 30, 1997. The bill was H.R. 3068.
plaw-104-262-1996:
Public Law 104-262, the Veterans' Health Care Eligibility Reform Act of 1996, approved October 9, 1996, amends title 38 to reform eligibility for health care provided by the Department of Veterans Affairs. It also authorizes major medical center construction projects for the department. And it aims to improve how the department runs health care.

Title I is the eligibility reform itself. Its sections cover who qualifies for hospital care and medical services. They also cover revised authority for priority health care for veterans exposed to specified toxic substances. Prosthetics and preventive care, and management of health care, are covered too. Funding approval and a review of how the reform is carried out follow. Title II authorizes major medical center projects and leases. It includes strategic planning and revised prospectus and building approval rules. Title III, on health care and administration, follows in the contents.
plaw-104-263-1996:
Veterans' disability checks rise with living costs under Public Law 104-263, the Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 1996, approved October 9, 1996. It increases, effective December 1, 1996, the rates of disability compensation for veterans with service-connected disabilities. It also increases the rates of dependency and indemnity compensation for survivors of certain service-connected disabled veterans.

The Secretary of Veterans Affairs shall raise each rate and limitation in the listed sections of title 38. Those are the sections the 1995 adjustment act had raised, as in effect on November 30, 1996. The percentage is not stated in the act. It is the same percentage by which Social Security title II benefit amounts increase effective December 1, 1996, under the Social Security Act's cost-of-living finding. A special rule lets the Secretary adjust rates for a small older class of people under a 1958 law. Notice of the change is tied to the Social Security announcement.
plaw-104-264-1996:
Federal aviation programs are renewed by Public Law 104-264, the Federal Aviation Reauthorization Act of 1996, approved October 9, 1996, which amends title 49 to renew programs of the Federal Aviation Administration. Its table of contents opens with Title I, Airport and Airway Improvements.

Subtitle A renews the core programs: the airport improvement program, the airway facilities improvement program, and FAA operations. Subtitle B turns to airport development financing. It covers shares of funds, the discretionary fund, use of shared amounts, and designating current and former military airports. Subtitle C modifies the airport improvement program itself. It covers intermodal planning, a pavement maintenance program, and access to airports by intercity buses. It also covers cost reimbursement for projects started before a grant award. And it covers selection of projects for grants from that fund.
plaw-104-265-1996: Public Law 104-265, the Walhalla National Fish Hatchery Conveyance Act, approved October 9, 1996. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey the Walhalla National Fish Hatchery to South Carolina within 180 days, without reimbursement. The hatchery will serve the state fish culture program. The hatchery sits on Indian Camp Creek and the East Fork of the Chattooga River, off State Secondary Highway 325 in northern Oconee County. It covers 76.2 acres, with its improvements, equipment, easements, leases, and water rights. Other uses trigger reversion to the United States.
plaw-104-266-1996:
Recycled water projects receive federal help under Public Law 104-266, the Reclamation Recycling and Water Conservation Act of 1996, approved October 9, 1996. It amends the Reclamation Wastewater and Groundwater Study and Facilities Act by adding new project sections to the Reclamation Projects Authorization and Adjustment Act of 1992.

The first new section authorizes the North San Diego County Area Water Recycling Project. The Secretary, working with state and local authorities, may take part in designing, planning, and building projects to reclaim and reuse water. The projects lie within the service areas of four California bodies. They are the San Elijo Joint Powers Authority, the Leucadia County Water District, the City of Carlsbad, and the Olivenhain Municipal Water District. The federal share of a project's cost may not exceed 25 percent of the total. The Secretary may not fund a project's operation or maintenance.
plaw-104-267-1996: Public Law 104-267, approved October 9, 1996, waives the Medicaid enrollment composition rule for a time. The rule is the 75/25 rule in section 1903(m)(2)(A)(ii) of the Social Security Act. The waiver covers three named health maintenance organizations. They are Catholic Health Services Plan of Brooklyn and Queens, doing business as Fidelis Health Plan, and Managed Healthcare Systems of New York. For those two, the waiver runs for contract periods through January 1, 1999. Health Partners of Philadelphia is covered through December 31, 1999. The single-section act names no others. Its bill was House bill 3871.
plaw-104-268-1996: Public Law 104-268, approved October 9, 1996, designates the United States Post Office building at 351 West Washington Street in Camden, Arkansas, as the David H. Pryor Post Office Building. Its references subsection directs that any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that building be deemed a reference to the David H. Pryor Post Office Building. The act, H.R. 3877, passed the House on September 24, 1996 and the Senate on September 27, in the closing days of the session.
plaw-104-269-1996: Public Law 104-269, approved October 9, 1996, makes certain Voice of America and Radio Marti tapes available for research. Despite two cited legal limits, the Director of the United States Information Agency may share them on request. The recipient is the Linguistic Data Consortium of the University of Pennsylvania. It receives computer readable multilingual text and speech recordings in various languages. It must reimburse the Director for the expenses of making the materials available. The authority ends five years after enactment. The bill was H.R. 3916.
plaw-104-270-1996:
A study of Alaska Native policy is ordered by Public Law 104-270, approved October 9, 1996. It provides for a study of the recommendations of the Joint Federal-State Commission on Policies and Programs Affecting Alaska Natives. Section 1 sets out Congress's findings about that commission and the report being studied.

The commission was established by Public Law 101-379. It followed a 1989 Alaska Federation of Natives report that called for action. Hearings had also shown the need for the first comprehensive assessment of Alaska Natives' social, cultural, and economic condition since the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act. The assessment covered 86,000 Natives. Its fourteen members held fifteen regional hearings across Alaska between July 1992 and October 1993, plus two statewide hearings in Anchorage. In May 1994 it issued a three-volume, 440-page report. It found many Native individuals, families, and communities in a crisis. The crisis showed in rampant unemployment, alcohol abuse, depression, and staggering illness and death rates.
plaw-104-271-1996:
Hydrogen energy research is authorized by Public Law 104-271, the Hydrogen Future Act of 1996, approved October 9, 1996. It authorizes the hydrogen research, development, and demonstration programs of the Department of Energy, and its early sections define the Department and the Secretary of Energy for its titles.

Title I, headed Hydrogen, amends the purposes in an earlier 1990 law, Public Law 101-566. The Secretary of Energy is to conduct a research, development, and demonstration program leading to the production, storage, transport, and use of hydrogen for industrial, residential, transportation, and utility applications. That four-part chain, from making hydrogen to using it in homes, vehicles, factories, and power systems, is the program's stated goal. Reports to Congress follow as the next section.
plaw-104-272-1996:
Boxers who travel from fight to fight are the stated concern of Public Law 104-272, the Professional Boxing Safety Act of 1996, approved October 9, 1996. It is an act to provide for the safety of journeymen boxers. Section 2 builds the act's vocabulary before its rules begin.

A boxer is an individual who fights in a professional boxing match. A boxing commission is an entity authorized under state law to regulate professional matches. A boxer registry is an entity certified by the Association of Boxing Commissions. It maintains records and identification of boxers. The cast around the fighter is also defined. A licensee serves as trainer, second, or cut man. A manager is paid to act as a boxer's agent or representative. A matchmaker proposes, selects, and arranges the boxers in a match. And a physician is a doctor legally authorized to practice in the state.
plaw-104-273-1996:
The federal helium business is opened to private parties by Public Law 104-273, the Helium Privatization Act of 1996, approved October 9, 1996. It amends the Helium Act to authorize the Secretary to enter into agreements with private parties for the recovery and disposal of helium on federal lands.

Sections 3, 4, and 5 of the Helium Act are rewritten, starting with the Secretary's authority. The Secretary may make such agreements on terms the Secretary deems fair, reasonable, and necessary, and may grant leasehold rights to the helium involved. One limit is built in: the Secretary may not sell such helium to anyone other than a private party holding an agreement for its recovery and disposal. Agreements may also be made subject to regulations the Secretary prescribes.
plaw-104-274-1996: Public Law 104-274, approved October 9, 1996, authorizes appropriations for the National Historical Publications and Records Commission for four fiscal years. It amends section 2504(f)(1) of title 44 by adding four subparagraphs to the commission's authorization list. Each subparagraph names 10 million dollars for one fiscal year: 1998, 1999, 2000, and 2001. That flat annual figure, repeated four times, is the whole act. The bill was S. 1577, with Senate Report 104-283.
plaw-104-275-1996:
Public Law 104-275, the Veterans' Benefits Improvements Act of 1996, approved October 9, 1996, amends title 38 to improve the benefits programs of the Secretary of Veterans Affairs. It also provides for a study of federal programs for veterans. Its table of contents divides the improvements into titles.

Title I covers education benefits. Its sections address the employment handicap for which a person may receive training and rehab assistance. They also cover permanent authority for other routes to teacher licensing. They end the distinction between open circuit television and independent study, and cover cooperative programs. Two sections widen the Montgomery GI Bill. One enrolls certain VEAP participants. The other covers who qualifies among active duty members of the Army and Air National Guard. Title II, Housing and Memorial Affairs, begins with extension of enhanced loan asset sale power and direct loans to refinance loans under a Native American veteran program.
plaw-104-276-1996: Public Law 104-276, approved October 9, 1996, directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey property containing a fish and wildlife facility. The property is Ranch A in Crook County, Wyoming. It goes to the state within 180 days, as-is and without reimbursement. About 600 acres pass, with buildings, improvements, and personal property. The list runs down to art, historic light fixtures, wildlife mounts, and furniture. It includes items on loan to museums. The United States retains an 80-acre portion, though its buildings and a permanent right of way across it are conveyed.
plaw-104-277-1996: Public Law 104-277, approved October 9, 1996, names the United States Post Office and Courthouse building at 9 East Broad Street in Cookeville, Tennessee. It is the L. Clure Morton United States Post Office and Courthouse. Its references section covers later mentions. Any law, map, rule, paper, or other record that names that building counts as naming the new name. The act was S. 1931. It passed the Senate in August 1996 and the House in September.
plaw-104-278-1996: Public Law 104-278 is the National Museum of the American Indian Act Amendments of 1996, approved October 9, 1996. It makes improvements to that museum act. One change to the board of trustees provision replaces an Assistant Secretary with a senior official. The listing rules are tightened. The Smithsonian's inventory of remains and objects must be done by June 1, 1998. The word means an itemized list. It names, as far as practicable, their geographic and cultural affiliation. Appropriations language is widened to cover a related section.
plaw-104-279-1996: Public Law 104-279, approved October 9, 1996, authorizes the Capitol Guide Service to accept voluntary services, replacing a subsection of the Legislative Reorganization Act of 1970. A volunteer must first agree in writing to waive claims against the United States arising from the services, other than claims under the federal employees' compensation chapter of title 5. Volunteers are not United States employees for any other purpose, and accepting their services may never reduce pay or displace any Guide Service employee. The bill was S. 2085.
plaw-104-280-1996: Public Law 104-280, approved October 9, 1996, extends certain authority for the Marshal of the Supreme Court and the Supreme Court Police. Its single section amends section 9(c) of the 1949 act on policing the Supreme Court building and grounds, codified at 40 U.S.C. 13n(c), by striking the year 1996 in its first sentence and inserting 2000, a four-year extension. Nothing else is amended. The bill was S. 2100, with a House companion, H.R. 4164, and both were passed by the House on September 27, 1996.
plaw-104-281-1996: Public Law 104-281, approved October 9, 1996, names the United States Post Office building in Brewer, Maine, as the Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain Post Office Building. The naming section gives the location, 22 Parkway South. The references section covers later mentions. Mentions of the building in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, and other records count as mentions of the new name. The bill, S. 2153, passed the Senate and House on the same day, September 28, 1996.
plaw-104-282-1996:
Tall ships and the bonds between nations are commended by Public Law 104-282, a joint resolution approved October 9, 1996. It praises Operation Sail for its advancement of brotherhood among nations. It praises its continuing commemoration of the history of the United States. And it praises its nurturing of young cadets through training in seamanship.

The recitals trace the organization: a nonprofit corporation dedicated to good will among nations, representing the United States in the international tall ship community since 1964. It has been a partner of every American President since John F. Kennedy. Operation Sail had made a tradition of marking major American events with gatherings of the world's tall ships. It would continue with OpSail 2000 in New York Harbor, celebrating the nation's 224th birthday and the new millennium, endorsed by President Clinton. The Navy's International Naval Review, with an aircraft carrier as a symbol of good will, was planned alongside it.
plaw-104-283-1996:
Ocean sanctuaries are reauthorized, and a famous shipwreck gets a preservation plan, under Public Law 104-283, the National Marine Sanctuaries Preservation Act, approved October 11, 1996. It reauthorizes the National Marine Sanctuaries Act, and its amendments are written as changes to that act.

Section 3 rewrites the authorization of appropriations in section 313. The scale rises: 12 million dollars for fiscal year 1997, 15 million for fiscal year 1998, and 18 million for fiscal year 1999. The money carries out the sanctuaries title. Section 4 turns to one site in particular. Within twelve months, the Secretary of Commerce shall prepare a long-range, comprehensive plan for the Monitor. The plan covers the management, stabilization, preservation, and recovery of its artifacts and materials. He shall send it to the House Resources Committee and the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
plaw-104-284-1996:
Propane gets an industry program under Public Law 104-284, the Propane Education and Research Act of 1996, approved October 11, 1996. The act authorizes and facilitates a program to enhance safety, training, research and development, and safety education in the propane gas industry, for the benefit of propane consumers and the public.

The findings make the industry's case. Propane, or liquefied petroleum gas, is an essential energy commodity providing heat, hot water, cooking fuel, and motor fuel to millions of Americans. Its use is especially important to rural citizens and farmers as an efficient and economical gas energy source. Propane has been recognized as a clean fuel that can help reduce pollution in cities and towns, and it is primarily domestically produced, providing energy security and American jobs. Definitions follow, starting with the Propane Education and Research Council the act creates.
plaw-104-285-1996:
Classic American films are the charge of Public Law 104-285, approved October 11, 1996, which reauthorizes the National Film Preservation Board. Title I carries its own name, the National Film Preservation Act of 1996, and it continues the film-saving machinery built by the acts of 1988 and 1992.

Section 102 directs the Librarian of Congress to continue the National Film Registry. The Registry maintains and preserves films that are culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant. The Librarian's duties include continuing a full national film preservation program for motion pictures. He works with other film archivists, teachers and historians, copyright owners, film industry representatives, and others involved in saving films. The program builds on the national film preservation study and plan conducted under the 1992 act. Talks with the Board established by the act run through the Librarian's work.
plaw-104-286-1996: Public Law 104-286, approved October 11, 1996, amends the Central Utah Project Completion Act. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to allow prepayment of repayment contracts with the Central Utah Water Conservancy District. The contracts are dated December 28, 1965 and supplemented November 26, 1985. The prepayment covers municipal and industrial water facilities. The terms are similar to a 1993 Jordan Aqueduct contract. Payment may be made in installments. It may not be adjusted based on the District's financing type. The District must exercise the right by the end of fiscal year 2002.
plaw-104-287-1996:
Public Law 104-287, approved October 11, 1996, codifies laws related to transportation without substantive change and improves the United States Code, as its title states.

The sample shows the work section by section. In title 18, an old list of statute names is replaced with citations to the Anti Car Theft Act titles and chapters of title 49. In title 23, a catchline reading fta becomes chapter 53 of title 49. In title 28, a citation to sections 51-60 of title 45 becomes the equivalent sections of the Act of April 22, 1908. And title 31 clauses are redesignated. It is a housekeeping law for the Code.
plaw-104-288-1996:
Promoting travel to the United States becomes an organized national effort under Public Law 104-288, the United States National Tourism Organization Act of 1996, approved October 11, 1996. It establishes the National Tourism Board and the National Tourism Organization to promote international travel and tourism to the United States, and its findings argue the industry deserved that effort.

Travel and tourism, Congress finds, was the second largest service and retail industry in the country and its largest export in 1995, generating an 18.6 billion dollar surplus. Expenditures totaled 433 billion dollars in 1995, receipts made up 6 percent of gross domestic product, and the industry directly employed 6.3 million people in 1994, with 8 million more jobs indirectly. Nearly all travel businesses, 99.7 percent, are small businesses. The 1995 White House Conference on Travel and Tourism had recommended the new national organization the act creates.
plaw-104-289-1996:
Metric measurements in federal building projects are softened by Public Law 104-289, the Savings in Construction Act of 1996, approved October 11, 1996. It provides for appropriate implementation of the Metric Conversion Act of 1975 in federal construction projects, and its findings explain the problem Congress saw.

The 1975 act set a national policy of converting to the metric system. It required federal agencies to use metric measurements in procurement, grants, and other business. An exception applied where that would cause significant cost or loss of markets to United States firms. Under it and a 1991 executive order, agencies increasingly built new federal buildings in round metric dimensions. Bidders were asked to supply materials in round metric sizes. The existing exemption for impractical or costly metric use, Congress finds, needed strengthening by amendment. The goal is to ensure that specific metric components in metric projects do not increase the cost of federal buildings to taxpayers.
plaw-104-290-1996:
Public Law 104-290, the National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996, approved October 11, 1996, amends the federal securities laws to promote efficiency and capital formation in the financial markets. It also amends the Investment Company Act of 1940 to promote better-run mutual funds, protect investors, and provide stronger, less burdensome regulation.

Title I, Capital Markets, opens with the creation of national markets. It then takes up broker-dealer exemptions from state law, broker-dealer funding, exemptive authority, and the promotion of efficiency, competition, and capital formation. Contracting out the EDGAR filing system, better teamwork in supervision, and increased access to foreign business information also appear. Title II, the Investment Company Act amendments, covers funds of funds, flexible registration, use of current information in fund advertising, and variable insurance contracts.
plaw-104-291-1996:
The National Transportation Safety Board is funded and its foreign work shielded by Public Law 104-291, approved October 11, 1996. It authorizes appropriations for the Board for fiscal years 1997, 1998, and 1999. Title I calls itself the National Transportation Safety Board Amendments of 1996 and begins with foreign investigations.

A new subsection of section 1114 of title 49 provides a nondisclosure rule. Neither the Board nor any agency receiving information from it shall disclose records or information about its participation in foreign aircraft accident investigations. Two releases are allowed. One comes when the country conducting the investigation issues its final report, or two years after the accident, whichever comes first. The other comes whenever that country authorizes disclosure. One activity is never restricted: the Board may refer to foreign accident investigation information at any time when making safety recommendations.
plaw-104-292-1996:
Lying to the government is restated by Public Law 104-292, the False Statements Accountability Act of 1996, approved October 11, 1996. It amends title 18 on false statements in government matters, replacing section 1001 in full.

The restored text covers whoever, in any matter within the jurisdiction of the executive, legislative, or judicial branch, acts knowingly and willfully. It covers a person who falsifies or conceals a material fact by trick, scheme, or device. It covers a person who makes a materially false or fraudulent statement. And it covers a person who uses a false writing knowing it contains such a statement. The penalty is a fine or imprisonment of not more than five years, or both. Two limits follow. The ban does not apply to parties or their counsel for submissions to a judge in a proceeding. And for legislative branch matters it applies only to administrative matters such as claims and procurement.
plaw-104-293-1996:
Public Law 104-293, the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1997, approved October 11, 1996, authorizes funding for fiscal year 1997 for intelligence and intelligence-related activities of the United States Government. It also covers the Community Management Account and the Central Intelligence Agency Retirement and Disability System.

Title I authorizes the intelligence activities funding itself. A classified schedule of amounts, staff ceiling changes, and the Community Management Account are handled in separate sections. They are a reminder that the spending details sit outside the public text. Title II authorizes money for the CIA retirement and disability system. Title III gathers general provisions. They cover increases in employee compensation and benefits authorized by law. They also cover a restriction on conduct of intelligence work, and a limitation on funds for automatic declassification of records over twenty-five years old. Application of sanctions laws to intelligence activities, and faster citizenship for some, complete the list.
plaw-104-294-1996:
The Economic Espionage Act of 1996 was the first federal law aimed squarely at the theft of trade secrets. Congress passed it as Public Law 104-294 in 1996. It added a new chapter on trade secrets to title 18 of the United States Code.

One part of the law targets spying for a foreign power. It is a crime to steal or take a trade secret while meaning to help a foreign government or its agents. A second part covers plain theft of trade secrets. The law also sets criminal forfeiture, lets courts keep secrets sealed during a case, and allows civil suits to stop the theft. Its rules reach acts done outside the United States.
plaw-104-295-1996:
Trade law accumulates small errors over time, and the Miscellaneous Trade and Technical Corrections Act of 1996 was Congress's cleanup bill. Public Law 104-295, enacted October 11, 1996, by the 104th Congress, makes technical corrections and miscellaneous amendments to the customs and trade laws already on the books.

Its sections clarify how duties and fees are paid, when customs user fees apply, and how drawback claims and entry reconciliations are handled. It suspends duties on specific goods, adjusts the tariff treatment of certain televisions, motor vehicles, and precious metal bars, and fixes chemical descriptions in the tariff schedules. It also ends the East-West Trade Statistics Monitoring System and makes technical fixes to the Uruguay Round Agreements Act and the North American trade law.
plaw-104-296-1996: Public Law 104-296 is a short joint resolution of the 104th Congress, approved October 11, 1996, that set two dates for the start of the next Congress. It provided that the first regular session of the One Hundred Fifth Congress would begin at noon on Tuesday, January 7, 1997. It also moved the joint meeting to count the electoral votes for President and Vice President cast in December 1996 to January 9, 1997, instead of the date otherwise fixed by law.
plaw-104-297-1996:
The Sustainable Fisheries Act became Public Law 104-297 on October 11, 1996. It changed the Magnuson Act, the main federal law on fishing in United States waters. The point, in the act's own words, was to provide for sustainable fisheries. It also renewed the money for the program.

The act rewrote the national standards for fishery plans. It set the duties of the regional fishery councils. It also covered plans for each fishery and action by the Secretary of Commerce. Later titles deal with fishery research, data systems, and the move to lasting fish stocks. Some parts treat highly migratory species, foreign fishing deals, and the North Pacific.
plaw-104-298-1996:
The Water Desalination Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-298 on October 11, 1996. It lets the Secretary of the Interior study how to turn salty water into usable water. It also covers the reuse of water.

The act defines its key terms in plain sections. Desalination means taking salt and other matter out of seawater, brackish water, or other poor water. The goal is water fit for farms, factories, towns, and nature. The studies were meant to find the cheapest and most efficient ways to make that water. The Interior Department runs the studies.
plaw-104-299-1996:
The Health Centers Consolidation Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-299 on October 11, 1996. It rewrote title III of the Public Health Service Act. The act joined the health center rules into one part and renewed them.

Under the act, a health center serves people who lack good access to care. It also serves farm workers, homeless people, and public housing residents. Centers must give basic health services. They may add more services where a center needs them. Care can come from the center's own staff or through contracts with others. The law dates from the 104th Congress.
plaw-104-300-1996:
The Fort Peck Rural County Water Supply System Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-300 on October 11, 1996. It serves a rural area in Montana. The act backs the building of a water supply system for the Fort Peck Rural County Water District. The district is a nonprofit group.

Federal help goes to the planning, design, and building of the system. The work follows a study from September 1994. That study is called the Final Engineering Report and Alternative Evaluation for the district. The Secretary of the Interior runs the federal side of the project.
plaw-104-301-1996:
For decades the Navajo and Hopi tribes disputed land in the Southwest, and the Navajo-Hopi Land Dispute Settlement Act of 1996 was meant to close the remaining issues. Public Law 104-301, approved October 11, 1996, provides for settlement of the dispute left over from the Navajo-Hopi Land Settlement Act of 1974.

Congress found that a fair and final settlement served the tribe, Navajo families living on the Hopi Partitioned Lands, and the United States. Working with a settlement agreement signed December 14, 1995, the act authorizes agreements letting eligible Navajo families stay on the Hopi Partitioned Lands for 75 years under an accommodation agreement. It also settles the tribe's multiple claims against the United States.
plaw-104-302-1996:
Foreign nurses on H-1A visas faced the end of their legal stay in 1996. Public Law 104-302 answered on October 11, 1996. It extends the stay of certain nurses through September 30, 1997.

The extension covers nurses who came in under the H-1A class. They had to be in the country on or after September 1, 1995. Their stay must have expired, or be set to expire, before the new date. The act does not extend any visa. It also bars these nurses from changing employers. The Attorney General had 30 days to issue rules for the change.
plaw-104-303-1996:
The Water Resources Development Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-303 on October 12, 1996. It is the big water projects bill of the 104th Congress. It lets the Secretary of the Army build projects on rivers and harbors across the United States.

Title I lists the projects. It also keeps small-project programs for flood control, bank work, navigation, and shore protection. Title II sets broad policy. It covers cost sharing, flood control, and the restoration of water habitats. It also deals with dredged material, environmental dredging, and park use and fees. It passed as Senate bill S. 640.
plaw-104-304-1996:
Pipelines carrying natural gas and hazardous liquids run under much of the country, and the Accountable Pipeline Safety and Partnership Act of 1996 aimed to cut the risks they pose. Public Law 104-304, signed October 12, 1996, amends the pipeline safety provisions of title 49 of the United States Code.

The act revises key definitions, including what counts as transporting gas through gathering lines in rural and nonrural areas. It introduces risk management into the statute, defined as the systematic use by a pipeline owner or operator of management policies, procedures, limited resources, and practices. Its stated purpose is to reduce risk to public safety and the environment from pipeline transportation.
plaw-104-305-1996:
The Drug-Induced Rape Prevention and Punishment Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-305 on October 13, 1996. It targets crimes where a victim is drugged without knowing it. Sexual assaults are a chief concern of the act.

The law adds a penalty of up to 20 years in prison. It applies when a person gives someone a controlled substance in secret. The act must be tied to a planned crime of violence. The law also raises penalties tied to flunitrazepam. Small amounts of that drug now count toward the higher sentence ranges. The change covers trafficking and import and export crimes.
plaw-104-306-1996: Public Law 104-306 is a short extension act from October 14, 1996. It keeps some programs under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act alive through September 30, 1997. It funds those parts of the act for fiscal year 1997. Two old dates in the law, both June 30, 1996, move to September 30, 1997. Nothing else in the energy law changes.
plaw-104-307-1996:
Old military planes got a new job under the Wildfire Suppression Aircraft Transfer Act of 1996. The act became Public Law 104-307 on October 14, 1996. It lets the Defense Department sell its excess planes and parts for fire fighting.

The sales run from October 1, 1996 to September 30, 2000. Buyers must hold federal contracts to drop fire retardant by air. The planes may serve only as airtankers against wildfire. They may not leave the United States in most cases. Trips abroad need a fire center dispatch or joint written approval from two cabinet secretaries. The sales window runs four years in all.
plaw-104-308-1996:
Public Law 104-308 is a patent act from October 19, 1996. It deals with owners whose patents the United States has used. Such owners may sue for fair payment. Small owners often could not afford the fight.

The act says fair payment now includes the owner's court costs. Fees for lawyers and expert witnesses count too. The rule helps independent inventors and nonprofit groups. It also helps firms with no more than 500 staff. But fees are denied if the government's stand was well founded. They are also denied where special facts make an award unjust. The change covers pending and new cases.
plaw-104-309-1996:
Public Law 104-309 dates from October 19, 1996. It states the sense of Congress on Nazi war crimes files. Federal agencies hold records on people accused of such crimes. Congress said those records should be made public.

The act's findings set the scene. Americans had just marked 50 years since the end of the Second World War. The Cold War was over. Other nations were opening their own files. United States agencies held facts on people who ordered or aided Nazi crimes. Some agencies had turned down requests for those facts under the Freedom of Information Act.
plaw-104-310-1996: Public Law 104-310, approved October 19, 1996, modifies the boundaries of the Talladega National Forest in Alabama. It adds two described parcels to the forest: about 399.40 acres in Cleburne County and 160 acres in Calhoun County, both surveyed under the Huntsville Meridian. The Secretary of the Interior transfers administrative jurisdiction over the federal lands to the Secretary of Agriculture without reimbursement, and the Forest Service administers them as part of the national forest. Existing rights-of-way, easements, leases, licenses, and permits on the land stay valid under their existing terms.
plaw-104-311-1996:
Florida's Wekiva River took a first step toward federal protection in 1996. Public Law 104-311 was signed on October 19, 1996. It adds the river to the study list in the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act. Seminole Creek and Rock Springs Run are on the list too.

Study status is not full protection. It starts a review of the whole river and both creeks. The study must be done within two years. A report then goes to Congress. Lawmakers can later decide if the river joins the national system. All three waters lie in Florida.
plaw-104-312-1996:
Mining research institutes got a new line of support for work on the ocean floor from Public Law 104-312, approved October 19, 1996. The act amends the Mining and Mineral Resources Research Institute Act of 1984 and renames it the Mining and Mineral Resources Institutes Act.

The act authorizes up to $1,800,000 for each fiscal year after 1996 for institutes experienced in studying the continental shelf, the deep seabed, near-shore island waters, and Arctic and cold water regions. The money supports building domestic skill at locating nonfuel minerals and recovering them from shallow and deep seabed in an efficient and environmentally sound way.
plaw-104-313-1996:
The Indian Health Care Improvement Technical Corrections Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-313 on October 19, 1996. It fixes the main federal law on health care for Native Americans. Its stated aim is to extend a test program. The program lets Indian health sites bill Medicare, Medicaid, and other payers directly.

The sample shows one set of fixes. The act widens the term health profession in the law. It adds allopathic medicine to the list of fields. The wording now reaches any allied health profession or other health profession. It is one of the health measures of the 104th Congress.
plaw-104-314-1996:
Pennsylvania's Clarion River joined the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System through Public Law 104-314, approved October 19, 1996. The act designates 51.7 miles of the river's main stem, running from near Ridgway Borough down to the backwaters of Piney Dam, to be administered by the Secretary of Agriculture.

The designated stretch is divided into four classified segments. Two segments, about 8.6 miles and about 26 miles long, are classed as recreational river. The other two, about 8 miles and about 9.1 miles, are classed as scenic river. The boundaries are fixed by landmarks including Portland Mills, the Allegheny National Forest boundary, and the State Game Lands 283 boundary near Cooksburg.
plaw-104-315-1996:
Medicaid rules for reviewing nursing home residents changed with Public Law 104-315, approved October 19, 1996. The act amends title XIX of the Social Security Act to repeal the requirement for an annual resident review for nursing facilities under the Medicaid program.

In place of the yearly review, the act requires reviews for mentally ill or mentally retarded residents when there is a significant change in physical or mental condition. A nursing facility must promptly notify the state mental health or developmental disability authority after such a change in one of those residents, and the review then follows from that notice. The repeal took effect on the date of enactment.
plaw-104-316-1996:
The General Accounting Office Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-316 on October 19, 1996. The office is Congress's own audit arm. Many laws tell it to audit or report on federal work. This act cleans up those laws.

Title I shifts some jobs to other agencies. When a law is changed to name a new office, the job moves with it. When a law is repealed, the job ends. The budget director may pass moved jobs on to other agencies. Staff, records, and funds move with the work. The act is a housekeeping measure, not a new program.
plaw-104-317-1996:
The Federal Courts Improvement Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-317 on October 19, 1996. It makes many small fixes to the way federal courts run.

Title I gives new powers to probation and pretrial services officers. Title II works on court process. It covers magistrate judges sent to help in emergencies. It also covers consent to trial and the use of judgments across districts. Other parts treat diversity cases and suits against the United States. Title III deals with court staff and pay. It takes up senior judges, survivors' benefits, and the reappointment of bankruptcy judges.
plaw-104-318-1996:
Severe drought in Texas prompted the Emergency Drought Relief Act of 1996. Public Law 104-318, approved October 19, 1996, provides emergency drought relief to the city of Corpus Christi, Texas, and to the Canadian River Municipal Water Authority, also in Texas.

For Corpus Christi, the Secretary of the Interior must defer all principal and interest payments, without penalty or added interest, for five years on the Nueces River Reclamation Project contract. The city must commit the freed funds only to acquiring or building facilities for alternative water supplies. Where those facilities need federal permits for Bureau of Reclamation land, the Secretary must issue them within 90 days. The act also recognizes the Canadian River authority's land and debt arrangements tied to the Lake Meredith National Recreation Area.
plaw-104-319-1996:
The Human Rights, Refugee, and Other Foreign Relations Provisions Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-319 on October 19, 1996. It bundles items on human rights, refugees, and foreign affairs.

Title I extends some court-related rules. It also covers exchange programs for students and scholars. Scholarships for Tibetans and Burmese are part of it. So is the International Boundary and Water Commission. Title II deals with foreign aid. It takes up human rights reports and aid for Mauritania. Title III funds the Claiborne Pell Institute for International Relations and Public Policy. The institute bears the name of Senator Claiborne Pell.
plaw-104-320-1996:
The Administrative Dispute Resolution Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-320 on October 19, 1996. It renews the use of mediation and like tools in federal disputes. The aim is to settle fights with agencies without a court case.

The act updates the terms in title 5 of the United States Code. It adds the use of ombuds to the list of approved methods. Arbitration was already on the list. The act also trims the secrecy rules for dispute talks. A talk shared with all sides in a case is not kept secret. The neutral's own papers get more protection.
plaw-104-321-1996:
States won the right to aid each other in disasters through Public Law 104-321. Congress gave its consent to the Emergency Management Assistance Compact on October 19, 1996. Thirteen states had already joined the compact. They run from Delaware and Florida to South Dakota and West Virginia.

The compact lets member states help in any declared emergency. The governor of the hit state must declare it first. Aid can cover natural disasters, civil unrest, and enemy attack. It can also cover joint drills and training. A state's National Guard forces may take part in the aid.
plaw-104-322-1996: Public Law 104-322 dates from October 19, 1996. It is a joint resolution on Washington area transit. Congress consents to changes made by Maryland, Virginia, and the District of Columbia. The changes amend the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Regulation Compact. One part restates the transit zone. It covers the District, named Virginia cities and counties, and two Maryland counties. A second part sets the transit board at six directors, two from each party.
plaw-104-323-1996:
The Cache La Poudre River Corridor Act became Public Law 104-323 on October 19, 1996. It sets up a heritage corridor in Colorado. The corridor lies in the Cache La Poudre River Basin.

The act says why the corridor exists. Its lands, waterways, and old buildings tell part of the nation's story. The aim is to present that story to the public. A new commission will write a plan for the corridor. The plan guides how the story is taught and shown. The Secretary of the Interior and Colorado's governor both have roles.
plaw-104-324-1996:
The Coast Guard Authorization Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-324 on October 19, 1996. It funds the Coast Guard for the year. It also sets the size of the force and its training levels.

Title I requires reports every three months on drug patrol work. It also states the sense of Congress on Coast Guard funds. Title II deals with the people of the service. It covers child care, recruiting, and keeping officers longer. It also treats Coast Guard housing and rescue diver training. One part gives relief tied to Hurricane Andrew. The act passed as a Senate bill, S. 1004.
plaw-104-325-1996:
Minerals lying under the ocean were the target of the Marine Mineral Resources Research Act of 1996. Public Law 104-325, approved October 19, 1996, promotes the research, identification, assessment, and exploration of marine mineral resources.

The act adds a new title to the Mining and Minerals Policy Act of 1970 creating a Marine Mineral Resources Research Program. It defines who may take part: eligible entities include research or educational bodies chartered under federal or state law, United States citizens, and state or regional agencies. The program works through contracts and cooperative agreements, using the standard federal meanings of those terms, to build knowledge of what mineral wealth the seabed holds.
plaw-104-326-1996: The Irrigation Project Contract Extension Act of 1996 is Public Law 104-326. It was signed on October 19, 1996. The act tells the Secretary of the Interior to extend water service contracts. The contracts are with irrigation districts in Kansas and Nebraska. Each one runs four more years past its old end date. The projects are units of the Missouri River Basin Project. They form part of the Pick-Sloan Missouri Basin Program. The list names the Bostwick Unit in both states. It also names the Farwell Unit and the Frenchman-Cambridge Unit.
plaw-104-327-1996: Public Law 104-327 dates from October 19, 1996. It makes technical fixes to the welfare law passed that same year. That law is the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996. The main fix clarifies a cap on federal duties for 1997. The math now uses two sums added together. One is the state's family assistance grant. The other is any sum the state could have drawn from the Contingency Fund for State Welfare Programs. The period runs to the day the state sent in its plan.
plaw-104-328-1996: Public Law 104-328 dates from October 19, 1996. It keeps one small federal body alive a bit longer. The body is the Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Relations. A 1996 funding act had cut the commission off. This act lets it stay open for one job only. That job is a contract under the National Gambling Impact Study Commission Act. The commission ends when the contract is done. Its staff keep their federal health and pension benefits in the meantime. A second part strikes two phrases from a 1997 funding act.
plaw-104-329-1996:
Collectors and several good causes were served by the United States Commemorative Coin Act of 1996. Public Law 104-329, approved October 20, 1996, establishes United States commemorative coin programs and sets the rules for how the coins are designed, made, and sold.

Title I covers the coin programs themselves, including design, legal tender status, sources of bullion, coin quality, sales, and financial assurances, with a general waiver of procurement regulations. Title II creates the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Maintenance Fund. Title III orders a study of a Fifty States commemorative coin program, fixes terms for members of the Citizens Commemorative Coin Advisory Committee, and reforms Mint managerial staffing.
plaw-104-330-1996:
Federal housing help for Native American tribes was rebuilt around tribal self-governance by the Native American Housing Assistance and Self-Determination Act of 1996. Public Law 104-330, approved October 26, 1996, provides federal assistance for Indian tribes in a manner that recognizes the right of tribal self-governance.

Title I replaces older programs with block grants: tribes submit Indian housing plans, which are reviewed under the act, and program income, labor standards, and environmental review are handled under its rules. Title II defines affordable housing activities, setting national objectives, the families eligible to benefit, and a low-income requirement with income targeting. Administration runs through the Office of Native American Programs.
plaw-104-331-1996:
The Presidential and Executive Office Accountability Act became Public Law 104-331 on October 26, 1996. It makes some workplace laws apply to the Executive Office of the President. Those laws had not reached the White House staff before.

The act adds a chapter to title 3 of the United States Code. The chapter extends rights and protections to presidential offices. The topics include job bias, family and medical leave, and fair hiring. The act also amends title 28. It sets how future job laws will apply. One part of the Government Employee Rights Act of 1991 is repealed.
plaw-104-332-1996:
Ships emptying ballast water can dump foreign species into American waters, and the National Invasive Species Act of 1996 attacked that route of invasion. Public Law 104-332, approved October 26, 1996, provides for ballast water management to prevent the introduction and spread of nonindigenous species into the waters of the United States.

The act amends the Nonindigenous Aquatic Nuisance Prevention and Control Act of 1990. Its updated findings describe how established foreign species compete with or prey on native plants, fish, and wildlife, carry diseases and parasites, and disrupt nearshore economies. It singles out the zebra mussel, unintentionally brought into the Great Lakes and since spread into the Mississippi drainage, the Arkansas River, the Hudson River, and Lake Champlain.
plaw-104-333-1996:
The Omnibus Parks and Public Lands Management Act of 1996 became Public Law 104-333 on November 12, 1996. It began as a bill on the Presidio of San Francisco. The aim was to run that site at low cost to taxpayers.

The final act is a large bundle of land measures. Part one sets up the Presidio Trust. It also caps funds for the site and orders a study of it. Part two changes the borders of many park units. The list names Zion, Yucca House, and Pictured Rocks. It also orders land transfers, such as the Taos Pueblo transfer.
plaw-104-89-1996: Public Law 104-89 is a short act from January 4, 1996. It extends powers under the Middle East Peace Facilitation Act of 1994 again. An earlier act had set the end at December 31, 1995. This act strikes that date. It inserts March 31, 1996. A newer policy paper counts for the consultation step. The paper is dated December 1, 1995. That rule covers acts before January 10, 1996.
plaw-104-90-1996: Public Law 104-90, approved January 4, 1996, is a joint resolution making further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1996 for the District of Columbia only. It funds the District out of its general and enterprise funds, continuing fiscal year 1995 projects and activities at a rate not exceeding the current rate. Where the House-passed and Senate-passed versions of the District's 1996 appropriations act differ, the lower rate governs.
plaw-104-91-1996: Public Law 104-91 is a land transfer act from January 6, 1996. It gives a federal lab to the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. The lab belongs to the National Marine Fisheries Service. It stands on Emerson Avenue in Gloucester. The Secretary of Commerce must make the transfer. The Commonwealth pays nothing for the site. It must keep up the property while it holds title. The fisheries service may stay in its lab space for up to five years. That stay rests on a written deal with the state.
plaw-104-92-1996:
Public Law 104-92 dates from January 6, 1996. Congress passed it during the budget fight of late 1995. The act funds a short list of chosen programs for fiscal year 1996. The programs run on under the fiscal year 1995 acts.

The list names meals and services for the elderly. It names state grants for child welfare. It names the Federal Parent Locator Service, which helps find parents who owe support. State jobless insurance offices stay funded. So do welfare and foster care payments under the Bureau of Indian Affairs. Family support payments to states are on the list too.
plaw-104-93-1996:
The Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1996 became Public Law 104-93 on January 6, 1996. It approves funds for the spy agencies for one year. It also funds the Community Management Account. The CIA Retirement and Disability System is funded as well.

Title I approves the money. The sums sit in a classified schedule, not in the act. Title II funds the CIA pension system. Title III adds broad rules. They limit how spy work may be done. They apply sanctions laws to spy work. They also treat secrecy deals and pension rights for spouses who help in security cases.
plaw-104-94-1996: Public Law 104-94, approved January 6, 1996, is a short joint resolution making further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1996. Its only funding change is a date: it amends Public Law 104-56 to strike December 15, 1995 and insert January 26, 1996, extending that stopgap. A second section ties delivery of the resolution to the President to a concurrent resolution making transmission depend on the President submitting a seven-year balanced budget built on Congressional Budget Office assumptions.
plaw-104-95-1996:
Public Law 104-95 dates from January 10, 1996. It guards retirees who move to a new state. A state may not tax pension income of a person who is not its resident. The rule sits in title 4 of the United States Code.

The act defines retirement income in broad terms. It covers pay from qualified trusts and pension plans. It covers individual retirement plans as well. Annuity plans and contracts are on the list. So are deferred pay plans and government plans. Series of equal payments over time also count. The act passed as H.R. 394.
plaw-104-96-1996:
The Smithsonian Institution's one hundred fiftieth birthday was marked in metal by the Smithsonian Institution Sesquicentennial Commemorative Coin Act of 1995. Public Law 104-96, approved January 10, 1996, requires the Secretary of the Treasury to mint coins commemorating the sesquicentennial of the Smithsonian's founding.

The act authorizes no more than one hundred thousand five dollar gold coins, each weighing 8.359 grams and containing ninety percent gold, and no more than six hundred fifty thousand one dollar silver coins of ninety percent silver. The Secretary may instead issue up to one hundred thousand five dollar platinum coins in place of the gold issue. The coins are legal tender and are treated as numismatic items.
plaw-104-97-1996: Public Law 104-97, approved January 11, 1996, reauthorizes the tied aid credit program of the Export-Import Bank of the United States. It changes a year in the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945 from 1995 to 1997 and authorizes such sums as necessary for the fund for each of fiscal years 1996 and 1997. A second section lets the Export-Import Bank conduct a personnel demonstration project under title 5, notwithstanding a limitation that would otherwise bar it.
plaw-104-98-1996:
The Federal Trademark Dilution Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-98 on January 16, 1996. It gives famous brand names a new shield in federal law. The act amends the Trademark Act of 1946.

The owner of a famous mark may sue over dilution. Dilution is a use that weakens the mark's distinct force. Old trademark law asked for proof of buyer confusion. This claim does not. A court weighs fairness when it grants relief. The act thus lets top brands act against copycat uses on unrelated goods. Such uses can blur or tarnish a name.
plaw-104-99-1996:
The Balanced Budget Downpayment Act, I became Public Law 104-99 on January 26, 1996. It is a stopgap funding act for fiscal year 1996. Its name ties the funding to a push for a balanced budget.

The act does not fund the whole government. It keeps two unfinished bills going at the current rate. One is the Interior Department bill. The other covers labor, health, and education. Programs run on under the fiscal year 1995 acts. Work already funded by Public Laws 104-91 and 104-92 is left out. The act passed as H.R. 2880 in the House. It is the first of its name.
plaw-1996: Private Law 104-4, approved on October 19, 1996, is a private law for the relief of one person, Nguyen Quy An. The law waives certain requirements for becoming a citizen under the Immigration and Nationality Act. It sets aside the rules on lawful permanent residence and on time spent living in the United States. If he is otherwise fit and files within two years, he may take the oath and be naturalized as a citizen.
plos-pbio-0020096:
Hajime Hirase, Lifen Qian, Peter Barthó, and their team imaged living brain support cells for PLOS Biology in 2004. Astrocytes are star-shaped cells that support neurons. They signal with waves of calcium, and the team watched those waves move through networks of astrocytes in living animals.

Seeing the waves in an intact brain, rather than in a dish, shows how they really spread and sync. Calcium waves may help astrocytes coordinate blood flow and neuron support across a wide area. The work pushes imaging methods forward as well. It gives researchers a way to watch non-neuron brain cells at work in real time, a view that was long out of reach.
plos-pbio-0020196:
Michèle Crozatier, Jean-Michel Ubeda, Alain Vincent, and their team studied fly immunity in PLOS Biology in 2004. When a wasp lays an egg inside a fruit fly larva, the larva must surround it with blood cells and kill it. That defense is called encapsulation.

A gene named collier, the fly version of a family of early B-cell factors, proves vital for the response. Without it, the larva cannot mount the cell attack properly. The study links a gene known from vertebrate blood development to an insect defense, hinting at deep shared roots. It also gives immunity research a clean genetic handle on how blood cells are called into action.
plos-pbio-0020296:
Matt Kaeberlein, Kathryn T. Kirkland, Stanley Fields, and their team tested an aging theory in yeast in PLOS Biology in 2004. Cutting food intake extends life in many species, an effect called calorie restriction. In yeast, the gene Sir2 was thought to be the required middleman for that benefit.

The team found yeast can live longer on less food even without Sir2. So the pathway forks: Sir2 helps in some settings but is not the only route. That result kept the field honest about a tidy story. It pushed aging research to map several paths from diet to lifespan, a map that remains central to work on healthy aging.
plos-pone-0000096:
Yuuki Hayashi, Takuyo Aita, Hitoshi Toyota, and their team charted a protein fitness landscape by experiment in PLOS ONE in 2006. A fitness landscape maps how each change in a protein's sequence affects how well it works. Theory draws these maps as hills and valleys, but real ones are hard to measure.

By making many variants of one protein and testing each, the team drew a real section of such a map. It proved rugged: small steps could help, harm, or do nothing, in no simple pattern. Rugged maps explain why protein evolution can get stuck at local peaks. Measured landscapes like this one ground a famous theory in laboratory fact.
plos-pone-0000196:
Evangelos Evangelou, Demetrius M. Maraganore, and John P. A. Ioannidis published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genome-wide association studies scan the whole genome for disease links, and meta-analysis pools many such studies for stronger evidence. The authors lay out strategies for doing that pooling well, applying them to Parkinson disease.

Single studies of gene effects are often too small to trust. A sound meta-analysis can separate real signals from chance hits. The paper gives practical guidance on combining genome-wide datasets and shows it at work on Parkinson's, where genetic clues have been hard to pin down.
plos-pone-0000296:
Nick J. B. Isaac, Samuel T. Turvey, Ben Collen, and colleagues published this conservation paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The EDGE approach ranks species by combining how threatened they are with how phylogenetically distinct they are, how much unique evolutionary history they carry. The authors apply it to mammals, setting conservation priorities on both grounds.

A species like the aardvark holds a whole branch of the mammal family tree. Losing it loses more history than losing one of many similar rodents. The paper lists which mammals score highest on threat plus distinctness. It gives conservation a defensible way to spend limited funds.
plos-pone-0000396:
Wei Zhang and colleagues hunted for DNA letter changes tied to where a gene is switched on, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genes make UGT1A enzymes, which help the body process drugs and its own chemicals, and different family members work in different tissues. The team searched for single-letter variants linked to those tissue-specific expression patterns.

A variant that changes where an enzyme is made can change how a person handles a drug. That makes this search part of pharmacogenetics, the study of how inherited differences shape drug response. Cataloging such variants is a step toward dosing medicines by a patient's genes rather than by averages.
plos-pone-0000496:
Antonio Graziano and colleagues improved stem cell bone building with a pitted surface, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. They grew stem cell-derived osteoblasts, bone-forming cells, on scaffold surfaces containing concave pits. The shaped surfaces improved the cells' performance and led to significant bone tissue formation.

Cells read the geometry of what they sit on: pits of the right size can nudge stem cells to become bone and lay down mineral. For regenerative medicine, the scaffold is half the therapy. A surface design that boosts bone formation could serve in implants for fractures and jaw work. Growing real bone there beats filling gaps with inert material.
plos-pone-0000596:
Thomas Karrasch and colleagues reported a warning about a plant compound often assumed to be protective, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Luteolin is a flavonoid found in vegetables and supplements. The team used NF-κB EGFP transgenic mice. These mice glow where the inflammation switch NF-κB is active. In them, the flavonoid luteolin worsened chemical-induced colitis. It did so by blocking NF-κB-dependent protective molecules.

NF-κB drives inflammation but also protects the gut lining; blocking it can backfire. The reporter mice made that double role visible in living tissue. The paper cautions against assuming natural antioxidants are safe in inflamed organs, and it refines where anti-inflammatory drugs should and should not act.
plos-pone-0000696:
Alexander Zumdieck, Karsten Kruse, Henrik Bringmann and colleagues gave a physical analysis of the ring that splits a cell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. During cytokinesis, a contractile ring of actin filaments squeezes the cell into two. The authors analyze how stress builds in that ring and how its filaments turn over, constantly replaced while the ring shrinks.

Their case study is the embryo of the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, a classic model. They present a general analysis of force balances and material exchange in the ring. Physics of this kind matters because division errors drive disease. A ring that both contracts and renews itself is an engineering puzzle worth solving exactly.
plos-pone-0000796:
Morten Nielsen, Claus Lundegaard, Thomas Blicher and colleagues presented NetMHCpan, a predictor for a core step in immune recognition, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Binding of peptides to MHC molecules is the single most selective step when the cellular immune system recognizes pathogens. The human MHC class I system, HLA-I, is extremely polymorphic, with a huge and growing registry of variants.

Older predictors handled only specific HLA types. NetMHCpan aims at any HLA-A and HLA-B protein of known sequence, giving quantitative binding predictions. Pan-specific prediction matters for vaccine design across diverse populations. A peptide vaccine must bind the HLA variants real people carry. Binding only the common laboratory ones is not enough.
plos-pone-0000896:
Jon Beadell, Colm Atkins, Erin Cashion and colleagues compared immune traits in four island bird groups, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hawaii's native birds have been hit hard by bird malaria and pox brought in by people. With fewer parasites around and smaller gene pools, island birds might share a changed immune profile.

The team measured immune signals across four island taxa and found they do not all point the same way. That divergence is itself the lesson: a parasite poor home does not reshape every species alike. For conservation, the work warns against treating island birds as one uniform case.
plos-pone-0000996:
Isabel Miranda, Rita Rocha, Maria Santos and colleagues showed that a changed genetic code creates variety in a human pathogen, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genetic code was once thought frozen and universal. Found exceptions in bacteria and eukaryotes alike ended that idea, showing codon assignments can shift.

Candida albicans, a fungus that infects people, reads one codon in an unusual way. The team argue this alteration acts as a phenotype diversity generator, producing varied cell surfaces and traits from one genome. Variety helps a pathogen dodge immunity and drugs. A code quirk once treated as a curiosity here becomes a survival strategy.
plos-pone-0001096:
Meei Ling Sheu, Shing Hwa Liu and Keng Hsin Lan tested a plant compound against gastric cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Honokiol is a small natural product from magnolia, reported to fight tumors and the blood vessels that feed them. Its molecular mechanisms, and whether it works against gastric cancer, were unknown.

The team report honokiol induces cleavage of a stress protein, GRP94, through calpain enzymes, and triggers apoptosis, ordered cell death, in human gastric cancer cells. It also reduced tumor growth in their model. Natural products often fail for lack of a mechanism; here the mechanism is the headline. Gastric cancer remains hard to treat, so new routes matter.
plos-pone-0001196:
Insulin affects the brain as well as the body, raising activity in the cerebral cortex of lean people. Otto Tschritter and colleagues tested a long-acting insulin, detemir, in overweight people, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. In obese individuals the brain's response to insulin is reduced, a sign of cerebrocortical insulin resistance.

The authors asked whether insulin detemir is a suitable tool to restore the cerebral insulin response in overweight humans. They tracked cerebrocortical beta activity, a rhythm of brain electrical activity that insulin stimulates. Their work bears on how brain insulin resistance might be reversed, with implications for appetite and weight control.
plos-pone-0001296:
Flu seasons differ around the world, but the global pattern had never been fully described for each virus type. Brian Finkelman and colleagues assembled laboratory-confirmed data on influenza activity from 1997 to 2005, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They covered the A/H3N2 and A/H1N1 subtypes and influenza B.

The authors describe global patterns in seasonal activity, including viral coexistence and latitudinal gradients, meaning how timing shifts with distance from the equator. Such maps help time vaccination campaigns and anticipate which strains circulate where. The work turns scattered national reports into one comparative picture.
plos-pone-0001396:
Joost Woltering and Antony Durston wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on body plan genes in zebrafish. Hox genes lay out the head to tail axis in animals. Small RNA genes sit inside the Hox clusters too, and they are kept across many species. The pair studied one such RNA, called miR-10, in fish embryos.

The authors show that miR-10 holds back two Hox genes in the fish. By curbing those genes, the small RNA helps set where body parts form. This adds a layer of fine control to the classic Hox plan. It also shows how tiny RNAs shape growth long before the animal takes its final form.
plos-pone-0001496:
Michael Rosenberg and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how muscle like motors build their bundles. Myosin motors form part of the cell's inner frame. Each motor has a long coiled tail, and tails must pack into bundles for the motor to pull at full force. The team asked what steers that packing.

They show the net charge along the tail rod rules both packing and where bundles sit in the cell. Charge is a simple trait with a large effect here. That rule helps labs predict how tail changes will alter cell pull. It may also guide design of man made motor materials.
plos-pone-0001596:
Andrew Kitchen, Michael Miyamoto, and Connie Mulligan wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how the Americas were first peopled. They weigh gene, dig, land, and climate proof in one frame. Past tales had split on route and pace. The team set out a three stage model that fits the full proof set.

In their model, a root group first split in Asia. It then waited out the ice age in the far north, then spread south in a swift wave. Each stage rests on a distinct line of proof. A model that honors all lines beats one that picks a favorite. It gives digs and gene hunts a shared map.
plos-pone-0001696:
Pablo Perel and co-authors checked whether clinical trials in Latin America match the region's health needs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article.
