Petherick's team at Oxford tracked how Brazilians felt about rival camps through the 2022 vote. Five planned survey waves followed two to three thousand people. Liking scales and smarts ratings measured affective polarization across waves. Groups spanned left-right labels, anti-voters, and candidate loyalists.

Lula versus Bolsonaro fans showed the fiercest mutual dislike before the race even began. That heat held through voting, then faded evenly on both sides. Fixing false beliefs about the other side's policy stances softened polarization a lot. Some fixes even shifted their own policy support on hot issues.
pmc-13241796:
Carmelo Betancort Acosta and a large team describe a 2026 trial protocol for a health app with artificial intelligence personalization. The WARIFA app supports healthier habits in the general public and self-care for type one diabetes. Risk factors for major chronic diseases are its main targets.

Around a hundred European participants were to be assigned by chance to the personalized or a plain version of the app. Personalized features include diet advice from food logs, step-based encouragement, and risk forecasts for several diseases. Diabetes participants also receive glucose predictions. Everyone gets an activity monitor and uses the app for roughly two to three months. Each person picks a personal goal at the start as the main outcome.
pmc-13242396:
De Plano's team in Messina traced Alzheimer's tau harm to a tiny RNA strangling mitochondria. Lab nerve cells made to overproduce mutant tau P301L formed the model. The cells grew in dishes in the lab. The microRNA miR-125b rose sharply in the tau-laden cells. Its likely gene targets clustered heavily in mitochondrial pathways.

Gene copies for breathing-chain parts one, four, and five fell sharply. Seahorse flux tests confirmed sagging basal breathing and ATP output. Spare breathing capacity shrank too. The team names miR-125b as the bridge between tau harm and energy failure.
pmc-13243296:
Qiyuan Lin and colleagues examine how people with early hip pain control their muscles during squats in 2026. Movement can look normal even when the control behind it has shifted. The team asked whether changing stance width would expose hidden differences.

Volunteers with hip pain and pain-free controls did standard squats at three stance widths. Sensors on both legs recorded muscle activity through the whole movement. Both groups used three stable muscle patterns, yet the pain group weighted and timed them in distinct ways. Differences grew as stance widened and peaked near the bottom of the squat. Muscle strength was also lower in the pain group, which suggests early change that routine checks can miss.
pmc-13243396:
Mingyi Yang and a large team test a grape-related compound against rheumatoid arthritis in 2026 lab work. The compound, piceatannol, is known for calming inflammation and fighting cell damage. The team wanted targets it might act on inside arthritic joints.

Computer screens first matched the compound against genes that differ in arthritis, yielding six hub genes. Models suggested it binds each hub well, with one kinase standing out. Cell tests then showed slower growth and more death in joint lining cells after treatment. Rats with induced arthritis also fared better on the compound. The authors present the results as early support for deeper study, not proof of a treatment.
pmc-13245396:
Bryan, Shields-Pruiett, and Berger tested last-resort antibiotics against the Pacific Northwest's toughest bacteria, in this 2026 JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance brief report. Carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative rods leave clinicians few options. The team assembled one hundred sixty-two isolates from unique patients and measured their susceptibility to five reserve beta-lactam drugs, including the newer cefiderocol and aztreonam-avibactam, and sequenced the genomes of selected Stenotrophomonas isolates.

Cefiderocol performed best overall, stopping nearly all Stenotrophomonas and most Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas isolates, while aztreonam-avibactam matched it in some groups but lagged in others. Sequencing linked reduced cefiderocol susceptibility to disruptive mutations in cell-wall building genes. In the bloodstream-infection subset, drawn from very ill patients, cefiderocol again showed the highest activity, guiding regional treatment choices.
pmc-13246596:
Cristina Valdovinos and co-authors track primary care visits in a public safety net system through COVID-19 in a 2026 study. Such systems serve many low-income patients and those with limited English. How remote care grew there, and for whom, was little known.

Records compared three spans: the year before the pandemic, its first year, and a second stretch into 2022. Remote visits jumped from under one in five patients to nearly all patients in year one. That share stayed high in the second period. Phone visits made up more than four fifths of remote care. The authors warn that ending payment for phone visits would hit underserved patients hardest.
pmc-13246796:
Wanas, Salama, and Abdelmotagaly ran two seasons of field trials on common beans under drought, in this 2026 Scientific Reports paper. Beans in dry regions suffer both water shortage and missing trace minerals. The team grew three varieties on sandy soil under full watering, moderate deficit, or severe deficit, spraying leaves with iron, zinc, and manganese at three dose levels.

The variety Giza 6 coped best, keeping higher chlorophyll and stronger antioxidant defenses, especially at the top spray dose. Moderate water deficit paired with the higher sprays preserved leaf minerals, growth, grain quality, and the best yield per unit of water. The authors say variety choice plus foliar feeding can blunt drought losses, though responses differed by genotype.
pmc-13247196:
A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2018 paper on a growth signal in bladder cancer, issued by the editors and publisher of OncoTargets and Therapy. The paper had claimed that the signal Nodal drives bladder cancer cell spread through a known pathway. Doubts about its figures were raised by a third party in 2024.

A journal inquiry confirmed odd similarities between image panels that were meant to show unlike conditions. Parts of figures also overlapped with blots in two papers by other groups on other topics. Such overlap breaks trust in the data behind the claims. The notice records the withdrawal so readers and future studies do not build on the work.
pmc-13247296:
Yeung, Tong, and Zhao make the case for very short personality questionnaires in digital mental health, in this 2026 Journal of Medical Internet Research article. Apps increasingly personalize messages and interventions, but the psychological traits that best guide personalization are usually measured with long scales nobody wants to complete on a phone. The authors review ways to shrink scales drastically while keeping their value.

They compare shortening methods, item-level regression, factor analysis, item response theory, ant colony optimization, and machine learning, each with conditions where it fits. Worked examples show how a few items might decide whether a user gets a story-style or a research-style message. Their three-tiered decision framework helps practitioners choose a method, arguing that a handful of well-chosen items beats an abandoned long form.
pmc-13247796:
Seana Camp, McKing Izeiza Amedari, and Adejare Atanda test whether having a usual care home predicts dental visits in a 2026 survey study. Primary care links patients to preventive services of many kinds. Whether that link extends to the dentist had not been checked in national data.

The team used survey records from 8,727 adults gathered between 2017 and 2020. Most adults had a routine care source, and about six in ten had seen a dentist in the past year. Adults with a care home were more than twice as likely to have had that visit. Black adults still lagged on dental visits even with care access and insurance. Joined medical-dental models may close the gap.
pmc-13248396:
Mestre Borras and a Swedish team engineered a cancer antibody that stays masked until needed, reported in 2026. Cetuximab attacks a growth receptor on tumors, but the same receptor sits in healthy tissue, causing side effects. The team built small binding proteins, called affibodies, that cover the antibody's active tip like a cap.

Screening a bacterial display library gave caps that blocked the antibody from its target. Fusing the best cap to the antibody made a prodrug far weaker when masked than when freed. In mice carrying human tumors, the prodrug could switch on where needed. The authors present masking as a route to safer antibody drugs.
pmc-13248896:
Bosch‐Capblanch and colleagues present OSSYRIS, an open-source system for running systematic reviews, in a 2026 paper. Reviews demand many unlike tasks, and data extraction is a known bottleneck because studies report results in wildly different styles. The team linked existing free tools rather than building everything from scratch.

References live in Zotero, screening and extraction run through KoboToolbox forms, and R code stitches the parts together and produces flow diagrams and tables automatically. Standard, pre-coded extraction forms keep data uniform across reviewers. The system has already served several real reviews, and the authors offer it as shared infrastructure for evidence teams.
pmc-13249096:
Zahoor and Rajra reviewed digital tools for sorting abnormal womb bleeding, in a 2026 Cureus article. Many patients cannot tell normal monthly variation from bleeding that needs a doctor, which delays care. Searching three databases, the authors screened one hundred twenty-two records and kept twenty-seven studies covering apps, diaries, remote visits, and artificial intelligence triage.

Tracking apps spotted abnormal patterns at scale, and picture-based charts measured blood loss more reliably than memory. Remote consultations worked for selected cases when safety nets were clear. Prediction models for womb lining disease looked promising but unproven. The authors call for validated triage rules and attention to privacy and fairness before wider rollout.
pmc-13249596:
Yuanquan Li and colleagues report a 2026 study of smell loss in people with obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea syndrome. The team asked which features of sleep track with a weaker sense of smell. They also tested whether the share of rapid eye movement sleep predicts smell problems on its own.

The group reviewed records from 198 patients whose apnea was confirmed by overnight sleep studies between 2020 and 2024. Each patient took a standardized smell test, and the researchers compared scores with sleep measures such as apnea severity and time in each sleep stage. Patients with smell problems had higher apnea scores and spent less of the night in rapid eye movement sleep. Statistical models singled out older age, worse apnea, and a lower share of rapid eye movement sleep as separate predictors. The authors suggest smell screening for older patients with severe apnea and little dream sleep.
pmc-13249996:
Xu and colleagues review how fertilizer shapes the health of rice paddy soil, in a 2026 Crop Health article. Flooded paddies host unusual microbes and store carbon differently from dry fields, because oxygen-starved soil slows decay. The authors summarize how nutrient cycles turn over through the planting season and how fertilizer choices ripple through the microbial community that runs them.

Organic fertilizers came out ahead of purely chemical ones for soil life and environmental cost, in their reading. Carbon storage has a ceiling, past which extra fertilizer buys nothing. Adjusting soil acidity and chemistry through sensible feeding can steer microbes toward locking carbon away. The authors look ahead to data-driven, precision feeding systems.
pmc-13250396:
Wakabayashi, Kimura, and Kawauchi review the gut lining as a layered gatekeeper that keeps harmful material out of the body. Their 2026 International Journal of Microbiology paper explains the puzzle: the intestine must absorb nutrients while blocking germs and toxins. Four layers share that job, namely physical, chemical, microbial, and immune defenses.

When the barrier weakens, gut contents leak into the bloodstream, a state often called leaky gut. The authors link such leaks to inflammation reaching the liver, brain, muscles, and kidneys, and note that damage differs between the small and large intestine. They also survey tests of barrier function, lab models, and repair strategies from diet and microbe therapies to lifestyle change. Restoring the barrier, they argue, could help prevent many body-wide diseases.
pmc-13250696:
Tsubasa Sasaki and Yoshiyuki Hirano explore a Japanese idea about belonging in this 2026 viewpoint paper on child psychiatry. The word ibasho means a place, physical or emotional, where a child feels accepted as their true self and safe with others.

The authors argue that feeling one has an ibasho tracks closely with mental health, since a sense of belonging predicts well-being through the teen years. Using a nationwide government survey of children and young people from 2022, they map where children find such places across home, school, and other settings, and how this shifts with age. They urge care that supports many kinds of ibasho, not just one.
pmc-13250896:
Zheng and a large team look for social and household factors that send Chinese COPD patients to hospital with flare-ups. Their 2026 International Journal of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease study follows nearly four thousand patients nationwide, split into smoking-related and non-smoking forms of the disease. Hospital flare-ups and total yearly hospital days were tracked for one year.

About three in ten patients in both groups suffered a hospitalized flare-up during follow-up. Rural living, larger households, and a hospital stay in the prior year raised the risk for everyone. Cooking smoke exposure mattered independently only for non-smokers, and low body weight added risk in that group too. The authors say flare prevention in China must reach beyond smoking history to home and social conditions.
pmc-13250996:
Peddle and a large Canadian network argue that emergency blood transfusion trials need a different consent model. Their 2026 Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine position statement covers trials of transfusion given before hospital arrival. Badly hurt patients usually cannot consent, time is short, and family decision-makers are rarely at hand.

The network backs an exception from advance consent paired with opt-out notification, as used in a Canadian whole-blood pilot trial. Patients and communities get notified through several channels, and anyone enrolled can withdraw afterward. The model rests on Canada's emergency research rules, which the authors cite in detail. They present it as a national template that balances workable trials with respect for patient autonomy.
pmc-13251696:
Devaraj Sankarganesh and colleagues update the state of estrus detection in dairy cattle in a 2026 review. Catching the brief fertile window accurately is essential because most dairy breeding uses artificial insemination. Missed or mistimed detection is a major drag on reproductive efficiency, and high-yielding cows often show only faint signs of heat.

The review covers hormone programs that synchronize cycles so the fertile window arrives on schedule. It then turns to sensor systems, from activity monitors worn on the neck or leg to implanted devices, and to chemical sensors that read biomarkers in milk or breath. A newer strand uses artificial intelligence on behavior data gathered by those sensors. The authors weigh each method's accuracy, practicality, and cost for farmers. They close by flagging experimental technologies that could sharpen detection further once validated on real farms.
pmc-13252796:
Shuai Wang and co-authors generalise the rules for drawing fractals in this 2026 mathematics paper. Fractals such as Mandelbrot and Julia sets are drawn by repeating a formula until points escape, and the escape test decides the picture's fine detail.

The team applies a two-step viscosity method to a family of complex formulas. They then widen it with two kinds of convexity. At each stage they derive fresh escape tests for Mandelbrot sets, Julia sets, and biomorph patterns. Side-by-side pictures made in MATLAB, at 50 iterations, show how each variant reshapes the same formula's output. The work adds options for both theory and fractal art.
pmc-13253096:
Laura Anna Bokor and colleagues link a glucose transporter to interferon activity and severity in cutaneous lupus in a 2026 study. Cutaneous lupus is an autoimmune skin disease driven by overactive type I interferon signaling. Whether disturbed glucose metabolism feeds that inflammation had not been examined in this condition.

The team took skin biopsies from fifty-one patients with active, untreated disease, covering its subacute and discoid forms, plus eight healthy controls. Staining showed the glucose transporter GLUT1 markedly increased in patient skin, alongside MxA, a marker protein switched on by interferon. The more GLUT1 in surface skin cells, the higher the interferon marker and the worse the clinical activity score. Public gene expression data backed the pairing across several cell types. The authors propose that heightened glucose uptake helps power the inflammatory process. They suggest metabolism deserves a place in future models of how this disease flares.
pmc-13253596:
Anna Seifert and colleagues compare two routes to the same brain cancer label in this 2026 study. Under current rules, a glioma can be called glioblastoma by its look under the microscope or by molecular markers, and whether those two groups fare alike was open.

The team studied 47 lower-looking tumours lacking the usual gene fault: 39 qualified as glioblastoma by molecular markers, mostly a promoter mutation, and eight had none of the defining changes. The molecular group showed lower cell growth rates and more seizures at presentation. Raw survival was similar between routes, but after adjusting for age, surgery extent, and treatment completion, the molecular group lived longer. The eight marker-free tumours were a mixed bag needing deeper testing.
pmc-13253696:
Chihyuan Cheng and colleagues derive a prognostic score for liver cancer from the immune cells gathered in tumor lymphoid hubs in a 2026 study. Tertiary lymphoid structures, improvised immune outposts inside tumors, have shown inconsistent links to survival in hepatocellular carcinoma when described by shape alone. A statistical method estimated each immune component's share in bulk tumor data from large cohorts. A penalized survival model kept just two features, regulatory T cells and a dendritic cell type called cDC2, as a compact risk score. The score separated survival in two international cohorts and tracked with response to PD-1 blockade therapy in a third. A tissue-staining version of the same two measures reproduced the split in hospital samples. The authors offer it as a translatable gauge of tumor immune state.
pmc-13253796:
Yueheng Zhang and colleagues profile a little-studied arm of the ruminant immune system in cattle and water buffalo in a 2026 sequencing study. Gamma-delta T cells make up an unusually large share of immune cells in these animals, and the delta chain of their receptor carries the key recognition region, called CDR3. The team sequenced that region at high depth in seven cattle and five buffalo.

Cattle showed the richer, more evenly spread repertoire, while buffalo leaned harder on a smaller set of heavily expanded receptor clones. Gene segment usage split the species cleanly: the variable segments differed with strong species-specific preferences, while the joining segments were highly conserved across both. Very few exact receptor sequences were shared between the species. The authors present the comparison as baseline data for understanding how these animals recognize threats differently.
pmc-13254196:
Vicky Muller Ferreira and Victor Ayres Muller pool trial data on GLP-1 drugs in heart failure in a 2026 meta-analysis. GLP-1 receptor agonists are drugs first made for diabetes that also help the heart. The team gathered 14 studies with 18,184 patients, covering all heart failure types.

Yet the death gain came from subgroup data, while direct heart failure trials leaned toward harm, so caution is urged.
pmc-13254896:

Dapagliflozin, a glucose-lowering drug, is known to protect arteries, but not entirely through sugar control. pmc-13255096:
Eshaan S. Patheria and colleagues report a 2026 battery study aimed at cathodes built from cheap, widely produced elements. Lithium-ion batteries need huge expansion for clean transport and energy, yet common cathode metals face supply limits. The team's earlier cathodes used aluminum, iron, and sulfur, storing charge partly through sulfur chemistry.

Here they added copper into the sulfide cathode across a range of amounts. Copper's strong bonding with sulfur let it hold positive charge itself, extending how the material balances charge during use. Copper also capped the total capacity, apparently by destabilizing the emptied structure. The authors say mapping both effects helps design future cathodes that squeeze more electrons from each atom.
pmc-13255196:
Yuanjia Zhong and colleagues report the full mitochondrial genome of a grasshopper in a 2026 study. Stauroderus scalaris is a grasshopper from Xinjiang, China, common in high meadow country. pmc-13257096:
Kamila Borowiec leads a 2026 study of two changed forms of quercetin, a plant pigment in foods. Adding one methyl group at unlike spots can change what the molecule does. The two forms, isorhamnetin and rhamnetin, were tested in dishes, in computer models, and in young zebrafish.

Four bench tests gauged how well each form mops up harmful oxygen forms. Rhamnetin scored higher in three of them. Isorhamnetin blocked an enzyme tied to pain and swelling more strongly, and models showed a unlike grip in the enzyme pocket. Young fish bore rhamnetin better at high doses. Both forms eased movement loss in a toxin model of nerve decay. The lesson is plain: where the group sits shapes both gain and risk.
pmc-13257696:
Zheng Ruan and co-authors compute the chemistry of a carnitine-making enzyme and its blocker drug in a 2026 study. The enzyme BBOX finishes carnitine production, and mildronate treats heart ischemia by interfering with it. In the drug, a nitrogen atom beside the reaction site made bond cleavage easier than the normal oxygen rebound, halting carnitine output. A previously proposed shortcut migration was ruled out, and a revised path through an imine intermediate was offered instead. Drug designers gain an electronic explanation for selectivity. The same logic may guide new blockers across this oxygen-using enzyme family.
pmc-13257996:
Paweł Możejko calculates what happens when electrons strike the building blocks of DNA. His 2026 paper covers deoxyribose, the sugar in DNA's backbone, and five nucleosides that pair sugars with bases. The figures he seeks, called ionization cross-sections, describe how likely electron impact is to knock out an electron.

He used the binary-encounter-Bethe model, fed by quantum chemical calculations of each molecule's electronic structure. Energies ran from the ionization threshold up to four thousand electron volts. Możejko also tests a shortcut: adding up cross-sections of smaller pieces to estimate bigger DNA blocks. Such data feed models of radiation damage in living tissue.
pmc-13258296:
André C. de Oliveira and a large team profile a pepper plant oil that kills mosquito larvae in a 2026 study. Piper humillimum oil was tested against dengue and malaria vectors whose resistance to synthetic insecticides keeps growing. Chemistry, larval assays, enzyme measures, and computer docking were combined for a full mechanism picture.

Two sesquiterpenes dominated the oil, and lethal doses sat in a useful range for both mosquito species. Treated larvae showed surging peroxide, damaged fats and proteins, and raised defense enzymes. Field persistence, non-target safety, and formulation stability remain the gates between this bench success and real breeding-site use.
pmc-13258496:
Elena Cesar-Rodo and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study on likely breakdown products of a drug family aimed at schistosomiasis. Earlier screening found two related compounds active against the worm that causes the disease. Inside parasites those drugs change through oxidation steps, and ring shaped products called benzoxanthones may form along the way.

Making the methoxy versions proved difficult because key starting materials were missing and some steps damaged the target groups. A revised route used protected groups and cheaper substitutes to finish the synthesis. Selected products were tested in parasite and cell assays. The authors argue environmental risk stays low because harm needs activation inside the parasite.
pmc-13258896:
Marina V. Parchaykina and coauthors test bacterial cellulose tubes as replacement blood vessels in a 2026 biomaterials study. Two modified versions of the cellulose conduit were compared for strength, stretch, and cell safety. Native vessel properties set the target range.

Both versions matched natural vessel behavior on the measured properties. One version stretched more while carrying lower tensile strength. Nanoscale pores in the fiber structure invited lining cells to attach inside the tube. Cell tests showed no toxicity and good oxygen passage. Heat tests tied elastic behavior to how the modifier bonded with cellulose fibers. Regenerative medicine gains a natural graft option with promising handling traits.
pmc-13259096:
Muntajin Rahman and coauthors review herbal treatments for cognitive disorders in a 2026 article. Memory and thinking disorders involve several transmitter systems plus inflammation, oxidative stress, and gut brain signaling. Standard drugs often give limited relief with notable side effects.

Herbs such as bacopa, ashwagandha, and ginkgo show protective effects in laboratory work and some small human studies. Proposed actions span antioxidant, anti inflammatory, and transmitter balancing effects. Delivery tricks like nanoparticles may raise brain uptake. Trial quality stays uneven, with small samples and short durations common. Clinicians get a balanced map of promise and proof gaps.
pmc-13259196:
Yubin Lin and coauthors coat water filter membranes with a two metal polyphenol network in a 2026 study. Tannic acid from plants bridges silver framework particles and iron ions during membrane formation. The goal was faster water flow with less fouling and added antibacterial action.

The best loading raised pure water flow to nearly double the plain membrane value. Protein rejection stayed high at the same time. Water loving, negatively charged surfaces resisted protein sticking and recovered flow well after cleaning. Silver release stayed controlled over long soaking. Water treatment gains a membrane that resists both clogging and bacterial growth.
pmc-13259296:
Mengwen Guo and coauthors formulate a screen printable liquid metal ink for silicone rubber sheets in a 2026 study. Gallium based inks usually bead up and stick poorly to silicone. A polymer modifier and a three solvent blend fixed wetting, flow, and drying together.

At the best recipe the ink spread flat instead of beading on the silicone surface. Viscosity could be tuned across the range screen printing needs. Laser treatment activated the printed traces into stable conductors. Resistance barely drifted after two weeks of storage or thousands of bends. Stretch cycles also left readings nearly unchanged. Wearable circuit makers gain a printable ink that survives daily flexing.
pmc-13259396:
Jiawei Song and coauthors polish tiny timing errors in passive seismic records in a 2026 paper. Even synchronized instruments drift slightly over long recordings, which blurs event locations. Their method works in the wavefield domain using quiet noise windows and controlled test events.

Station pairs yield residual lag estimates that are fused with confidence weights. A smooth correction curve then aligns the full record through fine interpolation. A sixty minute record from a six station local array validated the approach. Stacking quality and timing consistency improved after correction. Mine and city monitoring networks gain cleaner data without new hardware synchronization.
pmc-13259496:
Ruifeng Zhang and coauthors survey plant invasion in a high mountain wetland in a 2026 field study. Nearly three hundred plots in the Shennongjia reserve were checked for nine invasive species. Invaders appeared in just over half of all plots sampled.

Invaded plots held greener, thinner leaves on average than clean plots. Species diversity and family tree diversity fell as invasion intensity rose. Functional variety rose at the same time, showing reorganization rather than simple loss. Trait shifts grew stronger when invaders were counted inside the community measures. Reserve managers learn that invasion rewrites how the wetland works, not just which species live there.
pmc-13259596:
Qian Zhao, Magnus Rattray, and Guoqiang Yu present a software tool that merges gene tail site predictions in a 2026 paper. Single cell sequencing can reveal where RNA tails attach, yet three popular tools disagree widely on site lists. Their integrator offers two merging strategies for different user needs.

One strategy keeps only sites every tool supports, for high confidence work. Another keeps sites backed by a subset, for broader discovery. Sensitive tools paired with positionally precise tools gave the best combined behavior. Merged high confidence sites showed the expected biological sequence signatures. The tool is freely available for research groups to reuse.
pmc-13259996:
Alper Baydar and colleagues modeled in 2026 how climate change may alter the water footprint of rice in Mediterranean Türkiye. Rice needs steady water, and hotter, drier seasons threaten supply. Their work used a crop model already tuned for local conditions, driven by three climate models and two emission paths.

For irrigated rice, the water needed per ton of grain was highest in the near-future period and lower by the late century. Rainfed rice showed a far larger footprint in the near future, because low rainfall and water stress cut simulated yields. Footprints depended on yield response and irrigation regime as much as on water lost to the air. The authors present the approach as a planning tool for rice water management.
pmc-13260196:
Chen Xu leads a 2026 study adapting a scale that measures social media bullying harm among Chinese college students. The scale gauges how often students are targeted online. In Shanghai, 1,766 students from several universities filled in the adapted scale plus standard depression and anxiety surveys. The team checked the scale's content, structure, steadiness, and stability over time, and tested how well it predicted depression and anxiety scores.

Thirteen items were retained, forming two parts: information harassment, and harm to reputation and privacy. Together they explained 82.2 percent of the spread in answers. Both parts tracked closely with depression and anxiety. Overall, the scale proved steady, with a main coefficient of 0.959, and a test-retest value of 0.860 across two rounds. The scale showed fair accuracy in spotting depression and anxiety, with area-under-curve values near 0.74 for both outcomes.
pmc-13260296:
Manar Bani-Hani and colleagues surveyed in 2026 critical care nurses who treated COVID-19 patients in Lebanon during the pandemic. Lebanon faced a nursing shortage and a deep economic crisis at the same time. Their questionnaire reached 112 nurses at one university hospital and measured work stress, job satisfaction, and plans to quit.

Nurses reported high stress and only moderate satisfaction with their jobs. More than half said they intended to leave their current post. Stress tied to infection stigma, the shame attached to catching or spreading the virus, showed a clear negative link with satisfaction. The authors urge targeted mental health help and stronger organizational support to keep nurses in post. They also ask future studies to cover wider social and political pressures on staff.
pmc-13261596:
Yao Fang and colleagues proposed in 2026 a new way to estimate the health of lithium-ion batteries from electrical impedance signals. Judging battery aging accurately keeps vehicles and storage systems safe. Their method fuses mean and median impedance over a mid charge window into a single feature that balances trend sensitivity against noise.

A vision transformer reshaped for one-dimensional signals then reads that feature over time. An adaptive gated unit inside the model helps it handle the unsteady character of battery data. On an eight-cell pack the method reached very low error and explained nearly all variation in true health. It also performed well on other packs, including series strings with uneven cells. The authors target online monitoring inside battery management systems.
pmc-13263196:
S Müller and colleagues examine whether leakage after colon cancer surgery affects long-term survival in a 2026 journal article. A leak at the join between bowel ends is a major complication, but most earlier data mixed colon and rectal cancers. The team reviewed 166 patients operated on at one German university hospital between 2019 and 2021, tracking survival to mid-2025.

Fifteen patients, about 9 percent, developed a leak. Tumor site, stage, and complete removal rates were similar in patients with and without leaks. After accounting for age, stage, and other factors, a leak was linked to roughly triple the risk of death. Survival curves confirmed shorter survival after a leak. The authors stress prevention strategies around surgery.
pmc-13263496:
Ali Mawlood Ibrahim and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on breast self-examination and screening barriers among women with breast cancer in Baghdad, Iraq. They surveyed 325 diagnosed women aged eighteen to sixty-three about their habits before diagnosis and the obstacles they faced.

Engagement was low: about sixty-eight percent had never checked for lumps, and about ninety percent had never been trained to do so. Four in five had no screening before diagnosis. Reported barriers included trouble communicating with doctors, little personal power to decide on testing, and reluctance to waste doctors' time. Cancer stage was strongly tied to health insurance and to fear of visiting doctors. The authors urge sustained education and accessible screening.
pmc-13263696:
Mahtab Tavasoli and colleagues tested in 2026 a gene therapy for a rare muscular dystrophy caused by loss of the CHKB gene. The gene builds an enzyme in the pathway for a major membrane fat, and its loss weakens muscle from infancy. Their mouse model mirrors the human disease, with shrunken fibers, giant mitochondria, and fatty muscle.

A single injection of a virus carrying the human gene went to knockout mice at three dose levels. Every dose restored the missing enzyme's activity in muscle. Treated mice matched healthy animals in body and muscle weight, cell health, fat balance, and walking capacity. The authors describe the treated animals as indistinguishable from wild type on their measures. They propose the approach as a candidate treatment for the fewer than fifty known patients worldwide.
pmc-13264296:
Eslam Ahmed and colleagues report two-year outcomes after switching a stubborn eye disease to a newer drug in a 2026 real-world study. Wet age-related macular degeneration that responded poorly to a standard injection drug was switched to faricimab in over one hundred fifty eyes. After loading doses, intervals between injections were stretched as far as stability allowed, with vision, retinal thickness and fluid status tracked for at least twenty months.

Vision held essentially steady at two years while central retinal thickness fell substantially. Half the eyes achieved complete fluid clearance, and average treatment spacing lengthened considerably, with a minority reaching very long intervals. No severe inflammatory eye complications appeared, and side effects were uncommon. Resistant cases gained anatomical control without vision loss.
pmc-13264896:
Gagan Prakash and colleagues wrote a 2026 scoping review of penile cancer care and its uneven patterns worldwide. The cancer is rare, but staging, treatment, and outcomes vary a great deal by place. The team gathered evidence across staging, virus links, organ-saving care, node surgery, drug therapy, and life after treatment.

They note that current staging rules leave out tumor virus status, even though virus-linked tumors may respond differently to radiation and drugs, and testing is not yet routine. Early disease can often be treated while sparing the organ, but access differs widely. Node care lacks shared rules, and a gentler node biopsy method stays limited to big centers. Life-after-treatment support is poorly covered. The authors call for global consensus and shared long-term data.
pmc-13264996:
Hong-Zhen Li and co-authors wrote a 2026 study of Fu's subcutaneous needling, a shallow needle method, for neck and shoulder symptoms after neck spine surgery. The operation opens the back of the neck to relieve cord pressure, yet such axial symptoms remain common afterward. Records from a Beijing hospital let the team compare needled patients with those on standard rehabilitation alone.

Each group held 48 patients treated from 2023 to 2024 at Peking University People's Hospital. The needling group improved more on pain, neck disability, and function scores at every check, and the benefits held at twelve weeks. Neck alignment and range of motion recovered better, and brace-wearing time was shorter, while patients with worse starting pain seemed to gain most. No needling side effects were reported, and the authors call the method a safe, promising add-on that now needs prospective controlled trials.
pmc-13265196:
Song Wang and colleagues study a protein called periostin in papillary thyroid cancer, in a 2026 laboratory and patient study. This cancer type is the most common thyroid malignancy, and its incidence is rising. Periostin is involved in many cancers, with its role here unclear. Samples came from thirty patients and thirty healthy controls.

Periostin was higher in tumour tissue and blood, especially at advanced stages. Silencing the protein in cancer cells slowed growth and movement. Its suppression also raised cell death and self-eating activity, tied to a growth pathway. The authors propose periostin as a prognostic indicator and a possible treatment target.
pmc-13267496:
Shoichi Sugita, Kentaro Okano, and Atsunori Mori develop in 2026 a palladium-catalyzed route that folds quinoline-based amides into fused lactam rings. Their method activates two bonds in sequence: a carbon-hydrogen bond beside the amide on the quinoline and the amide's own nitrogen-hydrogen bond. Early runs in hot xylene solvent gave the ring product in modest yield.

Adding a phosphorus ligand and more catalyst lifted the yield sharply, reaching above eighty percent in the best cases. The reaction tolerated varied functional groups and worked with several two-halogen starting rings, including sulfur and nitrogen containing partners. Strong selectivity between the two halogen sites lets chemists branch from one product into many fused ring systems for materials and drug research.
pmc-13267696:
Afeng Wang and a large team report a 2026 survey of drug resistance genes in poultry farm bacteria in Zhejiang Province, China. Antibiotic resistance in farm animals is a shared threat to animal and human health. The team checked E. coli bacteria from poultry farms across the province for genes that defeat antibiotics, including genes against last-resort drugs.

All 106 isolates carried at least one resistance gene, and 99 percent resisted several drug types at once. Samples from Huzhou, a major poultry hub, carried more resistance genes than those from other areas. Moving gene carriers were linked to genes appearing together. The authors read the pattern as a sign of strong antibiotic pressure on farms. They call for tighter drug stewardship and joint monitoring across farms, environment, and clinics.
pmc-13267896:
Carolina Barbosa Carvalho do Carmo and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a rare tissue disorder that finally answered to a targeted drug. Rosai-Dorfman disease grows immune cells called histiocytes, usually mildly, but sometimes aggressively. Their patient was a 41-year-old woman with two years of spreading disease in neck and chest lymph nodes and her voice box.

Steroids, immune suppressants, other modulators, and chemotherapy all failed her. Gene sequencing of her tissue found a change in MAP2K1, a gene in a major cell growth pathway. She started cobimetinib, a drug that blocks the next step in that same pathway. Her disease cleared fully on scans and exams. The response has lasted over three years since she stopped the drug. The authors urge gene testing in stubborn cases.
pmc-13268196:
Manusnan Suriyalaksh and colleagues present a 2026 study using explainable machine learning on Thai rice farming. Thailand's rice yields trail its neighbors, and advice is usually one-size-fits-all. The team gathered data from 1,722 smallholder farmers in central Thailand, covering 58 farm and money variables. They compared four automated machine learning systems at predicting each farm's yield.

One system, AutoGluon, predicted best. An explanation method then ranked which factors drove the predictions. Farmers' social networks came first, followed by harvest rental costs and total harvest spending. Stronger social ties linked to higher yields, hinting that shared know-how lifts output. Grouping farmers by their explanation patterns produced six distinct cohorts, each ruled by different factors. The authors argue support programs should be tailored per cohort, not uniform.
pmc-13269096:
Regeru Njoroge Regeru and co-authors review in 2026 public health programs that aim to improve mental health and mental health literacy among young people in poorer countries. Young adults carry a heavy burden of depression and schizophrenia, while treatment gaps yawn wide where staff and money are scarce. Their systematic review gathered studies from medical and regional databases plus grey literature, ending with thirty programs.

Most programs taught behavior therapy skills, often adapted from established frameworks such as cognitive behavioral therapy. Ten used digital tools, from computerized therapy to messaging support. Twenty-five reported significant gains, though follow-up rarely passed six months. Literacy gains showed in social support, self-belief, and reframing of thoughts. Adapting proven frameworks to local settings emerged as a practical design lesson.
pmc-13269296:
Marius J P Zuidweg and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 reviewing 25 years of surgery for lung defects present at birth in Rotterdam. Most children were treated because the defect caused symptoms, above all trouble breathing. Records came from a structured long-term follow-up program.

Eighty patients had surgery over the period, at a median age of 108 days. Open chest surgery was used in 60 percent of cases and keyhole surgery in 29 percent. The median hospital stay after surgery was six days, and only 2.5 percent needed another operation. At the latest visit, 21 percent still had lung symptoms. The authors stress long-term management after early repair.
pmc-13270396:
Raj Kumar Sharma and co-authors published a pilot study in 2026 on detecting clear cell kidney cancer from blood plasma using proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy, a chemical fingerprinting method. Plasma came from 30 people split evenly: biopsy-confirmed cancer patients, patients with benign kidney masses, and healthy controls.

Cancer plasma profiles differed from both other groups. Several chemicals were significantly higher in cancer, including hydroxybutyrate, glucose, and creatinine. Two more were elevated in both benign and cancer plasma against healthy controls. Pathway analysis pointed to altered fat building, amino acid handling, nitrogen processing, and sugar breakdown, matching known cancer reprogramming. The authors present the method as a non-invasive detection route worth developing.
pmc-13271096:
Youngjune Kim and coauthors address in 2026 a practical problem in bone screening with chest scans. Doctors can spot weak bones on CT scans taken for other reasons, but bone density readings shift with scanner voltage and spinal level. Without a shared standard, the same patient can look healthier or sicker depending on scan settings.

The team studied 589 patients who had low-dose chest CT and a standard bone density test within three months. Their model linked density readings to the logarithm of tube voltage and to spinal level from T10 to L2. Converted thresholds matched scan-derived cutoffs closely, which could let hospitals screen for osteoporosis more consistently from scans already being taken.
pmc-13271296:
Dylan Evans is lead author of a 2026 systematic review on whether two changes in the EGFR gene predict response to EGFR-targeted drugs in recurrent glioblastoma, the most aggressive brain tumour type. Extra copies of EGFR and a mutated form called EGFRvIII are common in this cancer, yet their value for choosing treatment was unclear.

Searching three databases for studies from 2010 to 2025, the team kept twelve studies covering 565 patients. Median overall survival ranged from 5.7 to 10.3 months across studies, with no consistent survival benefit tied to either marker. Most studies were single-arm and mixed in design. The authors conclude neither marker should guide treatment choices outside clinical trials.
pmc-13271996:
Jia Xu and coauthors review in 2026 COVID-19 vaccination in pregnancy, with focus on newer second-generation vaccines. Pregnancy changes the immune system and breathing reserve, raising the risk of severe illness from the virus. Many pregnant women still hesitate over vaccine safety for themselves and their babies.

The review weighs protection and safety evidence for mothers and newborns, including outcomes after infection with the Omicron variant. It then examines why hesitancy persists despite reassuring data, from safety worries to access problems. The authors call for refined vaccination protocols and fairer access to cut infection risk during pregnancy.
pmc-13272196:
Chenming Zhang is lead author of a 2026 journal article on a long non-coding RNA called NORAD in spinal cord injury, severe trauma to the central nervous system. Such RNAs do not build proteins but regulate other genes, and the team explored whether NORAD drives oxidative stress and inflammation in nerve cells after injury.

The study enrolled 100 spinal cord injury patients and 80 healthy controls, plus rat and cell models. NORAD levels were high in patients and predicted the disease well. Blocking NORAD in rats improved hind-leg movement recovery and eased oxidative stress, cell damage, and nerve inflammation. Cell tests traced the chain: NORAD suppresses a small RNA, miR-22-3p, which normally restrains the gene PTEN, and rescue experiments confirmed the linked pathway.
pmc-13273396:
Dominique Turck leads a 2026 safety opinion from the European Food Safety Authority panel on zinc L-carnosine as a novel food and zinc source in supplements. The European Commission asked for the opinion under EU novel food law. The product is a powder chelate of zinc and L-carnosine, meant for people over 12, excluding pregnant and breastfeeding women.

The panel found the data do not rule out a fraction of very small particles, including nanoparticles, and do not show quick dissolving in stomach conditions. Studies provided were limited, so how much zinc the body actually absorbs at proposed levels remains uncharacterised. The panel concludes the product is insufficiently characterised, and neither its bioavailability nor its safety can be established.
pmc-13273496:
Jingya Li and co-authors evaluated four large language models on questions about bone metastasis and cancer bone pain in a 2026 study. Chatbots answer in a human like way, yet their reliability on complex medical topics is uncertain. The team built eighteen structured questions from a bibliometric scan of the field.

They put the same questions to four leading models and rated answers for accuracy, readability, completeness, brevity, and empathy across research, clinical, and patient viewpoints. The models gave clear and intuitive information efficiently. Weak points included data bias, hard to trace reasoning, and unclear accountability for errors. The authors say such tools should serve as supervised assistants for experts, not replacements, and they call for better model design and specialty specific scoring standards.
pmc-13273796:
Lepage and colleagues introduce CIVET-Chimp, a software pipeline that maps the surface of the chimpanzee cortex from MRI scans. Their 2026 journal article adapts a human brain tool for chimps. The cortex is the folded outer layer of the brain.

The team built the pipeline on the existing CIVET system. They tuned it for chimpanzee brain size and shape. Testing used a 3-tesla MRI data set from the National Chimpanzee Brain Resource. Automated surface extraction replaces slow manual tracing. Reliable surfaces let researchers compare brain folding across primates. The authors present the tool as a resource for neuroscience. It may support studies of brain evolution and cognition.
pmc-13273896:
Zhang and colleagues build a system from algae and nanoparticles to prevent sepsis-associated encephalopathy. Their 2026 journal article combines Chlorella algae with liposomes loaded with melatonin. The condition is brain dysfunction triggered by severe infection.

The system is named CV@MT-NPs. The algae carry the particles through the body. This extended how long melatonin stayed in circulation. More of the drug also reached and stayed in the brain. In mice with LPS-induced disease, survival improved. Thinking deficits and anxiety-like behaviors eased. The particles protected the blood-brain barrier. They restored tight junction proteins and calmed microglia. The gut barrier and gut microbes also improved. Short-chain fatty acids rose in both gut and brain. Safety tests showed no acute or chronic toxicity.
pmc-13274596:
Jiahao Hu and a large team present a 2026 journal article on generating exceptionally clean microwave signals from laser light. Optical frequency division trades a laser's stability down to microwave frequencies, but thermal noise in the references usually forces complex setups. Their reference lasers are two-color Brillouin lasers sharing one cavity and running at the fundamental quantum noise limit.

With references that pure, a far simpler comb divider sufficed to produce a ten-gigahertz signal with extremely low phase noise, meaning very steady timing. The system also synthesized signals anywhere from five to twenty gigahertz with millisecond tuning. The authors target atomic clocks, quantum sensors, and low-noise radar as uses for such compact, high-purity sources.
pmc-13274896:
Minmin Zheng and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on software that steers ships away from collisions in crowded waters. Their method first groups nearby ships with similar movement using a belief-rule system, an expert-logic framework, so the planner faces fewer, clearer targets. Safety zones around each ship or group scale with ship length.

A velocity obstacle algorithm, which maps which speeds would cause a crash, then plots a safe route to the goal. The team tested the combined approach in two encounter scenarios representing congested traffic. They report better navigational safety and operating efficiency than handling every ship separately. The work is aimed at intelligent decision support for maritime safety management.
pmc-13275396:
Lauriane Blavette and co-authors publish a 2026 survey of French health workers and their views on socially assistive robots. Robots that help with logistics, daily support, or social contact raise ethical and workplace questions. The survey measured perceived usefulness, willingness to use such robots, and the conditions staff want before adoption.

A 48-item questionnaire drew 148 responses, and most respondents already knew something about these robots. Staff rated robots highest for physical help and recreation, and lowest for feeding and therapy roles. Cluster analysis split respondents into low, moderate, and high acceptance groups. The authors call for clear rules, training, and careful local planning before wider use.
pmc-13275496:
Harmon S Khela and colleagues present a 2026 journal article testing whether pre-drawn steroid injection syringes stay sterile in storage. Hand surgeons often mix corticosteroid and lidocaine syringes ahead of clinic to save time, then throw unused ones away over contamination fears, wasting money and materials. The team simulated clinic workflows in a controlled lab study.

Forty syringes were stored at room temperature in a closed cabinet and sampled at one day, three days, one week, and two weeks using next-generation DNA sequencing, a highly sensitive germ detector. Thirty-nine of forty samples, 97.5 percent, showed no bacterial DNA. One fluid sample from the one-week group grew a Streptococcus signal. The authors support longer use windows to cut waste.
pmc-13275796:
Francesco Pagnini and co-authors published a 2026 author correction to a study known as the Batman effect. The original study watched whether an unexpected sight, a person dressed as Batman, made strangers act more kindly. The correction fixes numbers that clashed between the text and a table in the first version.

The corrected counts give sixty-one observation sessions for the Batman condition and seventy-seven for the control condition, still one hundred thirty-eight in total. Kind behavior was seen in about sixty-seven percent of Batman sessions and about thirty-eight percent of control sessions. The text now matches the table on these figures. The authors state that the correction changes neither the results nor the conclusions of the study.
pmc-13275996:
Timothy Perez and co-authors built a 2026 database article on how much heat plants can tolerate. Such data could show how species will cope with hotter extremes, but past studies used inconsistent methods and skipped key details. A shared, careful collection was missing.

The team gathered heat tolerance records from papers and older databases, adding notes on species, methods, place, and growing conditions. The result holds more than three thousand records, covering over seventeen hundred plant types across more than two hundred families, from 1935 to 2024. That more than doubles species coverage over earlier databases. The authors warn that methods still differ widely, and some regions and plant groups remain barely sampled. They offer the database to support stronger future studies.
pmc-13276396:
Nozomi Seki and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a refined heart test for horses at risk of sudden death. Sudden death, often from lethal rhythm disturbances, endangers horses and riders. Signal-averaged electrocardiography smooths many heartbeats into one trace, revealing tiny late signals that hint at damaged heart muscle.

The team recorded high-resolution traces from twenty-four healthy Thoroughbreds aged two to thirty-one. They also tested one horse with drug-induced heart injury and three with lasting heart murmurs. In healthy horses, one timing measure lengthened with age, likely reflecting scarring. The injured horse showed the classic late-signal pattern, confirmed by tissue examination. Horses with murmurs alone scored within the healthy range. The authors propose the test as a painless screen for dangerous rhythm risk, best used with other diagnostics.
pmc-13276496:
Yasuaki Yasuda and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on warning signs before ammonia crises in urea cycle disorders. In these inherited conditions, the liver cannot clear ammonia, and sudden spikes can damage the brain. Outpatient blood tests offer few practical predictors of a coming crisis.

The team reviewed eighteen patients over a decade, half with newborn-onset and half with later-onset disease. They tracked short-term changes in two blood markers, glutamine and ammonia, between clinic visits. In newborn-onset patients, a rising glutamine trend in the two months before a crisis signaled higher risk. A large rise pushed the estimated crisis chance to about two thirds. Ammonia changes did not predict crises. In later-onset patients, neither marker helped. The authors back glutamine trend monitoring for the newborn-onset form only.
pmc-13276596:
Xuesong Li and co-authors test brief air exposure as a hardening treatment for oyster larvae, in a 2026 study. Young Pacific oysters die easily under heat and other stresses in hatcheries. Intertidal oysters naturally endure periods out of water, which hints that controlled exposure might build resilience.

Larvae at the umbo stage went through two rounds of intermittent air exposure. Exposed larvae survived later high-temperature stress at higher rates than unexposed larvae. Their antioxidant capacity rose, and two stress-response genes became more active. The benefit carried into the juvenile stage, suggesting a lasting effect. The authors present air exposure as a cheap, chemical-free hatchery tool.
pmc-13276996:
Zhen-Long Wang leads a 2026 genome study of the plateau zokor, a burrowing rodent that lives high on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. The team built full genome maps for four zokor species that live at different heights. They focused on repeated DNA stretches that are often left out of genome work.

The plateau species had a larger genome, driven by growth of one repeated stretch found near centromeres, the parts that help chromosomes split evenly. Removing that repeat in cells harmed chromosome sorting, above all in low-oxygen conditions like those at altitude. The findings suggest the repeat helps guard the genome in thin air, linking junk-like DNA to survival.
pmc-13278396:
Alice Coffey leads a 2026 analysis of nutrition and carbon footprints for diets of United Kingdom children aged two to twelve. Plant-based diets are growing, but their adequacy for children is debated. The team analyzed three-day weighed food diaries from 39 children: fifteen omnivores, eleven vegetarians, and thirteen vegans, with emissions counted per ingredient.

No group met every nutrient target. Omnivores ate too much saturated fat and free sugar and too little fiber, while plant-based children sat in healthy ranges for those items. Vegan diets had the lowest emissions, forty-six percent below omnivore diets. Vitamin D and iodine gaps appeared across groups. Well-planned plant diets can meet most needs with fortified foods and supplements, the authors conclude.
pmc-13278796:
Raimondo Pittorru and colleagues report leadless pacing after heart transplantation in a 2026 case. A 36-year-old woman received a donor heart for restrictive cardiomyopathy using the older biatrial joining technique. Eleven months later she had a persistent slow junctional rhythm and tiredness on exertion.

Testing showed the donor and recipient atria beating out of sync, with no sinus node activity driving the heart. Normal wired pacing would be awkward in her altered anatomy and risky under immune suppression. A tiny leadless pacemaker was placed in the donor atrium using CT images fused with live X-ray guidance. Placement was precise, symptoms resolved fully, and her heart rate response to activity improved.
pmc-13279596:
Shunsuke Uehara and colleagues published a 2026 review arguing that osteoporosis treatment should target how bone-eating cells fuse and polarize, not simply how many exist. Today's main drugs cut fracture risk by suppressing osteoclasts wholesale. Yet osteoclasts also signal bone-building cells and blood vessels, so blanket suppression can stall healthy remodeling. The review gathers two processes: fusion of precursor cells into giant mature osteoclasts, and polarization, which lets a mature cell seal itself to bone and dissolve it.

Fusion depends on fusogen proteins and recognition systems at the cell surface. Polarization runs through adhesion signaling and shape-changing proteins, with the kinase LRRK1 identified as a hub joining both programs. Candidate drugs include antibodies and small molecules blocking fusion proteins or LRRK1 while sparing the coupling signals. The authors sketch a regimen that trims osteoclast numbers, blocks fusion to protect vessel formation, and tunes polarization: balance rather than shutdown.
pmc-13280596:
Muhammad Haaris Tiwana and team give a 2026 study of health worker views on how to mitigate moral distress in British Columbia, Canada. Moral distress can cause reduced morale, care quality loss, apathy, burnout and workforce attrition. Much research documents it, but few studies weigh how to mitigate it well. An online survey ran with primary care professionals from October to December 2022. It held physicians, nurses, homecare aides and long term care aides.

The survey gathered sociodemographic data, moral distress experiences and methods used to mitigate it. Two open ended answers were analysed by profession, gender and racial identity. With a socio ecological framework, the team organized mitigation strategies across four levels: individual, interpersonal, community and organizational, and societal and systemic. The title quote, they wait for us to break before they listen, captures worker frustration.
pmc-13280696:
Hui Li and colleagues published a 2026 brain wave study on how ADHD changes as children grow. ADHD affects focus and self-control. The team tested one hundred ten children with ADHD who had never taken drugs for it. One hundred matched peers joined as a comparison group. All were aged six to fourteen. The team read broad patterns in brain waves and one network used at rest.

Children with ADHD showed stronger broad wave patterns than peers. In healthy children those patterns fell with age, but the fall was weaker in ADHD. In younger children, front brain patterns tracked with poor focus and restless acts. In teens, the rest network linked up less well. The authors say ADHD brain signs shift with age, so tests and care may need to shift too.
pmc-13281896:
Bojun Liu and colleagues built a survival score for liver cancer patients with low cholesterol in a 2026 study. Low levels of the harmful cholesterol fraction mark higher risk in this cancer. The team read records of four hundred eighty-six patients at a Beijing hospital from 2015 to 2021. A bend in the risk curve appeared as cholesterol fell. Past a low point, death risk climbed as levels sank further. Patients in the low half lived shorter lives than the high half.

For the low group alone, the team built a chart that scores survival odds. It joins four facts: drinking history, cancer stage, tumor count, and a clotting time. The chart sorted patients fairly well at three and five years. Its risk groups split cleanly on survival curves. The authors say low cholesterol patients need their own yardstick. Standard models, built for all comers, blur this group's risks.
pmc-13282096:
Jake DeBroff and co-authors report a 2026 case linking a common COVID-19 drug to inflammation of the pancreas. The drug pair, nirmatrelvir and ritonavir, sold as Paxlovid, helps keep COVID-19 patients out of hospital. More than five hundred drugs are known to be able to trigger pancreatitis, where the pancreas grows swollen and painful. Ritonavir is one drug already flagged for this risk.

A seventy-one-year-old man developed upper belly pain and weight loss soon after finishing a five-day course of the drug. Tests showed acute pancreatitis, a sudden attack of that inflammation. His symptoms settled with supportive care alone, such as fluids and rest of the gut. No other cause is described in the summary. The authors aim to raise awareness that this rare side effect can follow a widely used treatment, so doctors consider drug causes when belly pain follows COVID-19 therapy.
pmc-13282396:
Hongjuan Jin and co-authors report a 2026 study testing whether a stool protein can help diagnose cow's milk protein allergy in extremely preterm infants. Such infants, born before thirty-two weeks, are fragile, and allergy signs overlap with other gut problems. The protein, shortened to ECP, is released by allergy-linked white blood cells. Sixty infants took part, thirty with confirmed allergy and thirty matched controls, with stool and blood tests over time.

Stool ECP spiked clearly during allergic episodes in the allergy group and stayed flat at all other times. Control infants held steady levels throughout. Outside episodes, the allergy group's levels matched controls, so a rise marked active disease rather than a lasting trait. The authors say stool testing offers a non-invasive aid for spotting this allergy in very early infants. It could support, not replace, careful feeding trials and clinical judgement in neonatal units.
pmc-13282596:
Paulomi Sudhir and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol for a lightly guided phone app aimed at adults in India who feel distressed yet are not in treatment. Many people with common mental health problems never seek care, due to stigma, low awareness, or poor access. The protocol tests whether the app can change that.

Adults will be split at random between the full app and a mood-logging app for comparison. Checks at baseline, five weeks, and one month will track real help-seeking, intent to seek help, felt barriers, and distress levels. Enrolment began in late 2025, so the protocol reports a plan and timeline rather than results.
pmc-13282796:
Chaemin Lim and colleagues introduced RMAD1 in 2026, a human-derived peptide that carries material into cells. Cancer vaccines often fail because their target proteins reach immune cells poorly and T cell priming stays weak. RMAD1 was drawn from the ADARB2 protein and found through a skin delivery search platform.

Peptide-linked vaccines gathered in draining lymph nodes and fed targets into the display route that wakes killer T cells. In two mouse tumour models, the vaccines sparked strong target-specific T cell responses, lowered regulatory T cells, and built memory that resisted a second tumour challenge. Effects in a lung spread model matched a standard chemotherapy drug, with a favourable safety picture in mice.
pmc-13283196:
Mine waste still clouds the Rio Doce a decade after its dam burst, river data from Luciana Pena Mello Brandao's team confirm in 2026. In 2015 the Fundao dam released huge mine waste volumes into the Rio Doce basin. Lasting harm to water and life was widely reported.

Three years of seasonal data covered one hit sub-basin and one clean reference river. Tests tracked cloudiness and metals such as manganese, arsenic, iron, and aluminum. The hit basin kept higher cloudiness and metal loads across seasons. Gaps grew worst in the rainy season in the analysis. Groups of sites formed a clear gradient tied to waste source and river joins. Long-term tracking stays vital.
pmc-13283396:
Ultrasound-based sizing trims overly high lens vaults versus chart sizing, Robert Edward T Ang's clinic comparison finds in 2026. The lens sits behind the iris to fix short sight without removing tissue. Correct size sets the gap, called vault, between lens and natural lens.

Records covered 227 eyes from 116 patients at one center in total. One group used a white-to-white chart, and the other used ultrasound measures. Vision and focus results matched closely between the two groups at one month. The ultrasound group had a lower mean vault and far fewer overly high vaults. Low vault rates were similar in both groups in this study. Ultrasound sizing may cut size errors.
pmc-13283496:
Chyong-Mei Chen and Yingwei Peng proposed a new statistics method in 2026 for survival data where some patients are cured. Their model looks at quantiles, meaning points across the spread of survival times, rather than averages alone. It also lets some measured factors act through smooth curve-shaped effects instead of straight-line ones.

The estimating approach carries a double protection: an error in one part of the cure model does not spoil estimates in the other part. It also loosens a strict log-linear rule found in older quantile methods, letting effects vary across quantile levels where the data allow. Tests on made-up data showed the protection and better efficiency. Applied to lung cancer data, the method found longer survival quantiles for one tumour cell type than another.
pmc-13283796:
Claudia Reytor-González and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how money hardship and food insecurity speed health decline in old age. About 28 percent of the world's people face moderate or severe food insecurity, and older adults in poor settings are hit hardest. Good food is basic to healthy ageing, yet tight budgets push people toward cheap, energy-dense, nutrient-poor diets.

Food-insecure older adults scored far lower on diet quality measures than secure peers. They also faced higher risk of muscle loss, frailty, and thinking decline, and were more likely to carry excess weight. The review traces these gaps to low income, limited schooling, weak safety nets, and poor local food access. The authors argue for system-level, culturally fitted fixes rather than advice aimed at individuals alone.
pmc-13283996:
Yuval Arbel and co-authors argued in 2026 that hearing loss in the United States shows a public health market failure. About 48 million American adults live with hearing loss, yet only a minority who could benefit from hearing aids use them. The team combined a game-theory model of adoption choices with national survey data on health spending.

People reporting hearing difficulty used more care and cost more across major service types, and model-based estimates put the spending gap tied to hearing loss as substantial. The dataset could not separate treated from untreated loss, so the savings from wider aid use could not be directly measured. The model frames low adoption as a social dilemma: private costs loom larger than private gains, while society pays the wider bill.
pmc-13284496:
Charlotte Ramdass and co-authors give a 2026 narrative review of preeclampsia outcomes for mothers and newborns, with and without HIV infection. Preeclampsia brings new high blood pressure after 20 weeks of pregnancy and can harm many organs. Long-term data from sub-Saharan Africa stay limited, despite a high HIV burden and likely links with HIV treatment.

Short-term risks extend past delivery for both mother and child, the review reports. Mothers face higher long-term risk of heart disease and kidney harm. pmc-13285596:

pmc-13286796:

pmc-13287596:

pmc-13288296:

pmc-13288396:

pmc-13288696:

pmc-13288896:

pmc-13289296:

pmc-13289896:

pmc-13290096:

pmc-13290696:

pmc-13290796:

pmc-13290996:

pmc-13291796:

pmc-13292296:

pmc-13292596:

pmc-13293396:

pmc-13293696:

pmc-13293796:

pmc-13293896:

pmc-13294196:

pmc-13294296:

pmc-13295896:

pmc-13296096:

pmc-13296196:

pmc-13296496:

pmc-13296696:

pmc-13296996:

pmc-13297096:

pmc-13297396:

pmc-13298096:

pmc-13298796:

pmc-13299696:

pmc-13300596:

pmc-13300696:

pmc-13300796:

pmc-13301196:

pmc-13301296:

pmc-13302196:

pmc-13302396:

The link held across subgroups and statistical approaches, including weighted and imputed analyses. Serial scanning, the authors suggest, could sharpen long-term risk estimates, especially in patients already taking statins.
pmc-13302896: Lucian-Daniel Peptine and colleagues issued this 2026 correction to their review of MRSA and vancomycin-resistant enterococci in hospital infections, published in the journal Microorganisms. The notice is a correction only. Two figures in the article were replaced with simpler versions to improve clarity. A few spelling slips in the main text were also fixed. The authors state that the review's conclusions stand unchanged. The correction was approved by the Academic Editor, and the published article has been updated to match.
pmc-13303096:
Two highly involved parents can leave a teenager feeling less in charge, Hongbo Cui and colleagues find in a 2026 survey of 680 adolescents. Fathers' and mothers' involvement were measured separately and crossed with the teens' internal locus of control, the belief that outcomes follow one's own actions. Response surface analysis mapped matched and mismatched parenting combinations.

Teens with low-involvement pairs on both sides scored higher on internal control than teens whose parents were both highly involved. In mismatched homes, an involved father beside a less involved mother beat the reverse pattern. The authors suggest heavy dual involvement may crowd out the autonomy adolescents need to feel self-directed.
pmc-13303796:
Mengyuan Zhang leads a 2026 study of parent bonds and shyness in teenagers with depression in Ningxia, China. Shyness can deepen social struggles for these teens, and bonds with mother and father may shape it jointly.

Questionnaires from 252 adolescents measured safety of bonds with each parent and levels of shyness. Both parents' bonds linked to lower shyness on their own. Surface analysis showed the lowest shyness when both bonds were strong and matched, while gaps between parents mattered less. Support that lifts both bonds together, and keeps them even, may best help social confidence and emotion control.
pmc-13304196:
Federica Li Pomi and co-authors follow, in a 2026 extension study, sun-damage skin spots treated with a five-day ointment to see how many stay gone at one year. Tirbanibulin clears actinic keratoses on face and scalp in the short term, but durability data were missing. Only spots fully cleared at two months entered the long-term check.

Thirty-seven patients returned at twelve months carrying 116 cleared lesions for review. About sixty percent remained clear, while the rest had relapsed at the same site, and thirty-five brand-new spots appeared in the treated fields. Thinner lesions held their clearance best, and thicker ones relapsed most. No delayed side effects appeared, satisfaction ran high, and nearly everyone would repeat the treatment.
pmc-13304296:
Claudiu Ioan Filip and colleagues compare flap surgery options for rebuilding the lower leg, ankle, and heel in a 2026 analysis. Wounds there are hard to cover because nearby tissue is scarce and many patients have diabetes or poor circulation.

Twenty-one studies supplied data on flap type, patients, and results such as survival of the flap, limb saving, function, and problems. Free flaps, moved with their own vessels, handled large or infected wounds with high survival. Attached pedicled flaps suited smaller wounds and frailer patients. Long-term sores on weight-bearing heels stayed common, and feeling plus blood flow predicted success best.
pmc-13305696:
Emily Nghiem, Ariel Tzamarot, and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether blocking two pathways at once beats either alone against colorectal cancer.
