The pair suppressed growth synergistically in flat cultures, spheres, and both organoid models. Mutant organoids were hit hardest, though cell lines responded regardless of mutation status. Growth signaling fell broadly, while death markers rose inconsistently across models, and the clearest cell-death boost appeared only in the mutant line. The authors read the results as preliminary support for the pairing, with escape routes through a parallel growth pathway suspected.
pmc-13306096:
Lara Marques and Nuno Vale run a virtual clinical trial in 2026 on propranolol, a widely used beta-blocker with highly variable handling in the body. They ask how kidney function and body size shape that variation, and how omeprazole co-treatment changes exposure. Physiologically based models were paired with population analysis of simulated patients.

A two-compartment model described propranolol best, with health status affecting clearance and body surface area affecting distribution volume. Omeprazole raised propranolol exposure, and the rise was larger in simulated patients with renal impairment. Levels still stayed below known toxicity thresholds in the simulations. The authors present virtual trials as a practical way to flag interaction risk and personalise dosing before real patients are exposed.
pmc-13306596:
Naresh Duvva measured how long excited anion radicals survive across ten related molecules in a 2026 photophysics study. Such radicals can drive electron-transfer chemistry under light, but short excited lives limit how much work they finish.

Radicals formed by chemical reduction in oxygen-free solvent stayed stable for testing with fast laser methods. Lifetimes spanned 2.9 to 565 ps in reported figures, a near 200-fold range across the family. Decay without light emission sped up as excited energy fell, matching the energy gap law closely and guiding catalyst design. Such rules may help chemists pick radicals that live long enough to do work.
pmc-13307296:
Hassan Osman fused body-worn motion sensors with full-body physics in one estimator in a 2026 study. Inertial units allow portable movement capture outside labs, yet magnetic disturbance and drift corrupt long recordings.

An iterated filter feeds accelerometer and gyroscope data straight into multibody dynamics, estimating joint motion and forces together under physical law. Optical tracking and torque readings can join the same filter for extra accuracy. Tests on a pendulum and a six-axis robot arm held joint angle error to a maximum reported difference of 3.75° in angle units.
pmc-13307896:
Rithu Chandran and colleagues review in 2026 whether plant compounds can cut poultry farming's leaning on antibiotics while controlling foodborne germs. Heavy drug use in food animals feeds resistance that reaches people through the food chain. Studies in dishes and in live birds covered Salmonella, Campylobacter, Listeria, and harmful E. coli.

Plant compounds hit germs by tearing membranes, jamming their signals, and muting virulence genes. Bird trials showed lower germ settling plus better gut health and growth. Host immunity and gut microbe balance also shifted for the better under treatment. Hurdles remain in uptake, dosing, batch sameness, and official sign-off, which the authors list plainly. Their verdict is that plant compounds belong inside wider drug-care plans rather than as drop-in swaps. Joint use could slow resistance spread from farms to dinner tables.
pmc-13308496:
Hassan Iqbal audits in 2026 what happens after gut endoscopy finds nothing in British patients referred urgently for iron deficiency anaemia. Eighty-nine patients at one centre were tracked through records from January 2024 to March 2025. Guidelines reserve small bowel and urinary tract checks for recurring or treatment-resistant cases, so the audit tests real practice.

Cancer was found in about ten percent of the referred group overall. Among patients with negative endoscopy, capsule studies and bowel imaging were used rarely, in under two percent and about thirteen percent respectively. Anaemia returned in roughly half of the negative group, yet further testing found an alternative cause in only one patient. Iqbal supports selective, guideline-based follow-up after a good negative examination. Single-centre design and short follow-up limit the message, and he says so plainly.
pmc-13308596:
Xuanhao Wang and co-authors present in 2026 a three dimensional photoacoustic imaging method that pairs a tight focus ultrasound sensor with a flipped phase rebuild method. Photoacoustic scans blend light detail with sound depth, yet sensor size trades off against sharpness, contrast, and reach in most builds.

Their paired fix gave about a twofold gain in sharpness and near a tenfold gain in contrast over noise in their tests. Checks spanned models, test objects, and live whole body scans that showed deep parts and tracked small drug paths. A barrel shaped sensor set widens the view for moving scenes. Faster, sharper deep scans could speed many lines of lab medicine.
pmc-13308796: Ian C Odland and co-authors issue a 2026 correction to their account of the THRIVE fellowship. That fellowship trains health workers in health innovation and entrepreneurship. The item itself is only a brief publishing notice. It adds no new data or outcome claims. It records that Joshua B Bederson was left off the byline and should stand as the thirteenth author, with Mount Sinai posts. It also swaps a wrong bar graph in Figure 4 for a fixed version. The fixed graph shows grants won after the fellowship.
pmc-13309596:
Marilia Bernadette Voigt and colleagues check for swelling around the aorta after leak repair in a 2026 hospital study. Aortic stent grafts can leak, and fixing leaks sometimes requires repeat procedures. Swelling beside the aorta, at times with abscess, is a feared late problem after such repairs.

Records covered 88 repair procedures in 59 patients between 2015 and 2025 at one center. Most leaks were the slow type fed by side branches. Follow-up scans found six cases of swelling around the aorta after that leak type was repaired. The authors flag the pattern as a risk worth watching and urge scan follow-up that looks for it after repair.
pmc-13310396:
Xiangnan Yao writes a 2026 letter on a rat study of wrist-ankle acupuncture for muscle pain. The study under discussion, by Mai and colleagues, compared needle stimulation against electrical stimulation at wrist and ankle points for inflamed calf muscle pain. Gene data pointed to a shared daily-rhythm pathway, a first for this comparison.

The letter praises the design, then raises method concerns for further debate. Group sizes were small, at four rats per group and three in some tests, with no separate validation cohort to confirm the gene findings. Sample size math rested on assumed values that may not hold. The author asks for larger, confirmed work before the method claims guide non-drug pain care.
pmc-13310796:
Elaheh Heidari and Amin Saeidinia report a 2026 case of juvenile myasthenia gravis first taken for another disease. A girl aged 4 years had drooping of one eyelid, then both lids within two days, then trouble walking and standing within five days. Two months earlier she had severe breathing trouble treated as Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Repeat nerve tests showed a fading response that fits myasthenia, and antibody tests were positive. A standard drug at weight based dose brought a good response. Early spotting avoids needless care and disease advance. Normal spinal fluid protein in a weak child should prompt a fresh look.
pmc-13310896:
Florencia Cora Jofre and colleagues pair a new calibration trick with fast digestion for food testing in a 2026 methods study. Labs must measure many elements in feed and animal foods with a plasma mass tool, yet complex mixes distort results. Infrared digestion cuts acid and energy use, while multi isotope calibration matches the sample matrix by design.

Tests on certified material gave recoveries from 85 to 118 percent of true values, with tight repeat scores. Six elements were measured in real feeds, and toxic cadmium and lead stayed below detection. Green scoring backed the low waste claim. The paired method offers a robust, leaner route for routine food checks.
pmc-13311196:
Eman Y Mohammady and colleagues test an insect and poultry meal blend as fishmeal swap in tilapia diets in a 2026 trial. Fishmeal costs and wild catch limits push farms toward new protein sources. A half and half blend of black soldier fly larvae meal and poultry byproduct meal was fed to Nile tilapia fry.

Four hundred fifty fry were split across five diets with graded swap levels for 70 days of feeding. Mid swap groups grew best, used feed well, digested more, and showed healthier guts, blood, and liver shields than controls. Full swap results trailed the mid groups. Blends at mid levels look like a sound farm choice.
pmc-13311296:
Kazi Md Azman Hossain and co-authors report phase one results of a 2026 trial on a strengthening home exercise plan for knee osteoarthritis. Exercise is a first-line care step, but proof for this home plan was thin.

The trial enrolled 247 people aged 45 to 70 with knee arthritis. One group did the home strengthening plan with lifestyle advice for eight weeks; the other took pain medicine with the same advice. Pain, pressure pain threshold, and daily function were measured before and after. The exercise group improved far more on pain and function scores. Full results from phase two will test whether gains hold.
pmc-13311796:
Nahuel Lofeudo and Gabriel Moncalian report a 2026 structural study of enzyme parts that help make omega-3 fats in thraustochytrids, single-celled marine microbes. The parts in question are the ER domains of the fat-building machine.

In these microbes, two ER domains sit on separate chains, PfaB and PfaC. Size and light-scattering tests showed the two pair up as a mixed dimer rather than matching pairs. A crystal structure at 2.2 angstrom resolution, with the FMN cofactor bound, confirms the pairing. Docking work supports a ping-pong chemistry between the pair. The finding clarifies how this fat factory holds together.
pmc-13311996:
Sien Guo and colleagues, in 2026, present a study on a protein called DCAF7 that speeds artery plaque growth in vessel lining cells. Dataset mining first flagged cell death as a key thread in atherosclerosis.

The iron-linked death factor SLC40A1 ran high in diseased vessels, and DCAF7 seemed to drive it. Cell and animal tests showed DCAF7 lifts SLC40A1 by way of TNF and NF-kappaB signaling, promoting cell death. In mice lacking ApoE, silencing DCAF7 slowed carotid plaque growth and cut cell death clearly. The authors name DCAF7 a candidate target for halting plaque progression.
pmc-13312096:
Uraiwan Sasang and colleagues report a 2026 cluster randomized trial in northeastern Thailand on adults whose high blood pressure stayed uncontrolled. Their program used transformative learning, an adult education approach meant to shift how people see their condition, to build health literacy and stronger self-management.

Two sub-district hospitals were assigned by lot so that 58 participants, 29 per site, received either the program or usual care. At 8 and 12 weeks, the program group scored higher on self-management behavior than controls and improved against its own starting point. Mean arterial pressure was also significantly lower in the program group after adjustment for baseline values. The authors present the approach as a workable route to better pressure control in primary care.
pmc-13312496:
Yu Liu and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study that overturns expectations about a metabolic enzyme in obesity-related heart disease. Faulty breakdown of branched-chain amino acids is implicated in obesity cardiomyopathy, and blocking the kinase BCKDK across the whole body helps the heart. The team asked what the enzyme does inside heart muscle cells themselves.

Mice lacking BCKDK only in cardiomyocytes fared worse on a high-fat diet, with deeper dysfunction and remodeling, even though heart amino acid levels fell. Forcing the enzyme higher did the opposite, protecting function while easing mitochondrial oxidative stress and quieting inflammatory MAPK signaling. A mitochondria-targeted antioxidant reversed the harm of deficiency in cells. The authors conclude the enzyme guards heart mitochondria by a route beyond amino acid control, and warn that whole-body inhibition may help mainly through organs outside the heart.
pmc-13313196:
Dan Yu and co-workers test lipoxin A4, a fat-based signal, in a 2026 mouse study of white fat browning. Browning turns stored white fat toward a heat-making form, and earlier cell work hinted that this signal helps that switch, but whole-animal proof and the path involved were missing.

Fat mice with insulin resistance got the signal while the team tracked weight, fat depots, food intake, blood fats, and insulin. Treated mice gained less weight, stored less fat, and showed better blood fat and insulin values, and their white fat took on brown-like traits. In cultured fat precursor cells the signal drove browning through a small RNA, miR-133a-3p, and its target SIRT1, checked with gene tests and reporter assays. The work names a path that drugs might copy to fight obesity.
pmc-13313296:
B Deva darshinii and co-authors review tissue engineering for oral cancer repair in a 2026 paper. Oral cancer ranks as the sixth most common cancer in the world, with about 377,000 new cases each year as stated in the report, and tobacco and alcohol drive much of it.

Surgery, radiation, and drug therapy have raised survival, but they often leave the mouth scarred and hard to use. The review looks at how engineered tissue could restore both form and function after treatment. It covers scaffold materials that mimic the natural cell matrix, stem cell methods, the use of a patient's own tissue, and gene tools such as CRISPR and changes to gene control marks. The authors frame these routes as a shift toward precise, patient-matched repair of the mouth.
pmc-13313796:
José L Fernández-Vásquez and colleagues document, in a 2026 case report, a piglet born with fused toes on every limb. Syndactyly, nicknamed mulefoot, ranks among the most common limb malformations in pigs. It can stem from genetic or environmental causes. The animal was seventeen days old and weighed 6.2 kilograms. The defect did not interfere with its daily activity. Its relevance for breeding and clinical practice, though, prompted a workup with blood tests, body measurements, and radiographs.

Imaging showed the malformation took two forms. In the front limbs the toe bones were fused. In the hind limbs an extra phalangeal element sat wedged between the main digits. Blood work showed mild elevation of white cells. The authors review how the defect arises when toes fail to separate during embryonic development. Severity runs from a skin bridge to bone fusion. Its genetic markers in pigs, they note, remain unmapped.
pmc-13314396:
Cun Ku and colleagues test genistein, a soy compound, against high blood pressure in a 2026 mouse study. The compound is known to guard the heart and vessels, but its role in hypertension was not pinned down.

Mice given angiotensin II, a hormone that raises pressure, also got genistein by mouth. Their systolic and diastolic pressures rose far less, with no change in body weight, as the authors report. Genistein eased thickening of the aorta wall and swelling of its muscle, and vessel tests showed better lining-led relaxation while other responses stayed intact. In loose aortic rings it undid the hormone-driven over-tightening and restored widening by acetylcholine. Tests in human vein cells added support. The work ties the benefit to restored nitric oxide and lower oxidative stress.
pmc-13314796:
Zi-Qi Fang and colleagues link a mix of metals in blood to oxidative stress and heart outcomes in diabetic patients, in a study from 2026. Metal exposure can raise oxidative stress, yet old tests read only single damage byproducts and miss the whole redox picture.

The team profiled 35 metals in plasma from a large cohort of 3142 patients with type 2 diabetes, as counted in the report. They also gauged global redox state by a newer marker, oxidation-reduction potential. A set of five metals stood out: nickel, zirconium, titanium, strontium, and vanadium, as listed in the report. High joint exposure tied not only to the redox marker but to standard signs of protein, fat, and DNA oxidation. The mix also tracked with coronary artery disease and outcomes after stent care, marking metals as a joint risk to weigh.
pmc-13315096:
Bénédicte Apouey and a team trace, in a 2026 analysis, how mosquito-borne epidemics ripple through France far beyond the fever ward. The tiger mosquito arrived in 2004 and by early 2025 had colonized 81 departments, bringing acquired dengue, chikungunya, and even Zika onto French soil. Locally caught cases, once novelties, reached 834 across dengue and chikungunya in 2025 alone. The authors set out to document what such outbreaks do to a high-income health system and society.

Their account maps three channels of damage: strain on healthcare services during surges, direct economic losses from illness, control campaigns, and disrupted activity, and social disruption in affected communities. Because the vector is now entrenched, they argue France must treat arboviral outbreaks as a recurring structural risk rather than an exotic surprise. The paper closes by pressing for intersectoral action and pre-committed resources for vector control, sized to the documented costs of reacting late.
pmc-13315196:
Biyan Zhou and co-authors used single-cell RNA sequencing in 2026 to compare early germ cells from the right and left sides of female chicken embryos. In birds the left ovary grows while the right side shrinks back, and the team asked whether germ cells already differ between sides at two early stages.

At the earlier stage, side differences centered on DNA damage response, cell-cycle arrest, ribosomes, and protein making. At the later stage the pattern shifted toward cell aging, cAMP signaling, and a form of cell death. Certain genes differed between sides, and signals in the NOTCH pathway between germ and support cells appeared only on the right side.
pmc-13315896:
Jon Stone traces in 2026 the role of Mark Hallett, who lived from 1943 to 2025, in reviving study of functional neurological disorder. Hallett brought deep skill in motor physiology and in questions of free will and agency to a common yet neglected condition, starting around 2003.

He pushed for understanding of the disorder's brain basis, course, and treatment, led research on abnormal brain networks and mixed causes, and helped organize global meetings and books. As first president of the International FND Society from 2019 to 2022, and with a major 2024 lecture, he embodied the field's renewed standing.
pmc-13315996:
Chelsea Ng and co-authors ran a user-centered design study in 2026 to build emotion-aware charts that help young kidney transplant patients and caregivers grasp kidney function values. Numbers such as creatinine are hard to act on, and visual analogies can connect abstract data to familiar ideas.

Two studies with youth recipients and caregivers first mapped which visual elements support patient needs, then shaped and tested a new display. Adding emotional framing aims to make trends feel meaningful rather than distant. Clearer self-management knowledge could help families spot change early and take part more fully in care.
pmc-13316096:
Berta Valente argues in 2026 that time should be reclaimed as a basic driver of health equity. Health is known to be shaped by social structure, yet time is mostly missing from public health frames, where it appears as a mere technical measure such as duration or life stage.

Blending sociology and epidemiology, the author splits time into availability and intensity. Scarce, rushed, and uncertain time falls unevenly by social position, gender, and money insecurity, limiting care, rest, and civic life, while illness and caregiving shrink time control further. Health systems built on standard clock time can also misfit patients' real lives.
pmc-13316196:
Shenglin Ye and a large team built artificial platelets in 2026 to fight deep vein thrombosis by competing for sticking sites in injured vessels. Knockout mice confirmed that STING fuels a clot-friendly setting through the NLRP3 inflammasome. The natural compound forsythoside A blocked STING, so the team loaded it into nanogels wrapped in activated platelet membrane. The coated particles home to adhesion sites and crowd out real platelets.
pmc-13316296:
Keisuke Okabe and colleagues, in a 2026 case report, describe rebuilding a very large buttock wound after removing severe hidradenitis suppurativa. That long-term skin disease causes painful lumps and draining tracts, lowers quality of life and can precede skin cancer or sepsis. Complete removal is advised, yet the resulting defect can be hard to cover.

Because no single known flap could cover most of both buttocks in one stage, the surgeons combined two flaps into one. A rotation flap based on a lumbar artery vessel covered the upper area. A split muscle and skin flap from the upper gluteus maximus covered the lower area. Blood flow stayed stable, drainage stopped and leg function was preserved.
pmc-13316696:
Wisoo Shin and co-authors report, in 2026, a relapsing blistering disease of the face linked to long-term cocaine use through the nose. Pemphigus vegetans is a rare form of pemphigus vulgaris where flaccid blisters turn into wart-like plaques. Certain drugs are known triggers, and reports tying cocaine to pemphigus are growing.

Their patient, a 45-year-old man, spent five months with an eroded, crusted plaque covering the lower nose and upper lip. The lesion began about a month after cocaine entered through a cut inside the nose. Several antibiotic courses failed, and repeated biopsies showed only mixed inflammation. The authors argue the case strengthens the link between intranasal cocaine and drug-induced pemphigus, and they review how the diagnosis was reached.
pmc-13317696:
Jinbo Li and colleagues fashion, in a 2026 study, electronic skin from pomelo pith, the spongy fruit waste, patterned with liquid metal and filled with sticky hydrogel. The cheap, porous fruit layer templates both the wiring and the glue in one green package.

Nickel-doped liquid metal lines were drawn with magnetic guidance across the pith's rough surface, while gel soaked into its pores by capillary pull. The skin heats quickly and evenly on demand, senses motion reliably, and, thanks to added glycerol, resists freezing and drying out. Conductivity, stickiness, and toughness rarely arrive together at this cost. The design points toward wearables built from farm waste rather than pricey synthetics.
pmc-13318096:
Intissar Lasfar and colleagues report, in 2026, successful endoscopic treatment of a rare bleeding lesion in the duodenum at a military hospital in Marrakech. A Dieulafoy lesion is an abnormally large artery just under the gut lining that can burst through a tiny erosion. Duodenal sites are exceptional, with few cases reported worldwide.

Their patient was 76 years old with several long-term illnesses. He arrived after four days of black stools and severe anaemia. Endoscopy found the lesion in the duodenum's second part, bleeding diffusely with no ulcer nearby. Injection of adrenaline followed by two metal clips stopped the bleeding, and the patient did well. The report also discusses managing blood-thinning medicines during active bleeding.
pmc-13318596:
Di Yang and co-authors deliver a 2026 systematic review of models that predict thinking problems after surgery in adults, known as postoperative cognitive dysfunction. They searched three major databases for model-building studies and judged quality with standard appraisal tools.

From 2,060 records, 13 studies with 14 models survived, built by logistic regression or machine learning on samples from 82 to 687 patients. Reported accuracy looked high, yet nearly all testing was internal, samples were often small, and age was the commonest predictor, appearing in ten models. Only two models faced outside testing over time, and both performed worse there. The authors say none is ready for routine care and urge large prospective cohorts with proper external checks.
pmc-13318796:
David Chen and colleagues offer a 2026 scoping review of health system efforts to widen access to external beam radiotherapy. Access varies sharply worldwide, most sharply in poorer countries. The team searched three databases through June 30, 2025. They sorted programmes by type, from building capacity to changing how services run.

Thirty-one studies were included in the synthesis. New buildings and kit appeared in 45 percent of studies, and staff training in 35 percent of them. Most programmes reported better use of treatment, shorter waits, and more finished treatments. Bundled plans worked best, joining buildings, staff, reshaped daily work, and remote support. Hub-and-spoke models and shorter treatment plans also helped. The authors call for shared access measures and fairness in reports.
pmc-13319096:
Minhuan Lin and a large team present a 2026 multicentre cohort study of uneven growth between twins and newborn outcomes. Growth-gap patterns over time were combined with the smaller twin's growth speed.

Four gap trajectories emerged from the modelling. A stable low gap covered 84.1 percent of pregnancies in their data. Two high-gap patterns, one easing and one rising, each roughly tripled the odds of bad newborn outcomes. Adding the smaller twin's growth velocity improved prediction beyond trajectory alone. The combined model reached an AUC of 0.696 in development and 0.733 in external validation. Growth speed of the smaller twin was the single strongest predictor.
pmc-13319996:
Giselle Coelho Resende Caselato and William D Freeman review, in 2026, holographic transmission for real-time teaching and medical care. Two demonstrations anchor the review. Surgeons in Boston mentored colleagues in São Paulo across continents, and a large educational link connected a United States clinic with a summit in Brazil. Both achieved two-way volumetric communication without noticeable delay. The authors credit fast cameras, high-bandwidth data links, graphics processors and low-latency 5G networks. Barriers remain: high cost, sensitivity to delay, narrow viewing fields and weak infrastructure in poorer regions. Privacy and fair access also need governance, they argue.
pmc-13320496:
A Hirschfeld and colleagues report a 2026 phase 2B trial of a cell therapy for advanced bowel cancer that had spread and no longer responded well to standard care. The patients had tumours classed as MSS and pMMR, a type often called cold because immune drugs rarely work on it. The therapy, AlloStim, aims to turn such tumours hot so the immune system attacks them.

Median survival reached 16.4 months in this hard to treat third-line group, and a second survival measure backed a lasting gain. Scans often looked worse before they looked better, a pattern the team calls pseudoprogression. Harm was mostly mild, with only 4.1 percent of side effects graded above level 3 in severity.
pmc-13320996:
Johanna Holschier and co-authors survey pain and sedation practice for children in intensive care across Australia and New Zealand in a 2026 report. Units that admit over 150 children a year and report to a regional registry were asked about protocols, drug choices, and quality work between December 2024 and May 2025. Fourteen of 16 eligible units replied.

Morphine was the favoured first pain drug and dexmedetomidine the favoured first sedative, though sedative choices varied. All units used standard pain scoring, and most scored sedation and drug withdrawal, but fewer than half had a set delirium protocol. Specialist children's units held pain and sedation protocols far more often than general units, and joint quality groups were rare.
pmc-13321196:
Zexuan Qi, Yangchun Yan, and Panpan Ren study trust in workplace AI teams in a 2026 survey article. Staff often resist new AI tools, yet raising safety concerns openly, called safety voice, may ease that resistance. The team asked whether speaking up about AI safety changes how willing staff feel to work with AI.

A multi-wave survey of 385 employees who routinely work with AI tested the pathway. Views of AI as capable and as well meaning linked safety voice to willingness to collaborate. Backing for speaking up, called voice endorsement, strengthened both links and thus the overall effect. Framing AI rollouts to welcome safety input may help human and AI teammates work better together.
pmc-13321796:
Tarun Mishra, Avary Edwards and Li Wu compare, in 2026, three drugs that block an enzyme placing chemical marks on RNA, testing whether that weakens HIV reawakening from latency. The mark, called m6A, influences how the virus hides in immune cells and how it can be flushed out, a step in cure strategies.

In a latently infected cell line, two inhibitors cut mark levels more potently than the third, but both caused notable cell damage at moderate doses after two days. The weaker drug was gentler across doses. In primary immune cells from healthy donors, all three usually lowered mark levels, with one exception in a single donor. Lower mark levels tracked with reduced virus reawakening in two models. The authors see potency and toxicity pulling in opposite directions.
pmc-13322196:
Huiqin Wang and co-authors test a cherry fruit extract against psoriasis in a 2026 study mixing computer analysis and animal work. Psoriasis is a long term immune skin disease with fast skin cell growth and stubborn inflammation, and current care suffers relapse and side effects. The extract, from Prunus cerasifera fruit powder, is called PCE10.

Network analysis flagged 67 psoriasis linked targets and 23 hub genes, with pathways tied to inflammation control. In mice with induced psoriasis-like skin change, the team scored skin severity, tissue change, and inflammatory signals to judge effect. Docking models predicted how extract compounds bind key targets. A hub gene, cyclin B1, is followed up as part of the mechanism story.
pmc-13322296:
Tiago Macedo and a large international team demonstrate, in 2026, a route from stored testicular tissue of childhood cancer survivors toward future fertility. Cancer treatment before puberty can destroy sperm-producing potential, and tissue freezing programmes are expanding, yet stored samples are often nearly empty of germ cells. Whether the remaining body cells could still seed new germ cells was unknown.

Tissue from two prepubertal patients, aged about six, had severely depleted sperm precursor counts. Support cells grown from those samples were reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells using a method that does not alter the genome. Those stem cells were then guided into early germ cell-like cells with high efficiency over a four-month pipeline. The authors present proof that depleted samples still hold regenerative value.
pmc-13322596:
D Jeenu and colleagues compare two pain control methods after planned caesarean birth in a 2026 randomised trial. Good pain control speeds walking, breastfeeding, and recovery, so the team weighed morphine given into the spinal fluid against a quadratus lumborum nerve block. Sixty women were randomised, and 59 were analysed over 48 hours.

Satisfaction also scored higher with spinal morphine, and no major safety gap appeared between groups.
pmc-13322796:

A second condition, tied to the MED13L gene, causes intellectual disability with speech and motor delay.

pmc-13322896:

They caution that clinical value stays unproven and needs studies built around basal-like cases alone.
pmc-13323296:

Working from a registered plan, the team sorted studies into three layers. These were functional coupling, interface control and direct genetic links. After screening, 168 studies fed a cross-domain synthesis. The synthesis charted where evidence clusters and where gaps remain. pmc-13323496:
Merritt Hayes and co-authors survey behaviour tests for frog tadpoles as a window on developing brain circuits, in a 2026 review. Xenopus frogs are a classic model for early development and now serve higher-throughput studies of genetic and environmental risk for brain disorders.

pmc-13324296:
Thomas Syphan and colleagues describe an advanced pelvic paraganglioma found through blood in the urine, in a 2026 case report. Their patient, a 60-year-old man, had four months of visible haematuria and urinary retention before a large mass inside the bladder area revealed metastatic disease.

pmc-13324496:

pmc-13324796:
Zhengyu Wei and colleagues fuse mineral clusters into an organic polymer to build a better sodium-ion battery anode in a 2026 study. Organic electrodes often hide their active sites, move charge slowly, and break down with cycling.

pmc-13325296:
A Pretta and colleagues compare metastatic colorectal cancer that starts at ages 30 to 39 against onset at 40 to 49 in a 2026 study. Early-onset cases are rising, and the youngest patients may form a distinct group.

pmc-13325396:
Jing Zhou and co-authors build a smart hydrogel that cleans oxidative stress and then feeds gum ligament stem cells in a 2026 study. Periodontitis bathes tissue in reactive oxygen, which cripples the very cells needed for bone regrowth.

On sensing high oxidant levels, the gel first soaks them up and falls apart, freeing the factor into a calmer space. That order matters: cells get a balanced setting before the growth signal arrives. pmc-13326596:
Yechao Sun and Yangyang Bai separate two kinds of math anxiety in a 2026 modeling study of high school students. Staying buoyant after setbacks matters under heavy study pressure, but which anxiety does the damage was unclear.

pmc-13326696:
Jane Ma and Patrick H. Poquiz present a case of coccidioidomycosis that first looked like bacterial pneumonia. Cough and low-grade fever followed. Chest X-ray suggested left lower lobe shadowing, pointing first toward bacterial pneumonia.

A positive immune screen and fungal studies of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid that grew Coccidioides immitis confirmed it. Fluconazole brought improvement. The authors highlight the presentation, tests, treatment, and follow-up labs as aids for clinicians managing this fungal disease long-term, especially where dust history matters.
pmc-13326896:
Mohammad Algarni and colleagues send mystery shoppers into Saudi pharmacies to grade insomnia care in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Pharmacists are often the first stop for sleepless patients, yet their practice there was unstudied.

A total of 251 simulated visits covered three regions, 43.4 percent urban and 49.4 percent suburban, with a rural remainder. Consultations lasted a median of just 1.5 minutes during the visits. Most pharmacists asked about sleep patterns, at 55.4 percent, and triggers, at 51 percent of visits. Melatonin led the over-the-counter picks at 64.5 percent. Lifestyle advice came in only 9.6 percent of visits, and safety notes in 4.9 percent.
pmc-13327396:
Devosri Sen and co-authors compare thinking skills across related mental disorders in a 2026 hospital study. Schizoaffective disorder sits between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder in symptoms and outlook, and all three can impair planning and control. Each group held 23 stable inpatients, matched for age, gender, and handedness, plus 23 healthy controls, and all took trail-making, Stroop, memory, and planning tests. pmc-13327896:
Minsuh Park, Kyung Jong Kim, and Young-hun Kim look for day-two warning signs after colorectal cancer surgery in a 2026 study. Catching complications early matters most, so they reviewed 109 patients who had planned surgery between January 2021 and May 2023. Outcomes were split into no, minor, and major complications by standard grades.

A lymphocyte count under 905 cells per microliter that day did the same in their analysis. Bowel obstruction at diagnosis also linked to minor trouble. pmc-13328096:
Carlos Frederico Lopes Benevides and co-authors type a cancer-causing virus in people living with HIV in Salvador, Brazil, in a 2026 study. Subtype A appeared in aggressive cases with organ disease, while subtype C leaned toward skin and mouth disease, though no link reached statistical significance. Most participants were men, with a median age of 34.
pmc-13329896:
Gabriel F. Martins, Cristiano Rocha, and Nuno Galamba simulate how heat changes two proteins tied to brain disease in a 2026 study. The authors frame clumping as a contest between inner and outer attractions, with outer ones winning in the end.
pmc-13330696:
Charlotte de Fouw and colleagues study heart rehab uptake after heart attack at a Dutch general hospital in a 2026 report. Records covered patients admitted from December 2019 to June 2022. Of 271 patients included, 63.5 percent joined rehab in the reported counts.

Younger age and bypass surgery predicted joining. Women were older than men at entry, scored worse on mood questionnaires during rehab, and finished less often in the group comparisons given. Joining rehab tied to far lower death risk over a median follow-up of 4.1 years in those models. Tailored help for older patients and for women facing mood burdens is needed, the authors argue.
pmc-13333396:
Kristen E. Rohli and co-authors report on pancreas surgery for babies born with congenital hyperinsulinism, a rare disorder of runaway insulin that crashes blood sugar. Removing most of the pancreas can stop the crashes when drugs fail. Life afterward, for children and parents, was undescribed.

pmc-13333496:
Yuhang Wu and co-authors pool trial evidence in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on whether immune-boosting tube feeds protect colorectal cancer patients after surgery. pmc-13334196:
Julia Rimmington and co-authors track how the mortality gap between people with bipolar disorder and the general population changed in Finland between 2000 and 2023. Across the period, people with bipolar disorder died at much higher rates: the age-standardised mortality ratio was 2.85 for men and 3.25 for women. The relative gap was largest in younger people and more pronounced in women. pmc-13334396:
Matthew R. Boyce surveyed American parents about tax credits tied to childhood vaccination in a 2026 policy study. The idea is to use the tax system to lift immunization coverage, and Boyce measured whether parents would back three versions of it.

A state-level version, rewarding families where at least 95 percent of children are immunized, drew 57.4 percent. Support varied by parent traits but, notably, not by political leaning or welfare participation.
pmc-13335796:
Hisato Takagi reported a 2026 case in which a heart clot formed after only two days of postoperative atrial fibrillation. The patient was an 84-year-old woman treated for a type-A aortic dissection.

Because imaging bracketed the event so tightly, the case pins clot formation to the two-day fibrillation window with unusual certainty. It warns surgical teams that even brief postoperative fibrillation can clot quickly in older patients.
pmc-13336496:
Guichuan Zhu and colleagues study 2026 a selenophene bridge that enables balanced two-way transport in high-power organic electric transistors. pmc-13336696:
Jingxiao Yu and colleagues designed new germ killing peptides in 2026 to attack Gram negative bacteria, whose tough outer coats block many drugs. pmc-13336796:

pmc-13336896:

pmc-13336996:

pmc-13337396:

pmc-13337696:

pmc-13337896:

pmc-13339496:

pmc-13339796:

pmc-13341496:

pmc-13341796:

pmc-13342196:

pmc-13343996:

pmc-13344096:

pmc-13344596:

pmc-13345796:

pmc-13348996:

pmc-13349896:

pmc-13349996:

pmc-13350596:

pmc-13350696:

pmc-13351096:

pmc-13351296:

The review helps anaesthetists judge where machine tools are ready for clinical testing and where they stay experimental.
pmc-13351596:

pmc-13351696:

pmc-13351896:
Fan Jiang and co-authors build a 2026 imaging model that predicts tumour subtype and EGFR mutation status in non-small cell lung cancer from PET and CT scans. Tissue sampling has limits for tracking change and tumour variety. The retrospective study held 384 patients across three separate cohorts.

Extra tests checked which parts of the model mattered, and the design aims to keep decisions readable for clinicians. The goal is a non-invasive route to guide personal treatment choices.
pmc-13352396:
James J Yue and co-authors told in 2026 of 24-month results for passive recharge burst spinal cord stimulation. The target was stubborn no-surgery low back pain. This state has few effective long-term options. Implanted stimulation aims to modulate pain paths with no surgery on the spine itself.

The trial tracked patients with no-surgery chronic low back pain for two years after implantation. Patient-reported outcomes were charted across common diagnoses. Passive recharge burst stimulation gave marked and sustained therapeutic gain at two years. Gains were steady across diagnostic subgroups. Predictors of success were also read. They help clinicians pick patients most likely to gain from this implantable therapy.
pmc-13352796:
Yao Teng, Xiaoyan Zhao, and Aiguo Liu review clock-guided cell therapy for blood cancers in 2026. Body clocks run on 24-hour cycles and steer blood formation and immune function, yet cancers often disrupt them. Disruption can fuel tumour growth, blunt anti-tumour immunity, and swing treatment response across the day.

Stem cell transplants and CAR T-cell therapy anchor modern care, but their results and harms shift with clock timing. The review gathers evidence on timed cell collection, manufacturing, infusion, and aftercare. Personal clock phase checks are proposed as a base for tailored schedules. Aligning therapy with body time may lift graft success, sharpen tumour kill, and trim toxicity at low extra cost.
pmc-13354796:
Koichi Hasegawa and others linked brain ageing to decline of the LINC complex on the neuronal nuclear envelope, in 2026. Ageing inevitably erodes brain function, yet its tiny drivers remain unclear. The team showed that falling LINC levels impairs excitability guided by the axon initial segment, the site where neurons fire.

The work points to nuclear envelope workings as a driver of brain ageing, and to Sun1 preservation as a possible plan for protecting ageing neurons.
pmc-13354996:
Imogen Sharkey Ochoa and Michael Okorie write a 2025 essay on sexism in surgical culture and whether it can be re-taught. Ochoa recounts months in a surgery unit where senior staff voiced open doubts about women's fitness for surgery and family life. Such views, the authors note, also shaped hiring talk and daily work.

The authors ask if doctors should wait for society to change or lead change themselves. They propose teaching against bias in medical school and safe ways to report bad conduct on placements.
pmc-13355196:

pmc-13355596:
Abubakar Saeed and Waseem Abbas present BioGraphX in 2026, a method to predict where a protein sits inside a cell using only its sequence. Knowing a protein's home helps explain cell work and disease, but lab checks are slow and costly, and most AI tools cannot say why they predict as they do. Paired with a language-style protein model, the system beat prior tools on a standard benchmark while using few parameters. Its checks showed that sequence signals act as broad filters, while chemistry traits pinpoint the exact compartment. Tests on a second task confirmed the signals are real.
pmc-13355696:
Panitchaya Limsiri and co-authors measured in 2026 how Thai preschoolers spend their day across activity, sitting, and sleep. Early childhood shapes lifelong health, and over 30 percent of Thai children under five show developmental delays. Motion trackers were worn by 518 children aged three to four, and results were checked against World Health Organization guidelines.

Only about a quarter met activity targets, half met sleep targets, and about seven in ten kept sitting within limits. Just 7.5 percent met all three. Low income, farm or government parent jobs, and single-parent homes linked to worse patterns. The authors call for safe play spaces and support for caregivers.
pmc-13355896:
Kumari Ayushi and co-authors compared leg alignment in 2026 between 200 sedentary young adults and 200 amateur athletes in India, aged 18 to 25. Two measures matter for knee mechanics: the Q-angle at the kneecap and tibial torsion, the twist of the shin bone. A single trained examiner measured both by hand tool, three times each.

Sedentary adults had a slightly higher Q-angle, by about one degree, which may raise kneecap load. Athletes had markedly greater shin twist, by about three degrees, though all values stayed in the normal range. Leg length did not differ. The authors read the gaps as adaptations to regular sport, with a small effect for Q-angle and a large one for twist.
pmc-13357096:
Yunna Zheng and co-authors mapped in 2026 the role of ADH1A, an alcohol-processing gene, across many solid cancers. pmc-13358596:
Gaia Cicioni and co-authors report a very rare cancer case in a 2026 paper. A 67-year-old man was found, by chance, to have a large mass on his left adrenal gland. Fewer than a handful of such adrenal cases appear in past reports, so the authors also review what is known about the disease. These vessel cancers make up only about one percent of soft tissue sarcomas. The case shows how doctors prove so rare a diagnosis and why full removal matters.
pmc-13358796:
Tatsuya Tanaka and co-authors report a near-miss in stroke care in a 2026 case. An 89-year-old woman with a heart rhythm disorder fell, arrived weak on her right side, and could not stay alert. Brain scans showed a fresh stroke from a blocked artery, with no bleeding. The team gave the standard clot-busting drug through a vein.

Only afterward did a second look at her body scans reveal a hidden break at the top of her thigh bone, on the weak side. The clot drug raised bleeding at the break, and she needed blood transfusions. The case warns that a fracture can hide behind stroke signs, even after careful first checks.
pmc-13358996:
Du Cheng and co-authors report a misleading eye case in a 2026 paper. A 58-year-old woman from Pakistan had a fast-growing mass in her eye socket that came back after removal. Tissue tests showed granulomas, a pattern of immune cell clusters, but no sign of infection or lymphoma. At first she had no other symptoms and her chest X-ray looked clear.

A chest CT then revealed lung nodules and swollen nodes, confirming sarcoidosis, the body-wide granuloma disease. Steroid drugs plus methotrexate shrank the inflammation. The case shows that a normal X-ray cannot rule out chest disease, and that CT can settle the diagnosis.
pmc-13359696:
Sotirios Sachanas and co-authors follow a quiet blood condition over time in a 2026 study. Some people carry a clone of B cells of marginal zone origin in their blood without having lymphoma. The team reviewed 98 such cases referred between 1999 and 2017 to learn how the condition evolves and what forecasts a worse course.

Most cases stayed stable or slowly gained cells, suggesting a pre-cancer state rather than true lymphoma. Heavy bone marrow involvement and a high level of one blood enzyme independently predicted shorter time without treatment. A rare few, about five percent, turned into splenic marginal zone lymphoma. The study helps doctors counsel patients who live with this finding.
pmc-13360696:
Caterina Nardella and co-authors report early proof in a 2026 study of a protein that teaches the immune system self-control. The protein, called AIRE, normally works in the thymus, where it shows young immune cells the body's own proteins so they learn not to attack them. AIRE also appears in immune organs outside the thymus, but its work there is less clear. The team tested blood cells from four healthy donors.

Using a method that fishes out DNA bound by a protein, they checked whether AIRE sits on the start switches of known self-antigen genes. They found AIRE at the start switches of every self-antigen gene they tested. That hints AIRE helps guard against autoimmunity in the blood as well as the thymus. The authors call the proof preliminary and a base for larger studies.
pmc-13361096:
Kanza Atif led a 2026 study on whether a simple frailty score can warn of problems after kidney cancer surgery. The surgery, open radical nephrectomy, removes a whole kidney through a large cut. The link held after accounting for age and kidney function, though the numbers were not precise. All problems seen were of moderate grade. The score flagged high-risk patients well but missed many who did develop problems. The authors call the tool promising yet in need of proof in larger groups.
pmc-13361196:
Vikas Chauhan wrote a 2026 review on anesthesia care for a brain blood-flow surgery in moyamoya disease. In this disease, brain arteries narrow over time, so blood flow leans heavily on body pressure and breathing gases. The surgery, EDAS, lays a scalp artery on the brain to grow new vessels over weeks. It does not boost flow during the operation itself, leaving a risky window.

Chauhan lays out a practical plan built on steady blood pressure near the patient's normal level. The plan stresses avoiding low pressure and low blood volume, keeping oxygen and body heat normal, and holding breathing gases in a safe range. Deep breathing must be avoided, since low carbon dioxide shrinks brain blood flow. Brain monitoring ties the plan together for safer care.
pmc-13361296:
Shausha Mohamed Anees led a 2026 study of infections that follow a stroke in Malaysia. Infection after ischemic stroke is common and is linked to worse recovery. Fresh data from Southeast Asia are scarce, so the team followed 390 adults admitted to a major center between August 2024 and November 2025. An infection counted if it was diagnosed within seven days of the stroke under set rules.

The team recorded how often such infections struck and which patient traits predicted them. Stroke severity was scored with a standard scale, and the state of patients at discharge was tracked. Local numbers like these help hospitals in the region plan watchfulness and early treatment. They also show whether lessons from other regions hold in Malaysian care.
pmc-13361396:
Maritza P Garrido and co-authors issued this 2026 correction to their 2020 paper on ovarian cancer cells. The authors explain that counting photos were taken at high magnification during the experiments. The display photos were shot later at lower magnification so readers could see the results better. A corrected figure replaces the faulty one, keeping the paper's data presentation honest.
pmc-13361796:
Rucai Chen and co-authors built a shelf-life model for a ready-to-eat snow fungus dish in a 2026 study. Tremella fuciformis cold dishes are popular, and predicting how long they stay safe and tasty is key for makers. The team stored the dishes at 5, 15, and 25 degrees and tracked quality over time. pmc-13363996:

The tuned blend started with high conductivity and lost only a small share when stretched by half. Microscopy confirmed the staged web formed as planned. pmc-13365596:

Sprayed plants show near two thirds less ill than bare ill plants, with far less fungus mass in their flesh. Guard genes in the plant switch on strong. Seed drug grade stays near well plant ranks, while sick bare plants lose much. A green spray path shows real worth.
pmc-13369296:

pmc-13373296:
Hasan F Buali and co-authors review the pros and cons of prostate checks in a 2026 paper. A blood test has been the main check since 1994. It finds many cancers, but it also finds some that would never harm, and care for those can harm life quality.

pmc-13376796:
Zamanali Khakhar and co-authors tell of a fast lung scar ill in a 2026 case report. A woman had a skin and muscle ill tied to one immune mark. That mark's ill can race in the lungs, scar them stiff, and turn grave in weeks.

pmc-13380196:

pmc-13381996:

pmc-13382296:
Aubree L Hawley and colleagues wrote a 2026 scoping review building a framework for nutrition literacy in adults in the United States. Poor eating habits drive much preventable chronic disease. pmc-13382896:
Susan L. Bannister and colleagues describe Cards, a self-testing study tool for Canadian medical students in pediatrics, in 2026 work. pmc-13383196:

pmc-13386796:

pmc-13386996:

pmc-13388496:

pmc-13389896:

The correction states the errors arose during manuscript preparation by the authors.
pmc-13392196:

pmc-13393496:

pmc-13393796: Yusha Chen, Suyu Li, and seven colleagues issue a correction to their study of cervical pathology outcomes when colposcopy impressions look fully normal. pmc-13394496:

pmc-13395296:

pmc-13395396:

pmc-13396296:

pmc-13396496:

pmc-13396596:

pmc-13397096:

pmc-13397596:

Each bar was scanned and laid over the design file in Geomagic Control X software to measure drift. The cast group averaged a discrepancy score near 0.1128 against about 0.1 for the sintered group, a gap the tests found not significant.
pmc-13397696:

pmc-13397796:

pmc-13398096:

pmc-13398496:

pmc-13398696:
Le Zheng, Meng Chen, Yun Su and Yurui Wu report a twisted lung remnant that masqueraded as a chest tumour in a boy. Their 2026 case concerns an 11-year-old with sudden chest pain. Growths at the back of the chest usually grow slowly and quietly, which clashed with his sudden pain.

pmc-13398796:
Hyung-Gyo Cho and John Fortunato present a 2026 case image report of a shot glass removed from a teenager's rectum with Magill forceps. The glass, measuring 4 by 5 cm, came out whole, and a follow-up scope check found no injury to the bowel lining. pmc-13398996:
Alexandre Natalis and co-authors describe sealing a wrist artery blister from inside the vessel, sparing a 93-year-old woman an operation. A clot sealed the leak while the artery stayed open; by three months only a fibrous remnant remained. Balloon sealing joins a short list of gentle fixes for this rare complication.
pmc-13399396:
Hinpetch Daungsupawong and Viroj Wiwanitkit wrote this 2026 letter commenting on a study that graded ChatGPT-4's answers about acute compartment syndrome, a limb-threatening emergency in orthopedic surgery. Only two expert physicians scored the answers, which narrows the viewpoint and risks expert bias. They propose judging medical AI on prioritization and risk communication, using messy, time-pressured case vignettes. They recast the chatbot's best role as a cognitive scaffold for clinicians rather than a decision maker.
pmc-13399596:
Akanksha Choudhary, Manoj K Paswan, and Anshu Jamaiyar studied how well the blood marker CA-125 separates benign from malignant ovarian tumors, in a 2026 observational study from eastern India. They used the standard cutoff of 35 units per milliliter.

Every malignant tumor showed a raised CA-125, while 89.1 percent of benign tumors stayed in the normal range. Those counts give the test a sensitivity of 100 percent, specificity of 87.7 percent, and overall accuracy of 90.7 percent in this series, as the authors compute. Their verdict is that CA-125 is a useful flag for malignancy, provided clinicians read it alongside examination, imaging, and tissue diagnosis rather than alone.
pmc-13400996:
John L Richards and a large team survey, in 2026, dental calculus, the hardened plaque on teeth, across mammals in museum collections. Calculus preserves molecules from the mouth over long timescales, making it a rich archive of past microbes. Outside humans and primates, its distribution was almost unknown.

Examining over sixteen hundred specimens from 142 species spanning nearly all mammal orders, they found calculus in 104 species. High-fiber diets linked most strongly to abundant deposits, while high protein and fat diets showed little or none. Evolutionary relatedness also mattered, pointing to mouth and tooth shape effects, and captivity changed formation in almost every diet group. The team predicts which unsurveyed species likely carry calculus.
pmc-13401296:
Arne Gessner and co-authors published a 2026 metabolomics study asking how two diabetes drugs, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin, change small molecules in blood and urine. These SGLT2 inhibitors protect the heart and kidneys even beyond blood sugar control, and the reasons are only partly understood.

A second study of 24 patients, comparing empagliflozin plus linagliptin against metformin plus insulin glargine over 12 weeks, served for confirmation. pmc-13401396:
Somaye Sohrabi and co-authors offer a 2026 perspective piece with twelve practical tips for bringing competency-based medical education into resource-limited settings. The approach ties training to patient care results and has spread worldwide. Scarce infrastructure, thin faculty capacity, and unready systems slow it down where resources are tight.

The tips grew out of the authors' own work rolling such reforms out, checked against a focused literature review and settled by group consensus. Early advice includes winning a formal pledge from school leadership, adapting the framework to local needs, and mapping skills onto the existing course plan. Making learners co-creators is another early step. Using entrustable professional activities turns skills into clinical action. Low-cost, high-impact testing methods and local testing champions keep the reform affordable and lasting.
pmc-13401596:
Marco Kramer and co-authors carried out a 2026 exploratory virtual reality study of how people with schizophrenia interact with environmental affordances, the action possibilities a place offers. Disturbed affordance perception has been linked to the disorder, but static laboratory tasks capture everyday perception-action loops poorly.

Nineteen patients and nineteen healthy controls explored natural and urban 360-degree video scenes and played an interactive VR game, after completing questionnaires on anomalous world experience. Their field of view was recorded and hand-coded, and mood, stress, and presence were rated before and after exposure. Patients scanned the scenes less, making fewer gaze shifts per minute than controls, especially in urban settings. In the game, object interaction patterns were broadly similar, though patients tended to hesitate longer before starting social interactions.
pmc-13401696:
Sithembile Mduduzi Tshomela, Isaac Tebogo Rampedi, and Phyllis Rumbidzai Kwenda surveyed household pharmaceutical waste habits in two South African areas in a 2026 one-time survey study. Medicine use and disposal keep rising with more people and wider health care access, and leftover drugs at home raise environmental questions.

A layered random sample brought a semi-set questionnaire to 303 locals, 221 in Katlehong Township and 82 in Lambton Suburb, within Ekurhuleni Municipality. Knowledge of what counts as drug waste was limited in both places, at roughly 39 and 43 percent of respondents in each place. Even so, 77 percent said they would adopt proper drop-off if teaching and drop-off options were offered. The most common storage spot in both places was inside a medicine box, and the study sets drop-off routes and awareness of harm to nature side by side across the two settings.
pmc-13401896:
Derk H C Nieuwenhuijsen, Moritz Eggelbusch, and Rob C I Wüst reviewed how myostatin, the body's brake on muscle growth, drives wasting during inactivity, in a 2026 mini-review. Muscle adapts fast to disuse: bed rest, a cast, or weightlessness can strip mass and strength in weeks.

Evidence from human and rodent studies shows inactivity raises myostatin expression and signalling, tipping protein balance toward breakdown. The protein docks at the activin type IIB receptor and fires Smad signals that suppress the Akt and mTOR growth pathway, cutting protein building. Weaker Akt signalling frees FoxO factors to switch on the cell's protein shredding machinery. Myostatin also keeps muscle stem cells asleep, blocking the MyoD-driven activation needed for repair. The review traces the time course of these changes during and after inactivity, a map for countermeasures.
pmc-13403096:
Gisela Meydilin Sanjaya and co-authors review trials of oral herbal pills against skin aging, asking whether swallowing plant products can do what creams promise. Twelve randomized trials from 2020 to 2025, found through database searches run in 2025, compared these products with placebo or standard care in adults. Outcomes spanned elasticity, hydration, wrinkle depth, smoothness, and inflammation markers.

Tested products included soy, bilberry, cranberry, Hydrangea serrata, and Pycnogenol among others. Most trials reported real gains in skin measures. The authors link the gains to antioxidant and anti-inflammatory action, collagen support, barrier repair, sun protection, DNA repair, and gut-skin effects acting together. Every trial carried some bias concerns on the Cochrane tool, though. The authors call the field promising and ask for larger, longer, marker-anchored studies before standard use.
pmc-13403396:
Gervas and co-authors audit, in 2026, the gap between Tanzania's insecticide resistance policy and its practice, as malaria gains stall and pyrethroid sprays stop working. They reviewed national malaria program documents spanning 2014 to 2024 against World Health Organization guidance, then spoke with 24 people from policymakers to district staff, sorting responses by theme.

pmc-13403596:
Haojun Tian and team tied a protein called Gremlin1 to early placenta aging in older mothers. Gremlin1, or GREM1, stood out as a possible driver in placenta trophoblast cells.

In lab trophoblast cells, extra GREM1 curbed growth, movement, and invasion while sparking aging, effects undone by knockdown. Lab work tied GREM1 to BMP4 signaling and SMAD phosphorylation, and mouse overexpression mimicked placenta aging traits. The work points to GREM1 signaling as a target for guarding placenta function.
pmc-13404096:
Itamar Beigel and co-authors grew four medical cannabis types in 2026 under a mix of four heavy metals at three dose levels. Metals in the flowers can harm users and may also change how the plant makes its active compounds. The team tracked where each metal piled up inside the plant.

Roots held the highest metal levels, which kept tender shoots partly shielded. Nickel moved upward most freely, while lead moved least. Even at a moderate-low dose, flower levels of cadmium and nickel passed world safety limits for healing plants. Effects on compound output shifted by dose and by plant type.
pmc-13404496:
Dominic Spicer and co-authors report a 2026 case that widens the known effects of a harmful change in the ASXL1 gene. Such changes usually cause Bohring-Opitz syndrome, a developmental condition seen in infants and teenagers. No muscle disease pattern had been linked to the gene before this report.

pmc-13405096:
Hamin Lee and co-authors screen seed extracts from seven Korean forest trees for useful biological effects, in 2026 work. Seeds grown for planting forests are mostly unused beyond sowing. The team tested whether they could serve as sources of antioxidants or other marketable compounds.

Extracts from species including Japanese alder, sawara cypress and Amur cork tree faced a battery of lab assays. Effects differed sharply by species rather than spreading evenly. Oak seed extract from Quercus glauca combined strong antioxidant action with anti-inflammatory and skin-whitening effects in the reported tests. Sawara cypress extract showed the clearest activity against cancer cell lines, while alder led on the whitening enzyme test.
pmc-13406296:
Bowei Yang and co-authors design a surface that boosts the faint light signal of bacterial slime, in a 2026 study. Staphylococcus aureus films are thin, so their infrared signal is weak. The team first read that signal with care, and gauged film depth with an atomic force tool.

Those reads fed models of a three-layer patterned surface tuned to the film's main bands. Two layouts were tried: one that favours light from one side, and one balanced for both. Boost factors reached 8.57 and 7.24 at the chosen wavelengths in the reported models. The design aims at fast checks for slime on medical and food gear.
pmc-13407596:
Omer Horovitz analyses, in 2026, how online wellness culture talks about orthorexia, an obsessive fixation on eating purely and correctly. Drawing on social theory that treats health as an identity project, the study reads orthorexia-related writing as moral identity work performed and contested on online platforms.

The corpus held 1,100 texts from Reddit, YouTube, and blogs published between 2020 and 2025, with 80 texts given close reading. Purity and contamination language, and self-positioning around it, appeared widely but shifted by genre. Close reading found restrictive eating framed as morally charged, self-defining, and non-negotiable, defended by boundary-drawing against critics and against being labelled ill. Recovery stories more often broke those binaries, separating self-worth from dietary purity. Prevention, Horovitz suggests, must engage the moralised self-concept itself.
pmc-13407796:
Janet E Pope and team tracked real-world staying power and outcomes for upadacitinib among Canadian patients with inflammatory arthritis. Their 2026 UPRAISE work draws on the AbbVie Care patient support program from January 2020 to July 2025, covering rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and axial spondyloarthritis. Rheumatoid patients improved function by a mean HAQ-DI drop of 0.40, with 62 percent hitting a clinically key difference. The work backs upadacitinib staying power and benefit, while program enrollment may skew results.
pmc-13407896:
Kai Zhang and co-authors identify, in 2026, a single protein that drives lung cancer's spread to bone and its resistance to immunotherapy. YBX1 is a gene-control factor. One target for two problems is the attraction.
pmc-13408196:

pmc-13408496:
Allegra Angeloni and a large Australian team ask in 2026 whether the wide erasure of DNA methylation in early embryos evolved with the placenta. Marsupials, which grow a short-lived placenta, offer the test case.

Yet it did so only in the trophectoderm, the placenta-forming lineage. The embryo proper stayed untouched. That pattern suggests placental erasure is the older state for mammals. pmc-13408696:

pmc-13410696:
Lovel Fornah and colleagues count in 2026 how many people in Sierra Leone drop out of HIV care after starting treatment. Records covered 1,544 patients, about two thirds of them women, followed for a median of just over four years. About 36 percent were lost to follow-up, defined as 90 days without a visit or refill. pmc-13411996:

The team proposes the hay as a low-cost feeding strategy.
pmc-13412996:

pmc-13413496:

pmc-13414796:
Sara Guibunda Tajú and colleagues hunt for schistosomiasis leads in a red seaweed, Ochtodes secundiramea, in a 2026 study. pmc-13415296:

Several model types, from elastic net regression to random forests, scored much alike, with accuracy measures near 0.71 to 0.72. Each model leaned on different patient features to decide. pmc-13416396:

pmc-13418496:

pmc-13418596:

pmc-13420296:

pmc-13420496:

pmc-13421096:
Cecilie Brandt Becker and colleagues compared post-mortem signs of diarrhea in young piglets in 2026, studying 145 pigs from a Danish herd followed from birth to ten weeks. pmc-13421196:

The team backs diffusion models as a tool for drug-dose studies.
pmc-13421696:

pmc-13421796:

pmc-13422096:

pmc-13423496:

pmc-13423996:

pmc-13424496:

pmc-13424796:

pmc-13424896:
Gabriela Soto-Canetti, Kristina Navrazhina, and Jordan Talia report using dupilumab to treat pemphigoid gestationis in a nursing mother who could not come off steroids. Their patient, a 34-year-old woman at thirty-two weeks, developed badly itchy raised plaques and tense blisters across her trunk and limbs, confirmed by biopsy.

High-dose prednisone barely held the disease, and every attempt to taper over four weeks failed. After delivery the condition worsened and the steroid dose climbed again. Because she was breastfeeding, dupilumab, an antibody blocking the interleukin-4 receptor, was started as a steroid-sparing option, letting prednisone be withdrawn with major gains. A review of published cases comes with the report.
pmc-13425096:
Witold Chmielnicki and coauthors examine immunology and quality of life in lichen sclerosus in a 2026 article. The chronic inflammatory skin condition mainly affects the anogenital area and is linked with genetic, autoimmune, tissue remodeling, oxidative stress, and urine occlusion factors. White plaques, thinning skin, redness, erosions, and scarring can markedly lower daily well-being.

Embarrassment, anxiety, and stigma trouble many patients, partly from mistaken links with sexually transmitted infections. Sexual problems also feature strongly, since appearance concerns and symptoms lead some people to avoid sexual activity, making psychological burden a core clinical issue here. Many of these men and women say the skin signs shape their mood, their work, and their close ties with other people.
pmc-13425596:
Douni Roger and colleagues present a 2026 case of Impella-assisted high-risk coronary intervention in a 69-year-old man in cardiogenic shock. He arrived after a mechanical fall with a non-ST-elevation heart attack, acute heart failure, low-flow low-gradient aortic stenosis, and multivessel coronary disease, and he was not a surgical candidate. A temporary Impella pump supported circulation during coronary revascularization that otherwise carried extreme risk. The case shows how mechanical support can create a window for treating blocked arteries when valve disease and shock coincide.
pmc-13425796:
Yuxi Liu and coauthors built a short form of a quality-of-life questionnaire for benign prostatic hyperplasia in a 2026 methods study. Each method selects items by different statistical rules, and agreement among them helps judge which short version is most trustworthy.

Shorter, validated questionnaires lower burden for older patients who complete repeated outcome measures. Urology services gain a candidate brief instrument whose measurement quality was checked under three separate frameworks.
pmc-13425996:
Chenxi Li and coauthors pooled three aging cohorts to study frailty, depressive symptoms, and combined heart disease with cancer in older adults in a 2026 analysis. Data harmonized the China, English, and United States retirement and ageing studies, giving 10,937 participants aged sixty-five and over free of cardio-oncology comorbidity at baseline. Frailty and mood symptoms were assessed together rather than in isolation.

Joint and interacting effects matter because each condition alone raises risk, and their combination may multiply it. Findings can guide combined screening, where a frailty check and mood check in one visit flag the highest-risk older patients.
pmc-13426196:
Karn Dhillon and Shuvro Roy report a 2026 case of a tumor-like brain lesion from neurosarcoidosis that responded to infliximab. Management is especially hard when disease resists steroids or patients depend on them long term. Response to infliximab, an antibody therapy, in this case offers a treatment data point for refractory tumefactive neurosarcoidosis.
pmc-13426296:
Cheung and co-authors ran a secondary check in 2026 on a computer pipeline that ranks antipsychotic drugs by their likely effects on blood lipids, the fats tied to heart risk. The pipeline mixes receptor binding data with gene expression signals linked to lipid traits.

The check removed the literature-based weights that tell the pipeline which receptors matter most, then rebuilt the rankings for 52 drugs across five lipid measures. What changed was credit: histamine and serotonin receptors dominated the weighted version, while dopamine receptors led once weights were equal. The exercise also flagged ADRB1 as a strong gene signal the literature weights had nearly ignored.
pmc-13426496:
Mei Xie and colleagues compared routine blood markers and lung function between asthma-COPD overlap and asthma alone in a 2026 retrospective study of 505 hospitalized asthma patients admitted from 2020 to 2024. Overlap cases numbered 190 and asthma-only cases 315, with records supplying disease history, lung function, blood counts, immunoglobulin E, and medication exposure. Separating true disease signals from drug effects helps clinicians interpret routine tests in mixed airway disease. Charts hold a full span of five years of stays, which gives the checks a broad base in men and women of all ages and grades of ill health.
pmc-13426896:
Mokhtar and colleagues interviewed in 2026 twenty-four adults living with obsessive-compulsive disorder about using artificial intelligence in their therapy and treatment. They prized the human side of care: trust in a therapist, empathy, and reassurance, which they felt no program could copy. Many also worried about privacy, security, and where their data might end up. Still, most accepted AI as a helper rather than a replacement.
