pmc-13426996:
Simon Frey and colleagues reviewed published cases of gnathostomiasis, a worm infection people catch mainly from eating raw fish. The worm's larvae wander through the body, and the review maps where cases occur and how the illness shows itself.

Most reports came from Asia and the Americas, with Thailand, Japan, and Mexico giving the highest case counts. Skin swellings from moving larvae made up about 84 percent of cases, far ahead of eye, nerve, and organ forms. Lasting harm was rare overall but hit about half of eye cases and about a third of nerve cases. Treatment with two worm drugs together cleared the infection in about 87 percent, beating either drug alone.
pmc-13427096:
Kerstin de Wit and a large Canadian group tracked emergency physician burnout longitudinally in a 2026 study begun in April 2020. Canadian emergency departments face record attendances, long waits, bed blocking, and crowding, and the team followed physicians through surveys in November 2020, September 2022, and January 2025. Primary outcomes measured emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and personal accomplishment scores.

Free-text answers from the 2025 round were analyzed thematically using the framework built from the 2022 survey. Five-year trends show how emergency practice has worn down physician well-being well beyond the pandemic peak. Five years of checks show wear that did not ease when the worst of the plague years passed, a point the team makes with care and weight.
pmc-13427996:
Lara Perrella and co-authors examine, in a 2026 Italian study, whether medicines known to raise fall risk send older people to hospital. Many common drugs, from painkillers to antidepressants, can cause dizziness or drowsiness. The team used health system records for community-dwelling adults aged 65 and older. People hospitalized for fall injuries in 2018 were matched one-to-one with similar people who had no fall injury, giving over 16,000 in each group.

Fall-risk drug use appeared in about 38 percent of cases versus about 26 percent of controls. Overall, use of such drugs came with about half again the odds of a fall hospitalization. Opioids and antidepressants carried the highest risks among drug classes. Long use and recent use raised the odds further. Careful prescribing reviews are the practical takeaway.
pmc-13428696:
Anju Shukla and colleagues issue, in a 2026 position statement for the Indian Academy of Medical Genetics, guidance on gene sequencing tests for rare disorders. Next-generation sequencing can scan a gene panel, all protein-coding regions, or the whole genome in one run. Use in India is growing fast, yet many ordering clinicians have limited genetics training. The statement aims to close that gap with practical direction.

Sections cover which test fits which clinical question, how to prepare families for possible findings, and how to read reports without over- or under-calling variants. A firm molecular diagnosis, the authors note, guides counseling, surveillance, and family planning for affected households. Judicious use is the theme throughout: the right test, ordered for the right reason, with results interpreted in context. Professional societies in fast-adopting health systems will find the template familiar and useful.
pmc-13428796:
Shahad E. Alraddadi and colleagues compare robotic and laparoscopic repair of inguinal hernias, groin hernias repaired through small incisions with or without a robot. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis follows standard reporting guidance and pools comparative studies in adults.

Nineteen reports covering 18 groups and 78,940 participants were included. Robotic repair was linked to a lower observed recurrence risk, though the certainty of that evidence was low and mostly non-randomised. Robotic operations took about 22 to 30 minutes longer and consistently cost more. Pooled results showed no clear difference in pain, hospital stay, or complications such as infection or urinary retention. The authors caution that the recurrence finding does not prove the robot is truly superior, so technique choice should weigh cost and local expertise.
pmc-13429996:
Stefan Bigge reviews, in a 2026 paper, an in-between laser wavelength for removing tattoos and treating skin pigment. Clinics mostly rely on 532 and 1064 nanometer picosecond lasers, ultrabroad pulses that shatter pigment particles. A 785 nanometer option, delivered by a titanium-sapphire laser, sits between them. The review gathers the direct clinical studies, lab work, comparison papers, and device documents that a targeted database search could find.

Direct evidence remains thin: small prospective studies, pilot series, and case reports. The clearest signal covers blue-green and other cool-colored tattoo inks that standard wavelengths handle poorly. Reports on freckles, melasma, and deeper brown patches are early and mixed. Lab data on pigment granule disruption support the idea without setting safe doses. The author casts 785 as a specialist adjunct, not a replacement, and asks for proper comparative trials.
pmc-13430796:
Zeeshan Ahmed and co-authors mined gene data in 2026 for shared drivers behind a stiff heart valve and a stiff heart muscle in people with heart failure. The valve fault raises the load on the heart, yet fresh clues hint that muscle stiffness can come first or grow in step. Blood cells from patients supplied both full gene reads and gene activity reads.

The team split its work into a hunt for gene changes and a hunt for gene activity shifts. Some markers tied to the valve fault alone, some to muscle stiffness alone, and some to both at once. Named genes also link to a wide spread of other heart faults, body-wide illness, and several cancers. The authors read the overlap as a sign of shared early paths worth tracking.
pmc-13431496:
Panchan Sitthicharoenchai and co-authors fed young pigs varied levels of vitamin D in 2026. Most groups then met a harsh strain of a major swine virus. The team watched effects on blood calcium and bone. The virus drives heavy losses in pig herds, and fresh outbreaks of this strain have grown worse. Forty-two pigs split into four groups, three dosed with the virus and one clean control.

Death rates ran high in every dosed group, no matter the diet. Blood calcium fell hard a week after dosing, which the authors read as a sign of high early demand. Across diets, blood calcium and kindred measures showed no clear split in the first two weeks. Rib bones from pigs that died early went under checks for ash, density, and growth plate scores.
pmc-13431896:
Rui Katano and co-authors told the case in 2026 of a 54-year-old woman whose heart muscle flared in a sudden, lethal form marked by a flood of allergy-linked white cells. She reached a local clinic with days of fever and short breath, in shock, with heart enzyme levels far above normal. Early tests mimicked a heart attack, yet artery scans showed no real block.

After her heart stopped, machines took over blood flow while a tissue snip from the heart showed dead muscle packed with the allergy-linked cells. Strong immune-calming drugs followed, with two more added as she failed to rally. Her heart fell silent in full and she died. The post-mortem found near-total loss of living heart cells with scar tissue in their place. The authors stress fast risk sorting for such cases.
pmc-13432896:
Helena Avermark, Maria Ström, and Sibylle Herzig van Wees heard school nurses in Stockholm in 2026 on the strain of giving a virus vaccine to teens in low-uptake areas. Sweden gives the shot free at school to all kids aged ten to twelve, yet trust and uptake trail other childhood shots, with wide gaps between groups. Twenty-one nurses gave deep talks across half a year.

Three themes rose. Nurses feel left alone to run the whole task. Each nurse also juggles two hats, private care for one child and health guard for the crowd. Talk around the shot snags on its link to sex, which needs a soft touch with kids and parents. Heavy loads rest on lone nurses, which the authors say risks the program's long life without more staff backing and talk tools.
pmc-13434196:
Hanson, Ennett, and Rogerson examine neighborhood measures and childhood asthma admissions in this 2026 retrospective study. Social conditions shape asthma outcomes, and researchers increasingly use composite indices of vulnerability, opportunity, and deprivation based on home address. The team analyzed 5,895 emergency encounters for 4,485 children aged two to eighteen in Indiana between 2021 and 2024, testing which index best predicted admission.

About twenty-eight percent of encounters ended in admission, split between ordinary wards and intensive care. Girls were more likely to be admitted. So were children with chronic illness. Children whose last outpatient visit was over a year earlier also faced higher odds. Black children and Spanish-preferring families were less likely in this dataset. None of the three neighborhood indices separated outcomes better than the others, yet neighborhood itself mattered, suggesting the indices miss whatever local factor drives disposition.
pmc-13434596:
Jacklyn M Huhn and a large team show how a gene switch feeds DNA copying in leukemia cells in 2026. The switch, ATF4, ramps up making of amino acids and of the letters that DNA is built from. Fast growth in cancer cells puts heavy strain on both supply lines.

The switch also boosts the tools that load amino acids onto carrier RNAs. Those carriers favor making of proteins that start DNA copying at the right time. Blocking the switch starved both supply lines and broke copy timing. Leukemia cells then matured and died. The work names a choke point for drug design.
pmc-13435596:
Rachel Wangari Kimani's team studied care ethics in 2026 as artificial intelligence and care robots enter health care. Standard ethics frames stress fairness, duties, and results, yet they often treat care as rule following, missing its moral core. Using Tronto's four stages, the paper compares human caregiving with machine-mediated care through idea analysis and robot literature.

Robots can improve watching, teamwork, and task work, but they do not take moral duty or do the moral judging that care requires. Robots shift all four stages: careful watch becomes sensing, duty becomes checks, skill becomes tuning, and response becomes live feedback. Ethics teams get a guide for judging what robots should and should not be asked to carry in care.
pmc-13437296:
Alexandra Lovatt and colleagues show that a channel protein in the eye's lens opens in response to carbon dioxide. The protein, connexin50, sits in lens fiber cells, and faults in it cause cataracts. Guided by recent structural images and prediction software, the team spotted a chemical motif that might sense carbon dioxide, much like one known in a sister protein.

Both the full protein and a natural shortened form opened their channels as carbon dioxide rose. Changing two key building blocks in the motif removed that response entirely. A known cataract-causing change also wiped out carbon dioxide sensitivity. In lens slices, the gas triggered calcium entry into fiber cells, partly through a chain in which the channels release glutamate, a signaling molecule. The authors propose that this sensing helps run the lens's internal circulation, a flow system the clear tissue needs to stay healthy.
pmc-13437396:
Amanda Caruso and co-authors review patient-derived organoids, tiny lab-grown copies of a person's tumor, as tools for choosing treatment. Gene reading alone often fails to say which drug will work for a given patient. Organoids keep much of a tumor's genetic makeup, gene activity, and look, and they can be grown, stored, and tested at scale.

Uses now span drug screening, modeling radiation response, pairing tumors with immune cells, and gene editing studies that hunt for weak points. In bowel, pancreatic, and breast cancers, organoid drug results have matched patient outcomes closely, and trials increasingly build them into care plans. Newer work links organoids with chip devices, artificial intelligence, and hospital workflows that return answers in time to matter. The authors argue this shifts precision oncology from gene lists toward live testing of each tumor.
pmc-13437596:
Serkan Guney, Saliha Guney, and Seydahmet Cay measured trace elements in honey from eight districts of Ordu Province in Türkiye, treating the jars as food and environmental sensors. Their 2026 study paired chemical readings with standard health risk formulas, then used pattern-sorting statistics to separate natural from human-made signals.

Samples differed clearly by district. One pattern grouped iron, nickel, and copper, a signature of the earth, while a second grouped cadmium, lead, and zinc, pointing to human sources. Toxic elements such as arsenic, cadmium, and lead sat at low levels, and cancer risk estimates stayed within accepted bounds. Chromium drove the non-cancer risk scores, though the authors caution the math treated all chromium as its worst form, likely overstating the danger. Their frame shows honey doubling as a cheap watchtower for regional contamination.
pmc-13437896:
Nadine Ikelaar and colleagues followed boys and young men with Duchenne muscular dystrophy to weigh the trade-off of steroid treatment on an on-off schedule. Steroids delay the spinal curve of this muscle-wasting disease but thin the bones. Their 2026 study used records from the Dutch national center for patients seen between 2002 and 2022. Yearly spine films and bone density scans tracked curves, fractures, and bone strength.

Three in four developed scoliosis, at a median age of eleven, mostly after walking was lost, and a quarter needed fusion surgery. Bone density fell below the worry line in a third. Set beside published figures for daily steroids, the intermittent group showed more spinal curves yet fewer fractures and stronger bones. The authors present the comparison carefully, since it leans on outside reports, not a head-to-head trial. Families choosing a dosing rhythm are picking which harm to lean against.
pmc-13438296:
Syed Hussein Fathi Syed Mahmud Shahab and co-authors report a surgical emergency traced to an improvised blood-taking trick in newborn care. Some units snap the plastic hub off a needle so blood flows straight from the vein into a tube, a shortcut called the broken needle technique. Their 2026 case concerns a ten-week-old baby born early, who arrived with a swollen patch on the left flank where a sharp point could be felt.

An X-ray showed a long, thin object in the flank, and a CT scan placed it against the hollow holding the spleen and kidney, with inflammation but no organ pierced. Surgeons explored the abdominal wall and removed a three-centimeter needle. They urge strict standard technique, proper neonatal sampling tools, trained staff, and safe disposal, framing the case as a preventable harm that equipment budgets, not luck, should stop.
pmc-13438496:
Giuseppe Comentale and colleagues compared blood-thinning strategies after coronary endarterectomy, an operation that peels diseased lining out of a heart artery when bypass grafting cannot clear it. Their 2026 analysis searched three databases with no limits on year or language and merged nineteen studies, with two reviewers screening blind and a third settling disputes.

Death rates, early and late, came out alike under both strategies. Early heart attacks, though, struck clearly less often in patients on dual platelet therapy, the paired aspirin-based regimens. Swapping the second platelet drug between clopidogrel and ticagrelor made no clear difference to whether grafts stayed open. The authors lean toward dual platelet therapy as the better buy, since it buys early protection at no survival cost. They frame the advice as the best reading of uneven studies, not a settled rule.
pmc-13438696:
Rin Yoshizato's team targeted CD80 in 2026 in Epstein-Barr virus linked B-cell lymphomas, cancers that resist standard chemotherapy and lack strong aimed options. Killing depended not only on the antibody tail but also on which target its variable region recognized, and CD80 antibodies spared T cell responses against virus-positive cells. Lymphoma teams get a promising new target with a favorable immune profile. Human trials will judge safety and benefit.
pmc-13439196:

Host actin switches Ceg14 on, while a bacterial partner, AnkJ, switches it off.

Frozen-state microscopy captured Ceg14 bound to actin, to AnkJ, and to both at once, each at near-atomic sharpness. Actin contact twists one end of Ceg14 and cycles its pocket through open and closed shapes as ATP splits. AnkJ grips the far side and locks a middle shape, halting the split. Together the pictures explain a tug-of-war over host energy during infection.
pmc-13439496:
Yikun Feng and colleagues review helper cells that shield lung tumours from treatment, focusing on cancer-associated fibroblasts in a 2026 article. Recent single-cell and spatial studies split these fibroblasts into distinct subtypes tied to scaffold building, immune exclusion, and treatment response. Tiny vesicles shed by fibroblasts carry further signals between tumour and immune cells. The review weighs therapies aimed at fibroblast pathways and favours normalising the stroma under biomarker guidance over wiping fibroblasts out wholesale.
pmc-13439696:
Gorringe and colleagues measured in 2026 how natural genetic variation in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana reshapes crossover rates near centromeres, the chromosome hubs that guide segregation in cell division. Crossovers, the swaps between paired chromosomes in meiosis, are usually suppressed around centromeres. Using fluorescent crossover reporters, the team counted over three million meioses across sixty hybrid crosses between the reference strain and varied wild accessions.

Most hybrids showed centromere-proximal crossover rates clearly above or below the inbred parents, so variation pushes both ways. Chromosome identity, accession, and their interaction together explained most of the spread, pointing to both local and genome-wide modifiers. A minority of hybrids also skewed how gene copies passed through meiosis, at times without any crossover change. The authors link the patterns to structural differences at centromeres and discuss how such heterozygosity can bend both recombination and inheritance.
pmc-13439796:
Isabel San Martín-Erice and colleagues measure how COVID-era confinement affected nursing home residents in Navarra, Spain, reporting a 2026 multi-centre study. All three measures worsened after lockdown. Daily ability and cognition scores fell by clear margins, while deterioration scores crept up. A nursing diagnosis of disrupted thought processes flagged patients headed for steeper cognitive loss. Trouble with complex daily tasks likewise tracked with deeper decline across scales, and men lost more daily function than women. The authors propose that the thought-process diagnosis can help staff spot patients who need protection during long isolation.
pmc-13439896:

pmc-13439996:
Raghuveer Kavarthapu's team mapped ovary defense in 2026 in classic milk-sugar disease, where early ovarian failure strikes about eighty percent of women with the disease. pmc-13441196:

Students then carry projects through over eight to sixteen weeks, ending in a poster presentation. pmc-13443196:

pmc-13445696:

Both groups urged early introduction, voluntary joining, and structured mentor selection. The findings show strong appetite for mentoring, with feasibility and outcome trials as the next step.
pmc-13446096:
Masoud Arabfard and colleagues search gene data for shared genes and pathways that might flag lung cancer risk in people with asthma or chronic lung disease, in a 2026 computing study. Shared pathways numbered twenty-eight for the asthma pair and twenty-two for the other. The authors frame the lists as early leads for risk tests, and they call for deeper study of the top genes before any clinic use.
pmc-13446196:
Lang Mai and colleagues trace a chain that drives cartilage cells toward an iron-linked death in osteoarthritis, in a 2026 lab study. The chain hands drug hunters a fresh target for joint care.
pmc-13446896:
Filipe Resende and colleagues review the role of neutrophils, the most plentiful white blood cells, in viral infections, in a 2026 paper. The authors back pro-resolving drugs: compounds that calm activation, set cell lifespan right, and speed clean-up, rather than blunt immune force that the body still needs to beat the virus.
pmc-13447196:
Dorota Godzina and a large team survey sleep and heart risk among Polish school leavers in a 2026 nationwide study. More than four in ten slept under seven hours on school nights, catching up at weekends. Short sleepers ate more processed food, drank and smoked more, moved less in winter and spent more time on screens. Few recognised short sleep itself as a heart and metabolic risk.
pmc-13447296:

The authors link the reframed idea to wider goals for health, equity and sustainable communities, with lessons for teaching and research.
pmc-13447796:
Rachael Goodman-Williams and colleagues study which sexual assault survivors report to police after seeking medical forensic care in 2026 work. Decisions seem shaped partly by perceived strength of evidence, the authors argue.
pmc-13448196:

Four phases are planned, covering app building, algorithm training, internal validation and independent clinical testing. Clinic patients will void with both the standard meter and the app, which guides phone placement for clean recordings. Sound features will train models for peak flow, average flow and total volume. Funding arrived in mid 2026, with first-phase recruitment planned to follow and results expected by early 2027.
pmc-13448896:
Jiawei Hu and colleagues present in 2026 a microscope method that maps two electronic properties of a material at the same time and at nanometer scale. Their technique joins microwave impedance imaging, which senses local conductivity, with Kelvin probe imaging, which senses chemical potential. They demonstrate it on graphene systems driven into quantum Hall states, where electrons organize into unusual collective phases.

In bilayer graphene the method resolved the energy spectrum of the many-body states directly. Turned on slightly twisted double bilayer graphene, it revealed a cascade of magnetic isospin phases, including states that unexpectedly reappear as conditions change. The measured spectra tie those phases to crossings between energy subbands and to the shapes of the underlying electron waves. From this the team assembled a full phase diagram, offering the probe as a general tool for electron correlation and topology studies.
pmc-13449396:
Yuwei Li and coauthors ran a 2026 randomized trial comparing two implants for neck surgery in cervical spondylotic myelopathy, a condition where the spinal cord is squeezed in the neck. The operation removes a damaged vertebra and fuses the spine, traditionally with a titanium mesh cage plus a front plate. The new implant is a 3D-printed vertebral body that locks itself in place without a separate plate.

Seventy-four patients were enrolled between early 2022 and early 2024 and assigned at random to one of the two implants. The team compared operating time, blood loss, hospital stay, pain and function scores, imaging measures, and swallowing difficulty. Sixty-two patients completed follow-up for the main comparison. Surgeons can weigh whether the self-locking design matches the older method on safety and recovery.
pmc-13449496:
Si Yu Zhao and colleagues study in 2026 which routine laboratory values warn that a dengue patient is heading toward liver failure. They draw on cases from Changsha, a Chinese city where dengue is newly emerging rather than endemic. They reviewed 86 confirmed patients hospitalized in 2023 and 2024, most showing low white cells, and about half showing low platelets or raised liver enzymes. After removing patients with prior liver disease or other infections, 79 remained for the risk analysis.

The 39 patients who developed liver failure had significantly lower platelet counts and higher ALT, AST, and LDH than the 40 who did not. A random forest model trained on separate data to tell dengue from health ranked AST, platelets, and ALT among its most important features, echoing the bedside findings. The authors propose these cheap, routine tests as early triage markers pending prospective confirmation.
pmc-13449696:
Peixun Zhao and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a mouth germ makes chronic stomach lining damage worse in rats. This stomach state can lead to cancer and has few cures, and the germ Fusobacterium nucleatum, tied to gut cancers, had a murky role in it. The team asked if the germ drives harm through swelling and energy failure in cells.

Rats with drug-induced stomach damage were fed the germ by mouth, while human stomach cells were grown with it at three doses. The germ settled in stomach tissue and deepened harm, with loss of glands, gut-like change, and white cells crowding in. Levels of swelling signals and measures of cell energy backed a two-part cause. The work flags a germ target for slowing stomach damage before cancer.
pmc-13449796:
Yongqiang Liu and colleagues survey in 2027 how artificial intelligence is reshaping the design of antimicrobial peptides, short natural antibiotics that kill broadly and rarely provoke resistance. Finding and tuning these peptides by experiment is slow because the link between a sequence and its behavior is tangled. Learning systems trained on large collections can now read the hidden patterns in sequences and propose candidates that are physically plausible and biologically sensible.

The review sorts the technology into two modes. Identification models judge whether existing sequences are likely to work, while generation models dream up new peptides with desired properties. Both cut the trial-and-error burden of the wet laboratory. The authors then catalog what still blocks progress, from thin and biased training data to candidates that fail in living systems. They point to finer-grained modeling and data enrichment as the way forward for this fast-moving field.
pmc-13449996:
Emma Murphy and colleagues review in 2026 whether tuning soldiers' gut microbes could harden them against the stresses of service and perhaps sharpen performance. Deployment brings ration packs, energy shortfalls, broken sleep, and physical extremes. All of these disturb the gut ecosystem that feeds into immunity, mineral uptake, muscle endurance, and even cognition through the gut-brain axis. The review surveys technologies built to remodel that ecosystem, from live bacterial products to targeted substrates.

Evidence from animal work and small studies in healthy people hints that cognition, endurance, structural resilience, and injury recovery all respond to the microbiome's state. Yet almost all regulation around these tools was written for treating disease, which fits enhancement uses awkwardly. The authors conclude the opportunity is real but premature. Far more research in healthy cohorts must come first, plus regulatory frameworks written for resilience rather than illness, before commanders can count on microbial support.
pmc-13450596:
Alyssa Smith and co-authors review in 2026 what psychiatrists should keep in mind when a patient has both bipolar disorder and cancer. People with bipolar disorder die of cancer more often than the wider public, yet the pairing is little studied. The review pulls work on outcomes, mood flare-ups from cancer drugs, and clashes between drug groups.

Cancer care can stall for these patients through late finds and lower uptake of standard treatment, while steroids and some cancer drugs can spark mood episodes. Mood drugs add their own risks to organs, the heart, and body salts. The authors press for early mind care, tight teamwork between cancer and mind clinics, and close watch on sleep and self-harm risk.
pmc-13450896:
Jon Harrison and a large team test in 2026 how far honey bee colonies can hold their hive heat as air soars. Bees are key crop pollinators, yet the true ceiling of colony cooling was untested, with books claiming success up to very high heat. The team tracked gas exchange and hive heat in standard colonies through a harsh heat spell.

Four hours at fifty degrees pushed brood zones to a harmful level in most colonies. Bees fanned and bearded, ate less pollen, and slowed body burn, while stored honey and wax soaked up most of the heat as a passive buffer. Water loss played only a small part, a finding that flips the textbook story and warns that coming heat waves may beat the bees.
pmc-13451296:
Florence Dadzoe, Jessica Boakye, and Egemen Okte ask in 2026 whether plain road upkeep can also make road quality fairer across neighborhoods. Repair plans rarely score fairness, so the team built two new measures: one for spread within local areas, and one that sets fairness-focused zones against others. They tested four repair ranking plans on a Massachusetts road district.

Every plan lifted both fairness scores over the base state, cutting one gap by as much as three quarters. Plans that weighted crowd exposure could widen town-versus-country gaps when budgets grew, while a plan based on road state alone kept its gains. The authors say fairness can ride along with upkeep if the ranking factors are picked with care.
pmc-13451796:
Babak Bagheri and co-authors pool in 2026 the world record on two ways to clear clots from man-made heart valves. Clots on a valve on the heart's left side can kill, and guidelines still split on clot-busting drugs versus open surgery. The team gathered 114 studies covering more than 6,500 patients.

Success rates ran near equal for the two routes, at about 84 to 85 percent. Death rates, though, ran lower with the drugs, and a slow drip form of the drug did best of all, with high success and very low deaths. Since most proof comes from watch-and-record studies, the authors urge caution and call for true head-to-head trials.
pmc-13451896:
Megumi Sumizono and co-authors test in 2026 whether exercise eases nerve pain in fat rats bred for diabetes-like traits. Nerve pain in diabetes grows from both nerve harm and swelling, so the team tied off a leg nerve in the rats and split them into exercise, rest, and healthy groups. Pain was gauged by how much touch the rats could bear.

Five weeks on, exercised rats bore more touch than rested ones. Swelling signals tied to spinal cord immune cells ran lower in the exercised group, as did two swelling signals in a memory zone of the brain. Memory tests and new cell growth did not shift. The authors name fresh targets beyond the usual one for diabetic nerve pain.
pmc-13452196:
Hamze Dahir, Abdisalam Jama Ibrahim, and Abdisalam Hassan Muse write in 2026 a letter urging a new plan against dengue fever in Somaliland. Outbreaks return each dry, windy summer in cities such as Hargeisa, the hub of the crisis, where crowding is high and mosquito control lags. The letter calls the present system stuck in a loop of late response.

Old data hide the true toll, since watch systems are weak across the region. Many sick people mistake dengue for malaria, buy pain pills and antibiotics on their own, and reach care late, which costs lives. The authors press for dengue care folded into primary health posts, fresher data, and public teaching ahead of each season.
pmc-13452396:
Tilki and colleagues report a multi-institutional experience in this 2026 study using stereotactic body radiotherapy, highly focused radiation delivered in few large doses, against bladder cancer that has spread only to bone. They reviewed patients whose disease was oligometastatic, meaning limited to a handful of deposits, treated at four institutions between 2012 and 2020.

Twenty-six patients with 41 bone metastases received the treatment to every lesion. Local control at the irradiated sites was excellent, reaching 94.7 percent at one year and 88.0 percent at two years in their estimates, and no severe toxicities of grade three or higher occurred. Survival told a harder story, though: median overall survival was 8.9 months, because cancer usually progressed elsewhere in the body. Only about a fifth of patients stayed off systemic drug therapy at one year, leading the authors to call for prospective trials of combined strategies.
pmc-13452796:
Ranran Zhang and others showed in 2026 that a soft fibrin matrix steers macrophages toward healing in fatty liver disease. Macrophage-driven inflammation drives metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, known as MASH, while fibrin deposits in diseased livers had an unclear role in macrophage behavior. The team tested whether matrix softness changes polarization.

Fibrin deposition was elevated in MASH patient and mouse livers and correlated with inflammatory macrophage infiltration. Macrophages grown in soft fibrin showed stronger anti-inflammatory M2 polarization, with higher Arg1 and CD206 and lower iNOS and TNF-alpha. Transfer of soft-matrix macrophages into high-fat diet mice eased disease in the reported results. The work links tissue mechanics to immune healing through FABP4 and fatty acid oxidation.
pmc-13452996:
Baungaard and colleagues reported in 2026 the case of a 24-year-old man with CREST syndrome whose brain aneurysm burst and bled around the brain. CREST is a limited form of scleroderma, a disease that hardens connective tissue. Aneurysms in this setting are rare, and whether the tissue disease helps cause them is unsettled.

The bleed came from an aneurysm at a fork of the right middle cerebral artery. Surgeons first clipped the bulge shut, and later scans found a leftover neck that was sealed with a stent and coils threaded through vessels. The patient recovered well, with mild lasting thinking deficits. A literature review found only a handful of similar cases. The authors suggest tissue disease, smoking, and past stimulant use may have combined to weaken the vessel wall.
pmc-13453496:
Zhang and a large team build a printable bone-repair scaffold in this 2026 study, mixing silk protein with the amino acid L-leucine. Their hydrogel ink, made from modified silk fibroin, hardens under light inside a 3D printer, letting them fabricate scaffolds whose pore structure matches a skull defect's geometry precisely.

Adding leucine strengthened the gel and made its surface more welcoming to cells without hurting print quality. Stem cells grown on the material multiplied and matured toward bone, and blood-vessel cells showed stronger vessel-forming activity. A formulation carrying 300 nanograms of leucine per milliliter performed best overall and went into rats with critical-size skull defects, where it markedly increased new bone, collagen, and mineralized tissue. Silencing a collagen-processing enzyme called PLOD2 erased much of the benefit, tying the effect to collagen remodeling.
pmc-13453696:
Huancheng Huang and five co-authors argue that bullying in sport is bred by training culture itself, not just by cruel individuals. Their 2026 paper mixes a review with case studies of two known abuse cases, one in the United States and one in China, plus interviews with 12 athletes. The authors frame harsh coaching as structural violence when a culture blesses it.

Two creeds do the damage: a culture of suffering, which treats pain as the price of growth, and a culture of obedience, which forbids pushback. Together they hide abuse five ways, by blessing it, making it routine, silencing protest, sinking it into the athlete's own beliefs, and drawing bystanders into collusion. Athletes then excuse their own mistreatment and feel helpless to stop it. The authors call for rebuilt cultures and real accountability, not punishments after the fact.
pmc-13453796:
Shota Inoue and eight co-authors set out a standard protocol for feeding a heart lung machine through the leg artery in keyhole heart surgery. That route can starve the leg of blood, a risk the protocol aims to prevent. Their 2026 study reviews 505 patients who had fully endoscopic surgery with this setup between June 2019 and July 2024.

The tube goes in shallow with its side hole aimed to keep blood flowing down the leg, and oxygen sensors watch both legs throughout. A drop of over half in leg oxygen triggered set steps, from raising pump flow to a drug sprayed on the vessel. No patient needed the last step, an added leg line, and none developed the crushing pressure syndrome feared after such surgery. Drops hit 28 patients and all recovered with the early steps alone.
pmc-13453996:
Mei Wu and others made an mRNA drug mix against ricin in 2026, to stretch the cure window past exposure. Ricin, a plant poison, is a bio threat with no approved cure, and old antibody cures work only briefly past exposure. The team used fat-bubble mRNA to make antibodies in the body.

Two mRNA antibodies that hit ricin A and B chains, mRNA-43RCA and mRNA-Sy1H3, were joined in one mix. One shot made blocking antibodies fast in mice, and shielded them from a later lethal ricin dose in the tests. The route saves time and cost next to making antibodies in a plant. Bio-defence teams gain a fast post-exposure shield platform.
pmc-13454196:
Guowei Liu and thirteen co-authors build a two channel memristor, a resistor with memory, that can hold a Bayesian network's uncertainty right in the hardware. Bayesian networks report how unsure they are, a trust feature edge devices need. Chip versions stall since a memristor's setting and its noise usually move together. Their 2026 device stacks an ion gel over zinc oxide to form two coupled channels.

The weight becomes the gap between the two channels' conductance, which lets the average and the spread be tuned apart. That split gives clean Gaussian weights straight from physics. A hardware tuned network then sorted human activities from several sensor types at 79.08 percent accuracy. It also flagged never seen activities as out of distribution, the honesty check such systems need. The team pitches the design as scalable, low power, and trustworthy by construction.
pmc-13454296:
Shayesteh Rounama and four colleagues describe, in 2026, a mouse model that joins two ways of studying drug reward in one animal. Mice drank oxycodone in a sweetened solution by choice, inside a two-chamber box. The team then checked whether the mice came to prefer the side paired with the drug, whether that liking faded, and whether a later dose brought it back.

Male and female mice drank the drug freely, though females drank less than males. Both sexes developed a clear place preference, lost it during drug-free weeks, and regained it after a challenge dose. Mice bred without the mu-opioid receptor showed no preference at all. The authors argue the model can help test how opioid reward forms and returns.
pmc-13454496:
Siyue Xu and eight colleagues review, in 2026, why the bacterium Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is so hard to treat in hospitals. The germ lives widely in nature and in clinics, and it preys on weakened patients. Built-in defenses make many standard antibiotics useless against it.

The review catalogs its shields: two home-grown enzymes that break key drugs, pumps that expel drugs, a tight outer coat, and slimy biofilms. The germ also picks up new resistance genes from neighbors and makes enzymes that aid invasion. A drug pair, trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, remains the first choice, though resistance is rising in places. Newer hopes include pump blockers, anti-virulence drugs, and virus-based phage therapy. The authors map where treatment stands and where fresh strategies are heading.
pmc-13454596:
Furong Yang and thirteen colleagues build, in 2026, a stretchable antenna that keeps its tuning while pulled in any direction. Wearable radios sit on skin that stretches unevenly during motion, which detunes ordinary antennas and breaks links. Earlier fixes worked only along one pull direction and often weakened the signal.

The team mapped how strain in each direction shifts an antenna's tone, then designed a two-port layout that cancels those shifts. Resonance moved by at most 40 megahertz at its 2.45 gigahertz band, even under 45 percent strain from varied directions. Strong signal gain held throughout. Demonstrations included wireless power harvesting that shrugged off stretching and a body-worn link that kept streaming health data during natural movement. The authors see the framework guiding deformation-proof wearables.
pmc-13455196:
Mahdis Mofidi and others found a new class 3 asparaginase in soil germs in 2026, as a new drug hope for child leukemia. Type II asparaginases treat child leukemia well, but side effects and antibody blocks from repeat shots spur a hunt for new classes. The team grew asparaginase-making germs from soil.

Of six germ strains, the top maker was Glutamicibacter, with asparaginase work of fifteen units per millilitre and glutaminase work of one point five units in broth. Gene reads tied it to fresh class 3 enzymes from Rhizobium etli. AlphaFold 3 drew its shape with high trust. Dock tests gave bind scores of minus nine point nine nine for both substrates, stronger than type IV and V enzymes. Motion tests found the asparagine knot more steady than the glutamine knot. The work names a new drug lead for child leukemia.
pmc-13455396:
Lucia La Sala and colleagues compare a simple blood-based insulin resistance score with older death predictors in obesity in a 2026 study. The triglyceride-glucose index, built from fasting triglycerides and glucose, has drawn interest as a cheap mortality marker, yet head-to-head checks against other indices were scarce. Two Italian cohorts with obesity were followed for nearly 14 years, a general cohort of 1,359 people with 11.5 percent mortality and a bariatric surgery cohort of 854 people with 5.5 percent mortality.

Many indices linked with death on their own, but age and the Charlson comorbidity index discriminated best in both cohorts, and combining indices did not reliably add value. Triglyceride-glucose scores thus remain useful for describing metabolic strain, not as front-line death predictors. Clinicians gain a sober ranking that keeps age and total illness burden at the centre of risk talk for patients with obesity.
pmc-13455496:
Danying Jing and Yawen Zhu followed Chinese high school students for six months to see whether being bullied predicts later depression, and whether the answer differs for boys and girls. Their 2026 study surveyed 457 tenth graders in Gansu Province, average age just under sixteen, in June 2024 and again that December. Students reported four kinds of victimization: physical, verbal, relational, and cyberbullying, along with their depressive symptoms at both time points.

All four forms of bullying at the first survey predicted higher depression scores six months later, even after demographic factors were accounted for. That held for physical attacks, insults, social exclusion, and online harassment alike. However, none of the gender interaction tests reached significance, so the bullying-to-depression link looked broadly similar for the 230 boys and 227 girls in this sample.
pmc-13456996:
Shouqiang Huang leads a twelve-author team building, in a 2026 study, a scoring chart for cognitive frailty in older patients living with chronic disease. The condition pairs physical frailty with thinking decline, and it is rising as populations age. The team assessed 752 patients aged sixty and over at three Chinese hospitals during 2025.

About 23 percent met the bar for cognitive frailty. Six traits traveled with it: sex, age, mouth frailty, muscle loss, low mood, and a measure of bodily resilience. The chart built from these scored well at sorting cases, with accuracy near 0.86 in its training group and 0.89 in a check group on a standard curve. Fit tests looked sound. The authors offer the chart for clinic screening, arguing that its inputs, from chewing strength to mood, are cheap to collect and point to where support can start.
pmc-13457296:
Caterina Formica and nine colleagues published this 2026 pilot study on brain responses to touch and temperature in patients with disorders of consciousness, such as vegetative or barely conscious states. Touch engages sensory pathways that may survive brain injury when sight and hearing routes fail. The team recorded EEG, the brain's electrical activity, before and after a month of touch and heat treatment, looking for signs of remaining cortical response.

Seven patients took part, receiving treatment to both hands. At baseline their EEG responses were weak and confined, dominated by slow waves. After the month of treatment, responses grew stronger and spread wider, with slow waves damped and faster activity better tuned over front-central and parietal regions. The authors read this as growth in cortical response linked to the treatment. They frame the EEG measures as markers to test in larger studies of diagnosis and care planning.
pmc-13457396:
Henry Leonhardt and colleagues report one-year results for jaw joint fractures fixed with a screw that the body slowly absorbs. Condylar head fractures, at the top of the lower jaw, are awkward to repair, and titanium hardware can demand a second removal operation. Their 2026 single-center series treated 20 patients with 22 fractures using a reduced-head magnesium-alloy screw, type WE43, whose surface was treated by plasma electrolytic oxidation.

Recovery of jaw function was strong. Maximum mouth opening grew from an average of 23.6 millimeters early on to 45.1 millimeters after a year, and bite alignment stabilized by about day 100. No patient suffered permanent facial nerve damage or an implant-related complication. Three-dimensional scans did show the condyle shrinking by roughly a quarter in volume and surface area, mostly during the first six months. That remodeling, the authors note, cost the patients nothing in function during the study year.
pmc-13457496:
Awwad, El-Salhi, and Igried built in 2026 an offline reader for the Arabic sign language alphabet. Deaf folk in Arabic lands lack the tech that American sign users have. Weak links and thin hardware rule out cloud tools there. Their stack pairs a shrink step with a trait puller, then a deep net to name each hand sign. A public set of sign shots fed the tests.

The stack named signs right near eighty seven times in a hundred. That beat the best old stack, a trait puller with a plain sorter, by a clear step. The shrink step cut the math load with no loss of skill. Signs that look near kin still blur at times. The authors pitch the tool for schools and daily talk.
pmc-13457696:
Xinran Gao and colleagues test calycosin, a plant isoflavone, for calming microglia, the brain's immune cells, when they overreact. Activated microglia can poison neurons and prune synapses, feeding brain illness. Their 2026 study inflamed BV2 mouse microglia with bacterial lipopolysaccharide, then asked whether calycosin could calm the cells and protect neurons bathed in microglia-conditioned medium.

Docking assays pointed to TLR4, the alarm-starting sensor, as calycosin's target. Treated microglia released less interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor, dialed down the TLR4/MyD88/NF-kappaB chain, and shifted from attack markers toward repair markers such as CD206. Medium from treated microglia partly rescued HT-22 neurons and brought back synaptic proteins including PSD95 and synapsin I. Matching tests in human HMC3 microglia and SH-SY5Y neurons echoed this. The authors conclude calycosin blunts microglia-driven neuron injury in cell models, a lead worth pursuing for neuroinflammatory disease.
pmc-13458396:
Le Ven and colleagues uncover a backup DNA repair partnership in human cells in this 2026 study. Certain DNA sites, called CpG sites, often carry a methyl tag, and when that tagged base decays it leaves a mismatched letter pair that can become a permanent mutation. These mutations mark both aging and cancer. A repair enzyme called MBD4 was known to handle most of them.

Using a targeted editing tool to create the damage at chosen sites, the team showed MBD4 recruits a non-standard mismatch repair team, including the protein pair MLH1-PMS1. Cells lacking PMS1 developed the same mutation signature as cells lacking MBD4, proving this pathway is a core job for PMS1. Part of the mutation burden in mismatch-repair-deficient tumors also traced back to this replication-independent damage.
pmc-13458696:
Zhaochu Wang and colleagues map the terpene synthase gene family in the medicinal plant Bidens alba in a 2026 genome study. Terpenoids give plants aroma, defence and drug value, and terpene synthases build them, yet the family in Bidens alba was uncharted. Whole-genome analysis found 84 BaTPS genes spread unevenly across 37 chromosome-scale scaffolds, sorted into five subfamilies, with TPS-a and TPS-b largest and TPS-g notably expanded.

Whole-genome and segmental duplication drove expansion under mainly purifying selection, with conserved gene structures and motifs including DDxxD. Promoters carried light, methyl jasmonate and abscisic acid response elements, and six genes expressed strongly in flowers, with two located in the cytoplasm. The work lays a foundation for tapping Bidens alba flowers as a terpenoid source and for testing individual synthase functions.
pmc-13459096:
Zelian Zhang and colleagues report in 2026 on a blood-based index and a breathing pattern called PRISm, where the ratio between two spirometry measures stays preserved while one of them is impaired. Their index, CALLY, combines C-reactive protein, albumin, and lymphocyte counts. The study compared 70 patients with PRISm against 119 without it, using hospital records.

Patients with PRISm had far lower CALLY values, and each one-unit rise in the index came with lower odds of the condition after adjustment for many other factors. People in the high group had odds about three quarters lower than the low group. Adding CALLY to a basic clinical model raised its accuracy noticeably, which the authors say could sharpen routine screening.
pmc-13459296:
Esther M Nasuuna and co-authors checked kidney health in young Ugandans living with HIV, focusing on whether the modern first line drug dolutegravir harms kidneys. Young people starting treatment young face decades of drug exposure, so early warning signs matter. Their 2026 study in Kampala measured 483 participants using urine protein tests and two estimates of kidney filtration. One estimate used creatinine and one used cystatin C, a marker less distorted by the drug in question.

Participants on the tenofovir plus dolutegravir combination showed higher creatinine and oddly inconsistent filtration estimates between the two methods. The cystatin based estimates, protein leakage rates, and shares with low filtration were similar across regimen groups, however. Elevated urine albumin appeared in 9.6 percent versus 13.0 percent of the compared groups, and proteinuria in 28.3 percent versus 30.2 percent. Kidney abnormalities were not tied to regimen, the authors conclude, but they want long term follow up.
pmc-13459396:
Yingjie Wang and co-authors studied how parental burnout, the exhaustion and emotional distancing that overwhelmed parenting can bring, relates to behavior problems in preschool children. Their 2026 survey covered 537 preschoolers and their parents in Shanghai, China. Parents filled out forms on burnout, family functioning, child behavior, and children's effortful control, the self control capacity that lets children inhibit impulses and focus. The team tested whether family functioning carries the burnout effect.

Parental burnout was significantly associated with more problem behaviors in the children. Family functioning mediated that link: burnout eroded how the family worked together, and a weaker family in turn tracked with more child problems. Children's effortful control softened the second half of the pathway. Children with stronger self control were buffered against the family level effects of a burned out parent.
pmc-13459496:
LaShae Nicholson and colleagues show how diet-caused insulin trouble worsens brain changes in memory-loss mice in a 2026 study. Fuel trouble raises memory-loss risk, yet the cell-level links between insulin trouble and brain decline were unclear. Normal and memory-loss knock-in mice, with human mutant APP and normal tau, were fed a high-fat, high-sugar diet, then tested for learning, glial flare-up and damage with single-cell RNA reads.

The diet caused weight gain and glucose trouble in both groups, but only memory-loss mice showed impaired spatial learning, without extra amyloid or tau damage. A distinct glial programme, termed fuel harm in brain decline, emerged alongside Meis2 rise in brain-surface layer 2 calming neurons and reduced calming synapse density. Experts gain cell targets linking fuel health to brain-surface weakness in memory-loss disease.
pmc-13459596:
Kateřina Heková and colleagues examine how general practice set-up shapes care teamwork in the Czech Republic in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Ageing, many ills and workforce gaps demand joined-up primary care, yet little was known about how practice models affect internal teamwork room. A survey of 356 general doctors on workforce, hand-off and teamwork, followed by structured expert talks on early findings, formed the design.

Small solo practices dominated, with limited non-doctor role, constrained hand-off and heavy paper loads, especially in rural areas. Younger doctors preferred group or staff models, while limited test access and weak gate control further curbed teamwork. Policy chiefs gain proof that teamwork gaps stem from set-up and system set-ups, not single doctor choices alone.
pmc-13460196:
Loïc Kouame and co-authors compared in 2026 two drugs that prevent bleeding, aprotinin and tranexamic acid, in urgent heart surgery involving the ascending aorta. Seventy-two non-elective operations at one tertiary center were reviewed, thirty-two using tranexamic acid in earlier years and forty using aprotinin later. A standardized bleeding score served as the main measure, with models adjusting for age, urgency, and bypass duration among other factors.

After adjustment, aprotinin came with a lower bleeding severity score, while greater urgency and longer bypass time each worsened bleeding. Transfusion rates and major complications did not differ significantly between drugs, although supporting blood products were used differently, and the mortality gap fell short of significance. Being retrospective and single-center, the study calls for further investigation.
pmc-13461896:
Coumba Gueye and colleagues describe building Papyrus, a digital patient-record platform for the oncology unit at Dalal Jamm hospital in Senegal. Cancer records there were paper-based and hand-carried between clinicians, so errors and lost data delayed care decisions.

Senegal sees about 6,646 new cancer cases a year with roughly 72 percent mortality, breast and cervical cancers leading. The platform lets the treating doctor edit records centrally, adding results, scans, pathology, allergy status, medicines, and discharge alerts. Coded access keeps entries secure, quick to reach, and traceable to whoever made them. Gueye reports the first milestone as a working, adopted platform, with adoption, reach, and feasibility to be assessed next.
pmc-13461996:
Muhammad Ibrahim and co-authors review the evidence for adding thyroid hormone to bipolar disorder treatment, grounding the old practice in the disorder's best replicated biology. Bipolar patients repeatedly show sluggish sodium pumps and excess sodium and calcium inside cells during mood episodes, a cellular energy problem. Thyroid hormone directly raises sodium pump expression and improves energy use. In their 2026 review, the authors gathered the clinical record on supraphysiological thyroid doses as an add on for bipolar depression and rapid cycling.

Across the literature, roughly 300 to 350 patients received high dose thyroid hormone, mostly for bipolar disorder, with generally very positive outcomes and minimal harm as reported. Benefits centered on lifting depression and slowing rapid cycling between mood states. No study found an increased risk of triggering mania, though mania itself has never been the treatment target in a trial. Dosing regimens vary enough to blur comparisons.
pmc-13462196:
Nick D Clement writes a 2026 commentary on a puzzle in robot-assisted joint replacement: the operation is more precise, yet patients feel no better than after standard surgery. Robots place hip and knee implants with better alignment and less variation, which appeals to surgeons. Randomized trials show pain, function, complication, and satisfaction scores that rarely differ in ways patients would notice. The gap raises a question about belief and expectation.

Clement asks whether part of the robotic benefit works like a placebo, where confidence in high-tech care speeds recovery, and whether that should trouble the field. Costs matter too: complications drive spending in joint surgery, and gear adds expense. Surgeon enthusiasm can run ahead of hard proof, he notes. The piece urges honest weighing of what robots add for patients, not just scan pictures. It invites study of how patient perception shapes recovery after joint replacement.
pmc-13462796:
Shankar and Dowlut-McElroy wrote this 2026 invited commentary on predicting ovarian decline in Turner syndrome, a condition in which one X chromosome is missing or altered. pmc-13462896:

pmc-13462996:
Shiping Lei and colleagues traced carbon chemistry off the Pearl River mouth in the northern South China Sea during spring 2023. pmc-13463396:
Malsha Dangedara and co-authors report a teenager whose dengue hemorrhagic fever spiraled into a rare immune overreaction that destroyed her blood from several directions at once. pmc-13463696:
Nader Maai and five co-authors map how labs use sound waves to find germs on removed joint and bone implants. Shaking implants with ultrasound frees trapped bacteria that normal tissue cultures can miss. Yet labs run the method in widely different ways, which blocks fair comparison.

Where steps were given, hard plastic tubs, salt fluids, and five minutes of shaking were most common. The authors press for one shared protocol so results can be trusted across hospitals.
pmc-13464096:
Hongyan Zhan and eight co-authors review how worn telomeres, the caps on chromosome ends, feed non-cancer lung diseases. Short caps and faulty repair of them turn up often in scarring lung disease, COPD, and asthma. The review covers cap biology first, then the gene faults behind the wear.

pmc-13464296:
Tooba Salar and three co-authors present two cases of Loeffler endocarditis, the fibrotic late stage of eosinophil heart injury. Long-running high eosinophil counts scar the heart lining and seed clots inside its chambers. Both men were in their late thirties and early forties when care began.

Steroids calmed his counts fast, and blood thinners guarded against clots. The second man's scans revealed the same disease, and gene testing found a treatable blood disorder behind it. A targeted pill normalized his counts promptly, which shows imaging can steer the hunt for causes.
pmc-13464896:
Li and co-authors described in 2026 a 73-year-old Chinese man whose chest tightness led scanners to a stalked mass inside his heart's left atrium. Occasionally, complete surgical removal alone appears to hold this cancer back.
pmc-13464996:

pmc-13465096:

No marker differed meaningfully between capillary and vein draws, and paired values tracked tightly with near-zero average bias. Risk classes matched in eleven of thirteen cases, with misses only between neighboring low classes.
pmc-13465196:
Yan and co-authors stress-tested two flagship artificial intelligence models for single-cell biology in 2026. pmc-13465896:

Recovery stayed steady across the weeks studied, with no clear drop in early or later groups. pmc-13466196:
Shuaiheng Song and colleagues built tiny drug carriers that fall open inside tumors, where reactive oxygen levels run high, in a 2026 study. Lab release tests freed most of the drug within a day under tumor-like conditions. The team also tracked two cell proteins, survivin and p21, whose shifts help explain how the treatment slows tumor growth.
pmc-13466896:

pmc-13467496:
Liang Kang and co-authors map in 2026 a family of enzymes in Corydalis saxicola, an endangered medicinal plant that grows in limestone karst country. pmc-13467996:

pmc-13468196:

pmc-13469096:

pmc-13469196:

pmc-13469696:

pmc-13469896:
Song and co-authors survey new chemistry aimed at bone metabolism disorders. Their 2026 review starts from osteoporosis, the dominant burden in this group. pmc-13470096:
Sharmake Gaiye Bashir leads a fifteen author review in 2026 asking whether the world is ready for Nipah virus, a high fatality infection carried by bats. Without that follow through, health systems stay exposed to a fast Nipah emergency or another unknown Disease X.
pmc-13470796:

The authors present the method as a practical front end for co-crystal design projects.
pmc-13471496:

Only 20.0% of invited students took part, so the authors call the evidence preliminary and urge testing in larger, required cohorts.
pmc-13471596:

The variant ranker placed the true culprit first in 95% of positive cases, in its top three in 98%, and in its top twenty in 99.6% of them. Neurological disorders dominated the positive set at 62.7% of cases, and metabolic disorders scored a perfect top-three rate. pmc-13471796:

pmc-13471996:

pmc-13472896:

pmc-13472996:

pmc-13473296:

pmc-13473496:

pmc-13473596:

pmc-13474496:

pmc-13474596:

pmc-13474696:

pmc-13474796:

pmc-13474896:

pmc-13476396:

pmc-13477396:

pmc-13478296:

pmc-13478396:

pmc-13478596:

pmc-13480196:

pmc-13480796:
Kirk and colleagues look back in 2026 over 19 years of treating kaposiform haemangioendothelioma at Sydney Children's Hospital, focusing on the chemotherapy drug vincristine. The rare vascular tumor strikes mostly newborns and traps blood cells inside its vessels, causing a dangerous clotting and bleeding disorder called the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. The series covered 21 children, 13 of them presenting as neonates, with limbs the commonest tumor site.

Nearly every child, 20 of 21, had the blood-consuming clotting problem, and six cases, 29 percent, had its severe form at presentation to the hospital. Six tumors were cut out, 16 children, 76 percent, received vincristine, and three later moved to the alternative drug sirolimus for their treatment course. No tumor recurred, and vincristine side effects, though common, were mostly mild, with one bloodstream infection and one line replacement, keeping it the authors' first-line choice.
pmc-13482396:
Sudhishna, Mondal, and Mondal squeeze gelatin rock models in 2026 to watch how injected fluid cracks layered stone, a scaled-down mirror of fracking in shale reservoirs. Their custom press applies load from two directions while cameras record fractures growing in real time through the transparent analogues. Water, thick SAE 140 oil, and oil-toluene mixes were injected at a steady 1 milliliter per minute under fixed confining and top loads.

Fracture shapes were measured frame by frame, tracking length and aspect ratio as the cracks chose paths through layered and uniform blocks under the loads applied. Computer simulations using a phase field damage model, which lets cracks emerge from the physics rather than being drawn in, reproduced the experiments well in the comparisons. Both also matched the classic analytical fracture model qualitatively, and the authors say the setup can serve carbon storage and gas hydrate studies as well.
pmc-13483096:
Li and co-authors reviewed in 2026 the part that a rare immune cell plays in ischemic stroke, the kind caused by a blocked brain artery. The cells are gamma delta T cells, which flood in after a stroke and spill a signal called IL-17 that stokes brain swelling. Most such cells live in the gut wall. The review reads the stroke story through the brain gut axis, the two way talk between head and belly.

After a stroke, gut flora shift, the gut wall leaks, and germ bits slip into the blood, which fans brain harm in a loop. The same cells can guard the gut wall, so their role cuts both ways. The authors map drug ideas that target the cells, the IL-17 signal, the leaky wall, or the flora. They note that hard proof in humans is still thin, and call for cell tracing work.
pmc-13483196:
Liu and Zhai proposed a self-teaching method for recognizing human actions from skeleton data, the stick-figure joint tracks that cameras extract from video. Labels for training are scarce, and standard tricks that warp the data can wreck the skeleton's structure. Their 2026 method, called HGCL, learns at two scales at once, whole-body motion and single body parts, while a contrast task teaches it which clips match.

On two public video benchmarks the method reached about 91 percent accuracy on the larger set and about 67 percent on the harder one in the reported tests. Its data warping respects bone lengths, with a proven cap on how far bones can distort. Detection confidence for each joint flows through the whole pipeline, muting unreliable joints instead of trusting them. Liu argues coupling the scales, rather than bolting on separate modules, is what makes the learning work.
pmc-13483496:
Shyryn Almerekova and co-authors present a 2026 family-tree study of Allium, the onion genus, drawing on species from Kazakhstan. The genus holds over a thousand species, yet its branches stayed tangled because older work sampled few genes. The team used a target kit to capture 302 nuclear loci across 47 samples covering 43 species.

Two tree-building routes agreed on three great lineages, then quarrelled inside the third. Several named subgroups failed to hold together as single branches. Tests traced the clashes to two sources: old gene variants sorted unevenly into young species, and outright gene flow between lineages. The genus itself dates to the early Eocene, near fifty-two million years ago, with a Miocene burst of splitting. Tangled ancestry, the authors show, is the genus's true shape.
pmc-13483696:
Haustine Patt Panganiban and co-workers set out a 2026 trial plan for alcohol withdrawal care in intensive care. When heavy drinkers stop at once in hospital, withdrawal can be hard to calm and can kill. Care in Australia now rests on one drug family, dosed bit by bit. Some regions use a second drug, phenobarbital, but proof that it works better is weak.

One center will assign 45 patients by chance to low-dose or standard-dose phenobarbital, or to usual care. Screening, group assignment, and drug orders will all run inside the health record system. The main test is whether such a trial can run at all inside routine care. Side checks will track withdrawal scores, extra drug needs, and patient health.
pmc-13486696:
Chen and colleagues asked whether preterm babies who received probiotics early still developed a devastating gut disease later, or on a different schedule. Necrotizing enterocolitis destroys premature infants' intestines, and probiotic prevention remains debated. Their 2026 review covered 216 preterm infants who developed the disease at two Chinese hospitals, comparing those with and without early mixed-species probiotic exposure.

Babies exposed to probiotics developed the disease at a median of about 23 days of life, against about 12 days in the unexposed group. They also resumed feeding sooner after the disease struck, with shorter fasting times recorded. Rates of surgery, intestinal perforation, death, and shock did not differ clearly between the groups. Chen cautions that exposure was not standardized, so the delay might reflect other care differences rather than the probiotics themselves.
pmc-13487296:
Feiyan Zhao and others test a probiotic strain, Lacticaseibacillus casei Zhang, against iron overload in mice. In 2026, the study feeds mice a high-iron diet, which raises blood iron and an immune signal called IL-22, lowers iron-binding capacity, and disturbs gut microbes and fuel use. The probiotic is then given to see whether it restores balance.

Treatment partly restored iron-binding capacity, lowered IL-22, and increased gut germs linked to health, including Bifidobacterium animalis, while easing bile acid and glucose disturbances. Mice lacking IL-22 gained no such benefit, showing the probiotic effect depends on that immune node. The work points to an IL-22-linked pathway as a target for reducing risks from excess iron.
pmc-13487996:
Longmei Si and colleagues develop nursing guidance for adults with a urostomy in China in a 2026 evidence synthesis and expert consensus study. A urostomy diverts urine through an opening in the belly, often after bladder removal, and skilled nursing helps patients gain confidence and avoid skin and infection problems. The team first gathered and graded published evidence, then ran a Delphi survey, where experts rate draft statements in rounds.

The final consensus holds fifty-seven recommendations across basic requirements, psychological support, care before surgery, and care after surgery. Every statement reached strong agreement among experts. The authors intend the set to raise the standard of stoma care across hospitals and improve daily life for patients.
pmc-13490596:
Gyimah and team raised malaria mosquitoes for ten rounds in three larval waters to watch bug spray hardiness evolve under each rearing environment. Hardiness management assumes bug sprays drive the change, but nursery water quality may steer it too. Their 2026 experiment split larvae from one Accra collection site into field water, tap water, and distilled water lines. Each round was tested against four bug spray classes, and two hardiness genes plus detox enzyme activity were read.

The three water lines diverged in hardiness profiles across the ten rounds, despite starting from the same mosquito population. Target-site gene change rates and detox enzyme levels shifted differently by habitat. Field water kept a broader hardiness signature than the cleaner lab waters. Gyimah warns that lab settling rewrites the hardiness biology researchers think they are studying, and that field-true water should be part of hardiness tracking.
pmc-13491796:
Jinpeng Li, Xiaoqing Jin, and Weicong Luo build in 2026 a fairer way to measure how quickly ambulances can reach patients in dense cities. Standard accessibility models count only the drive to the building, ignoring the minutes spent climbing stairs or riding elevators inside it. Their model adds that in-building leg and lets building height and occupancy shape the estimate, tested on the city of Wuhan, China.

In-building time followed a low-high-low pattern from center to suburbs, tracking where tall, crowded buildings cluster. Counting it shrank the population reachable within five minutes by about thirteen percent and pushed more people beyond the twelve-minute mark. Older methods flattered coverage most in transitional high-rise districts. The authors offer the model to planners deciding where to place ambulance stations.
pmc-13492196:
Stafford and colleagues studied in 2026 whether birth method shapes the first microbes in the gut of newborn beef calves. Birth route can seed a baby's gut, and the early community guides immune and metabolic growth. The team sampled five gut regions from Aberdeen Angus calves born naturally or by planned caesarean section on two research farms, and read their bacterial genes.

Stafford found the gut region itself was the main driver of community makeup, explaining about a quarter of the variation. Birth method explained almost none, and microbe counts and diversity were alike between the two groups at birth. A weak interaction hinted that any birth effect changed by site rather than running across the whole gut. Farm mattered little either. The authors conclude that life after birth, from surroundings and host contact, likely shapes the early calf gut more than delivery route.
pmc-13492496:
Jianhang Zhou leads a thirty-nine-author team showing in 2026 that harmless-looking heart scans can hide a warning that artificial intelligence can read. The study mined two international registries of hybrid perfusion imaging, narrowing more than forty thousand scans to 4,552 patients with no known coronary disease, mild calcium scores, and normal blood flow results. An AI tool measured calcium sitting in the first segments of the coronary arteries on the CT images used for scan correction.

About thirty-eight percent had calcium in those proximal segments. Over roughly three and a half years they suffered more major cardiac events and died more often than peers, even after accounting for total calcium and standard risk factors. Adding the proximal finding improved risk reclassification by about twelve percent. Patients once reassured by a normal scan, the authors argue, deserve a second look at where their calcium sits.
pmc-13493496:
Marcelo Ramos de Anchieta and Fabricio José Pereira test two dyes for locating Al and lead inside plant roots. In 2026, the method study uses Typha domingensis, a wetland plant grown for 180 days in waterlogged iron mine waste rich in Al and low in lead. Control plants came from an unpolluted site. Knowing where metals sit inside cells matters for understanding tolerance and cleanup.

Chrome Azurol S and Pyrogallol Red, tested at two solvents, two concentrations, and three reaction times, gave no reaction in clean roots but reacted in polluted roots under every condition. Al appeared in purple and red vesicles in outer and cortex cells, lead in pale-pink and red vesicles, and both coloured vessel cell walls. The dyes offer a practical tool for mapping metals in polluted root tissue.
pmc-13493796:
Sheng Luo, Xiaoyan Cheng, and Xianwen Liao engineer in 2026 a lightweight tracking system that lets drones follow many small objects at once without a power-hungry computer. Aerial footage is brutal for trackers: targets shrink to a few pixels, backgrounds clutter, and motion blurs everything. Their design injects edge information, drawn from image gradients, into both the detector and the tracker so weak shapes stand out.

A fusion module reconciles what the detector sees with what the tracker predicts, using overlap and speed agreement to decide which to trust. On three public benchmark sets the system led the field, and on the largest it scored about seventy-one percent tracking accuracy while running forty-three frames per second on an embedded drone computer. Cross-dataset tests added consistent gains of two to four and a half percent.
pmc-13493896:
Polock and colleagues examine what makes crashes involving child pedestrians more or less severe, using six years of Texas crash records from 2017 to 2022 for children under 15. Their 2026 model allows each risk factor's effect to vary rather than forcing one fixed value, which suits messy real-world data. They weighed road design, driver behaviour, lighting, time of day, and setting against how badly the child was hurt.

Crashes on two-lane two-way roads, on curves, and where no traffic control existed were tied to worse injuries, plausibly because drivers expect less and see children later there. Morning and late-evening crashes also ran more severe, pointing at poor visibility and tired or rushed drivers. By contrast, backing-up crashes and those in large cities tended to cause minor harm, likely thanks to low speeds and better infrastructure. The authors advise year-aware safety programmes and better lighting.
pmc-13495396:
Bao and colleagues mapped in 2026 the hidden subgroups inside psychological frailty in older adults, combining latent profile analysis with network modeling and computer simulation. Earlier work often treated older adults as one uniform group or studied single symptoms in isolation. The team instead looked for distinct frailty patterns and for how symptoms reinforce one another inside each pattern, using data from a large Chinese aging study.

Among 4,735 adults aged sixty-five or older, three profiles emerged: a relatively healthy group at 57.8 percent, a moderate distress group at 32.8 percent, and a severe cognitive deterioration group at 9.4 percent of participants. Symptom networks differed between profiles, with orientation problems central in one and emotional symptoms central in the other. In simulations, worsening powerlessness, depression, attention problems, and functional limits produced the largest increases in overall network burden. The authors call the framework exploratory.
pmc-13495496:
William Bro-Jørgensen and others challenge the standard story for two flow states of 4,4-prime-bipyridine in single-unit junctions. In 2026, the study uses a machine-learning force field to mimic break junction shifts, weighing the standard tilted-and-stretched single-unit picture with a multi-unit option. The unit is a classic testbed for small-scale circuits.

Models find the standard picture at odds with shifts, while two units in the junction steady a high-flow state over twice the low-flow rate, through kind shapes and gold reshuffles. The two-unit account also fits diverse test data better. The work warns that even simple junctions hide complex shifts between units.
pmc-13495596:
Weng Ian Che leads a large team hunting, in a 2026 genetics study, for DNA variants behind idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, rare diseases where the immune system attacks muscle. Too few patients exist for giant direct studies, so the team borrowed power from a genetically related family of cancers, the B cell lymphomas. Statistical methods that share signals across traits scanned both data sets for myopathy risk spots.

Six previously unreported regions surfaced, three tied to dermatomyositis and three to polymyositis, the two main disease forms. The variants sit in switches that control nearby genes, including several already tied to myopathy risk and others in immune control, fat handling, and protein cleanup. One pathway for shuttling materials inside cells stood out in polymyositis. The authors offer the regions as leads for lab work on how these diseases begin.
pmc-13500396:
Sho Goto and others report two-stage wound reconstruction in a dog after removal of a distal limb soft tissue sarcoma. In 2026, the case concerns a thirteen-year-old Chihuahua whose large skin defect could not be closed directly. That is a common problem on distal limbs where skin is scarce and motion and vessel limits threaten flaps and grafts. Amputation is often declined by owners.

First, a man-made dermis sponge impregnated with basic fiber cell growth factor produced uniform granulation tissue in ten days. Then an acellular fish skin graft achieved complete epithelialization twenty-five days later without further grafting, with no troubles or local recurrence at 320 days. The authors caution that growth factor use near tumours should stay restricted to carefully selected cases.
pmc-13501596:
Yonat Rum leads a seven-author team with a 2026 test of the double empathy problem, the theory that autistic and non-autistic people misunderstand each other in both directions. Volunteers watched video stories told by five autistic and five non-autistic adults, rating each storyteller's emotional tone throughout and judging which of twelve emotions they felt.
