Accuracy meant matching the storytellers' ratings. The sample held 141 autistic and 94 non-autistic adults recruited through a Cambridge database, with a mean age near 49 years.

Measured accuracy showed no clear main effect of viewer or storyteller neurotype. A trend-level pattern hinted that autistic viewers read autistic storytellers' tone better than non-autistic viewers. On self-report, non-autistic volunteers rated their empathy and interest higher no matter who told the story. Written responses suggested autistic volunteers may underrate their skills. The authors urge caution about treating either group as uniform.
pmc-13501796:
Amanda Nascimento leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 pilot study of a blood test for tracking lymphoma in dogs during chemotherapy. Ten client-owned dogs with confirmed multicentric lymphoma, each showing a response to the standard CHOP drug protocol, gave serial blood samples across treatment. The commercial Cancer Dx test, a liquid biopsy built to detect this cancer, returned positive or negative calls. Clinical status was graded by the veterinary oncology criteria for comparison.

Agreement between the test and clinical status was solid, with a Somers' D statistic of 0.70. Eight of the ten dogs turned test-negative as they entered remission, and seven stayed negative through complete remission. Half the dogs flipped back to positive at clinical relapse. Two dogs stayed positive during their first remission weeks, suggesting slow marker clearance. The authors judge the assay promising for monitoring but not reliable as a stand-alone tool.
pmc-13505096:
Guanghua Nie leads a team uncovering a three-protein complex that drives cartilage breakdown in osteoarthritis, in a 2026 study. The disease wears down the cushioning matrix in joints and has no drug that halts it. A known matrix-eating switch, Runx2, lacked a named partner crew until now.

From arthritic mouse cartilage, the team fished out two proteins bound to Runx2: EYA1 and CIITA. Together the three sit on the start lines of the main matrix-chewing genes and switch them on. Silencing any one member cut those genes sharply. EYA1 also strips a phosphate tag from CIITA at one spot, a step set by another enzyme under inflammatory attack. The authors propose blocking this crew as a route to protect joint cartilage.
pmc-13506796:
Ao Dong and colleagues report 2026 tests of a gene-silencing drug candidate for early fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. The drug, an antisense strand, targets STK25, a protein linked to fat droplets in liver cells. A sugar tag helps deliver it to the liver. The team tested it in human cells and in mice fed a high-fat diet.

One dose cut liver STK25 by more than half for over 35 days in mice. Treated mice showed better insulin response, less liver fat, and lower body weight, matching a known liver drug. A close variant strand worked unevenly, which highlights how exact the design must be. No drug is yet approved for this early stage.
pmc-13507196:
Yujie Yuan and colleagues report 2026 work on a catalyst that turns harmful nitrogen oxides in factory exhaust into harmless nitrogen using carbon monoxide already present in the gas. Oxygen-rich exhaust normally kills such reactions. Their catalyst pairs iridium and indium on a zeolite support, a porous mineral scaffold, with sulfur dioxide present in the gas.

Surface hydroxyl groups, tuned by the support silicon to aluminum ratio, speed a path through ammonium sulfate that breaks down at modest heat to release ammonia on site. That ammonia then runs a second cleaning cycle inside the same system. The best version converted most nitrogen oxides even with high oxygen and sulfur levels. Turning a pollutant into a helper is the core advance.
pmc-13507296:
Jing Bai, Qiaoni Shen, Kai Huang, and Yingchen C Bi examine, in 2026 work, how teacher criticism style shapes whether students intend to fix disruptive behavior in physical education classes. Questionnaires from 583 Chinese middle school students fed a model where classroom anger, anxiety, and helplessness carry the effects. Constructive criticism names the problem and offers a fix, while destructive criticism blames without guidance.

Constructive criticism worked through lower anger and helplessness, though not through anxiety. Destructive criticism flowed through all three emotions and fared worse overall. Students read respectful, specific feedback as guidance rather than personal attack. PE teachers should favor concrete, improvement-focused criticism to support self-correction.
pmc-13508196:
Ihsan Abdul Razak, Surianti Sukeri, Noor Aman Hamid, and Siti Nurbaya Shahrir survey patient satisfaction with virtual clinic visits in Malaysian public primary care, in 2026 work. The health ministry launched video consultations in 2019 and plans to expand them nationwide. Little was known about how patients judge the service. The study gathered 411 patients from clinics in West and East Malaysia through an online survey. A validated questionnaire scored how usable, acceptable, and satisfying people found the visits.

Patients rated the service highly, with an average satisfaction score near 21 out of 25. Feeling that the service was acceptable proved the strongest driver of satisfaction. Ease of use came next, and together those two factors explained most of the score differences. Demographic traits mattered far less. The authors urge planners to protect ease, privacy, and good interaction quality as the service scales up.
pmc-13508696:
Lili Wang and co-authors trace how metabolic crises in TANGO2 deficiency disorder, a genetic disease of faulty fat burning, trigger dangerous heart rhythm changes. Their 2026 study builds heart muscle cells from reprogrammed human stem cells carrying a TANGO2 deletion, and studies them fed on glucose or on fat.

On glucose the mutant cells' energy production looked normal. On fat, and worse after a day's fasting, energy output collapsed. During this crisis the cells' electrical signals lengthened, matching the QT prolongation seen in patients, unless energy molecules were supplied directly. A calcium channel blocker, verapamil, prevented the lengthening, and a two-week vitamin treatment prevented the crisis itself, echoing a clinical case that responded to these approaches. The crisis switched on another channel, TRPM4, and blocking that channel prevented the electrical prolongation without fixing the energy deficit. The authors propose TRPM4 as a treatment target.
pmc-13509396:
Yang, Huang, and Zhang wrote a 2026 review on killing bacteria through rust-like death in fat bubbles. Drug resistance is pushing medicine toward wholly new ways to kill germs. Ferroptosis-like death uses iron to wreck bacterial fats beyond repair. Liposomes, tiny fat bubbles, can ferry the trigger compounds safely to infections.

The review maps the death pathway inside bacteria step by step. It then shows how bubble design can sharpen aim and cut side damage. Stability and safety hurdles still block clinic use of the approach. Engineered bubbles with homing features form the authors' main design advice. They frame the pairing as a fresh paradigm against resistant infections. Poor water solubility has held back such inducer compounds until now.
pmc-13511696:
Artur Avelino Birk Preissler and colleagues measured pre-season fitness changes in under-15 male soccer players and compared them with early squad selection. Thirty-seven outfield players took jump, sprint, direction-change, and endurance tests before and after pre-season.

Jump heights and direction-change speed improved over pre-season, while sprint times and endurance scores did not change clearly. Fourteen players made early match squads, and they already tested higher than the rest at both time points. The sharpest gap came in post-season direction-change speed, where selected players ran clearly faster than non-selected ones. How much a player improved did not predict selection, Preissler notes, so current level mattered more than progress.
pmc-13513396:
Masaki Nakagaito and six co-authors test whether exercise testing is safe and useful in patients with advanced heart failure who need intravenous heart-boosting drugs, in 2026 work. Of 528 hospitalized patients who received such drugs, fifty highly selected patients completed a cardiopulmonary exercise test during the same stay. No exercise-related harm occurred.

Breathing efficiency during exercise, captured by the slope relating air breathed out to carbon dioxide produced, tied to later outcomes in early analyses. A slope above a cut point near the group median marked a far higher three-year rate of heart failure return or cardiovascular death. Peak oxygen use, the classic measure, showed no link here. Follow-up ran a median of about two years. The authors call the test feasible in chosen patients, with the slope as the signal to watch.
pmc-13514996:
Marko Igić and nine colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how fixed dental restorations such as crowns and bridges interact with gum and bone health. Problems can begin during fabrication itself, since choices about tooth shaping, gum displacement, and margin placement echo for years.

Crowns edged below the gumline or crowding the natural tissue attachment invite chronic inflammation, attachment loss, and bone shrinkage. Chemical agents used to push gums aside, especially ferric sulfate solutions, can spike inflammation and disturb the microbes under the gum. Newer preparation styles and computer-designed crowns improve fit precision, while zirconia crowns proved kinder to tissues and gathered fewer microbes than metal-ceramic ones. Igić's team keeps returning to one conclusion: careful plaque control and regular maintenance decide long-term gum health more than any material choice.
pmc-13515296:
James Darmey and colleagues work in 2026 on recovering aluminium from water treatment sludge, the waste left after alum is used to clear drinking water. Their separation method, Donnan dialysis, moves aluminium ions across a membrane without pressure, and they tuned it with a hybrid math approach.

A response-surface design first modeled how acidity, flow, starting aluminium, run time, and sweep strength affect recovery. A swarm optimization algorithm, which mimics flocking search, then hunted for the best settings. It predicted recovery above ninety-nine percent, and a real run reached about ninety percent, close enough to validate the model. The authors present the pairing as a strong template for turning sludge from a disposal problem into a resource.
pmc-13515496:
Haohua Fu and eight colleagues published this 2026 study evaluating a gut bacterium, Pediococcus acidilactici strain Pedio6-1, as a probiotic that breaks down purines. Purines are the compounds whose build-up causes gout and related disorders. The strain was isolated from pig intestine and tested in the dish. It cleared nearly all adenine offered and about a third of purines, while surviving acid, bile and digestive enzymes. The team then fed it to diet-induced obese mice for eight weeks.

Treated mice ended lighter, with lower liver weight ratios and reduced liver guanine, another purine. Two inflammatory signals in the liver, IL-1β and TLR4, were turned down. Blood metabolite profiling shifted the obese pattern back toward that of lean mice, with antioxidant regulators such as glutathione and bilirubin elevated. The authors conclude the strain both degrades purines and calms the metabolic disturbance and inflammation of obesity, at least in mice.
pmc-13516696:
Jun Kim and Seounghun Kang review precision strategies against pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma in a 2026 article. This cancer is among the deadliest, armoured by resistance, quick adaptation, and an immune-excluding scar tissue shell. The authors survey four fronts: drugs aimed at the KRAS driver gene, attacks on DNA repair weaknesses, immune redirection with engineered cells and two-headed antibodies, and remodelling of the tumour's surroundings.

New KRAS drugs, some fitted to the G12D variant and some broader, show real activity in early work, and tumours answer with varied escape routes. DNA repair attacks are widening beyond BRCA-mutant cases toward stress-based weaknesses. Immune approaches show early tumour shrinkage but stall against the stromal wall and patchy targets. Kim and Kang argue that progress needs treatment plans matched to each tumour's biology and adjusted as it adapts, tracked by repeat biomarkers.
pmc-13517296:
Shu Wu leads an eleven-author birth-cohort study linking air pollution in early life to toddler sleep in a 2026 paper. Five hundred fourteen mother-child pairs in Guangzhou, China, were followed to age two. The team estimated each child's exposure to particles of three sizes, plus the chemical ingredients of the finest fraction, from before birth through infancy, using detailed local grids. Parents reported sleep on a standard questionnaire.

Every particle size told the same story: more exposure meant shorter night sleep at age two. A mid-range rise in the finest particles trimmed roughly a quarter hour. The ingredients acted together, with sulfate the leading contributor. The pregnancy window showed the pattern as clearly as later exposure. Wu's team connects the finding to the first thousand days, when sleep circuits wire themselves. Cleaner air for pregnant women and infants may be sleep medicine in disguise.
pmc-13517996:
Offman and Baribeau reported a 2026 case in which intravenous lipid emulsion, a fat-based infusion, helped resuscitate a man whose heart stopped after massive cocaine ingestion. Cocaine blocks sodium channels in heart cells and floods the body with stimulant signals, producing lethal rhythms that respond poorly to standard care. Lipid emulsion is thought to work as a sink that soaks up fat-soluble toxins.

Offman recounts that the man, in his early thirties, arrested again after an initial revival despite bicarbonate and epinephrine, in a wide-complex pulseless rhythm pattern typical of sodium channel blockade. After the lipid emulsion was given in the setting of recurrent arrest and severe instability, he was successfully stabilized. The authors conclude the therapy, long used for local anesthetic poisoning, deserves consideration in cocaine-linked cardiac arrest, mainly with wide-complex rhythms or instability unresponsive to usual interventions.
pmc-13518796:
Panfeng Chen and five colleagues revisit a gloomy verdict on translation-based models for completing knowledge graphs in 2026 work. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked entities, yet missing links limit their use in search, health care, and question answering. Earlier theory claimed translation models had built-in limits on what relations they could express.

Chen and co-authors introduce RosE, a model adding two extra vectors that rotate entity and relation embeddings during translation. RosE beat older translation models on standard datasets including FB15k and WN18RR. Their analysis argues the old limits apply only when training stays in plain real-number space. Careful design, they conclude, keeps this model family promising.
pmc-13518996:
Mengjia Hong and a large team engineer triple base editors in 2026 that rewrite three DNA letters, adenine, cytosine, and guanine, within the same gene copy. Base editors mutate genes inside living cells for screening, yet earlier versions changed at most two letter types, limiting variant diversity.

By embedding engineered deaminase and DNA glycosylase variants inside the Cas9 protein, the team built smACGmax, reaching triple conversion rates up to 41 percent with low off-target RNA effects. Applied to the HBEGF gene, screening covered 94 percent of targeted variants and surfaced mutations resisting diphtheria toxin. A second screen dissected splicing factor SF3B1 variants. Complex single, double, and triple changes now become searchable in one pass.
pmc-13520296:
Saleem and colleagues reconstruct how Pakistan's illegal kidney trade actually operates, step by step, from the testimony of people who sold a kidney into it. Organ shortages feed a black market run by organised networks overlapping the legal health system. Their 2026 qualitative study found five former donors through snowball contacts. It interviewed them in depth under strict anonymity, and mapped their accounts onto crime script analysis, a criminology method that breaks an offence into its scenes.

The script runs in three acts. Brokers recruit the poor with deception before donation. Victims report being blindfolded and moved to hidden sites for coercive surgery during it. Afterwards come health decline, psychological trauma, and money that evaporates without lasting benefit. Collusive medical staff appear inside the script, not outside it. Many more potential witnesses refused to talk, fearing prosecution, stigma, or broker retaliation.
pmc-13520396:
Jing-wei Zhang and colleagues present in 2026 a 54-year-old woman with a rare heart tumour. Doctors first thought the growth was a benign myxoma that had come back. Tissue checks after surgery showed a spindle cell sarcoma of the left atrium instead. This cancer type is among the least reported heart cancers.

Several scan types were used before surgery. A complex past history kept the true nature unclear. Only tissue study after removal settled the question. The tumour showed low-grade features. The authors urge careful tissue checks for growths that look like repeat myxomas. They also urge long-term watch even when the grade looks low.
pmc-13520496:
Reine E. Jardine and colleagues test in 2026 whether routine brain scan measures can flag thinking problems in multiple sclerosis, where full cognitive testing is not always available. Brain shrinkage is known to track with cognition, so scans already on file might help triage referrals.

Scans and testing covered 120 clinic patients, with about one third showing thinking problems. Those patients showed lower total brain volume and lower white matter volume. Single scan measures sorted the problem only modestly, with sensitivity below the hoped level. Combining markers improved sorting in later analysis. The authors present scans as a possible aid, not a replacement for testing.
pmc-13520996:
Song Zhang and four colleagues published this 2026 feeding study on how the delivery form of lysophospholipids, fat-digesting additives, changes their benefit in broiler chickens fed energy-reduced diets. Four hundred and eighty Ross 308 broilers were split across five diets. One was normal, one reduced-energy, and three added the additive as a solid, pre-emulsified, or pre-mixed in oil. Growth, digestibility, gut structure and gene activity were tracked to day 42.

Cutting dietary energy worsened feed conversion. Both liquid forms beat the solid form and the plain diet on body weight and feed conversion in the finisher phase, with no difference between the liquid methods. All additive forms improved fat, energy and dry matter digestibility and restored villus structure damaged by the lean diet. Liquid forms raised expression of nutrient transporter genes. The authors recommend oil pre-mixing as the optimum.
pmc-13523196:
Yifei Geng and co-authors build a single-cell atlas of the diabetic retina in rats in a 2026 study of early eye disease. Diabetic retinopathy damages the inner blood-retinal barrier, a wall that controls what enters retinal tissue. Retinas from diabetic and normal rats yielded nearly thirty-seven thousand cells for sequencing, with a focus on microglia, the resident immune cells of the retina.

Microglia showed the strongest connections within the barrier environment and split into four subtypes. One subtype, marked by high expression of a gene called Spp1, rose sharply after diabetic lesions appeared and showed the greatest potential to change state. Tissue and biochemical checks supported its role in oxidative stress and cell death. The authors propose this cell type as a target for earlier diagnosis and treatment.
pmc-13524596:
Jun Zhou and colleagues explore, in a 2026 study, how silencing a protein called sirtuin 5 affects liver scarring through a form of cell death named ferroptosis. Liver fibrosis follows chronic injury, and activation of hepatic stellate cells drives it. Sirtuin 5 removes succinyl tags from proteins, a chemical editing step that can change protein stability.

Models included stellate cells treated with a growth factor that provokes fibrosis and mice given a liver toxin. Sirtuin 5 levels and overall succinylation rose in activated cells. Knocking the protein down reduced cell viability and antioxidant stores while raising iron, reactive oxygen, and damage markers, hallmarks of ferroptosis. The knockdown increased succinylation of GPX4, a protective enzyme, lowering its stability and amount. In mice, silencing improved liver structure, linking the pathway to fibrosis progression.
pmc-13525496:
Zhang and colleagues studied whether structured nursing risk management improves recovery after percutaneous coronary intervention, the catheter treatment that opens blocked heart arteries with a stent. Their 2026 study at a Chinese hospital looked back at 156 coronary heart disease patients treated between late 2024 and late 2025. They were matched evenly between risk-managed nursing and routine nursing care.

Zhang found the risk-managed group reported clearly better quality of life and left hospital sooner than the routine group. Problems were also clearly less frequent: major adverse cardiovascular events and everyday troubles such as stomach bloating, feeling on edge, and insomnia. Patients rated nursing care much higher under the program, at about nine in ten patients versus about four in five. The authors credit the gains to finding and preventing nursing risks step by step and recommend bigger trials across many hospitals to confirm the effect.
pmc-13526796:
Koen Kwakkenbos and colleagues built a model to spot high-risk breast cancer patients even after chemotherapy clears all visible tumor. Published in 2026, the retrospective study used a Dutch nationwide cohort of triple-negative breast cancer patients diagnosed from 2013 through 2021, focusing on 2,620 patients with pathological complete response. A complete response usually signals a good outlook, yet about one tenth still relapse.

The survival model discriminated well and split patients into low- and high-risk bands, with five-year survival near 97 percent in the low group against about 85 percent in the high group. Pre-treatment lymph node status predicted most strongly, followed by age and tumor stage. The authors argue that routine clinical data can guide extra post-surgery treatment for the high-risk fifth. Readers get a tool for personalizing follow-up after a seemingly clean result.
pmc-13527096:
Zirui Wang and colleagues use a 2026 UK Biobank cohort analysis to ask whether shortened telomeres help explain how a mother's smoking in pregnancy affects her adult children's brains. Telomeres, protective chromosome caps measured in white blood cells, mark biological aging and are shorter in exposed offspring. Brain scans, cognition, and mental health were all examined.

Nearly one hundred thousand offspring contributed data across hundreds of imaging measures, eleven cognitive tests, and four mental health outcomes. Exposed offspring showed shorter telomeres, shrinkage in thirty imaging measures, weaker scores on three cognitive tests, and higher symptom scores on all four mental health scales. Mediation analysis tied telomere shortening to part of the effect on eleven imaging measures, especially hippocampal shrinkage, plus reduced fluid intelligence and more depressive symptoms.
pmc-13527496:
Mechteld C. S. van Olden and colleagues validate, in a 2026 retrospective study, ultra-widefield autofluorescence imaging as a way to track disease progression in choroideremia, an inherited retinal wasting disease. Gene therapy trials in this condition missed their main vision endpoint, yet treatment effects in the far periphery might have gone unnoticed. Widefield imaging can capture that periphery.

Ninety-six images from fifteen patients with genetically confirmed disease were compared, pairing conventional thirty- or fifty-five-degree views with ultra-widefield images taken the same day. Two graders outlined atrophic areas and surviving pigment epithelium islands, with agreement ranging from good to excellent. Within the central field, total and atrophy measurements matched closely between methods, while preserved islands differed slightly in the narrower view. The authors support widefield imaging as a trial endpoint.
pmc-13527996:
Colleen Varcoe and thirteen colleagues report a 2026 process evaluation of EQUIP Emergency. The program helps hospital emergency departments build equity into everyday care. Work took place at three varied departments, with community and Indigenous leaders alongside staff. The team drew on a staff survey, interviews with 43 people, and hundreds of field notes.

Equity work kept being crowded out by urgent pressures. Staffing gaps, new staff training, drug poisoning emergencies, and later COVID-19 all took priority. Money, time, and skills shaped how much equity work each site could do. The authors offer ten suggestions for leaders. Their core message is to treat equity as a foundation, not an add-on. They also urge engaging leaders from every staff group from the start.
pmc-13528096:
Kie Maita and eight colleagues report a 2026 case of stiff-person syndrome linked to a thymus tumor. The syndrome causes painful muscle stiffness and spasms. A 60-year-old woman had worsening spasms and walking trouble in her legs. Scans showed no brain or spine fault. Blood and spinal fluid carried anti-GAD antibodies, which confirmed the diagnosis. Immune therapy and symptom drugs did not settle her.

A chest scan then found a small tumor in front of the heart. Surgeons removed the thymus widely through both sides of the chest. Tissue study confirmed a type B1 thymoma at an early stage. Her symptoms eased gradually after surgery. Two years on she walked alone and climbed stairs unaided. Antibody levels never normalized. The authors suggest removing the tumor can drive lasting gains in picked cases.
pmc-13528896:
Salomé Andres, Simon R. Cox, and Chloe Fawns-Ritchie track pain and thinking skills together over twenty-two years in a 2026 study. Most past work measured pain once, though pain comes and goes. This cohort followed both traits repeatedly from midlife onward. Models split steady differences between people from change within a person. Age and sex were handled first, then fuller adjustments.

Higher starting pain predicted faster thinking decline. So did pain that worsened over time. After full adjustment only the starting pain link survived. The authors note pain reports are personal yardsticks, which blurs measurement. Still, the long view beats single snapshots for untangling cause. Their design answers a recent pooled null result with richer data. Managing pain early may carry brain benefits, though proof needs trials.
pmc-13529696:
Patrick Doherty, Susan Duty, and Gareth Williams mine years of records before Parkinson's diagnosis in a 2026 study. The data came from a large British primary care database. Cases numbered 37,910, matched to 113,730 controls by age, sex, and practice. Body measures and prescriptions were read across two windows. One covered five to ten years before diagnosis. The other reached ten to twenty years back.

Future patients already showed higher blood pressure and kidney markers years ahead. A combined score sorted risk moderately well. Known drug links for salbutamol and propranolol were confirmed. Some drugs tied to lower risk were mostly given to healthier people, a warning sign for bias. Diabetes drugs called GLP-1 agonists stood out the other way. They went to higher-risk people yet tied to less disease. The authors back them for trial testing.
pmc-13530196:
Fisiha Derib leads a 2026 survey of patient safety habits among health workers in primary hospitals of northeast Ethiopia. Good safety practice blends proven procedures, clear communication, and a culture that reports errors openly. Random selection brought 419 professionals into the cross-sectional study.

Fewer than one in three showed good safety practice by the study measure. Prior safety training, willingness to report mistakes, joining safety programs, and a supportive workplace each raised the odds of good practice. Willingness to report errors showed the strongest link. The authors present the low overall level as a call for focused improvement.
pmc-13531196:
Cunha and colleagues wrote a 2026 editorial on a case of recurrent lung embolism after pulmonary endarterectomy, in a young patient treated where advanced testing and catheter therapies were unavailable. Pulmonary endarterectomy is surgery that clears chronic clots from the lung arteries. They argue the case exposes an underdiscussed truth in lung vascular disease: the line between inoperable and undeliverable care is often drawn by the resources around the patient.

Cunha stresses diagnostic honesty first, because chronic clot disease could not be confirmed without the invasive pressure measurement the center lacked. Acute recurrence, leftover obstruction, and chronic disease demand different treatments. With catheter options absent, systemic clot-dissolving therapy became the most feasible choice despite bleeding risk, which the authors judge defensible. Their broader lesson is that limited resources reshape, but do not erase, guideline-based reasoning, and uncertainty should structure the plan rather than be disguised.
pmc-13531596:
Clare R Goyder leads a 2026 interview study on the unsettled wait for a heart failure diagnosis in England. Twenty-four patients recruited through practices and community clinics described missed chances and the moment of diagnosis. Many were diagnosed only in hospital, despite earlier contact with primary care.

Patients described living in limbo: unwell, unnamed, sometimes even unaware a diagnosis sat in their records. Hearing the term brought relief mixed with shock, since many equated it with dying soon. Honest explanation, not the label alone, freed people from limbo. Clinicians guide that crossing through prompt detection and careful talk.
pmc-13531796:
Emel Cihan, Serap Sayar, and Emine Acar Uysal validate in 2026 a Turkish version of a questionnaire measuring how abdominal surgery affects recovery. A total of 181 patients, mostly hernia and gallbladder cases, answered the scale just after surgery and again one month later. Statistical checks covered content, structure, consistency, and change sensitivity.

Scores climbed steeply by one month, showing the scale senses recovery. Internal consistency ran high overall, though one gut-function section proved weak. Many patients hit the top score at one month, limiting fine grading. The authors advise testing in major gut surgery groups at several centers.
pmc-13531896:
Srujan Singh and co-authors map in 2026 how cold storage injures donor mouse kidneys region by region using spatial gene reading. Deceased donor kidneys sit on ice before transplant, and that cold wait can harm later function. Tissue slices after varying cold times were profiled spot by spot with a custom analysis pipeline.

The oxygen-poor inner zone oddly enriched energy-burning genes as cold time grew, a pattern distinct from warm injury. Follow-up tests in more mice confirmed the trends. Attention should shift from surface biopsy zones to the deep medulla when judging cold damage.
pmc-13531996:
Ying He and co-authors pool in 2026 cohort evidence on two nutrition scores as outcome predictors in leg artery disease. Fifteen studies with 6,830 patients linked the CONUT score and the prognostic nutritional index, both built from routine blood values, to death, major heart events, amputation, and ulcer healing.

Higher CONUT scores meant higher death and amputation risk. Higher nutritional index values meant lower death and amputation risk, the mirror image. Neither score tied firmly to heart events or ulcer healing. Cheap blood-based scores could flag high-risk patients early, pending larger prospective confirmation.
pmc-13534396:
Meryl Brod, Lori McLeod, and Alden Smith evaluate in 2026 two parent-report measures for children with achondroplasia, the most common genetic form of short-limb dwarfism. No strong condition-specific tools existed to track signs and daily impacts in children aged 2 to under 12. Data came from an observational study and a drug trial.

Factor checks shaped a 25-item impact scale with six areas and an 8-item signs scale with one area. Both tools proved reliable and valid for their planned use in the larger study. Trial data confirmed key traits and response to change, aiding future treatment studies.
pmc-13536696:
Ahmet Oğuz Akçay, Engin Karahan, and Ahmet Kara examine how thinking skills connect to felt success in primary school children in a 2026 study from Türkiye. The sample held 285 third and fourth graders aged 8 to 10 years who completed paper surveys in person. Four scales measured habits of critical thinking, problem solving, decision making, and views of personal success.

Path analysis showed that problem solving and decision making carried part of the link between critical thinking habits and views of success. Children stronger in all three skills were more likely to see themselves as doing well in school. The authors argue that lessons should build the three skills together rather than focus mainly on memorizing facts. They present the skills as a connected set that supports confidence and later learning.
pmc-13536796:
Oscar Flores-Flores and colleagues study how multiple chronic conditions, frailty, and depression cluster in older adults in Lima, Peru, in a 2026 survey. Adults aged 60 years or older in low-resource city neighborhoods were assessed for seven physical conditions, frailty signs, and depressive symptoms. Statistical grouping sorted participants into condition patterns, then linked each pattern to depression with and without frailty.

Three patterns emerged, described as heart-metabolic, multisystem, and apparently healthy. Only the multisystem pattern tracked with more depressive symptoms overall. That link grew much stronger among frail adults and faded among non-frail adults. About one in five participants had depression. The authors suggest that checking frailty alongside disease patterns helps spot older adults carrying the heaviest mood burden.
pmc-13538396:
Lumin Liu and co-authors present a physics-guided network for diagnosing bearing faults under changing work conditions in a 2026 engineering study. Vibration patterns shift with speed and load, breaking models trained in one setting. The design blends local filters with global attention across layers, then aligns features across settings using known links between fault tones and spin speed as pairing rules. Joint training balances sorting, alignment, and physics losses.

Tests on two public bearing collections across eighteen transfer tasks gave the highest average accuracy among compared leading methods. Performance held up under large setting shifts and strong noise. Removal tests and feature maps supported each design part. The authors argue that baking physics rules into learning yields sturdier, more readable fault diagnosis.
pmc-13538496:
Parisa Kahkhamoghadam and co-authors build a stacked learning model to predict how fast water moves through saturated soil in a 2026 study. The property guides irrigation and drainage design, yet direct measurement is slow. Four soil traits feed a tuned pipeline where a convolutional network compresses data, a ridge method predicts, and an error step mops up leftover gaps. A mutated grasshopper search tunes settings, with uncertainty bands added.

All four traits carried useful signal for prediction. The full stack beat simpler and hybrid rivals on accuracy, error size, and sturdiness by wide margins, slashing percentage error dramatically in comparisons. The authors offer the framework as a reliable stand-in for field measurement across varied conditions, easing water system design where lab access is thin.
pmc-13538696:
Methavee Poochanasri and colleagues link diabetes duration to cardiovascular disease in Thai adults in a 2026 nationwide data study. Records covered 34,131 adults with type 2 diabetes in 2018, grouped by years since diagnosis. Adjusted models compared heart and vessel outcomes across the bands. The models accounted for age, body size, blood pressure, fats, smoking, drinking, and sugar control.

Heart artery disease, heart failure, and leg artery disease all grew more common with longer diabetes history. Fifteen or more years carried clearly higher odds for all three versus under five years, with leg artery disease showing the steepest rise. Stroke showed no significant duration link. The authors note one-time data cannot prove cause and call for long-term follow-up studies.
pmc-13538796:
Moreno-Pérez and colleagues report in 2026 how finerenone performs in everyday Spanish practice. Finerenone is a drug that protects kidneys and the heart, used here in people who have type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease. Trial results do not always survive contact with routine care.

The retrospective study followed 844 patients who started the drug at eight Spanish centers, most of them older men at high kidney risk, and many already on other protective drugs. By six months the median level of protein leaking into urine had fallen by about a third. Just over half of patients reached the target drop of at least 30 percent in that measure during follow-up. High blood potassium, a watched side effect, appeared in under five percent of patients, and nearly nine in ten stayed on the drug.
pmc-13540096:
Azad and co-authors ran a 2026 indirect comparison of two hormone blocking drugs for metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, enzalutamide and apalutamide, each paired with androgen deprivation therapy. No head to head trial exists, so a matching adjusted indirect comparison bridges the two pivotal trials instead.

Patient level data from 971 men in the enzalutamide trial ARCHES were reweighted to match 1,052 men in the apalutamide trial TITAN. Azad found estimated overall survival was similar between the drugs in the matched analysis across both groups. Time to PSA progression also looked similar, leaning toward enzalutamide without reaching significance in the analysis. Scan based progression free survival favoured the first drug, though that edge faded in sensitivity analyses that matched scan methods. The authors urge caution given the method's built in limits.
pmc-13540896:
Jiazhuo Xiao and colleagues describe a computer pipeline in a 2026 study. The goal is new drugs against drug-resistant tuberculosis. One front-line drug is pyrazinamide. A mutant form of the germ resists it. The mutant lacks one building block in a protein the drug targets. That loss loosens the drug's grip.

A transformer model screened two large compound libraries. One held approved drugs, the other held traditional Chinese medicine compounds. Hundreds of candidates came back. Docking tests and long simulations then narrowed the field. One compound clung steadily to the mutant protein. It also calmed the protein's excess movement. Safety profiling of that compound looked good on paper.
pmc-13541996:
An, Watanabe, and Miyachi ask whether lifting weights in the morning burns more afterwards than lifting in the evening, a question of the afterburn effect, where energy expenditure stays elevated above rest. Thirteen trained men completed the same six-exercise session at both times of day in their 2026 crossover study. The team measured gas exchange for two hours afterwards. They then repeated the analysis after modelling out the body's daily circadian rhythm in resting metabolism.

Without adjustment, the morning session won: post-exercise energy use and the calculated afterburn both ran higher than after the evening session. The catch is the rhythm. Once the normal daily swing in resting metabolism was accounted for, the morning advantage shrank and lost statistical significance in the corrected comparison. The authors conclude the timing effect is the circadian system itself, not a bonus from morning training.
pmc-13542096:
Sisay Sitotaw Anberbr and six colleagues count, in a 2026 prospective study, drug therapy problems among children treated for infections at a teaching hospital in Debre Birhan, Ethiopia. Children are especially vulnerable to medicine problems, which lengthen stays and worsen outcomes.

Systematic sampling enrolled 163 young patients between March and August 2024, with data from carer interviews and chart review. About forty-three percent had at least one problem, and 201 problems were logged in total. Missing needed therapy was the commonest problem, followed by families not following the regimen. Adding drugs and counselling families were the top responses. Rural residence, herbal medicine use, and stays over ten days each raised the odds sharply.
pmc-13543496:
Makoto Watanabe and colleagues published a 2026 study probing Stevens-Johnson syndrome through the network of genes that regulate each other in the eye's surface cells. The syndrome is a rare, severe skin and mucous-membrane reaction usually triggered by drugs or infection. Earlier work from the group had named four susceptibility genes involved in the conjunctival response to immune stimulation. What remained unclear was how their pathways talk to one another.

The team built a gene regulatory network from mouse conjunctival cells under sixteen conditions, mixing stimulation with animals lacking or overexpressing each key gene. Targeted analysis surfaced many candidate mediator genes linking the four pathways, several from signalling routes never before connected to this disease. The disease may therefore arise when a balanced web of crosstalk breaks, not when one gene fails. That reframing, the authors argue, changes where researchers should hunt for mechanisms and treatments.
pmc-13543596:
Eva Philippon and colleagues published a 2026 study building a three-dimensional model of rheumatoid arthritis joint lining to test anti-inflammatory drugs. Real synovial tissue mixes macrophages, fibroblast-like cells, and blood-vessel cells, whose crosstalk drives inflammation and abnormal vessel growth. The team grew these three cell types together as spheroids in a collagen scaffold, using two macrophage flavours. They then challenged them with inflammatory signals or patients' joint fluid before adding two kinase-blocking drugs.

The macrophage types behaved differently, one staying in the core and the other migrating outward, and each produced its own molecular programme. Joint fluid switched on arthritis-like programmes that one drug, an NF-kappaB pathway blocker, suppressed broadly, while the approved drug tofacitinib trimmed only its targeted signalling branch. A bench model that answers drugs differently, the authors argue, can rank candidates before animal or human trials.
pmc-13546596:
Sogo Ito and colleagues described in 2026 a jaw reconstruction carried out with a patient-specific metal plate, a custom cutting guide, and mixed reality displays. After tumor removal, rebuilding the lower jaw with a plate normally means bending metal during surgery, which costs time and can weaken the plate. Japan's one available custom plate system ships without cutting guides, a gap the team set out to fill.

A 22-year-old man with a benign jaw tumor had part of his jaw removed and rebuilt with the planned system. Software let several surgeons view the anatomy and cutting margins together before and during the operation. The rebuilt bone matched the plan within a millimeter across more than 92 percent of the area, and function and appearance at one year were favorable.
pmc-13547396:
Lucky Singh and colleagues mapped in 2026 overweight and obesity among Indigenous adults in Odisha, eastern India, where the problem is new and poorly documented. Their survey covered nearly eighteen thousand adults in more than eight thousand households across thirteen tribal districts. About one adult in five met the Asian cutoff for overweight or obesity, and in about one household in eleven every adult did.

Household environment explained the largest share of the pattern, ahead of village and district levels. Excess weight clustered in wealthier households, and being married, male, from a non-particularly-vulnerable group, or living in town-leaning areas fed the wealth gap. The authors warn that eroding traditional diets and routines are seeding chronic disease in these communities.
pmc-13547896:
Fernando, Cotta, Kung, and colleagues report spinal fluid testing for narcolepsy in Australia. Their 2026 paper describes fifteen patients at two sleep centres. Narcolepsy type 1 causes overwhelming daytime sleepiness plus cataplexy. Cataplexy means sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotion. Low orexin in spinal fluid marks the type 1 form.

Orexin is a brain chemical that keeps people awake. Testing it can confirm narcolepsy type 1 objectively. Yet the test is rarely used across Australasia. Cataplexy can be atypical or absent early on. That makes bedside diagnosis genuinely uncertain at times. The case series shows where testing settled real doubts. Distinguishing type 1 from type 2 matters for treatment. Type 1 lasts lifelong, unlike milder look-alike conditions. Type 2 remits within five years in many cases. New targeted drugs make precise diagnosis more valuable. The authors urge wider use of the orexin test. General physicians, not only sleep specialists, should know it exists.
pmc-13548496:
Ambroce Stephen and colleagues evaluate a training method for newborn resuscitation in Dar es Salaam in a 2026 quasi-experimental study. Medical and nursing interns often start practice with weak skills in the Helping Babies Breathe program, where a one-day course leaves little room for hands-on practice. The team tested whether online lessons paired with low-cost simulation manikins could do better.

One group of 64 interns received a two-hour online session plus two days of guided practice, while 64 others kept their usual routine with reading materials. Knowledge and skills scores rose sharply in the trained group right after the course, and gains were still clear six weeks later. The authors present the blended format as a practical option for hospitals with limited budgets.
pmc-13548696:
Ke Zhang and ZhiHui Gu build a visual calculator for spotting nurses at risk of combined depression and anxiety after harmful events at work, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Nurses caught up in medical errors, the so-called second victims, suffer in proportion to the experience and the support they receive. An online survey drew 2,457 nurses from China's northeastern provinces, using standard mood questionnaires and a scale for second victim experience and support.

Four in ten nurses met the threshold for combined symptoms. Experience and support sorted nurses into four groups, from low experience with low support to high experience with low support. Long hours, many night shifts, heavy coffee use, and middle age raised risk, while exercise, decent pay, mental detachment after work, and a sense of empowerment protected. The calculator discriminated well in testing.
pmc-13551696:
Xu Zhang, with four colleagues, published a 2026 case report of a boy whose kidney disease changed within months. The boy was fourteen and first came in with blood in his urine. Kidney function was normal, and a key antibody test was negative. A biopsy showed IgA nephropathy, a common filter disease. He was treated with two drugs named in the report.

Four months later his kidney function collapsed. Repeat tests showed the antibody had turned strongly positive. A second biopsy found crescents in every filter unit, with antibody lining their walls. Plasma exchange, dialysis, and a strong drug cleared the antibody. His kidneys steadied without dialysis, though not back to baseline. The team urges care teams to watch for a second disease when IgA cases race ahead.
pmc-13551796:
Mohamad Qazreen Ahmad Shawaludin, with four colleagues, published a 2026 case report of a rare immune disorder in a small child. The boy was three years old. He came in with tiny abscesses in his spleen and a test pointing to a tropical infection. Since age one he had had chest infections again and again. His lymph nodes, liver, and spleen stayed swollen.

Blood tests showed high monocytes, low platelets, and high IgM. Gene sequencing found a harmful change in the NRAS gene. That result confirmed a disease called RALD, a rare fault of immune control. The family began preventive antibiotics and antibody replacement. They were counseled on immune drugs and stem cell transplant as later options.
pmc-13554296:
Mustafa Onur Yurdal and Remzi Y Kıncal compared digital peer support with face-to-face peer support for medical students learning hands-on procedures, publishing the trial in 2026. Good feedback is central to clinical training, yet students often get too little of it, and digital tools may widen access. Ninety-eight students were randomised to a digital peer-feedback platform, in-person peer support, or routine instructor feedback while training in injections, suturing, and intubation.

Exam scores right after training and seven weeks later varied by group in every skill, with the digital arm scoring highest and most steadily, and reflection scores also favoured that arm. Journals pointed to rewatchable video, clear criteria, and peer coaching as helps, while technical glitches slowed some learners. The trial supports digital peer feedback as a practical way to strengthen and retain procedural skill.
pmc-13554396:
Han and colleagues published a 2026 study on heart scans that may warn of transplant rejection. After a heart transplant, the immune system may attack the new organ. Fine blood flow in the heart muscle falters before rejection strikes fully. The team scanned 79 transplant patients three months after surgery.

Three flow measures from the scan set future rejection patients apart early. Slower peak flow and weaker flow rise tracked with later rejection. Over two years, about one in four patients faced a rejection episode. The scan measures predicted risk beyond age and body weight alone. Flow scanning could guide closer watch on high-risk patients, they say. The flow rise measure performed best of the three in their model.
pmc-13554796:
Bilal Ahmad and colleagues review how stone fruits build their hard pits through coordinated genes and hormones, publishing the review in 2026. The stone shields the seed, yet it complicates processing and germination, and growers increasingly want smaller or missing stones. The authors trace development from early tissue fate in the ovary through cell division, lignin laying, and programmed cell death that leaves a rigid shell.

Embryo signals switch on regulatory genes that set endocarp fate, then further factors drive the chemical pathway that deposits lignin. Faults in timing or signalling produce split pits, thin stones, or uneven hardening. The review closes by urging pangenomics, single-cell mapping, and precise gene editing to untangle how hormones and metabolites are steered into stone tissue, a step toward breeding better fruit.
pmc-13554896:
Stegmann and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a patient living with a durable heart pump, a left ventricular assist device. The patient developed a leaking aortic valve and a clot in the aorta. A catheter valve swap was ruled out: the valve ring was too wide, and the clot made catheter work unsafe.

The team chose a hybrid plan. Surgeons opened the aorta under brief circulatory arrest and removed the clot. They blocked the pump's outflow tube by catheter so surgery could proceed, and replaced the valve in open surgery.  Mixing open and catheter steps solved a problem neither approach could handle alone in such patients.
pmc-13555996:
Parya Karamdokht and three colleagues compared three exam formats used in dental education in a 2026 study. Senior dental students, 29 in all, sat end-of-semester exams in four courses that mixed extended-matching questions, standard multiple-choice questions, and short-answer questions. The researchers measured how hard each item was, how well it separated strong from weak students, and how well wrong answer choices worked.

Extended-matching questions proved the hardest of the three formats, while short-answer questions produced the highest mean scores. The formats did not differ in how well they separated students by ability, and wrong options in multiple-choice items worked most efficiently. Students also rated the extended-matching format through a validated questionnaire. The results help dental teachers weigh difficulty and fairness when they design exams.
pmc-13556096:
Lara E. Davis and seven colleagues piloted in 2026 a remotely delivered strength training programme for adults who had survived sarcoma, a cancer of bone or soft tissue. Treatment often leaves lasting weakness, and supervised progressive resistance training helps other cancer survivors, yet sarcoma survivors are rarely studied. Eligible volunteers were more than two years past treatment with no sign of recurrence, and each followed a personalised twelve-week plan.

Ten people aged 27 to 69 enrolled, most with leg tumours treated by surgery and chemotherapy. Nine finished the programme, attendance reached a strong level across twice-weekly sessions, and one weekly session was supervised live by video while the other was done alone. Self-reported physical function improved with a moderate to large effect. The pilot shows remote delivery is workable, setting up a larger trial.
pmc-13560396:
Huiming Huang and colleagues report in 2026 how rising salt reshapes flavonoid chemistry in a medicinal orchid prized in Chinese herbal practice. Flavonoids are plant compounds that defend against stress and carry much of the herb's health value.

The team grew the orchid at four salt levels and measured its chemicals, gene activity, and proteins together. Salt did not simply raise all flavonoids; it shifted the balance between branches of the pathway. A branch favoring reduced forms peaked under moderate salt, then eased under severe salt. Entry genes for the pathway switched on and stayed on, while one later gene was suppressed. The findings suggest growers could tune salinity to steer the plant's medicinal chemistry.
pmc-13562096:
Dinh Van Trung and colleagues test whether lung recruitability predicts who gains from recruitment maneuvers in acute respiratory distress syndrome. Their 2026 second look at a randomized trial studies fifty patients with moderate-to-severe disease. A chest belt sensor mapped air flow by region while a stepwise maneuver reopened collapsed lung, then set pressure support patient by patient.

Patients were split by a collapse index measured at a standard pressure level. In the high-recruitability half, blood oxygen and lung stretch rose clearly after the maneuver, driving pressure fell, and ventilation shifted toward the back of the lungs in the imaging. Low-recruitability patients gained nothing measurable, and spells of low blood pressure, rhythm trouble, and oxygen dips showed a bit more often among them. No lung rupture or cardiac arrest happened, and intensive care deaths matched. The authors back the tomography index for bedside triage of the maneuver.
pmc-13562696:
Kei Kawashima and colleagues asked whether a distinctive look under the microscope changes what breast cancer means for a patient. Apocrine morphology, cells resembling sweat-gland cells, has long been linked to unusual behaviour in hormone-negative tumours, but its role in hormone-positive disease was unclear. Combining records from 226,584 patients in the SEER registry with genomic data from 1,017 tumours in The Cancer Genome Atlas, their 2026 study tested whether estrogen receptor status changes the picture.

It does: apocrine tumours carried a better outlook when estrogen receptors were absent, but a worse outlook when they were present. The two groups also differed in growth rate, immune signals, and genome instability, and standard molecular groupings did not capture the distinction. The authors conclude that apocrine shape marks a distinct biological state whose meaning flips with hormone receptor status, a nuance that could sharpen prognosis.
pmc-13563696:
Michel Mpiene Kisubi and two colleagues report a tumour so rare that most brain surgeons will never meet one: a schwannoma growing inside a brain ventricle. These benign nerve-sheath tumours almost never appear within the fluid spaces of the brain, and their symptoms are vague. The patient, a 44-year-old Flemish woman, arrived after two days of memory trouble, with one bout of vomiting and a single fever spike. Scans showed a well-edged mass in her left lateral ventricle. Her brain-wave test showed no seizure activity.

After steroid cover, surgeons used navigation guidance to remove the whole tumour under the microscope. Tissue analysis confirmed the diagnosis. Her recovery was smooth and complete, with no memory problems and no new deficits. The authors add transient memory loss to the known presentations and restate the lesson: total removal is the treatment of choice and usually ends the story.
pmc-13563796:
Peri Newman and eight colleagues ask patients and doctors how they feel about easing off methotrexate, the anchor drug of rheumatoid arthritis, once the disease is quiet. Guidelines favour tapering this drug before the pricier biologics, yet acceptability decides whether anyone tries. Their 2026 survey covered two academic centres, one urban and one serving a rural area, collecting views from 2020 through 2022. In total, 143 patients answered, most of them women with a median twelve years of disease, alongside 24 rheumatology providers.

Taper attempts happened more at the urban centre. Doctors floated tapering more for men, for stable disease, and for longer disease histories. Worry ran higher among women who had taken the drug for eight years or more. Seasoned providers leaned on companion-drug cover when tapering and weighed patient reluctance less. The authors say future tapering programmes should be built around these human factors, not issued as blanket rules.
pmc-13566396:
Sheng-Nan Chang and colleagues scan, in a 2026 study of the Taiwan Biobank, genetic and gene-activity data for high blood pressure in more than ten thousand patients and nearly fifty thousand controls. Millions of genetic variants were tested, then combined with gene expression data and a polygenic risk score that adds up many small effects.

Fourteen regions linked to hypertension, including one new region tied to a gene active in blood. Fifty-five genes emerged from the expression analysis, several of them new and relevant to blood vessel biology. People in the highest tenth of genetic risk had over three times the risk of the lowest tenth, supporting risk prediction tuned to Asian populations.
pmc-13571796:
A. Gibbs and a large clinical team review, in a 2026 study, the value of reporting gene variants of uncertain significance during pregnancy. The laboratory behind the study provides prenatal sequencing for half of England. Such variants are discussed by a team only when they fit the baby's scan findings and sit close to a firmer classification.

Uncertain variants were reported in forty-one of 881 sequenced fetuses. Follow-up arrived for thirty-eight, and twenty-three were later upgraded to likely harmful, mostly thanks to new information from examination after birth or after death. One was downgraded. The authors conclude that careful, team-gated reporting resolves most uncertainty and helps families, rather than leaving useful clues unreported.
pmc-13575096:
MacKenzie D Trupp leads a 2026 trial asking whether guided viewing can raise the well-being gains of looking at art. Art visits link to better mood and mental health, yet gains vary by person and setting. The team tested two short videos at the National Gallery in London.

One video taught slow, style-focused looking, while the other led a mindful breathing exercise before viewing. In the main study 281 visitors were assigned to a video or a standard visit, with a small lab follow-up of 33 people. Well-being rose after gallery visits in all groups. Neither video clearly beat a plain visit, though guided viewing lifted positive mood more than the breathing video, and first-time visitors seemed to gain most.
pmc-13576296:
Jia Xie and four colleagues study what drives pain catastrophizing after leg injury surgery, and build a chart to predict it, in a 2026 paper. Pain catastrophizing means expecting the worst from pain, and it can slow recovery. The team gathered data on 320 patients with lower limb trauma.

Patients were split into a building set of 224 and a checking set of 96. Higher pain scores before surgery, worse injury severity, more anxiety and depression, and stronger fear-avoidance beliefs each raised the risk. A college education or higher lowered it. The prediction chart scored 0.850 on the accuracy curve in the building set and 0.815 in the checking set, with good calibration. The authors offer the tool for flagging patients who may need extra psychological support.
pmc-13577796:
Miray Erdem and colleagues answered a letter about their earlier work on nerve damage risk in Parkinson's disease patients treated with levodopa. The original study compared oral levodopa with levodopa delivered as an intestinal gel, using nerve tests and blood markers. Commentators had raised questions about drug dose, varied nerve findings, and the limits of one-time measurements.

The authors accept that dose differences may raise homocysteine and affect nerve function, and that combined nerve indices could sharpen future work. They also report a new prospective study in newly diagnosed, untreated patients, with nerve testing at baseline and after one year. That follow-up should clarify whether treatment exposure, metabolic change, and nerve damage unfold in sequence.
pmc-13578696:
Xiaohua Hu and colleagues build a machine learning tool that sorts people with diabetes by their current foot risk, in a 2026 study. Foot damage from nerve and vessel harm can end in ulcers and limb loss, so spotting high risk patients early guides prevention. Records came from close to two thousand patients at one hospital, with a second hospital group set aside to test the model cold.

Fifty measures spanned blood sugar, vessels, nerves, kidneys, and inflammation. A feature cutting step trimmed the list to sixteen, and ten model types were raced. A boosting model won, sorting risk with strong scores at home and holding nearly the same scores at the outside hospital. An explainer tool shows which measures drive each call, so clinicians can see the reasoning.
pmc-13582696:
Alison B. Tuck and colleagues tracked, moment by moment, how two kinds of feel-good emotion goals play out in daily life. Prohedonic regulation means steering feelings toward pleasure, either by lifting positive feelings or by cutting negative ones, but studies often lump the two together. Their 2026 study surveyed 179 adults five times a day for 14 days about the day's key event, their emotion goals, effort, difficulty, and success.

Goals to cut negative feelings were more common, and came with higher effort and difficulty but no extra success. Goals to lift or hold positive feelings came with lower difficulty and higher success, but no link to effort. Depression only changed one link: it strengthened the tie between holding positive feelings and feeling successful. The authors urge researchers and therapists to separate the two goal types.
pmc-13586196:
Kareem El-Ghazawi and colleagues mapped how wrap cells, the pericytes that hug brain capillaries, change in Alzheimer's disease by sex and brain region. Pericytes help guard the blood-brain barrier and vessel steadiness, but their role in Alzheimer's, above all sex gaps, was poorly defined. Their 2026 study used single-cell gene reads and cell-talk tools on temple-side cortex and front cortex from donors with and without Alzheimer's.

A pericyte-to-lining TGF-beta program rose in women with the disease only in temple-side cortex, while an oestrogen-linked wrap-cell-to-star-cell pathway fell, with wider cell gaps in spatial data. A brain-immune-cell-to-wrap-cell program tied to low oxygen and p53 rose in both sexes with by-region quirks. The authors argue wrap-cell signals help explain women's higher risk in Alzheimer's.
pmc-13587396:
Jamal Hasanli and colleagues ask whether the strict diet of celiac disease can tip into an unhealthy fixation on healthy eating. Celiac disease forces a lifelong ban on gluten, and that daily vigilance may feed orthorexia, an obsessive drive to eat only pure or correct food. Their 2026 study compared 156 patients with proven celiac disease against 182 people without it, using scored questionnaires on orthorexic traits, depression, and anxiety.

Patients scored higher on every part of the orthorexia scale, and their depression and anxiety scores also ran higher. Stronger orthorexic traits traveled with stronger distress in both measures. Having celiac disease was the single strongest predictor of orthorexic traits, with anxiety and age also counting. The authors urge clinics to pair diet coaching with mental health support at routine visits.
pmc-13590396:
Maria Flavia Bagaglini leads a study of early menopause in women with autoimmune thyroid disease, where the immune system attacks the thyroid gland. The team reviewed 7,690 postmenopausal women at a thyroid center. They compared women with no autoimmune hormone disease, women with thyroid autoimmunity alone, and women whose thyroid disease sat within a wider web of autoimmune ills.

Early loss of ovarian function was most common in that last, multi disease group, at close to six in a hundred women. Miscarriage was also more frequent there. Family history stood out as the strongest linked factor in the checks the team ran. Bagaglini and colleagues advise young women with this pattern to have their egg reserve checked early, so family plans can adapt in time.
pmc-13592196:
Yi Peng leads a team computing the traits of a new atom thin crystal built from tungsten, sulfur, and selenium. Single layer semiconductors promise tiny electronics and light sensors, yet most carry charges too slowly at room temperature. Their calculations checked five crystal arrangements of the same formula for stability, energy gaps, light uptake, and how fast charges move in each direction.

All five forms held together well on paper and acted as semiconductors with gaps near one electron volt. They drank in light strongly from infrared into visible bands. Electron speed along one direction reached values a hundred times past a known cousin crystal. Peng and the team offer the sheets as candidates for fast, direction aware nano devices.
pmc-13592296:
Chenxi Zhang, Sandra Olivero, Alice Mija, and Véronique Michelet report in 2026 a way to harden plant-based plastics using plain white light instead of ultraviolet light and chemical starters. Their starting materials come from limonene and carvone, scent compounds found in citrus peel and seeds.

Mixed with a partner compound and an imidazole catalyst, the plant-derived building blocks set into fully bio-based hard plastics under white light. Light curing opened the ring-shaped parts of the molecules at a different position than heat curing did, proof of a distinct pathway. The light-cured material was clear and colorless, and it resisted heat and stretching better than the heat-cured version. The team sees this as a cleaner route to renewable coatings and molded parts.
pmc-13592496:
Ewan S Nurse and three colleagues check, in 2026, how many full body convulsions patients fail to report during long home video EEG monitoring. Treatment and safety calls lean on seizure diaries, which assume such dramatic events get logged. Their Australian service records from 2018 to 2024 held 130 patients with at least one convulsion caught on camera. Diaries and follow up questions sorted each event as reported or not.

Nearly half the patients missed at least one event, and one in six reported none at all. At the event level, 45 percent of 754 convulsions went unlogged. Sleep raised the odds of a miss, while seizure type did not. Nurse and the team warn that diaries understate convulsive burden, skewing risk advice.
pmc-13592596:
Jingcong Li and four colleagues present a smarter way to train neural networks that solve physics equations. Standard physics informed networks check the equation only at scattered points, leaving gaps, and they train easy and hard regions alike. Their design, CoRoPINN, loops feedback between the two problems: gradient steadiness sets a safe neighborhood size, while each point's equation error gauges its difficulty. Hard points then get wider neighborhoods and heavier training weight.

Tests spanned three one dimensional equations, Poisson problems in two, three, and five dimensions, and a two dimensional flow case, across five network backbones. CoRoPINN posted the lowest average errors on the one dimensional set, cutting the runner up's error by roughly a fifth to three fifths. It also led on most higher dimensional tests.
pmc-13593396:
Christopher Yong-Zyn Lo leads a team weighing mixed reality help for kidney stone surgery through the back. The operation, called PCNL, threads a scope into the kidney to break large stones, and mixed reality tools promise surer punctures through holograms or fused imaging. Their review searched three databases to February 2026 and kept nine studies with 774 patients comparing assisted against standard guidance. Eight studies fed the pooled analysis.

Assisted surgery cleared stones slightly more often, with a relative gain of about nine percent. Complication rates matched the standard route, and puncture and operating times showed no firm difference. Reports also hinted at fewer puncture tries, less blood loss, and less radiation. Lo and the team call for bigger standardized trials before firm claims.
pmc-13594496:
Sung-Hao Huang and colleagues tested a delayed X-ray dye study of the left ventricle. They used it as a live visual check during left bundle branch pacing. That technique places the pacing lead deep in the heart's dividing wall. Electrical criteria usually confirm the lead reached the bundle, but they sometimes leave doubt, and their 2026 study covered seventy-six patients.

Fifty-one patients met the electrical definition of true bundle pacing and twenty-five had septal pacing instead. The dye images showed the lead tip sitting markedly closer to the left side of the wall in the bundle group at both phases of the heartbeat. Those leads also sat slightly deeper overall. No kidney harm from the dye appeared. The authors present delayed angiography as a practical backup for moments when the electrical picture stays ambiguous.
pmc-13597496:
Hughes examined in 2026 how reservation systems for United States national parks affect who gets in, using visitor data from seven parks. Demand for parks is at record levels, straining facilities and ecosystems, so many parks now require advance bookings. Hughes measured how two features, the length of the advance purchase window and the level of competition for permits, relate to the income of the areas visitors come from.

Hughes found both features tilt access toward higher-income users. In the most competitive markets, reservation holders came from zip codes with median household incomes about 3 to 5 percent higher than typical. Stretching the booking window to six months shifted reservations toward areas with incomes about 5 percent higher still. Extra checks pointed the same way. Hughes warns that crowding controls, unless designed with equity in mind, can deepen income gaps in access to public lands.
pmc-13598096:
Shidong Tan leads a thirteen-author team building an explainable AI tool. The tool flags pregnancies at risk of preterm premature rupture of membranes. That is the early breaking of the waters that drives many preterm births. Their 2026 model learned from more than one hundred fourteen thousand routine antenatal measurements, blending demographics, blood tests, and ultrasound findings.

The tuned algorithm discriminated risk with high accuracy. Two routine blood values topped its reasoning: raised C-reactive protein, a sign of inflammation, and falling albumin late in pregnancy, which the authors link to inflammation and oxidative stress. An explanation method exposed how risk patterns shift across gestation, keeping the model's logic inspectable rather than a black box. The authors position the noninvasive stratifier for late pregnancy, where timely warning could change monitoring and delivery planning.
pmc-13598596:
Logah Perumal presents in this 2026 methods paper new ways to compute integrals over curved regions whose borders are Bezier curves, the smooth shapes used in design software. Such calculations sit inside finite element analysis, where engineers split a shape into pieces and sum quantities over each piece.

Perumal derives formulas using a classic area-to-boundary theorem and a mapping trick that reshapes curved regions into simpler ones. For regions bounded by medium-order curves, the new formulas proved simpler than older surface methods. A further formula handles regions edged by circular arcs. When used inside two finite element methods on problems with round boundaries, the approach improved solution accuracy, which matters for stress and flow simulations on curved parts.
pmc-13599696:
Irene Polo-Blanco, Raúl Fernández-Cobos, and Agustín Vicente compare early number understanding in autistic and non-autistic children aged 4 to 7. Their 2026 study involved 82 children, half autistic, half matched peers, none with intellectual disability. The team tested cardinality, knowing the last number counted tells how many objects there are, and conservation, grasping that a spread-out row holds the same number. They also watched how each child counted.

Both groups handled cardinality about equally well. Autistic children scored lower on conservation tasks and needed more time when counting. They also counted aloud while pointing more often, and used instant recognition of small groups less often, even for tiny sets in familiar patterns. Both counting styles supported cardinality in both groups. The authors read this as a difference in strategy and conservation, not basic counting knowledge, which matters for teaching early math to autistic learners.
pmc-13601496:
Rachael A. Pearson, writing alone in 2026, reviews progress toward replacing lost light-sensing cells in the eye. Diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa and macular degeneration destroy photoreceptors, the rods and cones that catch light, and remain leading irreversible causes of blindness. Transplanting fresh photoreceptors offers a route to restore sight regardless of which disease did the damage.

The review covers growing replacement cells, delivering them into the retina, and wiring them into surviving circuitry. Results from lab and animal work are weighed against the steps still needed before routine clinical use. Pearson also considers how new photoreceptors might connect with bipolar cells, the next link in the visual pathway, and what patients with advanced degeneration could realistically gain. The piece serves as a compact map of a therapy moving from pre-clinical promise toward the clinic.
pmc-13602496:
Abdul-Mumin Amankwa and four colleagues explore in 2026 what paternal grandmothers in rural Ghana believe about caring for newborns. In Daboya, grandmothers guide how babies are fed, bathed, and protected, passing customs down the generations. Using the Theory of Planned Behaviour, the team interviewed 14 grandmothers who cared for newborns and analyzed transcripts by theme.

Attitudes mixed confidence, rejection, and uncertainty. Many grandmothers trusted herbal remedies and immediate bathing from long experience. Some rejected harmful customs such as tribal marking and force-feeding. Others blended home care with clinic medicine. Firm beliefs surrounded colostrum, the first milk some traditions discard, pre-lacteal feeds, infant seclusion, and spiritual protection. Newborn care here is deeply shaped by tradition, the authors conclude, and programs should work with grandmothers so safe practices and modern care reinforce each other.
pmc-13612196:
Rui Gao and Xu Li review whether MRI texture analysis can reveal a liver cancer marker without a biopsy. Glypican-3 is a protein that hepatocellular carcinoma displays and normal adult liver largely does not. It now guides diagnosis and targeted therapy selection, yet measuring it still requires tissue. Radiomics models extract numbers from routine MRI scans and try to predict the marker. The pair gathered such studies and pooled their accuracy with a bivariate model.

Seven retrospective studies with 1,209 patients fed the review; five, contributing eight model estimates, entered the pooled analysis. Sensitivity came to 0.81 and specificity to 0.87, with an overall area under the curve of 0.91. Sensitivity varied widely between studies while specificity was consistent, and radiomics quality scores ranged from middling to strong. The pooled figures are a benchmark, the authors present: MRI radiomics can approximate this tissue marker noninvasively, and standardized pipelines could follow.
pmc-13612796:
Mohamad El Iskandarani and Sara Lu Riggs tested how time pressure and reward value jointly shape visual search in virtual reality. Forty volunteers hunted for set objects in a virtual living room while eye trackers logged their gaze, under varied time pressure and reward terms. Time pressure is known to hurt performance, while reward may help, but whether reward can offset time pressure was unclear.

As expected, time pressure reduced accuracy, lengthening target acquisition yet shortening verification. Reward value improved acquisition efficiency and accuracy, and it helped most when time pressure was on, cutting search time while lifting accuracy. The two factors therefore act differently on finding versus confirming a target, while their interaction determines overall performance.
pmc-13613996:
Nicola Jones, Zilley Khan, and Kirsteen Watson present a case study of clinical teaching fellows in a British hospital. These fellows blend teaching medical students with work inside a busy education team. National Health Service staffing pressure has squeezed teaching time, so these fellow posts have grown. The authors wanted to see the role as part of a whole system, not as a lone job.

Eight of the ten team members joined a group interview, including three teaching fellows, two education facilitators, and three administrators. Using activity theory, a lens for studying work systems, the team mapped where duties and expectations clash. Fellows juggled teaching, course planning, and office work, while different groups understood their role in different ways. The study shows why new teaching posts can strain even when everyone involved means well.
pmc-13614896:
